$d$ if $s = \{a + n d : n \in \mathbb{N},\ n < l\}$ and $s$ has exactly $l$ elements, counting
the size of an infinite set as $\infty$; here $n d$ is the sum of $n$ copies of $d$.

articles.title: Sets that are arithmetic progressions
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive commutative monoid
and $l \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$. A set $s \subseteq \alpha$ is an arithmetic progression
of length $l$ if there are $a, d \in \alpha$ such that
$s = \{a + nd : n \in \mathbb{N},\ n < l\}$ and $s$ has exactly $l$ elements (infinitely many
when $l = \infty$). Here $nd$ denotes the sum of $n$ copies of $d$.

articles.title: Trivial upper bound for the largest progression-free subset
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$
and $N$, the largest size $r_k(N)$ of a subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ free of nontrivial
arithmetic progressions of length $k$ satisfies $r_k(N) \le N$.

articles.title: A largest progression-free subset is attained
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$ and $N$, let
$r_k(N)$ be the largest size of a subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ free of nontrivial arithmetic
progressions of length $k$. Then some subset $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ free of nontrivial
arithmetic progressions of length $k$ has exactly $r_k(N)$ elements.

articles.title: Largest size of a progression-free subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers
$k$ and $N$, $r_k(N)$ is the largest cardinality of a subset $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ that
is free of nontrivial arithmetic progressions of length $k$, meaning that if $k \ge 2$ then no
subset of $S$ is an arithmetic progression of length $k$ (for $k \le 1$ every subset
qualifies).

articles.title: A progression of length greater than one is not progression-free
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a set in an
additive commutative monoid and $l \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ with $l > 1$. If $s$ is an
arithmetic progression of length $l$, then $s$ is not free of nontrivial arithmetic progressions
of length $l$.

articles.title: Kelley–Meka: Roth numbers are below every power of the logarithm
articles.statement:
For every real $C > 0$
there is a real constant $K$ such that $r_3(N) \le K N / (\log N)^C$ for every natural number
$N \ge 2$, where $r_3(N)$ is the largest size of a subset of $\{0, 1, \dots, N - 1\}$ containing no
non-trivial three-term arithmetic progression.

This follows from the theorem of Kelley and Meka that for some $\beta > 0$ every subset of
$\{1, \dots, N\}$ of size at least $2^{-O((\log N)^\beta)} N$ contains a non-trivial three-term
progression, which gives $r_3(N) \le N \exp(-c (\log N)^\beta)$ for some $c > 0$.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #140, https://www.erdosproblems.com/140 (status PROVED (LEAN)); resolution: Z. Kelley and R. Meka, Strong bounds for 3-progressions, FOCS 2023, arXiv:2302.05537, abstract: every A ⊆ {1, …, N} with |A| ≥ 2^{-O((log N)^β)} N contains a non-trivial 3-term progression; erdosproblems.com/140, https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05537.

articles.title: Roth numbers below every power of the logarithm (Erdős Problem 140)
articles.statement:
The statement that
for every real $C > 0$ there is a real constant $K$ such that $r_3(N) \le K N / (\log N)^C$ for
every natural number $N \ge 2$, where $r_3(N)$ is the largest size of a subset of
$\{0, 1, \dots, N - 1\}$ containing no non-trivial three-term arithmetic progression.

articles.title: Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a set of natural numbers, and suppose there is a real
number $\delta > 0$ such that for every natural number $M$ there is a natural number $N \ge M$
with $\delta N \le |A \cap \{0, 1, \dots, N - 1\}|$. Then there are $a, b \in A$ and a natural
number $k > 0$ with $a < b$ and $b = a + k^2$.

## Sources

- A. Sárközy, Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. 31 (1978) and H. Furstenberg, J. Analyse Math. 31 (1977); Lean states positive upper density via `initialSegmentCount` with arbitrarily large N.

articles.title: Initial segment count
articles.statement:
For a set $A$ of natural numbers and a natural number $N$, the
initial segment count of $A$ at $N$ is the number of elements of $A$ that are less than $N$, that
is, $|A \cap \{0, 1, \dots, N - 1\}|$.

articles.title: Number of $k$-term arithmetic progressions in a set
articles.statement:
For a finite set
$A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and a natural number $k$, $\mathrm{AP}_k(A)$ is the number of pairs
$(a, d)$ of natural numbers with $a \in A$ and $1 \le d \le \max A$ such that $a + i d \in A$ for
every natural number $i < k$. For $k \ge 2$ the conditions $a \in A$ and $d \le \max A$ follow
from the others, so $\mathrm{AP}_k(A)$ counts the $k$-term progressions
$a, a + d, \dots, a + (k - 1) d$ in $A$ with $d \ge 1$.

articles.title: The progression threshold $F_k(N, \ell)$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $\ell$ and $N$,
$F_k(N, \ell)$ is the least natural number $m$ such that every $N$-element set
$A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with $\mathrm{AP}_k(A) \ge m$ contains an $\ell$-term arithmetic
progression, where $\mathrm{AP}_k(A)$ is the number of pairs $(a, d)$ with $a \in A$,
$1 \le d \le \max A$ and $a + i d \in A$ for all $i < k$ (for $k \ge 2$, the number of $k$-term
progressions in $A$ with $d \ge 1$); if no such $m$ exists, $F_k(N, \ell) = 0$.

For $k \ge 2$ such an $m$ always exists, since an $N$-element set has at most $N^2$ $k$-term
progressions.

articles.title: Containing a $k$-term arithmetic progression
articles.statement:
A finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$
contains a $k$-term arithmetic progression when there are natural numbers $a$ and $d \ge 1$ with
$a + i d \in A$ for every natural number $i < k$, that is, $a, a + d, \dots, a + (k - 1) d$ all
lie in $A$. For $k = 0$ this holds vacuously.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 179: $\log F_3(N, \ell) / \log N$ tends to $2$
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$\ell > 3$, $\log F_3(N, \ell) / \log N \to 2$ as $N \to \infty$ over the natural numbers, where
$F_3(N, \ell)$ is the least natural number $m$ such that every $N$-element set
$A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ containing at least $m$ three-term arithmetic progressions
$a, a + d, a + 2d$ with $d \ge 1$ contains an $\ell$-term arithmetic progression.

Fox and Pohoata prove that $\log f_{s,k}(n) / \log n \to 2$ for all $k > s \ge 3$, where
$f_{s,k}(n)$ is the largest number of $s$-term progressions in an $n$-element set with no
$k$-term progression; since $F_3(N, \ell) = f_{3,\ell}(N) + 1$, taking $s = 3$ and $k = \ell$
gives the statement.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #179, https://www.erdosproblems.com/179 (status PROVED); resolution: J. Fox and C. Pohoata, Sets without k-term progressions can have many shorter progressions, Random Structures Algorithms 58 (2021), 383-389, arXiv:1908.09905, main theorem: for all k > s ≥ 3, log f_{s,k}(n) / log n → 2, where f_{s,k}(n) = F_s(n, k) - 1 is the largest number of s-term progressions in an n-set with no k-term progression; erdosproblems.com/179: F_k(N, ℓ) ≤ N² / (log log N)^{C_ℓ}, https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.09905.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 179: does $\log F_3(N, \ell) / \log N$ tend to $2$?
articles.statement:
**Erdős Problem 179: does $\log F_3(N, \ell) / \log N$ tend to $2$?** The statement that for
every natural number $\ell > 3$, $\log F_3(N, \ell) / \log N \to 2$ as $N \to \infty$ over the
natural numbers, where $F_3(N, \ell)$ is the least $m$ such that every $N$-element set
$A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ containing at least $m$ three-term arithmetic progressions
$a, a + d, a + 2d$ with $d \ge 1$ contains an $\ell$-term arithmetic progression.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 179: $F_3(N, 4) = o(N^2)$
articles.statement:
As $N \to \infty$ over the natural numbers,
$F_3(N, 4) / N^2 \to 0$, that is, $F_3(N, 4) = o(N^2)$, where $F_3(N, 4)$ is the least natural
number $m$ such that every $N$-element set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ containing at least $m$
three-term arithmetic progressions $a, a + d, a + 2d$ with $d \ge 1$ contains a $4$-term
arithmetic progression.

Write $F_k(N, \ell)$ for the same threshold with $k$-term progressions in place of three-term ones
and $\ell$-term progressions in place of $4$-term ones. Fox and Pohoata bound $F_k(N, \ell)$ above
by $(r_\ell(N) / N)^{O(1)} N^2$, where $r_\ell(N)$ is the largest size of a subset of
$\{1, \dots, N\}$ without $\ell$-term progressions; since $r_\ell(N) = o(N)$ by Szemerédi's
theorem, this bound is $o(N^2)$. erdosproblems.com/179 records
$F_k(N, \ell) \le N^2 / (\log \log N)^{C_\ell}$ for a constant $C_\ell$ depending only on $\ell$.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #179, https://www.erdosproblems.com/179 (status PROVED); resolution: J. Fox and C. Pohoata, Sets without k-term progressions can have many shorter progressions, Random Structures Algorithms 58 (2021), 383-389, arXiv:1908.09905, main theorem: for all k > s ≥ 3, log f_{s,k}(n) / log n → 2, where f_{s,k}(n) = F_s(n, k) - 1 is the largest number of s-term progressions in an n-set with no k-term progression; erdosproblems.com/179: F_k(N, ℓ) ≤ N² / (log log N)^{C_ℓ}, https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.09905.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 179: is $F_3(N, 4) = o(N^2)$?
articles.statement:
**Erdős Problem 179: is $F_3(N, 4) = o(N^2)$?** The statement that $F_3(N, 4) = o(N^2)$ as
$N \to \infty$ over the natural numbers, that is, $F_3(N, 4) / N^2 \to 0$, where $F_3(N, 4)$ is the
least $m$ such that every $N$-element set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ containing at least $m$
three-term arithmetic progressions $a, a + d, a + 2d$ with $d \ge 1$ contains a $4$-term
arithmetic progression.

articles.title: Triangle-free subsets of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$
articles.statement:
A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n$ is
triangle-free if there are no $x, y \in A$ with $x + y \in A$ (the case $x = y$ is allowed).

articles.title: Polynomial triangle removal holds in $\mathbb{F}_2^n$
articles.statement:
There are real constants $c > 0$
and $C > 0$ such that for every natural number $n$, every finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n$
and every real number $\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon \le 1$ the following holds: if every
triangle-free $B \subseteq A$ misses at least $\varepsilon 2^n$ elements of $A$, then the
triangle count of $A$ is at least $c \varepsilon^C 4^n$. Here a set $B \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n$
is triangle-free when there are no $x, y \in B$ with $x + y \in B$ (the case $x = y$ is allowed),
and the triangle count of $A$ is the number of ordered pairs $(x, y) \in A \times A$ with
$x + y \in A$, so that it divided by $4^n$ is the probability that $x, y, x + y \in A$ for
independent uniform $x, y \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$.

This answers O'Donnell's Problem 14 in the affirmative. Fox and Lovász proved it with the
essentially tight exponent $C = 1 + 1/(5/3 - \log_2 3) \approx 13.239$.

## Sources

- R. O'Donnell, Open Problems in Analysis of Boolean Functions (2012), arXiv:1204.6447, Problem 14 (Triangle Removal in 𝔽₂ⁿ); resolution: J. Fox and L. M. Lovász, A tight bound for Green's arithmetic triangle removal lemma in vector spaces, Adv. Math. 321 (2017), 287-297, arXiv:1606.01230, Theorem 1: for 0 < ε < 1 and δ = (ε/3)^{C_p}, if X, Y, Z ⊆ 𝔽_pⁿ span fewer than δ N² triangles (N = pⁿ) then removing εN elements of X ∪ Y ∪ Z kills all triangles; C₂ = 1 + 1/(5/3 - log₂ 3) ≈ 13.239 (applied with X = Y = Z = A and p = 2; the case ε = 1 follows from ε < 1), https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.01230.

articles.title: Polynomial triangle removal in $\mathbb{F}_2^n$
articles.statement:
This is the statement that there are
real constants $c > 0$ and $C > 0$ such that for every $n$, every $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n$
and every real $\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon \le 1$: if every triangle-free $B \subseteq A$
misses at least $\varepsilon 2^n$ elements of $A$, then the triangle count of $A$ is at least
$c \varepsilon^C 4^n$, that is, $\Pr_{x,y}[x, y, x + y \in A] \ge c \varepsilon^C$ for
independent uniform $x, y \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$.

This is Green's question as posed by O'Donnell (Problem 14); the answer is yes.

articles.title: Number of triangles in a subset of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$
articles.statement:
For $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n$,
the triangle count of $A$ is the number of ordered pairs $(x, y) \in A \times A$ with
$x + y \in A$. Divided by $4^n$, it is the probability that $x, y, x + y \in A$ for independent
uniform $x, y \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 199 is false
articles.statement:
There is a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ containing no three-term
arithmetic progression (no $x, y, z \in A$ with $x + z = 2y$ and $x \ne y$) such that for all reals
$a$ and $d \ne 0$ some term $a + nd$, with $n$ a natural number, lies in $A$: the complement
$\mathbb{R} \setminus A$ contains no infinite arithmetic progression $a, a + d, a + 2d, \dots$
with $d \ne 0$.

Baumgartner constructed such a set with the axiom of choice, from a basis of $\mathbb{R}$ over
$\mathbb{Q}$.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #199, https://www.erdosproblems.com/199 (status DISPROVED (LEAN)); resolution: J. E. Baumgartner, Partitioning vector spaces, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 18 (1975), 231-233; formal proof plby/lean-proofs, erdosproblems.com/199: answered no by Baumgartner (construction using a Hamel basis), https://doi.org/10.1016/0097-3165(75)90011-8.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 199
articles.statement:
The statement that for every set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ containing no
three-term arithmetic progression (no $x, y, z \in A$ with $x + z = 2y$ and $x \ne y$) there are
reals $a$ and $d \ne 0$ with $a + nd \notin A$ for every natural number $n$, that is, the
complement $\mathbb{R} \setminus A$ contains the infinite arithmetic progression
$a, a + d, a + 2d, \dots$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 1185 is false
articles.statement:
The following statement is false: for every real $\delta > 0$
and every natural number $k \ge 3$ there is a natural number $m \ge 1$ such that for all
sufficiently large natural numbers $N$, whenever $A$ and $B$ are subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$
with $|A| \ge \delta N$ and $|B| \ge m$, there are natural numbers $a$ and $d > 0$ such that
$b_1 = b_2 + d$ for some $b_1, b_2 \in B$ and $a + i d \in A$ for every natural number $i < k$.

The answer is negative already for $k = 3$: Furstenberg gave an infinite set $B$ such that
$B - B$ is not $2$-intersective, that is, some set of positive density contains no $3$-term
progression with common difference in $B - B$; truncating both sets at $N$ gives
counterexamples with $|B \cap [1, N]|$ unbounded.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #1185, https://www.erdosproblems.com/1185 (status SOLVED); resolution: H. Furstenberg, Recurrence in Ergodic Theory and Combinatorial Number Theory, Princeton University Press (1981), erdosproblems.com/1185: false already at k = 3, since Furstenberg gave an infinite set B such that B - B is not 2-intersective.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 1185: progressions with difference in a difference set
articles.statement:
This is the
statement that for every real $\delta > 0$ and every natural number $k \ge 3$ there is a natural
number $m \ge 1$ such that for all sufficiently large natural numbers $N$, whenever $A$ and $B$
are subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ with $|A| \ge \delta N$ and $|B| \ge m$, there are natural
numbers $a$ and $d > 0$ such that $b_1 = b_2 + d$ for some $b_1, b_2 \in B$ and $a + i d \in A$
for every natural number $i < k$; that is, $A$ contains the $k$-term arithmetic progression
$a, a + d, \dots, a + (k - 1) d$, whose common difference $d$ is positive and lies in $B - B$.

articles.title: Largest cap set in dimension five
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{F}_3$ be the field with three elements.
The largest subset of $\mathbb{F}_3^5$ containing no three-term arithmetic progression, that is,
no elements $a, b, c$ of the subset with $a + c = 2b$ and $a \neq b$, has exactly $45$ elements.

Over $\mathbb{F}_3$ these subsets are exactly the caps: sets with no three distinct collinear
points.

## Sources

- Y. Edel, S. Ferret, I. Landjev, and L. Storme, *The classification of the largest caps in AG(5,3)*, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 99 (2002), 95–110; OEIS A090245; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/CapSet/README.md`.

articles.title: Largest cap set in dimension four
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{F}_3$ be the field with three elements.
The largest subset of $\mathbb{F}_3^4$ containing no three-term arithmetic progression, that is,
no elements $a, b, c$ of the subset with $a + c = 2b$ and $a \neq b$, has exactly $20$ elements.

Over $\mathbb{F}_3$ these subsets are exactly the caps: sets with no three distinct collinear
points.

## Sources

- G. Pellegrino, *Sul massimo ordine delle calotte in S₄,₃*, Matematiche (Catania) 25 (1970), 149–157; OEIS A090245; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/CapSet/README.md`.

articles.title: Largest cap set in dimension six
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{F}_3$ be the field with three elements.
The largest subset of $\mathbb{F}_3^6$ containing no three-term arithmetic progression, that is,
no elements $a, b, c$ of the subset with $a + c = 2b$ and $a \neq b$, has exactly $112$ elements.

Over $\mathbb{F}_3$ these subsets are exactly the caps: sets with no three distinct collinear

## Sources

- A. Potechin, *Maximal caps in AG(6,3)*, Des. Codes Cryptogr. 46 (2008), 243–259; OEIS A090245; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/CapSet/README.md`.

articles.title: Largest cap set in dimension three
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{F}_3$ be the field with three elements.
The largest subset of $\mathbb{F}_3^3$ containing no three-term arithmetic progression, that is,
no elements $a, b, c$ of the subset with $a + c = 2b$ and $a \neq b$, has exactly $9$ elements.

Over $\mathbb{F}_3$ these subsets are exactly the caps: sets with no three distinct collinear
points.

## Sources

- exhaustive search; OEIS A090245; listed in leansolving/SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/CapSet/README.md`.

articles.title: Roth numbers from five to fourteen
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, let $r_3(n)$ be the largest
size of a subset of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ containing no three-term arithmetic progression,
that is, no elements $a, b, c$ of the subset with $a + c = 2b$ and $a \neq b$. Then the values
$r_3(5), r_3(6), \dots, r_3(14)$ are $4, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8$, in this order.

## Sources

- OEIS A003002; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/Roth/README.md`.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 658 is true
articles.statement:
For every real number $\delta > 0$ there is a natural number $N_0$
such that for every $N \ge N_0$, every set $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}^2$ of pairs of natural
numbers with $|A| \ge \delta N^2$ contains the four vertices $(a, b)$, $(a + d, b)$, $(a, b + d)$
and $(a + d, b + d)$ of an axis-parallel square, for some natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $d \ge 1$.

This follows from the density Hales–Jewett theorem of Furstenberg and Katznelson; Solymosi gave a
quantitative proof.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #658, https://www.erdosproblems.com/658 (status PROVED (LEAN)); resolution: H. Furstenberg and Y. Katznelson, A density version of the Hales-Jewett theorem, J. Anal. Math. (1991), 64-119, erdosproblems.com/658: the qualitative statement follows from the density Hales-Jewett theorem; a quantitative proof was given by Solymosi (Combin. Probab. Comput. 2004), https://www.erdosproblems.com/658.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 658 (axis-parallel squares in dense subsets of the grid)
articles.statement:
The statement that
for every real number $\delta > 0$ there is a natural number $N_0$ such that for every $N \ge N_0$,
every set $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}^2$ of pairs of natural numbers with $|A| \ge \delta N^2$
contains the four vertices $(a, b)$, $(a + d, b)$, $(a, b + d)$ and $(a + d, b + d)$ of an
axis-parallel square, for some natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $d \ge 1$.

articles.title: Szemerédi's theorem
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k \ge 1$ and every real number $\delta > 0$
there is a natural number $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$, every set
$A \subseteq \{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ with $\delta n \le |A|$ contains an arithmetic progression
of length $k$: there are natural numbers $a$ and $d > 0$ with $a + i d \in A$ for all $i < k$.

Proof: We derive the result from the density Hales–Jewett theorem by averaging coordinate-sum
translates and mapping combinatorial lines to arithmetic progressions.

## Sources

- E. Szemerédi, Acta Arith. 27 (1975); Lean states finitary density form equivalent to infinitary positive upper density k-AP existence.

articles.title: Three-term arithmetic progressions in a sequence of points
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number
and let $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ be a sequence of points of $\mathbb{R}^d$. The sequence contains a
three-term arithmetic progression when there are indices $i$, $j$, $k$ with $a_i \ne a_j$ and
$a_i + a_k = 2 a_j$.

articles.title: Unit-step walks
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number. A sequence
$a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ of points of $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a unit-step walk when for every $i$ the
step $a_{i+1} - a_i$ is a standard unit vector $e_j$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ for some $j$.

articles.title: Solution of Erdős Problem 192 on three-term progressions in unit-step walks
articles.statement:
For every
natural number $d$, every sequence $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ of points of $\mathbb{R}^d$ whose steps
$a_{i+1} - a_i$ are all standard unit vectors contains a three-term arithmetic progression
(indices $i$, $j$, $k$ with $a_i \ne a_j$ and $a_i + a_k = 2 a_j$) if and only if $d \le 3$.

Points $a_i, a_j, a_k$ form a progression exactly when the step words from $i$ to $j$ and from
$j$ to $k$ are permutations of each other (an abelian square). Over at most three letters every
long enough word contains an abelian square, and Keränen's infinite abelian-square-free word over
four letters gives, for every $d \ge 4$, a walk with no three-term progression.
erdosproblems.com/192 lists the problem as solved.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #192, https://www.erdosproblems.com/192 (status SOLVED (LEAN)); resolution: V. Keränen, Abelian squares are avoidable on 4 letters, Automata, Languages and Programming (ICALP 1992), Lecture Notes in Comput. Sci. 623, Springer (1992), 41-52, erdosproblems.com/192: true for d ≤ 3 and false for d ≥ 4, via an infinite abelian-square-free word over 4 letters (Keränen), https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-55719-9_62.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 192 on three-term progressions in unit-step walks
articles.statement:
The statement that for
every natural number $d$, every sequence $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ of points of $\mathbb{R}^d$ whose
steps $a_{i+1} - a_i$ are all standard unit vectors contains a three-term arithmetic progression
(indices $i$, $j$, $k$ with $a_i \ne a_j$ and $a_i + a_k = 2 a_j$) if and only if $d \le 3$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 847 is false
articles.statement:
Call a set of natural numbers 3AP-free if it contains no
$a, b, c$ with $a + c = 2b$ and $a \ne b$. There is an infinite set $A$ of natural numbers such
that, for some real number $\varepsilon > 0$, every finite subset $B \subseteq A$ has a 3AP-free
subset of size at least $\varepsilon |B|$, but $A$ is not the union of finitely many 3AP-free sets
of natural numbers.

## Sources

- Christian Reiher, Vojtěch Rödl, and Marcelo Sales, Colouring versus density in integers and Hales–Jewett cubes, Journal of the London Mathematical Society (2024), e12987, https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms.12987.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 847
articles.statement:
Call a set of natural numbers 3AP-free if it contains no $a, b, c$ with
$a + c = 2b$ and $a \ne b$. The proposition asserts that every infinite set $A$ of natural numbers
such that, for some real number $\varepsilon > 0$, every finite subset $B \subseteq A$ has a
3AP-free subset of size at least $\varepsilon |B|$, is a finite union of 3AP-free sets: there are
a natural number $n$ and 3AP-free sets $S_0, \dots, S_{n-1}$ of natural numbers with
$A = S_0 \cup \dots \cup S_{n-1}$.

articles.title: Sets with uniformly large 3AP-free subsets
articles.statement:
A set $A$ of natural numbers has this property
if there is a real number $\varepsilon > 0$ such that every finite subset $B \subseteq A$ contains
a subset $C \subseteq B$ with $|C| \ge \varepsilon |B|$ that contains no nontrivial three-term
arithmetic progression, that is, no $a, b, c \in C$ with $a + c = 2b$ and $a \ne b$.

articles.title: $B_h$-set
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an additive commutative semigroup, $A \subseteq G$ and $h$ a natural
number. $A$ is a $B_h$-set if $A$ is nonempty, $h \ge 1$, and whenever two sequences
$(a_1, \dots, a_h)$ and $(b_1, \dots, b_h)$ of elements of $A$ satisfy
$a_1 + \dots + a_h = b_1 + \dots + b_h$, the sequence $(b_1, \dots, b_h)$ is a rearrangement of
$(a_1, \dots, a_h)$.

Repeated summands are allowed: the entries of each sequence need not be distinct. No zero element
is assumed.

articles.title: The sum of a nonempty list does not depend on the nonemptiness proof
articles.statement:
For every list $l$
of elements of a type with an addition and any two proofs $e_1$ and $e_2$ that $l$ is nonempty,
the sum of $l$ computed with $e_1$ equals the sum of $l$ computed with $e_2$.

articles.title: Sum of a nonempty list
articles.statement:
For a nonempty list $(a_1, \dots, a_k)$ of elements of a type with
an addition, its sum is obtained by adding the entries from left to right starting from the head:
it is $a_1$ when $k = 1$, and $(\cdots((a_1 + a_2) + a_3) + \cdots) + a_k$ in general. No zero
element is needed, and the proof that the list is nonempty does not affect the value.

articles.title: Eventual bounds for $R_h(n)$ and $R_h^{-1}(k)$
articles.statement:
Let $h \ge 2$. Write $R_h(n)$ for the
largest size of a $B_h$-set contained in $\{1, \dots, n\}$ and $R_h^{-1}(k)$ for the least $n$
such that $\{1, \dots, n\}$ contains a $B_h$-set with $k$ elements. Then
$R_h(n) \ge n^{1/h} - n^{21/(40h)}$ for all sufficiently large natural numbers $n$, and
$R_h^{-1}(k) \le k^h + 2^h k^{h - 19/40}$ for all sufficiently large natural numbers $k$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 5(c) (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-5`).

articles.title: Bounds for $R_h(n)$ and $R_h^{-1}(k)$ beyond $e^{e^{34}}$
articles.statement:
Let $h \ge 2$. Write $R_h(n)$ for
the largest size of a $B_h$-set contained in $\{1, \dots, n\}$ and $R_h^{-1}(k)$ for the least
$n$ such that $\{1, \dots, n\}$ contains a $B_h$-set with $k$ elements. Then every natural number
$n \ge e^{e^{34}}$ satisfies $R_h(n) \ge n^{1/h} - 7 n^{2/(3h)}$, and every natural number
$k \ge e^{e^{34}}$ satisfies $R_h^{-1}(k) \le k^h + (3k)^{h - 1/3}$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 5(b) (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-5`).

articles.title: Riemann Hypothesis bounds for $R_h(n)$ and $R_h^{-1}(k)$
articles.statement:
Assume the Riemann Hypothesis
and let $h \ge 2$. Write $R_h(n)$ for the largest size of a $B_h$-set contained in
$\{1, \dots, n\}$, with $R_h(0) = 0$ (a $B_h$-set is nonempty), and $R_h^{-1}(k)$ for the least
$n$ such that $\{1, \dots, n\}$ contains a $B_h$-set with $k$ elements, and let $\log$ be the
natural logarithm, with the convention $\log 0 = 0$. Then every natural number $k \ge 1$
satisfies $R_h^{-1}(k) < k^h + \log(20k)\, k^{h - 1/2} + 2 k^{h - 1} (\log(20k))^{2h}$, and
every natural number $n$ satisfies $R_h(n) \ge n^{1/h} - (7 + (\log n)/h)\, n^{1/(2h)}$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 5(d) (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-5`).

articles.title: Unconditional bounds for $R_h(n)$ and $R_h^{-1}(k)$
articles.statement:
Let $h \ge 2$. Write $R_h(n)$ for the
largest size of a $B_h$-set contained in $\{1, \dots, n\}$, with $R_h(0) = 0$, and $R_h^{-1}(k)$
for the least $n$ such that $\{1, \dots, n\}$ contains a $B_h$-set with $k$ elements, with
$R_h^{-1}(0) = 0$ (a $B_h$-set is nonempty). Then every natural number $n$ satisfies
$R_h(n) \ge n^{1/h} - 2^{44} n^{154/(155h)}$, and every natural number $k$ satisfies
$R_h^{-1}(k) \le k^h + 3^{155h} k^{h - 1/155}$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 5(a) (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-5`).

articles.title: $R_h(n)$ is at most $n$
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $h$ and $n$, let $R_h(n)$ be the largest
size of a $B_h$-set contained in $\{1, \dots, n\}$, or $0$ if there is no such set (for example
when $h = 0$ or $n = 0$). Then $R_h(n) \le n$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, the definition of `R_h(n)` before Theorem 5.

articles.title: $R_h(1) = 1$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $h \ge 1$, the largest size $R_h(1)$ of a $B_h$-set
contained in $\{1\}$ equals $1$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, the definition of `R_h(n)` before Theorem 5.

articles.title: Maximum size of a $B_h$-set in $\{1, \dots, n\}$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $h$ and $n$, $R_h(n)$
is the largest number of elements of a $B_h$-set of natural numbers contained in
$\{1, \dots, n\}$. If no $B_h$-set is contained in $\{1, \dots, n\}$ (for example when $n = 0$),
then $R_h(n) = 0$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, the paragraph before Theorem 5.

articles.title: Eventual strict upper bound for $R_h^{-1}(k)$ and lower bound for $R_h(n)$
articles.statement:
Let $h \ge 2$.
Write $R_h(n)$ for the largest size of a $B_h$-set contained in $\{1, \dots, n\}$ and
$R_h^{-1}(k)$ for the least $n$ such that $\{1, \dots, n\}$ contains a $B_h$-set with $k$
elements. Then $R_h^{-1}(k) < k^h + 2^h k^{h - 19/40}$ for all sufficiently large natural
numbers $k$, and $R_h(n) \ge n^{1/h} - n^{21/(40h)}$ for all sufficiently large natural
numbers $n$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 11 (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-11`).

articles.title: Unconditional bounds for $R_h^{-1}(k)$, $k \ge 4$, and $R_h(n)$, $n \ge h + 3$
articles.statement:
Let
$h \ge 2$. Write $R_h(n)$ for the largest size of a $B_h$-set contained in $\{1, \dots, n\}$ and
$R_h^{-1}(k)$ for the least $n$ such that $\{1, \dots, n\}$ contains a $B_h$-set with $k$
elements. Then every natural number $k \ge 4$ satisfies
$R_h^{-1}(k) < k^h + 3^{155h} k^{h - 1/155}$, and every natural number $n \ge h + 3$ satisfies
$R_h(n) \ge n^{1/h} - 2^{44} n^{154/(155h)}$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 7 (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-7`).

articles.title: Riemann Hypothesis bounds for $R_h^{-1}(k)$, $k \ge 4$, and $R_h(n)$, $n \ge h + 3$
articles.statement:
Assume
the Riemann Hypothesis and let $h \ge 2$. Write $R_h(n)$ for the largest size of a $B_h$-set
contained in $\{1, \dots, n\}$ and $R_h^{-1}(k)$ for the least $n$ such that $\{1, \dots, n\}$
contains a $B_h$-set with $k$ elements, and let $\log$ be the natural logarithm. Then every
natural number $k \ge 4$ satisfies
$R_h^{-1}(k) < k^h + \log(20k)\, k^{h - 1/2} + 2 k^{h - 1} (\log(20k))^{2h}$, and every natural
number $n \ge h + 3$ satisfies $R_h(n) \ge n^{1/h} - (7 + (\log n)/h)\, n^{1/(2h)}$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 13 (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-13`).

articles.title: Strict bounds for thick $B_h$-sets beyond $e^{e^{34}}$
articles.statement:
Let $h \ge 2$. For natural
numbers $n$ and $k$, let $R_h(n)$ be the largest size of a $B_h$-set of natural numbers contained
in $\{1, \dots, n\}$, and let $R_h^{-1}(k)$ be the smallest $n$ such that $\{1, \dots, n\}$
contains a $B_h$-set with exactly $k$ elements. Then every natural number $k > e^{e^{34}}$
satisfies $R_h^{-1}(k) < k^h + (3k)^{h - 1/3}$, and every natural number $n > e^{e^{34}}$
satisfies $R_h(n) > n^{1/h} - 7 n^{2/(3h)}$.

The printed theorem leaves $n$ unquantified; the hypothesis on $n$ is taken from Theorem 5(b).

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 9 (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-9`).

articles.title: The shortest interval holding a one-element $B_h$-set
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$h \ge 1$, the smallest natural number $n$ such that $\{1, \dots, n\}$ contains a $B_h$-set with
exactly one element is $1$; that is, $R_h^{-1}(1) = 1$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, the paragraph before Theorem 7 ("Clearly, `R_h⁻¹(1) = 1`").

articles.title: Shortest interval containing a $B_h$-set of given size
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $h$ and $k$,
$R_h^{-1}(k)$ is the smallest natural number $n$ such that some $B_h$-set of natural numbers with
exactly $k$ elements is contained in $\{1, \dots, n\}$; it is $0$ when no such $n$ exists, for
example when $k = 0$, since a $B_h$-set is nonempty.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, the paragraph before Theorem 5.

articles.title: Generalized Bose set
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite field with $q$ elements, $K$ a field extension
of $F$, $h$ and $b$ natural numbers and $\theta \in K$. The generalized Bose set
$\mathrm{Bose}_h(q, b)$ is the set of residues $a \in \mathbb{Z}/(q^h - 1)\mathbb{Z}$ such that
$\theta^a = \theta^b + v$ for some $v \in F$, where $\theta^a$ is computed with the least
nonnegative representative of $a$ (for $h = 0$ the modulus is $0$, $a$ ranges over $\mathbb{Z}$
and $\theta^a$ means $\theta^{|a|}$).

In the paper $K$ has degree $h$ over $F$ and $\theta$ generates $K^\times$; the definition does
not need these assumptions.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Definition 1.

articles.title: Baker–Harman–Pintz theorem
articles.statement:
There is a real number $x_0$ such that for every real
$x \ge x_0$ there is a prime $p$ with $x - x^{21/40} \le p \le x$ and a prime $p'$ with
$x \le p' \le x + x^{21/40}$.

This is the form quoted in the paper, which prints the first interval as $[x - x^{21/40}, n]$
with $n$ undefined; the right endpoint is read as $x$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 10 (Baker, Harman and Pintz) (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-10`).

articles.title: Cully-Hugill's theorem for cubes
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n > \exp(\exp(32.537))$ there
is a prime $p$ with $n^3 < p < (n + 1)^3$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 8 (Cully-Hugill) (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-8`).

articles.title: Cully-Hugill's theorem for 155th powers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 1$ there is a
prime $p$ with $n^{155} < p < (n + 1)^{155}$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 6 (Cully-Hugill) (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-6`).

articles.title: Dudek–Grenié–Molteni theorem
articles.statement:
Assume the Riemann Hypothesis. Then for every natural
number $n \ge 2$ there is a prime $p$ with
$n^2 < p < \bigl(n + (1 + 1/\log n)^2 \log n\bigr)^2$, where $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 12 (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-12`).

articles.title: Bose's construction of $B_h$-sets
articles.statement:
Let $h \ge 2$, let $F$ be a finite field with $q$
elements, let $K$ be a field extension of $F$ of degree $h$, let $\theta$ be a generator of the
multiplicative group $K^\times$, and let $b$ be a natural number such that $\theta^b$ has degree
$h$ over $F$. Then the generalized Bose set $\mathrm{Bose}_h(q, b)$, a subset of
$\mathbb{Z}/(q^h - 1)\mathbb{Z}$, is a $B_h$-set with exactly $q$ elements.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 3 (first sentence) (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-3`).

articles.title: Singer's construction of $B_h$-sets
articles.statement:
Let $h \ge 2$, let $F$ be a finite field with $q$
elements, let $K$ be a field extension of $F$ of degree $h + 1$, let $\theta$ be a generator of
the multiplicative group $K^\times$, and let $b$ be a natural number such that $\theta^b$ has
degree $h + 1$ over $F$. Then the generalized Singer set $\mathrm{Singer}_h(q, b)$, a subset of
$\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$ with $M = (q^{h+1} - 1)/(q - 1)$, is a $B_h$-set with exactly $q + 1$
elements.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 3 (second sentence) (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-3`).

articles.title: Membership in a Bose set
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite field with $q$ elements, let $K$ be a field
extension of $F$, let $\theta \in K$, and let $h$ and $b$ be natural numbers. A residue
$a \in \mathbb{Z}/(q^h - 1)\mathbb{Z}$ lies in the Bose set $\mathrm{Bose}_h(q, b)$ built from
$F$, $K$ and $\theta$ if and only if $\theta^a = \theta^b + v$ for some $v \in F$, where
$\theta^a$ means $\theta$ raised to the least nonnegative representative of $a$ (or to $|a|$
when $h = 0$, since then $\mathbb{Z}/(q^h - 1)\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}$).

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Definition 1.

articles.title: Membership in a Singer set
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite field with $q$ elements, let $K$ be a
field extension of $F$, let $\theta \in K$, let $h$ and $b$ be natural numbers, and put
$M = (q^{h+1} - 1)/(q - 1)$. A residue $a \in \mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$ lies in the Singer set
$\mathrm{Singer}_h(q, b)$ built from $F$, $K$ and $\theta$ if and only if
$\theta^a = u\theta^b + v$ for some $u, v \in F$, where $\theta^a$ means $\theta$ raised to the
least nonnegative representative of $a$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Definition 2.

articles.title: Generalized Singer set
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite field with $q$ elements, let $K$ be a field
extension of $F$, let $\theta \in K$, let $h$ and $b$ be natural numbers, and put
$M = (q^{h+1} - 1)/(q - 1)$. The generalized Singer set $\mathrm{Singer}_h(q, b)$ is the set of
residues $a \in \mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$ such that $\theta^a = u\theta^b + v$ for some
$u, v \in F$, where $\theta^a$ means $\theta$ raised to the least nonnegative representative
of $a$.

The construction is intended for $[K : F] = h + 1$ and $\theta$ a generator of $K^\times$; the
definition itself does not assume either.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Definition 2.

articles.title: Affine equivalences between Bose sets
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite field with $q$ elements and
characteristic $p$, let $h \ge 2$, let $K$ be a field extension of $F$ of degree $h$, and let
$\theta \in K$ have order $|K| - 1$, that is, generate $K^\times$. Let $b$ and $e$ be natural
numbers such that the minimal polynomials of $\theta^b$ and $\theta^e$ over $F$ both have
degree $h$. Suppose that (i) $b \equiv e \pmod{(q^h - 1)/(q - 1)}$, or
(ii) $\theta^b - \theta^e \in F$, or (iii) $b \equiv p^i e \pmod{q^h - 1}$ for some natural
number $i$. Then the Bose sets $\mathrm{Bose}_h(q, b)$ and $\mathrm{Bose}_h(q, e)$ built from
$F$, $K$ and $\theta$ are affinely equivalent.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 4 (items (i)–(iii)) (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-4`).

articles.title: Affine equivalence is reflexive
articles.statement:
For every natural number $M$, every subset $A$ of
$\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$ is affinely equivalent to itself (take $d = 1$ and $s = 0$).

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, the definition before Theorem 4.

articles.title: Affine equivalences between Singer sets
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite field with $q$ elements and
characteristic $p$, let $h \ge 2$, let $K$ be a field extension of $F$ of degree $h + 1$, and
let $\theta \in K$ have order $|K| - 1$, that is, generate $K^\times$. Put
$M = (q^{h+1} - 1)/(q - 1)$. Let $b$ and $e$ be natural numbers such that the minimal
polynomials of $\theta^b$ and $\theta^e$ over $F$ both have degree $h + 1$. Suppose that
(iv) $b \equiv e \pmod{M}$, or (v) $b \equiv p^i e \pmod{q^{h+1} - 1}$ for some natural number
$i$, or (vi) $\theta^b - \theta^e \in F$, or (vii) $r\theta^b + t\theta^{e+b} + w\theta^e \in F$
for some $r, t, w \in F$ with $r$ and $t$ not both $0$. Then the Singer sets
$\mathrm{Singer}_h(q, b)$ and $\mathrm{Singer}_h(q, e)$ built from $F$, $K$ and $\theta$ are
affinely equivalent.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, Theorem 4 (items (iv)–(vii)) (`jis-2024-24.1.2-thm-4`).

articles.title: Affine equivalence of sets of residues
articles.statement:
For a natural number $M$, sets
$A_1, A_2 \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$ are affinely equivalent, written $A_1 \sim A_2$, if
there are a unit $d$ of $\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$ and an element $s \in \mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$
such that $A_2 = \{d a + s : a \in A_1\}$.

## Sources

- Kevin O'Bryant, *Constructing Thick `B_h`-Sets*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.2, the definition before Theorem 4.

articles.title: Nonzero differences of the Bose–Chowla set avoid the subgroup of order $g$
articles.statement:
Let $q$
and $g$ be natural numbers with $g \mid q - 1$, let $K$ be a finite field with $q^2$ elements, and
let $\theta \in K$ be a primitive $(q^2 - 1)$-th root of unity, that is, a generator of $K^\times$.
If $a$ and $b$ are natural numbers less than $q^2 - 1$ with
$(\theta^a - \theta)^q = \theta^a - \theta$ and $(\theta^b - \theta)^q = \theta^b - \theta$, and
$(q^2 - 1)/g$ divides $a - b$, then $a = b$.

Equivalently, let $\mathbb{F}_q = \{x \in K : x^q = x\}$, let
$B_q = \{a \in \mathbb{Z}/(q^2 - 1) : \theta^a - \theta \in \mathbb{F}_q\}$ be the Bose–Chowla set
and let $H$ be the subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}/(q^2 - 1)$ generated by $(q^2 - 1)/g$; then
$(B_q - B_q) \cap H = \{0\}$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Lemma 9, quoting Bose–Chowla and Brandão–Debarre–Tait / Gómez–Trujillo–Tait.

articles.title: Upper bound for sets with bounded difference multiplicities
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $g$ and
$n$, let $\alpha_g(n)$ be the largest size of a set $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ such that every
nonzero integer $x$ is the difference $a - a'$ of at most $g$ ordered pairs
$(a, a') \in A \times A$. If $g \ge 1$, then for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ we have
$\alpha_g(n) \le (1 + \varepsilon)\sqrt{gn}$ for all sufficiently large $n$; that is,
$\alpha_g(n) \le (1 + o(1))\sqrt{gn}$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Trivial upper bound for sets with bounded difference multiplicities
articles.statement:
For natural numbers
$g$ and $n$, let $\alpha_g(n)$ be the largest size of a set $A \subseteq [n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$
such that every nonzero integer $x$ is the difference $a - a'$ of at most $g$ ordered pairs
$(a, a') \in A \times A$. Then $\alpha_g(n) \le n$, since these sets are subsets of $[n]$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Section 4.

articles.title: The value $\alpha_g(1) = 1$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $g$ and $n$, let $\alpha_g(n)$ be the
largest size of a set $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ such that every nonzero integer $x$ is the
difference $a - a'$ of at most $g$ ordered pairs $(a, a') \in A \times A$. Then for every natural
number $g$ we have $\alpha_g(1) = 1$: the singleton $\{1\}$ has no nonzero differences.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Section 4.

articles.title: Maximal sets with bounded difference multiplicities
articles.statement:
For a finite set
$A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ and $x \in \mathbb{Z}$, write $r_{A-A}(x)$ for the number of ordered
pairs $(a, a') \in A \times A$ with $a - a' = x$. For natural numbers $g$ and $n$, $\alpha_g(n)$
is the largest size of a set $A \subseteq [n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ with $r_{A-A}(x) \le g$ for
every nonzero integer $x$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Sections 1 and 4.

articles.title: Upper bound for the $g$-difference basis number
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $g$ and $n$, let
$\eta_g(n)$ be the least size of a finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ such that every
$x \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ is the difference $a - a'$ of at least $g$ ordered pairs
$(a, a') \in A \times A$. Then for all natural numbers $g$ and $n$,

$$\frac{\eta_g(n)}{\sqrt{n}} \le 2\left(1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\right) g,$$

where for $n = 0$ both quotients are read with the convention that division by $0$ gives $0$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Scaling bound for the $g$-difference basis number
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $g$ and $m$, let
$\eta_g(m)$ be the least size of a finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ such that every
$x \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ is the difference $a - a'$ of at least $g$ ordered pairs
$(a, a') \in A \times A$. If $q$ is a prime and $n$ and $v$ are natural numbers with
$n \le q^2 v$, then $\eta_g(n) \le (q + 1)\,\eta_g(v)$.

For $v \ge 1$ the hypothesis $n \le q^2 v$ says $\sqrt{n/v} \le q$. Corrected reading: the paper
prints the factor $q$, obtained from the misprinted Lemma 4; its proof gives $q + 1$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Corollary 3.

articles.title: Comparing $g$-difference bases with difference bases
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $g$ and $n$,
let $\eta_g(n)$ be the least size of a finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ such that every
$x \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ is the difference $a - a'$ of at least $g$ ordered pairs
$(a, a') \in A \times A$. If $n > 1$ and $g \ge 1$, then
$\eta_1(n) \le \eta_g(n) \le g\,\eta_1(n)$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Corollary 2.

articles.title: The value $\eta_1(1) = 2$
articles.statement:
Let $\eta_1(1)$ be the least size of a finite set
$A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ containing elements $a, a'$ with $a - a' = 1$. Then $\eta_1(1) = 2$: such a
set needs two elements, and $\{0, 1\}$ is one.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Section 1.

articles.title: The $g$-difference basis number
articles.statement:
For a finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ and
$x \in \mathbb{Z}$, write $r_{A-A}(x)$ for the number of ordered pairs $(a, a') \in A \times A$
with $a - a' = x$. For natural numbers $g$ and $n$, a finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ is a
$g$-difference basis for $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ if $r_{A-A}(x) \ge g$ for every $x \in [n]$, and
$\eta_g(n)$ is the least size of such a set.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Section 1.

articles.title: Lower-bound construction for sets with bounded difference multiplicities
articles.statement:
For every
integer $g \ge 1$ there are finite sets $A_n \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ of integers, one for each
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, such that for every $n$ each nonzero integer $x$ equals $a - a'$ for at most
$g$ ordered pairs $(a, a') \in A_n \times A_n$, and $|A_n| / \sqrt{gn} \to 1$ as $n \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Proposition 2.

articles.title: Square-root bound for difference bases of finite fields
articles.statement:
For every finite field $K$ with
$q$ elements, the least size $\eta_1(K)$ of a set $A \subseteq K$ such that every element of $K$
is a difference $a - a'$ of two elements of $A$ satisfies $\eta_1(K) \le 100 \sqrt{q}$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Lemma 7.

articles.title: Difference basis number of $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$
articles.statement:
The least size
$\eta_1(\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z})$ of a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ such that every
element of $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ is a difference $a - a'$ of two elements of $A$ equals $2$:
the set $\{0, 1\}$ has differences $0, 1, 2$, and one element is not enough.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Section 3.

articles.title: Difference bases of the square of a finite field
articles.statement:
For an abelian group $G$ let
$\eta_1(G)$ be the least size of a set $A \subseteq G$ such that every element of $G$ is a
difference $a - a'$ of two elements of $A$. If $K$ is a finite field with $q$ elements whose
characteristic is not $2$, then $\eta_1(K \times K) \le q + \eta_1(K)$, where $K$ and
$K \times K$ are taken as additive groups.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Lemma 6.

articles.title: Difference bases of the integers modulo a prime
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$, the least size
$\eta_1(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})$ of a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ such that every
residue modulo $p$ is a difference $a - a'$ of two elements of $A$ satisfies
$\eta_1(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}) \le 2 \lceil \sqrt{p} \rceil$.

The bound comes from reducing the Rédei–Rényi set modulo $p$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, equation (5) after Lemma 5.

articles.title: Difference basis number of an abelian group
articles.statement:
For an abelian group $G$ and
$g \in \mathbb{N}$, a $g$-difference basis of $G$ is a finite set $A \subseteq G$ such that every
$x \in G$ equals $a - a'$ for at least $g$ ordered pairs $(a, a') \in A \times A$. The difference
basis number $\eta_g(G)$ is the least size of a $g$-difference basis of $G$, and $0$ if $G$ has
none.

There is no $g$-difference basis when $G$ is infinite and $g \ge 1$, or when $G$ is finite and
$g > |G|$, since each element is $a - a'$ for at most $|A| \le |G|$ pairs; in these cases the
value $0$ is a convention. When $G$ is finite and $g \le |G|$, the set $A = G$ is a
$g$-difference basis, so $\eta_g(G)$ is a true minimum. This is the paper's $\eta_g(S)$ with
$S = G$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Sections 1 and 3.

articles.title: Rédei–Rényi difference basis
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and $k = \lceil \sqrt{n} \rceil$. The set
of integers $B_n = \{1, \dots, k - 1\} \cup \{k, 2k, \dots, k^2, (k + 1)k\}$ has $2k$ elements,
and every $x \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ is a difference $b - b'$ of two elements of $B_n$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Singer product construction of difference bases
articles.statement:
Let $g, q, v \in \mathbb{N}$ and
$m = q^2 + q + 1$. Let $a_0, \dots, a_q$ be integers in $\{1, \dots, m\}$ such that every
$r \in \{1, \dots, m - 1\}$ is congruent modulo $m$ to $a_i - a_j$ for exactly one ordered pair
$(i, j)$ with $i \ne j$ (a Singer difference set modulo $m$). Let $B$ be a finite set of
integers such that every $x \in \{1, \dots, v\}$ equals $b - b'$ for at least $g$ ordered pairs
$(b, b') \in B \times B$. Then, with $F = \{a_i + mb : 0 \le i \le q,\ b \in B\}$, every
$s \in \{1, \dots, mv\}$ equals $f - f'$ for at least $g$ ordered pairs $(f, f') \in F \times F$.

All $q + 1$ Singer elements are used; the paper prints $1 \le i \le q$, for which the statement
fails.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Trivial lower bound for difference bases of an interval
articles.statement:
Let $g, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n > 1$, and let $\eta_g(n)$ be the least size of a finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ such that
every $x \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ equals $a - a'$ for at least $g$ ordered pairs
$(a, a') \in A \times A$. Then $\eta_g(n) / \sqrt{n} \ge \sqrt{2g}$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Products of difference bases
articles.statement:
Let $G_1, G_2$ be abelian groups, $g_1, g_2 \in \mathbb{N}$,
and $A_1 \subseteq G_1$, $A_2 \subseteq G_2$ finite sets. If every element of $G_1$ equals $a - a'$
for at least $g_1$ ordered pairs $(a, a') \in A_1 \times A_1$, and every element of $G_2$ equals
$a - a'$ for at least $g_2$ ordered pairs $(a, a') \in A_2 \times A_2$, then every element of
$G_1 \times G_2$ equals $z - z'$ for at least $g_1 g_2$ ordered pairs
$(z, z') \in (A_1 \times A_2) \times (A_1 \times A_2)$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Representations of zero as a difference
articles.statement:
For every finite subset $A$ of an abelian
group, $r_{A-A}(0) = |A|$: the number of ordered pairs $(a, a') \in A \times A$ with
$a - a' = 0$ equals the number of elements of $A$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Section 1.

articles.title: Difference representation function
articles.statement:
For a finite subset $A$ of an abelian group $G$ and
an element $x \in G$, the difference representation function $r_{A-A}(x)$ is the number of
ordered pairs $(a, a') \in A \times A$ with $a - a' = x$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Section 1.

articles.title: Asymptotics of the largest sets with bounded difference counts
articles.statement:
For a finite set $A$ of
integers and an integer $x$, write $r_{A-A}(x)$ for the number of ordered pairs
$(a, a') \in A \times A$ with $a - a' = x$. For every integer $g \ge 1$, let $\alpha_g(n)$ be the
largest size of a set $A$ of integers in the interval $[1, n]$ with $r_{A-A}(x) \le g$ for every
nonzero integer $x$. Then $\alpha_g(n) / \sqrt{gn} \to 1$ as $n \to \infty$, that is,
$\alpha_g(n) = (1 + o_g(1)) \sqrt{gn}$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Kravitz's question: the normalized difference basis numbers converge
articles.statement:
For a finite set
$A$ of integers and an integer $x$, write $r_{A-A}(x)$ for the number of ordered pairs
$(a, a') \in A \times A$ with $a - a' = x$. For every integer $g \ge 1$, let $\eta_g(n)$ be the
least size of a finite set $A$ of integers with $r_{A-A}(x) \ge g$ for every integer
$x \in [1, n]$. Then there is a real number $c > 0$ with $\eta_g(n) / \sqrt{n} \to c$ as
$n \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Even and odd limits for difference bases of $\mathbb{F}_p^n$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and
$g \ge 1$ an integer. For a finite abelian group $G$, a set $A \subseteq G$ and $x \in G$, write
$r_{A-A}(x)$ for the number of ordered pairs $(a, a') \in A \times A$ with $a - a' = x$, and let
$\eta_g(G)$ be the least size of a set $A \subseteq G$ with $r_{A-A}(x) \ge g$ for every $x \in G$.
Then there are real numbers $L_e > 0$ and $L_o > 0$ such that, as $k \to \infty$,
$\eta_g(\mathbb{F}_p^{2k}) / \sqrt{p^{2k}} \to L_e$ and
$\eta_g(\mathbb{F}_p^{2k+1}) / \sqrt{p^{2k+1}} \to L_o$, where $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ is the additive
group of $n$-tuples over the field $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p$ elements.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Difference bases of $\mathbb{F}_{p^t} \times \mathbb{F}_{p^t}$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime.
For a finite abelian group $G$, a set $A \subseteq G$ and $x \in G$, write $r_{A-A}(x)$ for the
number of ordered pairs $(a, a') \in A \times A$ with $a - a' = x$, and let $\eta_1(G)$ be the
least size of a set $A \subseteq G$ with $r_{A-A}(x) \ge 1$ for every $x \in G$. Then
$\eta_1(\mathbb{F}_{p^t} \times \mathbb{F}_{p^t}) / p^t \to 1$ as $t \to \infty$, that is,
$\eta_1(\mathbb{F}_{p^t} \times \mathbb{F}_{p^t}) = (1 + o(1))\, p^t$, where $\mathbb{F}_{p^t}$
is the field with $p^t$ elements.

The restriction to odd $p$ is deliberate: for $p = 2$ the claim fails.

## Sources

- Eric Schmutz and Michael Tait, *Cardinalities of g-Difference Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A77, Lemma 8.

articles.title: Ruzsa's theorem on difference sets of sparse sets
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an infinite set of natural
numbers whose counting function $A(N) = |A \cap \{1, \dots, N\}|$ satisfies $A(N)/N \to 0$ as
$N \to \infty$, and let $D(N)$ be the number of integers $d \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ of the form
$d = a - b$ with $a, b \in A$. Then $\limsup_{N \to \infty} D(N)/A(N) = +\infty$, where the ratio
is computed in the extended reals and taken to be $0$ when $A(N) = 0$.

This answers Erdős Problem 899 affirmatively.

## Sources

- I. Z. Ruzsa, On the cardinality of A+A and A-A (1978), 933–938, https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet-getitem?mr=519317.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 899 on difference sets of sparse sets
articles.statement:
The proposition asserts the following
for every infinite set $A$ of natural numbers. Write $A(N) = |A \cap \{1, \dots, N\}|$ for its
counting function and $D(N)$ for the number of integers $d \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ of the form
$d = a - b$ with $a, b \in A$. If $A(N)/N \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$, then
$\limsup_{N \to \infty} D(N)/A(N) = +\infty$.

The ratio $D(N)/A(N)$ is computed in the extended reals and taken to be $0$ when $A(N) = 0$.

articles.title: Golomb ruler lengths
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, the set of Golomb ruler lengths with $m$
marks consists of the natural numbers $L$ for which there is a finite Sidon set $S$ of natural
numbers with $S \subseteq \{0, 1, \dots, L\}$, exactly $m$ elements, and $L \in S$. A mark at
$0$ is not required.

For finite sets of integers the Sidon condition is equivalent to all positive pairwise
differences being distinct.

articles.title: Optimal Golomb rulers with 3 to 11 marks
articles.statement:
The optimal Golomb ruler lengths with
$m = 3, 4, \dots, 11$ marks are, in order, $3, 6, 11, 17, 25, 34, 44, 55, 72$.

## Sources

- exhaustive searches; OEIS A003022; listed in leansolving/SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/Golomb/README.md`.

articles.title: Optimal 28-mark Golomb ruler
articles.statement:
The optimal Golomb ruler length with $28$ marks is $585$.

## Sources

- distributed.net OGR-28 exhaustive search, completed 2022; OEIS A003022; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/Golomb/README.md`.

articles.title: Optimal 27-mark Golomb ruler
articles.statement:
The optimal Golomb ruler length with $27$ marks is $553$.

## Sources

- distributed.net OGR-27 exhaustive search, completed 2014; OEIS A003022; listed in SqueezeBench `SqueezeBench/Problems/Golomb/README.md`.

articles.title: Optimal Golomb ruler length
articles.statement:
For $m \ge 1$, the optimal Golomb ruler length $G(m)$ is
the infimum in $\mathbb{N}$ of the set of Golomb ruler lengths with $m$ marks, that is, of the
natural numbers $L$ such that some $m$-element Sidon set of natural numbers contained in
$\{0, 1, \dots, L\}$ contains $L$; for $m = 0$ we set $G(0) = 0$.

For $m \ge 2$ this is OEIS A003022, the length of a shortest Golomb ruler with $m$ marks.

articles.title: Lower bound for the fourth greedy $B_h$ term
articles.statement:
Let $h$ and $a$ be natural numbers with
$h \ge 2$. If $a$ is the fourth positive element $a_4(h)$ of the greedy $B_h$-set, then
$a \ge v(h)$, where $v(h) = (h^3 + 3h^2 + 3h + 1)/2$ if $h$ is odd and
$v(h) = (h^3 + 2h^2 + 3h + 2)/2$ if $h$ is even.

## Sources

- Melvyn B. Nathanson and Kevin O'Bryant, "The Fourth Positive Element in the Greedy `B_h`-Set", Lemma 2.

articles.title: Quasipolynomial for the fourth greedy $B_h$ term
articles.statement:
For a natural number $h$, the value
$v(h)$ is $(h^3 + 3h^2 + 3h + 1)/2$ if $h$ is odd and $(h^3 + 2h^2 + 3h + 2)/2$ if $h$ is even.

Both numerators are even, so the divisions are exact.

articles.title: Formula for the fourth greedy $B_h$ term
articles.statement:
For every integer $h \ge 1$, the fourth positive
element $a_4(h)$ of the greedy $B_h$-set is $(h^3 + 3h^2 + 3h + 1)/2$ if $h$ is odd and
$(h^3 + 2h^2 + 3h + 2)/2$ if $h$ is even.

## Sources

- Melvyn B. Nathanson and Kevin O'Bryant, "The Fourth Positive Element in the Greedy `B_h`-Set", Theorem 1.

articles.title: Upper bound for the fourth greedy $B_h$ term
articles.statement:
Let $h$ and $a$ be natural numbers with
$h \ge 1$. If $a$ is the fourth positive element $a_4(h)$ of the greedy $B_h$-set, then
$a \le v(h)$, where $v(h) = (h^3 + 3h^2 + 3h + 1)/2$ if $h$ is odd and
$v(h) = (h^3 + 2h^2 + 3h + 2)/2$ if $h$ is even.

## Sources

- Melvyn B. Nathanson and Kevin O'Bryant, "The Fourth Positive Element in the Greedy `B_h`-Set", Lemma 3.

articles.title: Fourth positive term of the greedy $B_h$-set
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $h$ and $a$, we say that
$a$ is the fourth positive element $a_4(h)$ of the greedy $B_h$-set if $1$ is the next greedy
$B_h$ choice after $\{0\}$, $h + 1$ is the next greedy $B_h$ choice after $\{0, 1\}$,
$h^2 + h + 1$ is the next greedy $B_h$ choice after $\{0, 1, h + 1\}$, and $a$ is the next
greedy $B_h$ choice after $\{0, 1, h + 1, h^2 + h + 1\}$.

articles.title: Next term of a greedy $B_h$-set
articles.statement:
Let $h$ and $a$ be natural numbers and $A$ a set of natural
numbers. Then $a$ is the next greedy $B_h$ choice after $A$ if $a$ is greater than every element
of $A$, the set $A \cup \{a\}$ is a $B_h$-set, and for every natural number $b < a$ that is
greater than every element of $A$, the set $A \cup \{b\}$ is not a $B_h$-set.

articles.title: Largest Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ (Erdős Problem 861)
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$,
$f(N)$ is the largest cardinality of a Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 861, second question: negative answer
articles.statement:
Let $A(N)$ be the number of Sidon
subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$, including the empty set and the singletons, and let $f(N)$ be the
largest size of a Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$. Then the ratio $\log_2 A(N) / f(N)$ does not
tend to $1$ as $N \to \infty$; that is, $A(N) = 2^{(1 + o(1)) f(N)}$ fails.

Saxton and Thomason proved $A(N) \ge 2^{(1.16 + o(1)) \sqrt{N}}$ (Theorem 2.11), and
$f(N) \sim \sqrt{N}$, so $\log_2 A(N) / f(N) \ge 1.16 + o(1)$.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #861, https://www.erdosproblems.com/861 (status SOLVED); resolution: D. Saxton and A. Thomason, Hypergraph containers, Invent. Math. (2015), 925-992, arXiv:1204.6595 (lower bound); Y. Kohayakawa, S. J. Lee, V. Rödl and W. Samotij, The number of Sidon sets and the maximum size of Sidon sets contained in a sparse random set of integers, Random Structures Algorithms (2015), 1-25 (upper bound), Saxton-Thomason Theorem 2.11: there are between 2^{(1.16 + o(1)) √n} and 2^{(55 + o(1)) √n} Sidon subsets of [n], the lower bound answering negatively whether there are only 2^{(1 + o(1)) √n}; erdosproblems.com/861: f(N) ∼ N^{1/2}, both questions are settled, the first positively and the second negatively, and 2^{1.16 f(N)} ≤ A(N) ≤ 2^{6.442 f(N)} for large N, https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.6595.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 861, second question
articles.statement:
Let $A(N)$ be the number of Sidon subsets of
$\{1, \dots, N\}$, including the empty set and the singletons, and let $f(N)$ be the
largest size of a Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$. The statement is that
$\log_2 A(N) / f(N) \to 1$ as $N \to \infty$, that is, $A(N) = 2^{(1 + o(1)) f(N)}$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 861, first question: positive answer
articles.statement:
Let $A(N)$ be the number of Sidon
subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$, including the empty set and the singletons, and let $f(N)$ be the
largest size of a Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$. Then $A(N) / 2^{f(N)} \to \infty$ as
$N \to \infty$.

Saxton and Thomason proved $A(N) \ge 2^{(1.16 + o(1)) \sqrt{N}}$ (Theorem 2.11), and
$f(N) \sim \sqrt{N}$, so $A(N) / 2^{f(N)} \ge 2^{(0.16 + o(1)) \sqrt{N}} \to \infty$.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #861, https://www.erdosproblems.com/861 (status SOLVED); resolution: D. Saxton and A. Thomason, Hypergraph containers, Invent. Math. (2015), 925-992, arXiv:1204.6595 (lower bound); Y. Kohayakawa, S. J. Lee, V. Rödl and W. Samotij, The number of Sidon sets and the maximum size of Sidon sets contained in a sparse random set of integers, Random Structures Algorithms (2015), 1-25 (upper bound), Saxton-Thomason Theorem 2.11: there are between 2^{(1.16 + o(1)) √n} and 2^{(55 + o(1)) √n} Sidon subsets of [n], the lower bound answering negatively whether there are only 2^{(1 + o(1)) √n}; erdosproblems.com/861: f(N) ∼ N^{1/2}, both questions are settled, the first positively and the second negatively, and 2^{1.16 f(N)} ≤ A(N) ≤ 2^{6.442 f(N)} for large N, https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.6595.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 861, first question
articles.statement:
Let $A(N)$ be the number of Sidon subsets of
$\{1, \dots, N\}$, including the empty set and the singletons, and let $f(N)$ be the
largest size of a Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$. The statement is that
$A(N) / 2^{f(N)} \to \infty$ as $N \to \infty$.

articles.title: Sidon subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$, this is the finite family
of all subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ that are Sidon sets of natural numbers, including the empty
set and the singletons.

articles.title: The almost thin ideal is contained in the Sidon ideal
articles.statement:
Every set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$
that is contained in a finite union of almost thin sets is contained in a finite union of Sidon
sets; that is, the ideal generated by the almost thin sets is contained in the Sidon ideal.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Theorem 4.

articles.title: The ideal of sets avoiding large difference sets
articles.statement:
For a set $Z \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, let
$D(Z) = \{a - b : a, b \in Z,\ b < a\}$ be its set of positive differences. The ideal
$D_{\mathrm{fin}}$ consists of the sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ for which there is a natural
number $n$ such that $D(Z) \not\subseteq A$ for every $n$-element set $Z \subseteq \mathbb{N}$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Definition 3.

articles.title: The empty set lies in the difference-set ideal
articles.statement:
The empty set belongs to the ideal
$D_{\mathrm{fin}}$ of sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ for which some natural number $n$ satisfies
$D(Z) \not\subseteq A$ for every $n$-element set $Z \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, where $D(Z)$ is the set
of positive differences $a - b$ with $a, b \in Z$ and $b < a$.

One can take $n = 2$: every two-element set has a positive difference.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Definition 3.

articles.title: The empty set lies in the van der Waerden ideal
articles.statement:
The empty subset of $\mathbb{N}$ belongs to
the van der Waerden ideal.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Definition 9.

articles.title: Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi lower bound for an infinite Sidon set
articles.statement:
There exist a Sidon set
$A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and a real constant $c > 0$ such that
$|A \cap \{1, \dots, n\}| > c\, (n \log n)^{1/3}$ for every natural number $n \ge 1$, where $\log$
is the natural logarithm.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Theorem 3, item 2, quoting M. Ajtai, J. Komlós and E. Szemerédi, *A dense infinite Sidon sequence*, European J. Combin. 2 (1981).

articles.title: Mian–Chowla lower bound for an infinite Sidon set
articles.statement:
There exist a Sidon set
$A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and a real constant $c > 0$ such that
$|A \cap \{1, \dots, n\}| > c\, n^{1/3}$ for every natural number $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Theorem 3, item 1, quoting A. M. Mian and S. Chowla, *On the B₂ sequences of Sidon*, Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. India Sect. A 14 (1944).

articles.title: Ruzsa's lower bound for an infinite Sidon set
articles.statement:
There is a Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$
such that for every real $\varepsilon > 0$, the inequality
$|A \cap \{1, \dots, n\}| > n^{\sqrt{2} - 1 - \varepsilon}$ holds for all sufficiently large
natural numbers $n$; that is, $|A \cap \{1, \dots, n\}| > n^{\sqrt{2} - 1 - o(1)}$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Theorem 3, item 3, quoting I. Z. Ruzsa, *An infinite Sidon sequence*, J. Number Theory 68 (1998).

articles.title: A Sidon set outside the almost thin ideal
articles.statement:
There is a Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$
that is not contained in any finite union of almost thin sets; that is, $A$ does not belong to the
ideal generated by the almost thin sets.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Proposition 1.

articles.title: A set in the van der Waerden, lacunary and difference-set ideals outside the Sidon ideal
articles.statement:
There is a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that belongs to the van der Waerden ideal, is contained in
a finite union of gap-lacunary sets (infinite sets whose gaps between consecutive elements tend to
infinity), and belongs to the ideal $D_{\mathrm{fin}}$ of sets avoiding large difference sets, but
is not contained in any finite union of Sidon sets.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Weak Sidon sets split into two Sidon sets
articles.statement:
Every weak Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is
the union of two disjoint Sidon sets $B$ and $C$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Weak Sidon sets generate the Sidon ideal
articles.statement:
The ideal on $\mathbb{N}$ generated by the weak
Sidon sets equals the Sidon ideal.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Generated ideals are closed under subsets
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a property of subsets of
$\mathbb{N}$. If $A$ lies in the ideal generated by $P$ and $B \subseteq A$, then $B$ also lies in
the ideal generated by $P$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Section 1 (ideals, item 2).

articles.title: Ideal generated by a property
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a property of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$. The ideal
generated by $P$ is the family of all sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that are contained in the union
of finitely many sets with property $P$. The empty union is allowed, so the empty set always
belongs to it.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Section 1 (ideals) and Definitions 5, 8 and 13 (ideals generated by a family).

articles.title: Almost thin sets are infinite
articles.statement:
Every almost thin set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is infinite.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Definition 7.

articles.title: Gap-lacunary sets are infinite
articles.statement:
Every gap-lacunary set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is infinite.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Definition 4.

articles.title: Almost thin set
articles.statement:
A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is *almost thin* if it is infinite and,
writing $A(n)$ for its $n$-th element in increasing order (counting from $n = 0$), there is a
real number $\alpha < 1$ such that $A(n)/A(n+1) \le \alpha$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

Since the ratios $A(n)/A(n+1)$ lie in $[0, 1]$, this is equivalent to
$\limsup_{n \to \infty} A(n)/A(n+1) < 1$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Definition 7.

articles.title: Gap-lacunary set
articles.statement:
A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is *gap-lacunary* (called *lacunary* in
the source) if it is infinite and, writing $A(n)$ for its $n$-th element in increasing order
(counting from $n = 0$), the gaps $A(n+1) - A(n)$ tend to infinity as $n \to \infty$.

This differs from Hadamard lacunarity, where consecutive elements grow by a factor at least
$q > 1$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Definition 4.

articles.title: Positive sets whose elements at least double are Sidon
articles.statement:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with
$0 \notin A$, and write $A(n)$ for the $n$-th element of $A$ in increasing order, counting from
$n = 0$, with $A(n) = 0$ when $A$ has at most $n$ elements. If $2 A(n) \le A(n+1)$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $A$ is a Sidon set.

The hypotheses force $A$ to be empty or infinite, so the source's standing assumption that $A$
is infinite is not needed.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Sidon sets are weak Sidon sets
articles.statement:
Every Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a weak Sidon
set.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Definitions 10 and 11.

articles.title: Weak Sidon set
articles.statement:
A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a *weak Sidon set* (or *well spread*) if
sums of two distinct elements of $A$ are distinct: whenever $a, b, c, d \in A$ satisfy $a < b$,
$c < d$ and $a + b = c + d$, then $a = c$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Definition 11.

articles.title: Sets with a property lie in the ideal it generates
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a property of subsets
of $\mathbb{N}$. Every set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with property $P$ lies in the ideal
generated by $P$, the family of all subsets of finite unions of sets with property $P$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Section 1 (ideals).

articles.title: A block not covered by few Sidon sets
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and $C \ge 1$ be natural
numbers, and put $M = C \cdot 2^n + 1$ and $K = (n - 1)\binom{n}{2} + 1$. Then the block
$\mathrm{Block}(n, C, M, K) = \{M l + C \cdot 2^k : 0 \le k < n,\ 1 \le l \le K\}$ is not
contained in the union of any $n - 1$ Sidon subsets of $\mathbb{N}$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Positive difference set
articles.statement:
For a set $Z \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the positive difference set
$D(Z)$ is the set of all differences $a - b$ with $a, b \in Z$ and $a > b$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Section 1 (notation `A - B` and `D(A)`).

articles.title: One-term blocks
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $C$ and $M$, the block
$\mathrm{Block}(1, C, M, 1) = \{M l + C \cdot 2^k : 0 \le k < 1,\ 1 \le l \le 1\}$ is the
singleton $\{M + C\}$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Section 3 (definition of `Block` before Lemma 2).

articles.title: Block sets
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$, $C$, $M$ and $K$, the block
$\mathrm{Block}(n, C, M, K)$ is the set of natural numbers $M l + C \cdot 2^k$ with
$0 \le k < n$ and $1 \le l \le K$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Section 3 (definition of `Block` before Lemma 2).

articles.title: The Sidon ideal is $F_\sigma$
articles.statement:
Give the Cantor space $\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ the product
topology and identify each set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with its indicator function. Then the set
of indicator functions of the members of the Sidon ideal is a countable union of closed subsets
of $\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Corollary 2.

articles.title: The Sidon ideal is contained in the lacunary ideal
articles.statement:
Call a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$
lacunary if it is infinite and the gaps $A(n + 1) - A(n)$ between consecutive elements tend to
infinity, where $A(n)$ is the $n$-th element of $A$ in increasing order. Every set in the Sidon
ideal is contained in a finite union of lacunary sets, that is, it lies in the ideal
$\mathrm{Lac}$ generated by the lacunary sets.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Sidon ideal
articles.statement:
The Sidon ideal $\mathrm{Si}$ is the ideal on $\mathbb{N}$ generated by the
Sidon sets: it consists of all sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ contained in a finite union of
Sidon subsets of $\mathbb{N}$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Definition 13.

articles.title: Generated ideals are closed under unions
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a property of subsets of
$\mathbb{N}$, and consider the ideal generated by $P$, the family of all subsets of finite unions
of sets with property $P$. If $A$ and $B$ lie in this ideal, then so does $A \cup B$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Section 1 (ideals, item 3).

articles.title: Van der Waerden ideal
articles.statement:
The van der Waerden ideal $W$ consists of the sets
$A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ for which there is an $n > 0$ such that $A$ contains no arithmetic
progression $a, a + r, \dots, a + (n - 1) r$ of $n$ terms with $a \in \mathbb{N}$ and $r > 0$.

## Sources

- Andrzej Nowik, *On the Sidon Ideal*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A91, Definition 9.

articles.title: Perfect difference sets modulo $v$
articles.statement:
A set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a perfect difference
set modulo a natural number $v$ when every nonzero residue $x$ modulo $v$ satisfies
