Resolved true: Erdős and Szemerédi proved it for all large primes $p$, and Gao, Hamidoune and Wang
for every modulus.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #541, https://www.erdosproblems.com/541 (status PROVED (LEAN)); resolution: W. Gao, Y. O. Hamidoune and G. Wang, Distinct length modular zero-sum subsequences: a proof of Graham's conjecture, J. Number Theory (2010), 1425-1431, erdosproblems.com/541: proved by Erdős and Szemerédi for large p and by Gao, Hamidoune and Wang for all moduli, https://www.erdosproblems.com/541.

articles.title: Graham's zero-sum statement (Erdős Problem 541)
articles.statement:
This is the statement that for every
prime $p$ and every sequence $a_0, \dots, a_{p-1}$ of residues modulo $p$, not necessarily
distinct, if there is a natural number $r$ such that every nonempty set
$S \subseteq \{0, \dots, p-1\}$ with $\sum_{i \in S} a_i = 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ has
exactly $r$ elements, then at most two distinct residues occur among $a_0, \dots, a_{p-1}$.

articles.title: Perfect covers with exactly one odd element
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be an abelian group of order $2^m$,
let $n \ge 1$ and let $G = H \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$. Call an element of $G$ odd when its
$\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$-coordinate, taken as a representative in $\{0, 1, \dots, 2^n - 1\}$, is odd.
Then the number of perfect covers of $G$ with exactly one odd element is
$2^m \cdot 2^{n-1} \cdot C(H \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{2^{n-1}})$, where $C(K)$ denotes the number of
perfect covers of a group $K$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Lemma 21 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-lem-21`). "`y_1` odd, all other `y_i` even" is read as "exactly one odd `y`" for the unordered set; `y` odd means `y.val` odd; `n ≥ 1` added (`ℤ_{2^{n-1}}`).

articles.title: Perfect covers containing a perfect cover of a subgroup
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an abelian group of
order $2^n$ and $H$ a subgroup of order $2^m$. Then the number of perfect covers of $G$ that
contain a perfect cover of $H$ is $2^{m(n-m)} \cdot C(G/H) \cdot C(H)$, where $C(K)$ denotes the
number of perfect covers of a group $K$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Lemma 17 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-lem-17`).

articles.title: Perfect covers of $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^m \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$
articles.statement:
Write $C(K)$ for the number
of perfect covers of a group $K$, and for natural numbers $m$ and $n$ let
$b_{m,n} = C((\mathbb{Z}_2)^m \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{2^n})$. Then:
for every $m \ge 0$, $C((\mathbb{Z}_2)^m) \cdot m! = \prod_{i=0}^{m-1} (2^m - 2^i)$;
for all $m, n \ge 1$, writing $B_{m,k} = 2^m \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} (2^m - 2^i) / (k+1)!$ for
$1 \le k \le m$, we have $b_{m,n} = 2^{m+n-1} b_{m,n-1} +
\sum_{k=1}^{m} B_{m,k} \, 2^{k(m-k)} \, 2^{(k+1)(n-1)} \, b_{m-k,n-1}$;
and for every $m \ge 0$ there is a polynomial $q$ of degree $m$ with rational coefficients such
that $b_{m,n} = 2^{m(n-1)} \, 2^{n(n-1)/2} \, q(n)$ for all $n \ge 0$, where the power
$2^{m(n-1)}$ has an integer exponent (it is $2^{-m}$ at $n = 0$).

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Theorem 4 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-thm-4`).

articles.title: Perfect covers of an elementary abelian group of order 4 or 8 times a cyclic 2-group
articles.statement:
Write $C(K)$ for the number of perfect covers of a group $K$. For every $n \ge 0$,
$C((\mathbb{Z}_2)^2 \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{2^n}) = 2^{2n-2} \, 2^{n(n-1)/2} \, (3n^2 + 13n + 12)$
and
$C((\mathbb{Z}_2)^3 \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{2^n}) =
2^{3n-3} \, 2^{n(n-1)/2} \, (28n^3 + 196n^2 + 392n + 224)$,
where $2^{2n-2}$ and $2^{3n-3}$ are integer powers of $2$ (fractional at $n = 0$).

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Corollary 26 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-cor-26`). The record's third identity, for `(ℤ₂)^4 ⊕ ℤ_{2^n}`, is omitted: it fails as printed at `n = 1` (`C((ℤ₂)^5) = 83328`, formula `72328`).

articles.title: Perfect cover count as a finset cardinality
articles.statement:
For a finite abelian group $G$, the number
$C(G)$ of perfect covers of $G$ equals the number of elements of the finite set of all subsets of
$G$ that are perfect covers.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Section 1 (`C(G)`).

articles.title: Small values of the perfect cover count
articles.statement:
Writing $C(K)$ for the number of perfect covers
of a group $K$, we have $C(\mathbb{Z}_2) = 1$, $C(\mathbb{Z}_4) = 2$ and
$C(\mathbb{Z}_2 \oplus \mathbb{Z}_2) = 3$.

The two perfect covers of $\mathbb{Z}_4$ are $\{1, 2\}$ and $\{2, 3\}$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Theorems 2 and 4 at `n = 1, 2` and `m = 2`.

articles.title: Perfect covers of a product of two cyclic 2-groups
articles.statement:
Write $C(K)$ for the number of
perfect covers of a group $K$, and $a_{m,n} = C(\mathbb{Z}_{2^m} \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{2^n})$.
For all $m \ge n \ge 1$,
$a_{m,n} = 2^{m+n-1} (a_{m-1,n} + 2 a_{m,n-1}) -
3 \cdot 2^{2m+2n-4} \, a_{m-1,n-1}$.
Moreover, for every $n \ge 0$ there is a polynomial $p$ of degree $n$ with rational coefficients
such that $a_{m,n} = 2^{(m-1)n} \, 2^{m(m-1)/2} \, p(m)$ for all $m \ge n$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Theorem 3 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-thm-3`).

articles.title: Perfect covers of a cyclic 2-group times a cyclic group of order 2, 4 or 8
articles.statement:
Write
$C(K)$ for the number of perfect covers of a group $K$. For every $n \ge 0$,
$C(\mathbb{Z}_{2^n} \oplus \mathbb{Z}_2) = 2^{n-1} \, 2^{n(n-1)/2} \, (n + 2)$, where $2^{n-1}$
is an integer power of $2$ (equal to $1/2$ at $n = 0$). For every $n \ge 1$,
$C(\mathbb{Z}_{2^n} \oplus \mathbb{Z}_4) = 2^{2n-2} \, 2^{n(n-1)/2} \, (n^2 + 11n + 4)$.
For every $n \ge 2$,
$C(\mathbb{Z}_{2^n} \oplus \mathbb{Z}_8) =
2^{3n-3} \, 2^{n(n-1)/2} \, (4n^3 + 108n^2 + 512n - 384)/3$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Corollary 25 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-cor-25`). The record gives no range; the second identity fails at `n = 0` (`C(ℤ₄) = 2`, formula `1`) and the third at `n = 0, 1` (`C(ℤ₈) = 8`, formula `-16`; `C(ℤ₂ ⊕ ℤ₈) = 160`, formula `80`), matching Theorem 3's range `m ≥ n`.

articles.title: Number of perfect covers of a cyclic 2-group
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 0$, the cyclic group
$\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$ has exactly $2^{n(n-1)/2}$ perfect covers.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Theorem 2 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-thm-2`).

articles.title: Number of perfect covers
articles.statement:
For an abelian group $G$, $C(G)$ is the number of perfect
covers of $G$: finite subsets $S \subseteq G$ such that every element of $G$ is the sum of
exactly one subset of $S$ (the empty subset has sum $0$).

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Section 1 (`C(G)`).

articles.title: Removing the last element of a perfect $2^j$-cover
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an abelian group, let
$s = (x_1, \dots, x_{k+1})$ be a family in $G$ that is a perfect $2^j$-cover of $G$, and let
$S_1 = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$. For every $a \in G$, if $S_1$ covers $a$ exactly $c$ times, then
$S_1$ covers $a + x_{k+1}$ exactly $2^j - c$ times.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Lemma 8 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-lem-8`). The paper's `|G| = 2^n` and `k + 1 = j + n` are not needed.

articles.title: Shifting by multiples of the last element of a perfect $2^j$-cover
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an
abelian group, let $s = (x_1, \dots, x_{k+1})$ be a family in $G$ that is a perfect $2^j$-cover
of $G$, and let $S_1 = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$. For every $b \in G$, if $S_1$ covers $b$ exactly $c$
times, then for every integer $t$ it covers $b + 2t\,x_{k+1}$ exactly $c$ times and
$b + (2t + 1)\,x_{k+1}$ exactly $2^j - c$ times.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Corollary 9 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-cor-9`). `t` ranges over `ℤ`.

articles.title: Distinct subset sums from the odd-combination condition
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an abelian group,
and for a finite set $A \subseteq G$ write $\mathcal{T}(A)$ for the set of odd combinations of
$A$. Let $x = (x_1, \dots, x_m)$ be a family in $G$ such that
$x_i \notin \mathcal{T}(\{x_1, \dots, x_{i-1}\})$ for every $i$ (for $i = 1$ this says
$x_1 \ne 0$, and for $i \ge 2$ it forces $x_i \ne 0$). Then $x$ covers every element of $G$ at
most once, that is, all subset sums of $x$ are distinct; if moreover $|G| = 2^m$, then $x$ is a
perfect $1$-cover of $G$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Lemma 16 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-lem-16`). The paper's "nonzero" hypothesis is the `i = 1` case of `hx`; distinctness needs no finiteness, and "`m = n`" is `Nat.card G = 2 ^ m`.

articles.title: Cover count
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an abelian group, $s = (s_i)_{i \in \iota}$ a family in $G$
indexed by a finite type $\iota$ (a colored multiset), and $g \in G$. The cover count of $g$ by
$s$ is the number of index sets $I \subseteq \iota$ with $\sum_{i \in I} s_i = g$: the number of
times $s$ covers $g$ by its subset sums (the empty set covers $0$).

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Section 1 (subset sums, "covered `m` times", Lemma 8).

articles.title: Elements of order $2$ in perfect covers of $\mathbb{Z}_{2^m} \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$
articles.statement:
Let $m, n$ be natural numbers with $m + n > 0$. Every perfect cover of
$\mathbb{Z}_{2^m} \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$ contains an element of order $2$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Lemma 19 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-lem-19`). Hypothesis `0 < m + n` added: the trivial group's perfect cover is empty.

articles.title: Perfect covers with a prescribed number of odd last coordinates
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a finite
abelian group of order $2^m$, let $n \ge 1$, and let $G = H \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$. For every
$k$ with $1 \le k \le m + 1$, some perfect cover $S$ of $G$ has exactly $k$ elements $(h, y)$
whose coordinate $y \in \mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$ is odd.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Lemma 20 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-lem-20`). The setting `G = H ⊕ ℤ_{2^n}`, `|H| = 2^m`, is the one fixed before the lemma in Section 5; `y` odd means `y.val` odd; `n ≥ 1` added (for `n = 0` no `y` is odd).

articles.title: Existence of perfect covers
articles.statement:
Every finite abelian group $G$ of order $2^n$ has a perfect
cover, and every nonzero $x \in G$ lies in some perfect cover of $G$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Theorem 1 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-thm-1`).

articles.title: Which families are perfect $m$-covers of $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$
articles.statement:
Let $s = (s_i)_{i \in \iota}$
be a family in $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$ indexed by a finite type $\iota$ (a colored multiset). Then $s$
is a perfect $m$-cover of $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$ for some $m$ if and only if for every $j$ with
$1 \le j \le n$ some $s_i$ has additive order $2^j$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Theorem 12 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-thm-12`). The multiplicity `m` is existentially quantified.

articles.title: Perfect $m$-covers of $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$ contain perfect covers
articles.statement:
Let
$s = (s_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a family in $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$ indexed by a finite type $\iota$. If
$s$ is a perfect $m$-cover of $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$, then there is a finite set $T \subseteq \iota$
such that the subfamily $(s_i)_{i \in T}$ is a perfect $1$-cover of $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Corollary 13 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-cor-13`).

articles.title: Orders of second coordinates in perfect $m$-covers
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a finite abelian group of
order $2^r$ and let $s = (s_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a family in $H \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$ indexed by
a finite type $\iota$. If $s$ is a perfect $m$-cover of $H \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$, then for
every $j$ with $1 \le j \le n$ the second coordinate of some $s_i$ has additive order $2^j$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Corollary 14 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-cor-14`). The family has any finite index type (the record reuses `n` for its length).

articles.title: Perfect covers of ℤ₄: an example and a non-example
articles.statement:
In the cyclic group
$\mathbb{Z}_4 = \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$, the set $\{1, 2\}$ is a perfect cover and the set
$\{1, 3\}$ is not, since $1 + 3 = 0$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Section 1 (perfect covers).

articles.title: Perfect cover
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an abelian group. A finite set $S \subseteq G$ is a perfect cover
of $G$ when every element of $G$ is the sum of exactly one subset of $S$ (the empty subset has
sum $0$); that is, the family of the elements of $S$ is a perfect $1$-cover of $G$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Section 1 (perfect covers, Lemma 16).

articles.title: Replacing an entry of a perfect $2^k$-cover by an odd multiple
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an abelian
group, let $k$ and $N$ be natural numbers, and let $a, b, s_1, \dots, s_N \in G$. If the family
$(a, s_1, \dots, s_N)$ is a perfect $2^k$-cover of $G$ and $b = (2j + 1)a$ for some integer $j$,
then the family $(b, s_1, \dots, s_N)$ is also a perfect $2^k$-cover of $G$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Lemma 11 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-lem-11`). The paper's `|G| = 2^n` and length `n + k` are not needed.

articles.title: Adjoining an element doubles the multiplicity of a perfect cover
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an abelian
group and let $s = (s_1, \dots, s_k)$ be a perfect $m$-cover of $G$. For every $g \in G$, the
family $(g, s_1, \dots, s_k)$ is a perfect $2m$-cover of $G$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Lemma 5 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-lem-5`).

articles.title: Projections of a perfect cover of a direct sum
articles.statement:
Let $H$ and $K$ be finite abelian groups
with $|H| = 2^m$ and $|K| = 2^n$, and let $s = (s_i)_{i \in \iota}$, indexed by a finite set
$\iota$, be a perfect $l$-cover of $H \oplus K$. Then the first coordinates of the $s_i$ form a
perfect $2^n l$-cover of $H$, and the second coordinates form a perfect $2^m l$-cover of $K$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Lemma 6 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-lem-6`).

articles.title: Perfect $m$-cover
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an abelian group, $m$ a natural number and
$s = (s_i)_{i \in \iota}$ a family of elements of $G$ indexed by a finite set $\iota$ (a colored
multiset: repeated values count separately). The family $s$ is a perfect $m$-cover of $G$ when
every $g \in G$ equals $\sum_{i \in I} s_i$ for exactly $m$ subsets $I \subseteq \iota$ (the
empty subset has sum $0$).

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Section 1 (perfect `m`-covers, Lemmas 5 and 8).

articles.title: Elements of a finite set are odd combinations of it
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an abelian group and $A$ a
finite subset of $G$, and let $\mathcal{T}(A)$ be the set of combinations $\sum_{y \in A} c_y y$
in which every integer coefficient $c_y$ is $0$ or odd. Every $x \in A$ lies in $\mathcal{T}(A)$:
take $c_x = 1$ and $c_y = 0$ for $y \neq x$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Section 3 (the operator `𝒯`).

articles.title: Elements of order two among odd combinations of part of a perfect cover
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an
abelian group of order $2^n$, let $S$ be a perfect cover of $G$, and let $A \subseteq S$ contain
no element of order $2$. Let $\mathcal{T}(A)$ be the set of combinations $\sum_{x \in A} c_x x$ in
which every integer coefficient $c_x$ is $0$ or odd. Then $\mathcal{T}(A)$ does not contain
exactly one element of order $2$: it contains none or at least two.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Lemma 18 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-lem-18`). "No elements of order `2`, or at least two" is stated as "not exactly one".

articles.title: Odd combinations of the empty set
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an abelian group and, for a finite
$A \subseteq G$, let $\mathcal{T}(A)$ be the set of combinations $\sum_{x \in A} c_x x$ in which
every integer coefficient $c_x$ is $0$ or odd. Then $\mathcal{T}(\emptyset) = \{0\}$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Section 3 (the operator `𝒯`).

articles.title: Odd combinations of disjoint parts of a perfect cover
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an abelian group of
order $2^n$ and $S$ a perfect cover of $G$. For a finite $A \subseteq G$, let $\mathcal{T}(A)$ be
the set of combinations $\sum_{x \in A} c_x x$ in which every integer coefficient $c_x$ is $0$
or odd. Then: (a) for disjoint $A, B \subseteq S$, $\mathcal{T}(A) \cap \mathcal{T}(B) = \{0\}$;
(b) if $A \subseteq S$ and $s \in S \setminus A$, then $s \notin \mathcal{T}(A)$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Theorem 15 (a), (b) (`jis-2025-25.7.8-thm-15`).

articles.title: Odd combinations
articles.statement:
For a finite subset $A$ of an abelian group $G$, $\mathcal{T}(A)$ is the
set of all sums $\sum_{x \in A} c_x x$ with integer coefficients $c_x$ such that every $c_x$ is
either $0$ or odd.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Section 3 (the operator `𝒯`).

articles.title: Odd multiples and replacement in perfect covers
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of order
$2^n$ and let $a, b \in G$ be nonzero. Then $b = (2j+1)a$ for some integer $j$ if and only if, for
every perfect cover $S$ of $G$ with $a \in S$, the set $(S \setminus \{a\}) \cup \{b\}$ is again a
perfect cover of $G$. If moreover $a \ne b$, then $b = (2j+1)a$ for some integer $j$ if and only if
no perfect cover of $G$ contains both $a$ and $b$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Theorem 10 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-thm-10`). `a, b ≠ 0` added and `a ≠ b` added for (3): for `a = 0, b ≠ 0` conditions (2) and (3) hold vacuously while (1) fails, and for `a = b ≠ 0` condition (3) fails (Theorem 1 puts `a` in a perfect cover) while (1) holds.

articles.title: Removing one element from a perfect cover
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of order $2^n$,
let $S$ be a perfect cover of $G$, let $z \in S$ and let $S_1 = S \setminus \{z\}$. Then (a) every
element of $G$ is the sum of at most one subset of $S_1$, and exactly half of the $2^n$ elements
of $G$ are the sum of a subset of $S_1$; (b) if $g \in G$ is the sum of a subset of $S_1$ and $j$
is an integer with $j \ge 1$, then $g + 2jz$ is the sum of a subset of $S_1$ and $g + (2j-1)z$ is
not.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Lemma 7 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-lem-7`).

articles.title: The even tail of a perfect cover
articles.statement:
Let $s = (s_1, \dots, s_{m+n})$, $s_i = (x_i, y_i)$, be a
family in $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^m \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$ that is a perfect $1$-cover: every element of
the group is the sum of the $s_i$ over exactly one set of indices. Let $k + 1 \le m + n$ and suppose
that $y_i$, read as an integer in $\{0, \dots, 2^n - 1\}$, is odd exactly when $i \le k + 1$. Let
$V$ be the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-span of $x_{k+2}, \dots, x_{m+n}$ in $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^m$. Then every
$(x, y)$ with $x \in V$ and $y$ even (again read in $\{0, \dots, 2^n - 1\}$) is the sum of the
$s_i$ over exactly one set of indices taken from $\{k+2, \dots, m+n\}$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Lemma 24 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-lem-24`). The family's elements lie in `V ⊕ 2ℤ_{2^n}` by hypothesis and by definition of `V`; only the covering statement is stated.

articles.title: Spans of the odd and even entries of a perfect cover
articles.statement:
Let $m$, $n$ and $k$ be natural
numbers with $k + 1 \le m + n$, and let $s = (s_1, \dots, s_{m+n})$, $s_i = (x_i, y_i)$, be a
family in $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^m \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$ that is a perfect $1$-cover: every element of
the group is the sum of the $s_i$ over exactly one set of indices. Suppose that $y_i$, read as an
integer in $\{0, \dots, 2^n - 1\}$, is odd exactly when $i \le k + 1$. Let $U$ be the
$\mathbb{Z}_2$-span of $x_1 + x_2, \dots, x_1 + x_{k+1}$ and $V$ the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-span of
$x_{k+2}, \dots, x_{m+n}$ in $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^m$. Then $\dim U = k$, $\dim V = m - k$,
$U \cap V = 0$ and $U + V = (\mathbb{Z}_2)^m$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Lemma 23 (`jis-2025-25.7.8-lem-23`). Indices are `0`-based (`i < k + 1` are the odd ones, and `k + 1 ≤ m + n` makes `y_1, …, y_{k+1}` exist); the perfect cover is an indexed family (perfect covers have distinct entries); `(ℤ₂)^m = U ⊕ V` is stated as `U ⊔ V = ⊤`.

articles.title: Zero is an odd combination
articles.statement:
For every finite subset $A$ of an abelian group $G$, $0$ lies
in the set $\mathcal{T}(A)$ of odd combinations of $A$ (take every coefficient equal to $0$).

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Section 3 (the operator `𝒯`).

articles.title: Odd combinations are closed under odd multiples
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite subset of an abelian
group $G$. If $g$ lies in the set $\mathcal{T}(A)$ of odd combinations of $A$, then
$(2j+1)g \in \mathcal{T}(A)$ for every integer $j$.

## Sources

- John Greene and Clayton Higgins, *Maximal Subset Sums in a Group of Order a Power of 2*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.8, Theorem 15 (c) (`jis-2025-25.7.8-thm-15`). "Union of equivalence classes" is stated as closure under odd multiples (`0 ∈ 𝒯(A)` is `zero_mem_oddCombinations`).

articles.title: Valid orderings of finite sets of nonzero integers
articles.statement:
Every finite set $A$ of nonzero
integers has a valid ordering: its elements can be listed as $a_1, \dots, a_m$, each exactly
once, so that the partial sums $a_1, a_1 + a_2, \dots, a_1 + \cdots + a_m$ are pairwise
distinct. The empty sum $0$ is not counted among the partial sums.

## Sources

- Noah Kravitz, "Rearranging Small Sets for Distinct Partial Sums", Theorem 2.

articles.title: Lev's rectification principle
articles.statement:
Let $\ell \ge 2$ be a natural number, $p$ a prime and
$A$ a subset of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ with $|A| \le \lceil \log p / \log \ell \rceil$. Then
there are a finite set $B$ of integers and a map $f \colon \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$
that is a Freiman isomorphism of order $\ell$ from $A$ to $B$: $f$ maps $A$ bijectively onto
$B$, and for all $a_1, \dots, a_\ell, b_1, \dots, b_\ell \in A$ we have
$f(a_1) + \cdots + f(a_\ell) = f(b_1) + \cdots + f(b_\ell)$ if and only if
$a_1 + \cdots + a_\ell = b_1 + \cdots + b_\ell$.

## Sources

- Noah Kravitz, "Rearranging Small Sets for Distinct Partial Sums", Theorem 3.

articles.title: Bounded subsequence sums as a generalized h-fold sumset when zero is a term
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be
an abelian group, let $m$ be a natural number, let $a_1, \dots, a_m$ be distinct nonzero elements
of $G$, and put $a_0 = 0$. Let $t_0, \dots, t_m$ be positive integers, let $\mathcal{A}$ be the
sequence in which each $a_i$ occurs $t_i$ times, and let $h = t_0 + \dots + t_m$ be its length.
If $\alpha, \beta$ are natural numbers with $\alpha \ge 1$, $\beta \le h - 1$ and
$\alpha + \beta \le h$, then $\Sigma^\beta_\alpha(\mathcal{A})$, the set of sums of subsequences
of $\mathcal{A}$ with at least $\alpha$ and at most $h - \beta$ terms, equals the generalized
$(h - \beta)$-fold sumset $(h - \beta)^{(\bar r)} A$ of $A = (a_0, a_1, \dots, a_m)$ with
$\bar r = (h - \alpha - \beta + t_0, t_1, \dots, t_m)$, that is, the set of sums
$\sum_{j=0}^{m} s_j a_j$ with $0 \le s_j \le r_j$ for all $j$ and $\sum_j s_j = h - \beta$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Bounded subsequence sums as a generalized h-fold sumset when zero is not a term
articles.statement:
Let $G$
be an abelian group and let $a_1, \dots, a_k$ be distinct nonzero elements of $G$. Let
$t_1, \dots, t_k$ be positive integers, let $\mathcal{A}$ be the sequence in which each $a_i$
occurs $t_i$ times, and let $h = t_1 + \dots + t_k$ be its length. If $\alpha, \beta$ are natural
numbers with $\alpha \ge 1$ and $\alpha + \beta \le h - 1$, then $\Sigma^\beta_\alpha(\mathcal{A})$,
the set of sums of subsequences of $\mathcal{A}$ with at least $\alpha$ and at most $h - \beta$
terms, equals the generalized $(h - \beta)$-fold sumset $(h - \beta)^{(\bar r)} A_0$ of
$A_0 = (a_0, a_1, \dots, a_k)$, where $a_0 = 0$, with
$\bar r = (h - \alpha - \beta, t_1, \dots, t_k)$, that is, the set of sums
$\sum_{j=0}^{k} s_j a_j$ with $0 \le s_j \le r_j$ for all $j$ and $\sum_j s_j = h - \beta$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Inverse theorem for bounded subsequence sums of mixed-sign sequences containing zero
articles.statement:
Let
$1 \le n \le p$, let $c_1 < \dots < c_n < 0 < d_1 < \dots < d_p$ be integers and
$A = \{c_1, \dots, c_n, 0, d_1, \dots, d_p\}$, a set of $k = n + p + 1$ elements, let
$s_1, \dots, s_n, z, t_1, \dots, t_p$ be positive integers, let $\mathcal{A}$ be the sequence in
which each $c_i$ occurs $s_i$ times, $0$ occurs $z$ times and each $d_j$ occurs $t_j$ times, and
let $h = s_1 + \dots + s_n + z + t_1 + \dots + t_p$. Let $\alpha, \beta$ be natural numbers with
$1 \le \alpha \le h - 2$, $\beta \le h - 2$ and $\alpha + \beta \le h$, put
$\bar r = (s_1, \dots, s_n, h - \alpha - \beta + z, t_1, \dots, t_p)$, and write $E$ for the
equality $|\Sigma^\beta_\alpha(\mathcal{A})| = L(\bar r, h - \beta)$, where $L$ is the Yang–Chen
bound. For an integer $e$ and a set $X$ write $e \cdot X = \{e x : x \in X\}$. Then:
(a) if $k = 3$ and $\alpha + \beta = h$, then $E$ holds when $z = 1$, and for $z \ge 2$, $E$ holds
if and only if $A = e \cdot \{-1, 0, 1\}$ for some integer $e > 0$;
(b) if $k = 3$ and $\alpha + \beta \le h - 1$, then $E$ holds if and only if
$A = e \cdot \{-1, 0, 1\}$ for some integer $e > 0$;
(c) if $k = 4$ and $\alpha + \beta = h$, then for $z = t_1 = 1$, $E$ holds if and only if
$A = \{x - y, 0, x, y\}$ for some integers $0 < x < y$, and for $z \ge 2$ or $t_1 \ge 2$, $E$
holds if and only if $A = e \cdot \{-1, 0, 1, 2\}$ for some integer $e > 0$;
(d) if $k = 4$ and $\alpha + \beta \le h - 1$, then $E$ holds if and only if
$A = e \cdot \{-1, 0, 1, 2\}$ for some integer $e > 0$;
(e) if $k \ge 5$, then $E$ holds if and only if $A = e \cdot \{-n, \dots, p\}$ for some integer
$e > 0$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 20.

articles.title: Inverse theorem for bounded subsequence sums of mixed-sign sequences without zero
articles.statement:
Let
$1 \le n \le p$, let $c_1 < \dots < c_n < 0 < d_1 < \dots < d_p$ be integers and
$A = \{c_1, \dots, c_n, d_1, \dots, d_p\}$, let $s_1, \dots, s_n, t_1, \dots, t_p$ be positive
integers, let $\mathcal{A}$ be the sequence in which each $c_i$ occurs $s_i$ times and each $d_j$
occurs $t_j$ times, and let $h = s_1 + \dots + s_n + t_1 + \dots + t_p$, with $h \ge 3$. Let
$\alpha, \beta$ be natural numbers with $1 \le \alpha \le h - 2$, $\beta \le h - 2$ and
$\alpha + \beta \le h - 1$, put $\bar r = (s_1, \dots, s_n, h - \alpha - \beta, t_1, \dots, t_p)$,
and write $E$ for the equality $|\Sigma^\beta_\alpha(\mathcal{A})| = L(\bar r, h - \beta)$, where
$L$ is the Yang–Chen bound. Then:
(a) if $n + p = 3$, $\alpha + \beta = h - 1$ and $t_1 = 1$, then $E$ holds if and only if
$A = \{x - y, x, y\}$ for some integers $0 < x < y$;
(b) in every other case, except $n + p = 2$ with $\alpha + \beta = h - 1$, $E$ holds if and only
if $A = \{e x : x \in \{-n, \dots, -1, 1, \dots, p\}\}$ for some integer $e > 0$.

The source states (b) also for $n + p = 2$ and $\alpha + \beta = h - 1$, but there $E$ holds for
every $A$: for $A = \{-2, 7\}$ with $s_1 = 1$, $t_1 = 2$ and $\alpha = \beta = 1$ one has
$|\Sigma^1_1(\mathcal{A})| = |\{-2, 5, 7, 14\}| = 4 = L((1, 1, 2), 2)$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 19.

articles.title: Inverse theorem for bounded subsequence sums of nonnegative sequences containing zero
articles.statement:
Let
$m \ge 2$, let $0 < a_1 < \dots < a_m$ be integers, put $a_0 = 0$ and
$A = \{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_m\}$, let $t_0, t_1, \dots, t_m$ be positive integers, let
$\mathcal{A}$ be the sequence in which each $a_i$ occurs $t_i$ times, and let
$h = t_0 + t_1 + \dots + t_m$. Let $\alpha, \beta$ be natural numbers with
$1 \le \alpha \le h - 2$, $\beta \le h - 2$ and $\alpha + \beta \le h - 1$, put
$\bar r = (h - \alpha - \beta + t_0, t_1, \dots, t_m)$, and write $E$ for the equality
$|\Sigma^\beta_\alpha(\mathcal{A})| = L(\bar r, h - \beta)$, where $L$ is the Yang–Chen bound.
For an integer $e$ and a set $X$ write $e \cdot X = \{e x : x \in X\}$. Then:
(a) if $m = 2$ and $t_1 = 1$, then $E$ holds; if $m = 2$ and $t_1 \ge 2$, then $E$ holds if and
only if $A = e \cdot \{0, 1, 2\}$ for some integer $e > 0$;
(b) if $m = 3$ and $t_1 = t_2 = 1$, then $E$ holds if and only if $A = \{0, x, y, x + y\}$ for
some integers $0 < x < y$; if $m = 3$ and $t_1 \ge 2$ or $t_2 \ge 2$, then $E$ holds if and only
if $A = e \cdot \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ for some integer $e > 0$;
(c) if $m \ge 4$, then $E$ holds if and only if $A = e \cdot \{0, 1, \dots, m\}$ for some integer
$e > 0$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 18.

articles.title: Inverse theorem for bounded subsequence sums of positive sequences
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$, let
$a_1 < \dots < a_k$ be positive integers and $A = \{a_1, \dots, a_k\}$, let $t_1, \dots, t_k$ be
positive integers, let $\mathcal{A}$ be the sequence in which each $a_i$ occurs $t_i$ times, and
let $h = t_1 + \dots + t_k$. Let $\alpha, \beta$ be natural numbers with
$1 \le \alpha \le h - 2$, $\beta \le h - 2$ and $\alpha + \beta \le h - 1$, put
$\bar r = (h - \alpha - \beta, t_1, \dots, t_k)$, and write $E$ for the equality
$|\Sigma^\beta_\alpha(\mathcal{A})| = L(\bar r, h - \beta)$, where $L$ is the Yang–Chen bound.
For an integer $e$ and a set $X$ write $e \cdot X = \{e x : x \in X\}$. Then:
(a) if $k = 2$ and $t_1 = 1$, then $E$ holds; if $k = 2$ and $t_1 \ge 2$, then $E$ holds if and
only if $A = e \cdot \{1, 2\}$ for some integer $e > 0$;
(b) if $k = 3$ and $t_1 = t_2 = 1$, then $E$ holds if and only if $A = \{x, y, x + y\}$ for some
integers $0 < x < y$; if $k = 3$ and $t_1 \ge 2$ or $t_2 \ge 2$, then $E$ holds if and only if
$A = e \cdot \{1, 2, 3\}$ for some integer $e > 0$;
(c) if $k \ge 4$, then $E$ holds if and only if $A = e \cdot \{1, 2, \dots, k\}$ for some integer
$e > 0$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 17.

articles.title: An example of bounded subsequence sums
articles.statement:
For the sequence of integers
$\mathcal{A} = (-2, 7, 7)$, in which $-2$ occurs once and $7$ twice,
$\Sigma^1_1(\mathcal{A}) = \{-2, 5, 7, 14\}$: the sums of the subsequences with at least one and
at most two terms are $-2$, $7$, $-2 + 7 = 5$ and $7 + 7 = 14$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Section 4 (definition of `Σ^β_α(𝒜)`).

articles.title: Subsequence sums with a bounded number of terms
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $\alpha, \beta$ and a
finite sequence $\mathcal{A}$ (a multiset) in an additive commutative monoid $G$,
$\Sigma^\beta_\alpha(\mathcal{A})$ is the finite set of the sums $\sigma(\mathcal{B})$ of the
terms of the subsequences $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathcal{A}$ (sub-multisets) with
$\alpha \le |\mathcal{B}|$ and $|\mathcal{B}| + \beta \le |\mathcal{A}|$, that is, with at least
$\alpha$ and at most $|\mathcal{A}| - \beta$ terms; it is empty when $\beta > |\mathcal{A}|$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Section 4 (definition of `Σ^β_α(𝒜)`).

articles.title: Bounded subset sums as a generalized h-fold sumset when zero is in the set
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an
abelian group, let $m$ be a natural number, let $a_1, \dots, a_m$ be distinct nonzero elements
of $G$, put $a_0 = 0$ and $k = m + 1$, and let $A = \{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_m\}$, a set of $k$
elements. If $\alpha, \beta$ are natural numbers with $\alpha \ge 1$, $\beta \le k - 1$ and
$\alpha + \beta \le k$, then $\Sigma^\beta_\alpha(A)$, the set of sums of subsets $B \subseteq A$
with $\alpha \le |B| \le k - \beta$, equals the generalized $(k - \beta)$-fold sumset
$(k - \beta)^{(\bar r)} A$ of $A$ listed as $(a_0, a_1, \dots, a_m)$, with
$\bar r = (k - \alpha - \beta + 1, 1, \dots, 1)$, that is, the set of sums
$\sum_{j=0}^{m} s_j a_j$ with $0 \le s_j \le r_j$ for all $j$ and $\sum_j s_j = k - \beta$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Bounded subset sums as a generalized h-fold sumset when zero is not in the set
articles.statement:
Let $G$
be an abelian group and let $A = \{a_1, \dots, a_k\}$ be a set of $k$ distinct nonzero elements
of $G$. If $\alpha, \beta$ are natural numbers with $\alpha + \beta \le k - 1$, then
$\Sigma^\beta_\alpha(A)$, the set of sums of subsets $B \subseteq A$ with
$\alpha \le |B| \le k - \beta$, equals the generalized $(k - \beta)$-fold sumset
$(k - \beta)^{(\bar r)} A_0$ of $A_0 = (a_0, a_1, \dots, a_k)$, where $a_0 = 0$, with
$\bar r = (k - \alpha - \beta, 1, \dots, 1)$, that is, the set of sums $\sum_{j=0}^{k} s_j a_j$
with $0 \le s_j \le r_j$ for all $j$ and $\sum_j s_j = k - \beta$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Inverse theorem for subset sums of a mixed-sign set containing zero
articles.statement:
Let $n, p, \alpha,
\beta$ be natural numbers with $1 \le n \le p$, put $k = n + p + 1$, and assume
$1 \le \alpha \le k - 2$, $\beta \le k - 2$ and $\alpha + \beta \le k - 1$. Let $A$ be a finite set
of integers that contains $0$, exactly $n$ negative integers and exactly $p$ positive integers.
Then $|\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(A)| = L_0(\alpha, \beta, A)$ if and only if
$A = d \cdot \{-n, -n + 1, \dots, p\}$ for some integer $d > 0$. Here $\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(A)$
is the set of sums of subsets $B \subseteq A$ with $\alpha \le |B| \le |A| - \beta$, and
$L_0(\alpha, \beta, A)$ is the mixed-sign bound with zero, which depends only on $n$, $p$,
$\alpha$ and $\beta$.

The factor $d$ is then the least positive element of $A$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 11.

articles.title: Inverse theorem for subset sums of a mixed-sign set
articles.statement:
Let $n, p, \alpha, \beta$ be natural
numbers with $1 \le n \le p$, put $k = n + p$, and assume $1 \le \alpha \le k - 2$,
$\beta \le k - 2$ and $\alpha + \beta \le k - 1$. Let $A$ be a finite set of integers that does
not contain $0$ and has exactly $n$ negative and exactly $p$ positive elements, and write $E$ for
the equation $|\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(A)| = L(\alpha, \beta, A)$. If $k = 3$, $\alpha = 1$ and
$\beta = 0$, then $E$ holds if and only if $A = d \cdot \{-1, 1, 2\}$ for some integer $d > 0$.
If $k = 3$ and $\alpha = \beta = 1$, then $E$ holds if and only if $A = \{x, x + y, y\}$ for some
integers $x, y$ with $x < 0 < x + y < y$. If $k \ge 4$, then $E$ holds if and only if
$A = d \cdot \{-n, \dots, -1, 1, \dots, p\}$ for some integer $d > 0$. Here
$\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(A)$ is the set of sums of subsets $B \subseteq A$ with
$\alpha \le |B| \le |A| - \beta$, and $L(\alpha, \beta, A)$ is the mixed-sign bound, which
depends only on $n$, $p$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

The factor $d$ is then the least positive element of $A$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 10.

articles.title: Inverse theorem for subset sums of nonnegative sets
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 3$ and let $\alpha, \beta$
be natural numbers with $1 \le \alpha \le k - 2$, $\beta \le k - 2$ and $\alpha + \beta \le k - 1$.
Let $A$ be a set of $k$ integers, and let $\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(A)$ be the set of sums of
subsets $B \subseteq A$ with $\alpha \le |B| \le k - \beta$. If all elements of $A$ are positive
and $|\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(A)| = \binom{k+1}{2} - \binom{\alpha+1}{2} - \binom{\beta+1}{2} + 1$,
then $A = d \cdot \{1, 2, \dots, k\}$ for some integer $d > 0$ when $k \ne 3$, and
$A = \{x, y, x + y\}$ for some integers $0 < x < y$ when $k = 3$. If all elements of $A$ are
nonnegative, $0 \in A$ and
$|\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(A)| = \binom{k}{2} - \binom{\alpha}{2} - \binom{\beta}{2} + 1$, then
$A = d \cdot \{0, 1, \dots, k - 1\}$ for some integer $d > 0$ when $k \ge 5$,
$A = \{0, x, y\}$ for some integers $0 < x < y$ when $k = 3$, and
$A = \{0, x, y, x + y\}$ for some integers $0 < x < y$ when $k = 4$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 9.

articles.title: Bounded subset sums of $\{-1, 1, 2\}$
articles.statement:
The set $\Sigma^{1}_{1}(\{-1, 1, 2\})$ of sums of
subsets of the integer set $\{-1, 1, 2\}$ with at least $1$ and at most $2$ elements is
$\{-1, 0, 1, 2, 3\}$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Section 1 (definition of `Σ^β_α(A)`).

articles.title: Subset sums with a bounded number of terms
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $\alpha, \beta$ and a
finite subset $A$ of an additive commutative monoid $G$, the set $\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(A)$ is
the union of the restricted sumsets $m^{\wedge} A$ over $\alpha \le m \le |A| - \beta$, that is,
the set of sums $\sum_{b \in B} b$ over subsets $B \subseteq A$ with
$\alpha \le |B| \le |A| - \beta$. Here $|A| - \beta$ is read as $0$ when $\beta > |A|$.

The source assumes $\alpha + \beta \le |A|$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Section 1 (definition of `Σ^β_α(A)`).

articles.title: Lower bound for bounded subsequence sums of a mixed-sign sequence containing zero
articles.statement:
Let
$1 \le n \le p$, let $t_0, \dots, t_{n-1}$, $t_n$ and $t_{n+1}, \dots, t_{n+p}$ be positive
integers, let $h = t_0 + t_1 + \dots + t_{n+p}$, and let $\alpha, \beta$ be natural numbers with
$1 \le \alpha$ and $\alpha + \beta \le h - 1$. Put
$\bar r = (t_0, \dots, t_{n-1}, h - \alpha - \beta + t_n, t_{n+1}, \dots, t_{n+p})$. For integers
$c_0 < \dots < c_{n-1} < 0 < d_1 < \dots < d_p$, let $\mathcal{A}$ be the sequence in which
$c_i$ occurs $t_i$ times, $0$ occurs $t_n$ times and $d_j$ occurs $t_{n+j}$ times. Then
$|\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{A})| \ge L(\bar r, h - \beta)$ for all such $c$ and $d$, and
equality holds for some such $c$ and $d$. Here $\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{A})$ is the set
of sums of subsequences of $\mathcal{A}$ with at least $\alpha$ and at most $h - \beta$ terms, and
$L$ is the Yang–Chen bound.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 16.

articles.title: Lower bound for bounded subsequence sums of a mixed-sign sequence
articles.statement:
Let $1 \le n \le p$, let
$t_0, \dots, t_{n-1}$ and $t_{n+1}, \dots, t_{n+p}$ be positive integers, let $h$ be their sum,
and let $\alpha, \beta$ be natural numbers with $1 \le \alpha$ and $\alpha + \beta \le h - 1$.
Put $\bar r = (t_0, \dots, t_{n-1}, h - \alpha - \beta, t_{n+1}, \dots, t_{n+p})$. For integers
$c_0 < \dots < c_{n-1} < 0 < d_1 < \dots < d_p$, let $\mathcal{A}$ be the sequence in which
$c_i$ occurs $t_i$ times and $d_j$ occurs $t_{n+j}$ times. Then
$|\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{A})| \ge L(\bar r, h - \beta)$ for all such $c$ and $d$, and
equality holds for some such $c$ and $d$. Here $\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{A})$ is the set
of sums of subsequences of $\mathcal{A}$ with at least $\alpha$ and at most $h - \beta$ terms, and
$L$ is the Yang–Chen bound.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 15.

articles.title: Lower bound for bounded subsequence sums of a nonnegative sequence containing zero
articles.statement:
Let
$m \ge 1$, let $t_0, \dots, t_m$ be positive integers, let $h = t_0 + \dots + t_m$, and let
$\alpha, \beta$ be natural numbers with $1 \le \alpha$, $\beta \le h - 1$ and
$\alpha + \beta \le h$. Put $\bar r = (h - \alpha - \beta + t_0, t_1, \dots, t_m)$. For integers
$0 < b_1 < \dots < b_m$, let $\mathcal{A}$ be the sequence in which $0$ occurs $t_0$ times and
$b_i$ occurs $t_i$ times. Then $|\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{A})| \ge L(\bar r, h - \beta)$
for all such $b$, and equality holds for some such $b$. Here $\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{A})$
is the set of sums of subsequences of $\mathcal{A}$ with at least $\alpha$ and at most $h - \beta$
terms, and $L$ is the Yang–Chen bound.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 14.

articles.title: Lower bound for bounded subsequence sums of a positive sequence
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$, let
$t_1, \dots, t_k$ be positive integers, let $h = t_1 + \dots + t_k$, and let $\alpha, \beta$ be
natural numbers with $1 \le \alpha$ and $\alpha + \beta \le h - 1$. Put
$\bar r = (h - \alpha - \beta, t_1, \dots, t_k)$. For integers $0 < b_1 < \dots < b_k$, let
$\mathcal{A}$ be the sequence in which $b_i$ occurs $t_i$ times. Then
$|\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{A})| \ge L(\bar r, h - \beta)$ for all such $b$, and equality
holds for some such $b$. Here $\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{A})$ is the set of sums of
subsequences of $\mathcal{A}$ with at least $\alpha$ and at most $h - \beta$ terms, and $L$ is the
Yang–Chen bound.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 13.

articles.title: Lower bound for subset sums of a mixed-sign set containing zero
articles.statement:
Let $n, p, \alpha, \beta$
be natural numbers with $1 \le n \le p$, $1 \le \alpha$ and $\alpha + \beta \le n + p$. Every
finite set $A$ of integers that contains $0$, exactly $n$ negative integers and exactly $p$
positive integers satisfies $|\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(A)| \ge L_0(\alpha, \beta, A)$, and some
such set $A$ attains equality. Here $\Sigma^{\beta}_{\alpha}(A)$ is the set of sums of subsets
$B \subseteq A$ with $\alpha \le |B| \le |A| - \beta$, and $L_0(\alpha, \beta, A)$ is the
mixed-sign bound with zero, which depends only on $n$, $p$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 8.

articles.title: Lower bound for bounded subset sums of a mixed-sign set
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $p$, $\alpha$, $\beta$ be
natural numbers with $1 \le n \le p$, $1 \le \alpha$ and $\alpha + \beta + 1 \le n + p$, and let
$L_{n,p}(\alpha, \beta)$ be the mixed-sign subset-sum bound. For a finite set $A$ of integers write
$\Sigma_\alpha^\beta(A)$ for the set of sums of subsets $B \subseteq A$ with
$\alpha \le |B| \le |A| - \beta$. Every finite set $A$ of nonzero integers with exactly $n$
negative and exactly $p$ positive elements satisfies
$|\Sigma_\alpha^\beta(A)| \ge L_{n,p}(\alpha, \beta)$, and some such set $A$ attains equality.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Sharp lower bounds for bounded subset sums of nonnegative sets
articles.statement:
Let $k$, $\alpha$, $\beta$
be natural numbers with $k \ge 2$, $\alpha \ge 1$ and $\alpha + \beta + 1 \le k$. For a finite set
$A$ of integers write $\Sigma_\alpha^\beta(A)$ for the set of sums of subsets $B \subseteq A$ with
$\alpha \le |B| \le |A| - \beta$. Every set $A$ of $k$ positive integers satisfies
$|\Sigma_\alpha^\beta(A)| \ge \binom{k+1}{2} - \binom{\alpha+1}{2} - \binom{\beta+1}{2} + 1$,
and every set $A$ of $k$ nonnegative integers containing $0$ satisfies
$|\Sigma_\alpha^\beta(A)| \ge \binom{k}{2} - \binom{\alpha}{2} - \binom{\beta}{2} + 1$. Both
bounds are attained: the first by $A = \{1, 2, \dots, k\}$ and the second by
$A = \{0, 1, \dots, k - 1\}$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Length of a sequence with repetitions
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a set, $a_0, \dots, a_{k-1} \in G$ (not
necessarily distinct), $t_0, \dots, t_{k-1}$ natural numbers, $A = (a_0, \dots, a_{k-1})$ and
$\bar t = (t_0, \dots, t_{k-1})$. The multiset $(A, \bar t)$, made of $t_i$ copies of $a_i$ for
each $i$, has $t_0 + \dots + t_{k-1}$ elements counted with multiplicity.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Section 4 (notation `(A, t̄)` for a finite sequence).

articles.title: Reordering invariance of the generalized $h$-fold sumset
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an additive
commutative monoid, $a_0, \dots, a_{k-1} \in G$, $r_0, \dots, r_{k-1}$ and $h$ natural numbers,
and write $h^{(\bar r)}A = \{\sum_j s_j a_j : 0 \le s_j \le r_j, \sum_j s_j = h\}$ for the
generalized $h$-fold sumset of $A = (a_0, \dots, a_{k-1})$ with $\bar r = (r_0, \dots, r_{k-1})$.
For every permutation $\pi$ of $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, the generalized $h$-fold sumset of
$(a_{\pi(0)}, \dots, a_{\pi(k-1)})$ with $(r_{\pi(0)}, \dots, r_{\pi(k-1)})$ equals
$h^{(\bar r)}A$.

The paper assumes $h \ge 2$, all $r_j$ positive and the $a_j$ distinct; none of this is assumed
here.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Lemma 3.

articles.title: A generalized $2$-fold sumset of $\{0, 1, 2\}$
articles.statement:
For $A = (0, 1, 2)$ in the integers and
$\bar r = (1, 1, 1)$, the generalized $2$-fold sumset $2^{(\bar r)}A$, the set of sums
$s_0 \cdot 0 + s_1 \cdot 1 + s_2 \cdot 2$ with $s_0, s_1, s_2 \in \{0, 1\}$ and
$s_0 + s_1 + s_2 = 2$, equals $\{1, 2, 3\}$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Section 1 (definition of `h^{(r̄)}A`).

articles.title: Generalized $h$-fold sumset
articles.statement:
For elements $a_0, \dots, a_{k-1}$ of an additive commutative
monoid $G$ (not necessarily distinct), natural numbers $\bar r = (r_0, \dots, r_{k-1})$ and a
natural number $h$, the generalized $h$-fold sumset of $A = (a_0, \dots, a_{k-1})$ is the finite
set $h^{(\bar r)}A = \{\sum_j s_j a_j : s_j \in \mathbb{N}, s_j \le r_j, \sum_j s_j = h\}$, where
$s_j a_j$ is the sum of $s_j$ copies of $a_j$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Section 1 (definition of `h^{(r̄)}A`).

articles.title: A value of the mixed-sign subset-sum bound
articles.statement:
For $n = 1$, $p = 2$ and $\alpha = \beta = 1$,
the mixed-sign subset-sum bound is $L_{1,2}(1, 1) = 5$; this value comes from its second case.

It is attained by $A = \{-1, 1, 2\}$: the sums of subsets of $A$ with one or two elements form
$\{-1, 0, 1, 2, 3\}$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 7 (definition of `L(α, β, A)`).

articles.title: Mixed-sign subset-sum bound
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$, $p$, $\alpha$, $\beta$ (the numbers
of negative and positive elements of a set $A$, and the bounds on subset sizes), let
$\kappa = n + p - \beta$, computed in the integers, $T(x) = x(x+1)/2$ and
$S = T(p) + T(n) + 1$. The integer $L_{n,p}(\alpha, \beta)$, written $L(\alpha, \beta, A)$ in
the source, is $S - T(\beta - n) - T(\beta - p)$ if $1 \le \alpha < \kappa < n \le p$;
$S - T(\beta - n)$ if $1 \le \alpha < n \le \kappa < p$ or $1 \le \alpha = n < \kappa \le p$;
$S$ if $1 \le \alpha < n \le p \le \kappa$, or $1 \le \alpha = n < p < \kappa$, or
$1 \le \alpha = n = p < \kappa$; $S - T(\beta - n) - T(\alpha - n)$ if
$1 \le n < \alpha < \kappa \le p$; $S - T(\alpha - n)$ if $1 \le n < \alpha < p < \kappa$ or
$1 \le n < \alpha = p < \kappa$; $S - T(\alpha - n) - T(\alpha - p)$ if
$1 \le n \le p < \alpha < \kappa$; and $0$ otherwise.

These six cases are mutually exclusive, and when $1 \le n \le p$, $1 \le \alpha$ and
$\alpha + \beta + 1 \le n + p$ exactly one of them applies.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 7 (definition of `L(α, β, A)`).

articles.title: A value of the mixed-sign subset-sum bound with zero
articles.statement:
For $n = p = 1$ and
$\alpha = \beta = 1$, the mixed-sign subset-sum bound with zero is $L^0_{1,1}(1, 1) = 3$; this
value comes from its third case.

It is attained by $A = \{-1, 0, 1\}$: the sums of subsets of $A$ with one or two elements form
$\{-1, 0, 1\}$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 8 (definition of `L₀(α, β, A)`).

articles.title: Mixed-sign subset-sum bound with zero
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$, $p$, $\alpha$, $\beta$
(the numbers of negative and positive elements of a set $A$ that also contains $0$, and the
bounds on subset sizes), let $\kappa = n + p + 1 - \beta$, computed in the integers,
$T(x) = x(x+1)/2$, $T_0(x) = x(x-1)/2$ and $S = T(p) + T(n) + 1$. The integer
$L^0_{n,p}(\alpha, \beta)$, written $L_0(\alpha, \beta, A)$ in the source, is
$S - T_0(\beta - n) - T_0(\beta - p)$ if $1 \le \alpha < \kappa < n \le p$;
$S - T_0(\beta - n)$ if $1 \le \alpha < n \le \kappa < p$ or $1 \le \alpha = n < \kappa \le p$;
$S$ if $1 \le \alpha < n \le p \le \kappa$, or $1 \le \alpha = n < p < \kappa$, or
$1 \le \alpha = n = p < \kappa$; $S - T_0(\beta - n) - T_0(\alpha - n)$ if
$1 \le n < \alpha < \kappa \le p$; $S - T_0(\alpha - n)$ if $1 \le n < \alpha < p < \kappa$ or
$1 \le n < \alpha = p < \kappa$; $S - T_0(\alpha - n) - T_0(\alpha - p)$ if
$1 \le n \le p < \alpha < \kappa$; and $0$ otherwise.

These six cases are mutually exclusive, and when $1 \le n \le p$, $1 \le \alpha$ and
$\alpha + \beta + 1 \le n + p + 1$ exactly one of them applies.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 8 (definition of `L₀(α, β, A)`).

articles.title: Sequence with prescribed multiplicities
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a type, $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
$A = (a_0, \dots, a_{k-1})$ a $k$-tuple of elements of $G$ and $\bar t = (t_0, \dots, t_{k-1})$ a
$k$-tuple of natural numbers. The sequence $(A, \bar t)$ is the finite multiset of elements of $G$
obtained by taking $t_i$ copies of $a_i$ for each $i < k$; an element $x \in G$ thus occurs
$\sum_{i : a_i = x} t_i$ times.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Section 4 (notation `(A, t̄)` for a finite sequence).

articles.title: Yang–Chen bound at $(1, 1, 1)$ and $h = 2$
articles.statement:
The Yang–Chen bound $L(\bar r, h)$ for
$\bar r = (1, 1, 1)$ and $h = 2$ equals $3$.

Here $\mu = 2$, $\eta = 0$ and $\delta = \theta = 0$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Section 1.1 (definition of `L(r̄, h)`).

articles.title: Yang–Chen bound at $(1, 1, 2)$ and $h = 2$
articles.statement:
The Yang–Chen bound $L(\bar r, h)$ for
$\bar r = (1, 1, 2)$ and $h = 2$ equals $4$.

Here $\mu = 2$, $\eta = 1$ and $\delta = \theta = 0$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Section 1.1 (definition of `L(r̄, h)`).

articles.title: The Yang–Chen bound
articles.statement:
Let $k, h \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\bar r = (r_0, \dots, r_{k-1})$ with
all $r_j \in \mathbb{N}$; all sums below run over indices $j \in \{0, \dots, k-1\}$. Let $\mu$ be
the largest $m \in \{0, \dots, k\}$ with $\sum_{j < m} r_j \le h$, let $\eta$ be the integer such
that $\eta + 1$ is the least $m \in \{0, \dots, k\}$ with $\sum_{j \ge m} r_j \le h$ (so
$\eta = -1$ when $h \ge \sum_j r_j$), and set $\delta = h - \sum_{j < \mu} r_j$ and
$\theta = h - \sum_{j > \eta} r_j$. The Yang–Chen bound is the integer

$$L(\bar r, h) = \sum_{j > \eta} j r_j - \sum_{j < \mu} j r_j + \theta \eta - \delta \mu + 1.$$

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Section 1.1 (definitions of `μ`, `η`, `δ`, `θ` and `L(r̄, h)`).

articles.title: Yang–Chen inverse theorem for at least five terms
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 5$ and $h \ge 2$ be integers,
let $\bar r = (r_0, \dots, r_{k-1})$ be positive integers with $h \le r_0 + \dots + r_{k-1} - 2$,
and let $L(\bar r, h)$ be the Yang–Chen bound. For all integers $a_0 < a_1 < \dots < a_{k-1}$,
with $A = \{a_0, \dots, a_{k-1}\}$, the generalized $h$-fold sumset $h^{(\bar r)}A$ has exactly
$L(\bar r, h)$ elements if and only if $A$ is an arithmetic progression of length $k$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 3 (Yang and Chen).

articles.title: Yang–Chen inverse theorem for three terms
articles.statement:
Let $a_0 < a_1 < a_2$ be integers,
$A = \{a_0, a_1, a_2\}$, $\bar r = (r_0, r_1, r_2)$ positive integers and $h \ge 2$ an integer
with $h \le r_0 + r_1 + r_2 - 2$, and let $L(\bar r, h)$ be the Yang–Chen bound. If $r_1 = 1$,
then the generalized $h$-fold sumset $h^{(\bar r)}A$ has exactly $L(\bar r, h)$ elements. If
$r_1 \ge 2$, then $h^{(\bar r)}A$ has exactly $L(\bar r, h)$ elements if and only if $A$ is an
arithmetic progression of length $3$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 4 (Yang and Chen).

articles.title: Yang–Chen inverse theorem for four terms
articles.statement:
Let $a_0 < a_1 < a_2 < a_3$ be integers,
$A = \{a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3\}$, $\bar r = (r_0, r_1, r_2, r_3)$ positive integers and $h \ge 2$ an
integer with $h \le r_0 + r_1 + r_2 + r_3 - 2$, and let $L(\bar r, h)$ be the Yang–Chen bound.
If $r_1 = r_2 = 1$, then the generalized $h$-fold sumset $h^{(\bar r)}A$ has exactly
$L(\bar r, h)$ elements if and only if $a_1 - a_0 = a_3 - a_2$. If $r_1 \ge 2$ or $r_2 \ge 2$,
then $h^{(\bar r)}A$ has exactly $L(\bar r, h)$ elements if and only if $A$ is an arithmetic
progression of length $4$.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 5 (Yang and Chen).

articles.title: Yang–Chen lower bound for generalized $h$-fold sumsets
articles.statement:
Let $k, h \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$\bar r = (r_0, \dots, r_{k-1})$ be positive integers with $2 \le h \le r_0 + \dots + r_{k-1}$, and
let $L(\bar r, h)$ be the Yang–Chen bound. For all integers $a_0 < a_1 < \dots < a_{k-1}$, the
generalized $h$-fold sumset $h^{(\bar r)}A$ of $A = (a_0, \dots, a_{k-1})$ has at least
$L(\bar r, h)$ elements; and there exist integers $a_0 < a_1 < \dots < a_{k-1}$ for which
$h^{(\bar r)}A$ has exactly $L(\bar r, h)$ elements.

## Sources

- Raj Kumar Mistri, *Subset and Subsequence Sums with Bounded Numbers of Terms*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A116, Theorem 2 (Yang and Chen).

articles.title: Consecutive weighted zero-sum subsequences
articles.statement:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ and let
$S = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$ be a sequence in $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Then $S$ has an $A$-weighted
zero-sum consecutive subsequence if there are indices $1 \le l \le h \le k$ and weights
$a_l, \dots, a_h \in A$ with $\sum_{i=l}^{h} a_i x_i = 0$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Introduction.

articles.title: Weighted zero-sum subsequences
articles.statement:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ and let
$S = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$ be a sequence in $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Then $S$ has an $A$-weighted
zero-sum subsequence if there are a nonempty set $J \subseteq \{1, \dots, k\}$ of indices and
weights $a_i \in A$ for $i \in J$ with $\sum_{i \in J} a_i x_i = 0$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Introduction.

articles.title: Weighted zero-sum sequences
articles.statement:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ and let
$S = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$ be a sequence in $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Then $S$ is an $A$-weighted
zero-sum sequence if there are weights $a_1, \dots, a_k \in A$ with
$a_1 x_1 + a_2 x_2 + \dots + a_k x_k = 0$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Introduction.

articles.title: Weighted zero-sum free sequences
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an additive commutative monoid and $A$ a
finite set of natural numbers. A finite sequence $s = (s_1, \dots, s_n)$ over $G$ is
$A$-weighted zero-sum free when, for every non-empty set $I \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ of
positions and every choice of weights $a_i \in A$ for $i \in I$, the weighted sum
$\sum_{i \in I} a_i s_i$ is non-zero, where $a_i s_i$ is the sum of $a_i$ copies of $s_i$.
Terms are indexed by position, so repeated terms count separately.

## Sources

- Md Ibrahim Molla, *New Families of Weight Sets Yielding Prescribed Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A89, Section 2 (weighted zero-sum subsequences, as used in Lemmas 2 and 3).

articles.title: Lower bound for the weighted Davenport constant
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an additive commutative
monoid, $A$ a finite set of natural numbers and $D_A(G)$ the $A$-weighted Davenport constant
of $G$. If a sequence over $G$ of length $L$ is $A$-weighted zero-sum free, then $L < D_A(G)$.

## Sources

- Md Ibrahim Molla, *New Families of Weight Sets Yielding Prescribed Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A89, Section 2 (definition of `D_A(G)`).

articles.title: Membership in the weight representatives
articles.statement:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.
A natural number $a$ lies in the set of weight representatives of $A$ if and only if $a < n$ and
the residue of $a$ modulo $n$ lies in $A$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Introduction.

articles.title: Weighted zero-sum subsequences are monotone in the weight set
articles.statement:
Let
$A \subseteq B \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ and let $S$ be a finite sequence in
$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. If $S$ has an $A$-weighted zero-sum subsequence, then $S$ has a
$B$-weighted zero-sum subsequence.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Introduction.

articles.title: Nonzero squares modulo $n$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $S(n)$ is the set of elements $x$
of $\mathbb{Z}_n = \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ with $x \neq 0$ and $x = y^2$ for some
$y \in \mathbb{Z}_n$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Introduction.

articles.title: Prefixes of weighted zero-sum free sequences
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an additive commutative monoid
and $A$ a finite set of natural numbers. If a sequence $s$ over $G$ is $A$-weighted zero-sum
free, then for every $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ the prefix of $s$ formed by its first $\ell$ terms
(all of $s$ when $\ell$ is at least its length) is $A$-weighted zero-sum free.

## Sources

- Md Ibrahim Molla, *New Families of Weight Sets Yielding Prescribed Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A89, Section 2 (definition of `D_A(G)`).

articles.title: Units modulo n
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $U(n)$ is the set of units of the ring
$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ of integers modulo $n$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Introduction.

articles.title: Squares of units modulo n
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $U(n)^2$ is the set of elements of
$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ of the form $u^2$ with $u$ a unit of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Introduction.

articles.title: Weighted consecutive zero-sum constant
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and $A$ a subset of
$\mathbb{Z}_n = \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. The $A$-weighted consecutive constant $C_A$ of
$\mathbb{Z}_n$ is the least positive integer $k$ such that every sequence $(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ of
elements of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ has a nonempty block of consecutive terms $x_i, \dots, x_j$ with
weights $a_i, \dots, a_j \in A$ such that $a_i x_i + \dots + a_j x_j = 0$; it is $0$ when no
such $k$ exists.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Introduction.

articles.title: Lengths forcing a consecutive weighted zero sum
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and $A$ a
subset of $\mathbb{Z}_n = \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. This is the set of positive integers $k$ such
that every sequence $(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ of elements of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ has a nonempty block of
consecutive terms $x_i, \dots, x_j$ with weights $a_i, \dots, a_j \in A$ such that
$a_i x_i + \dots + a_j x_j = 0$. Its least element, or $0$ when it is empty, is the $A$-weighted
consecutive constant $C_A$ of $\mathbb{Z}_n$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Introduction.

articles.title: The weighted Davenport constant as a least length
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an additive commutative
monoid, $A$ a finite set of natural numbers and $D_A(G)$ the $A$-weighted Davenport constant
of $G$. If there is a length $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ such that no sequence over $G$ of length
$\ell$ is $A$-weighted zero-sum free, then $D_A(G)$ is finite and equals the least such length.

## Sources

- Md Ibrahim Molla, *New Families of Weight Sets Yielding Prescribed Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A89, Section 2 (definition of `D_A(G)`).

articles.title: When the weighted Davenport constant is infinite
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an additive commutative
monoid, $A$ a finite set of natural numbers and $D_A(G)$ the $A$-weighted Davenport constant
of $G$. Then $D_A(G) = \infty$ if and only if for every $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ there is an
$A$-weighted zero-sum free sequence over $G$ of length $\ell$.

## Sources

- Md Ibrahim Molla, *New Families of Weight Sets Yielding Prescribed Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A89, Section 2 (definition of `D_A(G)`).

articles.title: Upper bound for the weighted Davenport constant
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an additive commutative
monoid, $A$ a finite set of natural numbers, $D_A(G)$ the $A$-weighted Davenport constant of
$G$ and $\ell$ a natural number. If no sequence over $G$ of length $\ell$ is $A$-weighted
zero-sum free, that is, every sequence over $G$ of length $\ell$ has a non-empty $A$-weighted
zero-sum subsequence, then $D_A(G) \le \ell$.

## Sources

- Md Ibrahim Molla, *New Families of Weight Sets Yielding Prescribed Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A89, Section 2 (definition of `D_A(G)`).

articles.title: Davenport constant of the group of order two
articles.statement:
The ordinary Davenport constant of
$\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, that is, its $\{1\}$-weighted Davenport constant, is
$D_{\{1\}}(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}) = 2$.

## Sources

- Md Ibrahim Molla, *New Families of Weight Sets Yielding Prescribed Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A89, Section 2 (characteristic value of `D_A`).

articles.title: Weighted Davenport constant of the trivial group
articles.statement:
For every non-empty finite set $A$ of
natural numbers, the $A$-weighted Davenport constant of the trivial group $\mathbb{Z}/1\mathbb{Z}$
is $D_A(\mathbb{Z}/1\mathbb{Z}) = 1$.

## Sources

- Md Ibrahim Molla, *New Families of Weight Sets Yielding Prescribed Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A89, Section 2 (characteristic value of `D_A`).

articles.title: Weighted Davenport constant
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an additive commutative monoid and $A$ a finite
set of natural numbers. The $A$-weighted Davenport constant $D_A(G) \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$
is the least length $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ such that no sequence over $G$ of length $\ell$ is
$A$-weighted zero-sum free, that is, such that every sequence over $G$ of length $\ell$ has a
non-empty $A$-weighted zero-sum subsequence; it is $\infty$ when no such length exists.

For example $D_A(G) = \infty$ when $A = \emptyset$, or when $A = \{1\}$ and $G = \mathbb{Z}$. For
a finite group $G$ and a non-empty weight set $A$ it is finite. The ordinary Davenport constant of
$G$ is $D_{\{1\}}(G)$.

## Sources

- Md Ibrahim Molla, *New Families of Weight Sets Yielding Prescribed Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A89, Section 2 (definition of `D_A(G)`).

articles.title: Representatives of a set of residues
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and $A$ a subset of
$\mathbb{Z}_n$. The representatives of $A$ form the finite set of natural numbers $a$ with
$0 \le a < n$ whose residue modulo $n$ lies in $A$.

A natural number $a$ acts on $\mathbb{Z}_n$ by $x \mapsto a x$. For $n \ge 1$ every residue has
exactly one representative below $n$, so the weighted Davenport constant of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ with
the representatives of $A$ as weights is the paper's $D_A$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Introduction.

articles.title: Two units without square-weighted zero sums modulo any prime divisor
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 2$ be
odd, and write $S(m)$ for the set of nonzero squares in $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$. Then there are
units $u, v$ of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ such that for every prime $p$ dividing $n$, the sequence
$(u \bmod p, v \bmod p)$ in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ has no $S(p)$-weighted zero-sum subsequence.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Proposition 17.

articles.title: Scaled unit squares modulo a prime power
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and $r, k$ natural numbers
with $k = 0$ or $2k < r$, and write $U(m)^2$ for the set of squares of units of
$\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$. Then the set $p^{2k} U(p^r)^2 = \{p^{2k} x : x \in U(p^r)^2\}$ in
$\mathbb{Z}/p^r\mathbb{Z}$ has the same number of elements as $U(p^{r-2k})^2$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Number of nonzero squares modulo a prime power
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and $r \ge 1$, and write
$S(m)$ for the set of nonzero squares and $U(m)^2$ for the set of squares of units in
$\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$. If $r$ is even, then
$|S(p^r)| = \sum_{k=0}^{r/2-1} |U(p^{r-2k})^2|$, and if $r$ is odd, then
$|S(p^r)| = \sum_{k=0}^{(r-1)/2} |U(p^{r-2k})^2|$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Three-term sequences without square-weighted zero-sum subsequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and
$r$ a nonzero even natural number, and write $S(m)$ for the set of nonzero squares in
$\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$. Let $z_1, z_2$ be units of $\mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z}$ whose reduction
$(z_1 \bmod p, z_2 \bmod p)$ is not an $S(p)$-weighted zero-sum sequence. Let $T = (x_1, x_2, y_1)$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{Z}/p^r\mathbb{Z}$ whose reduction modulo $p^2$ is $(z_1, z_2, p)$. Then
$T$ has no $S(p^r)$-weighted zero-sum subsequence.

The paper states the lemma for sequences of units modulo $p^r$, which no $y_1$ reducing to the
nonunit $p$ can be; following the paper's proof and its application in Theorem 12, the sequence is
taken in $\mathbb{Z}/p^r\mathbb{Z}$. Then $x_1, x_2$ are automatically units, since $z_1, z_2$ are.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Lemma 11.

articles.title: Square-weighted zero-sum free unit pairs lift to odd prime powers
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd
prime, let $r \ge 1$, and let $x_1, x_2$ be units of $\mathbb{Z}_{p^r}$. Write $S(m)$ for the set
of nonzero squares in $\mathbb{Z}_m$, and say that a sequence $(y_i)$ in $\mathbb{Z}_m$ has an
$A$-weighted zero-sum subsequence when there are a non-empty set $J$ of indices and weights
$a_j \in A$ for $j \in J$ with $\sum_{j \in J} a_j y_j = 0$. If the reduction
$(\bar x_1, \bar x_2)$ of $(x_1, x_2)$ modulo $p$ has no $S(p)$-weighted zero-sum subsequence,
then $(x_1, x_2)$ has no $S(p^r)$-weighted zero-sum subsequence.

The paper states the hypothesis with $Q_p$, the set of nonzero quadratic residues modulo $p$,
which equals $S(p)$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Lemma 18.

articles.title: Square-weighted zero-sum free unit triples modulo even powers of two
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a nonzero
even natural number, and let $x_1, x_2, x_3$ be units of $\mathbb{Z}_{2^r}$ that are each
congruent to $1$ modulo $4$. Write $S(2^r)$ for the set of nonzero squares in $\mathbb{Z}_{2^r}$.
Then $(x_1, x_2, x_3)$ has no $S(2^r)$-weighted zero-sum subsequence: there are no non-empty set
$J$ of indices and weights $a_j \in S(2^r)$ for $j \in J$ with $\sum_{j \in J} a_j x_j = 0$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Lemma 10.

articles.title: Square-weighted constants of even squares
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 2$ be an even perfect square and let
$S(n)$ be the set of nonzero squares in $\mathbb{Z}_n$. Then the $S(n)$-weighted Davenport
constant of $\mathbb{Z}_n$, with weights the representatives in $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ of the
elements of $S(n)$, equals $4$. Moreover, some positive length $k$ forces every sequence of
length $k$ in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ to have a non-empty consecutive $S(n)$-weighted zero-sum
subsequence, and the least such length, the consecutive constant $C_{S(n)}$, equals $4$.

Since the infimum of the empty set of natural numbers is $0$, the existence clause makes the
equality $C_{S(n)} = 4$ nonvacuous.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Corollary 16.

articles.title: Square-weighted constants modulo $p^r$, for $p \ge 2$ and nonzero even $r$, are at most unit-square constants modulo $p^2$
articles.statement:
**Square-weighted constants modulo $p^r$, for $p \ge 2$ and nonzero even $r$, are at most
unit-square constants modulo $p^2$.** Let $p \ge 2$ be a natural number and let $r$ be a nonzero
even natural number. Write $S(p^r)$ for the set of nonzero squares in $\mathbb{Z}_{p^r}$ and
$U(p^2)^2$ for the set of squares of units in $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$. For a weight set
$A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_m$, write $D_A(\mathbb{Z}_m)$ for the $A$-weighted Davenport constant of
$\mathbb{Z}_m$, where $A$ acts through its representatives in $\{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ and the value
lies in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, and write $C_A$ for the least positive length $k$ such that
every sequence of length $k$ in $\mathbb{Z}_m$ has a non-empty consecutive $A$-weighted zero-sum
subsequence, or $0$ if there is no such length. Then
$D_{S(p^r)}(\mathbb{Z}_{p^r}) \le D_{U(p^2)^2}(\mathbb{Z}_{p^2})$ and
$C_{S(p^r)} \le C_{U(p^2)^2}$, the first constant in each inequality taken in $\mathbb{Z}_{p^r}$
and the second in $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$.

The paper says $p$ positive; $p = 1$ is excluded (the paper assumes throughout that the modulus is
at least $2$), since then $S(1)$ is empty, so $D_{S(1)}(\mathbb{Z}_1) = \infty$, while
$D_{U(1)^2}(\mathbb{Z}_1) = 1$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Corollary 14.

articles.title: Square-weighted constants of nonsquares with even $2$-adic valuation
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 2$ be a
natural number that is not a perfect square and whose $2$-adic valuation $v_2(n)$ is even
(possibly zero), and let $S(n)$ be the set of nonzero squares in $\mathbb{Z}_n$. Then the
$S(n)$-weighted Davenport constant of $\mathbb{Z}_n$, with weights the representatives in
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ of the elements of $S(n)$, equals $3$. Moreover, some positive length $k$
forces every sequence of length $k$ in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ to have a non-empty consecutive
$S(n)$-weighted zero-sum subsequence, and the least such length, the consecutive constant
$C_{S(n)}$, equals $3$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Corollary 22.

articles.title: Decomposition of the nonzero squares modulo a prime power
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, let
$r \ge 1$, and let $l = \lfloor (r - 1)/2 \rfloor$. Write $S(p^r)$ for the set of nonzero squares
in $\mathbb{Z}_{p^r}$, $U(p^r)^2$ for the set of squares of units in $\mathbb{Z}_{p^r}$, and
$p^{2k} U(p^r)^2 = \{p^{2k} x : x \in U(p^r)^2\}$. Then

$$S(p^r) = \bigcup_{k=0}^{l} p^{2k} U(p^r)^2,$$

and the sets $p^{2k} U(p^r)^2$ for $k = 0, \dots, l$ are pairwise disjoint.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Square-weighted zero sums lift from a prime-power component
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 2$, let $p$ be a
prime dividing $n$, and let $r$ be the exponent of $p$ in $n$. Write $S(m)$ for the set of
nonzero squares in $\mathbb{Z}_m$. Let $x_1, \dots, x_k$ be a sequence in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ whose
reduction $\bar x_1, \dots, \bar x_k$ modulo $p^r$ has an $S(p^r)$-weighted zero sum, that is,
there are $b_1, \dots, b_k \in S(p^r)$ with $\sum_i b_i \bar x_i = 0$. Then there are
$a_1, \dots, a_k \in S(n)$ with $\sum_i a_i x_i = 0$.

## Sources

- Krishnendu Paul and Shameek Paul, *Square-Weighted Zero-Sum Constants*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.6, Lemma 7.

articles.title: Square-weighted zero sums lift from $p$ to odd powers $p^r$
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 2$ be a natural
number and $r$ an odd natural number. Write $S(m)$ for the set of nonzero squares in
$\mathbb{Z}_m$. Let $x_1, \dots, x_k$ be a sequence in $\mathbb{Z}_{p^r}$ whose reduction
$\bar x_1, \dots, \bar x_k$ modulo $p$ has an $S(p)$-weighted zero sum, that is, there are
$b_1, \dots, b_k \in S(p)$ with $\sum_i b_i \bar x_i = 0$. Then there are
