A convex function on `[0, 1]` that is nonpositive at both endpoints is nonpositive on `[0, 1]`.
 See also `ConvexOn.le_max_of_mem_Icc`.

articles.title: Finite sum of convex functions is convex
articles.statement: A finite sum of convex functions is convex.

articles.title: Convexity of the damped total weight
articles.statement: The damped total weight `u ↦ ∑_S 4 |S| (1-u)^{|S|-1} f̂(S)²` is convex on `[0, 1]`.

articles.title: Small-influence case implies the full capped estimate on $(1/2, q)$
articles.statement: `cvg_smallDeltaResidue q` implies `mxd_martingaleHC_statement q`.

articles.title: Maximal influence of a Boolean function is at most one
articles.statement: The maximal influence of a Boolean function is at most `1`.

articles.title: Convexity of $(1 - u)^k$ on $(0, 1)$
articles.statement: `u ↦ (1 - u)^k` is convex on `[0, 1]`.

articles.title: Capped estimate when the maximal influence is at least $e^{-1}$
articles.statement: The capped estimate holds for all `u ∈ (0, 1)` when the maximal influence is at least `e^{-1}`.

articles.title: Capped estimate on $(0, 1)$ from concavity of the right side
articles.statement: If the right side of the capped estimate is concave in `u`, the estimate holds on `(0, 1)`.

articles.title: Small-influence case implies the open-interval case
articles.statement: `cvg_smallDeltaResidue q` implies `frh_openResidue q`.

articles.title: Concavity of $\exp(m u/(2-u))$ for $-1 \le m \le 0$
articles.statement: `u ↦ exp (m · u/(2-u))` is concave on `[0, 1]` for `-1 ≤ m ≤ 0`.

articles.title: Concavity of $\delta^{u/(2-u)} T$ for $e^{-1} \le \delta \le 1$
articles.statement: `u ↦ δ^{u/(2-u)} T` is concave on `[0, 1]` for `e^{-1} ≤ δ ≤ 1` and `T ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Small-influence residual case of the capped estimate
articles.statement:
The capped estimate for all `p ∈ (1/2, q)` with `p < 1`, all Boolean functions with maximal
 influence `δ < e^{-1}`, and all `u ∈ (0, 1)`.

articles.title: Low-range case condition fails for some $u$
articles.statement:
For `p > 1/2` and `0 < δ < 1`, the case condition in `hcq_lowRangeResidue` fails for some `u ∈
 (0, 1)`.

articles.title: Capped estimate in the hypercontractive range with matching $q'$
articles.statement: The capped estimate in the hypercontractive range, with the matching `q'`.

articles.title: Under the gap condition the hypercontractive bound is dominated
articles.statement:
If `δ^{gap} ≥ 4p(1-p)`, the bound with exponent `2/q' - 1` and factor `4p(1-p)` is at most
 `δ^{u/(2-u)}`.

articles.title: Gap condition holds at $u = 1$
articles.statement: At `u = 1` (`q' = 1`) the gap condition holds.

articles.title: Hypercontractive exponent is at most the target exponent
articles.statement: In the hypercontractive range the exponent `2/q' - 1` is at most the target exponent `u/(2-u)`.

articles.title: Closed form of the exponent gap
articles.statement: Closed form of the exponent gap `u/(2-u) - (2/q' - 1)`.

articles.title: Upper bound on the exponent gap
articles.statement: Upper bound on the exponent gap.

articles.title: Right side of the capped estimate is nonnegative
articles.statement: The right side `δ^{u/(2-u)} ∑ₑ Infₑ` of the capped estimate is nonnegative.

articles.title: Low-range residual case of the capped estimate
articles.statement:
The capped estimate for all `p ∈ (1/2, q)` with `p < 1`, `δ < e^{-1}`, and `u ∈ (0, 1)` either
 below the hypercontractive range or failing the gap condition.

articles.title: Low-range case implies the full capped estimate on $(1/2, q)$
articles.statement: `hcq_lowRangeResidue q` implies `mxd_martingaleHC_statement q`.

articles.title: Gap condition holds at some $u < 1$ in the hypercontractive range
articles.statement:
For `p > 1/2` and `0 < δ < 1`, some `u ∈ (0, 1)` lies in the hypercontractive range and
 satisfies the gap condition.

articles.title: Low-range case implies the small-influence case
articles.statement: `hcq_lowRangeResidue q` implies `cvg_smallDeltaResidue q`.

articles.title: Capped estimate at $p = 1/2$ for all $u \in (0, 1)$
articles.statement:
At `p = 1/2` the capped estimate `∑_S 4 |S| (1-u)^{|S|-1} f̂(S)² ≤ δ^{u/(2-u)} ∑ₑ Infₑ` holds
 for all `u ∈ (0, 1)`.

articles.title: Target-exponent capped estimate under the gap condition
articles.statement:
The capped estimate with exponent `u/(2-u)` in the hypercontractive range, under the gap
 condition `δ^{gap} ≥ 4p(1-p)`.

articles.title: Target-exponent capped estimate from a domination bound
articles.statement: The capped estimate with exponent `u/(2-u)` from a domination of the hypercontractive bound.

articles.title: Power bound $s \le \delta^g$ from a logarithmic exponent bound
articles.statement: `s ≤ δ^g` when `g ≤ log (1/s) / log (1/δ)`.

articles.title: Damped total weight at $u = 0$ is at most the total influence
articles.statement: At `u = 0` the damped total weight is at most the total influence.

articles.title: Capped estimate in the hypercontractive range
articles.statement:
The capped estimate in the hypercontractive range: if `1 - u = 4p(1-p)(q'-1)` with `1 ≤ q' ≤ 2`,
 then `∑_S 4 |S| (1-u)^{|S|-1} f̂(S)² ≤ 4p(1-p) * δ^{2/q'-1} ∑ₑ Infₑ`.

articles.title: Parametrization of the hypercontractive range by $q' \in (1, 2)$
articles.statement: Every `u ∈ [1 - 4p(1-p), 1]` has the form `1 - u = 4p(1-p)(q'-1)` with `q' ∈ [1, 2]`.

articles.title: Capped estimate at the endpoint $u = 1$
articles.statement: At `u = 1` the capped estimate holds.

articles.title: Damped total weight as a sum of per-coordinate weights
articles.statement: The damped total weight is `4p(1-p) ∑ₑ Dₑ(u)`.

articles.title: Hypercontractive range misses an interval near $u = 0$
articles.statement:
For `p > 1/2` the hypercontractive range `u ≥ 1 - 4p(1-p)` excludes a nonempty interval near `u
 = 0`.

articles.title: Open-interval case implies the full capped estimate on $(1/2, q)$
articles.statement: `frh_openResidue q` implies `mxd_martingaleHC_statement q`, by adding the endpoints.

articles.title: Open-interval residual case of the capped estimate
articles.statement:
The capped estimate `∑_S 4 |S| (1-u)^{|S|-1} f̂(S)² ≤ δ^{u/(2-u)} ∑ₑ Infₑ` for all `p ∈ (1/2,
 q)` with `p < 1` and all `u ∈ (0, 1)`.

articles.title: Per-coordinate damped weight
articles.statement:
The per-coordinate damped weight `Dₑ(u) = ∑_{S ∋ e} (1-u)^{|S|-1} (f̂(S)/√(p(1-p)))²` under
 `μ_p`.

articles.title: Measure–influence form of KKL with constant 0 holds trivially
articles.statement: `klo_DeltaUpgrade 0` holds trivially.

articles.title: Fourier-form KKL inequality given the measure–influence bound
articles.statement:
The KKL inequality at `p = 1/2` in Fourier form, with the bound `m - m^{2/(1+ρ²)} ≤ (1 - ρ²) I /
 4` (for all `ρ ∈ [0, 1]`) as a hypothesis, where `m` is the measure and `I` the total influence
 of `φ`. The hypothesis always holds (`klo_master_le`).

articles.title: Edge-isoperimetric inequality
articles.statement:
**Edge-isoperimetric inequality** on the discrete cube (S. Hart, *A note on the edges of the
 n-cube*, Discrete Math. 1976): an event of uniform measure `m > 0` has total influence at least
 `2 m log (1 / m)`. Here `log` is the natural logarithm, so this is weaker by the factor `log 2`
 than the sharp bound `2 m log₂ (1 / m)`.

articles.title: Measure–influence form of KKL implies the indicator-bound form
articles.statement: `klo_DeltaUpgrade c` implies `kls_LogOptimisation c`.

articles.title: Measure–influence form of KKL implies the KKL inequality at $p = 1/2$
articles.statement: `klo_DeltaUpgrade c` implies the KKL inequality `KKLHypercontractive (1/2) c`.

articles.title: Bound on $m - m^{2/(1+\rho^2)}$ by total influence
articles.statement:
For an event of uniform measure `m` and total influence `I = ∑_S 4 |S| f̂(S)²`, `m -
 m^{2/(1+ρ²)} ≤ (1 - ρ²) I / 4` for `0 ≤ ρ ≤ 1`.

articles.title: Bernoulli's inequality $1 - x^k \le k(1 - x)$
articles.statement:
Bernoulli's inequality in the form `1 - x^k ≤ k (1 - x)` for `0 ≤ x` (the hypothesis
`x ≤ 1` is not needed). See also `one_add_mul_le_pow`.

articles.title: Kahn–Kalai–Linial inequality
articles.statement:
**Kahn–Kalai–Linial inequality** for the uniform measure with constant `2` (J. Kahn, G. Kalai,
 N. Linial, *The influence of variables on Boolean functions*, FOCS 1988; proof after D. Falik,
 A. Samorodnitsky, 2007): for every finite nonempty `E` and every Boolean function `φ` on `{0,
 1}^E`, `2 · Var(φ) · log (1 / maxₑ Infₑ(φ)) ≤ ∑ₑ Infₑ(φ)`, where `Infₑ(φ)` is the probability
 that `e` is pivotal. This is the `p = 1/2` case of the `p`-biased KKL inequality.

articles.title: Squared $p$-biased and Walsh coefficients agree at $p = 1/2$
articles.statement: At `p = 1/2` the squared `p`-biased and Walsh Fourier coefficients agree.

articles.title: $p$-biased character at $p = 1/2$ is the Walsh character up to sign
articles.statement: At `p = 1/2` the `p`-biased character is `(-1)^{|S|}` times the Walsh character.

articles.title: Normalized bit at $p = 1/2$ is $-(-1)^b$
articles.statement: At `p = 1/2` the normalized bit is `-(-1)^b`.

articles.title: Total influence at $p = 1/2$ via $p$-biased Fourier coefficients
articles.statement: Total influence at `p = 1/2` in terms of the `p`-biased Fourier coefficients.

articles.title: Kahn–Kalai–Linial inequality
articles.statement:
**Kahn–Kalai–Linial inequality** for events under the uniform measure (J. Kahn, G. Kalai, N.
 Linial, *The influence of variables on Boolean functions*, FOCS 1988), with constant `2`: `2 ·
 P(A)(1 - P(A)) · log (1 / maxₑ Infₑ(A)) ≤ ∑ₑ Infₑ(A)`, where `Infₑ(A)` is the probability that
 `e` is pivotal for `A`.

articles.title: KKL inequality with constant 2 at $p$ implies its event form
articles.statement:
The KKL inequality `KKLHypercontractive p 2` for an event: `2 · P_p(A)(1 - P_p(A)) · log (1 /
 maxₑ Infₑ(A)) ≤ ∑ₑ Infₑ(A)`.

articles.title: KKL on the interior of $(1/2, q)$ implies its event form there
articles.statement: `kklw_hkkl_of_hypercontractive` at every `p` in the interior of `[1/2, q]`.

articles.title: Pivotal-probability influence as the OSSS influence of an indicator
articles.statement: `StatMech.BeffaraDC.influence` is the OSSS influence of the indicator of `A`.

articles.title: Logarithm of the reciprocal maximal influence of an event
articles.statement: `log (1 / maxₑ Infₑ(A))` under the Bernoulli(`p`) product measure.

articles.title: Event probability as the OSSS expectation of its indicator
articles.statement: `StatMech.prob p A` is the OSSS expectation of the indicator of `A`.

articles.title: Sharp-threshold window bound assuming the KKL inequality on $(1/2, q)$
articles.statement:
Window form of `kklw_sharpThreshold`: under the same hypotheses, if `P_q(A) ≤ 1 - ε` then `q -
 1/2 ≤ (1/2 - ε) / (2 v₀ L)`.

articles.title: Sharp-threshold bound assuming the KKL inequality on $(1/2, q)$
articles.statement:
Sharp-threshold bound: for an increasing event with `P_{1/2}(A) = 1/2`, if the KKL inequality
 holds for all `p ∈ (1/2, q)` and there `P_p(A)(1 - P_p(A)) ≥ v₀` and `log (1 / maxₑ Infₑ(A)) ≥
 L`, then `P_q(A) ≥ 1/2 + 2 v₀ L (q - 1/2)`.

articles.title: Variance of an event indicator is $P(A)(1 - P(A))$
articles.statement: The variance of the indicator of `A` is `P(A)(1 - P(A))`.

articles.title: OSSS Bernoulli weight equals the configuration weight
articles.statement: The OSSS Bernoulli weight of a configuration is `StatMech.configWeight`.

articles.title: Bound on the integral of $e^{-tu/2}$ over $(0, 1)$
articles.statement: `∫₀¹ exp (-(t/2) u) du ≤ 2 / t` for `t > 0`.

articles.title: Integral of $e^{cx}$ over an interval
articles.statement: `∫_a^b exp (c x) dx = (exp (c b) - exp (c a)) / c` for `c ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Integral of damped total-influence weights over the noise parameter
articles.statement:
Integrating the damped total-influence weights over the noise parameter: `∫₀¹ ∑_S 4 |S|
 (1-u)^{|S|-1} c_S du = 4 ∑_{S ≠ ∅} c_S`.

articles.title: Integral of $(1 - u)^n$ over $(0, 1)$
Bound on the integral of $\delta^{u/(2-u)}$ over $(0, 1)$
Capped estimate rewritten in the variable $u = 1 - \rho^2$
articles.statement:
The capped estimate in the variable `u = 1 - ρ²`: `∑_S 4 |S| (1-u)^{|S|-1} f̂(S)² ≤ δ^{u/(2-u)}
 ∑_S 4 |S| f̂(S)²`.

articles.title: KKL inequality
articles.statement:
**KKL inequality** for the uniform measure, Fourier form with constant `2` (after J. Kahn, G.
 Kalai, N. Linial, *The influence of variables on Boolean functions*, FOCS 1988; this proof
 follows D. Falik, A. Samorodnitsky, *Edge-isoperimetric inequalities and influences*, 2007): `2
 · ∑_{S ≠ ∅} f̂(S)² · log (1 / maxₑ Infₑ) ≤ ∑_S 4 |S| f̂(S)²` for every Boolean function.

articles.title: KKL inequality with constant 0 holds trivially
articles.statement: `KKLHypercontractive p 0` holds trivially, since total influence is nonnegative.

articles.title: Kahn–Kalai–Linial inequality
articles.statement:
**Kahn–Kalai–Linial inequality**, maximal-influence form (J. Kahn, G. Kalai, N. Linial, *The
 influence of variables on Boolean functions*, FOCS 1988): under `KKLHypercontractive p c`, `c ·
 Var(φ) · log (1 / δ) ≤ |E| · δ` with `δ = maxₑ Infₑ(φ)`, so `δ` is at least of order `Var(φ) ·
 log |E| / |E|`.

articles.title: Kahn–Kalai–Linial inequality
articles.statement:
**Kahn–Kalai–Linial inequality**, total-influence form (J. Kahn, G. Kalai, N. Linial, *The
 influence of variables on Boolean functions*, FOCS 1988): under `KKLHypercontractive p c`, `c ·
 Var(φ) · log (1 / maxₑ Infₑ(φ)) ≤ ∑ₑ Infₑ(φ)`.

articles.title: KKL inequality with constant $c$ for the $p$-biased measure
articles.statement:
The KKL inequality with constant `c` for the Bernoulli(`p`) product measure: for every finite
 nonempty index type `E` and every Boolean function `φ` on `{0, 1}^E`, `c · Var(φ) · log (1 /
 maxₑ Infₑ(φ)) ≤ ∑ₑ Infₑ(φ)`, with `Infₑ(φ)` the probability that `e` is pivotal.

Despite its name, this is the conclusion of the KKL theorem, not a hypercontractivity estimate.
 It holds trivially for `c = 0` (`kkl_hypercontractive_zero`) and is proved for `p = 1/2`, `c =
 2` in `fsr_pbiased_endpoint`. When `maxₑ Infₑ(φ) = 0`, `log (1 / 0) = 0` in Lean and the
 inequality is trivial.

articles.title: Maximal influence under a product weight
articles.statement: The maximal influence `maxₑ Infₑ(g)` of `g` under the product weight `ν`.

articles.title: Total influence under a product weight
articles.statement: The total influence `∑ₑ Infₑ(g)` of `g` under the product weight `ν`.

articles.title: Coordinatewise complement of a configuration
articles.statement: The coordinatewise complement `ω ↦ ¬ω` of a configuration.

articles.title: KKL hypothesis on $(1/2, q)$ restated on the interior of $(1/2, q)$
articles.statement: `kpb_PBiasedHC q` in the form used by `StatMech.TwoDim.kklw_sharpThreshold`.

articles.title: Reflection of the KKL inequality from $p$ to $1 - p$
articles.statement: The KKL inequality with constant `2` at `p` implies it at `1 - p`.

articles.title: KKL inequality with constant 2 on $(1/2, q)$
articles.statement: The KKL inequality with constant `2` for every Bernoulli parameter `p ∈ (1/2, q)`.

articles.title: KKL inequality with constant 0 holds trivially on $(1/2, q)$
articles.statement: The KKL inequality with constant `0` holds for every `p`; this is trivial.

articles.title: Sharp-threshold window under the $p$-biased KKL hypothesis
articles.statement: `StatMech.TwoDim.kklw_sharpThreshold_window` under `kpb_PBiasedHC q`.

articles.title: Sharp-threshold bound under the $p$-biased KKL hypothesis
articles.statement: `StatMech.TwoDim.kklw_sharpThreshold` under `kpb_PBiasedHC q`.

articles.title: Complement swaps the Bernoulli $p$ and $1 - p$ weights
articles.statement: Complementing sends the Bernoulli(`p`) weight to the Bernoulli(`1 - p`) weight.

articles.title: Cube bijection induced by an index bijection
articles.statement: The bijection `{0, 1}^ι ≃ {0, 1}^κ` induced by `e : κ ≃ ι`.

articles.title: Walsh coefficient is the canonical Fourier coefficient up to sign
articles.statement:
On `Fin n`, the Fourier coefficient is `BooleanCube.boolFourierCoeff` up to the sign
`(-1)^{|S|}`.

articles.title: Fourier coefficients are invariant under reindexing
articles.statement: Fourier coefficients are unchanged when both the function and its index are reindexed.

articles.title: Fourier–Walsh coefficient under the uniform measure
articles.statement:
The Fourier–Walsh coefficient `f̂(S) = 𝔼[f χ_S]` under the uniform measure.

This retains the legacy signs; `khc_fourierCoeff_eq_boolFourierCoeff` transports
 the canonical Fourier identities used below.

articles.title: Fourier inversion on the Boolean cube
articles.statement: Fourier inversion: `f = ∑_S f̂(S) χ_S`.

articles.title: Bonami–Beckner hypercontractive inequality
articles.statement:
**Bonami–Beckner hypercontractive inequality** (A. Bonami, *Étude des coefficients de Fourier
 des fonctions de Lᵖ(G)*, Ann. Inst. Fourier 1970; W. Beckner, *Inequalities in Fourier
 analysis*, Ann. of Math. 1975): `‖T_ρ g‖₂ ≤ ‖g‖_{1+ρ²}` on `{0, 1}^ι` for `0 ≤ ρ ≤ 1`.

articles.title: Event influence is four times the canonical influence
articles.statement: Event influence is four times canonical quarter-square influence after reindexing.

articles.title: Influence of a coordinate as Fourier weight
articles.statement: The influence of `e` on a Boolean function is `∑_{S ∋ e} 4 f̂(S)²`.

articles.title: Hypercontractive form of KKL implies the KKL inequality at $p = 1/2$
articles.statement:
The Fourier form `khc_LogSobolevStep c` implies the KKL inequality `KKLHypercontractive (1/2)
 c`.

articles.title: Hypercontractive form of KKL with constant 0 holds trivially
articles.statement: `khc_LogSobolevStep 0` holds trivially.

articles.title: Fourier-form KKL inequality given the hypercontractive bound
articles.statement:
The KKL inequality at `p = 1/2` in Fourier form, with the hypercontractive bound as a
 hypothesis: for every Boolean `φ`, if `∑_S ρ^{2|S|} f̂(S)² ≤ ‖f‖²_{1+ρ²}` for all `ρ ∈ [0, 1]`,
 then `c · ∑_{S ≠ ∅} f̂(S)² · log (1 / maxₑ Infₑ(f)) ≤ ∑_S 4 |S| f̂(S)²`, where `f = 1_φ`. The
 hypothesis always holds (`khc_lowDegreeWeight_le`).

articles.title: Hypercontractivity in Fourier form
articles.statement: Hypercontractivity in Fourier form: `∑_S ρ^{2|S|} f̂(S)² ≤ ‖f‖²_{1+ρ²}`.

articles.title: Noise operator is diagonal in the Walsh basis
articles.statement:
The noise operator acts diagonally on the Walsh basis: `T_ρ f = ∑_S ρ^{|S|} f̂(S) χ_S`.

Transported from `BooleanCube.boolNoiseOp_eq_sum`, for every real `ρ`.

articles.title: Parseval's identity on the Boolean cube
articles.statement:
Parseval's identity: `𝔼[f g] = ∑_S f̂(S) ĝ(S)`.

Transported from `BooleanCube.expect_mul_eq_sum_boolFourierCoeff_mul`.

articles.title: Reindexing preserves values at corresponding cube points
articles.statement: Reindexing back at the corresponding cube point recovers the original value.

articles.title: Reindexing a cube function along an index bijection
articles.statement: The function `f` on `{0, 1}^ι` transported to `{0, 1}^κ` along the bijection `e : κ ≃ ι`.

articles.title: $\pm 1$ value of a bit
articles.statement: The `±1` value of a bit: `false ↦ 1`, `true ↦ -1`.

articles.title: Total influence as Fourier weight
articles.statement: The total influence of a Boolean function is `∑_S 4 |S| f̂(S)²`.

articles.title: Variance as Fourier weight off the empty set
articles.statement: Variance under the uniform measure is the Fourier weight off the empty set.

articles.title: Uniform variance agrees with the canonical Boolean variance
articles.statement: On `Fin n`, the variance under the uniform product weight is `BooleanCube.boolVariance`.

articles.title: Walsh character agrees with the canonical cube character up to sign
articles.statement:
On `Fin n`, the Walsh character is `BooleanCube.cubeChi` up to the sign `(-1)^{|S|}`:
`BooleanCube.cubeVal` sends `true` to `1`, while `khc_sign` sends it to `-1`.

articles.title: Reindexing a Walsh character reindexes its coordinate set
articles.statement: Reindexing a Walsh character reindexes its finite set of coordinates.

articles.title: Walsh character on the Boolean cube
articles.statement:
The Walsh character `χ_S(x) = ∏_{i ∈ S} (-1)^{x i}` on `{0, 1}^ι`.

This legacy sign convention is retained for KKL consumers; its proofs use
 `BooleanCube.cubeChi` through `khc_walshChar_eq_cubeChi`.

articles.title: Linear threshold function
articles.statement:
A function $f : \{-1, 1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is a linear
threshold function if there are reals $w_0, w_1, \dots, w_n$ such that for every
$x \in \{-1, 1\}^n$ we have $f(x) = \operatorname{sgn}(w_0 + w_1 x_1 + \dots + w_n x_n)$, where
$x_i \in \{-1, 1\}$ is the $i$-th coordinate of $x$, $\operatorname{sgn} z = 1$ for $z \ge 0$ and
$\operatorname{sgn} z = -1$ for $z < 0$.

articles.title: Majority Is Least Stable fails in every odd dimension at least five
articles.statement:
For every odd natural
number $n \ge 5$, the Majority Is Least Stable conjecture in $n$ variables fails: there are a
linear threshold function $f : \{-1, 1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ and a real number $\rho$ with
$0 \le \rho \le 1$ such that $\mathrm{Stab}_\rho[f] < \mathrm{Stab}_\rho[\mathrm{Maj}_n]$, where
$\mathrm{Stab}_\rho$ is the noise stability and $\mathrm{Maj}_n$ is the majority function.

Biswas and Sarkar exhibit, for every odd $n \ge 5$, a linear threshold function $g_n$ with
$\mathrm{Stab}_\rho[g_n] < \mathrm{Stab}_\rho[\mathrm{Maj}_n]$ for all small $\rho > 0$. The
conjecture holds for $n = 1$ and $n = 3$.

## Sources

- R. O'Donnell, Open problems in analysis of Boolean functions, arXiv:1204.6447 (2012), 'Majority Is Least Stable Conjecture' (Benjamini, Kalai, Schramm); resolution: A. Biswas, P. Sarkar, On the "majority is least stable" conjecture, Inform. Process. Lett. 179 (2023), 106295, arXiv:2202.09024, Theorem 2 of arXiv:2202.09024v2: the conjecture is true for n = 1 and n = 3 and false for every odd n ≥ 5; for odd n ≥ 5 the linear threshold function g_n(x) = sgn(2(x₁ + ⋯ + x_{n-3}) + x_{n-2} + x_{n-1} + x_n) has W⁰[g_n] = 0 and W¹[g_n] < W¹[Maj_n] (Lemmas 3 and 4), hence Stab_ρ[g_n] < Stab_ρ[Maj_n] for all small ρ > 0 (Lemma 1); the case n = 5 is V. Jain, arXiv:1703.07657, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ipl.2022.106295.

articles.title: Majority Is Least Stable in some odd dimension at least five
articles.statement:
There is an odd natural
number $n \ge 5$ for which the Majority Is Least Stable conjecture in $n$ variables holds: every
linear threshold function $f : \{-1, 1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies
$\mathrm{Stab}_\rho[f] \ge \mathrm{Stab}_\rho[\mathrm{Maj}_n]$ for every real $\rho$ with
$0 \le \rho \le 1$, where $\mathrm{Stab}_\rho$ is the noise stability and $\mathrm{Maj}_n$ is the
majority function.

articles.title: Majority Is Least Stable conjecture in $n$ variables
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the
statement that every linear threshold function $f : \{-1, 1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies
$\mathrm{Stab}_\rho[f] \ge \mathrm{Stab}_\rho[\mathrm{Maj}_n]$ for every real $\rho$ with
$0 \le \rho \le 1$, where $\mathrm{Stab}_\rho$ is the noise stability and $\mathrm{Maj}_n$ is the
majority function.

articles.title: Majority function
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the majority function
$\mathrm{Maj}_n : \{-1, 1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is given by $\mathrm{Maj}_n(x) = 1$ if
$x_1 + \dots + x_n \ge 0$ and $\mathrm{Maj}_n(x) = -1$ otherwise, where $x_i \in \{-1, 1\}$ is the
$i$-th coordinate of $x$.

articles.title: Noise stability
articles.statement:
For a real number $\rho$ and a function $f : \{-1, 1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$,
the noise stability of $f$ at $\rho$ is
$\mathrm{Stab}_\rho[f] = \sum_{S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}} \rho^{|S|} \hat f(S)^2$, where
$\hat f(S)$ is the Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $S$.

For $-1 \le \rho \le 1$ this is the Fourier expansion of $\mathbb{E}[f(x) f(y)]$ for uniform $x$
and a $\rho$-correlated copy $y$ of $x$.

articles.title: Bernoulli product weight
articles.statement: The Bernoulli(`p`) product weight: every coordinate is `true` with probability `p`.

articles.title: Root step of the OSSS induction
articles.statement:
Root step of the OSSS induction: the covariance of a function whose discrete derivative in `e`
 is bounded by `1` with the martingale increment `g - 𝔼[g | ω_{≠e}]` is at most `Infₑ(g)`.

articles.title: Subtree step of the OSSS induction
articles.statement:
Subtree step of the OSSS induction: for `G` independent of the root variable `e`, the covariance
 with a tree rooted at `e` splits into the covariances with the two subtrees under the
 conditioned weights.

articles.title: Conditional expectation given the other coordinates
articles.statement: The conditional expectation of `g` given all coordinates except `e`.

articles.title: Covariance under a product weight
articles.statement: The covariance `𝔼[f g] - 𝔼[f] 𝔼[g]` under the product weight `ν`.

articles.title: Binary decision tree
articles.statement:
A binary decision tree on the variables `E`: a leaf outputs a Boolean value, and a node queries
 a variable and continues in the first subtree if it is `true` and in the second otherwise.

articles.title: Real-valued function computed by a decision tree
articles.statement: The function computed by the decision tree, as a `0/1`-valued real function.

articles.title: Boolean function computed by a decision tree
articles.statement: The Boolean function computed by the decision tree.

articles.title: Bernoulli product weight computes product-measure integrals
articles.statement:
The Bernoulli(`p`) product weight computes integrals against
`StatMech.bernoulliProductMeasure`, the corresponding product probability measure.

articles.title: Expectation under a product weight
articles.statement: The expectation `∑_ω weight ν ω * g ω` of `g` under the product weight `ν`.

articles.title: Configuration with one coordinate flipped
articles.statement:
The configuration `ω` with coordinate `e` flipped.

See also `BooleanCube.flipCoord`, the same operation on `Fin n → Bool`.

articles.title: Decision tree querying every variable
articles.statement:
The decision tree that queries every variable and then outputs the value of `φ`; it computes `φ`
 and has revealment `1` at every variable.

articles.title: Decision tree querying a list of variables
articles.statement:
The decision tree that queries the variables of `l` in order and then outputs the value of `φ`
 at the configuration that agrees with the answers on `l` and is `false` elsewhere. It computes
 `φ` when `φ` depends only on the variables in `l` (`eval_fullTree`).

articles.title: Influence on an indicator is the pivotal probability
articles.statement: The influence of `e` on the indicator of `A` is the probability that `e` is pivotal for `A`.

articles.title: Influence of a coordinate
articles.statement:
The influence of coordinate `e` on `g`: `𝔼 |g(ω^{e ↦ 1}) - g(ω^{e ↦ 0})|`. For the indicator of
 an event this is the probability that `e` is pivotal (`infl_indicator_eq_pivotal`).

See also `BooleanCube.boolInfluence`, the uniform-measure influence `𝔼 ((f x - f x^{⊕i}) / 2)²`;
 for `0/1`-valued functions on the uniform cube the two differ by the factor `4`.

articles.title: Function depending only on listed coordinates
articles.statement: `φ` depends only on the coordinates in the list `l`.

articles.title: Product probability weight
articles.statement: `ν` is a product probability weight: each `ν e` is a probability vector on `Bool`.

articles.title: OSSS inequality for the Bernoulli product measure
articles.statement: The OSSS inequality for the Bernoulli(`p`) product measure.

articles.title: OSSS covariance inequality over all product weights
articles.statement:
The OSSS covariance inequality, stated for all product weights at once so that it can be proved
 by induction on the decision tree. Use `osss` for the usual argument order.

articles.title: OSSS inequality
articles.statement:
**OSSS inequality** (O'Donnell, Saks, Schramm, Servedio, *Every decision tree has an influential
 variable*, FOCS 2005): if the decision tree `T` computes `f`, then `Var(f) ≤ ∑ᵢ δᵢ(T) Infᵢ(f)`
 under every product probability measure.

articles.title: OSSS inequality
articles.statement:
**OSSS inequality**, covariance form (O'Donnell, Saks, Schramm, Servedio, *Every decision tree
 has an influential variable*, FOCS 2005; in this form Duminil-Copin, Raoufi, Tassion, Ann. of
 Math. 2019): if the decision tree `T` computes the Boolean function `f`, then for every real
 function `g` and every product probability measure, `Cov(f, g) ≤ ∑ᵢ δᵢ(T) Infᵢ(g)`, where
 `Infᵢ(g) = 𝔼 |g(ω^{i ↦ 1}) - g(ω^{i ↦ 0})|`.

This is `osss_cov` with the weight and its hypothesis as leading arguments.

articles.title: Poincaré inequality for the Bernoulli product measure
articles.statement: `poincare` for the Bernoulli(`p`) product measure.

articles.title: Covariance form of the Poincaré inequality
articles.statement: Covariance form of `poincare`: `Cov(1_A, g) ≤ ∑ₑ Infₑ(g)` for every real function `g`.

articles.title: Poincaré inequality for Boolean functions under a product measure
articles.statement:
Poincaré inequality for Boolean functions under a product measure: `Var(1_A) ≤ ∑ₑ Infₑ(1_A)`,
 where `Infₑ(1_A)` is the probability that `e` is pivotal. This is the OSSS inequality for the
 full decision tree; it is weaker than the Efron–Stein inequality `Var(f) ≤ ∑ₑ pₑ(1 - pₑ) 𝔼[(∂ₑ
 f)²]` by the factor `pₑ(1 - pₑ) ≤ 1/4`.

articles.title: Point-mass weight on the Booleans
articles.statement: The point mass at `b`, as a weight on `Bool`. Replacing `ν e` by `pt b` conditions on `ω e = b`.

articles.title: Variables queried by a decision tree on an input
articles.statement: The set of variables the decision tree queries on input `ω`.

articles.title: Revealment of a variable by a decision tree
articles.statement: The revealment `δₑ(T)`: the probability that the decision tree `T` queries the variable `e`.

articles.title: Variance under a product weight
articles.statement: The variance of `g` under the product weight `ν`.

articles.title: Probability of a configuration under a product weight
articles.statement: The probability `∏ₑ ν e (ω e)` of the configuration `ω` under the product weight `ν`.

articles.title: At most half of field pairs have dot product one
articles.statement:
For one exponent `E`, at most half of all field pairs satisfy
`dotProduct (bits (a ^ E)) (bits b) = 1`.

articles.title: At least 15/32 of field pairs have odd parity
articles.statement:
Under `16 * m ≤ 2 ^ s`, at least `15 / 32` of the field pairs have odd
parity across any nonempty exponent set `V`.  Fractions are cleared in the
statement.

articles.title: Lower bound on odd-parity pairs in a finite field
articles.statement:
Let a finite field be written as `s` binary coordinates.  For a nonempty
set `V` of exponents below `m`, the number of pairs `(a, b)` for which an odd
number of the dot products `bits (a ^ E) ⬝ᵥ bits b` equal one satisfies the
cleared-denominator lower bound

`|F| ^ 2 ≤ 2 * oddPairs + (m - 1) * |F|`.

This is a one-sided odd-frequency estimate.

articles.title: Even indicator of a natural number
articles.statement: The integer indicator that a natural number is even.

articles.title: Coefficients of the even-indicator expansion
articles.statement:
The coefficients of the even-indicator expansion: one at zero and
`(-1) ^ i * 2 ^ (i - 1)` at positive indices.

articles.title: Truncated subset expansion of parity products modulo powers of two
articles.statement:
A product of even-cardinality indicators and parity signs is congruent to its finite
subset expansion cut off at total degree `M`. Each even-indicator factor costs at most one
power of two, so the cutoff must satisfy `ν - 1 + #J₁ ≤ M`, with `1 ≤ ν`.
Indices outside `J₁ ∪ J₂` select only the empty subset.

articles.title: Subset sum of parity coefficients is the even-cardinality indicator
articles.statement: Summing parity coefficients over all subsets gives the even-cardinality indicator.

articles.title: Twice the even indicator is one plus the parity sign
articles.statement: Twice the even indicator is one plus the parity sign.

articles.title: Twice a parity coefficient is a sign coefficient
articles.statement: Twice the parity coefficient is the sign coefficient, with a correction at zero.

articles.title: Concatenation at the all-false input
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$ and a finite list
$W = (W_0, \dots, W_{m-1})$ of Boolean functions on $n$ variables, the concatenation of $W$ on
$n + k$ variables takes the value $W_0(\mathrm{false}, \dots, \mathrm{false})$ at the all-false
input when $W$ is nonempty, and the value false when $W$ is empty.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, the concatenation representation of `D_n^{B^k}` before Theorem 10.

articles.title: Concatenation of a list of Boolean functions
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers and let
$W = (W_0, W_1, \dots, W_{m-1})$ be a finite list of Boolean functions on $n$ variables. The
concatenation $W_0 \cdot W_1 \cdots W_{m-1}$ on $n + k$ variables is the Boolean function that
sends $(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}, y_0, \dots, y_{k-1})$ to $W_i(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$, where
$i = \sum_{j < k} y_j 2^j$ is the number whose binary digits are the last $k$ variables (true
counted as $1$ and false as $0$), and to false when $i \ge m$.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, the concatenation representation of `D_n^{B^k}` before Theorem 10.

articles.title: Duality reverses order and exchanges joins and meets
articles.statement:
Let $f$ and $g$ be monotone
Boolean functions on $n$ variables, ordered pointwise, with duals $f^*$ and $g^*$. If $f \le g$
then $g^* \le f^*$. Moreover $(f \lor g)^* = f^* \land g^*$ and $(f \land g)^* = f^* \lor g^*$,
where $\lor$ and $\land$ are pointwise disjunction and conjunction.

Part 1 of the paper's lemma, $f^{**} = f$, holds for every Boolean function.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Lemma 2 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-lem-2`).

articles.title: Duality of Boolean functions is an involution
articles.statement:
For every $n$ and every Boolean function
$f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$, writing $f^\star$ for the dual of $f$, we have
$(f^\star)^\star = f$.

articles.title: Dual of a Boolean function
articles.statement:
For a Boolean function $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$, its
dual is the Boolean function $f^\star \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ given by
$f^\star(x) = \lnot f(\bar x)$, where $\bar x$ is the coordinatewise complement of $x$.

articles.title: Permuting variables preserves monotonicity, duals and self-duality
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a Boolean
function on $n$ variables, let $\pi$ be a permutation of the $n$ coordinates, and let $f^\pi$
be the function $x \mapsto f(x \circ \pi)$. If $f$ is monotone, then $f^\pi$ is monotone and
$(f^*)^\pi = (f^\pi)^*$, where $f^*$ is the dual of $f$. If $f$ is self-dual monotone, then so
is $f^\pi$.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Lemma 5 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-lem-5`).

articles.title: Complementation of Boolean vectors is an involution
articles.statement:
For every $n$ and every Boolean
vector $x \in \{0,1\}^n$, writing $\bar x$ for the coordinatewise complement of $x$, we have
$\bar{\bar x} = x$.

articles.title: Complement of a Boolean vector
articles.statement:
The complement of a Boolean vector $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ is
the vector $\bar x \in \{0,1\}^n$ obtained by negating every coordinate: $\bar x_i = \lnot x_i$
for every $i < n$.

## Sources

- JIS VOL28/Pawelski, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL28/Pawelski/pawelski22.tex>, lines 72–81.

articles.title: Counting self-dual monotone functions on $n + 4$ variables
articles.statement:
Let $D_n$ be the set of
monotone Boolean functions on $n$ variables, ordered pointwise, with $\lor$ the pointwise
disjunction and $f^*$ the dual of $f$. For $x, h \in D_n$ let $\mathrm{re}(x, h)$ be the number
of $z \in D_n$ with $x \le z \le h$. Then the number of self-dual monotone Boolean functions on
$n + 4$ variables equals

$$
\sum_{a, b, c \in D_n} \ \sum_{h \in D_n,\ h \ge a \lor b \lor c \lor a^* \lor b^* \lor c^*}
\mathrm{re}(a \lor b \lor c, h) \, \mathrm{re}(a \lor b^* \lor c^*, h) \,
\mathrm{re}(b \lor a^* \lor c^*, h) \, \mathrm{re}(c \lor a^* \lor b^*, h).
$$

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Theorem 13 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-thm-13`).

articles.title: Counting self-dual monotone functions on $n + 2$ variables
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 0$ and let
$\lambda_{n+2}$ be the number of self-dual monotone Boolean functions on $n + 2$ variables. For
a monotone Boolean function $b$ on $n$ variables let $r(b)$ be the number of monotone Boolean
functions $z$ on $n$ variables with $b \lor b^* \le z$, where $b^*$ is the dual of $b$, $\lor$
is pointwise disjunction and functions are ordered pointwise. Then $\lambda_{n+2}$ is the sum
of $r(b)$ over all monotone Boolean functions $b$ on $n$ variables. Moreover, for a permutation
$\pi$ of the $n$ coordinates write $b^\pi$ for the function $x \mapsto b(x \circ \pi)$, and let
$R$ be any finite set of monotone Boolean functions on $n$ variables such that for every
monotone $f$ there is exactly one $b \in R$ with $f = b^\pi$ for some permutation $\pi$. Then
$\lambda_{n+2} = \sum_{b \in R} \gamma(b) \, r(b)$, where $\gamma(b)$ is the number of distinct
functions $b^\pi$ as $\pi$ ranges over all permutations.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Theorem 10 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-thm-10`).

articles.title: Recursion for self-dual monotone functions from $n$ to $n + 1$ variables
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$,
let $\lambda_m$ be the number of self-dual monotone Boolean functions on $m$ variables, and let
$d_n$ be the number of monotone Boolean functions on $n$ variables. For a Boolean function $b$
on $n$ variables let $b^*$ be its dual and $\ell(b)$ the number of inputs at which $b$ is true,
order functions pointwise, and for a permutation $\pi$ of the $n$ coordinates write $b^\pi$ for
the function $x \mapsto b(x \circ \pi)$. Let $R$ be any finite set of monotone Boolean
functions on $n$ variables such that for every monotone $f$ there is exactly one $b \in R$ with
$f = b^\pi$ for some permutation $\pi$, and let $\gamma(b)$ be the number of distinct functions
$b^\pi$ as $\pi$ ranges over all permutations. Then

$$
\lambda_{n+1} = \lambda_n + \sum_{b \in R,\ \ell(b) < 2^{n-1},\ b \le b^*} \gamma(b),
$$

and $2 \lambda_{n+1} \le d_n + \lambda_n$.

The bound is the paper's $\lambda_{n+1} \le (d_n + \lambda_n) / 2$ with the division cleared.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Theorem 9 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-thm-9`).

articles.title: Upper bound for self-dual monotone functions on $n + 1$ variables
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 0$,
the number of self-dual monotone Boolean functions on $n + 1$ variables is at most the number
of monotone Boolean functions on $n$ variables.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Corollary 7 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-cor-7`).

articles.title: Counting self-dual monotone functions on $n + 1$ variables
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 0$, the
number of self-dual monotone Boolean functions on $n + 1$ variables equals the number of
monotone Boolean functions $b$ on $n$ variables with $b \le b^*$, where $b^*$ is the dual of $b$
and functions are ordered pointwise. Moreover, for a permutation $\pi$ of the $n$ coordinates
write $b^\pi$ for the function $x \mapsto b(x \circ \pi)$, and let $R$ be any finite set of
monotone Boolean functions on $n$ variables such that for every monotone $f$ there is exactly
one $b \in R$ with $f = b^\pi$ for some permutation $\pi$. Then the number of self-dual
monotone Boolean functions on $n + 1$ variables equals $\sum_{b \in R,\ b \le b^*} \gamma(b)$,
where $\gamma(b)$ is the number of distinct functions $b^\pi$ as $\pi$ ranges over all
permutations.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Theorem 6 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-thm-6`).

articles.title: For odd $n$, every permutation fixes a self-dual monotone function
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be odd and
let $\pi$ be a permutation of the $n$ coordinates. Then there is a self-dual monotone Boolean
function $f$ on $n$ variables with $f(x \circ \pi) = f(x)$ for every input $x$.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Lemma 17 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-lem-17`).

articles.title: Self-dual monotone Boolean functions
articles.statement:
A Boolean function $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$
is self-dual monotone when it is monotone, that is, $f(x) \le f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \{0,1\}^n$
with $x_i \le y_i$ for every $i < n$, and it equals its dual, that is, $f = f^\star$, where
$f^\star(x) = \lnot f(\bar x)$ and $\bar x$ is the coordinatewise complement of $x$.

articles.title: Dedekind numbers bound self-dual counts from below (Corollary 11)
articles.statement:
For a natural number
$n$, let $d_n$ be the number of monotone Boolean functions $\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ (for the
coordinatewise order with $0 < 1$) and let $\lambda_{n+2}$ be the number of self-dual monotone
Boolean functions $\{0,1\}^{n+2} \to \{0,1\}$, that is, monotone functions $f$ with
$f(\bar x) = \lnot f(x)$ for every $x$, where $\bar x$ is the coordinatewise complement of $x$.
Then $d_n \le \lambda_{n+2}$.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Corollary 11 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-cor-11`).

articles.title: Maximal intersecting families split complementary pairs (Lemma 3, L2)
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and
let $\mathcal U$ be a maximal intersecting family of subsets of $X = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$: any two
members of $\mathcal U$, not necessarily distinct, have nonempty intersection, and no family of
subsets of $X$ strictly containing $\mathcal U$ has this property. Then for every
$A \subseteq X$, $A \in \mathcal U$ if and only if $X \setminus A \notin \mathcal U$.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is needed: for $n = 0$ the empty family is the maximal intersecting
family, and it contains neither $\emptyset$ nor its complement $\emptyset$.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Lemma 3 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-lem-3`).

articles.title: A criterion for maximal intersecting families (Lemma 4)
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and
let $\mathcal U$ be a family of subsets of $X = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that $\mathcal U$ is an
upper set (if $A \in \mathcal U$ and $A \subseteq B \subseteq X$ then $B \in \mathcal U$) and,
for every $A \subseteq X$, $A \in \mathcal U$ if and only if $X \setminus A \notin \mathcal U$.
Then $\mathcal U$ is a maximal intersecting family: any two members of $\mathcal U$, not
necessarily distinct, have nonempty intersection, and no family of subsets of $X$ strictly
containing $\mathcal U$ has this property.

The paper's hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is not needed: for $n = 0$ the complement of $\emptyset$ is
$\emptyset$, so no family satisfies the second condition.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Lemma 4 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-lem-4`).

articles.title: Currying monotone Boolean functions (Lemma 1)
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, let $D_m$ be the
poset of monotone Boolean functions $\{0,1\}^m \to \{0,1\}$, where $0 < 1$, inputs are ordered
coordinatewise and functions are ordered pointwise. Then for all natural numbers $n$ and $k$,
$D_{n+k}$ is order-isomorphic to the poset of monotone maps $\{0,1\}^k \to D_n$, ordered
pointwise.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Lemma 1 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-lem-1`).

articles.title: Weights of monotone Boolean functions and their duals (Lemma 8)
articles.statement:
Order $\{0,1\}$ by
$0 < 1$, inputs in $\{0,1\}^n$ coordinatewise and Boolean functions on $\{0,1\}^n$ pointwise. For
such a function $f$, let $f^*(x) = \lnot f(\bar x)$ be its dual, where $\bar x$ is the
coordinatewise complement of $x$, and let $\ell(f)$ be the number of $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ with
$f(x) = 1$. Let $b$ be a monotone Boolean function on $\{0,1\}^n$. Then: if $b \le b^*$, then
$2\ell(b) \le 2^n$; if $2\ell(b) = 2^n$ and $b \le b^*$, then $b = b^*$; if $b = b^*$, then
$2\ell(b) = 2^n$; and $\ell(b^*) = 2^n - \ell(b)$. Moreover, the number of monotone Boolean
functions $f$ on $\{0,1\}^n$ with $2\ell(f) < 2^n$ equals the number of those with
$2\ell(f) > 2^n$.

For $n \ge 1$ the comparisons of $2\ell$ with $2^n$ are the paper's comparisons of $\ell$ with
$2^{n-1}$; written this way the statement also covers $n = 0$.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Lemma 8 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-lem-8`).

articles.title: Self-dual monotone functions on $n+4$ variables, interval form (Theorem 14)
articles.statement:
Order
$\{0,1\}$ by $0 < 1$, inputs coordinatewise and Boolean functions pointwise, with $\vee$ the
pointwise maximum. Let $D_n$ be the set of monotone Boolean functions on $\{0,1\}^n$, and let
$f^*(x) = \lnot f(\bar x)$ be the dual of $f$, where $\bar x$ is the coordinatewise complement of
$x$; a Boolean function $F$ is self-dual monotone if it is monotone and $F^* = F$. The
concatenation $W_0 \cdot W_1 \cdots W_{15}$ of Boolean functions on $\{0,1\}^n$ is the Boolean
function on $\{0,1\}^{n+4}$ sending $(x, y_0, y_1, y_2, y_3)$, with $x \in \{0,1\}^n$, to
$W_i(x)$, where $i = y_0 + 2y_1 + 4y_2 + 8y_3$. Let $a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h \in D_n$ satisfy
$h^* \le h$, $h^* \le a \le h$, $h^* \le b \le h$, $h^* \le c \le h$,
$a \vee b \vee c \le d \le h$, $a \vee b^* \vee c^* \le e \le h$,
$b \vee a^* \vee c^* \le f \le h$ and $c \vee a^* \vee b^* \le g \le h$. Then the concatenation

$$h^* \cdot g^* \cdot f^* \cdot a \cdot e^* \cdot b \cdot c \cdot d \cdot
d^* \cdot c^* \cdot b^* \cdot e \cdot a^* \cdot f \cdot g \cdot h$$

is a self-dual monotone Boolean function on $\{0,1\}^{n+4}$. Conversely, every self-dual
monotone Boolean function on $\{0,1\}^{n+4}$ equals this concatenation for some
$a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h \in D_n$ satisfying these inequalities.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Theorem 14 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-thm-14`).

articles.title: Self-dual monotone functions on $n+4$ variables as concatenations (Theorem 12)
articles.statement:
Order
$\{0,1\}$ by $0 < 1$, inputs coordinatewise and Boolean functions pointwise, with $\vee$ the
pointwise maximum. Let $D_n$ be the set of monotone Boolean functions on $\{0,1\}^n$, and let
$f^*(x) = \lnot f(\bar x)$ be the dual of $f$, where $\bar x$ is the coordinatewise complement of
$x$; a Boolean function $F$ is self-dual monotone if it is monotone and $F^* = F$. The
concatenation $W_0 \cdot W_1 \cdots W_{15}$ of Boolean functions on $\{0,1\}^n$ is the Boolean
function on $\{0,1\}^{n+4}$ sending $(x, y_0, y_1, y_2, y_3)$, with $x \in \{0,1\}^n$, to
$W_i(x)$, where $i = y_0 + 2y_1 + 4y_2 + 8y_3$. Let $a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h \in D_n$ satisfy
$a \vee b \vee c \vee a^* \vee b^* \vee c^* \le h$, $a \vee b \vee c \le d \le h$,
$a \vee b^* \vee c^* \le e \le h$, $b \vee a^* \vee c^* \le f \le h$ and
$c \vee a^* \vee b^* \le g \le h$. Then the concatenation

$$h^* \cdot g^* \cdot f^* \cdot a \cdot e^* \cdot b \cdot c \cdot d \cdot
d^* \cdot c^* \cdot b^* \cdot e \cdot a^* \cdot f \cdot g \cdot h$$

is a self-dual monotone Boolean function on $\{0,1\}^{n+4}$. Conversely, every self-dual
monotone Boolean function on $\{0,1\}^{n+4}$ equals this concatenation for some
$a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h \in D_n$ satisfying these inequalities.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Theorem 12 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-thm-12`).

articles.title: Permutations of eight variables fixing no self-dual monotone function (Corollary 16)
articles.statement:
Let $\pi$ be one of the permutations $(0\,1\,2\,3\,4\,5\,6\,7)$, $(0\,1)(2\,3\,4\,5\,6\,7)$,
$(0\,1\,2\,3)(4\,5\,6\,7)$, $(0\,1)(2\,3)(4\,5\,6\,7)$ and $(0\,1)(2\,3)(4\,5)(6\,7)$ of
$\{0, \dots, 7\}$, in cycle notation. Let $f : \{0,1\}^8 \to \{0,1\}$ be self-dual monotone,
that is, monotone for the coordinatewise order with $0 < 1$ and such that
$f(\bar x) = \lnot f(x)$ for every $x$, where $\bar x$ is the coordinatewise complement of $x$.
Then $f$ is not fixed by $\pi$: the function $x \mapsto f(x \circ \pi)$, where
$(x \circ \pi)_i = x_{\pi(i)}$, differs from $f$.

In the paper the points are numbered $1, \dots, 8$, so these permutations are $(12345678)$,
$(12)(345678)$, $(1234)(5678)$, $(12)(34)(5678)$ and $(12)(34)(56)(78)$.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Corollary 16 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-cor-16`).

articles.title: Permutations with only even cycles fix no self-dual monotone function (Lemma 15)
articles.statement:
Let
$\pi$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ all of whose cycles have even length, that is,
every point has an orbit of even size under $\pi$. Let $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ be self-dual
monotone, that is, monotone for the coordinatewise order with $0 < 1$ and such that
$f(\bar x) = \lnot f(x)$ for every $x$, where $\bar x$ is the coordinatewise complement of $x$.
Then $f$ is not fixed by $\pi$: the function $x \mapsto f(x \circ \pi)$, where
$(x \circ \pi)_i = x_{\pi(i)}$, differs from $f$.

The paper also assumes that $n$ is even; this follows from the condition on the cycles.

## Sources

- Bartłomiej Pawelski and Andrzej Szepietowski, *Counting Self-Dual Monotone Boolean Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.5, Lemma 15 (`jis-2025-25.6.5-lem-15`).

articles.title: Coordinate projections are self-dual monotone
articles.statement:
For every $n$ and every index $i < n$, the
projection $x \mapsto x_i$ on $\{0,1\}^n$ is a self-dual monotone Boolean function.

articles.title: Balanced unate and balanced monotone functions have equally many NN- and NPN-classes
articles.statement:
For every $n$, call an $n$-variable Boolean function $f$ balanced when $2\,\mathrm{wt}(f) = 2^n$,
where $\mathrm{wt}(f)$ is the weight of $f$. The number of NN-inequivalent balanced unate
$n$-variable Boolean functions equals the number of NN-inequivalent balanced monotone ones, and
the number of NPN-inequivalent balanced unate $n$-variable Boolean functions equals the number of
NPN-inequivalent balanced monotone ones. Here monotone means nondecreasing for the coordinatewise
order with $0 < 1$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 14(b) (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-14`).

articles.title: The empty property has no classes
articles.statement:
For every relation $R$ on $n$-variable Boolean
functions, the number of $R$-inequivalent $n$-variable Boolean functions with the property that
holds for no function is $0$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 2.1.

articles.title: Unate and monotone functions have equally many NN- and NPN-classes
articles.statement:
For every $n$, the
number of NN-inequivalent unate $n$-variable Boolean functions equals the number of
NN-inequivalent monotone ones, and the number of NPN-inequivalent unate $n$-variable Boolean
functions equals the number of NPN-inequivalent monotone ones. Here monotone means nondecreasing
for the coordinatewise order with $0 < 1$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 14(a) (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-14`).

articles.title: Permutation classes counted by non-degenerate ones
articles.statement:
Let $(P_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a family of
properties, $P_n$ a property of $n$-variable Boolean functions, that is invariant under renaming
variables: for all $m$ and $n$, every injection $e$ from $\{1, \dots, m\}$ to $\{1, \dots, n\}$
and every $m$-variable function $g$, the $n$-variable function $x \mapsto g(x \circ e)$ has $P_n$
if and only if $g$ has $P_m$. Write $[P]_n$ for the number of classes of $n$-variable functions
with $P_n$ under permutation of the variables, and $\mathrm{nd}[P]_n$ for the same count over the
non-degenerate $n$-variable functions with $P_n$. Then for every $n$,

$$[P]_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \mathrm{nd}[P]_i.$$

The paper assumes only closure under permutations of the variables; the counting argument also
needs invariance under adding or removing dummy variables. Closure under permutations alone is not
enough: if $P_1$ holds for all four $1$-variable functions and $P_n$ holds for none when
$n \ne 1$, then $[P]_1 = 4$ but $\mathrm{nd}[P]_0 + \mathrm{nd}[P]_1 = 0 + 2 = 2$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 11 (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-11`).

articles.title: Non-degenerate permutation classes as a difference
articles.statement:
Let $(P_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a family of
properties, $P_n$ a property of $n$-variable Boolean functions, that is invariant under renaming
variables: for all $m$ and $n$, every injection $e$ from $\{1, \dots, m\}$ to $\{1, \dots, n\}$
and every $m$-variable function $g$, the $n$-variable function $x \mapsto g(x \circ e)$ has $P_n$
if and only if $g$ has $P_m$. Write $[P]_n$ for the number of classes of $n$-variable functions
with $P_n$ under permutation of the variables, and $\mathrm{nd}[P]_n$ for the same count over the
non-degenerate $n$-variable functions with $P_n$. Then for every $n$,

$$\mathrm{nd}[P]_{n+1} = [P]_{n+1} - [P]_n,$$

where the subtraction is truncated at $0$; this is the paper's
$\mathrm{nd}[P]_n = [P]_n - [P]_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 1$.

The paper assumes only closure under permutations of the variables, which is not enough; see the
summation form of Proposition 11.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 11 (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-11`).

articles.title: Unate versus monotone permutation classes
articles.statement:
Write $[Q]_n$ for the number of classes of
$n$-variable Boolean functions with property $Q$ under permutation of the variables. Let $U$, $M$,
$B$ and $\mathrm{nd}$ be the properties of being unate, monotone (nondecreasing for the
coordinatewise order with $0 < 1$), balanced (true of a function $f$ when $2\,\mathrm{wt}(f) = 2^n$,
where $\mathrm{wt}(f)$ is the weight of $f$) and non-degenerate, and write juxtaposition for
conjunction, so that $BU$ is the property of being balanced and unate. Then for every $n$,
$[\mathrm{nd}\,U]_n \le 2^n [\mathrm{nd}\,M]_n$, $[\mathrm{nd}\,BU]_n \le 2^n [\mathrm{nd}\,BM]_n$,
$[U]_n \le 2^n [M]_n$ and $[BU]_n \le 2^n [BM]_n$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 12 (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-12`).

articles.title: Number of classes of Boolean functions
articles.statement:
Given a relation $R$ and a property $P$ of
$n$-variable Boolean functions, the number of $R$-inequivalent $n$-variable functions with $P$ is
the number of distinct sets $\{g : P(g) \text{ and } R(f, g)\}$ as $f$ ranges over the functions
with $P$. When $R$ is an equivalence relation, this is the number of equivalence classes of $R$
restricted to the functions with $P$. The paper's $[P]_n$ is this count when $R$ is equivalence
under permutation of the variables.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 2.1.

articles.title: Evaluating a concatenation
articles.statement:
For $n$-variable Boolean functions $g$ and $h$, every
$b \in \{0, 1\}$ and every $x \in \{0, 1\}^n$, the concatenation $g \,\|\, h$ takes the value $g(x)$
at the input $(b, x_1, \dots, x_n)$ if $b = 0$ and the value $h(x)$ there if $b = 1$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 2, equation (1).

articles.title: Concatenation of two Boolean functions
articles.statement:
The concatenation $g \,\|\, h$ of two $n$-variable
Boolean functions $g$ and $h$ is the $(n+1)$-variable function whose truth table is that of $g$
followed by that of $h$: its value at $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{n+1})$ is $g(x_2, \dots, x_{n+1})$ if
$x_1 = 0$ and $h(x_2, \dots, x_{n+1})$ if $x_1 = 1$. Equivalently,
$(g \,\|\, h)(x) = \bar{x}_1 g(x_2, \dots, x_{n+1}) \oplus x_1 h(x_2, \dots, x_{n+1})$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 2, equation (1).

articles.title: Weight of the constant one function
articles.statement:
For every $n$, the constant function $1$ on $n$
variables has weight $2^n$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 2.

articles.title: Weight of a Boolean function
articles.statement:
The weight $\mathrm{wt}(f)$ of an $n$-variable Boolean
function $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ is the number of inputs $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ with
$f(x) = 1$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 2.

articles.title: Counting Boolean functions by their non-degenerate restrictions
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a property
of Boolean functions on any number of variables that is invariant under renaming variables
along injections: for all $m, n$, every injective map $e$ from $\{1, \dots, m\}$ to
$\{1, \dots, n\}$ and every $m$-variable function $g$, the $n$-variable function
$x \mapsto g(x_{e(1)}, \dots, x_{e(m)})$ has $P$ if and only if $g$ has $P$. Write $P_n$ for the
number of $n$-variable Boolean functions with $P$ and $\mathrm{nd}\text{-}P_i$ for the number of
non-degenerate $i$-variable Boolean functions with $P$. Then for every $n \ge 0$,

$$P_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} \, \mathrm{nd}\text{-}P_i.$$

The invariance hypothesis cannot be dropped: if $P$ holds exactly for the four $1$-variable
functions, then $P_1 = 4$ but the right-hand side is $0 + 2 = 2$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 1 (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-1`).

articles.title: Weight symmetry of monotone Boolean functions
articles.statement:
For all $n \ge 0$ and all $w$ with
$0 \le w \le 2^n$, the number of monotone $n$-variable Boolean functions of weight $w$ equals
the number of monotone $n$-variable Boolean functions of weight $2^n - w$.

The source assumes $n \ge 1$; the case $n = 0$ is included here.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 8 (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-8`).

articles.title: Counting non-degenerate Boolean functions by inclusion–exclusion
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a property
of Boolean functions on any number of variables that is invariant under renaming variables
along injections: for all $m, n$, every injective map $e$ from $\{1, \dots, m\}$ to
$\{1, \dots, n\}$ and every $m$-variable function $g$, the $n$-variable function
$x \mapsto g(x_{e(1)}, \dots, x_{e(m)})$ has $P$ if and only if $g$ has $P$. Write $P_i$ for the
number of $i$-variable Boolean functions with $P$ and $\mathrm{nd}\text{-}P_n$ for the number of
non-degenerate $n$-variable Boolean functions with $P$. Then for every $n \ge 0$,

$$\mathrm{nd}\text{-}P_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-i} \binom{n}{i} P_i.$$

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 1 (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-1`).

articles.title: Unate versus monotone Boolean function counts
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 0$, write $U_n$ and $M_n$ for
the numbers of unate and of monotone $n$-variable Boolean functions, $BU_n$ and $BM_n$ for the
numbers of those that are moreover balanced, that is, twice their weight equals $2^n$, and write
the prefix $\mathrm{nd}\text{-}$ for the same counts restricted to non-degenerate functions.
Then $\mathrm{nd}\text{-}U_n = 2^n \, \mathrm{nd}\text{-}M_n$,
$\mathrm{nd}\text{-}BU_n = 2^n \, \mathrm{nd}\text{-}BM_n$, $U_n \le 2^n M_n$ and
$BU_n \le 2^n BM_n$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 3 (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-3`).

articles.title: Weight symmetry of unate Boolean functions
articles.statement:
For all $n \ge 0$ and all $w$ with
$0 \le w \le 2^n$, the number of unate $n$-variable Boolean functions of weight $w$ equals the
number of unate $n$-variable Boolean functions of weight $2^n - w$.

The source assumes $n \ge 1$; the case $n = 0$ is included here.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 9 (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-9`).

articles.title: Boolean functions decreasing in a variable
articles.statement:
An $n$-variable Boolean function $f$ is
monotone decreasing in the variable $x_i$ if for every input $x$ with $x_i = 0$, changing $x_i$
to $1$ does not increase the value: $f(x') \le f(x)$, where $x'$ agrees with $x$ except that
$x'_i = 1$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 2.

articles.title: Boolean functions increasing in a variable
articles.statement:
An $n$-variable Boolean function $f$ is
monotone increasing in the variable $x_i$ if for every input $x$ with $x_i = 0$, changing $x_i$
to $1$ does not decrease the value: $f(x) \le f(x')$, where $x'$ agrees with $x$ except that
$x'_i = 1$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 2.

articles.title: NN-equivalence of monotone Boolean functions
articles.statement:
Let $f$ and $g$ be monotone $n$-variable
Boolean functions. Then $f$ and $g$ are NN-equivalent ($g$ is obtained from $f$ by negating
some inputs and possibly the output) if and only if either $g = f$, or $g(x) = \lnot f(x \oplus a)$
for all $x$, where $a \in \{0,1\}^n$ has $a_i = 1$ exactly for the variables $x_i$ on which $f$
is non-degenerate and $\oplus$ is coordinatewise exclusive or.

This does not mean that every NN-class of monotone functions has two elements: for $n = 1$
and $f(x) = x_1$, the only monotone function NN-equivalent to $f$ is $f$ itself.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 13 (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-13`).

articles.title: NN-equivalence is reflexive
articles.statement:
Every Boolean function is NN-equivalent to itself.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 13.

articles.title: NN-equivalence of Boolean functions
articles.statement:
An $n$-variable Boolean function $f$ is
NN-equivalent to $g$ when $g$ is obtained from $f$ by negating some of the inputs and
possibly the output: there are $a \in \{0,1\}^n$ and $c \in \{0,1\}$ such that
$g(x) = f(x \oplus a) \oplus c$ for every $x \in \{0,1\}^n$, where $\oplus$ is exclusive or
(coordinatewise on vectors).

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 13.

articles.title: A projection is non-degenerate on its own variable
articles.statement:
For every $n$ and every index
$i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$, the projection $x \mapsto x_i$ on $\{0,1\}^n$ is non-degenerate on
the variable $x_i$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 2.

articles.title: Non-degeneracy in a variable
articles.statement:
An $n$-variable Boolean function $f$ is non-degenerate
on the variable $x_i$ when flipping $x_i$ changes the value of $f$ at some input: there is
$x \in \{0,1\}^n$ with $f(x) \ne f(x')$, where $x'$ is $x$ with its $i$-th coordinate negated.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 2.

articles.title: NPN-equivalence is reflexive
articles.statement:
Every $n$-variable Boolean function is NPN-equivalent to
itself.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 14.

articles.title: NPN-equivalence of Boolean functions
articles.statement:
An $n$-variable Boolean function $f$ is
NPN-equivalent to $g$ when $g$ is obtained from $f$ by permuting the variables, negating some
of the inputs and possibly negating the output: there are a permutation $\sigma$ of
$\{1, \ldots, n\}$, a vector $a \in \{0,1\}^n$ and a bit $c \in \{0,1\}$ such that
$g(x) = f(x_{\sigma(1)} \oplus a_1, \ldots, x_{\sigma(n)} \oplus a_n) \oplus c$ for every
$x \in \{0,1\}^n$, where $\oplus$ is exclusive or.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 14.

articles.title: Permutation equivalence is reflexive
articles.statement:
Every $n$-variable Boolean function is
permutation-equivalent to itself.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 2.1.

articles.title: Permutation equivalence of Boolean functions
articles.statement:
An $n$-variable Boolean function $f$ is
permutation-equivalent to $g$ when $g$ is obtained from $f$ by permuting the variables: there
is a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ such that
$g(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = f(x_{\sigma(1)}, \ldots, x_{\sigma(n)})$ for every $x \in \{0,1\}^n$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 2.1.

articles.title: Non-degenerate Boolean functions
articles.statement:
An $n$-variable Boolean function $f$ is non-degenerate
when it is non-degenerate on every variable $x_i$, $1 \le i \le n$: for each $i$ there is an input
$x \in \{0,1\}^n$ with $f(x) \ne f(x')$, where $x'$ is $x$ with its $i$-th coordinate negated.
For $n = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so both $0$-variable (constant) functions are
non-degenerate, matching the paper's convention.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 2 and Remark 2.

articles.title: Unateness of a concatenation
articles.statement:
Let $g$ and $h$ be $n$-variable Boolean functions and let
$g \| h$ be their concatenation, the $(n+1)$-variable function equal to $g$ of the remaining
variables when the first variable is $0$ and to $h$ of them when it is $1$. Then $g \| h$ is
unate if and only if $g$ and $h$ are unate, for each variable $x_i$ either both $g$ and $h$
are monotone increasing in $x_i$ or both are monotone decreasing in $x_i$, and $g \le h$
pointwise or $h \le g$ pointwise.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 6 (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-6`).

articles.title: The negation of a unate function is unate
articles.statement:
If an $n$-variable Boolean function $f$ is
unate, then so is its negation $x \mapsto \lnot f(x)$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 7 (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-7`).

articles.title: Monotone Boolean functions are unate
articles.statement:
Every Boolean function $f$ on $n$ variables that
is monotone, for the coordinatewise order on $\{0,1\}^n$ with $0 \le 1$, is unate.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 1.

articles.title: Unate Boolean function
articles.statement:
A Boolean function $f$ on $n$ variables, with Boolean values
$0 < 1$, is unate when for each variable $i$ either $f$ is increasing in $x_i$ (changing $x_i$
from $0$ to $1$, with the other variables fixed, never decreases the value of $f$) or $f$ is
decreasing in $x_i$ (that change never increases the value of $f$).

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Section 1.

articles.title: Monotone concatenations of Boolean functions (Bakoev)
articles.statement:
Let $g$ and $h$ be Boolean
functions on $n$ variables, and let $g \parallel h$ be their concatenation, the function on
$n + 1$ variables that equals $g$ of the remaining variables when its first variable is $0$ and
$h$ of them when it is $1$. Then $g \parallel h$ is monotone if and only if $g$ and $h$ are both
monotone and $g(x) \le h(x)$ for every $x \in \{0,1\}^n$.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 4 (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-4`), quoting Bakoev.

articles.title: The dual of a monotone Boolean function is monotone
articles.statement:
If a Boolean function $f$ on $n$
variables is monotone, then so is its dual $f^\star$, defined by $f^\star(x) = \neg f(\bar{x})$,
where $\bar{x}$ is the coordinatewise complement of $x \in \{0,1\}^n$.

In the notation of the source, $f^\star$ is $\overline{f^r}$, where $f^r(x) = f(\bar{x})$ is
the function whose truth table is that of $f$ reversed.

## Sources

- Biswas and Sarkar, *Counting Unate and Monotone Boolean Functions under Restrictions of Balancedness and Non-Degeneracy*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.4, Proposition 5 (`jis-2025-25.3.4-prop-5`).

articles.title: Catalan numbers other than $1$ are not perfect powers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 2$, the
$n$-th Catalan number $C_n$ is not a perfect power: there are no natural numbers $m$ and $k$
with $k \ge 2$ and $C_n = m^k$.

The proof of Checcoli and D'Adderio checks small cases directly, and for $n \ge 6$ uses a
Ramanujan prime $p$ with $n + 2 \le p < 2n$, which divides $C_n$ exactly once, so $C_n = m^k$
with $k \ge 2$ is impossible.

## Sources

- Nathaniel Benjamin, Grant Fickes, Eugene Fiorini, Edgar Jaramillo Rodriguez, Eric Jovinelly, and Tony W. H. Wong, "Primes and Perfect Powers in the Catalan Triangle," Journal of Integer Sequences 22 (2019), Article 19.7.6, Theorem [Checcoli–D'Adderio], lines 148–150, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL22/Fiorini/fiorini3.tex

articles.title: Parity of Catalan numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the $n$th Catalan number $C_n$
is odd if and only if $n = 2^a - 1$ for some natural number $a$.

## Sources

- Alon Regev, "The Central Component of a Triangulation", Journal of Integer Sequences 16 (2013), Article 13.4.1, theorem `oddcats`, lines 132–147 of <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL16/Regev/regev4.tex>. This entry records the displayed theorem statement. Lines 85–88 define `C_n` with the standard indexing used by Mathlib's `catalan`, so no index shift is required. The natural subtraction in `2 ^ a - 1` is safe because `2 ^ a` is positive. No parallel Catalan definition is introduced.

articles.title: Closed form of the Catalan generating function
articles.statement:
Let $C_n$ be the $n$th Catalan number.
For every real number $x$ with $|x| < 1/4$ and $x \neq 0$,

$$
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} C_n x^n = \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - 4x}}{2x}.
$$

The hypothesis $x \neq 0$ excludes the removable singularity of the right-hand side at $x = 0$.

## Sources

- Paul Barry, "A Note on a Family of Generalized Pascal Matrices Defined by Riordan Arrays", Journal of Integer Sequences 16 (2013), Article 13.5.4, proposition lines 380–388, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL16/Barry2/barry231.tex>. Mathlib has `PowerSeries.catalanSeries` and its quadratic functional equation, but its source file explicitly lists the square-root closed form as a TODO; this theorem records the analytic closed form rather than duplicating the formal series definition.

articles.title: Catalan numbers are at most $4^n$
articles.statement: The `n`th Catalan number is at most `4 ^ n`.

articles.title: Explicit formula for the Fine numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the Fine number
$F(n)$, indexed from $0$ so that $F(0) = 1$, satisfies

$$F(n) = \frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{i=0}^{n} (-2)^i \, (i+1) \binom{2(n+1)}{n-i}.$$

The source indexes from $1$: writing $\mathbb{F}_m = F(m - 1)$ for $m \ge 1$, it states
$\mathbb{F}_m = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} (-2)^{i-1} \, i \binom{2m}{m-i}$, which becomes the
formula above on setting $m = n + 1$ and shifting the summation index down by one.

articles.title: Fine numbers
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the Fine number $F(n)$, indexed from $0$ so
that $F(0) = 1$, is the rational number

$$F(n) = \frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{i=0}^{n} (-2)^i \, (i+1) \binom{2(n+1)}{n-i}.$$

## Sources

- Fine numbers (OEIS A000957), zero-based: `fineNumber n` is source `𝔽_(n+1)`. Source explicit formula `𝔽_n = (1/n) * ∑_{i=1}^n (-2)^(i-1) * i * C(2n, n-i)` with `𝔽_1 = 1`, from JIS VOL21/Janjic3/janjic96.tex lines 105-108 and 157-158. <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL21/Janjic3/janjic96.tex>.

articles.title: Closed form of the Eloe–Kublik gamma array
articles.statement:
Let $\gamma_{n,k}$, for natural numbers $n$ and
$k$, be real numbers such that $\gamma_{n,0} = 1$ for every $n$, $\gamma_{2n-1,n} = 0$ for every
$n \ge 1$, and

$$\gamma_{n,k} = (1 + \frac{2k}{n+2})\,\gamma_{n-1,k} + \frac{2k-n-1}{n+2}\,\gamma_{n-1,k-1}$$

whenever $n \ge 2$ and $1 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. Then
$\gamma_{n,k} = (-\frac{1}{4})^k \binom{n}{2k} C_k$ for all natural numbers $n$ and $k$ with
$k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, where $C_k$ is the $k$-th Catalan number.

## Sources

- Paul Eloe and Catherine Kublik, "When Numerical Analysis Crosses Paths with Catalan and Generalized Motzkin Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 21 (2018), Article 18.8.4, Theorem `closedform_thm`, lines 390-396, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL21/Kublik/kublik2.tex>; the recursion and initial conditions are equation `gamma_linear_recursion`, lines 87-91.

articles.title: Generating function of the generalized Catalan–Schröder numbers
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative
ring, let $s, t, p \in R$, and let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence in $R$ with $a_0 = 1$,
$a_1 = p$ and

$$a_n = s\,a_{n-1} + t \sum_{k=0}^{n-3} a_{k+1}\,a_{n-k-2} \qquad (n \ge 2).$$

Let $g$ and $f$ be formal power series over $R$ with

$$(1 - (s - 2t)X)\,g = 1 + (p - s + t)X, \qquad (1 - (s - 2t)X)^2 f = tX\,(1 + (p - s + t)X),$$

and let $C(X) = \sum_{n \ge 0} C_n X^n$, where $C_n$ is the $n$-th Catalan number viewed in $R$.
Then $\sum_{n \ge 0} a_n X^n = g \cdot C(f)$, where $C(f)$ is the power series obtained by
substituting $f$ for $X$ in $C$. Since $1 - (s - 2t)X$ is invertible in $R[[X]]$, these
equations determine $g$ and $f$, and $f$ has zero constant term.

Barry prints $f$ without the factor $X$ in $1 + (p - s + t)X$. That version is false: for
$s = 2$, $t = 1$, $p = 2$ the resulting series $g \cdot C(f)$ has coefficient $3$ at $X$, not
$a_1 = 2$. The recurrence forces the factor restored here.

The proof substitutes $f$ into the Catalan equation $C = 1 + X C^2$, shows that $g \cdot C(f)$
satisfies the same quadratic functional equation as $\sum_{n \ge 0} a_n X^n$, and concludes by
comparing coefficients.

## Sources
