- Paul Barry, "Generalized Catalan Recurrences, Riordan Arrays, Elliptic Curves, and Orthogonal Polynomials", Journal of Integer Sequences 24 (2021), Article 21.5.1, Proposition lines 367-373, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL24/Barry/barry431.tex>.

articles.title: Functional equation of the generalized Catalan–Schröder recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a
commutative ring, let $s, t, p \in R$, and let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence in $R$ with
$a_0 = 1$, $a_1 = p$ and

$$a_n = s\,a_{n-1} + t \sum_{k=0}^{n-3} a_{k+1}\,a_{n-k-2} \qquad (n \ge 2).$$

Then the power series $A = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n X^n$ over $R$ satisfies
$A - 1 = pX + sX\,(A - 1) + tX\,(A - 1)^2$.

articles.title: Second formula for the Narayana number
articles.statement:
For positive integers $n$ and $k$, the Narayana
number $N(n, k)$ satisfies $N(n, k) = \lfloor \binom{n-1}{k-1}\binom{n}{k-1} / k \rfloor$.

articles.title: Defining formula for the Narayana number
articles.statement:
For positive integers $n$ and $k$, the Narayana
number $N(n, k)$ satisfies $N(n, k) = \lfloor \binom{n}{k}\binom{n}{k-1} / n \rfloor$.

articles.title: Narayana polynomial coefficients at positive indices
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n$ and
$k$, the Narayana polynomial coefficient in row $n + 1$ and degree $k + 1$ equals the Narayana
number $N(n + 1, k + 1)$.

This holds by definition.

articles.title: Narayana polynomial coefficients
articles.statement:
The Narayana polynomial coefficients are the natural
numbers $a(n, k)$, for natural numbers $n$ and $k$, given by $a(0, 0) = 1$, $a(0, k) = 0$ for
$k \ge 1$, $a(n, 0) = 0$ for $n \ge 1$, and $a(n, k) = N(n, k)$ for $n, k \ge 1$, where $N(n, k)$
is the Narayana number. So row zero is $1$ and every positive row has zero constant term.

articles.title: Narayana polynomials
articles.statement:
For a semiring $R$ and a natural number $n$, the $n$-th Narayana
polynomial is

$$N_n(X) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a(n, k)\, X^k \in R[X],$$

where $a(n, k)$ is the Narayana polynomial coefficient, taken in $R$. Since $a(0, 0) = 1$ and,
for $n \ge 1$, $a(n, 0) = 0$ and $a(n, k)$ is the Narayana number $N(n, k)$ for $k \ge 1$, the
first polynomials are $N_0 = 1$, $N_1 = X$, $N_2 = X^2 + X$ and $N_3 = X^3 + 3X^2 + X$.

articles.title: Narayana number
articles.statement:
For positive integers $n$ and $k$, the Narayana number $N(n, k)$ is the
natural number $\lfloor \binom{n}{k}\binom{n}{k-1} / n \rfloor$.

articles.title: Palindromic Narayana numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the palindromic Narayana
number is the rational number $\tilde{N}(n, k) = \binom{n}{k} \binom{n+1}{k} / (k+1)$.

The value is taken in $\mathbb{Q}$ so that the displayed quotient is represented literally.

## Sources

- Paul Barry, "Generalized Catalan Numbers Associated with a Family of Pascal-like Triangles," <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL22/Barry3/barry422.tex>.

articles.title: Binomial coefficient with rational upper argument
articles.statement:
For a rational number $r$ and a natural
number $k$, the generalized binomial coefficient is the rational number
$\binom{r}{k} = r(r-1)\cdots(r-k+1)/k!$, which is $1$ for $k = 0$.

It is the binomial coefficient with fractional upper argument used in the $(p,q)$-Patalan
numbers.

## Sources

- Thomas M. Richardson, "The Super Patalan Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.3.3, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Richardson/rich2.tex>.

articles.title: The (p,q)-Patalan numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $p$ and $q$ with $p > 1$ and $0 < q < p$,
the $(p,q)$-Patalan number with index $n \in \mathbb{N}$ is the rational number
$b(n) = -p^{2n+1} \binom{n - q/p}{n+1}$, where $\binom{r}{k} = r(r-1)\cdots(r-k+1)/k!$ is the
binomial coefficient with rational upper argument $r$.

## Sources

- Thomas M. Richardson, "The Super Patalan Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.3.3, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Richardson/rich2.tex>.

articles.title: The (p,q)-super Patalan numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $p$ and $q$ with $p > 1$ and
$0 < q < p$, and natural numbers $i$ and $j$, the $(p,q)$-super Patalan number is the rational
number $Q(i,j) = (-1)^j p^{2(i+j)} \binom{i - q/p}{i+j}$, where
$\binom{r}{k} = r(r-1)\cdots(r-k+1)/k!$ is the binomial coefficient with rational upper
argument $r$.

## Sources

- Thomas M. Richardson, "The Super Patalan Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.3.3.

articles.title: Admissible parameters for the (p,q)-Patalan numbers
articles.statement:
An admissible parameter pair for the
$(p,q)$-Patalan numbers is a pair of natural numbers $p$ and $q$ with $p > 1$ and $0 < q < p$.

## Sources

- Thomas M. Richardson, "The Super Patalan Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.3.3, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Richardson/rich2.tex>.

articles.title: Super Patalan numbers of order p
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p > 1$ and natural numbers $i$ and
$j$, the super Patalan number of order $p$ is the $(p,q)$-super Patalan number with $q = 1$, that
is, the rational number $(-1)^j p^{2(i+j)} \binom{i - 1/p}{i+j}$, where
$\binom{r}{k} = r(r-1)\cdots(r-k+1)/k!$ is the binomial coefficient with rational upper
argument $r$.

articles.title: Raney's cycle lemma for arbitrary integer lists
articles.statement:
Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be a
list of integers whose entries sum to $-1$. Then there is exactly one index $r$ with $0 \le r < n$
such that every proper prefix of the rotation $(a_r, \dots, a_{n-1}, a_0, \dots, a_{r-1})$ has
nonnegative sum: for every $t$ with $0 \le t < n$, the sum of the first $t$ entries of this
rotation is at least $0$.

articles.title: Raney's cycle lemma
articles.statement:
Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be a list of integers, each at least
$-1$, whose entries sum to $-1$. Then there is exactly one index $r$ with $0 \le r < n$ such that
every proper prefix of the rotation $(a_r, \dots, a_{n-1}, a_0, \dots, a_{r-1})$ has nonnegative
sum: for every $t$ with $0 \le t < n$, the sum of the first $t$ entries of this rotation is at
least $0$.

The hypothesis that every entry is at least $-1$ is not needed; Raney's cycle lemma for arbitrary
integer lists proves the same conclusion without it.

## Sources

- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL24/Haupt/haupt4.tex>, lines 804-807. Lean's zero-based left rotation is a bijective reindexing of the source's cut after `a_r`; `t < a.length` ranges over every proper prefix, with `t = 0` giving the true empty-prefix condition. The lower bound `hlower` is not needed; see `raney_cycle_lemma_sum_neg_one_general`.

articles.title: Riordan numbers as an alternating Catalan sum
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the $n$-th
Riordan number $r_n$ equals

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} \binom{n}{k} C_k,$$

where $C_k$ is the $k$-th Catalan number.

articles.title: Riordan numbers
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the $n$-th Riordan number is the integer

$$r_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} \binom{n}{k} C_k,$$

where $C_k$ is the $k$-th Catalan number.

## Sources

- closed form (Kirgizov lines 436-438).

articles.title: Fine numbers as an alternating binomial sum
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 2$, the Fine
number $F(n)$ satisfies

$$F(n) = \frac{1}{2} (-1)^n +
\frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} \left(1 - \frac{n}{k+1}\right) \binom{n+k}{k}.$$

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Corollary 3.

articles.title: Fine numbers from Sabar's triangle
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 2$, the Fine number
$F(n)$ is the difference of two entries of row $2n$ of Sabar's triangle $s$:
$F(n) = s(2n, n+1) - s(2n, n-1)$.

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Harmonic numbers from Sabar's triangle
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 2$, the harmonic
number $H_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k}$ and the entries $s(n-1, i)$ of Sabar's triangle satisfy

$$H_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \binom{n-1}{i}^{-1} +
\sum_{i=0}^{n-2} \frac{(-1)^{n-i} \, s(n-1, i)}{n-i}.$$

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Central entries of Sabar's triangle and Fine numbers
articles.statement:
Let $F(m)$ denote the Fine numbers
and $C_m$ the Catalan numbers. For every natural number $n \ge 1$, the entries of Sabar's
triangle $s$ satisfy

$$s(2n, n) = \frac{1}{6} \binom{2n+2}{n+1} + \frac{2}{3} F(n) + (-1)^{n+1},$$



$$s(2n, n) = \frac{1}{3} (2n+1) C_n + \frac{2}{3} F(n) + (-1)^{n+1},$$



$$s(2n, n) = \frac{2}{3} \binom{2n}{n} - \frac{1}{3} F(n-1) + (-1)^{n+1},$$

and

$$s(2n-1, n) = \frac{2}{3} \binom{2n-1}{n} + \frac{1}{3} F(n-1) + (-1)^n.$$

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Central entries of Sabar's triangle and Whitt's numbers
articles.statement:
Let $C(2, m)$ denote Whitt's
generalized Catalan numbers at $\alpha = 2$. For every natural number $n \ge 1$, the central
entry $s(2n, n)$ of Sabar's triangle satisfies

$$s(2n, n) = \frac{2}{3} \binom{2n}{n} - \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{C(2, n)}{2^{n+1}} +
(-1)^{n+1} + \frac{(-1)^n}{2^{n+1}}.$$

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Theorem 7.

articles.title: A recurrence for Sabar's triangle in small cases
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n$ and $i$ with
$i < n < 8$, the entries of Sabar's triangle $s$ satisfy
$s(n + 2, i + 1) = s(n, i + 1) + \binom{n+1}{i}$.

This is the source's third basic identity $s(n, i) = s(n-2, i) + \binom{n-1}{i-1}$, stated here
only in these cases. It fails for $i = n$ and $i = n + 1$ (for $i \ge n + 2$ both sides are $0$):
for example $s(2, 1) = 2$ but $s(0, 1) + \binom{1}{0} = 1$.

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Section 2 (identities following from the definition).

articles.title: Rows 5 and 10 of Sabar's triangle
articles.statement:
The entries $s(5, i)$ of Sabar's triangle for
$i = 0, 1, \dots, 4$ are $1, 2, 7, 6, 5$, and the entries $s(10, i)$ for $i = 0, 1, \dots, 9$
are $0, 6, 24, 71, 129, 167, 147, 92, 36, 10$.

These are rows $n = 5$ and $n = 10$ of the source's Table 1.

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Table 1.

articles.title: Sabar's triangle
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $i$, the entry $s(n, i)$ of Sabar's triangle
is the integer

$$s(n, i) = \sum_{j=i+1}^{n} (-1)^{n-j} \binom{j}{i}.$$

In particular $s(n, i) = 0$ for $i \ge n$, the empty sum.

In the source, $s(n, i)$ counts certain grid paths; for $0 \le i \le n - 1$ these numbers form
OEIS A341091.

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Section 2 (definition of `s(n, i)`).

articles.title: Consecutive binomial sums weighted by powers of 2
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, let
$V_m(2) = \sum_{k=0}^{m} \binom{m+k}{k} 2^k$. For every natural number $n \ge 1$,
$V_n(2) + V_{n+1}(2) = 3 \cdot 2^n \binom{2n+2}{n+1}$.

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Reciprocal binomial sums from Sabar's triangle
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 2$, the
entries $s(n-1, i)$ of Sabar's triangle satisfy

$$\frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i}^{-1} =
1 + \sum_{i=0}^{n-2} \frac{(-1)^{n-i-1} \, s(n-1, i)}{(n-i)(n+1-i)}.$$

This is the source's Corollary 1 with the sign used in its proof. As printed, with $(-1)^{n-i}$,
it fails at $n = 2$: the left side is $5/6$ but $1 + s(1, 0)/(2 \cdot 3) = 7/6$.

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Sabar's alternating binomial sum equal to $n$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 2$, in the
rational numbers,

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k+1} \left(1 - \frac{2k}{n+1} + \frac{n}{k+1}\right) \binom{n+k}{k} = n.$$

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Corollary 2.

articles.title: The harmonic numbers as an alternating sum of Sabar numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n \ge 2$, writing $s(m, i)$ for Sabar's triangle and $H_n = \sum_{j=1}^{n} 1/j$ for the $n$-th
harmonic number, in the rational numbers

$$\sum_{i=0}^{2n-2} \frac{(-1)^i \, s(2n-1, i)}{i+1} = H_n.$$

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Fine numbers from Whitt's generalized Catalan numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 1$,
the Fine number $F(n)$, indexed so that $F(0) = 1$ and $F(1) = 0$, and Whitt's generalized Catalan
number $C(2, n+1)$ at $\alpha = 2$ satisfy

$$2^{n+2} F(n) = C(2, n+1) + 3(-1)^n.$$

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Corollary 4.

articles.title: Consecutive Whitt generalized Catalan numbers at $\alpha = 2$
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n \ge 1$, Whitt's generalized Catalan numbers at $\alpha = 2$ satisfy

$$C(2, n) + C(2, n+1) = 2^{n+1} c_n,$$

where $c_n = \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ is the $n$-th Catalan number.

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Touchard's Catalan identity
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, writing
$C_k = \binom{2k}{k}/(k+1)$ for the $k$-th Catalan number,

$$C_{n+1} = \sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} \binom{n}{2i} 2^{n-2i} C_i.$$

## Sources

- https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL20/Dershowitz/dersh3.tex, lines 274-277. A second JIS source prints the finite upper bound as `floor(n/2)`.

articles.title: Von Szily's identity for super Catalan numbers
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $m$ and $n$,

$$
\left\lfloor \frac{(2m)!\,(2n)!}{m!\,n!\,(m+n)!} \right\rfloor
= \sum_{k=\max(-m,-n)}^{\min(m,n)} (-1)^k \binom{2m}{m+k} \binom{2n}{n+k},
$$

where the sum runs over the integers $k$ with $\max(-m, -n) \le k \le \min(m, n)$.

The quotient inside the floor is the super Catalan number $S(m, n)$. The source sums over all
$k \in \mathbb{Z}$; only the terms in this range are nonzero.

## Sources

- Kendra Killpatrick, *Super FiboCatalan Numbers and Their Lucas Analogues*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.5.8, von Szily identity quoted in the Open problems section, lines 671–674, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL28/Killpatrick/killp6.tex>, citing I. Gessel, *Super ballot numbers*, J. Symbolic Comput. 14 (1992), p. 11.

articles.title: Whitt's generalized Catalan number at one
articles.statement:
For every rational number $\alpha$, Whitt's
generalized Catalan number $C(\alpha, 1)$ equals $1$.

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Section 5 (definition of `C(α, n+1)` at `n = 0`).

articles.title: Whitt's generalized Catalan numbers in the source's indexing
articles.statement:
For every rational number
$\alpha$ and every natural number $n$, Whitt's generalized Catalan number $C(\alpha, n + 1)$ is

$$C(\alpha, n + 1) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \left(1 - \frac{k}{n+1}\right) \binom{n+k}{k} \alpha^k.$$

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Section 5 (definition of `C(α, n+1)`).

articles.title: First values of Whitt's generalized Catalan numbers with parameter two
articles.statement:
Whitt's
generalized Catalan numbers with parameter $\alpha = 2$ satisfy $C(2, 1) = 1$, $C(2, 2) = 3$,
$C(2, 3) = 13$ and $C(2, 4) = 67$.

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Section 5 (OEIS A064062).

articles.title: Whitt's generalized Catalan numbers with parameter zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n \ge 1$, Whitt's generalized Catalan number $C(0, n)$ equals $1$: only the term $k = 0$ of the
defining sum survives.

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Section 5 (definition of `C(α, n+1)`).

articles.title: Whitt's generalized Catalan number at zero
articles.statement:
For every rational number $\alpha$, Whitt's
generalized Catalan number $C(\alpha, 0)$ equals $0$, being an empty sum.

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Section 5 (definition of `C(α, n+1)`).

articles.title: Whitt's generalized Catalan numbers
articles.statement:
For a rational number $\alpha$ and a natural number
$n$, Whitt's generalized Catalan number $C(\alpha, n)$ is the rational number

$$C(\alpha, n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \left(1 - \frac{k}{n}\right) \binom{n-1+k}{k} \alpha^k.$$

In particular $C(\alpha, 0) = 0$, the empty sum. Writing $n + 1$ for $n$ gives the source's form
$C(\alpha, n+1) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \left(1 - \frac{k}{n+1}\right) \binom{n+k}{k} \alpha^k$. For
$\alpha = 2$ and $n \ge 1$ these are the terms of OEIS A064062.

## Sources

- Sabar Taoufik, *A New Triangle of Numbers: Properties and Observations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A27, Section 5 (definition of `C(α, n+1)`, quoting W. Whitt, J. Integer Seq. 14 (2011)).

articles.title: Parity of a sum of adjacent binomial coefficients
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$
with $k \ge 1$, $\binom{n}{k} + \binom{n+1}{k} \equiv \binom{n}{k-1} \pmod 2$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Lemma 15 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-lem-15`).

articles.title: First horizontal sums of a Delannoy array with binomial seeds
articles.statement:
Let $R(m, n)$, for
$m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, be integers with $R(m+1, n+1) = R(m, n+1) + R(m+1, n) + R(m, n)$ for all
$m, n$. Let $k \ge 1$ and suppose $R(0, n) = \binom{k+n}{k}$ for all $n$. Then for all $m$ and
$n$, $R(m, n) + R(m, n+1) \equiv \binom{k+n}{k-1} \pmod 2$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Theorem 17 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-thm-17`).

articles.title: Parity of iterated horizontal sums of a Delannoy array with binomial seeds
articles.statement:
Let $R(m, n)$,
for $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, be integers with $R(m+1, n+1) = R(m, n+1) + R(m+1, n) + R(m, n)$ for
all $m, n$. For an array $S$ let $(HS)(m, n) = S(m, n) + S(m, n+1)$, and write $R^i = H^i R$ for
the $i$-fold horizontal sum, so $R^0 = R$. Let $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and suppose
$R(0, n) = \binom{k+n}{k}$ for all $n$; the values $R(m, 0)$ for $m \ge 1$ are arbitrary. Then
every entry of $R^{k+1}$ is even, and for every $j \le k$ some entry of $R^j$ is odd.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Lemma 16 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-lem-16`).

articles.title: Powers of two dividing iterated horizontal sums of a Delannoy array
articles.statement:
Let $R(m, n)$, for
$m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, be integers with $R(m+1, n+1) = R(m, n+1) + R(m+1, n) + R(m, n)$ for all
$m, n$. For an array $S$ let $(HS)(m, n) = S(m, n) + S(m, n+1)$, and write $R^i = H^i R$ for the
$i$-fold horizontal sum. Let $k, i \in \mathbb{N}$ with $i \ge 1$, and suppose
$R(0, n) = \binom{k+n}{k}$ for all $n$. Then every entry of $R^{k+i}$ is divisible by $2^i$, and
some entry of $R^{k+i}$ is not divisible by $2^{i+1}$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Theorem 18 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-thm-18`).

articles.title: Rows of iterated horizontal sums of a Delannoy array agree mod 2
articles.statement:
Let $R(m, n)$, for
$m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, be integers with $R(m+1, n+1) = R(m, n+1) + R(m+1, n) + R(m, n)$ for all
$m, n$. For an array $S$ let $(HS)(m, n) = S(m, n) + S(m, n+1)$, and write $R^i = H^i R$ for the
$i$-fold horizontal sum. Then for every $i \ge 1$ and all $m, m', n \in \mathbb{N}$,
$R^i(m, n) \equiv R^i(m', n) \pmod 2$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Corollary 14 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-cor-14`).

articles.title: Parity of adjacent rows of a Delannoy array
articles.statement:
Let $R(m, n)$, for $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, be
integers with $R(m+1, n+1) = R(m, n+1) + R(m+1, n) + R(m, n)$ for all $m, n$, and let
$m \in \mathbb{N}$. If $R(m, 0) \equiv R(m+1, 0) \pmod 2$, then $R(m, i) \equiv R(m+1, i) \pmod 2$
for all $i$; if $R(m, 0) \not\equiv R(m+1, 0) \pmod 2$, then
$R(m, i) \not\equiv R(m+1, i) \pmod 2$ for all $i$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Theorem 13 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-thm-13`).

articles.title: Delannoy numbers as a sum of powers of two
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $m$ and $n$, the
Delannoy number $D(m, n)$, that is, the Delannoy triangle entry $T(m + n, m; 1)$, satisfies
$D(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(m, n)} \binom{m}{j} \binom{n}{j} 2^j$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Theorem 8 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-thm-8`).

articles.title: Unified power-of-two sums for generalized Delannoy numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $m$,
$n$, write $D_k(m, n)$ and $D^k(m, n)$ for the lower and upper generalized Delannoy numbers. If
$m \ge k$ and $n \ge k$, then
$D_k(m, n) = \sum_{j=k}^{\min(m, n)} \binom{m-k}{j-k} \binom{n}{j} 2^j$; and, for all $k$, $m$, $n$,
$D^k(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(m, n)} \binom{m+k}{j+k} \binom{n}{j} 2^j$.

With the convention $D_{-k} = D^k$, the second formula is the first with $k$ replaced by $-k$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Theorem 11 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-thm-11`).

articles.title: Lower generalized Delannoy numbers as a sum of powers of two
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $m$,
$n$ with $m \ge k$ and $n \ge k$, the lower generalized Delannoy number $D_k(m, n)$ satisfies
$D_k(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(m-k, n-k)} \binom{m-k}{j} \binom{n}{j+k} 2^{j+k}$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Theorem 9 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-thm-9`).

articles.title: A value of the lower generalized Delannoy number
articles.statement:
The lower generalized Delannoy number
$D_1(2, 2)$ equals $8$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Section 1 (central theorem `D_k(m, n) = 2^k D^k(n - k, m - k)`).

articles.title: Relationship identities for generalized Delannoy numbers
articles.statement:
The four relationship identities for `D_k` (`k ≥ 1`, `m, n ≥ k`):
`D_k(m, n) + D_k(m, n + 1) = 2 D_(k-1)(m, n)`, `D_k(m, n) + D_k(m + 1, n) = D_(k+1)(m + 1, n + 1)`,
`D_k(m, n + 1) - D_k(m, n) = 2 D_(k-1)(m - 1, n)`, `D_k(m + 1, n) - D_k(m, n) = D_(k+1)(m + 1, n)`.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Theorem 7 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-thm-7`).

articles.title: The lower and upper generalized Delannoy numbers agree at index zero
articles.statement:
For natural
numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$, let
$D_k(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{m + n - k - j}{n - k} \binom{n}{j}$ (with subtraction
truncated at $0$) and
$D^k(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{m + n + k - j}{n + k} \binom{n}{j}$ be the lower
and upper generalized Delannoy numbers. Then $D_0(m, n) = D^0(m, n)$ for all natural numbers
$m$ and $n$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Section 1.

articles.title: Lower generalized Delannoy number
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$, the generalized
Delannoy number $D_k(m, n)$ is

$$D_k(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{m + n - k - j}{n - k} \binom{n}{j},$$

where each subtraction is truncated at $0$. The definition is intended for $m, n \ge k$, where
no truncation occurs.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Section 1 (definition of `D_k(m, n)`).

articles.title: Vertical sum identity for the upper generalized Delannoy numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$, write
$D^k(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{m + n + k - j}{n + k} \binom{n}{j}$ for the upper
generalized Delannoy numbers. For all natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$ with $k \ge 1$,
$D^k(m, n) + D^k(m + 1, n) = D^{k-1}(m + 1, n + 1)$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Theorem 4 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-thm-4`).

articles.title: Horizontal sum identity for the upper generalized Delannoy numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$, write
$D^k(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{m + n + k - j}{n + k} \binom{n}{j}$ for the upper
generalized Delannoy numbers. For all natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$,
$D^k(m, n) + D^k(m, n + 1) = 2 D^{k+1}(m, n)$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Theorem 3 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-thm-3`).

articles.title: Powers-of-two formula for the upper generalized Delannoy numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$, write
$D^k(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{m + n + k - j}{n + k} \binom{n}{j}$ for the upper
generalized Delannoy numbers. For all natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$,

$$D^k(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(m, n)} \binom{m + k}{j + k} \binom{n}{j} 2^j.$$

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Theorem 10 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-thm-10`).

articles.title: An upper generalized Delannoy number equal to $44$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$, write
$D^k(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{m + n + k - j}{n + k} \binom{n}{j}$ for the upper
generalized Delannoy numbers. Then $D^1(3, 2) = 44$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Table 1.

articles.title: Vertical difference identity for the upper generalized Delannoy numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$, write
$D^k(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{m + n + k - j}{n + k} \binom{n}{j}$ for the upper
generalized Delannoy numbers. For all natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$ with $k \ge 1$,
$D^k(m + 1, n) - D^k(m, n) = D^{k-1}(m + 1, n)$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Corollary 6 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-cor-6`).

articles.title: Horizontal difference identity for the upper generalized Delannoy numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$, write
$D^k(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{m + n + k - j}{n + k} \binom{n}{j}$ for the upper
generalized Delannoy numbers. For all natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$ with $m \ge 1$,
$D^k(m, n + 1) - D^k(m, n) = 2 D^{k+1}(m - 1, n)$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Corollary 5 (`jis-2024-24.1.8-cor-5`).

articles.title: An upper generalized Delannoy number equal to $13$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$, write
$D^k(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{m + n + k - j}{n + k} \binom{n}{j}$ for the upper
generalized Delannoy numbers. Then $D^0(2, 2) = 13$.

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Table 1.

articles.title: Generalized Delannoy number with upper index
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$, the
generalized Delannoy number $D^k(m, n)$ is the natural number

$$D^k(m, n) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{m + n + k - j}{n + k} \binom{n}{j}.$$

## Sources

- Steven Edwards and William Griffiths, *Delannoy Constructions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.1.8, Section 1 (definition of `D^k(m, n)`).

articles.title: Gessel alphabet
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the Gessel alphabet over
$S = [n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ is the disjoint union of an unbarred copy and a barred copy of $[n]$:
it has an unbarred letter $i$ and a barred letter $\bar{i}$ for each $i \in [n]$.

Each copy is indexed by $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, the index $j$ standing for the label $j + 1$.

articles.title: Signed balance of a label
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $w$ be a word over the Gessel
alphabet over $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ and let $m$ be a natural number. The signed balance of $m$
in $w$ is the integer obtained by subtracting the number of occurrences of the barred letter
$\bar{m}$ in $w$ from the number of occurrences of the unbarred letter $m$ in $w$; it is $0$ when
$m \notin [n]$.

articles.title: Barred occurrences of a label
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $w$ be a word (a finite
sequence of letters) over the Gessel alphabet over $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ and let $m$ be a
natural number. The barred count of $m$ in $w$ is the number of positions of $w$ that hold the
barred letter $\bar{m}$; it is $0$ when $m \notin [n]$.

articles.title: Unbarred occurrences of a label
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $w$ be a word (a finite
sequence of letters) over the Gessel alphabet over $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ and let $m$ be a
natural number. The unbarred count of $m$ in $w$ is the number of positions of $w$ that hold the
unbarred letter $m$; it is $0$ when $m \notin [n]$.

articles.title: Complete Gessel words are the Gessel words of zero balance
articles.statement:
A word $w$ over the Gessel
alphabet of $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ is a complete Gessel word if and only if it is a Gessel word
and, for every $m \in [n]$, the signed balance of $m$ in $w$ (the number of occurrences of the
unbarred letter $m$ minus the number of occurrences of the barred letter $\bar m$) is zero.

articles.title: Complete Gessel words
articles.statement:
A word $w$ over the Gessel alphabet of $S = [n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$
is a complete Gessel word when it is a Gessel word and, for every $m \in [n]$, the unbarred
letter $m$ and the barred letter $\bar m$ occur the same number of times in $w$.

articles.title: Gessel word
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number. For a word $u$ over the Gessel alphabet over
$S = [n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ and a natural number $m$, write $\beta_u(m)$ for the signed balance of
$m$ in $u$: the number of occurrences of the unbarred letter $m$ in $u$ minus the number of
occurrences of the barred letter $\bar{m}$ in $u$. A word $w$ over this alphabet is a Gessel word
when, for every prefix $w'$ of $w$ (including the empty word and $w$ itself) and every $k$ with
$1 \le k \le n$, we have $\sum_{i=1}^{k} \beta_{w'}(n + 1 - i) \ge 0$, that is, the signed
balances in $w'$ of the $k$ largest labels $n, n - 1, \dots, n + 1 - k$ have nonnegative sum.

articles.title: Augmentation of a $k$-Dyck word
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 0$ and let $w$ be a word in the letters
$U = (1,1)$ and $D^{(k)} = (k,-k)$, for example a $k$-Dyck path. The augmented path of $w$ is the
word in the skew Dyck steps $U$, $D$, $L$ obtained from $w$ by keeping each letter $U$ and
replacing each letter $D^{(k)}$ by $U D^{k-1} L D$, where $D^{k-1}$ means $k - 1$ copies of $D$
(none when $k \le 1$).

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 2.

articles.title: Generating function of augmented $k$-Dyck paths
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 0$ and let $\hat D_n^{(k)}$
be the set of augmented $k$-Dyck paths of size $n$. Then $G_k(x)$ is the formal power series with
integer coefficients

$$
G_k(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} |\hat D_n^{(k)}| \, x^n \in \mathbb{Z}[[x]].
$$

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 6.

articles.title: Long-ascent generating function of augmented $k$-Dyck paths
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 0$, let
$\hat D_n^{(k)}$ be the set of augmented $k$-Dyck paths of size $n$, and for a path $\mu$ let
$\operatorname{asc}(\mu)$ be its number of long ascents. Then $\acute{G}_k(t, x)$ is the formal
power series

$$
\acute{G}_k(t, x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{\mu \in \hat D_n^{(k)}} t^{\operatorname{asc}(\mu)} x^n
$$

in $\mathbb{Z}[t][[x]]$. Its constant term is $1$, coming from the empty path.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 7.

articles.title: Augmented $k$-Dyck paths
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, write $U = (1,1)$ and
$D^{(k)} = (k,-k)$. A $k$-Dyck path of size $n$ is a word of length $(k+1)n$ in the letters $U$
and $D^{(k)}$ that has exactly $n$ letters $D^{(k)}$ and $k$ times as many letters $U$ as letters
$D^{(k)}$, and in which every prefix has at least $k$ times as many letters $U$ as letters
$D^{(k)}$. The augmented path of such a word is the word in the skew Dyck steps $U$, $D$, $L$
obtained by keeping each letter $U$ and replacing each letter $D^{(k)}$ by $U D^{k-1} L D$, where
$D^{k-1}$ means $k - 1$ copies of $D$ (none when $k \le 1$). The set $\hat{D}_n^{(k)}$ of
augmented $k$-Dyck paths of size $n$ is the set of the augmented paths of the $k$-Dyck paths of
size $n$.

The definition is used for $k \ge 2$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 2.

articles.title: The $k$-box factor
articles.statement:
For $k \ge 0$, the $k$-box factor is the word $U D^k L$ in the skew
Dyck steps: one step $U$, then $k$ steps $D$, then one step $L$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 3.

articles.title: The box word for $k = 1$ and $a = (3, 2)$
articles.statement:
For $k = 1$ and $a = (3, 2)$, the box word
$U^{a_1} D^k L D \, U^{a_2} D^k L$ equals $UUUDLDUUDL$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Box words
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 0$ and let $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ be a list of natural numbers
with $n \ge 1$. The box word of $k$ and $a$ is the word in the skew Dyck steps

$$
U^{a_1} D^k L D \; U^{a_2} D^k L D \; \cdots \; U^{a_{n-1}} D^k L D \; U^{a_n} D^k L,
$$

that is, the blocks $U^{a_i} D^k L D$ for $i < n$ followed by $U^{a_n} D^k L$. For the empty
list it is $D^k L$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Number of $k$-box paths with $j$ long ascents
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$, $n \ge 1$ and $j \ge 1$,
and let $a_{k,n,j}$ be the number of $k$-box paths of size $n$ with exactly $j$ long ascents.
Then

$$
j \, a_{k,n,j} = \binom{(k+1)n - 2}{j - 1} \binom{n - 1}{j - 1}.
$$

For $j > n$ both sides vanish.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Theorem 13 (`jis-2024-24.2.4-thm-13`).

articles.title: Number of $k$-box paths with $j$ returns
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and $1 \le j \le n$, and let
$r_{k,n,j}$ be the number of $k$-box paths of size $n$ with exactly $j$ returns. Then

$$
((k+2)n - j - 1) \, r_{k,n,j} = (j(k+1) - 1) \binom{(k+2)n - j - 1}{n - j},
$$

and if moreover $j < n$, then

$$
(n - j) \, r_{k,n,j} = (j(k+1) - 1) \binom{(k+2)n - j - 2}{n - j - 1}.
$$

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Theorem 9 (`jis-2024-24.2.4-thm-9`).

articles.title: Number of $k$-box paths of size $n$
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$, and let $f_{k,n}$ be
the number of $k$-box paths of size $n$. Then

$$
((k+2)n - 1) \, f_{k,n} = \binom{(k+2)n - 1}{n},
$$

and if moreover $n \ge 2$, then

$$
(n - 1) \, f_{k,n} = (k+1) \binom{(k+2)n - 2}{n - 2}.
$$

The source also identifies $f_{k,n}$ with the number of $(k+1)$-tuples of $(k+2)$-ary trees
with $n - 1$ nodes; that identification is not part of this statement.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Theorem 5 (`jis-2024-24.2.4-thm-5`).

articles.title: Three $2$-Dyck paths of size $2$
articles.statement:
The number of $2$-Dyck paths of size $2$ is $3$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 2.

articles.title: Three skew Dyck paths of semilength $2$
articles.statement:
The number of skew Dyck paths of semilength
$2$ is $3$.

They are $UUDD$, $UDUD$ and $UUDL$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 1.

articles.title: Counting tailed $k$-box paths
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$, and let $T$ be the number of
$k$-box paths of size $n$ that end with $U^{k+1} D^k L$. Then
$((k+2)(n-1)+1) \cdot T = \binom{(k+2)(n-1)+1}{n-1}$, and if $n \ge 2$ then also
$(n-1) \cdot T = \binom{(k+2)(n-1)}{n-2}$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Proposition 7 (`jis-2024-24.2.4-prop-7`).

articles.title: $k$-Dyck words
articles.statement:
A word $w$ over the Booleans is a $k$-Dyck word when the number of
letters $\mathrm{true}$ in $w$ is $k$ times the number of letters $\mathrm{false}$, and every
prefix of $w$ contains at least $k$ times as many letters $\mathrm{true}$ as letters
$\mathrm{false}$.

Reading $\mathrm{true}$ as the step $U = (1,1)$ and $\mathrm{false}$ as the step
$D^{(k)} = (k,-k)$, this says that the path ends on the $x$-axis and never goes below it.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 2.

articles.title: Skew Dyck words
articles.statement:
A word $w$ in the steps $U$, $D$, $L$ is a skew Dyck word when neither
$UL$ nor $LU$ occurs in $w$ as two consecutive letters, the number of $U$s in $w$ equals the
number of $D$s and $L$s together, and no prefix of $w$ has more $D$s and $L$s together than
$U$s.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 1.

articles.title: Long-ascent functional equations for $k$-box paths
articles.statement:
Let $\acute F_k(t, x)$ be the
long-ascent generating function of $k$-box paths and $\acute G_k(t, x)$ that of augmented
$k$-Dyck paths, including the empty path, both in $\mathbb{Z}[t][[x]]$. Then for every $k \ge 1$

$$
\acute F_k = x \, \acute G_{k+1}^{k} \, (\acute G_{k+1} - 1 + t),
$$

and for every $k \ge 2$

$$
\acute G_k = 1 + x \, \acute G_k^{k} \, (\acute G_k - 1 + t).
$$

The source's displayed sum for $\acute G_k$ omits the empty path; here $\acute G_k$ includes it
(constant term $1$), as both equations require.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Lemma 12 (`jis-2024-24.2.4-lem-12`).

articles.title: Long-ascent generating function of $k$-box paths
articles.statement:
Let $B_n^{(k)}$ be the set of $k$-box
paths of size $n$, and let $\mathrm{la}(\mu)$ be the number of long ascents of a path $\mu$. The
long-ascent generating function of $k$-box paths is the power series

$$
\acute F_k(t, x) = \sum_{n \ge 1} \sum_{\mu \in B_n^{(k)}} t^{\mathrm{la}(\mu)} x^n
$$

in $\mathbb{Z}[t][[x]]$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 7.

articles.title: Decomposition of $k$-box paths
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$. A word $w$ in the steps $U$, $D$, $L$ is a
$k$-box path of some size $n \ge 1$ if and only if $w = \mu_1 U \mu_2 U \cdots \mu_{k+1} U D^k L$
for some augmented $(k+1)$-Dyck paths $\mu_1, \ldots, \mu_{k+1}$, each of some size.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Lemma 4 (`jis-2024-24.2.4-lem-4`).

articles.title: Mean and variance of long ascents in $k$-box paths
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$. Over the
$k$-box paths of size $n$, taken with equal weight, the mean number of long ascents is

$$
\frac{n((k+1)n-1)}{(k+2)n-2}
$$

and the variance (the mean of the square minus the square of the mean) is

$$
\frac{((k+1)n-1)((k+1)n-2)\,n(n-1)}{((k+2)n-2)^2\,((k+2)n-3)}.
$$

When $k = n = 1$ the variance is $0$, and the last fraction reads $0/0$, which is taken to be $0$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Proposition 18 (`jis-2024-24.2.4-prop-18`).

articles.title: The $1$-box path of size $1$
articles.statement:
The only $1$-box path of size $1$ is $UUDL$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 3.

articles.title: Mean and variance of the number of returns of $k$-box paths
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$,
and let $R(\mu)$ be the number of returns (steps ending on the $x$-axis) of a path $\mu$. The
average of $R$ over the $k$-box paths of size $n$ is

$$\frac{(k+2)((k+2)n-1)}{(k+1)((k+1)n+1)},$$

and the average of $R^2$ over these paths minus the square of the average of $R$ is

$$\frac{(k+2)((k+2)n-1)((2k+1)(k+1)n-2)(n-1)}{(k+1)^2((k+1)n+1)^2((k+1)n+2)}.$$

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Corollary 11 (`jis-2024-24.2.4-cor-11`).

articles.title: Structure of $k$-box paths
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$. For a list
$a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ of natural numbers write
$w_k(a) = U^{a_1} D^k L D \cdots U^{a_{n-1}} D^k L D\, U^{a_n} D^k L$. Every $k$-box path of
size $n$ equals $w_k(a)$ for some list $a$ of $n$ positive integers. Conversely, if $a$ is a
list of $n$ positive integers with $a_1 + \cdots + a_n = (k+2)n - 1$ and no prefix of $w_k(a)$
has more $D$s and $L$s together than $U$s, then $w_k(a)$ is a $k$-box path of size $n$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Lemma 2 (`jis-2024-24.2.4-lem-2`).

articles.title: $k$-box paths
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, the set $B_n^{(k)}$ of $k$-box paths of
size $n$ consists of the skew Dyck paths of semilength $(k+2)n - 1$ that contain exactly $n$
occurrences of the factor $U D^k L$. The subtraction is truncated at $0$, so $B_0^{(k)}$
consists of the empty path alone.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 3.

articles.title: Functional equation for the returns generating function
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$, let
$F_k(t, x) \in \mathbb{Z}[t][[x]]$ be the generating function of $k$-box paths of size at least
$1$ by number of returns (exponent of $t$) and size (exponent of $x$), and let $G_{k+1}(x)$ be
the generating function of augmented $(k+1)$-Dyck paths by size, viewed in $\mathbb{Z}[t][[x]]$.
Then

$$\bigl(1 - t x G_{k+1}^{k+1}\bigr) F_k = t x G_{k+1}^k.$$

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Lemma 8 (`jis-2024-24.2.4-lem-8`).

articles.title: Generating function of $k$-box paths by returns
articles.statement:
For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $F_k(t, x)$ is
the power series in $\mathbb{Z}[t][[x]]$ with constant term $0$ whose coefficient of $x^n$ for
$n \ge 1$ is the sum of $t^{\operatorname{ret}(\mu)}$ over the set $B_n^{(k)}$ of $k$-box paths
$\mu$ of size $n$, where $\operatorname{ret}(\mu)$ is the number of returns of $\mu$; that is,
$F_k(t, x) = \sum_{n \ge 1} \sum_{\mu \in B_n^{(k)}} t^{\operatorname{ret}(\mu)} x^n$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 6.

articles.title: $k$-Dyck paths of size $n$
articles.statement:
Write $U = (1,1)$ and $D^{(k)} = (k,-k)$. The $k$-Dyck paths
of size $n$ are the words of length $(k+1)n$ over $\{U, D^{(k)}\}$ with exactly $n$ steps
$D^{(k)}$ that have $k$ times as many $U$s as $D^{(k)}$s and in which every prefix has at least
$k$ times as many $U$s as $D^{(k)}$s.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 2.

articles.title: Minimal semilength of skew Dyck paths with $n$ box factors
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$.
Some skew Dyck path with exactly $n$ occurrences of the factor $U D^k L$ has semilength
(number of $U$ steps) $(k+2)n - 1$, and every skew Dyck path with exactly $n$ occurrences of
$U D^k L$ has semilength at least $(k+2)n - 1$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Proposition 1 (`jis-2024-24.2.4-prop-1`).

articles.title: Second polygonal numbers count box paths with two long ascents
articles.statement:
Let $K \ge 4$ and
$n \ge 1$. Then $n\bigl((K-2)n + (K-4)\bigr)$ is twice the number of $(K-3)$-box paths of size
$n + 1$ with exactly two long ascents (maximal runs of at least two $U$ steps). Equivalently,
the $n$th second $K$-gonal number $n\bigl((K-2)n + (K-4)\bigr)/2$, the $K$-gonal formula
$m\bigl((K-2)m - (K-4)\bigr)/2$ at $m = -n$, equals this number of paths.

The source states this for $K \ge 3$, where the case $K = 3$ uses its convention for $0$-box
paths.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Theorem 15 (`jis-2024-24.2.4-thm-15`).

articles.title: Skew Dyck steps
articles.statement:
A skew Dyck path is built from three kinds of step: the up step
$U = (1,1)$, the down step $D = (1,-1)$ and the left step $L = (-1,-1)$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 1.

articles.title: Skew Dyck paths of semilength $m$
articles.statement:
For $m \in \mathbb{N}$, the skew Dyck paths of
semilength $m$ are the words of length $2m$ over $\{U, D, L\}$ that avoid the factors $UL$ and
$LU$, have as many $U$s as $D$s and $L$s together, and have no prefix with more $D$s and $L$s
together than $U$s.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 1.

articles.title: Occurrences of a factor in a skew Dyck word
articles.statement:
For words $f$ and $w$ over the skew Dyck
steps $U$, $D$, $L$, the factor count of $f$ in $w$ is the number of suffixes of $w$, including
$w$ itself and the empty suffix, that begin with $f$. Equivalently, it is the number of positions
of $w$ at which an occurrence of $f$ as a contiguous block starts, overlapping occurrences all
being counted; in particular the empty word has factor count $|w| + 1$ in $w$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 1.

articles.title: Long ascents of a skew Dyck word
articles.statement:
A long ascent of a word $w$ over the skew Dyck steps
$U$, $D$, $L$ is a maximal run of consecutive $U$ steps of length at least $2$. The long ascent
count of $w$ is the number of long ascents of $w$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 7.

articles.title: Returns and long ascents of an example skew Dyck path
articles.statement:
The word $U D U^5 D L^2 D U D L$
over the skew Dyck steps has exactly two returns and exactly one long ascent.

This is the source's example of a skew Dyck path.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Figure 1.

articles.title: Returns of a skew Dyck word
articles.statement:
Read a word $w$ over the skew Dyck steps $U = (1,1)$,
$D = (1,-1)$ and $L = (-1,-1)$ as a lattice path starting at the origin. The number of returns of
$w$ is the number of steps of $w$ that end on the $x$-axis, that is, the number of nonempty
prefixes of $w$ that contain as many $U$ steps as $D$ and $L$ steps together.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Section 3.

articles.title: Long ascents of box paths: sum and sum of squares
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$, let
$B_n^{(k)}$ be the set of $k$-box paths of size $n$, and for a path $w$ let $\mathrm{la}(w)$ be
its number of long ascents. Then

$$\sum_{w \in B_n^{(k)}} \mathrm{la}(w) = \binom{(k+2)n-3}{n-1}$$

and

$$\bigl((k+2)n-3\bigr) \sum_{w \in B_n^{(k)}} \mathrm{la}(w)^2 =
\bigl((k+1)n^2-n-1\bigr) \binom{(k+2)n-3}{n-1}.$$

The source states the second identity divided by $(k+2)n-3$, that is, with the sum of
$\mathrm{la}(w)^2$ equal to $\frac{(k+1)n^2-n-1}{(k+2)n-3}\binom{(k+2)n-3}{n-1}$; at $k = n = 1$
the cleared form reads $0 = 0$.

## Sources

- Zhang and Zhuang, *A Subfamily of Skew Dyck Paths Related to `k`-ary Trees*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.2.4, Lemma 17 (`jis-2024-24.2.4-lem-17`).

articles.title: Lindström–Gessel–Viennot lemma
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n$ be a natural
number, and let $E$ be a relation on a type $V$, read as a directed graph on $V$ with an edge
from $u$ to $v$ whenever $E(u, v)$. Suppose there is a function $r : V \to \mathbb{N}$ with
$r(u) < r(v)$ whenever $E(u, v)$, so the graph is acyclic. A path from $u$ to $w$ is a nonempty
list of vertices that starts at $u$, ends at $w$, and in which there is an edge from each vertex
to the next one. Let $A_0, \dots, A_{n-1}$ and $B_0, \dots, B_{n-1}$ be vertices, and suppose
that for all $i, j < n$ the paths from $A_i$ to $B_j$ form a finite set $P_{ij}$. Let $e$ be the
$n \times n$ matrix over $R$ with $e_{ij} = |P_{ij}|$. Suppose further that whenever $i < j$ and
$l < k$, every path from $A_i$ to $B_k$ shares a vertex with every path from $A_j$ to $B_l$. Let
$S$ be the finite set of families $(F_0, \dots, F_{n-1})$ in which each $F_i$ is a path from
$A_i$ to $B_i$ and $F_i$ and $F_j$ share no vertex whenever $i \ne j$. Then the number of
elements of $S$, taken in $R$, equals $\det e$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindstr%C3%B6m%E2%80%93Gessel%E2%80%93Viennot_lemma

articles.title: Marked tail
articles.statement:
A multi-marked Dyck path $P$ has a marked tail when its final run of
vertical steps (the steps after its last horizontal step $E$, or all of $P$ if $P$ has no step
$E$) contains a marked vertical step $N^*_t$ for some index $t \ge 2$.

articles.title: Unmarked tail
articles.statement:
A multi-marked Dyck path $P$ has an unmarked tail when it does not
have a marked tail, that is, when its final run of vertical steps (the steps after its last
horizontal step $E$, or all of $P$ if $P$ has no step $E$) contains no marked vertical step.

articles.title: Marked step of a marked Dyck path
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a marked Dyck path with $\ell$ steps. For a
position $i$ with $0 \le i < \ell$, the step of $P$ at position $i$ is marked when it is the
marked vertical step $N^*$ (rather than an unmarked vertical step $N$ or a horizontal step $E$).

articles.title: Number of horizontal steps in a marked Dyck step sequence
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence $P$ of
marked Dyck steps, $E(P)$ is the number of horizontal steps $E$ in $P$.

articles.title: Number of unmarked vertical steps
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence $P$ of marked Dyck steps,
$N(P)$ is the number of unmarked vertical steps $N$ in $P$.

articles.title: Number of marked vertical steps
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence $P$ of marked Dyck steps,
$N^*(P)$ is the number of marked vertical steps $N^*$ in $P$.

articles.title: Marked Dyck path
articles.statement:
Let $E(Q)$, $N(Q)$ and $N^*(Q)$ denote the numbers of horizontal steps
$E$, unmarked vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*$ in a finite sequence $Q$ of
marked Dyck steps. A marked Dyck path is a finite sequence $P$ of marked Dyck steps such that
$E(P) = N(P) + N^*(P)$ and every prefix $Q$ of $P$ satisfies $N(Q) + N^*(Q) \le E(Q)$: a
lattice path from $(0, 0)$ that ends on the diagonal and never goes above it.

articles.title: Steps of a marked Dyck path
articles.statement:
A step of a marked Dyck path is one of three kinds: a
horizontal step $E = (1, 0)$, an unmarked vertical step $N = (0, 1)$, or a marked vertical step
$N^* = (0, 1)$.

articles.title: Number of horizontal steps in a multi-marked step sequence
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence $P$ of
multi-marked steps (horizontal steps $E$, plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps
$N^*_t$ with index $t \ge 2$), $E(P)$ is the number of horizontal steps $E$ in $P$.

articles.title: Equal horizontal and vertical step counts
articles.statement:
For every multi-marked Dyck path $P$, the
number $E(P)$ of horizontal steps of $P$ equals the number of vertical steps of $P$, plain steps
$N$ and marked steps $N^*_t$ counted together.

articles.title: Number of marked steps of a given index
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence $P$ of multi-marked steps
(horizontal steps $E$, plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*_s$ with index
$s \ge 2$) and a natural number $t$, $N^*_t(P)$ is the number of marked steps in $P$ whose index
is exactly $t$.

articles.title: Number of plain vertical steps
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence $P$ of multi-marked steps
(horizontal steps $E$, plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*_t$ with index
$t \ge 2$), $N(P)$ is the number of plain (unmarked) vertical steps $N$ in $P$.

articles.title: Number of steps
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence $P$ of multi-marked steps (horizontal steps $E$,
plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*_t$ with index $t \ge 2$), this is the
total number of steps in $P$, that is, the length of $P$.

articles.title: Number of vertical steps
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence $P$ of multi-marked steps (horizontal
steps $E$, plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*_t$ with index $t \ge 2$),
this is the number of vertical steps in $P$, plain steps $N$ and marked steps $N^*_t$ counted
together.

articles.title: Multi-marked Dyck paths of a given size
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $\tilde P_n$ is the
set of multi-marked Dyck paths $P$ of size $n$. Here the size of $P$ is $E(P) + \sum (t - 1)$,
where $E(P)$ is the number of horizontal steps of $P$ and the sum runs over the marked steps
$N^*_t$ of $P$, each occurrence counted separately.

articles.title: Multi-marked Dyck path
articles.statement:
A multi-marked Dyck path is a finite sequence $P$ of steps, each
a horizontal step $E = (1,0)$, a plain vertical step $N = (0,1)$ or a marked vertical step
$N^*_t = (0,1)$ carrying an index $t \ge 2$, such that every prefix of $P$, including the empty
prefix and $P$ itself, has at most as many vertical steps (plain and marked) as horizontal
steps, and $P$ has exactly as many vertical steps as horizontal steps.

Read as a lattice path from $(0,0)$, $P$ never rises above the diagonal and ends on it.

articles.title: Index sum of a multi-marked step sequence
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence $s$ of steps of a
multi-marked Dyck path, the index sum of $s$ is the sum of the indices $t$ over all occurrences
of marked steps $N^*_t$ in $s$, each occurrence counted separately; the steps $E$ and $N$
contribute nothing.

Grouping the occurrences by index, the index sum equals $\sum_t t \cdot N^*_t(s)$, where
$N^*_t(s)$ is the number of marked steps of index $t$ in $s$.

articles.title: Vertical steps of a multi-marked Dyck path
articles.statement:
A step of a multi-marked Dyck path is
vertical when it is the plain step $N$ or a marked step $N^*_t$; the horizontal step $E$ is not
vertical. This test delimits the final run of vertical steps of a step sequence.

articles.title: Shifted index sum of a multi-marked step sequence
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence $s$ of steps of
a multi-marked Dyck path, the shifted index sum of $s$ is the sum of $t - 1$ over all
occurrences of marked steps $N^*_t$ in $s$, each occurrence counted separately; the steps $E$
and $N$ contribute nothing.

Grouping the occurrences by index, the shifted index sum equals
$\sum_t (t - 1) \cdot N^*_t(s)$, where $N^*_t(s)$ is the number of marked steps of index $t$ in $s$.

articles.title: Two expressions for the size of a multi-marked Dyck path
articles.statement:
For every multi-marked Dyck
path $P$, the size $E(P) + \sum (t - 1)$ of $P$ equals $N(P) + \sum t$, where $E(P)$ is the
number of horizontal steps $E$ of $P$, $N(P)$ is the number of plain vertical steps $N$ of $P$,
and both sums run over all occurrences of marked steps $N^*_t$ in $P$.

Grouped by index, this reads
$E(P) + \sum_t (t - 1) N^*_t(P) = N(P) + \sum_t t N^*_t(P)$, where $N^*_t(P)$ is the number of
marked steps of index $t$ in $P$.

articles.title: Size of a multi-marked step sequence
articles.statement:
The size of a finite sequence $s$ of steps of a
multi-marked Dyck path is $E(s) + \sum (t - 1)$, where $E(s)$ is the number of horizontal steps
$E$ in $s$ and the sum runs over all occurrences of marked steps $N^*_t$ in $s$.

articles.title: Steps of a multi-marked Dyck path
articles.statement:
A step of a multi-marked Dyck path is one of the
horizontal step $E = (1, 0)$, the plain vertical step $N = (0, 1)$, or, for an integer
$t \ge 2$, the marked vertical step $N^*_t = (0, 1)$ of index $t$. There are no marked steps
of index less than $2$.

articles.title: Final run of vertical steps
articles.statement:
The final run of vertical steps of a finite sequence $s$
of steps of a multi-marked Dyck path is the longest suffix of $s$ consisting of vertical steps
($N$ or $N^*_t$): the part of $s$ after its last horizontal step $E$, or all of $s$ if $s$ has
no step $E$.

articles.title: Multi-marked Dyck paths with an unmarked tail
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $\tilde R_n$ is
the set of multi-marked Dyck paths of size $n$ with an unmarked tail, that is, whose final
run of vertical steps contains no marked step.

articles.title: Vertical count plus shifted index sum
articles.statement:
For every finite sequence $s$ of steps of a
multi-marked Dyck path, the number of vertical steps of $s$ plus the shifted index sum of $s$
equals the number of plain vertical steps $N$ of $s$ plus the index sum of $s$.

Each marked step $N^*_t$ contributes $1 + (t - 1)$ to the left side and $t$ to the right side.

articles.title: Size of a marked Dyck path
articles.statement:
The size of a marked Dyck path $P$ is $N^*(P) + E(P)$,
where $N^*(P)$ is the number of marked vertical steps of $P$ and $E(P)$ the number of its
horizontal steps.

articles.title: Size of a marked Dyck path in vertical steps
articles.statement:
For every marked Dyck path $P$, the size of
$P$ equals $N(P) + 2N^*(P)$, where $N(P)$ and $N^*(P)$ are the numbers of unmarked and marked
vertical steps of $P$.

articles.title: Minimal lattice walks with unit and diagonal steps
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $a$ and $b$,
the number of sequences of $\max(a, b)$ steps, each taken from $\{(1,0), (0,1), (1,1)\}$,
whose sum is $(a, b)$ equals $\binom{\max(a, b)}{\min(a, b)}$.

Every walk from the origin to $(a, b)$ with these steps has at least $\max(a, b)$ steps, since
each step raises each coordinate by at most $1$, and walks of exactly that length exist; so the
sequences counted are the minimal-length walks from the origin to $(a, b)$.

## Sources

- Jackson Evoniuk, Steven Klee, and Van Magnan, "Enumerating Minimal Length Lattice Paths," Journal of Integer Sequences 21 (2018), Article 18.3.6, Theorem (section Minimal walks for S = {(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)}, label sec2), lines 273–275, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL21/Klee/klee2.tex

articles.title: Peak descents of a sample Dyck path
articles.statement:
The Dyck path $UUUUDDDUDDUUDUUDDD$, which factors
as $U\,U\,U\,(UD^3)(UD^2)\,U\,(UD)\,U\,(UD^3)$, has four peaks $UD$, and the lengths of the
maximal runs of $D$ steps starting at the $D$ of each peak are, from left to right,
$3, 2, 1, 3$.

## Sources

- Gil, Hoover, and Shearer, *Bijections Between Colored Compositions, Dyck Paths, and Polygon Partitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.2, Section 2.

articles.title: Peak descents
articles.statement:
Let $l$ be a finite sequence of up steps $U$ and down steps $D$. A peak
of $l$ is a position where a step $U$ is immediately followed by a step $D$. The peak descents
of $l$ form the list that has, for each peak from left to right, the length $j$ of the maximal
run of consecutive steps $D$ that starts at the $D$ of that peak, so that the peak and its
descent form the primitive block $U D^j$.

## Sources

- Gil, Hoover, and Shearer, *Bijections Between Colored Compositions, Dyck Paths, and Polygon Partitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.2, Section 2 (Dyck paths).

articles.title: Maximal runs of the word $1001100$
articles.statement:
Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the maximal
runs of the Boolean word $1001100$, listed from left to right as pairs (letter, length), are
$(1, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2), (0, 2)$.

This word is the block word of the source's example path $U\,(UD)\,(DU)^2\,(UD)^2\,(DU)^2\,D$.
In the source's factorization $U\,(UD)^{p_1}\,(DU)^{v_1}\,(UD)^{p_2}\,(DU)^{v_2}\,D$ of that path
into maximal blocks of $1$-peaks $UD$ and $0$-valleys $DU$, the block lengths are $p_1 = 1$,
$v_1 = 2$, $p_2 = 2$, $v_2 = 2$.

## Sources

- Barcucci, Bernini, Bilotta, and Pinzani, *Rational Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.2, Section 3, Example.

articles.title: Maximal runs of a Boolean word
articles.statement:
The run decomposition of a Boolean word is the list,
from left to right, of its maximal runs of equal consecutive letters, each recorded as the pair
(letter, length of the run).

## Sources

- Barcucci, Bernini, Bilotta, and Pinzani, *Rational Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.2, Section 3 (blocks of maximal length of consecutive `1`-peaks and `0`-valleys).

articles.title: Path counts for $q = 3/2$
articles.statement:
Let $r = 3$ and $s = 2$. The set $Q_4^{3/2}$ of $Q$-bonacci
paths of semilength $4$, that is, the Dyck paths of semilength $4$ and height at most $2$ whose
block word's maximal runs satisfy the $Q$-bonacci run condition, has $7$ elements, while the set
$\tilde R_5^{3/2}$ of Dyck paths of semilength $5$ and height at most $2$ whose block word's
maximal runs satisfy the rational run condition has $6$ elements.

Here $t = \lfloor (s - 1)/r \rfloor = 0$ and $s \ne t r + 1$.

## Sources

- Barcucci, Bernini, Bilotta, and Pinzani, *Rational Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.2, Definitions 3 and 4.

articles.title: Block word of a Dyck path of height at most $2$
articles.statement:
For a Dyck word
$P = P_0 P_1 \cdots P_{2n-1}$ of semilength $n$, with steps indexed from $0$, the block word of
$P$ is the Boolean word of length $n - 1$ (empty when $n = 0$) whose entry $i$, for
$0 \le i < n - 1$, is true exactly when $P_{2i+1} = U$.

When $P$ has height at most $2$ and $n \ge 1$, it factorizes as $P = U X_1 \cdots X_{n-1} D$
with each $X_{i+1} = P_{2i+1} P_{2i+2}$ a $1$-peak $UD$ or a $0$-valley $DU$, so entry $i$ is
true for a $1$-peak and false for a $0$-valley.

## Sources

- Barcucci, Bernini, Bilotta, and Pinzani, *Rational Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.2, Section 3, factorization (1).

articles.title: $Q$-bonacci and rational-run paths correspond exactly when $s \equiv 1 \pmod r$
articles.statement:
Let
$r, s \ge 1$ be coprime natural numbers and let $t = \lfloor (s - 1)/r \rfloor$, so that
$t r + 1 \le s \le (t + 1) r$. For $m \in \mathbb{N}$ write $Q_m^{r/s}$ for the set of $Q$-bonacci
paths of semilength $m$ and $\tilde R_m^{r/s}$ for the set of Dyck paths of semilength $m$ and
height at most $2$ whose block word's maximal runs satisfy the rational run condition for
$q = r/s$. Then $\tilde R_{n+t+1}^{r/s}$ and $Q_n^{r/s}$ are in bijection for every $n \ge 0$ if
and only if $s = t r + 1$.

## Sources

- Barcucci, Bernini, Bilotta, and Pinzani, *Rational Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.2, Proposition 7 (`jis-2025-25.3.2-prop-7`).

articles.title: Dyck words of height at most $2$
articles.statement:
A Dyck word has height at most $2$ when no prefix of it
has more than two more up steps $U$ than down steps $D$.

## Sources

- Barcucci, Bernini, Bilotta, and Pinzani, *Rational Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.2, Section 2.

articles.title: Examples of the $Q$-bonacci run condition for $q = 4/5$
articles.statement:
Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for
false, for $r = 4$ and $s = 5$ the maximal runs of the Boolean word $1001100$ do not satisfy the
$Q$-bonacci run condition, while the maximal runs of $100111100$ and of $100111$ do.

These are the block words of the source's paths $U\,(UD)\,(DU)^2\,(UD)^2\,(DU)^2\,D$, which is
not in the set $Q^{4/5}$ of $Q$-bonacci paths for $q = 4/5$, and
$U\,(UD)\,(DU)^2\,(UD)^4\,(DU)^2\,D$ and $U\,(UD)\,(DU)^2\,(UD)^3\,D$, which are. Writing each
path as $U\,(UD)^{p_1}\,(DU)^{v_1}\,(UD)^{p_2}\,(DU)^{v_2}\,D$ with maximal blocks, the second
has last block $p_2 = 4 = r$ and the third has $p_2 = 3 < r$ and $v_2 = 0$.

## Sources

- Barcucci, Bernini, Bilotta, and Pinzani, *Rational Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.2, Example after Definition 4.

articles.title: The $Q$-bonacci run condition
articles.statement:
Let $r, s \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $R$ be a list of runs,
each a pair (letter, length) with a Boolean letter. For the run at position $i$, let $v_i$ be the
length of the run at position $i + 1$ if that run exists and has letter false, and $v_i = 0$
otherwise. Then $R$ satisfies the $Q$-bonacci run condition for $q = r/s$ when every run of
letter true, say of length $p$ at position $i$, has $p \le r$ and also $p s \le r v_i$, except
that $p s \le r v_i$ may fail when both this run is the last run of letter true in $R$ and
either $p = r$ or $v_i = 0$.

Applied to the maximal runs of the block word of a Dyck path, the runs of letter true are the
blocks of $p$ consecutive $1$-peaks and $v_i$ counts the $0$-valleys that follow them: every
block but the last needs $p s \le r v_i$, and the last block, of $p_k$ peaks followed by $v_k$
valleys, needs it only when $p_k < r$ and $v_k \ne 0$.

## Sources

- Barcucci, Bernini, Bilotta, and Pinzani, *Rational Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.2, Definition 4.

articles.title: The rational Dyck path run condition
articles.statement:
Let $r, s \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $R$ be a list of
runs, each a pair (letter, length) with a Boolean letter. For the run at position $i$, let $v_i$
be the length of the run at position $i + 1$ if that run exists and has letter false, and
$v_i = 0$ otherwise. Then $R$ satisfies the rational run condition for $q = r/s$ when every run
of letter true, say of length $p$ at position $i$, has $p \le r$ and $p s \le r v_i$.

Applied to the maximal runs of the block word of a Dyck path, this says that every block of $p$
consecutive $1$-peaks has $p \le r$ and is followed by $v$ consecutive $0$-valleys with
$p s \le r v$, that is, $v \ge \lceil p s / r \rceil$ when $r \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Barcucci, Bernini, Bilotta, and Pinzani, *Rational Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.2, Definition 3.

articles.title: $Q$-bonacci and rational-run paths are in bijection when $s = t r + 1$
articles.statement:
Let $r \ge 1$
and $t$ be natural numbers and $s = t r + 1$. Then for every $n \ge 0$ the set $Q_n^{r/s}$ of
$Q$-bonacci paths of semilength $n$ is in bijection with the set $\tilde R_{n+t+1}^{r/s}$ of Dyck
paths of semilength $n + t + 1$ and height at most $2$ whose block word's maximal runs satisfy
the rational run condition for $q = r/s$.

## Sources

- Barcucci, Bernini, Bilotta, and Pinzani, *Rational Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.2, Proposition 6 (`jis-2025-25.3.2-prop-6`).

articles.title: The $Q$-bonacci paths $Q_n^{r/s}$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $r$, $s$ and $n$, $Q_n^{r/s}$ is
the finite set of Dyck paths of semilength $n$ and height at most $2$ that satisfy the following
run condition. For $n \ge 1$ such a path factors as $U X_1 \cdots X_{n-1} D$ with each $X_i$
either a $1$-peak $UD$ or a $0$-valley $DU$, and its block word $X_1 \cdots X_{n-1}$ (empty for
$n = 0$) splits into maximal runs of equal blocks. Every run of $p$ consecutive $1$-peaks must
have $p \le r$, and also $p s \le r v$, where $v$ is the length of the run of $0$-valleys
immediately after it ($v = 0$ if no run follows it); for the last run of $1$-peaks, the
inequality $p s \le r v$ is required only when $p < r$ and $v \ne 0$.

## Sources

- Barcucci, Bernini, Bilotta, and Pinzani, *Rational Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.2, Definition 4.

articles.title: Valleys following a run
articles.statement:
Let $R = ((b_0, m_0), \dots, (b_{k-1}, m_{k-1}))$ be a list of
pairs of a Boolean letter and a natural number, read as the maximal runs of a block word in which
the letter $\mathrm{false}$ stands for a $0$-valley $DU$. For $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the number of
$0$-valleys immediately after run $i$ is $m_{i+1}$ if $i + 1 < k$ and $b_{i+1} = \mathrm{false}$,
and $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Barcucci, Bernini, Bilotta, and Pinzani, *Rational Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.2, Section 3 (`vᵢ` after `pᵢ`).

articles.title: The path sets $\tilde R_n^{r/s}$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $r$, $s$ and $n$,
$\tilde R_n^{r/s}$ is the finite set of Dyck paths of semilength $n$ and height at most $2$
that satisfy the following run condition. For $n \ge 1$ such a path factors as
$U X_1 \cdots X_{n-1} D$ with each $X_i$ either a $1$-peak $UD$ or a $0$-valley $DU$, and its
block word $X_1 \cdots X_{n-1}$ (empty for $n = 0$) splits into maximal runs of equal blocks.
Every run of $p$ consecutive $1$-peaks must have $p \le r$ and $p s \le r v$, where $v$ is the
length of the run of $0$-valleys immediately after it ($v = 0$ if no run follows it).

## Sources

- Barcucci, Bernini, Bilotta, and Pinzani, *Rational Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.2, Definition 3.

articles.title: Thirteen non-decreasing Dyck paths of semilength 4
articles.statement:
There are exactly $13$
non-decreasing Dyck paths of semilength $4$.

They are all $14$ Dyck paths of semilength $4$ except $UUDUDDUD$.

## Sources

- Flórez, Junes, Montoya, and Ramírez, *Counting Subwords in Non-Decreasing Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.6, Section 1.

articles.title: Five non-decreasing Dyck paths of semilength 3
articles.statement:
There are exactly $5$ non-decreasing
Dyck paths of semilength $3$.

These are all five Dyck paths of semilength $3$.

## Sources

- Flórez, Junes, Montoya, and Ramírez, *Counting Subwords in Non-Decreasing Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.6, Section 1.

articles.title: Last peak height of UDUUDD
articles.statement:
The last peak of the Dyck path $UDUUDD$ has height $2$.

## Sources

- Flórez, Junes, Montoya, and Ramírez, *Counting Subwords in Non-Decreasing Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.6, Theorem 16.

articles.title: Height of the last peak
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence $l$ of up steps $U$ and down steps $D$,
the last peak height of $l$ is undefined when $l$ has no factor $UD$. Otherwise it is the
height of the peak of the rightmost factor $UD$: the number of $U$ steps minus the number of
$D$ steps in $l$ up to and including the $U$ of that factor, taken to be $0$ when negative.

## Sources

- Flórez, Junes, Montoya, and Ramírez, *Counting Subwords in Non-Decreasing Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.6, Theorem 16.

articles.title: Occurrences of UDU in UDUDUD
articles.statement:
The contiguous subword $UDU$ occurs exactly $2$ times in
$UDUDUD$; the two occurrences overlap.

## Sources

- Flórez, Junes, Montoya, and Ramírez, *Counting Subwords in Non-Decreasing Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.6, Section 1.

articles.title: Occurrences of UU in UUUDDD
articles.statement:
The contiguous subword $UU$ occurs exactly $2$ times in
$UUUDDD$; the two occurrences overlap.

## Sources

- Flórez, Junes, Montoya, and Ramírez, *Counting Subwords in Non-Decreasing Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.6, Section 1.

articles.title: Number of occurrences of a subword
articles.statement:
For finite words $w$ and $l$ in the up step $U$ and
the down step $D$, the number of occurrences of $w$ in $l$ is the number of suffixes of $l$,
including $l$ itself and the empty suffix, that begin with $w$. Thus every occurrence of $w$ as a
contiguous subword of $l$ is counted, overlapping occurrences separately.

## Sources

- Flórez, Junes, Montoya, and Ramírez, *Counting Subwords in Non-Decreasing Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.6, Section 1.

articles.title: Valley heights of UDUUDUDD
articles.statement:
The Dyck path $UDUUDUDD$ has exactly two valleys, of heights
$0$ and $1$ from left to right.

## Sources

- Flórez and Ramírez, *Restricted Dyck paths on valleys sequence*, arXiv:2108.08299, Section 1.

articles.title: Valley heights of UUDUDDUD
articles.statement:
The Dyck path $UUDUDDUD$ has exactly two valleys, of heights
$1$ and $0$ from left to right.

In particular this path is not non-decreasing.

## Sources

- Flórez and Ramírez, *Restricted Dyck paths on valleys sequence*, arXiv:2108.08299, Section 1.

articles.title: Valley heights
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence $l$ of up steps $U$ and down steps $D$, the valley
heights of $l$ form the list with one entry for each factor $DU$ of $l$, from left to right:
the number of $U$ steps minus the number of $D$ steps in $l$ up to and including the $D$ of
that factor, taken to be $0$ when negative.

## Sources

- Flórez and Ramírez, *Restricted Dyck paths on valleys sequence*, arXiv:2108.08299, Section 1, the definition of non-decreasing Dyck paths used by Flórez, Junes, Montoya, and Ramírez, *Counting Subwords in Non-Decreasing Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.6.

articles.title: Non-decreasing Dyck paths
articles.statement:
A Dyck path is non-decreasing when its valley heights (the
heights reached after the $D$ of each factor $DU$), read from left to right, form a
non-decreasing sequence.

## Sources

- Flórez and Ramírez, *Restricted Dyck paths on valleys sequence*, arXiv:2108.08299, Section 1 (the `0`-Dyck paths), as used by Flórez, Junes, Montoya, and Ramírez, *Counting Subwords in Non-Decreasing Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.6.

articles.title: Non-decreasing Dyck paths of semilength four with last peak at height one
articles.statement:
Exactly four
non-decreasing Dyck paths of semilength $4$ have their last peak at height $1$; that is,
$l_{4,1} = 4$, where $l_{n,k}$ is the number of non-decreasing Dyck paths of semilength $n$
whose last peak has height $k$.

## Sources

- Flórez, Junes, Montoya, and Ramírez, *Counting Subwords in Non-Decreasing Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.6, Theorem 16.

articles.title: Non-decreasing Dyck paths by height of the last peak
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$,
$l_{n,k}$ is the number of non-decreasing Dyck paths of semilength $n$ whose last peak (the last
factor $UD$) has height $k$.

## Sources

- Flórez, Junes, Montoya, and Ramírez, *Counting Subwords in Non-Decreasing Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.6, Theorem 16.

articles.title: Bivariate generating function of a subword in non-decreasing Dyck paths
articles.statement:
For a word $w$
in the steps $U$ and $D$, let $D_n$ be the set of non-decreasing Dyck paths of semilength $n$,
and let $\#w(P)$ be the number of occurrences of $w$ as a contiguous subword of a path $P$,
overlapping occurrences counted separately. The bivariate generating function $F_w(x, y)$ is
the power series in $x$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}[y]$ given by

$$F_w(x, y) = \sum_{n \ge 1} \sum_{P \in D_n} y^{\#w(P)} x^n,$$

so its constant coefficient is $0$: the empty path is not counted.

## Sources

- Flórez, Junes, Montoya, and Ramírez, *Counting Subwords in Non-Decreasing Dyck Paths*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.6, Section 1.

articles.title: The subword $DDD$ in non-decreasing Dyck paths
articles.statement:
Let $F_{DDD}(x, y)$ and $D_{DDD}(x)$ be
the bivariate and univariate generating functions of the subword $DDD$ in non-decreasing Dyck
paths, let $d_{DDD}(n)$ be the total number of occurrences of $DDD$ over all non-decreasing Dyck
paths of semilength $n$, and let $F_n$ and $L_n$ denote the Fibonacci and Lucas numbers. Then

$$(1 - x(1 + y) - x^2(1 - y)) (1 - x(1 + 2y) - x^2(1 - y - y^2)) F_{DDD}(x, y) =
