words of length $n$ consists of the smooth words of length $n$ in which no two adjacent letters
are both equal to $1$.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Section 4, definition of restricted smooth words.

articles.title: Boundary values of the capacity distributions of smooth words
articles.statement:
For letters $i$, let
$r(n, i; q)$ be the capacity distribution of the smooth words of length $n$ ending in $i$, and
$s(n, i; q)$ that of those smooth words of length $n$ ending in $i$ whose largest letter is $i$.
For $n \ge 1$, $r(n, n; q) = s(n, n; q) = s(n, 1; q) = 1$, and if $n \ge 2$ then
$r(n, 1; q) = r(n - 1, 1; q) + r(n - 1, 2; q)$.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Lemma 7.

articles.title: Zero-capacity smooth words with a given last letter
articles.statement:
For $2 \le i \le n$, the number of
smooth words of length $n$ ending in $i$ with capacity $0$, that is, the value at $q = 0$ of their
capacity distribution $r(n, i; q)$, equals $\sum_{j=i-2}^{n-2} \binom{n-2}{j}$.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Recurrence for the capacity distribution of smooth words by last letter
articles.statement:
Let $r(n, i; q)$
be the capacity distribution of the smooth words of length $n$ ending in $i$, let $s(n, i; q)$ be
that of those smooth words of length $n$ ending in $i$ whose largest letter is $i$, and let
$t(m, j; q)$ be the area distribution (the area of a word is the sum of its letters) of the words
of length $m$ over $\{1, \dots, j\}$ that begin and end with $j$ and whose adjacent letters
differ by at most $1$. For $1 < i < n$, in the ring $\mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}]$ of Laurent
polynomials,

$$
r(n, i; q) = r(n - 1, i; q) + r(n - 1, i + 1; q) + s(n - 1, i - 1; q) +
\sum_{m=1}^{n-i-1} q^{mi}\, r(n - m - 1, i; q)\, t(m, i - 1; 1/q).
$$

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Lemma 7.

articles.title: Capacity distribution of smooth words by last letter
articles.statement:
For $n, i \ge 0$, $r(n, i; q)$ is the
polynomial $\sum_w q^{\operatorname{cap}(w)} \in \mathbb{Z}[q]$, where $w$ runs over the smooth
words of length $n$ whose last letter is $i$ and $\operatorname{cap}(w)$ is the capacity of $w$.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Section 3, definition of `r(n, i; q)`.

articles.title: Generating function of smooth words ending in their largest letter
articles.statement:
For $i \ge 1$, let
$s(n, i; q)$ be the capacity distribution of the smooth words of length $n$ that end in $i$ and
have largest letter $i$, and let $t(m, j; q)$ be the area distribution (the area of a word is the
sum of its letters) of the words of length $m$ over $\{1, \dots, j\}$ that begin and end with $j$
and whose adjacent letters differ by at most $1$. In the ring of formal power series in $x$ over
the Laurent polynomials $\mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}]$,

$$
\sum_{n \ge 0} s(n, i; q)\, x^n = x^i \prod_{j=0}^{i-1}
\Bigl(1 - x - x \sum_{m \ge 0} q^{(j+1)m}\, t(m, j; 1/q)\, x^m\Bigr)^{-1}.
$$

The factor for $j = 0$ is $(1 - x)^{-1}$, since $t(m, 0; q) = 0$ for every $m$.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Lemma 9.

articles.title: Recurrence for the capacity distribution of smooth words ending in their largest letter
articles.statement:
Let $s(n, i; q)$ be the capacity distribution of the smooth words of length $n$ that end in $i$ and
have largest letter $i$, and let $t(m, j; q)$ be the area distribution (the area of a word is the
sum of its letters) of the words of length $m$ over $\{1, \dots, j\}$ that begin and end with $j$
and whose adjacent letters differ by at most $1$. For $1 < i < n$, in the ring
$\mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}]$ of Laurent polynomials,

$$
s(n, i; q) = s(n - 1, i; q) + s(n - 1, i - 1; q) +
\sum_{m=1}^{n-i-1} q^{mi}\, s(n - m - 1, i; q)\, t(m, i - 1; 1/q).
$$

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Lemma 7.

articles.title: Capacity distribution of smooth words ending in their largest letter
articles.statement:
For $n, i \ge 0$,
$s(n, i; q)$ is the polynomial $\sum_w q^{\operatorname{cap}(w)} \in \mathbb{Z}[q]$, where $w$ runs
over the smooth words of length $n$ whose last letter is $i$ and all of whose letters are at most
$i$, and $\operatorname{cap}(w)$ is the capacity of $w$.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Section 3, definition of `s(n, i; q)`.

articles.title: Continued fraction for smooth words from $j$ to $j$ by area
articles.statement:
Let $t(m, j; q)$ be the area
distribution of the words of length $m$ over $\{1, \dots, j\}$ that begin and end with $j$ and whose
consecutive letters differ by at most $1$. Define power series $K_k$ in $x$ over $\mathbb{Z}[q]$ by
$K_1 = 1 - qx$ and $K_k = 1 - q^k x - q^{2k-1} x^2 / K_{k-1}$ for $k \ge 2$; each $K_k$ has constant
term $1$. Then for every $j \ge 1$, in $\mathbb{Z}[q][[x]]$,

$$\sum_{m \ge 0} t(m, j; q)\, x^m = \frac{q^j x}{K_j}.$$

This is Mansour and Shattuck's Lemma 8: $q^j x / K_j$ is the finite continued fraction
$q^j x / (1 - q^j x - q^{2j-1} x^2 / (1 - q^{j-1} x - \cdots / (1 - q^2 x - q^3 x^2 / (1 - qx))))$,
and for $j = 1$ it is $qx / (1 - qx)$. The term $m = 0$ vanishes.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Lemma 8.

articles.title: Recurrence for the area distribution of smooth words from $j$ to $j$
articles.statement:
Let $t(m, j; q)$ be
the area distribution of the words of length $m$ over $\{1, \dots, j\}$ that begin and end with $j$
and whose consecutive letters differ by at most $1$. For all $m \ge 2$ and $j \ge 2$,

$$t(m, j; q) = q^j\, t(m-1, j; q) + q^j \sum_{\ell=1}^{m-2} t(\ell, j-1; q)\, t(m-\ell-1, j; q),$$

and for every $k \ge 1$, $t(k, 1; q) = t(1, k; q) = q^k$ (Mansour and Shattuck's Lemma 6).

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Lemma 6.

articles.title: Area distribution of smooth words from $j$ to $j$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$ and $j$, let
$\mathcal{T}_{m,j}$ be the set of words $w = w_1 \cdots w_m$ with letters in $\{1, \dots, j\}$
such that $w_1 = w_m = j$ and $|w_{i+1} - w_i| \le 1$ for $1 \le i < m$; in particular
$\mathcal{T}_{0,j}$ is empty. The area distribution of $\mathcal{T}_{m,j}$ is the polynomial
$t(m, j; q) = \sum_{w \in \mathcal{T}_{m,j}} q^{w_1 + \cdots + w_m}$ in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Section 3, definition of `𝒯_{m,j}` and `t(m, j; q)`.

articles.title: Maximum capacity of smooth words
articles.statement:
A smooth word is a word of positive integers with first
letter $1$ whose consecutive letters differ by at most $1$. Let
$r(n; q) = \sum_w q^{\mathrm{cap}(w)}$, summed over the smooth words $w$ of length $n$, where
$\mathrm{cap}(w)$ is the capacity of $w$. For all $m \ge 1$ and $0 \le p \le 3$, the degree of
$r(4m + p; q)$ in $q$ is $m(2m + p - 1)$. Since $r(n; q)$ is a nonzero polynomial with
nonnegative coefficients, this degree is the maximum capacity of a smooth word of length
$4m + p$ (Mansour and Shattuck's Theorem 5).

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Number of smooth words of capacity zero
articles.statement:
Let $r(n, i; q)$ be the capacity distribution of
the smooth words of length $n$ ending in $i$ and $r(n; q)$ that of all smooth words of length $n$,
so that $r(n, i; 0)$ and $r(n; 0)$ count the smooth words of capacity $0$. Then $r(1, 1; 0) = 1$
and $r(n, 1; 0) = 2^{n-2}$ for every $n \ge 2$; moreover $r(1; 0) = 1$, $r(2; 0) = 2$ and
$r(n; 0) = (n + 2) \cdot 2^{n-3}$ for every $n \ge 3$ (Mansour and Shattuck's Theorem 6, totals).

The paper states the formula for $r(n; 0)$ for $n \ge 2$; at $n = 2$ it reads $4 \cdot 2^{-1} = 2$,
so that case is stated separately.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Smooth words
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 0$, the set $\mathcal{R}_n$ of smooth words of length $n$ consists
of the words $w = w_1 \cdots w_n$ of positive integers with $w_1 = 1$ (when $n \ge 1$) and
$|w_{i+1} - w_i| \le 1$ for $1 \le i < n$.

The letters of a smooth word of length $n$ are at most $n$, so $\mathcal{R}_n$ is finite.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Section 1, definition of smooth words.

articles.title: A recursion for binomial sums of odd-indexed Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let $F_k$ be the Fibonacci
numbers, with the convention $F_{-1} = 1$. For all integers $n \ge 1$ and $2 \le i \le n + 1$,

$$\sum_{m=0}^{n-i+1} \binom{n-m-1}{i-2} F_{2m-1} =
\binom{n-1}{i-2} + \sum_{j=i}^{n} \sum_{m=0}^{n-j} \binom{n-m-2}{j-2} F_{2m-1}$$

(Mansour and Shattuck's Lemma 5, identity (21)). All differences in the binomial coefficients and
in the summation bounds are nonnegative.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Area of a word
articles.statement:
The area of a word $w = w_1 \cdots w_n$ of natural numbers is the sum
$w_1 + \cdots + w_n$ of its letters, the area of its bargraph.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Section 2, definition of the area statistic.

articles.title: Capacity of the word $122341123212323$
articles.statement:
The word
$w = 1\,2\,2\,3\,4\,1\,1\,2\,3\,2\,1\,2\,3\,2\,3$ of length $15$ has capacity $10$ (Mansour and
Shattuck's Figure 1).

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Section 1, Figure 1.

articles.title: Capacity of a word
articles.statement:
The capacity of a word $w = w_1 \cdots w_n$ of natural numbers,
viewed as a bargraph, is

$$\mathrm{cap}(w) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}
\max\Bigl(0, \min\bigl(\max_{j < i} w_j, \max_{j > i} w_j\bigr) - w_i\Bigr),$$

the number of cells of water held above the columns, where an empty maximum is $0$. In particular
the first and last columns hold no water.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Section 1, definition of capacity.

articles.title: Words with all letters at most a bound
articles.statement:
Given a finite set $S$ of words of length $n$
with letters in $\mathbb{N}$ and a natural number $k$, this is the set of words in $S$ all of
whose letters are at most $k$. Applied to the words of $S$ whose last letter is $k$, it gives
those whose largest letter is $k$.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Section 2, definition of `ℬ_{n,i}`.

articles.title: Words ending in a given letter
articles.statement:
Given a finite set $S$ of words $w = w_1 \cdots w_n$
of length $n$ with letters in $\mathbb{N}$ and a natural number $k$, this is the set of words
in $S$ whose last letter $w_n$ is $k$. When $n = 0$ this set is empty.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, *Enumeration of Catalan and Smooth Words According to Capacity*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A5, Section 2, definition of `𝒜_{n,i}`.

articles.title: Recurrence for words avoiding the pattern $z, z+1, z$
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and, for each
natural number $n$, let $f_k(n)$ be the number of words of length $n$ over the alphabet
$\{0, 1, \dots, k-1\}$ that avoid the consecutive pattern $z, z+1, z$. Then $f_k(0) = 1$,
$f_k(1) = k$, $f_k(2) = k^2$, and $f_k(n) = k f_k(n-1) - f_k(n-2) + f_k(n-3)$ for every $n \ge 3$.

At $k = 0$ the recurrence would read $0 = 1$ at $n = 3$.

## Sources

- Sela Fried, "Proofs of Several Conjectures From the OEIS", Theorem 3.

articles.title: Words avoiding the consecutive pattern $z, z+1, z$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$,
$f_k(n)$ is the number of words $w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{n-1}$ of length $n$ over the alphabet
$\{0, 1, \dots, k-1\}$ with no position $i$ such that $i + 2 < n$, $w_{i+1} = w_i + 1$ and
$w_{i+2} = w_i$.

articles.title: Floor of a sum of cube roots
articles.statement:
For every integer $m \ge 1$, the sum
$S_m = \sum_{i=1}^{10^{3m}} i^{1/3}$ of the real cube roots of $1, 2, \dots, 10^{3m}$ satisfies

$$\lfloor S_m \rfloor = \frac{3 \cdot 10^{4m}}{4} + 5 \cdot 10^{m-1} - 1.$$

## Sources

- Sela Fried, "Proofs of Several Conjectures From the OEIS", Theorem 7.

articles.title: Bit length of $\binom{2^n}{2^{n-1}}$
articles.statement:
For every integer $n \ge 1$, the binary expansion of
the binomial coefficient $\binom{2^n}{2^{n-1}}$ has exactly $2^n - \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ digits.

## Sources

- Sela Fried, "Proofs of Several Conjectures From the OEIS", Theorem 6.

articles.title: Reversal preserves equilibrious words
articles.statement:
A finite word $u$ over the binary alphabet
$\{0, 1\}$ is equilibrious if and only if its reversal is equilibrious.

articles.title: Equilibrious binary words
articles.statement:
A finite word $u$ over the binary alphabet $\{0, 1\}$ is
equilibrious when the letters $0$ and $1$ occur the same number of times in $u$.

The letters $a$ and $b$ of the source alphabet $\Sigma = \{a, b\}$ are represented by $0$ and $1$.

## Sources

- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL28/Coons/coons6.tex>, lines 543–575.

articles.title: Non-intersecting pairs of words
articles.statement:
Fix natural numbers $k$, $n \ge 1$ and $r \ge 1$, and call
a pair of words over an alphabet of $k$ letters non-intersecting when no letter occurs in both.
Write $[x^m] F$ for the coefficient of $x^m$ in a formal power series $F$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ and
$S(m, j)$ for the Stirling numbers of the second kind. Let $N$ be the number of non-intersecting
pairs $(u, v)$ with $u$ of length $n$ and $v$ of length $r$. Then
$N = \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \binom{k}{j} \,
[x^n]\Bigl(j! \, x^j \bigl(\prod_{i=1}^{j} (1 - i x)\bigr)^{-1}\Bigr) \,
[x^r]\bigl((k-j) x \, (1 - (k-j) x)^{-1}\bigr)$
and
$N = \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \binom{k}{j} \, j! \, S(n, j) \,
[x^r]\bigl((k-j) x \, (1 - (k-j) x)^{-1}\bigr)$.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher and Arnold Knopfmacher, *Intersections in Pairs of Words*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A107, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Non-intersecting pairs of words of equal length
articles.statement:
Let $S(n, j)$ denote the Stirling numbers
of the second kind. For natural numbers $k$ and $n \ge 1$, the number of pairs $(u, v)$ of words
of length $n$ over an alphabet of $k$ letters such that no letter occurs in both $u$ and $v$ is
$\sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \binom{k}{j} \, j! \, S(n, j) \, (k-j)^n$.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher and Arnold Knopfmacher, *Intersections in Pairs of Words*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A107, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Generating function of non-intersecting pairs of words of equal length
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a
natural number, let $S(n, j)$ denote the Stirling numbers of the second kind, and for $n \ge 1$ let
$h(n)$ be the number of pairs $(u, v)$ of words of length $n$ over an alphabet of $k$ letters such
that no letter occurs in both. Then, as formal power series over $\mathbb{Q}$,
$\sum_{n \ge 1} h(n) x^n = \sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \binom{k}{j} \, j! \, S(n, j) \,
(k-j)^n x^n$.

The constant term on the right is $0$ because $S(0, j) = 0$ for $j \ge 1$: the empty pair is not
counted.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher and Arnold Knopfmacher, *Intersections in Pairs of Words*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A107, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Generating function of non-intersecting pairs of weakly decreasing words
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a
natural number and order an alphabet of $k$ letters. In the ring of formal power series in $x$
and $y$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ let
$f(x, y) = \bigl(x (1-x)^{-1} + (1-y)^{-1}\bigr)^k - (1-x)^{-k} - (1-y)^{-k} + 1$.
Then for all natural numbers $n$ and $r$, the coefficient of $x^n y^r$ in $f$ is $0$ if $n = 0$
or $r = 0$, and otherwise equals the number of pairs $(u, v)$ of weakly decreasing words over this
alphabet, $u$ of length $n$ and $v$ of length $r$, such that no letter occurs in both.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher and Arnold Knopfmacher, *Intersections in Pairs of Words*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A107, Corollary 4.

articles.title: Non-intersecting pairs of weakly decreasing words of equal length
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$
and $n \ge 1$, the number of pairs $(u, v)$ of weakly decreasing words of length $n$ over an
ordered alphabet of $k$ letters such that no letter occurs in both is
$\sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \binom{k}{j} \binom{n-1}{j-1} \binom{n+k-j-1}{n}$.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher and Arnold Knopfmacher, *Intersections in Pairs of Words*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A107, Corollary 5.

articles.title: Non-intersecting pairs of weakly decreasing words
articles.statement:
Fix natural numbers $k$, $n \ge 1$ and
$r \ge 1$, and order an alphabet of $k$ letters. Write $[x^m] F$ for the coefficient of $x^m$ in a
formal power series $F$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. The number of pairs $(u, v)$ of weakly decreasing words
over this alphabet, $u$ of length $n$ and $v$ of length $r$, such that no letter occurs in both is
$\sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \binom{k}{j} \, [x^n]\bigl(x^j (1-x)^{-j}\bigr) \,
[x^r]\bigl((1-x)^{-(k-j)} - 1\bigr)$.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher and Arnold Knopfmacher, *Intersections in Pairs of Words*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A107, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Overlap statistic on pairs of weakly decreasing words
articles.statement:
Fix natural numbers $k$, $n \ge 1$,
$r \ge 1$ and a rational number $q$, and order an alphabet of $k$ letters. For words $u$ and $v$
over this alphabet, the overlap of $(u, v)$ is the number of positions of $v$ whose letter occurs
in $u$. Write $[x^m] F$ for the coefficient of $x^m$ in a formal power series $F$ over
$\mathbb{Q}$. Let $T$ be the sum of $q^{\text{overlap}}$ over all pairs $(u, v)$ of weakly
decreasing words, $u$ of length $n$ and $v$ of length $r$. Then
$T = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \binom{k}{j} \, [x^n]\bigl(x^j (1-x)^{-j}\bigr) \,
[x^r]\Bigl((1-x)^{-(k-j)} - 1 + (1-x)^{-(k-j)} \sum_{m \ge 1} \binom{m+j-1}{m} q^m x^m\Bigr)$
and
$T = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \binom{k}{j} \, [x^n]\bigl(x^j (1-x)^{-j}\bigr) \,
[x^r]\bigl(-1 + (1-x)^{-(k-j)} (1 - qx)^{-j}\bigr)$.

The paper prints these sums over $j$ with upper limit $k - 1$, which omits the pairs whose first
word uses all $k$ letters ($j = k$, which Theorem 2 includes): for $k = 1$ and $n = r = 1$ the
only pair contributes $q$, while the printed sum is empty.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher and Arnold Knopfmacher, *Intersections in Pairs of Words*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A107, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Overlap statistic on pairs of words
articles.statement:
Fix natural numbers $k$, $n \ge 1$, $r \ge 1$ and a
rational number $q$. For words $u$ and $v$ over an alphabet of $k$ letters, the overlap of
$(u, v)$ is the number of positions of $v$ whose letter occurs in $u$. Write $[x^m] F$ for the
coefficient of $x^m$ in a formal power series $F$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, $S(m, j)$ for the Stirling
numbers of the second kind, and $c_j = qj + k - j$. Then the sum of $q^{\text{overlap}}$ over all
pairs $(u, v)$ with $u$ of length $n$ and $v$ of length $r$ equals
$\sum_{j=1}^{k} \binom{k}{j} \, [x^r]\bigl(c_j x \, (1 - c_j x)^{-1}\bigr) \, j! \, S(n, j)$.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher and Arnold Knopfmacher, *Intersections in Pairs of Words*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A107, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Overlap statistic on pairs of words of equal length
articles.statement:
Fix natural numbers $k$ and $n \ge 1$
and a rational number $q$. For words $u$ and $v$ over an alphabet of $k$ letters, the overlap of
$(u, v)$ is the number of positions of $v$ whose letter occurs in $u$. Let $S(n, j)$ denote the
Stirling numbers of the second kind. Then the sum of $q^{\text{overlap}}$ over all pairs $(u, v)$
of words of length $n$ equals $\sum_{j=1}^{k} \binom{k}{j} \, j! \, S(n, j) \, (qj + k - j)^n$.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher and Arnold Knopfmacher, *Intersections in Pairs of Words*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A107, Corollary 3.

articles.title: Keyword classes are counted by partial sums of $m$-step Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let
$m, n \ge 1$ and let $F_0, F_1, F_2, \dots$ be the $m$-step Fibonacci numbers: $F_0 = 1$,
$F_k = 2^{k-1}$ for $1 \le k \le m - 1$, and $F_k = F_{k-1} + F_{k-2} + \dots + F_{k-m}$ for
$k \ge m$. Then for every binary keyword $a$ of length $m + 1$, the number of equivalence
classes of the relation $\sim_a$ on binary words of length $n$ is $F_0 + F_1 + \dots + F_n$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Theorem 1 (`jis-2025-25.6.6-thm-1`).

articles.title: Keywords with equally many singleton classes
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be binary keywords of
length $m + 1$. The relations $\sim_a$ and $\sim_b$ have the same number of one-element
equivalence classes on binary words of length $n$ for every $n \ge 0$ if and only if, for every
$i$ with $1 \le i \le m + 1$, the following holds for $a$ exactly when it holds for $b$: the
prefix of length $i$ of the keyword equals its suffix of length $i$ or the letterwise negation
of that suffix.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Proposition 10 (`jis-2025-25.6.6-prop-10`).

articles.title: Parity of the smallest index in a non-commuting list
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be a binary keyword of
length $m + 1$, let $n$ and $i$ be natural numbers with $i < n$, and for each index $k$ let
$\varphi_k$ be the simple map of $a$ at letter $k$ on binary words of length $n$. Let
$l = [j_1, \dots, j_r]$ be a list of indices that are all greater than $i$, and let
$\varphi_l = \varphi_{j_r} \circ \dots \circ \varphi_{j_1}$ be the map that applies
$\varphi_{j_1}$ first. Suppose that $\varphi_i \circ \varphi_l \ne \varphi_l \circ \varphi_i$
as maps on words of length $n$, and that the list $[i, j_1, \dots, j_r, i]$, applied from left
to right, acts completely on some word of length $n$ (each map in turn changes the word). Then
every entry $j$ of $l$ with $j \le j'$ for all entries $j'$ of $l$ occurs an even number of
times in $l$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Lemma 8 (`jis-2025-25.6.6-lem-8`).

articles.title: Complete action of a one-element list
articles.statement:
For a binary keyword $a$, an index $j$ and a
binary word $u$, the one-element list $[j]$ acts completely on $u$ if and only if the simple map
$\varphi_j$ of $a$ changes $u$, that is, $\varphi_j(u) \ne u$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Section 2.2 (action by lists of simple maps).

articles.title: Lists of simple maps acting completely
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be a binary keyword and $u$ a binary
word. A list $[j_1, \dots, j_r]$ of indices acts completely on $u$ when applying the simple maps
$\varphi_{j_1}, \varphi_{j_2}, \dots, \varphi_{j_r}$ of $a$ in this order changes the word at
every step: with $u_0 = u$ and $u_q = \varphi_{j_q}(u_{q-1})$, we have $u_q \ne u_{q-1}$ for
$1 \le q \le r$. In particular the empty list acts completely on every word.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Section 2.2 (action by lists of simple maps).

articles.title: Applicability of a keyword
articles.statement:
Let $a = a_0 a_1 \cdots a_m$ be a binary keyword of length
$m + 1$ and $u = u_0 u_1 \cdots u_{n-1}$ a binary word of length $n$. The keyword $a$ is
applicable to $u$ at the ($0$-indexed) letter $i$ when $i + m < n$ and the subword
$u_i u_{i+1} \cdots u_{i+m}$ of $u$ equals $a$ or the letterwise negation of $a$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Section 2.1 (definition of substitutions involving the keyword).

articles.title: Keyword equivalence is stable under concatenation
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be a binary keyword, let $u$
and $v$ be binary words of length $n$, and let $w$ be a binary word of length $n'$. Writing $xy$
for the concatenation of words $x$ and $y$, we have $u \sim_a v$ if and only if
$uw \sim_a vw$, and $u \sim_a v$ if and only if $wu \sim_a wv$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Lemma 6 (`jis-2025-25.6.6-lem-6`).

articles.title: Reflexivity of keyword equivalence
articles.statement:
For every binary keyword $a$ and every binary word
$u$, we have $u \sim_a u$: the empty composition of simple maps sends $u$ to itself.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Section 2.1 (equivalence relation induced by the keyword).

articles.title: Keyword equivalence of binary words
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be a binary keyword of length $m + 1$.
Two binary words $u$ and $v$ of length $n$ satisfy $u \sim_a v$ when some finite composition
of simple maps of $a$, possibly the empty composition, sends $u$ to $v$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Section 2.1 (equivalence relation induced by the keyword).

articles.title: Adjacency in the keyword substitution graph
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be a binary keyword and let $u$
and $v$ be binary words of length $n$. Then $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in the graph
$\mathcal{G}_n^{(a)}$ if and only if $u \ne v$ and some simple map $\varphi_i$ of $a$ sends $u$
to $v$ or sends $v$ to $u$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Section 3.2 (graph structure within equivalence classes).

articles.title: Intertwining bijections preserve distances in the substitution graph
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be
keywords of length $m + 1$, and write $\varphi_i^{(a)}$ and $\varphi_i^{(b)}$ for the simple maps
of $a$ and $b$ at letter $i$ on binary words of length $n$. Let $f$ be a bijection of the set of
binary words of length $n$ and $\sigma$ a permutation of the positions $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, and
suppose that $f(\varphi_i^{(a)}(u)) = \varphi_{\sigma(i)}^{(b)}(f(u))$ for every word $u$ and
every position $i$. Then for all words $u$ and $v$ of length $n$, the extended graph distance
(possibly $\infty$) between $u$ and $v$ in the substitution graph $\mathcal{G}_n^{(a)}$ equals the
extended graph distance between $f(u)$ and $f(v)$ in $\mathcal{G}_n^{(b)}$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Lemma 16 (`jis-2025-25.6.6-lem-16`).

articles.title: The substitution graph is bipartite
articles.statement:
For every keyword $a$ of length $m + 1$ and every
$n \ge 0$, the substitution graph $\mathcal{G}_n^{(a)}$ on binary words of length $n$ is
bipartite.

The paper states this for $n \ge 1$; it also holds at $n = 0$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Proposition 17 (`jis-2025-25.6.6-prop-17`).

articles.title: Keyword symmetries of the substitution graph
articles.statement:
Let $a = a_0 a_1 \cdots a_m$ be a keyword of
length $m + 1$ and let $n \ge 0$. Write $\neg a$ for the letterwise negation of $a$,
$\rho(a) = a_m a_{m-1} \cdots a_0$ for its reversal, and $\bar a$ for its seminegation, which keeps
$a_t$ for even $t$ and negates $a_t$ for odd $t$. Then the substitution graphs satisfy
$\mathcal{G}_n^{(a)} = \mathcal{G}_n^{(\neg a)}$, and $\mathcal{G}_n^{(a)}$ is isomorphic both to
$\mathcal{G}_n^{(\rho(a))}$ and to $\mathcal{G}_n^{(\bar a)}$.

In the paper's numbering, which counts letters from $1$, the seminegation negates the letters in
even positions. The paper states this for $n \ge 1$; it also holds at $n = 0$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Proposition 15 (`jis-2025-25.6.6-prop-15`).

articles.title: Substitution graph
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be a keyword, a binary word of length $m + 1$, and let
$n \ge 0$. The substitution graph $\mathcal{G}_n^{(a)}$ is the simple graph on the binary words of
length $n$ in which distinct words $u$ and $v$ are adjacent when $\varphi_i(u) = v$ or
$\varphi_i(v) = u$ for some $i \in \mathbb{N}$, where $\varphi_i$ is the simple map of $a$ at
letter $i$. Equivalently, $u$ and $v$ are adjacent when one is obtained from the other by
replacing an occurrence of $a$ by $\neg a$ or an occurrence of $\neg a$ by $a$, where $\neg a$ is
the letterwise negation of $a$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Section 3.2 (graph structure within equivalence classes).

articles.title: The empty list of simple maps acts trivially
articles.statement:
For every keyword $a$ and every binary word
$u$, applying the empty list of simple maps of $a$ to $u$ returns $u$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Section 2.2 (action by lists of simple maps).

articles.title: Action of a list of simple maps
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be a keyword and, for $j \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$\varphi_j$ be the simple map of $a$ at letter $j$. A list $[j_1, \dots, j_r]$ of natural numbers
acts on a binary word $u$ of length $n$ by
$u \mapsto \varphi_{j_r}(\cdots(\varphi_{j_1}(u))\cdots)$: the head of the list acts first, and
the empty list acts as the identity.

The paper writes this list as $(\varphi_{j_r}, \dots, \varphi_{j_1})$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Section 2.2 (action by lists of simple maps).

articles.title: An applicable simple map negates its window
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be a keyword of length $m + 1$ and $u$
a binary word of length $n$, and suppose that $a$ is applicable to $u$ at letter $i$. Then the
simple map $\varphi_i$ of $a$ negates the letters of $u$ at positions $i, \dots, i + m$ and leaves
every other letter unchanged: for every position $j$, $\varphi_i(u)_j = \neg u_j$ if
$i \le j \le i + m$, and $\varphi_i(u)_j = u_j$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Section 2.1 (simple maps).

articles.title: When two simple maps commute
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be a keyword of length $m + 1$ and let $n$ be a
natural number. Let $i < j$ be natural numbers with $j + m < n$, and put $\Delta = j - i$. The
simple maps $\varphi_i$ and $\varphi_j$ of $a$ on binary words of length $n$ satisfy
$\varphi_i \circ \varphi_j = \varphi_j \circ \varphi_i$ if and only if $\Delta \ge m + 1$, or the
prefix of $a$ of length $m + 1 - \Delta$ differs both from the suffix of $a$ of length
$m + 1 - \Delta$ and from the letterwise negation of that suffix.

In the paper's numbering, which counts letters from $1$, the hypothesis reads $i < j \le n - m$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Proposition 12 (`jis-2025-25.6.6-prop-12`).

articles.title: A simple map that is not applicable is the identity
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be a keyword and $u$ a binary
word. If $a$ is not applicable to $u$ at letter $i$, then the simple map $\varphi_i$ of $a$ leaves
$u$ unchanged: $\varphi_i(u) = u$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Section 2.1 (simple maps).

articles.title: Simple map
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be a keyword, a binary word of length $m + 1$, and let
$i \in \mathbb{N}$. The simple map $\varphi_i$ sends a binary word $u$ of length $n$ to the word
obtained by negating the letters of $u$ at positions $i, \dots, i + m$ (positions counted from
$0$) if $a$ is applicable to $u$ at letter $i$, that is, if $i + m < n$ and the subword of $u$ at
positions $i, \dots, i + m$ equals $a$ or its letterwise negation $\neg a$; otherwise
$\varphi_i(u) = u$.

The paper counts letters from $1$, so its simple map $\varphi_i$ is $\varphi_{i-1}$ in this
numbering.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Section 2.1 (simple maps).

articles.title: Recurrence for partial sums of $m$-step Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and let
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $F(0) = 1$, $F(k) = 2^{k-1}$ for $1 \le k \le m - 1$,
and $F(k) = F(k-1) + \cdots + F(k-m)$ for $k \ge m$ (the $m$-step Fibonacci numbers). Then a
real sequence $(S_n)_{n \ge 0}$ satisfies $S_n = F(0) + F(1) + \cdots + F(n)$ for all $n$ if
and only if $S_n = 2^n$ for $0 \le n \le m$ and $S_n = 2 S_{n-1} - S_{n-m-1}$ for $n \ge m + 1$.

## Sources

- Erik Bates, Blan Morrison, Mason Rogers, Arianna Serafini and Anav Sood, *A New Combinatorial Interpretation of Partial Sums of m-Step Fibonacci Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.6, Lemma 9 (`jis-2025-25.6.6-lem-9`).

articles.title: Witt's formula for the number of Lyndon words of given content
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a natural
number and let $n_0, \dots, n_{r-1}$ be natural numbers with $n = n_0 + \dots + n_{r-1} > 0$.
Order the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$ as the natural numbers and order words over it
lexicographically. Then the number of Lyndon words over this alphabet in which each letter $i$
occurs exactly $n_i$ times equals, as a rational number, Witt's multigraded value
$M(n_0, \dots, n_{r-1}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{d \mid g} \mu(d) \binom{n/d}{n_0/d, \ldots, n_{r-1}/d}$,
where $g = \gcd(n_0, \dots, n_{r-1})$, the sum runs over the positive divisors $d$ of $g$, and
$\mu$ is the Möbius function.

articles.title: Words of given content are counted by the multinomial coefficient
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a natural
number, let $n_0, \dots, n_{r-1}$ be natural numbers, and let $n = n_0 + \dots + n_{r-1}$. The
number of words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$ in which each letter $i$ occurs exactly
$n_i$ times is the multinomial coefficient
$\binom{n}{n_0, \ldots, n_{r-1}} = \frac{n!}{n_0! \cdots n_{r-1}!}$.

articles.title: Lyndon word
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered alphabet, and order the words over
$\alpha$ lexicographically. A word $w$ over $\alpha$ of length $n$ is a Lyndon word if it is
nonempty and, for every $k$ with $0 < k < n$, $w$ is strictly smaller than its rotation by $k$,
the word obtained by moving the first $k$ letters of $w$ to the end.

articles.title: Primitivity via distinct rotations
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be a word of length $n$, and for
$0 \le k < n$ let $w_k$ be the rotation of $w$ by $k$, obtained by moving the first $k$ letters
of $w$ to the end. Then $w$ is primitive if and only if $w$ is nonempty and the $n$ words
$w_0, w_1, \dots, w_{n-1}$ are pairwise distinct.

articles.title: Lyndon words are primitive
articles.statement:
Every Lyndon word over a linearly ordered alphabet is
primitive.

articles.title: Primitive word
articles.statement: A nonempty finite word is primitive if it is not a proper power of another word.

articles.title: Lyndon words of given content
articles.statement:
For a natural number $r$ and natural numbers
$n_0, \dots, n_{r-1}$, the set of Lyndon words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$, ordered as
the natural numbers, in which each letter $i$ occurs exactly $n_i$ times.

articles.title: Primitive words of given content
articles.statement:
For a natural number $r$ and natural numbers
$n_0, \dots, n_{r-1}$, the set of primitive words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$ in which
each letter $i$ occurs exactly $n_i$ times.

articles.title: Nontrivial rotations move a primitive word
articles.statement:
If $w$ is a primitive word of length $n$
and $0 < k < n$, then the rotation of $w$ by $k$, obtained by moving the first $k$ letters of $w$
to the end, is different from $w$.

articles.title: The content of a word sums to its length
articles.statement:
For a natural number $r$ and a word $w$ over
the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$, summing over all letters $i$ the number of occurrences of $i$
in $w$ gives the length of $w$.

articles.title: Content is additive under concatenation
articles.statement:
For a natural number $r$, words $u$ and $v$ over
the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$, and every letter $i$, the number of occurrences of $i$ in the
concatenation $uv$ is the number of occurrences of $i$ in $u$ plus the number of occurrences
of $i$ in $v$.

articles.title: Content of a word after prepending a letter
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a natural number, let $w$ be a word
over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$, let $i$ be a letter, and write $c(u)$ for the content of a
word $u$ (the number of occurrences of each letter in $u$). If $iw$ denotes $w$ with $i$ prepended,
then $c(iw)(i) = c(w)(i) + 1$ and $c(iw)(j) = c(w)(j)$ for every letter $j \ne i$.

articles.title: Content of a one-letter word
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a natural number. For every letter $i$ of the
alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$, the content of the one-letter word $i$ takes the value $1$ at $i$ and
the value $0$ at every other letter.

articles.title: Content of a word
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a natural number. The content of a word $w$ over the alphabet
$\{0, \dots, r-1\}$ is the function that assigns to each letter $i$ the number of occurrences of $i$
in $w$.

articles.title: Words with prescribed content
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a natural number. Given a function $d$ from the
alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$ to the natural numbers, the words of content $d$ are the words $w$ over
this alphabet whose content equals $d$, that is, in which each letter $i$ occurs exactly $d(i)$
times.

articles.title: Generating function for $1 \times s$ rectangles in nondecreasing words
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and
$s \ge 1$, and let $f_k(n)$ be the total number of $1 \times s$ rectangles over all nondecreasing
words of length $n$ over $[k] = \{1, \dots, k\}$. Then, as formal power series over $\mathbb{Z}$,

$$
\Big(\sum_{n \ge 0} f_k(n)\, x^n\Big) (1 - x)^{k+1} =
x^s \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} (-1)^i \binom{i+s-2}{i} \binom{k+s}{s+i+1} x^i,
$$

and for every $n \ge s$,

$$
f_k(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{\min(k-1,\, n-s)} (-1)^i \binom{i+s-2}{i} \binom{k+s}{s+i+1}
\binom{n-s-i+k}{k}.
$$

For $s = 1$ the factor $\binom{i+s-2}{i} = \binom{i-1}{i}$ is $1$ at $i = 0$ and $0$ for $i \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Sela Fried and Toufik Mansour, *Counting Rectangles of Size r × s in Nondecreasing and Smirnov Words*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.4, Corollary 2 (`jis-2024-24.8.4-cor-2`).

articles.title: Generating function for $r \times s$ rectangles in nondecreasing words
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$,
$r \ge 1$ and $s \ge 1$, let $g_k(n)$ be the total number of $r \times s$ rectangles over all
nondecreasing words of length $n$ over $[k] = \{1, \dots, k\}$, and let $m = \max(k + 1 - r, 0)$.
Then, as formal power series over $\mathbb{Z}$,

$$
\Big(\sum_{n \ge 0} g_k(n)\, x^n\Big) (1 - x)^{k+1} =
x^s \sum_{0 \le i \le k+1-r} (-1)^i \binom{i+s-2}{i} \binom{m+s}{s+i+1} x^i,
$$

where the sum is empty when $r \ge k + 2$, and for every $n \ge s$,

$$
g_k(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{\min(m,\, n-s)} (-1)^i \binom{i+s-2}{i} \binom{m+s}{s+i+1}
\binom{n-s-i+k}{k}.
$$

For $s = 1$ the factor $\binom{i+s-2}{i} = \binom{i-1}{i}$ is $1$ at $i = 0$ and $0$ for $i \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Sela Fried and Toufik Mansour, *Counting Rectangles of Size r × s in Nondecreasing and Smirnov Words*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.4, Corollary 6 (`jis-2024-24.8.4-cor-6`).

articles.title: Example: $1 \times 2$ rectangles in nondecreasing words of length $2$
articles.statement:
The nondecreasing
words of length $2$ over $[2] = \{1, 2\}$ are $11$, $12$ and $22$, which contain $1$, $1$ and $2$
rectangles of size $1 \times 2$ respectively, so the total number of $1 \times 2$ rectangles over
all nondecreasing words of length $2$ over $[2]$ is $4$.

## Sources

- Sela Fried and Toufik Mansour, *Counting Rectangles of Size r × s in Nondecreasing and Smirnov Words*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.4, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Total number of $r \times s$ rectangles in nondecreasing words
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$,
$r$, $s$ and $n$, this is the sum, over all nondecreasing words $w_1 \le w_2 \le \cdots \le w_n$ of
length $n$ over the alphabet $[k] = \{1, \dots, k\}$ (the set $W^{\nearrow}_{n,k}$), of the number
of $r \times s$ rectangles in the bargraph of $w$.

## Sources

- Sela Fried and Toufik Mansour, *Counting Rectangles of Size r × s in Nondecreasing and Smirnov Words*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.4, Corollaries 2 and 6.

articles.title: Example: $3 \times 2$ rectangles in the word $345134$
articles.statement:
The bargraph of the word $345134$
contains exactly four rectangles of height $3$ and width $2$.

## Sources

- Sela Fried and Toufik Mansour, *Counting Rectangles of Size r × s in Nondecreasing and Smirnov Words*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.4, Figure 2.

articles.title: Number of $r \times s$ rectangles in a bargraph
articles.statement:
Let $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{m-1}$ be a word
of natural numbers, drawn as a bargraph whose column $i$ has height $w_i$. The number of
occurrences of an $r \times s$ rectangle (height $r$, width $s$) in $w$ is the number of pairs
$(i, y)$ of natural numbers with $i < m$, $i + s \le m$ and $y \le w_0 + \cdots + w_{m-1}$ such
that $y + r \le w_{i+j}$ for every $j < s$.

Here $(i, y)$ is the rectangle whose lower left cell is in column $i$ and row $y$, both counted
from $0$. For $s \ge 1$ the conditions $i < m$ and $y \le w_0 + \cdots + w_{m-1}$ follow from the
others; for $s = 0$ the count is $m(w_0 + \cdots + w_{m-1} + 1)$.

## Sources

- Sela Fried and Toufik Mansour, *Counting Rectangles of Size r × s in Nondecreasing and Smirnov Words*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.4, Introduction and Figure 2.

articles.title: $k$-strings
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, a $k$-string is a finite sequence (possibly empty)
of elements of $\{0, 1, \ldots, k-1\}$.

articles.title: The reverse-permute relation
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, a $k$-string $s$ is related to a
$k$-string $t$ by the reverse-permute (RP) relation when there is a permutation $\sigma$ of
$\{0, 1, \ldots, k-1\}$ such that $t$ is obtained, either from $s$ or from the reversal of $s$,
by replacing each entry $x$ with $\sigma(x)$.

articles.title: Counting Ulam words with a single one
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$, the number of
$a \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ for which the word $0^a 1 0^{n-1-a}$ ($a$ zeros, then a one, then
$n - 1 - a$ zeros) is an Ulam word equals $2^{s_2(n-1)}$, where $s_2(m)$ is the sum of the binary
digits of $m$. This number is the term $G(n - 1)$ of Gould's sequence.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Theorem 5 (Corollary 3.4 of Bade, Cui, Labelle, and Li).

articles.title: The first stage of the discrete Sierpiński triangle
articles.statement:
The stage $S_1$ of the discrete
Sierpiński triangle is $\{(2, 1), (3, 1), (3, 2)\}$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Section 4.

articles.title: Stages of the discrete Sierpiński triangle
articles.statement:
The stages
$S_n \subseteq \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ of the discrete Sierpiński triangle are defined by
$S_0 = \{(2, 1)\}$ and $S_{n+1} = S_n \cup (S_n + (2^n, 0)) \cup (S_n + (2^n, 2^n))$, where
$S + (u, v) = \{(x + u, y + v) : (x, y) \in S\}$ denotes a translate.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Section 4 (recursive definition of `S_n`).

articles.title: The discrete Sierpiński triangle
articles.statement:
The discrete Sierpiński triangle is the set
$\mathcal{S} = \bigcup_{n \ge 0} S_n \subseteq \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, the union of all the
stages $S_n$ of the discrete Sierpiński triangle.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Section 4.

articles.title: Ulam words of length four: examples
articles.statement:
The words $0001$ and $1011$ are Ulam words, while
$0011$ and $0110$ are not.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Section 1 (displayed `U₄`).

articles.title: Complement symmetry of Ulam words
articles.statement:
For a word $w$ over $\{0, 1\}$, let $\bar w$ be its
complement (every letter swapped) and let $\pi(w)$ be the integer whose binary expansion is $w$,
most significant letter first. If $w$ is an Ulam word of length $n$, then $\bar w$ is an Ulam
word and $\pi(\bar w) + \pi(w) = 2^n - 1$. Moreover, for all natural numbers $N$ and $n$ and every
$a \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, the number of Ulam words $w$ of length $n$ with
$\pi(w) \equiv a \pmod N$ equals the number of Ulam words $w$ of length $n$ with
$\pi(w) \equiv 2^n - 1 - a \pmod N$.

For $n \ge 1$, writing $\rho_{a,N}(n)$ for the proportion of Ulam words $w$ of length $n$ with
$\pi(w) \equiv a \pmod N$ among all Ulam words of length $n$, the second statement says
$\rho_{a,N}(n) = \rho_{2^n-1-a,N}(n)$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Theorem 11.

articles.title: Ulam words made of ones followed by zeros
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $x$ and $y$ with
$1 \le y \le x$, the word $1^y 0^{x-y}$ ($y$ ones followed by $x - y$ zeros) is an Ulam word if
and only if $(x, y) = (1, 1)$ or $(x, y)$ belongs to the discrete Sierpiński triangle
$\mathcal{S}$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Theorem 9 (precise form of Theorem 3).

articles.title: Ulam words of length at most three
articles.statement:
The empty word is not an Ulam word, and both words
$0$ and $1$ of length one are Ulam words. The Ulam words of length two are exactly $01$ and $10$,
and the Ulam words of length three are exactly $001$, $011$, $100$ and $110$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Section 1 (displayed `U₁, …, U₄`).

articles.title: Ulam words with three leading ones
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 3$, the word $1^3 0^{n-3}$ (three
ones followed by $n - 3$ zeros) is an Ulam word if and only if $n \equiv 0 \pmod 4$ or
$n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Padding the word 10101 with zeros
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$ and $b$ with $a + b \ge 1$, the
word $0^a 10101 0^b$ ($a$ zeros, then $10101$, then $b$ zeros) is an Ulam word if and only if $a$
and $b$ are both even and at least one of $a$ and $b$ is zero.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Theorem 10.

articles.title: Ulam words with a block of four ones
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$ and $b$ with $a + b \ge 1$,
the binary word $0^a 1111 0^b$ ($a$ zeros, then four ones, then $b$ zeros) is an Ulam word if
and only if $a + b \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Ulam words with one 101 block
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$ and $b$ with $a + b \ge 2$, the
binary word $0^a 101 0^b$ ($a$ zeros, then the letters $1, 0, 1$, then $b$ zeros) is an Ulam word
if and only if $a + b$ is odd.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Theorem 7 (Theorem 3.6 of Bade, Cui, Labelle, and Li).

articles.title: Parity criterion for Ulam words with a single one
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$ and $b$, the
binary word $0^a 1 0^b$ ($a$ zeros, then a one, then $b$ zeros) is an Ulam word if and only if
the binomial coefficient $\binom{a + b}{a}$ is odd.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Theorem 8 (Theorem 3.4 of Bade, Cui, Labelle, and Li).

articles.title: Ulam words with a block of two ones
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$ and $b$, the binary word
$0^a 11 0^b$ ($a$ zeros, then two ones, then $b$ zeros) is an Ulam word if and only if $a + b$ is
odd.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Theorem 6 (Theorem 3.5 of Bade, Cui, Labelle, and Li).

articles.title: Ulam words
articles.statement:
Ulam words are finite words over the alphabet $\{0, 1\}$, defined by
recursion on the length. The empty word is not an Ulam word, and the two words $0$ and $1$ of
length $1$ are Ulam words. A word $w$ of length at least $2$ is an Ulam word if and only if there
is exactly one way to write $w = uv$ with $u$ and $v$ nonempty, distinct Ulam words.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Section 1 (definition of Ulam words, after Bade, Cui, Labelle, and Li).

articles.title: Linear lower bound on the number of Ulam words
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 6$, the
number of Ulam words of length $n$ is at least $2n + 4$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Theorem 1.

articles.title: The inverse Ulam density has the order of the mean gap
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $U_n$
be the set of Ulam words of length $n$, and let $\mu_g(n)$ be the mean gap of the binary values
of the words in $U_n$. Then $2^n / |U_n|$ (the reciprocal of the density $|U_n| / 2^n$) and
$\mu_g(n)$ have the same order of growth as $n \to \infty$: there are constants $c, C > 0$ such
that $c \, \mu_g(n) \le 2^n / |U_n| \le C \, \mu_g(n)$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Theorem 4 (first sentence).

articles.title: Mean gap of the Ulam values
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, read each Ulam word of length $n$
as a binary numeral, most significant letter first, and list the resulting values in increasing
order as $u_1 < u_2 < \dots < u_k$. The mean gap of these values is the rational number

$$\mu_g(n) = \frac{1}{k - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} (u_{i+1} - u_i),$$

where a quotient by $0$ is read as $0$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Section 1 (Conjecture 2, `μ_g(n)` as the mean of the gap distribution `p_n`).

articles.title: Residue symmetries of Ulam words modulo 2 and 3
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $N$ and $n$ and a
residue $a \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, let $c_{a,N}(n)$ be the number of Ulam words of length
$n$ whose value as a binary numeral, most significant letter first, is congruent to $a$ modulo
$N$. Then for every $n \ge 1$ we have $c_{0,2}(n) = c_{1,2}(n)$, and for every
$a \in \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ we have $c_{a,3}(n) = c_{-a,3}(n)$ if $n$ is even and
$c_{a,3}(n) = c_{1-a,3}(n)$ if $n$ is odd.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Residues of the Ulam words of length 2 modulo 3
articles.statement:
Read the Ulam words of length $2$ as
binary numerals, most significant letter first. None of their values is congruent to $0$ modulo
$3$, exactly one is congruent to $1$, and exactly one is congruent to $2$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Section 6.

articles.title: Ulam words in a residue class
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $N$ and $n$ and a residue class
$a \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, this is the number of Ulam words $w$ of length $n$ in the letters
$0$ and $1$ whose binary value $\pi(w)$, read with the most significant letter first, lies in the
class $a$ modulo $N$. For $N = 0$, $\mathbb{Z}/0\mathbb{Z}$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ and the condition is
$\pi(w) = a$.

The paper's relative density $\rho_{a,N}(n)$ is this number divided by the number $\#U_n$ of
Ulam words of length $n$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Section 1 (Conjecture 3, definition of `ρ_{a,N}(n)`).

articles.title: Binary values of the Ulam words of length 3
articles.statement:
The increasing list of the distinct binary
values $\pi(w)$, read with the most significant letter first, of the Ulam words $w$ of length $3$
has exactly the entries $1, 3, 4, 6$.

These values come from the Ulam words $001$, $011$, $100$, $110$ of length $3$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Section 1.

articles.title: Sorted binary values of Ulam words
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, this is the list
$u_1 < u_2 < \dots < u_k$ of the distinct binary values $\pi(w)$, read with the most significant
letter first, of the Ulam words $w$ of length $n$, in increasing order.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Section 1 (Conjecture 2, ordered elements of `π(U_n)`).

articles.title: Fuel-bounded Ulam test
articles.statement:
For a natural number $f$ (the fuel) and a word $w$ in the letters
$0$ and $1$, the test returns false when $f = 0$. With fuel $f + 1$ it returns true when $w$ has
length $1$; otherwise it returns true exactly when there is exactly one $k$ with
$1 \le k < |w|$ such that the prefix $w_1 \cdots w_k$ and the suffix $w_{k+1} \cdots w_{|w|}$
are distinct and both pass the test with fuel $f$.

This is the Ulam recursion: with fuel at least $|w|$, the test decides whether $w$ is an Ulam
word.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Section 1 (definition of Ulam words, after Bade, Cui, Labelle, and Li).

articles.title: Exponential lower bound for Ulam word counts along a subsequence
articles.statement:
Let $\#U_n$ be the
number of Ulam words of length $n$ and $\alpha_0 = (\#U_{30} / (2 \cdot 31))^{1/30}$. For every
real $\alpha$ with $1 < \alpha < \alpha_0$, every real $C$ and every natural number $N$, there
is some $n \ge N$ with $C \alpha^n \le \#U_n$; that is,
$\limsup_{n \to \infty} \#U_n / \alpha^n = \infty$.

Here $\alpha_0$ is the constant from the paper's proof, with $n_1 = 30$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Numbers of short Ulam words
articles.statement:
There are $2$, $2$, $4$ and $8$ Ulam words of length $1$,
$2$, $3$ and $4$ respectively: $\#U_1 = 2$, $\#U_2 = 2$, $\#U_3 = 4$ and $\#U_4 = 8$, where
$\#U_n$ is the number of Ulam words of length $n$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Section 1 (displayed `U₁, …, U₄`).

articles.title: Square of the Ulam word count is at most a block sum
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$,
$(\#U_n)^2 \le \sum_{i=n}^{2n} \#U_i$, where $\#U_i$ is the number of Ulam words of length $i$.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Number of Ulam words of a given length
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $\#U_n$ denotes the
number of Ulam words of length $n$, that is, of words $w_1 \cdots w_n$ of length $n$ in the
letters $0$ and $1$ that are Ulam words.

## Sources

- Adutwum, Clark, Emerson, A. Sheydvasser, A. Sheydvasser, and Tougouma, *Distributions of Ulam Words up to Length 30*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A102, Section 1.

articles.title: Existence of universal cycles for $k$-subsets
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$ there is a
natural number $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ for which $k$ divides $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$, there
is a universal cycle for the $k$-subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Here $n - 1$ and $k - 1$ are
truncated at $0$, so for $k = 0$ the divisibility condition reads $0 \mid 1$ and never holds.

This is the Chung–Diaconis–Graham conjecture. Glock, Joos, Kühn and Osthus (Theorem 1.1)
proved it for every $k \ge 2$ in the language of tight Euler tours of the complete
$k$-uniform hypergraph; the case $k = 1$ is elementary.

## Sources

- Stefan Glock, Felix Joos, Daniela Kühn, Deryk Osthus, Euler tours in hypergraphs, Combinatorica 40 (2020), 679-690; arXiv:1808.07720, https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.07720.

articles.title: Chung–Diaconis–Graham universal cycle conjecture
articles.statement:
The statement that for every natural
number $k$ there is a natural number $N$ such that every $n \ge N$ for which $k$ divides
$\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ admits a universal cycle for the $k$-subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Here
$n - 1$ and $k - 1$ are truncated at $0$, so for $k = 0$ the divisibility condition reads
$0 \mid 1$ and never holds.

## Sources

- Chung/Diaconis/Graham as cited in Cooper, Combinatorial Problems I Like, Words and Codes bullet 78 [AMR-030-0078].

articles.title: Universal cycle for $k$-subsets
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, let $N = \binom{n}{k}$.
A sequence $c_0, \dots, c_{N-1}$ of elements of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, read cyclically, is a
universal cycle for the $k$-subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ when, for every starting position
$i < N$, the $k$ consecutive entries $c_i, c_{i+1}, \dots, c_{i+k-1}$ (indices taken modulo $N$)
are pairwise distinct, and every $k$-element subset of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is the set of these
entries for exactly one starting position $i$.

## Sources

- Chung/Diaconis/Graham as cited in Cooper, Combinatorial Problems I Like, Words and Codes bullet 78 [AMR-030-0078].

articles.title: Factor as a list
articles.statement:
For a right-infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over an alphabet
$\alpha$ and natural numbers $k$ and $i$, the length-$k$ factor of $u$ at position $i$, as a
list, is $[u_i, u_{i+1}, \ldots, u_{i+k-1}]$ (the empty list when $k = 0$).

articles.title: Set of factors of a given length
articles.statement:
For a right-infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$
over an alphabet $\alpha$ and a natural number $k$, the set of length-$k$ factors of $u$ is the
set of the maps $\{0, \ldots, k-1\} \to \alpha$, $s \mapsto u_{i+s}$, for $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Factor of an infinite word
articles.statement:
A right-infinite word over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a
sequence $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ of letters $u_n \in \alpha$. For natural numbers $k$ and $i$,
the length-$k$ factor of $u$ at position $i$ is the word $u_i u_{i+1} \cdots u_{i+k-1}$, given
as the map $\{0, \ldots, k-1\} \to \alpha$, $s \mapsto u_{i+s}$.

articles.title: Finitely many factors of each length
articles.statement:
If the alphabet $\alpha$ is finite, then for every
right-infinite word $u$ over $\alpha$ and every natural number $k$, the set of length-$k$
factors of $u$ is finite.

articles.title: Initial segment of an infinite word
articles.statement:
For a right-infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$
over an alphabet $\alpha$ and a natural number $k$, the length-$k$ initial segment of $u$ is the
word $u_0 u_1 \cdots u_{k-1}$, given as the map $\{0, \ldots, k-1\} \to \alpha$, $s \mapsto u_s$;
it is the length-$k$ factor of $u$ at position $0$.

articles.title: Occurrence via list-valued factors
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be a finite list of length $\ell$ over an
alphabet $\alpha$ and $u$ a right-infinite word over $\alpha$. Then $w$ is a factor of $u$ if and
only if there is a position $i \in \mathbb{N}$ such that the length-$\ell$ factor of $u$ at
position $i$, as a list, equals $w$.

articles.title: Factors as lists and as tuples agree
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number, $v$ a map
$\{0, \ldots, k-1\} \to \alpha$, written $j \mapsto v_j$, and $u$ a right-infinite word over
$\alpha$. Then the list $[v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_{k-1}]$ is a factor of $u$ if and only if $v$
belongs to the set of length-$k$ factors of $u$. This holds also for $k = 0$.

articles.title: Lists occurring in an infinite word
articles.statement:
A finite list $w$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a
factor of a right-infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over $\alpha$ when, writing $\ell$ for
the length of $w$, there is a position $i \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$w = [u_i, u_{i+1}, \ldots, u_{i+\ell-1}]$. In particular, the empty list is a factor of every
right-infinite word over $\alpha$.

articles.title: Nonempty factors via list-valued factors
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be a finite list of length $\ell$ over
an alphabet $\alpha$ and $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ a right-infinite word over $\alpha$. Then $w$
is a nonempty factor of $u$ if and only if $w$ is nonempty and there is a position
$i \in \mathbb{N}$ with $[u_i, u_{i+1}, \ldots, u_{i+\ell-1}] = w$.

articles.title: Nonempty factors are the factors that are nonempty
articles.statement:
For a finite list $w$ over an
alphabet $\alpha$ and a right-infinite word $u$ over $\alpha$, $w$ is a nonempty factor of $u$ if
and only if $w$ is nonempty and $w$ is a factor of $u$.

articles.title: Nonempty factors of an infinite word
articles.statement:
Let $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ be a right-infinite
word over an alphabet $\alpha$, viewed as a map $\mathbb{N} \to \alpha$. A finite word
$w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{n-1}$ over $\alpha$ is a nonempty factor of $u$ when $n \ge 1$ and there
is a position $i \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $w_j = u_{i+j}$ for every $j < n$.

The empty word is excluded, following the convention in which a factor is given by its
endpoints $r \le s$.

articles.title: Factor complexity at length zero
articles.statement:
For every infinite word $w$ over a finite alphabet,
the factor complexity of $w$ at length $0$ equals $1$, that is, $p_w(0) = 1$: the empty word is
the only factor of $w$ of length $0$.

articles.title: Factor complexity of an infinite word
articles.statement:
Let $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ be an infinite word
over a finite alphabet $A$. For $n \ge 0$ and a position $i \ge 0$, the factor of $w$ of length
$n$ at position $i$ is the word $w_i w_{i+1} \cdots w_{i+n-1}$. The factor complexity $p_w(n)$ is
the number of distinct factors of $w$ of length $n$, each word being counted once however often it
occurs in $w$.

## Sources

- Fabien Durand, Julien Leroy, and Gwenaël Richomme, *Do the Properties of an S-adic Representation Determine Factor Complexity?*, Journal of Integer Sequences 16 (2013), Article 13.2.6, complexity-function definition, lines 117–128, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL16/Durand/durand2.tex>.

articles.title: Finite Fibonacci words agree with the infinite Fibonacci word
articles.statement:
Let $f_0 = 0$ and let
$f_{k+1}$ be the image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$). For
all natural numbers $m$ and $n$ such that $n$ is less than the length of $f_m$, the letter of $f_m$
at index $n$ equals the letter at index $n$ of the one-sided infinite Fibonacci word (indices start
at $0$). In other words, every $f_m$ is a prefix of the infinite Fibonacci word.

articles.title: The finite Fibonacci word of index $n + 2$ has more than $n$ letters
articles.statement:
Let $f_0 = 0$ and
let $f_{k+1}$ be the image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$).
For every natural number $n$, the length of $f_{n+2}$ is greater than $n$.

articles.title: Factorization of the infinite Fibonacci word into finite Fibonacci words
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be the
infinite Fibonacci word and let $f_0, f_1, f_2, \ldots$ be the finite Fibonacci words. For every
natural number $N$, the finite word $w_N = 0\,1\,f_0 f_1 \cdots f_{N-1}$ (so $w_0 = 01$) consists of
the first $|w_N|$ letters of $f$, and for every natural number $k$ the first $k$ letters of $f$
form a prefix of $w_N$ for some $N$. In this sense
$f = 0 \cdot 1 \cdot f_0 \cdot f_1 \cdot f_2 \cdots$.

## Sources

- Gabriele Fici, "Factorizations of the Fibonacci Infinite Word", Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.9.3, equation `fibo`.

articles.title: Infinite Fibonacci word
articles.statement:
Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$ be the image of $f_k$ under the
Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$), so that $f_0, f_1, f_2, \ldots$ are the finite
Fibonacci words $0, 01, 010, 01001, \ldots$. The one-sided infinite Fibonacci word is the infinite
binary word whose letter at index $n$ (indices start at $0$) is the letter of $f_{n+2}$ at index
$n$.

Each $f_k$ is a prefix of $f_{k+1}$ and $f_{n+2}$ has more than $n$ letters, so this word is the
limit of the finite Fibonacci words.

articles.title: The Fibonacci morphism respects concatenation
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the Fibonacci morphism on
finite binary words, induced by $0 \mapsto 01$ and $1 \mapsto 0$. For all finite binary words $a$
and $b$, $\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$, where juxtaposition denotes concatenation.

articles.title: The Fibonacci morphism does not shorten words
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the Fibonacci morphism on
finite binary words, induced by $0 \mapsto 01$ and $1 \mapsto 0$. For every finite binary word $w$,
the length of $\varphi(w)$ is at least the length of $w$, that is, $|w| \le |\varphi(w)|$.

The reason is that every letter maps to a nonempty word.

articles.title: Fibonacci morphism
articles.statement:
The Fibonacci morphism $\varphi$ extends the Fibonacci substitution
$\sigma$, which maps $0$ to $01$ and $1$ to $0$, to finite binary words by concatenation: $\varphi$
maps the empty word to the empty word, and $\varphi(bw) = \sigma(b)\varphi(w)$ for every letter
$b$ and every finite binary word $w$.

articles.title: Fibonacci substitution
articles.statement:
The Fibonacci substitution sends each letter of the binary
alphabet $\{0, 1\}$ to a finite binary word: it maps $0$ to $01$ and $1$ to $0$.

The letters $0$ and $1$ are represented by the Booleans false and true.

articles.title: Recurrence for the finite Fibonacci words
articles.statement:
Let $f_0, f_1, f_2, \ldots$ be the finite
Fibonacci words. For every natural number $n$, $f_{n+2} = f_{n+1} f_n$, where juxtaposition
denotes concatenation.

articles.title: Finite Fibonacci words are prefixes of the infinite Fibonacci word
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $n$, the finite Fibonacci word $f_n$ is the word formed by the first $|f_n|$ letters of the
infinite Fibonacci word.

articles.title: Concatenating the finite Fibonacci words
articles.statement:
For every natural number $N$, prepending the
letters $0$ and $1$ to the concatenation $f_0 f_1 \cdots f_{N-1}$ of the first $N$ finite Fibonacci
words gives $f_{N+1}$: that is, $0\,1\,f_0 f_1 \cdots f_{N-1} = f_{N+1}$, where the concatenation
is empty when $N = 0$.

articles.title: Letters of the finite Fibonacci words stabilize
articles.statement:
Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$ be the
image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$). For all natural
numbers $n \le m$ and every index $i$ less than the length of $f_n$ (indices start at $0$), the
letter of $f_m$ at index $i$ equals the letter of $f_n$ at index $i$.

articles.title: Finite Fibonacci words begin with $0$
articles.statement:
Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$ be the image of
$f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$). For every natural number $n$,
there is a finite binary word $t$ such that $f_n = 0t$, that is, the first letter of $f_n$ is $0$.

articles.title: Lower bound on the length of the finite Fibonacci words
articles.statement:
Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$
be the image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$). For every
natural number $n$, the word $f_n$ has length at least $n + 1$.

articles.title: Consecutive finite Fibonacci words are nested
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the $n$-th
finite Fibonacci word $f_n$ is a prefix of $f_{n+1}$: there is a finite word $t$ in the letters
$0$ and $1$ with $f_{n+1} = f_n t$.

articles.title: Earlier finite Fibonacci words are prefixes of later ones
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers
$n \le m$, the $n$-th finite Fibonacci word $f_n$ is a prefix of the $m$-th finite Fibonacci word
$f_m$: there is a finite word $t$ in the letters $0$ and $1$ with $f_m = f_n t$.

articles.title: Finite Fibonacci words
articles.statement:
The finite Fibonacci words $f_n$, for natural numbers $n$, are
the words in the letters $0$ and $1$ defined by $f_0 = 0$ and $f_{n+1} = \varphi(f_n)$, where
$\varphi$ is the Fibonacci morphism, which replaces each letter $0$ by $01$ and each letter $1$
by $0$.

The first words are $0$, $01$, $010$, $01001$, $01001010$, and so on.

articles.title: The infinite Fibonacci word as $0$ followed by the finite Fibonacci words
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be an
infinite word over $\{0, 1\}$ and let $f_1, f_2, f_3, \ldots$ be finite words over $\{0, 1\}$ with
$f_1 = 1$, $f_2 = 0$ and $f_{n+3} = f_{n+2} f_{n+1}$ for every natural number $n$, such that for
every natural number $n$ the word $f_{n+2}$ consists of the first $|f_{n+2}|$ letters of $f$.
Then for every natural number $N$ the word $w_N = 0\,f_1 f_2 \cdots f_N$ (so $w_0 = 0$) consists of
the first $|w_N|$ letters of $f$, and for every natural number $k$ the first $k$ letters of $f$
form a prefix of $w_N$ for some $N$. In this sense $f = 0 \cdot f_1 \cdot f_2 \cdot f_3 \cdots$.

## Sources

- Gabriele Fici, "Factorizations of the Fibonacci Infinite Word", Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.9.3, Proposition lines 188-195 (equation `fibo`), <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Fici/fici5.tex>.

articles.title: Appending a word does not change earlier letters
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $t$ be finite words in the
letters $0$ and $1$, and let $k$ be a natural number smaller than the length of $a$. Then the
letter at position $k$ of the concatenation $a t$ equals the letter at position $k$ of $a$,
counting positions from $0$.

articles.title: Kimberling's set modulo 2 is the Fibonacci word
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be the set of natural numbers
obtained from $1$ by finitely many applications of the maps $x \mapsto 2x$ and
$x \mapsto 4x - 1$. Let $S$ be a strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers whose set
of values is $K$, and let $w$ be the binary sequence with $w(n) = 1$ if $S(n + 1)$ is odd
and $w(n) = 0$ if $S(n + 1)$ is even. Let $\varphi$ be the morphism of binary words with
$\varphi(0) = 01$ and $\varphi(1) = 0$. Then for every $k \ge 0$, the first
$|\varphi^k(0)|$ terms $w(0) w(1) \cdots$ of $w$ spell the word $\varphi^k(0)$. In other
words, $S$ modulo $2$ with its first term dropped is the infinite Fibonacci word.

The source gives a third proof of this theorem of Kimberling, via a transducer
construction; Allouche and Shallit also reproved it.

## Sources

- Tomi Kärki, Anne Lacroix, and Michel Rigo, "On the Recognizability of Self-Generating Sets," Journal of Integer Sequences 13 (2010), Article 10.2.2, Theorem (section Kimberling set and the Fibonacci word, label secKF), lines 710–714, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL13/Rigo/rigo6.tex

articles.title: First difference of a finite binary word
articles.statement:
For a finite word $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_m$ over
$\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, its first difference is the word
$(w_1 - w_0)(w_2 - w_1) \cdots (w_m - w_{m-1})$ of length $m$, computed in $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.
The first difference of the empty word is the empty word.

articles.title: First difference of an infinite binary word
articles.statement:
For an infinite word $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$
over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, its first difference is the infinite word $\Delta w$ over
$\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ with $(\Delta w)_i = w_{i+1} - w_i$ for every natural number $i$.

articles.title: A morphic word is the coding of its generator
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet, $u$ an
infinite word over $A$, $\tau : A \to B$ a map and $w$ an infinite word over $B$. If $w$ is
morphic with generator $u$ and coding $\tau$, then $w(n) = \tau(u(n))$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Building a morphic word from its generator
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet, $u$ a pure
morphic infinite word over $A$, $\tau : A \to B$ a map and $w$ an infinite word over $B$. If
$w(n) = \tau(u(n))$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $w$ is morphic with generator $u$ and
coding $\tau$.

articles.title: Morphic words via a coding
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet, $B$ any alphabet, $u$ an
infinite word over $A$, $\tau : A \to B$ a map (a coding) and $w$ an infinite word over $B$.
Then $w$ is morphic with generator $u$ and coding $\tau$ if $u$ is a pure morphic word and
$w(n) = \tau(u(n))$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Non-erasing letter maps
articles.statement:
A map $f$ sending each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a finite
word over $A$ is non-erasing when the word $f(a)$ is nonempty for every letter $a \in A$.

articles.title: Infinite word as the limit of iterates
articles.statement:
Let $f$ send each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a
finite word over $A$, extended to finite words by concatenation, with iterates $f^n$ (where $f^0$
is the identity), let $a \in A$, and let $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ be an infinite word over $A$.
Then $w$ is the limit of the iterates of $f$ at $a$ when the lengths of the words $f^n(a)$
(iterates applied to the one-letter word $a$) are unbounded as $n$ ranges over the natural
numbers, and for every $n$ and every position $i$ of $f^n(a)$, counted from $0$, the letter of
$f^n(a)$ at position $i$ is $w_i$.

articles.title: Prolongable letter maps
articles.statement:
Let $f$ send each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a finite word
over $A$, extended to finite words by concatenation, with iterates $f^n$ (where $f^0$ is the
identity). Then $f$ is prefix-preserving (prolongable) at a letter $a \in A$ when
$f(a) = a\alpha$ for some finite word $\alpha$ over $A$ such that the word $f^n(\alpha)$ is
nonempty for every natural number $n$, including $n = 0$.

articles.title: Pure morphic words
articles.statement:
An infinite word $w$ over a finite alphabet $A$ is pure morphic when
