Such a word contains both letters infinitely often, so no separate hypothesis that both letters
occur infinitely often is needed.

## Sources

- Michael Coons, Christopher Ramsey and Nicolae Strungaru, *Relative Position in Binary Substitutions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.5, Corollary 31 (`jis-2025-25.1.5-cor-31`).

articles.title: Number of ones in a factor
articles.statement:
For an infinite binary word $x = x_0 x_1 x_2 \cdots$ over
$\{0, 1\}$ and natural numbers $i$ and $n$, this is the number of indices $k < n$ with
$x_{i+k} = 1$, that is, the number of $1$s in the factor $x_i x_{i+1} \cdots x_{i+n-1}$ of length
$n$ starting at position $i$ (it is $0$ when $n = 0$).

articles.title: Aperiodic infinite words
articles.statement:
An infinite binary word $x = x_0 x_1 x_2 \cdots$ over $\{0, 1\}$
is aperiodic when it is not ultimately periodic: there are no natural numbers $p > 0$ and $N$
such that $x_{n+p} = x_n$ for all $n \ge N$.

articles.title: Balanced infinite words
articles.statement:
An infinite binary word $x = x_0 x_1 x_2 \cdots$ over $\{0, 1\}$
is balanced when for all natural numbers $i$, $j$ and $n$, the numbers of $1$s in the factors
$x_i x_{i+1} \cdots x_{i+n-1}$ and $x_j x_{j+1} \cdots x_{j+n-1}$ of length $n$ differ by at
most $1$.

articles.title: Sturmian words
articles.statement:
An infinite binary word $x = x_0 x_1 x_2 \cdots$ over $\{0, 1\}$ is
Sturmian when it is both aperiodic and balanced.

articles.title: Length of the generalized Thue–Morse blocks
articles.statement:
Let $L > 1$ and $k > 1$ be natural numbers
and let $\kappa$ assign a shift $\kappa(j, n) \in \mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z}$ to each
$j \in \{1, \dots, k-1\}$ and each $n \ge 0$. For every $n \ge 0$, the block $A_n$ of the
$(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence has exactly $k^n$ letters.

articles.title: Each generalized Thue–Morse block is a prefix of the next
articles.statement:
Let $L > 1$ and $k > 1$ be
natural numbers and let $\kappa$ assign a shift $\kappa(j, n) \in \mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z}$ to each
$j \in \{1, \dots, k-1\}$ and each $n \ge 0$. For every $n \ge 0$, the block $A_n$ of the
$(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence is a prefix of $A_{n+1}$: there is a word $w$ with
$A_{n+1} = A_n w$.

articles.title: The generalized Thue–Morse blocks form a chain of prefixes
articles.statement:
Let $L > 1$ and $k > 1$ be
natural numbers and let $\kappa$ assign a shift $\kappa(j, n) \in \mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z}$ to each
$j \in \{1, \dots, k-1\}$ and each $n \ge 0$. For all natural numbers $m \le n$, the block $A_m$
of the $(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence is a prefix of $A_n$: there is a word $w$ with
$A_n = A_m w$.

articles.title: Blocks of the generalized Thue–Morse sequence
articles.statement:
Let $L > 1$ and $k > 1$ be natural numbers,
take the letters $0, 1, \dots, L-1$ (the elements of $\mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z}$), and let $\kappa$
assign a shift $\kappa(j, n) \in \mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z}$ to each $j \in \{1, \dots, k-1\}$ and
each $n \ge 0$. For a word $w$ and $t \in \mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z}$, let $f^t(w)$ be the word
obtained from $w$ by adding $t$ modulo $L$ to every letter. The blocks $A_n$ of the
$(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence are the words given by $A_0 = 0$ (a word of one letter)
and $A_{n+1} = A_n \, f^{\kappa(1, n)}(A_n) \, f^{\kappa(2, n)}(A_n) \cdots
f^{\kappa(k-1, n)}(A_n)$.

articles.title: Classical Thue–Morse block of order 0
articles.statement:
The classical Thue–Morse block $A_0$ is the
one-letter word $0$.

articles.title: Classical Thue–Morse block of order 1
articles.statement:
The classical Thue–Morse block $A_1$ is the word
$01$.

articles.title: Classical Thue–Morse block of order 2
articles.statement:
The classical Thue–Morse block $A_2$ is the word
$0110$.

articles.title: Classical Thue–Morse block of order 3
articles.statement:
The classical Thue–Morse block $A_3$ is the word
$01101001$.

articles.title: Classical Thue–Morse blocks
articles.statement:
The classical Thue–Morse blocks are the blocks $A_n$ of the
$(2, 2, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence with $\kappa(1, n) = 1$ for every $n \ge 0$. Thus $A_0$ is
the one-letter word $0$, and $A_{n+1}$ is $A_n$ followed by the word obtained from $A_n$ by
exchanging the letters $0$ and $1$.

articles.title: The classical Thue–Morse word begins with 01101001
articles.statement:
Let $A_\infty$ be the infinite word
of the $(2, 2, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence with $\kappa(1, n) = 1$ for every $n \ge 0$. The
letters of $A_\infty$ at positions $0, 1, \dots, 7$ are $0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1$, so $A_\infty$
begins with $01101001$.

articles.title: Classical shift schedule
articles.statement:
The classical shift schedule is the map $\kappa$ that assigns
to the index $j = 1$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ the letter $\kappa(1, n) = 1$ of the alphabet
$\{0, 1\}$. It is the schedule of the classical Thue–Morse sequence, the
$(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence with $L = k = 2$.

## Sources

- the classical $(2, 2, 1)$ example after JIS Definition 2.2.

articles.title: Length of the classical Thue–Morse blocks
articles.statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the classical
Thue–Morse block $A_n$ (the block $A_n$ of the $(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence with
$L = k = 2$ and $\kappa(1, i) = 1$ for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$) has exactly $2^n$ letters.

## Sources

- the classical $(2, 2, 1)$ example after JIS Definition 2.2.

articles.title: Indexing into a concatenation
articles.statement:
Let $l_1$ and $l_2$ be lists over a type, and let $m$ be a
natural number less than the length of $l_1$. Then the entry at position $m$ of the concatenation
of $l_1$ followed by $l_2$ equals the entry at position $m$ of $l_1$ (positions start at $0$).

## Sources

- JIS Definition 2.2.

articles.title: Later blocks agree with the infinite word
articles.statement:
Let $L, k \ge 2$, let
$\kappa : \{1, \dots, k-1\} \times \mathbb{N} \to \{0, \dots, L-1\}$ be a shift schedule, and let
$A_0, A_1, \dots$ be the blocks and $A_\infty$ the infinite word of the
$(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence. For all $m, N \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m + 1 \le N$ and $m$
less than the length of $A_N$, the letter at position $m$ of $A_N$ equals the letter at
position $m$ of $A_\infty$ (positions start at $0$).

## Sources

- JIS Definition 2.2.

articles.title: The infinite generalized Thue–Morse word
articles.statement:
Let $L, k \ge 2$, let
$\kappa : \{1, \dots, k-1\} \times \mathbb{N} \to \{0, \dots, L-1\}$ be a shift schedule, and let
$A_0, A_1, \dots$ be the blocks of the $(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence. The infinite word
$A_\infty$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, L-1\}$ has, for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$, as its letter
at position $m$ (positions start at $0$) the letter at position $m$ of the block $A_{m+1}$,
which has $k^{m+1} > m$ letters.

The letter is read by checked indexing, with no default letter.

## Sources

- JIS Definition 2.2.

articles.title: Length of a concatenation of equal-length lists
articles.statement:
Let $l$ be a list of lists over a type
and let $m \in \mathbb{N}$. If every list in $l$ has length $m$, then the concatenation of the
lists in $l$ has length $n \cdot m$, where $n$ is the number of lists in $l$.

## Sources

- JIS Definition 2.2.

articles.title: A crude exponential bound
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k > 1$ and every $m \in \mathbb{N}$,
we have $m < k^{m+1}$.

## Sources

- JIS Definition 2.2.

articles.title: Value of the cyclic letter shift
articles.statement:
For every $L \in \mathbb{N}$ and all letters $a, t$ of
the alphabet $\{0, \dots, L-1\}$, the cyclic shift of $a$ by $t$ is the letter
$(a + t) \bmod L$.

## Sources

- JIS Definition 2.2.

articles.title: Cyclic letter shift
articles.statement:
For $L \in \mathbb{N}$ and letters $a, t$ of the alphabet
$\{0, \dots, L-1\}$, the cyclic shift of $a$ by $t$ is the letter $(a + t) \bmod L$. Writing the
letters as $a_0, \dots, a_{L-1}$, it sends $a_i$ to $a_{(i + t) \bmod L}$.

## Sources

- JIS Definition 2.2.

articles.title: Cyclic shifting preserves word length
articles.statement:
For every $L \in \mathbb{N}$, every letter $t$ of
the alphabet $\{0, \dots, L-1\}$ and every finite word $w$ over that alphabet, the word obtained
from $w$ by shifting each letter cyclically by $t$ has the same length as $w$.

## Sources

- JIS Definition 2.2.

articles.title: Letters of a cyclically shifted word
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a natural number and let $t$ and $b$ be
letters of the alphabet $\{0, 1, \dots, L - 1\}$. For a letter $a$ write
$\sigma_t(a) = (a + t) \bmod L$ for its cyclic shift by $t$, and for a word $w$ over this
alphabet write $\sigma_t(w)$ for the word obtained by shifting each letter of $w$. Then $b$
occurs in $\sigma_t(w)$ if and only if $b = \sigma_t(a)$ for some letter $a$ occurring in $w$.

articles.title: Cyclic shift of a word
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a natural number and let $t$ be a letter of the
alphabet $\{0, 1, \dots, L - 1\}$. The cyclic shift by $t$ of a word $w = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$
over this alphabet is the word $\sigma_t(a_1) \sigma_t(a_2) \cdots \sigma_t(a_n)$ of the same
length, where $\sigma_t(a) = (a + t) \bmod L$ is the cyclic shift of a letter.

articles.title: Thue–Morse blocks
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be the Thue–Morse substitution, $\sigma(0) = 01$ and
$\sigma(1) = 10$, applied to finite words over $\{0, 1\}$ letter by letter. For a natural number
$n$, the $n$th Thue–Morse block is the finite word $\sigma^n(0)$: the $0$th block is the
one-letter word $0$, and the $(n+1)$st block is obtained from the $n$th by replacing each letter
$a$ with $\sigma(a)$.

articles.title: Thue–Morse substitution
articles.statement:
The Thue–Morse substitution $\sigma$ on the alphabet $\{0, 1\}$
sends each letter to a word of length two: $\sigma(0) = 01$ and $\sigma(1) = 10$.

## Sources

- Example 2 in Scott Balchin and Dan Rust, *Computations for Symbolic Substitutions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 20 (2017): https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL20/Rust/rust3.tex.

articles.title: Thue–Morse sequence
articles.statement:
The Thue–Morse sequence $t_0 t_1 t_2 \cdots$ over $\{0, 1\}$ is
indexed from $0$, and $t_n = 1$ exactly when the binary expansion of $n$ has an odd number of
digits equal to $1$; otherwise $t_n = 0$.

## Sources

- Eiji Miyanohara, *Transcendence of Digital Expansions Generated by a Generalized Thue-Morse Sequence*, Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), which lists the initial blocks `0`, `01`, `0110` and `01101001` and the limit beginning `0110100110010110`: https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Miyanohara/miy5.tex. Evaluation here uses the binary digits of the index, in time and space logarithmic in it, rather than an exponentially long block.

articles.title: The Tribonacci alphabet
articles.statement:
The Tribonacci word is written over the three-letter alphabet
whose letters are $a$, $b$ and $c$.

articles.title: Recursion for the finite Tribonacci words
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 0$, the finite Tribonacci
word $W(n + 3)$ is the concatenation $W(n + 2)\,W(n + 1)\,W(n)$.

articles.title: Length recurrence for finite Tribonacci words
articles.statement:
Writing $|w|$ for the length of a word
$w$, for every $n \ge 0$ the finite Tribonacci words satisfy
$|W(n + 3)| = |W(n + 2)| + |W(n + 1)| + |W(n)|$.

articles.title: Length lower bound for finite Tribonacci words
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 0$, the finite
Tribonacci word $W(n)$ has length at least $n + 1$.

articles.title: Lengths of finite Tribonacci words are monotone
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $m \le n$,
the length of the finite Tribonacci word $W(m)$ is at most the length of $W(n)$.

articles.title: Each finite Tribonacci word is a prefix of the next
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 0$, the finite
Tribonacci word $W(n)$ is a prefix of $W(n + 1)$.

articles.title: Finite Tribonacci words form a prefix chain
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $m \le n$, the
finite Tribonacci word $W(m)$ is a prefix of $W(n)$.

articles.title: Finite Tribonacci words
articles.statement:
The finite Tribonacci words $W(n)$, for $n \ge 0$, are the
words over the alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$ defined by $W(0) = a$, $W(1) = ab$, $W(2) = abac$ and
$W(n + 3) = W(n + 2)\,W(n + 1)\,W(n)$ for every $n \ge 0$, where juxtaposition denotes
concatenation.

articles.title: Finite Tribonacci words agree with the infinite word
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers
$k \le n$ such that $k$ is less than the length of the finite Tribonacci word $W(n)$, the
letter of $W(n)$ at position $k$ equals the letter of the infinite Tribonacci word at
position $k$, positions being counted from $0$.

articles.title: The infinite Tribonacci word
articles.statement:
The infinite Tribonacci word is the sequence over the
alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$ whose letter at each position $k \ge 0$ (positions counted from $0$) is
the letter at position $k$ of the finite Tribonacci word $W(k)$; this position exists because
$W(k)$ has length at least $k + 1$.

articles.title: $k$-abelian equivalence
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, two words $u$ and $v$ over an alphabet
are $k$-abelian equivalent when $k \ge 1$, both $u$ and $v$ are nonempty, $u$ and $v$ have the
same prefix of length $k - 1$ and the same suffix of length $k - 1$ (a word shorter than
$k - 1$ counting as its own prefix and suffix), and every word $t$ of length $k$ occurs as a
factor of $u$, counting overlapping occurrences, exactly as often as it occurs in $v$.

articles.title: $k$-abelian square-free words
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, a finite word $w$ is
$k$-abelian square-free when $k \ge 1$ and no factor of $w$ (a word $x$ with $w = pxs$ for some
words $p$ and $s$) is a $k$-abelian square.

articles.title: $k$-abelian squares
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, a word $w$ is a $k$-abelian square when
$w = uv$ for two nonempty words $u$ and $v$ that are $k$-abelian equivalent.

articles.title: $3$-abelian equivalence of ternary words
articles.statement:
Two words $u$ and $v$ over the alphabet
$\{0, 1, 2\}$ are $3$-abelian equivalent when they are $k$-abelian equivalent for $k = 3$: both
are nonempty, they have the same prefix and the same suffix of length $2$ (a shorter word
counting as its own prefix and suffix), and every word of length $3$ occurs as a factor of $u$,
counting overlapping occurrences, exactly as often as it occurs in $v$.

articles.title: $3$-abelian square-free ternary words
articles.statement:
A finite word $w$ over the alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$
is $3$-abelian square-free when no factor of $w$ (a word $x$ with $w = pxs$ for some words $p$
and $s$) is a $3$-abelian square.

articles.title: $3$-abelian squares over a ternary alphabet
articles.statement:
A word $w$ over the alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$ is
a $3$-abelian square when $w = uv$ for two nonempty words $u$ and $v$ that are $3$-abelian
equivalent.

articles.title: Number of occurrences of a factor
articles.statement:
For words $w$ and $t$ over an alphabet with $t$
nonempty, the factor count of $t$ in $w$ is the number of positions of $w$ at which an occurrence
of $t$ starts, overlapping occurrences all being counted. The factor count of the empty word is
$0$.

articles.title: Exponential lower bound for ternary abelian-cube-free words
articles.statement:
An abelian cube is a word
$xyz$ with $x$, $y$, $z$ nonempty such that each letter occurs equally often in $x$, $y$ and $z$.
Let $a_n$ be the number of words of length $n$ over $\{0, 1, 2\}$ that contain no abelian cube
as a factor. Then $2^{n/24} = O(a_n)$ as $n \to \infty$: there is a constant $C$ such that
$2^{n/24} \le C a_n$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

## Sources

- Ali Aberkane and James D. Currie, *The Number of Ternary Words Avoiding Abelian Cubes Grows Exponentially*, Journal of Integer Sequences 7 (2004), Article 04.2.7, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL7/Currie/currie18.tex>, Second Main Theorem, lines 558-561.

articles.title: Avoiding additive cubes
articles.statement:
An infinite word $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ over the alphabet
$\{0, 1, 3, 4\}$ avoids PVHH-cubes (additive cubes) if there are no natural numbers $s$ and
$\ell \ge 1$ such that the three consecutive factors $w_s \cdots w_{s+\ell-1}$,
$w_{s+\ell} \cdots w_{s+2\ell-1}$ and $w_{s+2\ell} \cdots w_{s+3\ell-1}$ of length $\ell$ all have
the same sum of letter values.

articles.title: The Cassaigne–Currie–Schaeffer–Shallit word avoids additive cubes
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be the
substitution $0 \mapsto 03$, $1 \mapsto 43$, $3 \mapsto 1$, $4 \mapsto 01$ on the alphabet
$\{0, 1, 3, 4\}$, extended to words by replacing each letter with its image. There is an infinite
word $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ over $\{0, 1, 3, 4\}$ such that $\sigma^k(0)$ is a prefix of $w$ for
every $k \ge 0$, and $w$ contains no additive cube: there are no natural numbers $s$ and
$\ell \ge 1$ such that the three consecutive factors of length $\ell$ starting at positions $s$,
$s + \ell$ and $s + 2\ell$ all have the same sum of letter values.

## Sources

- Julien Cassaigne, James D. Currie, Luke Schaeffer and Jeffrey Shallit, Avoiding three consecutive blocks of the same size and same sum, J. ACM 61(2) (2014), Article 10, arXiv:1106.5204, https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.5204.

articles.title: Additive-cube-free fixed point conjecture
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be the substitution
$0 \mapsto 03$, $1 \mapsto 43$, $3 \mapsto 1$, $4 \mapsto 01$ on the alphabet $\{0, 1, 3, 4\}$,
extended to words by replacing each letter with its image. The proposition that there is an
infinite word $w$ over $\{0, 1, 3, 4\}$ such that $\sigma^k(0)$ is a prefix of $w$ for every
$k \ge 0$ and $w$ avoids PVHH-cubes (additive cubes): no three consecutive nonempty factors of $w$
of equal length have equal sums of letter values.

articles.title: Sum of a factor
articles.statement:
For an infinite word $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ over the alphabet
$\{0, 1, 3, 4\}$ and natural numbers $s$ and $\ell$, the sum of the factor of length $\ell$
starting at position $s$ is the integer $\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1} w_{s+i}$, where each letter counts
as its value.

articles.title: The fixed point generated from $0$
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be the substitution $0 \mapsto 03$,
$1 \mapsto 43$, $3 \mapsto 1$, $4 \mapsto 01$ on the alphabet $\{0, 1, 3, 4\}$, extended to words
by replacing each letter with its image. An infinite word $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ over
$\{0, 1, 3, 4\}$ is the fixed point generated from $0$ if the word $\sigma^k(0)$ is a prefix of $w$
for every $k \ge 0$.

articles.title: Value of a letter
articles.statement:
Each letter of the alphabet $\{0, 1, 3, 4\}$ has as its value the
integer it names: the letters $0$, $1$, $3$ and $4$ have values $0$, $1$, $3$ and $4$.

articles.title: The alphabet $\{0, 1, 3, 4\}$
articles.statement:
The alphabet with four distinct letters, written $0$, $1$,
$3$ and $4$.

articles.title: Iterates of the substitution on $0$
articles.statement:
For $k \ge 0$, the word $\sigma^k(0)$ obtained from
the one-letter word $0$ by applying the substitution $\sigma$ ($0 \mapsto 03$, $1 \mapsto 43$,
$3 \mapsto 1$, $4 \mapsto 01$) $k$ times, where $\sigma$ acts on a word by replacing each letter
with its image: $\sigma^0(0) = 0$ and $\sigma^{k+1}(0) = \sigma(\sigma^k(0))$.

articles.title: The substitution $0 \mapsto 03$, $1 \mapsto 43$, $3 \mapsto 1$, $4 \mapsto 01$
articles.statement:
The map
sending each letter of the alphabet $\{0, 1, 3, 4\}$ to a word: $0$ to $03$, $1$ to $43$, $3$ to
$1$ and $4$ to $01$.

articles.title: Dejean's theorem on repetition thresholds
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a real number
$r$, call an infinite word $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$
*$r^+$-free* if for all natural numbers $s$, $\ell$ and $p$ with $0 < p \le \ell$ such that
$w_{s+i+p} = w_{s+i}$ for every natural number $i$ with $i + p < \ell$, we have $\ell / p \le r$;
that is, no factor of $w$ has exponent strictly greater than $r$. Let $\mathrm{RT}(n)$, the
repetition threshold, be the infimum of the set of real numbers $r > 1$ for which there is an
infinite $r^+$-free word over $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Then $\mathrm{RT}(2) = 2$,
$\mathrm{RT}(3) = 7/4$, $\mathrm{RT}(4) = 7/5$, and $\mathrm{RT}(n) = n/(n-1)$ for every
$n \ge 5$.

This is a proved result (Dejean's conjecture of 1972): the last cases were proved in 2011 by
Currie and Rampersad and, independently, by Rao.

Paper: James D. Currie, Lucas Mol, and Narad Rampersad, "The Number of Threshold
Words on n Letters Grows Exponentially for Every n ≥ 27", Journal of Integer
Sequences 23 (2020), Article 20.3.1.

## Sources

- Period/exponent and `r`/`r⁺`-free definitions, lines 93--99; repetition-threshold definition and exact values, lines 100--113. Original definition/conjecture: Françoise Dejean, "Sur un théorème de Thue", Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A 13(1) (1972), 90--99, DOI 10.1016/0097-3165(72)90011-8. Final cases confirmed in 2011 by James D. Currie and Narad Rampersad, "A proof of Dejean's conjecture", Mathematics of Computation 80 (2011), 1063--1070, arXiv:0905.1129, and independently by Michaël Rao, "Last cases of Dejean's conjecture", Theoretical Computer Science 412(27) (2011), 3010--3018, DOI 10.1016/j.tcs.2010.06.020. Lean representation: `Fin n` harmlessly relabels the source `n`-letter alphabet `A_n`; the universal period clause expresses absence of factors with exponent strictly greater than `r`, i.e. `r⁺`-freeness; `RT` is the real-valued `sInf` over `r > 1` admitting such an infinite word.
- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL23/Mol/mol2.tex>.

articles.title: Kurosaki's words are $(7/4)^+$-power-free
articles.statement:
On the alphabet $\{1, 2, 3\}$, let $\sigma$ be the
permutation that swaps $1$ and $2$ and fixes $3$, let $\rho$ be the permutation that swaps $2$ and
$3$ and fixes $1$, and for a finite word $w$ let $\varphi(w) = \sigma(w)\,w\,\rho(w)$, where
$\sigma(w)$ and $\rho(w)$ apply the permutation to each letter of $w$. Call $p \ge 1$ a period of
a finite word $u = u_0 u_1 \cdots$ when $u_i = u_{i+p}$ for every $i$ with $i + p < |u|$. For every
$n \ge 1$, every factor $u$ of the word $\varphi^n(2)$ and every period $p$ of $u$ satisfy
$4|u| \le 7p$; that is, every factor of $\varphi^n(2)$ has exponent at most $7/4$.

## Sources

- Serina Camungol and Narad Rampersad, "Concerning Kurosaki's Squarefree Word," Journal of Integer Sequences 16 (2013), Article 13.9.4, Theorem, lines 184–188, with the σ/ρ/φ definitions at lines 116–124, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL16/Camungol/ramper4.tex

articles.title: Overlap-free binary words
articles.statement:
A finite binary word is overlap-free when none of its
contiguous factors is an overlap.

articles.title: Overlaps in words
articles.statement:
A finite word $o$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ is an overlap if
$o = xyxyx$ for some finite words $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$ with $x$ nonempty; $y$ may be empty.

Here $x$ may have any positive length, not only length one.

articles.title: Crochemore's square-freeness test
articles.statement:
Let $f$ map each letter of the three-letter alphabet
$\{a, b, c\}$ to a finite word over a set $T$, and extend $f$ to words by concatenation,
$f(x_1 \cdots x_n) = f(x_1) \cdots f(x_n)$. Then $f$ maps every square-free word over
$\{a, b, c\}$ to a square-free word if and only if it maps every square-free word over
$\{a, b, c\}$ of length at most $5$ to a square-free word.

A word is square-free when no factor has the form $uu$ with $u$ nonempty. No non-erasing
hypothesis is assumed: the image of a letter may be empty.

Proof: reduce erasing morphisms first, then apply Currie's synchronization
method to a shortest square occurrence and its shortest source-word cover.

## Sources

- Currie, lines 99-100 of <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL22/Currie/currie20.tex>; primary reference Crochemore, Theoret. Comput. Sci. 18(2) (1982), DOI 10.1016/0304-3975(82)90023-8.

articles.title: Square-free infinite word
articles.statement:
An infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over an alphabet
$\alpha$ is square-free if it contains no two adjacent equal nonempty blocks: for all $i \ge 0$ and
all $k \ge 1$ there is some $j < k$ with $u_{i+j} \ne u_{i+k+j}$.

articles.title: Square-free infinite ternary word
articles.statement:
An infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over the
ternary alphabet is a square-free infinite ternary word if it is square-free as an infinite word.

articles.title: Square-freeness via prefixes of suffixes
articles.statement:
A finite word $w$ is square-free if and only if,
for every prefix $s$ of a suffix of $w$ and every nonempty prefix $x$ of $s$, we have $s \ne xx$,
where $xx$ denotes the concatenation of $x$ with itself.

This form is directly decidable when letter equality is decidable.

articles.title: Square-free finite word
articles.statement:
A finite word $w$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ is square-free if no
factor of $w$ is a square, where a factor of $w$ is a word $s$ with $w = psq$ for some words $p$
and $q$, and a square is a word $xx$ with $x$ nonempty.

articles.title: Square-free ternary words of length $n$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, a finite word $w$ over
the ternary alphabet is a square-free ternary word of length $n$ if $w$ is square-free and $w$ has
length exactly $n$.

articles.title: Square word
articles.statement:
A word $w$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a square if $w = xx$ for some nonempty
word $x$, where $xx$ denotes the concatenation of $x$ with itself.

articles.title: Factors of square-free words are square-free
articles.statement:
If a finite word $v$ is square-free and $u$
is a factor of $v$, that is, $v = puq$ for some words $p$ and $q$, then $u$ is square-free.

articles.title: The ternary alphabet for square-free words
articles.statement:
The ternary alphabet is the set $\{0, 1, 2\}$
of natural numbers less than $3$; its three letters play the role of $a$, $b$ and $c$.

articles.title: Intervals and residues of the anti-$k$-bonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k > 1$, let $A_n$ be the
anti-recurrence numbers of the linear form $(1, \dots, 1)$ of length $k$, and put
$i = \lfloor k/2 \rfloor$ and $\kappa = k^2 + 1$. Then for every $n \ge 1$, $A_n$ lies in the
interval $[\kappa(n - 1) + 1, \kappa n]$, and $A_n \equiv ik + c \pmod{\kappa}$ for some natural
number $c$ with $1 \le c \le k$ if $k$ is even and $i + 1 \le c \le i + k$ if $k$ is odd.

The paper attaches the condition $k > 2$ to $\kappa$; it is not needed, since $k = 2$ is the
anti-Fibonacci case (Zaslavsky's formula $A_n = 5n - 2 + PD_{n-1}$, with $PD$ the
period-doubling sequence).

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Lemma 3.

articles.title: First summands of the anti-Fibonacci construction
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 1$, $A_n$ is the first
entry of the $n$-th triple $(A_n, B_n, C_n)$ of the anti-Fibonacci construction: $A_1 = 1$, and
for $n \ge 2$, $A_n$ is the least positive integer that is not among the values $A_k$, $B_k$,
$C_k$ with $1 \le k < n$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives $A_0 = A_1 = 1$.

In the source's notation $A_n = Y_{2n-1}$, where $Y_1 < Y_2 < \dots$ are the non-anti-Fibonacci
numbers.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: Second summands of the anti-Fibonacci construction
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 1$, $B_n$ is the second
entry of the $n$-th triple $(A_n, B_n, C_n)$ of the anti-Fibonacci construction: $B_1 = 2$, and
for $n \ge 2$, $B_n$ is the second smallest positive integer that is not among the values $A_k$,
$B_k$, $C_k$ with $1 \le k < n$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives $B_0 = B_1 = 2$.

In the source's notation $B_n = Y_{2n}$, where $Y_1 < Y_2 < \dots$ are the non-anti-Fibonacci
numbers.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: Anti-Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 1$, the anti-Fibonacci number $X_n = C_n$ is the third
entry of the $n$-th triple $(A_n, B_n, C_n)$ of the anti-Fibonacci construction, so
$C_n = A_n + B_n$ and $C_1 = 3$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives $C_0 = C_1 = 3$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: First anti-Fibonacci and non-anti-Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
In the anti-Fibonacci construction
with triples $(A_n, B_n, C_n)$, the first four anti-Fibonacci numbers are $C_1 = 3$, $C_2 = 9$,
$C_3 = 13$ and $C_4 = 18$, and $(A_1, B_1) = (1, 2)$, $(A_2, B_2) = (4, 5)$,
$(A_3, B_3) = (6, 7)$ and $(A_4, B_4) = (8, 10)$.

Since $A_1, B_1, A_2, B_2, \dots$ are the non-anti-Fibonacci numbers, the first eight
non-anti-Fibonacci numbers are $1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: The anti-Fibonacci construction
articles.statement:
For each $n \ge 0$, entry $n$ of the construction is the
triple $(A_{n+1}, B_{n+1}, C_{n+1})$ of natural numbers together with the finite set $U_{n+1}$ of
values used so far. Entry $0$ is $(1, 2, 3)$ with $U_1 = \{1, 2, 3\}$. For $n \ge 1$, $A_{n+1}$ is
the least positive integer not in $U_n$, $B_{n+1}$ is the least positive integer not in
$U_n \cup \{A_{n+1}\}$, $C_{n+1} = A_{n+1} + B_{n+1}$, and
$U_{n+1} = U_n \cup \{A_{n+1}, B_{n+1}, C_{n+1}\}$.

The $C_n$ are the anti-Fibonacci numbers (OEIS A075326 without its initial $0$) and the missing
numbers $A_1, B_1, A_2, B_2, \dots$ are the non-anti-Fibonacci numbers $Y_1, Y_2, \dots$
(OEIS A249031).

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: Kimberling's bounds for the anti-Jacobsthal numbers
articles.statement:
Let $A_n$ be the anti-recurrence
numbers of the linear form $a = (2, 1)$ (the anti-Jacobsthal numbers), let $B_m$ be its
non-anti-recurrence numbers, and put $B^1_n = B_{2n-1}$ and $B^2_n = B_{2n}$. Then for every
$n \ge 1$ we have $0 \le A_n - 7n + 4 \le 3$, $0 \le 3B^1_n - 7n + 6 \le 4$ and
$0 \le 3B^2_n - 7n + 2 \le 3$.

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Kimberling's bounds for the anti-Pell numbers
articles.statement:
Let $A_n$ be the anti-recurrence numbers
of the linear form $a = (1, 2)$ (the anti-Pell numbers), let $B_m$ be its non-anti-recurrence
numbers, and put $B^1_n = B_{2n-1}$ and $B^2_n = B_{2n}$. Then for every $n \ge 1$ we have
$0 \le A_n - 7n + 3 \le 2$, $0 \le 3B^1_n - 7n + 6 \le 3$ and $0 \le 3B^2_n - 7n + 2 \le 3$.

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Gaps between successive anti-recurrence numbers
articles.statement:
Let $a = (a_1, \dots, a_k)$ be a linear
form with positive integer coefficients and $k > 1$, let $\tau = a_1 + \dots + a_k$ be its trace,
and let $A_n$ and $B_m$ be the anti-recurrence and non-anti-recurrence numbers of $a$; for
$m \ge 1$, block $m$ consists of $B_{(m-1)k+1}, \dots, B_{mk}$, and it is an interval when
$B_{mk} = B_{(m-1)k+1} + k - 1$. Then for every $n \ge 1$ we have $A_{n+1} \ge A_n + k\tau$.
Equality holds if $B_{(n-1)k+1+j} = B_{(n-1)k+1} + j$ for every $j$ with $0 \le j < 2k$, that
is, if $B_{(n-1)k+1}, \dots, B_{(n+1)k}$ are consecutive integers. The inequality is strict if
exactly one of the blocks $n$ and $n + 1$ is an interval.

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Lemma 1.

articles.title: First anti-Fibonacci anti-recurrence numbers
articles.statement:
The anti-recurrence numbers
$A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4$ of the linear form $(1, 1)$ are $3, 9, 13, 18$, and the first four
anti-Fibonacci numbers $C_1, C_2, C_3, C_4$ of the Walnut anti-Fibonacci construction
(OEIS A075326) are also $3, 9, 13, 18$; so the two sequences agree for $1 \le n \le 4$.

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Section 1.

articles.title: First anti-Jacobsthal numbers
articles.statement:
The anti-recurrence numbers $A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4$ of the
linear form $(2, 1)$, the anti-Jacobsthal numbers (OEIS A304499), are $4, 11, 19, 25$.

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Section 3.

articles.title: First anti-Pell numbers
articles.statement:
The anti-recurrence numbers $A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4$ of the linear
form $(1, 2)$, the anti-Pell numbers (OEIS A304502), are $5, 11, 20, 26$, and its first eight
non-anti-recurrence numbers $B_1, \dots, B_8$ are $1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9$ (so
$B^1_n = B_{2n-1}$ starts $1, 3, 6, 8$ and $B^2_n = B_{2n}$ starts $2, 4, 7, 9$).

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Section 3.

articles.title: First anti-Tribonacci anti-recurrence numbers
articles.statement:
The anti-recurrence numbers
$A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4$ of the linear form $(1, 1, 1)$ are $6, 16, 27, 36$, and the first four
anti-Tribonacci numbers $D_1, D_2, D_3, D_4$ of the Walnut anti-Tribonacci construction
(OEIS A265389) are also $6, 16, 27, 36$; so the two sequences agree for $1 \le n \le 4$.

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Section 4.

articles.title: Block of successive mex values
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$ and a finite set $s$ of natural
numbers, the mex block of length $m$ from $s$ is the list $(x_1, \dots, x_m)$ in which each $x_j$
is the least positive integer not in $s \cup \{x_1, \dots, x_{j-1}\}$.

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Section 2 (proof of Lemma 2, the mex rule).

articles.title: Non-anti-recurrence numbers
articles.statement:
Let $a = (a_1, \dots, a_k)$ be a linear form with natural
number coefficients. Its non-anti-recurrence numbers $B_1, B_2, \dots$ are produced in blocks of
$k$ by the mex rule: for $n \ge 1$, each of $B_{(n-1)k+1}, \dots, B_{nk}$ in turn is the least
positive integer not among $B_1, \dots, B_{(n-1)k}$, the anti-recurrence numbers
$A_1, \dots, A_{n-1}$ and the earlier entries of its block, and then
$A_n = a_1 B_{(n-1)k+1} + \dots + a_k B_{nk}$. For $k = 2$ the subsequences $B^1_n = B_{2n-1}$
and $B^2_n = B_{2n}$ are the paper's $B^1$ and $B^2$.

By Lemma 2 of the source, for a positive form with $k > 1$ the numbers $B_m$ are the positive
integers that are not anti-recurrence numbers, listed in increasing order.

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Section 2 (definition of anti-recurrence sequences).

articles.title: Interval location of anti-recurrence numbers for bounded forms
articles.statement:
Let
$a = (a_1, \dots, a_k)$ be a linear form with positive integer coefficients and $k > 1$, of trace
$\tau = a_1 + \dots + a_k$, with anti-recurrence numbers $A_1, A_2, \dots$ and non-anti-recurrence
numbers $B_1, B_2, \dots$, and let $\kappa = k\tau + 1$. Suppose that $a$ is $A_1$-bounded, that
is, $A_1 \le (k - 1)\tau + 2$. Then for every $n \ge 1$, $A_n$ lies in the interval
$I_n = [\kappa(n - 1) + 1, \kappa n]$, and the first $k$ numbers of $I_n$ are non-anti-recurrence
numbers: $B_{(n-1)k\tau + j} = \kappa(n - 1) + j$ for $1 \le j \le k$.

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Lower bound for the first anti-recurrence number
articles.statement:
Let $a = (a_1, \dots, a_k)$ be a linear
form with positive integer coefficients, of trace $\tau = a_1 + \dots + a_k$, and let $A_1$ be its
first anti-recurrence number. Then $\tau + (k - 1)k/2 \le A_1$, and the inequality is strict if
and only if $a_j > 1$ for some $j$ with $2 \le j \le k$.

This corrects the printed strictness condition ("$k > 2$ and not anti-bonacci"), which fails for
$a = (2, 1, 1)$: there $A_1 = 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 = \tau + 3$. The correction follows the paper's
proof, $A_1 = \tau + \sum_j (j - 1) a_j$. The paper's hypothesis $k > 1$ is not needed.

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Lemma 4.

articles.title: State of the anti-recurrence construction
articles.statement:
Let $a = (a_1, \dots, a_k)$ be a finite list of
natural numbers. The state at step $0$ is the pair of the empty list and the empty set. If the
state at step $n$ has set $S$, then the state at step $n + 1$ is the pair $(\beta, S')$, where
$\beta = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$ is the mex block of length $k$ from $S$ (each $x_j$ is the least
positive integer not in $S \cup \{x_1, \dots, x_{j-1}\}$) and
$S' = S \cup \{x_1, \dots, x_k\} \cup \{a_1 x_1 + \dots + a_k x_k\}$.

In the notation of the source, for $n \ge 1$ the block at step $n$ is
$(B_{(n-1)k+1}, \dots, B_{nk})$ and the set at step $n$ is
$\{B_1, \dots, B_{nk}\} \cup \{A_1, \dots, A_n\}$, where the $B_m$ are the non-anti-recurrence
numbers and the $A_m$ are the anti-recurrence numbers of $a$.

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Section 2 (definition of anti-recurrence sequences and Lemma 2).

articles.title: Bounded anti-recurrence sequences are automatic up to a linear term
articles.statement:
Let
$a = (a_1, \dots, a_k)$ be a linear form with positive integer coefficients and $k > 1$, of trace
$\tau = a_1 + \dots + a_k$, with anti-recurrence numbers $A_1, A_2, \dots$, and let
$\kappa = k\tau + 1$. If $a$ is $A_1$-bounded, that is, $A_1 \le (k - 1)\tau + 2$, then the
integer sequence $n \mapsto A_{n+1} - \kappa(n + 1)$, indexed from $n = 0$, is $\tau$-automatic:
$\tau \ge 2$ and its $\tau$-kernel is finite.

Automaticity is stated through Eilenberg's characterization by a finite kernel, in place of the
paper's definition by a finite automaton with output.

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Characterization of anti-recurrence sequences
articles.statement:
Let $a = (a_1, \dots, a_k)$ be a linear
form with positive integer coefficients and $k > 1$, with anti-recurrence numbers
$A_1, A_2, \dots$ and non-anti-recurrence numbers $B_1, B_2, \dots$. Let $(x_i)_{i \ge 0}$ and
$(y_i)_{i \ge 0}$ be sequences of natural numbers. Then $x$ and $y$ are strictly increasing, every
$y_i$ is positive, every positive integer is a term of exactly one of $x$ and $y$, and
$x_i = \sum_{j=1}^{k} a_j y_{ik+j-1}$ for all $i$, if and only if $x_i = A_{i+1}$ and
$y_i = B_{i+1}$ for all $i$.

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Anti-recurrence numbers
articles.statement:
Let $a = (a_1, \dots, a_k)$ be a linear form with natural number
coefficients. The non-anti-recurrence numbers $B_1, B_2, \dots$ are produced in blocks of $k$ by
the mex rule, and each block $B_{(n-1)k+1}, \dots, B_{nk}$ generates the anti-recurrence number
$A_n = \sum_{j=1}^{k} a_j B_{(n-1)k+j}$. Here $B_m$ is the least positive integer that differs
from $B_1, \dots, B_{m-1}$ and from the anti-recurrence numbers of earlier blocks. By convention
$A_0 = 0$, following Hofstadter.

## Sources

- Robbert Fokkink and Gandhar Joshi, *Anti-Recurrence Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A24, Section 2 (definition of anti-recurrence sequences).

articles.title: First summands of the anti-Tribonacci construction
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 1$, $A_n$ is the first
entry of the $n$-th quadruple $(A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n)$ of the anti-Tribonacci construction:
$A_1 = 1$, and for $n \ge 2$, $A_n$ is the least positive integer that is not among the values
$A_k$, $B_k$, $C_k$, $D_k$ with $1 \le k < n$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives $A_0 = A_1 = 1$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: Second summands of the anti-Tribonacci construction
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 1$, $B_n$ is the second
entry of the $n$-th quadruple $(A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n)$ of the anti-Tribonacci construction:
$B_1 = 2$, and for $n \ge 2$, $B_n$ is the second smallest positive integer that is not among
the values $A_k$, $B_k$, $C_k$, $D_k$ with $1 \le k < n$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives
$B_0 = B_1 = 2$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: Third summands of the anti-Tribonacci construction
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 1$, $C_n$ is the third
entry of the $n$-th quadruple $(A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n)$ of the anti-Tribonacci construction:
$C_1 = 3$, and for $n \ge 2$, $C_n$ is the third smallest positive integer that is not among
the values $A_k$, $B_k$, $C_k$, $D_k$ with $1 \le k < n$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives
$C_0 = C_1 = 3$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: First anti-Tribonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Writing $D_n$ for the $n$-th anti-Tribonacci number,
the first four anti-Tribonacci numbers are $D_1 = 6$, $D_2 = 16$, $D_3 = 27$ and $D_4 = 36$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: Anti-Tribonacci numbers
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 1$, the anti-Tribonacci number $D_n$ (OEIS A265389) is
the fourth entry of the $n$-th quadruple $(A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n)$ of the anti-Tribonacci
construction, so $D_n = A_n + B_n + C_n$ and $D_1 = 6$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives
$D_0 = D_1 = 6$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: Mex of $\{1, 2, 3, 6\}$
articles.statement:
The least positive integer not in $\{1, 2, 3, 6\}$ is $4$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: The mex is at most every missing positive integer
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{mex}(s)$ for the least
positive integer not in a finite set $s$ of natural numbers. If $m$ is a positive integer with
$m \notin s$, then $\mathrm{mex}(s) \le m$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: The mex of a finite set lies outside the set
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{mex}(s)$ for the least positive
integer not in a finite set $s$ of natural numbers. For every such $s$, $\mathrm{mex}(s) \notin s$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: The mex of a finite set is positive
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{mex}(s)$ for the least positive integer
not in a finite set $s$ of natural numbers. For every such $s$, $\mathrm{mex}(s) > 0$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: Least positive integer missing from a finite set
articles.statement:
For a finite set $s$ of natural numbers,
this is the least positive integer not in $s$ (the source's $\mathrm{mex}$ over the positive
integers, used to build the anti-Tribonacci sequence). It always lies among $1, \dots, |s| + 1$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: Anti-Tribonacci construction
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{mex}(U)$ for the least positive integer not in
a finite set $U$ of natural numbers. Set $(A_1, B_1, C_1, D_1) = (1, 2, 3, 6)$ and
$U_1 = \{1, 2, 3, 6\}$. For $k \ge 1$ let $A_{k+1} = \mathrm{mex}(U_k)$,
$B_{k+1} = \mathrm{mex}(U_k \cup \{A_{k+1}\})$,
$C_{k+1} = \mathrm{mex}(U_k \cup \{A_{k+1}, B_{k+1}\})$, $D_{k+1} = A_{k+1} + B_{k+1} + C_{k+1}$
and $U_{k+1} = U_k \cup \{A_{k+1}, B_{k+1}, C_{k+1}, D_{k+1}\}$. Entry $n$ of the construction is
the pair $((A_{n+1}, B_{n+1}, C_{n+1}, D_{n+1}), U_{n+1})$, where $U_{n+1}$ is the set of all
values used so far.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: Hajdu–Tijdeman–Varga theorem on $(x-1)^c (x+1)^d$ modulo $3$
articles.statement:
Let $c$ and $d$ be natural
numbers. If none of the coefficients of $x^0, x^1, \dots, x^{c+d}$ in the integer polynomial
$(x-1)^c (x+1)^d$ is divisible by $3$, then there are natural numbers $i > j$ such that $c + d + 1$
equals $3^j$, $2 \cdot 3^j$, $3^i + 3^j$ or $2 \cdot 3^i + 3^j$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Theorem 10 (`jis-2025-25.3.8-thm-10`), citing Hajdu, Tijdeman, and Varga.

articles.title: First members of $S_{1,2,3}$
articles.statement:
The members of the greedy $3$-subsumfree sequence
$S_{1,2,3}$ below $26$ are exactly $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 13, 14, 15, 25$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 6.

articles.title: Members of a greedy $3$-subsumfree sequence below a bound
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $x$, $y$
and $z$ (the source takes $x < y < z$), let $S_{x,y,z}$ consist of $x$, $y$, $z$ and every natural
number $n > z$ that is not a sum $a + b + c$ of members $a < b < c$ of $S_{x,y,z}$ smaller than
$n$. This definition gives, for each natural number $m$, the finite set of members of $S_{x,y,z}$
below $m$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 6.

articles.title: Markers among the unsum gaps
articles.statement:
A natural number $i$ is a *marker* if $i \ge 10$ and the
$i$-th gap between consecutive unsums of upper Wythoff numbers (counted from zero) equals $2$.

The source marks the entries $2$ of A260311 that follow the irregular prefix $1111122121$ of
length ten.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 2.

articles.title: The unsums up to 21
articles.statement:
The unsums (OEIS A260317) that are at most $21$ are exactly
$1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 19, 21$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 2.

articles.title: Unsums of upper Wythoff numbers
articles.statement:
A positive integer $p$ is an *upper Wythoff number* when
the letter at index $p - 1$ (indices start at $0$) of the infinite Fibonacci word
$0100101001001\ldots$ is $1$; that is, the upper Wythoff numbers are the positions of the letter
$1$ in the Fibonacci word counted from one. A positive integer $x$ is an *unsum* (OEIS A260317)
if there are no upper Wythoff numbers $p < q$ with $p + q = x$.

The source writes the Fibonacci word over the letters $a$ and $b$; its letter $b$ is the letter
$1$ here.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 2, defining unsums as the members of OEIS A260317.

articles.title: Kimberling's conjecture on the anti-Tribonacci sequence
articles.statement:
Let $A_1 = 1$, $B_1 = 2$,
$C_1 = 3$ and $D_1 = 6$, and for $n \ge 1$ let $A_{n+1} < B_{n+1} < C_{n+1}$ be the three
smallest positive integers that are not among $A_i, B_i, C_i, D_i$ for $i \le n$, and
$D_{n+1} = A_{n+1} + B_{n+1} + C_{n+1}$ (the $D_n$ are the anti-Tribonacci numbers). For every
integer $n \ge 1$, $0 \le 10n - 6 - 3A_n \le 2$, $0 \le 10n - 2 - 3B_n \le 3$,
$0 \le 10n + 1 - 3C_n \le 3$ and $0 \le 10n - 3 - D_n \le 2$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Theorem 12 (`jis-2025-25.3.8-thm-12`).

articles.title: Length of the period-doubling iterates
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the word obtained by
applying the period-doubling substitution $1 \mapsto 10$, $0 \mapsto 11$ to the one-letter word
$1$ a total of $n$ times has length $2^n$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: Membership in three greedy 3-subsumfree sequences
articles.statement:
For $x < y < z$, the greedy
$3$-subsumfree sequence $S_{x,y,z}$ consists of $x$, $y$, $z$ and every $m > z$ that is not the
sum of three different members of $S_{x,y,z}$ smaller than $m$. For every positive integer $n$:
$n \in S_{1,2,3}$ if and only if $n \in \{1, 5, 13\}$ or $n \bmod 23 \in \{2, 3, 4, 14, 15\}$;
$n \in S_{1,3,4}$ if and only if $n \in \{1, 7, 19\}$ or
$n \bmod 33 \in \{3, 4, 5, 6, 20, 21, 22\}$; and $n \in S_{1,4,5}$ if and only if
$n \in \{1, 9, 25\}$ or $n \bmod 43 \in \{4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 26, 27, 28, 29\}$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Theorem 15 (`jis-2025-25.3.8-thm-15`).

articles.title: First letters of the period-doubling word
articles.statement:
The letters at indices $0, 1, \ldots, 7$ of the
period-doubling word (the fixed point of $1 \mapsto 10$, $0 \mapsto 11$ that starts with $1$) are
$1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: Letters of the period-doubling iterates
articles.statement:
Let $w_m$ be the word obtained by applying the
period-doubling substitution $1 \mapsto 10$, $0 \mapsto 11$ to the one-letter word $1$ a total of
$m$ times. For all natural numbers $m$ and $k$ with $k < 2^m$, the letter of $w_m$ at index $k$
(indices start at $0$) equals the letter of the period-doubling word at index $k$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: Iterates of the period-doubling substitution
articles.statement:
Write the period-doubling substitution
$a \mapsto ab$, $b \mapsto aa$ over the letters $a = 1$ and $b = 0$, so that it sends $1$ to $10$
and $0$ to $11$. The $n$-th period-doubling iterate is the word obtained by applying this
substitution $n$ times to the one-letter word $1$; the iterates begin $1$, $10$, $1011$,
$10111010$, and their limit is the period-doubling word (Walnut's PD).

The source's prose takes $a = 0$ and $b = 1$, but its Walnut definition `antifib`
(`PD[k]=@1` gives $9 + 10k$) and its displayed anti-Fibonacci numbers $0, 3, 9, 13, \ldots$ need
the first letter of PD to be $1$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: The period-doubling word
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, the letter at index $k$ (indices start
at $0$) of the period-doubling word is the letter at index $k$ of the word obtained by applying
the period-doubling substitution $1 \mapsto 10$, $0 \mapsto 11$ to the one-letter word $1$ a total
of $\lfloor \log_2 k \rfloor + 1$ times, where $\lfloor \log_2 0 \rfloor$ is taken to be $0$.
That word has length $2^{\lfloor \log_2 k \rfloor + 1} \le 2k + 2$, so it contains index $k$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 4.

articles.title: The upper Wythoff numbers below 30
articles.statement:
The positive integers $p < 30$ such that the letter at
index $p - 1$ (indices start at $0$) of the infinite Fibonacci word is $1$, that is, the upper
Wythoff numbers below $30$, are exactly $2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23, 26, 28$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 2.

articles.title: The last gap of size one between unsums
articles.statement:
Let $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ be the unsums
(OEIS A260317), and for $i \ge 0$ let $g_i = a_{i+2} - a_{i+1}$ be the $i$-th gap between
consecutive unsums, counted from zero. Then $g_9 = 1$, and $g_i \ne 1$ for every $i \ge 10$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Lemma 1 (`jis-2025-25.3.8-lem-1`).

articles.title: The first thirteen gaps between unsums
articles.statement:
Let $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ be the unsums
(OEIS A260317) and let $g_i = a_{i+2} - a_{i+1}$ for $i \ge 0$. Then the gaps
$g_0, g_1, \dots, g_{12}$ are $1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 2.

articles.title: Gaps between unsums
articles.statement:
Let $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ be the unsums (OEIS A260317): the
positive integers that are not a sum $p + q$ of upper Wythoff numbers $p < q$. For $i \ge 0$,
the $i$-th gap between consecutive unsums (counted from zero) is $a_{i+2} - a_{i+1}$; this
is OEIS A260311 shifted by one.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 2.

articles.title: The first two markers
articles.statement:
Call a gap index $i$ a marker if $i \ge 10$ and the $i$-th gap
between consecutive unsums (counted from zero) equals $2$. The smallest marker is $10$ and
the second smallest is $12$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 2.

articles.title: Markers in the gaps between unsums
articles.statement:
Call a gap index $i$ a marker if $i \ge 10$ and the
$i$-th gap between consecutive unsums (counted from zero) equals $2$. For $j \ge 0$, the
$j$-th marker is the $j$-th marker in increasing order, counted from zero, so the $0$-th
marker is the smallest one.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 2.

articles.title: The palindromes begin and end with the digit 3
articles.statement:
Let $g_k$ be the $k$-th gap between
consecutive unsums (OEIS A260317), counted from zero, and let $m_0 < m_1 < \cdots$ be the
markers, the indices $k \ge 10$ with $g_k = 2$, in increasing order. For $i \ge 1$ let $W_i$
be the word of the gaps $g_k$ with $m_{2i-2} < k < m_{2i-1}$, in increasing order of $k$. Then
for every $i \ge 1$, the word $W_i$ is nonempty, its first digit is $3$, and its last digit
is $3$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Lemma 5 (`jis-2025-25.3.8-lem-5`).

articles.title: When one palindrome is a prefix of the next
articles.statement:
Let $g_k$ be the $k$-th gap between
consecutive unsums (OEIS A260317), counted from zero, and let $m_0 < m_1 < \cdots$ be the
markers, the indices $k \ge 10$ with $g_k = 2$, in increasing order. For $i \ge 1$ let $W_i$
be the word of the gaps $g_k$ with $m_{2i-2} < k < m_{2i-1}$, in increasing order of $k$. Then
for every $i \ge 1$, the word $W_i$ is a prefix of $W_{i+1}$ if and only if $i$ is odd.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Lemma 7 (`jis-2025-25.3.8-lem-7`).

articles.title: The first palindrome
articles.statement:
Let $g_k$ be the $k$-th gap between consecutive unsums
(OEIS A260317), counted from zero, and let $m_0 < m_1 < \cdots$ be the markers, the indices
$k \ge 10$ with $g_k = 2$, in increasing order. The word $W_1$ of the gaps $g_k$ with
$m_0 < k < m_1$, in increasing order of $k$, consists of the single digit $3$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 2.

articles.title: The gap words are palindromes
articles.statement:
Let $g_k$ be the $k$-th gap between
consecutive unsums (OEIS A260317), counted from zero, and let $m_0 < m_1 < \cdots$ be the
markers, the indices $k \ge 10$ with $g_k = 2$, in increasing order. For $i \ge 1$ let $W_i$
be the word of the gaps $g_k$ with $m_{2i-2} < k < m_{2i-1}$, in increasing order of $k$. Then
for every $i \ge 1$, the word $W_i$ read backwards is $W_i$ itself.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Lemma 4 (`jis-2025-25.3.8-lem-4`).

articles.title: Recursion for the words $W_i$ of the unsum gap sequence
articles.statement:
For each $i$ let $V_i$ be the
word $W_i$ with its first and last digit removed, write $|W|$ for the length of a word $W$, and
denote concatenation of words by juxtaposition. For every $i \ge 2$: if $i$ is odd, then
$W_{i+1} = W_i \, 5 \, V_{i-1} \, 3$; if $i$ is even, then $W_{i+1} = 3 \, V_i \, 5 \, W_{i-1}$;
and in both cases $|W_{i+1}| = |W_i| + |W_{i-1}|$. Moreover $|W_1| = 1$, $|W_2| = 2$, and
$|W_i| = F_{i+1}$ for every $i \ge 1$, where $F_m$ is the $m$-th Fibonacci number ($F_0 = 0$,
$F_1 = 1$).

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Lemma 8 (`jis-2025-25.3.8-lem-8`).

articles.title: The words $W_i$ converge to $3$ followed by the coded Fibonacci word
articles.statement:
Let
$u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ be the infinite Fibonacci word over $\{0, 1\}$, indexed from $0$, and let
$\mathbf{V}$ be the infinite word obtained from it by replacing each $0$ by $5$ and each
$1$ by $3$. Then the words $W_i$ of the unsum gap sequence converge to the infinite word
$3\mathbf{V}$: for every $k \ge 0$ there is $N$ such that for every $i \ge N$ the word $W_i$ has
more than $k$ digits and its digit at position $k$ (counted from zero) is the digit of
$3\mathbf{V}$ at position $k$, that is, $3$ if $k = 0$, and for $k \ge 1$ it is $3$ if
$u_{k-1} = 1$ and $5$ if $u_{k-1} = 0$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Lemma 9 (`jis-2025-25.3.8-lem-9`).

articles.title: The words $W_i$ of the unsum gap sequence
articles.statement:
For $i \ge 1$, the word $W_i$ is the word of
gaps strictly between the $(2i-2)$-th and $(2i-1)$-th markers of the unsum gap sequence, with
markers counted from zero; for $i = 0$ the definition gives the same word as for $i = 1$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 2.

articles.title: A word $3V3$ between markers is followed by a word starting with $3V$
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a
finite word of natural numbers, and suppose that the $j$-th word between markers of the unsum
gap sequence is $3V3$. Then $3V$ is a prefix of the $(j+1)$-th word between markers, and if the
$(j+1)$-th word has the same digit sum as the $j$-th word, then the two words are equal.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Lemma 6 (`jis-2025-25.3.8-lem-6`).

articles.title: Digit sums between markers are two less than Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
For every $j$, the digit
sum of the $j$-th word between markers of the unsum gap sequence, plus $2$, is a Fibonacci
number: it equals $F_m$ for some natural number $m$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Lemma 2 (`jis-2025-25.3.8-lem-2`).

articles.title: Digit sums of the words between markers
articles.statement:
Let $F_n$ be the Fibonacci numbers, with
$F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$. For every $j$ (words counted from zero), the digit sum of the $j$-th
word between markers of the unsum gap sequence, plus $2$, equals $F_{\lfloor j/2 \rfloor + 5}$.

So the digit sums are $3, 3, 6, 6, 11, \ldots$; adding the preceding marker digit $2$ gives
$F_5, F_5, F_6, F_6, F_7, \ldots$, which is how the source's Lemma 3 must be read, since the
bare digit sum of the first word is $3 \ne F_5 = 5$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Lemma 3 (`jis-2025-25.3.8-lem-3`).

articles.title: Words between markers in the unsum gap sequence
articles.statement:
Let $g_0, g_1, g_2, \ldots$ be the
gaps between consecutive unsums, and call an index $i \ge 10$ with $g_i = 2$ a marker. Let
$m_0 < m_1 < m_2 < \cdots$ be the markers in increasing order. For each $j$, the $j$-th word
between markers is $g_{m_j + 1} g_{m_j + 2} \cdots g_{m_{j+1} - 1}$, the word of the gaps
strictly between the $j$-th and the $(j+1)$-th marker.

The source writes the gap sequence after its prefix as $2 W_1 2 W_1 2 W_2 2 W_2 2 W_3 2 \cdots$,
so these words are $W_1, W_1, W_2, W_2, \ldots$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Section 2.

articles.title: Zaslavsky's formulas for the anti-Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let $A_1 = 1$, $B_1 = 2$,
$C_1 = 3$, and for $n \ge 1$ let $A_{n+1} < B_{n+1}$ be the two smallest positive integers not
among $A_1, B_1, C_1, \ldots, A_n, B_n, C_n$ and $C_{n+1} = A_{n+1} + B_{n+1}$. Let
$\mathrm{PD}[0], \mathrm{PD}[1], \ldots$ be the letters of the period-doubling word, the fixed
point of $1 \mapsto 10$, $0 \mapsto 11$ starting with $1$. Then for every $k \ge 0$,
$C_{2k+1} = 10k + 3$, $C_{2k+2} = 10k + 8 + \mathrm{PD}[k]$, $A_{2k+1} = 5k + 1$,
$B_{2k+1} = 5k + 2$, $A_{2k+2} = 5k + 3 + \mathrm{PD}[k]$, and $B_{2k+2} = 5(k + 1)$.

In the source's notation the anti-Fibonacci numbers are $X_n = C_n$ and the
non-anti-Fibonacci numbers are $Y_{2n-1} = A_n$ and $Y_{2n} = B_n$, so the formulas read
$X_{2k+1} = 10k + 3$, $X_{2k+2} = 10k + 8 + \mathrm{PD}[k]$, $Y_{4k+1} = 5k + 1$,
$Y_{4k+2} = 5k + 2$, $Y_{4k+3} = 5k + 3 + \mathrm{PD}[k]$ and $Y_{4k+4} = 5(k + 1)$ (the
source's $Y_{4k} = 5k$ for $k \ge 1$). The source's prose writes the period-doubling word
over letters $a, b$ with $a = 0$, but its Walnut code and its values $X_2 = 9$ and $Y_3 = 4$
need $\mathrm{PD}[0] = 1$.

## Sources

- Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl, and Tromp, *Using Walnut to Solve Problems from the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.8, Theorem 11 (`jis-2025-25.3.8-thm-11`), due to Zaslavsky.

articles.title: Existence and uniqueness of the Aronson transform, general form
articles.statement:
Let $n_0$ be a natural
number and let $\beta : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be strictly increasing such that infinitely
many integers $m \ge n_0$ are not values of $\beta$. Then there is exactly one sequence
$\alpha : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that $\alpha$ is strictly increasing, $\alpha_i \ge n_0$
for every $i$, $\alpha_0$ is the least integer $m \ge n_0$ such that $m = n_0$ holds exactly when
$m$ is a value of $\beta$, and, for every $i \ge 0$, $\alpha_{i+1}$ is the least integer
$m > \alpha_i$ such that $n_0 + i + 1 \in \{\alpha_0, \dots, \alpha_i, m\}$ holds exactly when $m$
is a value of $\beta$.

The values of $\beta$ are not required to be at least $n_0$.

articles.title: Existence and uniqueness of the Aronson transform
articles.statement:
Let $n_0$ be a natural number and let
$\beta : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be strictly increasing with $\beta_i \ge n_0$ for every $i$,
such that infinitely many integers $m \ge n_0$ are not values of $\beta$. Then there is exactly
one sequence $\alpha : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that $\alpha$ is strictly increasing,
$\alpha_i \ge n_0$ for every $i$, $\alpha_0$ is the least integer $m \ge n_0$ such that $m = n_0$
holds exactly when $m$ is a value of $\beta$, and, for every $i \ge 0$, $\alpha_{i+1}$ is the
least integer $m > \alpha_i$ such that $n_0 + i + 1 \in \{\alpha_0, \dots, \alpha_i, m\}$ holds
exactly when $m$ is a value of $\beta$.

The hypothesis $\beta_i \ge n_0$ is not used in the proof.

## Sources

- Benoit Cloitre, N. J. A. Sloane, and Matthew J. Vandermast, "Numerical Analogues of Aronson's Sequence," Journal of Integer Sequences 6 (2003), Article 03.2.2, Theorem `ThAT1`, lines 782–784 (transform defined lines 761–780), https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL6/Cloitre/cloitre2.tex

articles.title: Approximants of Cloitre's sequence
articles.statement:
The finite words $A_k$ of natural numbers are defined
by $A_0 = (1, 1)$ and $A_{k+1} = A_k A_k^r$, the concatenation of $A_k$ with its mirror image
$A_k^r$: reverse $A_k$, then replace a leading $2$ by $1, 1$, or two leading letters $1, 1$ by
$2$, and otherwise leave it unchanged.

For example $A_1 = (1, 1, 2)$, $A_2 = (1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1)$ and
$A_3 = (1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1)$, and $A_4$ continues with $2, 2$.

articles.title: First-letter complement of a word
articles.statement:
For a finite list of natural numbers, a leading letter
$2$ is replaced by the two letters $1, 1$, and two leading letters $1, 1$ are replaced by the single
letter $2$; the empty list and every list beginning otherwise (with a letter other than $1$ or $2$,
or with a $1$ not followed by another $1$) are left unchanged.

Every word this is applied to in Cloitre's construction begins with $1, 1$ or with $2$, so the
last case does not arise there.

articles.title: Mirror image with first-letter complement
articles.statement:
For a finite list $A$ of natural numbers, the
mirror image $A^r$ is obtained by reversing $A$ and then complementing the first letter: a leading
$2$ of the reversed list becomes $1, 1$, two leading letters $1, 1$ become $2$, and any other list
is left unchanged. For example $(1, 1, 2)^r = (1, 1, 1, 1)$ and
$(1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1)^r = (2, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1)$.

articles.title: Sum of a sequence over a run
articles.statement:
For sequences $s, b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, the $n$-th run sum is $\sum_{b(n) \le j < b(n+1)} s(j)$, the sum of $s$ over
the block $[b(n), b(n+1))$; it is $0$ when $b(n+1) \le b(n)$.

articles.title: Cloitre's sequence
articles.statement:
Let $A_0 = (1, 1)$ and $A_{k+1} = A_k A_k^r$ be the approximants of
Cloitre's sequence, where $A_k^r$ is the mirror image of $A_k$: reverse $A_k$, then replace a
leading $2$ by $1, 1$, or two leading letters $1, 1$ by $2$, and otherwise leave it unchanged.
Cloitre's sequence $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is defined by letting $s(n)$ be the letter at
position $n$ (counting from $0$) of $A_{n+2}$, or $0$ if $A_{n+2}$ has at most $n$ letters.

Each approximant is a prefix of the next and $A_{n+2}$ has more than $n$ letters, so $s$ is the
limit of the approximants. It begins $1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, \ldots$

articles.title: Cloitre's self-describing property
articles.statement:
A sequence $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is
self-describing in Cloitre's sense when there is a sequence $b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with
$b(0) = 0$, $b$ strictly increasing, $s$ constant on each block $[b(n), b(n+1))$ and each value of
$s$ on a block different from each value on the next block (so the blocks are the maximal runs of
$s$), such that for every $n$, $2 s(n) = \sum_{b(n) \le j < b(n+1)} s(j)$.

In words, for every $n$ the $n$-th term $s(n)$ is half the sum of the $n$-th run; the condition is
stated with $2 s(n)$ to avoid truncated division in $\mathbb{N}$. For example, run sums
$2, 2, 4, 2, 2, 2, 2, 4, \ldots$ correspond to the terms $1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, \ldots$

articles.title: Run boundaries of a sequence
articles.statement:
For sequences $s, b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, $b$ marks
the maximal runs of $s$ when $b(0) = 0$, $b$ is strictly increasing, $s$ is constant on each
block $[b(n), b(n+1))$, and for every $n$ each value of $s$ on the block $[b(n), b(n+1))$ differs
from each value of $s$ on the next block $[b(n+1), b(n+2))$.

Because $b$ is strictly increasing with $b(0) = 0$, the blocks partition $\mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Entries of the Connell triangle
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$, $r$, $j$ and $k$, the entry with
zero-based index $k$ in row $j$ of the Connell $(m, r)$ triangle is $s_j + mk$, where $s_j$ is the
first entry of row $j$. The formula is used for every $k$, also at or beyond the row length.

articles.title: Next position in the Connell triangle
articles.statement:
For a natural number $r$, the position following
row $j$, zero-based column $k$, is row $j$, column $k + 1$ if $k + 1 < 1 + r(j - 1)$ (the length
of row $j$, with $j - 1$ read as $0$ when $j = 0$), and row $j + 1$, column $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Connell parameters
articles.statement:
A pair of natural numbers $(m, r)$ with $m \ge 2$ and $r \ge 1$; these
are the admissible parameters of a Connell $(m, r)$ sequence.

articles.title: Position of a term in the Connell triangle
articles.statement:
For a natural number $r$, the position
$p_n = (j_n, k_n)$ (row $j_n$, zero-based column $k_n$) of index $n \ge 0$ is defined by
$p_0 = (1, 0)$ and $p_{n+1} = (j_n, k_n + 1)$ if $k_n + 1 < 1 + r(j_n - 1)$ (the length of row
$j_n$, with $j_n - 1$ read as $0$ when $j_n = 0$), and $p_{n+1} = (j_n + 1, 0)$ otherwise.

articles.title: Rows of the Connell triangle
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$, $r$ and $j$, row $j$ of the
Connell $(m, r)$ triangle is the finite set of the numbers $s_j + mk$ with $0 \le k < \ell_j$, where
$s_j$ is the first entry of row $j$ and $\ell_j = 1 + r(j - 1)$ is its length, with $j - 1$ read
as $0$ when $j = 0$.

articles.title: Row lengths of the Connell triangle
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $r$ and $j$, the length of
row $j$ is $1 + r(j - 1)$, where $j - 1$ is read as $0$ when $j = 0$. For $j \ge 1$ this is the
number of entries in row $j$ of the Connell $(m, r)$ triangle for every $m$; the source numbers
rows from one, and the value at $j = 0$ is a convention.

articles.title: First entries of the rows of the Connell triangle
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$ and $r$, the
numbers $s_j$ are defined by $s_0 = s_1 = 1$ and $s_{j+1} = s_j + m(\ell_j - 1) + 1$ for
$j \ge 1$, where $\ell_j = 1 + r(j - 1)$ is the length of row $j$. For $j \ge 1$, $s_j$ is the
first entry of row $j$ of the Connell $(m, r)$ triangle: each row starts one above the last
entry $s_j + m(\ell_j - 1)$ of the row before. The source numbers rows from one, and the value
$s_0 = 1$ is a convention.

articles.title: Connell sequence
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m \ge 2$ and $r \ge 1$, the Connell $(m, r)$
sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ reads the Connell triangle row by row: row $j \ge 1$ has
$\ell_j = 1 + r(j - 1)$ entries $s_j, s_j + m, \dots, s_j + m(\ell_j - 1)$, where $s_1 = 1$ and
$s_{j+1} = s_j + m(\ell_j - 1) + 1$. Thus $a_n = s_j + mk$, where row $j$, zero-based column $k$
is the position reached from row $1$, column $0$ after $n$ steps, each step moving one column
right within a row and from the last entry of a row to the first entry of the next.

articles.title: Regular fractal sequence
articles.statement:
A regular fractal sequence is a sequence $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of
positive integers together with a position array $(p_i(j))_{i, j \ge 0}$ of natural numbers such
that: for every $i \ge 0$, the strictly increasing sequence $p_i(0) < p_i(1) < \cdots$ lists
exactly the positions $n$ with $x_n = i + 1$ (so every positive integer occurs infinitely often);
for all $i$ and $n$ with $x_n = i + 2$, some $m < n$ has $x_m = i + 1$; for all $h$, $i$ and $j$
with $h < i$, exactly one $k$ satisfies $p_i(j) < p_h(k) < p_i(j + 1)$; and for every $j$,
$p_i(j)$ is strictly increasing in $i$.

Source JIS VOL25/Kimberling,
<https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Kimberling/kimber16.tex>, lines 103–219.

Source positive value `i + 1` is represented directly as the natural `i + 1`,
and `pos i j` is the zero-based position of its `j`-th occurrence.

articles.title: Every value occurs infinitely often in a regular fractal sequence
articles.statement:
Let $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$
be a regular fractal sequence. Then for every positive integer $k$ there are infinitely many $n$
with $x_n = k$.

articles.title: Occurrence positions are distinct
articles.statement:
In a regular fractal sequence with position array
$p$, for every $i \ge 0$ the map $j \mapsto p_i(j)$, sending $j$ to the position of the $j$-th
occurrence of $i + 1$ (counting from $j = 0$), is injective.

articles.title: Curling number of block words with small exponents
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and $u \ge 2$, and let
$a_1, \dots, a_{u-1} \in \{0, \dots, m\}$ with $a_1 \ne 0$. Writing $B_t = B_t^{(m+1)}$ for the
blocks of the $(m+1)$th order Gijswijt sequence $A^{(m+1)}$, the string
$P = B_{u-1}^{a_{u-1}} \cdots B_2^{a_2} B_1^{a_1}$ has curling number $\mathcal{C}(P) \le m$.

## Sources

- Levi van de Pol, *The Growth Rate of Gijswijt's Sequence*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.6, Lemma 13 (`jis-2025-25.4.6-lem-13`).

articles.title: Curling number of block words with a maximal exponent
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and $u \ge 1$, and
let $a_1, \dots, a_{u-1} \in \{0, \dots, m+1\}$ with $a_i = m + 1$ for some $1 \le i \le u - 1$.
Writing $B_t = B_t^{(m+1)}$ for the blocks of the $(m+1)$th order Gijswijt sequence $A^{(m+1)}$,
the string $P = B_{u-1}^{a_{u-1}} \cdots B_2^{a_2} B_1^{a_1}$ has curling number
$\mathcal{C}(P) = m + 1$.

## Sources

- Levi van de Pol, *The Growth Rate of Gijswijt's Sequence*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.6, Lemma 12 (`jis-2025-25.4.6-lem-12`).

articles.title: Curling number of $112112223$
articles.statement:
The string $112112223$ has curling number
$\mathcal{C}(112112223) = 1$.

## Sources

- Levi van de Pol, *The Growth Rate of Gijswijt's Sequence*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.6, Section 1 (curling number examples).

articles.title: Curling number of $222322232223$
articles.statement:
The string $222322232223$ has curling number
$\mathcal{C}(222322232223) = 3$.

## Sources

- Levi van de Pol, *The Growth Rate of Gijswijt's Sequence*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.6, Section 1 (curling number examples).

articles.title: The curling number is monotone under suffixes
articles.statement:
For strings $S$ and $T$ of natural numbers,
if $T$ is a suffix of $S$, then $\mathcal{C}(T) \le \mathcal{C}(S)$.

## Sources

- Levi van de Pol, *The Growth Rate of Gijswijt's Sequence*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.6, Lemma 3 (`jis-2025-25.4.6-lem-3`).

articles.title: Curling number of the empty string
articles.statement:
The empty string $\varepsilon$ has curling number
$\mathcal{C}(\varepsilon) = 1$.

## Sources

- Levi van de Pol, *The Growth Rate of Gijswijt's Sequence*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.6, Section 1.2 (`𝒞(ε) := 1`).

articles.title: Curling number
articles.statement:
The curling number $\mathcal{C}(S)$ of a finite string $S$ of natural
numbers is the largest integer $k$ such that $S = X Y^k$ for some strings $X$ and $Y$ with $Y$
nonempty; for the empty string $\varepsilon$ it is $\mathcal{C}(\varepsilon) = 1$.

## Sources

- Levi van de Pol, *The Growth Rate of Gijswijt's Sequence*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.6, Section 1 (curling number) and Section 1.2 (`𝒞(ε) := 1`).

articles.title: Recursive estimate for the block index
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and $n \ge m + 3$, and for $k \ge 1$
let $t(k, n)$ be the index $t$ such that the first occurrence of $n$ in the $k$th order Gijswijt
sequence $A^{(k)}$ is the last element of the block $B_t^{(k)}$ of $A^{(k)}$. Then
$m (m+1)^{t(m+1,n) - 2} \le t(m, n) \le (m+1)^{t(m+1,n) - 1} + 1$, and the second inequality is
strict when $n = m + 3$.

## Sources

- Levi van de Pol, *The Growth Rate of Gijswijt's Sequence*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.6, Proposition 19 (`jis-2025-25.4.6-prop-19`).

articles.title: Block index of the first occurrence
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$ and $n$, let $p$ be the
position of the first occurrence of $n$ in the $m$th order Gijswijt sequence $A^{(m)}$, with
$p = 0$ if $n$ does not occur. Then $t(m, n)$ is the least $t \ge 1$ such that the block length
$\beta^{(m)}(t)$ equals $p$, so that when $n$ occurs, this first $n$ is the last element of the
block $B_t^{(m)}$; if there is no such $t$, then $t(m, n) = 0$.

## Sources

- Levi van de Pol, *The Growth Rate of Gijswijt's Sequence*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.6, Section 3 (definition of `t(m, n)`).

articles.title: Upper bound on block lengths
articles.statement:
Let $M_7 = 4$ and $M_{k+1} = M_k (1 + 9 (k+1)^{1.59} / 2^k)$
for $k \ge 7$. Then for all $m \ge 1$ and $u \ge 7$, the block lengths $\beta^{(m)}(u)$ of the
$m$th order Gijswijt sequence $A^{(m)}$ satisfy $\beta^{(m)}(u) / (m+1)^{u-1} < M_u$.

## Sources

- Levi van de Pol, *The Growth Rate of Gijswijt's Sequence*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.6, Lemma 20 (`jis-2025-25.4.6-lem-20`).

articles.title: Bounds on the block lengths of order $m+1$
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and $u \ge 2$. Write
$\beta^{(m+1)}(u)$ for the length of the block $B_u^{(m+1)}$ of the $(m+1)$th order Gijswijt
