in $w$ and each $s_i$ is a (possibly empty) string without $0$. The result is the list of strings
$a s_0, s_1, \dots, s_m$, in this order, where $a s_0$ is the concatenation of $a$ and $s_0$.

articles.title: Splitting a ternary string at its zeros
articles.statement:
For a string $w$ over $\{0, 1, 2\}$, the list of
the segments of $w$ obtained by cutting at every $0$: the part before the first $0$, the parts
between consecutive $0$s and the part after the last $0$, in order and including empty parts.
A string with $m$ zeros gives $m + 1$ segments; the empty string gives one empty segment.

articles.title: Admissible ternary strings
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$ and $n$, the strings $w$ over
$\{0, 1, 2\}$ of length $n - 1$ (truncated subtraction, so length $0$ when $n = 0$) such that
every segment of $w$ obtained by cutting at its zeros (before the first zero, between
consecutive zeros and after the last zero, empty segments included) either consists only of
$1$s and has length at least $b - 1$, or consists only of $2$s and has length at least $b$.
In particular an empty segment is allowed exactly when $b \le 1$.

This is the segment form of the conditions in Theorem 2 of Hopkins and Wang (no $12$ or $21$
subwords, run-length bounds, and separation of successive zeros).

articles.title: Identity for $t(n) + t(n-2)$ when $n \ge 3$ and $n \equiv 2 \pmod 3$
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be the
tribonacci numbers with $t(0) = 1$, $t(1) = 0$, $t(2) = 1$ and
$t(n) = t(n-1) + t(n-2) + t(n-3)$ for $n \ge 3$, extended by $t(n) = 0$ for $n < 0$. For every
natural number $k \ge 1$, with $n = 3k + 2$,

$$t(n) + t(n-2) = 2 + 2 \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} t(n-3i-1).$$

## Sources

- Brian Hopkins and Hua Wang, "Allowing or Prohibiting Two Consecutive Colors in `n`-Color Compositions", Theorem 9.

articles.title: Identity for $t(n) + t(n-2)$ when $n \ge 3$ and $n \equiv 0, 1 \pmod 3$
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be the
tribonacci numbers with $t(0) = 1$, $t(1) = 0$, $t(2) = 1$ and
$t(n) = t(n-1) + t(n-2) + t(n-3)$ for $n \ge 3$, extended by $t(n) = 0$ for $n < 0$. For every
natural number $k \ge 1$, both $n = 3k$ and $n = 3k + 1$ satisfy

$$t(n) + t(n-2) = 2 \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} t(n-3i-1).$$

## Sources

- Brian Hopkins and Hua Wang, "Allowing or Prohibiting Two Consecutive Colors in `n`-Color Compositions", Theorem 9.

articles.title: Tribonacci numbers from $t(n-1)$ and alternate earlier terms
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be the tribonacci
numbers with $t(0) = 1$, $t(1) = 0$, $t(2) = 1$ and $t(n) = t(n-1) + t(n-2) + t(n-3)$ for
$n \ge 3$, extended by $t(n) = 0$ for $n < 0$. For every integer $n \ge 3$,

$$t(n) = t(n-1) + 1 + 2 \sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 1} t(n-2i-1).$$

## Sources

- Brian Hopkins and Hua Wang, "Allowing or Prohibiting Two Consecutive Colors in `n`-Color Compositions", Proposition 7.

articles.title: Tribonacci numbers from $t(n-2)$ and a partial sum
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be the tribonacci numbers
with $t(0) = 1$, $t(1) = 0$, $t(2) = 1$ and $t(n) = t(n-1) + t(n-2) + t(n-3)$ for $n \ge 3$,
extended by $t(n) = 0$ for $n < 0$. For every integer $n \ge 3$,

$$t(n) = t(n-2) + 2 \sum_{i=3}^{n} t(n-i).$$

## Sources

- Brian Hopkins and Hua Wang, "Allowing or Prohibiting Two Consecutive Colors in `n`-Color Compositions", Proposition 6.

articles.title: Tribonacci numbers with initial values $1, 0, 1$
articles.statement:
The sequence
$t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ with $t(0) = 1$, $t(1) = 0$, $t(2) = 1$ and
$t(n) = t(n-1) + t(n-2) + t(n-3)$ for $n \ge 3$.

articles.title: Tribonacci partial-sum identity for $t(3k+1)$
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be the tribonacci numbers with
$t(0) = 1$, $t(1) = 0$, $t(2) = 1$ and $t(n) = t(n-1) + t(n-2) + t(n-3)$ for $n \ge 3$,
extended by $t(n) = 0$ for $n < 0$. For every natural number $k$,

$$t(3k+1) = -1 + \sum_{i=0}^{k} \bigl(t(3k-3i) + t(3k-3i-1)\bigr).$$

## Sources

- Brian Hopkins and Hua Wang, "Allowing or Prohibiting Two Consecutive Colors in `n`-Color Compositions", Theorem 8.

articles.title: Tribonacci partial-sum identity for $t(3k+2)$
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be the tribonacci numbers with
$t(0) = 1$, $t(1) = 0$, $t(2) = 1$ and $t(n) = t(n-1) + t(n-2) + t(n-3)$ for $n \ge 3$,
extended by $t(n) = 0$ for $n < 0$. For every natural number $k$,

$$t(3k+2) = \sum_{i=0}^{k} \bigl(t(3k-3i+1) + t(3k-3i)\bigr).$$

## Sources

- Brian Hopkins and Hua Wang, "Allowing or Prohibiting Two Consecutive Colors in `n`-Color Compositions", Theorem 8.

articles.title: Tribonacci partial-sum identity for $t(3k)$
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be the tribonacci numbers with
$t(0) = 1$, $t(1) = 0$, $t(2) = 1$ and $t(n) = t(n-1) + t(n-2) + t(n-3)$ for $n \ge 3$,
extended by $t(n) = 0$ for $n < 0$. For every natural number $k$,

$$t(3k) = 1 + \sum_{i=0}^{k} \bigl(t(3k-3i-1) + t(3k-3i-2)\bigr).$$

## Sources

- Brian Hopkins and Hua Wang, "Allowing or Prohibiting Two Consecutive Colors in `n`-Color Compositions", Theorem 8.

articles.title: Hopkins–Wang tribonacci numbers on the integers
articles.statement:
Let $t(0) = 1$, $t(1) = 0$,
$t(2) = 1$ and $t(n) = t(n-1) + t(n-2) + t(n-3)$ for natural numbers $n \ge 3$. This
extends $t$ to an integer-valued function on all integers by setting $t(n) = 0$ for
$n < 0$.

articles.title: Compositions with two types of part 1 and no equal adjacent 1s
articles.statement:
For a natural
number $n$, $C^*_{1,2}(n)$ is the set of compositions of $n$ whose parts are $1_1$, $1_2$
(two types of part of size $1$) and $2$, such that no two adjacent parts are parts $1$ of
the same type.

A composition is encoded as a list over the symbols $0$, $1$, $2$, where $0$ and $1$ stand
for $1_1$ and $1_2$ and the symbol $2$ stands for the part $2$.

articles.title: Restricted weighted composition count
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $S$ a finite set
of natural numbers and $f \colon \mathbb{N} \to R$ a weight function. For natural numbers $n$
and $k$, $d_{S,f}(n, k)$ is the sum, over all $k$-tuples $(\pi_1, \dots, \pi_k)$ of natural
numbers with every $\pi_i \in S$ and $\pi_1 + \dots + \pi_k = n$, of the weight
$f(\pi_1) \cdots f(\pi_k)$.

Since every part of a composition of $n$ is at most $n$, the tuples range over the finite set
of maps from $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$ to $\{0, \dots, n\}$.

articles.title: Vandermonde convolution for restricted weighted compositions
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative
ring, $S$ a finite set of natural numbers and $f \colon \mathbb{N} \to R$ a weight function, and
write $d_{S,f}(n, k)$ for the weighted count of $S$-restricted $f$-weighted compositions of $n$
with $k$ parts. Then for all natural numbers $n$, $k$ and $j$ with $j \le k$,

$$d_{S,f}(n, k) = \sum_{m=0}^{n} d_{S,f}(m, j) \, d_{S,f}(n - m, k - j).$$

articles.title: Shade of the composition 4
articles.statement:
The one-part composition $4$ has shade $6$: its
bargraph has $6$ shaded cells.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher, Arnold Knopfmacher and Michael Mays, *Shade in Compositions of Integers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.6, Figure 5.

articles.title: The total shade bounds the shade of each composition
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$
and every composition $x$ of $n$, the shade of $x$ is at most the total shade $c(n)$ of the
compositions of $n$.

For example, since the composition $4$ has shade $6$, this gives $c(4) \ge 6$.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher, Arnold Knopfmacher and Michael Mays, *Shade in Compositions of Integers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.6, Section 2.

articles.title: Shade of the composition 1 + 3
articles.statement:
The composition $1 + 3$ has shade $3$: its bargraph
has $3$ shaded cells.

All three shaded cells lie to the right of the bargraph.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher, Arnold Knopfmacher and Michael Mays, *Shade in Compositions of Integers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.6, Figure 5.

articles.title: Shade of a composition
articles.statement:
Let $x = (x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_{k-1})$ be a finite list of
natural numbers (the parts of a composition), drawn as a bargraph whose column $c$ has height
$x_c$, with $x_c = 0$ for $c \ge k$. A cell $(c, h)$ with column $c \ge 0$ and height $h \ge 1$
is shaded when $h > x_c$ and $x_j \ge h + (c - j)$ for some column $j < c$. The shade of $x$
is the number of shaded cells.

Every shaded cell satisfies $c < k + s$ and $h \le s$, where $s = x_0 + \cdots + x_{k-1}$,
so the number of shaded cells is finite.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher, Arnold Knopfmacher and Michael Mays, *Shade in Compositions of Integers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.6, Section 1.

articles.title: Generating function for the total shade of compositions
articles.statement:
Let $c(n)$ be the total
shade of the compositions of $n$, and let $q$ be a real number with $0 < q < 1/4$. For natural
numbers $i_2, i_3, s_1, s_3$ put

$$A_{i_2, i_3, s_1, s_3} = (s_1 - s_3) \prod_{i_3 < i < i_2} (1 - q^{s_1 - i + 1}) +
\sum_{i_3 < j < i_2} \Big( \prod_{i_3 < i < i_2, i \ne j} (1 - q^{s_1 - i + 1}) \Big)
\frac{j(q - 1) + q^{s_1 + 1 - j} + s_1 - q(1 + s_1)}{1 - q},$$



$$B_{i_2} = 1 + \sum_{m \ge 1} q^{-i_2 m - m(m - 1)/2} (1 - q)^{-m} q^{m(1 + 2 i_2 + m)/2},$$

and for natural numbers $i, j, s$ put

$$E_{i, j, s} = -1 - q^{1 - i - j + s} (-2 + i + j - s) + q^{2 - i - j + s} (-1 + i + j - s).$$

Let

$$D_L(q) = \sum_{i_1 \ge 1} \sum_{s_1 \ge i_1 + 2} \Big( \frac{1}{1 - q} \Big)^{i_1 - 2}
\Big( \prod_{r=1}^{i_1 - 1} (1 - q^{s_1 - r}) \Big) q^{i_1 (i_1 - 1)/2 - i_1 s_1}
\sum_{i_2 = i_1 + 2}^{s_1 + 1} \sum_{s_2 \ge s_1 + 1} \sum_{i_3 = i_1 + 1}^{i_2 - 1}
\sum_{s_3 = i_3}^{s_1 - 1} q^{i_3 s_1 + s_2 + s_3 - (i_3 + i_3^2)/2}
\Big( \frac{1}{1 - q} \Big)^{i_2 - i_3} A_{i_2, i_3, s_1, s_3} B_{i_2},$$



$$D_R(q) = \sum_{i \ge 1} \sum_{s \ge i} \Big( \prod_{r=1}^{i-1} (1 - q^{s - r}) \Big)
\frac{q^s}{(1 - q)^{i-1}} \Big( \binom{s - i + 1}{2} \sum_{m=0}^{s-1} \frac{q^m}{(1 - q)^m}
\prod_{r=1}^{m} (1 - q^{s + 1 - i - r}) +
\frac{1}{(1 - q)^2} \sum_{m=1}^{s-1} \sum_{j=1}^{m} \frac{q^m}{(1 - q)^{m-1}}
\Big( \prod_{1 \le r \le m, r \ne j} (1 - q^{s + 1 - i - r}) \Big) E_{i, j, s} \Big).$$

Then

$$\sum_{n \ge 0} c(n) q^n = D_L(q) + D_R(q).$$

Empty sums are $0$ and empty products are $1$; all exponents are integers and may be
negative. For $0 < q < 1/4$ all these series converge absolutely.

This is Theorem 1 of the paper with two corrected readings. In the paper's display for
$D_L(q)$ the outer double sum over $i_1, s_1$ (and the left-hand side $L(x, q, u)$) is
duplicated, a typesetting slip; reading it once reproduces the printed expansion
$2q^6 + 6q^7 + 24q^8 + \cdots$. In the display for $D_R(q)$ the product in the double sum
over $m, j$ runs over $r \ne j$, as in the paper's display (R) from which it is obtained by
setting $x = 1$; with the product over all $r$ as printed, the coefficient of $q^4$ in
$D_R(q)$ is $14$ instead of the printed $13$, and $D_L + D_R$ no longer matches the total
shade.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher, Arnold Knopfmacher and Michael Mays, *Shade in Compositions of Integers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.6, Theorem 1 (`jis-2024-24.5.6-thm-1`).

articles.title: Total shade of the compositions of zero
articles.statement:
The total shade $c(0)$ of the compositions
of $0$ is zero: $c(0) = 0$.

The only composition of $0$ is the empty one, whose bargraph has no shaded cells.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher, Arnold Knopfmacher and Michael Mays, *Shade in Compositions of Integers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.6, Section 2.

articles.title: Total shade of compositions
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the total shade $c(n)$ is the
sum of the shades of all compositions of $n$.

## Sources

- Aubrey Blecher, Arnold Knopfmacher and Michael Mays, *Shade in Compositions of Integers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.6, Section 2.

articles.title: Expected symmetric peaks and valleys in geometric words
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 2$, let
$0 < p < 1$ and $q = 1 - p$, and let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent random variables, each
geometric on $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ with $\Pr(X_i = k) = q^k p$, and consider the word
$X_1 X_2 \cdots X_n$. The expected number of its symmetric peaks is
$p^2 q (n - 2)/(1 - q^3)$, the expected number of its symmetric valleys is
$p^2 \left(\frac{1}{1 - q^2} - \frac{1}{1 - q^3}\right)(n - 2)$, the expected sum of the
heights of its symmetric peaks is $p q (n - 2)/(1 - q^3)$, and the expected sum of the depths
of its symmetric valleys is $q \left(\frac{p}{1 - q^3} - \frac{1}{(1 + q)^2}\right)(n - 2)$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Trivariate generating function for symmetric peaks in compositions
articles.statement:
For a composition
$c$ write $\ell(c)$ for its number of parts, $\mathrm{sp}(c)$ for the number of symmetric peaks
and $\mathrm{hsp}(c)$ for the symmetric peak height sum of its sequence of parts. In the ring
$\mathbb{Z}[y, q, h][[x]]$ of formal power series in $x$ whose coefficients are polynomials in
$y, q, h$ with integer coefficients,

$$
\sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{c \models n} x^n y^{\ell(c)} q^{\mathrm{sp}(c)} h^{\mathrm{hsp}(c)} =
\frac{1}{1 - \sum_{a \ge 1} \frac{x^a y}{1 - y^2 x^{2a+1} \left(\frac{qh}{1 - hx} -
\frac{1}{1 - x}\right)}},
$$

where $c \models n$ ranges over the compositions of $n$ and
$\frac{qh}{1 - hx} - \frac{1}{1 - x}$ stands for the series $\sum_{j \ge 0} (q h^{j+1} - 1) x^j$.
Precisely: for every $n \ge 0$ the coefficients of $x^n$ on the two sides agree when the sum
over $a$ is restricted to $1 \le a \le n$ (the terms with $a > n$ do not contribute to them).

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Number of symmetric peaks
articles.statement:
For a finite word $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_m$ of natural
numbers, a symmetric peak is a factor $w_i w_{i+1} w_{i+2}$ of three consecutive letters with
$w_i = w_{i+2} < w_{i+1}$. The number of symmetric peaks of $w$ is the number of indices $i$
with $1 \le i \le m - 2$ at which $w$ has a symmetric peak (overlapping peaks all count); it
is $0$ when $m < 3$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Section 1 (symmetric peaks).

articles.title: Bivariate generating function of the total symmetric peak height over compositions
articles.statement:
For $n, k \ge 0$ let $\mathrm{hsp}(n, k)$ be the sum, over all compositions $c$ of $n$ with
exactly $k$ parts, of the symmetric peak height sum of the sequence of parts of $c$. Then in
the ring $\mathbb{Z}[y][[x]]$ of formal power series in $x$ over $\mathbb{Z}[y]$,

$$
\left(\sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{k \ge 0} \mathrm{hsp}(n, k)\, y^k x^n\right)
(1 - x^3)(1 - x - yx)^2 = y^3 x^4,
$$

that is, $\sum_{n, k \ge 0} \mathrm{hsp}(n, k)\, x^n y^k = y^3 x^4 / ((1 - x^3)(1 - x - yx)^2)$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Closed form for the total symmetric peak height over compositions
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 0$ let
$\mathrm{hsp}(n)$ be the sum, over all compositions $c$ of $n$, of the symmetric peak height
sum of the sequence of parts of $c$, and let $\omega_\pm = 1 \pm i\sqrt{3}$. Then for every
$n \ge 0$, as complex numbers,

$$
\mathrm{hsp}(n) = \frac{2^n}{2} \cdot \frac{7n - 24}{49} +
\frac{(-33 - 15 i \sqrt{3})(-2)^n}{441\, \omega_+^{n+1}} +
\frac{(-33 + 15 i \sqrt{3})(-2)^n}{441\, \omega_-^{n+1}} + \frac{1}{3}.
$$

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Corollary 1, (6).

articles.title: Generating function of the total symmetric peak height over compositions
articles.statement:
For
$n \ge 0$ let $\mathrm{hsp}(n)$ be the sum, over all compositions $c$ of $n$, of the symmetric
peak height sum of the sequence of parts of $c$. Then in $\mathbb{Z}[[x]]$

$$
\left(\sum_{n \ge 0} \mathrm{hsp}(n)\, x^n\right)(1 - 2x)^2 (1 - x^3) = x^4,
$$

that is, $\sum_{n \ge 0} \mathrm{hsp}(n)\, x^n = x^4 / ((1 - 2x)^2 (1 - x^3))$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Lemma 1, (5).

articles.title: Total symmetric peak height over compositions with a fixed number of parts
articles.statement:
For
$n, k \ge 0$ let $\mathrm{hsp}(n, k)$ be the sum, over all compositions $c$ of $n$ with exactly
$k$ parts, of the symmetric peak height sum of the sequence of parts of $c$. If $k > 3$, then
for every $n \ge 0$

$$
\mathrm{hsp}(n, k) = (k - 2) \sum_{m=2}^{n-k+1} \sum_{b=1}^{\min(m-1,\, t_m)}
\binom{n - 2b - m - 1}{k - 4} (m - b),
\qquad t_m = \left\lfloor \frac{n - m - k + 3}{2} \right\rfloor,
$$

where an empty sum is $0$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Theorem 2(a).

articles.title: Symmetric peak examples among the compositions of 5
articles.statement:
The symmetric peak height sums of
the words $1\,3\,1$, $1\,2\,1\,1$, $1\,1\,2\,1$ and $1\,1\,1\,1\,1$ are $2$, $1$, $1$ and $0$
respectively, and the word $1\,3\,1$ has exactly one symmetric peak.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, example after Corollary 1.

articles.title: Sum of the heights of symmetric peaks
articles.statement:
For a finite word $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_m$ of
natural numbers, a symmetric peak is a factor $w_i w_{i+1} w_{i+2}$ of three consecutive
letters with $w_i = w_{i+2} < w_{i+1}$, and its height is $w_{i+1} - w_i$. The symmetric peak
height sum of $w$ is the sum of the heights of the symmetric peaks of $w$ over all indices $i$
with $1 \le i \le m - 2$ at which one occurs; it is $0$ when $m < 3$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Section 1 (heights of symmetric peaks).

articles.title: Trivariate generating function for symmetric valleys in compositions
articles.statement:
For a composition
$c$ write $\ell(c)$ for its number of parts, $\mathrm{sv}(c)$ for the number of symmetric
valleys and $\mathrm{dsv}(c)$ for the symmetric valley depth sum of its sequence of parts. In
the ring $\mathbb{Z}[y, p, d][[x]]$ of formal power series in $x$ whose coefficients are
polynomials in $y, p, d$ with integer coefficients,

$$
\sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{c \models n} x^n y^{\ell(c)} p^{\mathrm{sv}(c)} d^{\mathrm{dsv}(c)} =
\frac{1}{1 - \sum_{a \ge 1} \frac{x^a y}{1 - y^2 x^{a+1}
\sum_{b=1}^{a-1} (p d^{a-b} - 1) x^{b-1}}},
$$

where $c \models n$ ranges over the compositions of $n$. Precisely: for every $n \ge 0$ the
coefficients of $x^n$ on the two sides agree when the sum over $a$ is restricted to
$1 \le a \le n$ (the terms with $a > n$ do not contribute to them). The inner sum equals
$p(x^{a-1} - d^{a-1})/(x/d - 1) - (x^{a-1} - 1)/(x - 1)$.

Corrected reading: the paper prints $(p x^{a-1} - d^{a-1})/(x/d - 1)$, with $p$ on the first
term only; that is false (at $n = 3$ it gives the composition $111$ a symmetric valley of depth
$0$). The corrected term $p(x^{a-1} - d^{a-1})/(x/d - 1)$ is the penultimate line of the
paper's proof, $x^a y^2 p d^a ((x/d)^a - x/d)/(x/d - 1)$, and agrees with the paper's
specialization $d = 1$, $(x^{a-1} - 1)(p - 1)/(x - 1)$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Number of symmetric valleys of a word
articles.statement:
For a word $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_\ell$ of natural
numbers, a symmetric valley is a position $i$ with $1 < i < \ell$ such that $w_{i-1} = w_{i+1}$
and $w_i < w_{i-1}$, that is, a factor $a\,b\,a$ with $b < a$. The symmetric valley count of $w$
is the number of such positions; in particular it is $0$ when $\ell < 3$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Section 1 (symmetric valleys).

articles.title: Closed form for the total depth of symmetric valleys over compositions
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 0$,
let $\operatorname{dsv}(n)$ be the sum, over all compositions $c$ of $n$, of the total depth of
the symmetric valleys of the sequence of parts of $c$, and write $\omega_\pm = 1 \pm i\sqrt{3}$.
Then, as complex numbers,

$$\operatorname{dsv}(n) = \frac{(-6n+7)(-1)^n}{108} + \frac{2^n(21n-79)}{1323} +
\frac{(-33-15\sqrt{3}\,i)(-2)^n}{441\,\omega_+^{n+1}} +
\frac{(-33+15\sqrt{3}\,i)(-2)^n}{441\,\omega_-^{n+1}} + \frac{1}{12}.$$

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Corollary 2, (12).

articles.title: Total depth of symmetric valleys over compositions with $k > 3$ parts
articles.statement:
For natural
numbers $n$ and $k$ with $k > 3$, the sum, over all compositions $c$ of $n$ with exactly $k$
parts, of the total depth of the symmetric valleys of the sequence of parts of $c$ equals

$$(k-2) \sum_{m=1}^{\lfloor (n-k+1)/3 \rfloor} \sum_{b=m+1}^{\lfloor (n-m-(k-3))/2 \rfloor}
\binom{n-2b-m-1}{k-4}(b-m),$$

where a difference of natural numbers that would be negative is read as $0$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Theorem 4(a).

articles.title: Total depth of symmetric valleys over compositions with three parts
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $n$, the sum, over all compositions $c$ of $n$ with exactly three parts, of the total
depth of the symmetric valleys of the sequence of parts of $c$ equals
$\sum_{m=1}^{\lfloor (n-2)/3 \rfloor} d_m$, where $d_m = (n-3m)/2$ if $n - m$ is even and
$d_m = 0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Theorem 4(b).

articles.title: Generating function for the total depth of symmetric valleys over compositions
articles.statement:
For
$n \ge 0$, let $\operatorname{dsv}(n)$ be the sum, over all compositions $c$ of $n$, of the total
depth of the symmetric valleys of the sequence of parts of $c$. Then in the ring $\mathbb{Z}[[x]]$
of formal power series,

$$\Big(\sum_{n \ge 0} \operatorname{dsv}(n)\, x^n\Big)(1-2x)^2(1-x^3)(1-x^2)^2 = x^5 - 2x^6 + x^7,$$

that is, $\sum_{n \ge 0} \operatorname{dsv}(n)\, x^n$ equals
$(x^5 - 2x^6 + x^7)/((1-2x)^2(1-x^3)(1-x^2)^2)$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Lemma 2, (11).

articles.title: Symmetric valleys in three compositions of eight
articles.statement:
The word $2\,1\,2\,1\,2$ has two
symmetric valleys and total symmetric valley depth $2$, the word $3\,1\,3\,1$ has total symmetric
valley depth $2$, and the word $3\,2\,3$ has total symmetric valley depth $1$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, example after Corollary 2.

articles.title: Total depth of the symmetric valleys of a word
articles.statement:
For a word $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_\ell$ of
natural numbers, a symmetric valley is a position $i$ with $1 < i < \ell$ such that
$w_{i-1} = w_{i+1}$ and $w_i < w_{i-1}$; its depth is $w_{i-1} - w_i$. The symmetric valley depth
sum of $w$ is the sum of the depths of all its symmetric valleys; in particular it is $0$ when
$\ell < 3$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *The Heights of Symmetric Peaks and the Depths of Symmetric Valleys over Compositions of an Integer*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A65, Section 1 (depths of symmetric valleys).

articles.title: Bijection removing $k$ copies of a part from partitions
articles.statement:
Removing `k` copies of the positive part `v` gives a bijection from partitions of `E`
containing at least `k` copies of `v` to partitions of `E - k * v`.

articles.title: Exponential upper bound for the partition function
articles.statement:
The number of integer partitions of `n` is at most
`exp (π * sqrt (2 / 3) * sqrt n)`.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the partition function
articles.statement: The number of integer partitions is monotone in the integer being partitioned.

articles.title: Exponential lower bound for the partition function
articles.statement:
The number of partitions of `n` is at least
`H * exp (pi * sqrt (2 / 3) * sqrt n) / n ^ B` for some `H > 0` and natural `B`, when `n ≥ 1`.

articles.title: Logarithmic bounds for the partition function
articles.statement:
There are constants `B` and `C` such that the base-two logarithm of the number of integer
partitions of `n` differs from its leading square-root term by at most a logarithmic lower-order
term below and a constant above.

articles.title: Sum-of-parts recurrence for the partition function
articles.statement:
A recurrence obtained by summing all parts of all partitions of `E`, first by partition
and then by part value and multiplicity threshold.

articles.title: Linear lower bound for the partition function
articles.statement: The number of partitions of `n` is at least `(n + 1) / 2`.

articles.title: The Landau function is attained
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, some partition of $n$
has least common multiple of its parts equal to the Landau function at $n$.

articles.title: Landau's function
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, Landau's function at $n$ is the maximum, over
all partitions $p$ of $n$, of the least common multiple of the parts of $p$.

articles.title: The Landau function bounds the LCM of the parts
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and every
partition $p$ of $n$, the least common multiple of the parts of $p$ is at most the Landau function
at $n$.

articles.title: Least common multiple of the parts of a partition
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a
partition $p$ of $n$, this is the least common multiple of the parts of $p$, taken with
the convention that it equals $1$ when $p$ has no parts.

articles.title: Three-colored distinct-part partitions of $1$
articles.statement:
The number $D_3(1)$ of partitions of $1$ into
parts of three colors, with the parts of each color distinct, equals $3$: the single part $1$
takes one of the three colors.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Definition of `D_3(n)`.

articles.title: Three-colored distinct-part partitions of $2$
articles.statement:
The number $D_3(2)$ of partitions of $2$ into
parts of three colors, with the parts of each color distinct, equals $6$: the single part $2$ in
one of three colors, or two parts $1$ in two different colors.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Definition of `D_3(n)`.

articles.title: Three-colored distinct-part partitions of $0$
articles.statement:
The number $D_3(0)$ of partitions of $0$ into
parts of three colors, with the parts of each color distinct, equals $1$: the empty partition is
the only one.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Definition of `D_3(n)`.

articles.title: Three-colored distinct-part partitions
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $D_3(n)$ is the number of
triples $(A, B, C)$ of subsets of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ such that the sum of the elements of $A$, the
sum of the elements of $B$ and the sum of the elements of $C$ add up to $n$. Here $A$, $B$, $C$
are the parts of the three colors of a partition of $n$ whose parts of each color are distinct.

A size may occur in several colors but at most once in each, as in the product
$\prod_{m \ge 1} (1 + q^m)^3$.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Definition of `D_3(n)`.

articles.title: Eta-quotient congruence for sums of overpartition minimal excludants
articles.statement:
Let $r \ge 1$ and
$k \ge 1$ be integers, and for $n \ge 0$ let $\sigma_r \overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n)$ be the sum, over
all overpartitions of $n$, of the least positive integer occurring fewer than $r$ times among the
non-overlined parts. Then there are integers $c_0, c_1, c_2, \dots$ such that for every complex $q$
with $|q| < 1$, writing $f_d = (q^d; q^d)_\infty = \prod_{m \ge 1} (1 - q^{dm})$,

$$q^{3r} \frac{f_{48} f_{24r}^{2^k - 1}}{f_{24}^2 f_{48r}^{2^{k-1} - 2}} = \sum_{j \ge 0} c_j q^j,$$

and for every $j \ge 0$ we have $c_j \equiv \sigma_r \overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n) \pmod{2^k}$ when
$j = 24n + 3r$ with $n \ge 0$, and $c_j \equiv 0 \pmod{2^k}$ otherwise.

The exponent $2^{k-1} - 2$ is an integer; at $k = 1$ it equals $-1$, so $f_{48r}$ then appears
in the numerator.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Proposition 16.

articles.title: Ingham's Tauberian theorem
articles.statement:
Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be nonnegative and weakly
increasing, let $A : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ be a function, and let $\alpha$, $\beta$, $C$
be real numbers with $C > 0$. Suppose that for every complex $q$ with $|q| < 1$ the series
$\sum_{n \ge 0} a(n) q^n$ is summable with sum $A(q)$, and that for every complex $q$ with
$|q| > 1$ it is not summable. Suppose also that $A(e^{-t}) \sim \alpha t^\beta e^{C/t}$ as
$t \to 0^+$ through positive reals, and that for every $\Delta > 0$,
$A(e^{-z}) = O(|z|^\beta e^{C/|z|})$ as $z \to 0$ within the cone
$\{z \in \mathbb{C} : \mathrm{Re}\, z > 0,\ |\mathrm{Im}\, z| \le \Delta\, \mathrm{Re}\, z\}$.
Then, as $n \to \infty$,

$$a(n) \sim \frac{\alpha}{2\sqrt{\pi}} C^{(2\beta + 1)/4} n^{-(2\beta + 3)/4} e^{2\sqrt{Cn}}.$$

Nothing is assumed about the series on the circle $|q| = 1$, since radius of convergence one
permits either behavior there.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Proposition 9.

articles.title: Minimal excludant of an overpartition with a multiplicity bound
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $r \ge 1$
and $n$ and an overpartition $O$ of $n$, $\overline{\mathrm{mex}}_r(O)$ is the least positive
integer $k$ that occurs fewer than $r$ times among the non-overlined parts of $O$. Such a $k$
exists, since $n + 1$ is not a part of $O$. For $r = 0$, which the paper does not use, the value
is $0$ by convention.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Definition of `mex̄_r`.

articles.title: Number of non-overlined copies of a part size
articles.statement:
For an overpartition $O$ of $n$ and a natural
number $a$, the number of non-overlined parts of size $a$ in $O$ is the multiplicity of $a$ in the
underlying partition of $O$, minus $1$ if $a$ is overlined in $O$ and minus $0$ otherwise.

This matches the convention that only the first occurrence of a part size may be overlined: an
overpartition records each overlined size once.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Definition of `mex̄_r`.

articles.title: The number of overpartitions of zero
articles.statement:
The number $\overline{p}(0)$ of overpartitions of
$0$ equals $1$: the empty overpartition is the only one.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Section 1 (`p̄(0) = 1`).

articles.title: Number of overpartitions
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $\overline{p}(n)$ is the number of
overpartitions of $n$, that is, of pairs consisting of a partition $p$ of $n$ and a set of
overlined part sizes, each of which occurs as a part of $p$. For example, $\overline{p}(3) = 8$.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Section 1.

articles.title: Asymptotic formula for the overpartition mex sum
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n)$ be
the sum, over all overpartitions $\pi$ of $n$, of $\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(\pi)$, the least
positive integer that does not occur among the non-overlined parts of $\pi$. Then
$\sigma\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n) \sim e^{\pi\sqrt{n}} / (8 n^{3/4})$ as $n \to \infty$, that is,
the ratio of the two sides tends to $1$.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Theorem 3.

articles.title: The overpartition mex sum counts three-colored distinct-part partitions
articles.statement:
For an
overpartition $\pi$, let $\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(\pi)$ be the least positive integer that does
not occur among the non-overlined parts of $\pi$, and let $\sigma\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n)$ be
the sum of $\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(\pi)$ over all overpartitions $\pi$ of $n$. For every
positive integer $n$, $\sigma\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n) = D_3(n)$, the number of partitions of
$n$ into distinct parts in three colors: the number of triples $(A, B, C)$ of subsets of
$\{1, \dots, n\}$ whose three element sums add up to $n$.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Theorem 2.

articles.title: The r-mex sum of overpartitions as a sum of overpartition counts
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $r$ be
natural numbers with $r \ge 1$, let $\overline{p}(m)$ be the number of overpartitions of $m$, let
$T_k = k(k+1)/2$ be the $k$-th triangular number, and let $\sigma_r\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n)$ be
the sum over all overpartitions $\pi$ of $n$ of $\overline{\mathrm{mex}}_r(\pi)$, the least
positive integer occurring fewer than $r$ times among the non-overlined parts of $\pi$. Then

$$\sigma_r\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n) = \sum_{k \ge 0,\; rT_k \le n} \overline{p}(n - rT_k).$$

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Proposition 10.

articles.title: Generating function of the overpartition r-mex sums
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a positive integer and $q$
a complex number with $|q| < 1$. Write $(a;q)_\infty = \prod_{j \ge 0} (1 - a q^j)$, and let
$\sigma_r\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n)$ be the sum over all overpartitions $\pi$ of $n$ of
$\overline{\mathrm{mex}}_r(\pi)$, the least positive integer occurring fewer than $r$ times among
the non-overlined parts of $\pi$. Then

$$
\sum_{n \ge 0} \sigma_r\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n)\, q^n =
\frac{(-q;q)_\infty\,(q^{2r};q^{2r})_\infty}{(q;q)_\infty\,(q^r;q^{2r})_\infty}.
$$

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Parity of the overpartition mex sum
articles.statement:
For an overpartition $\pi$, let
$\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(\pi)$ be the least positive integer that does not occur among the
non-overlined parts of $\pi$, and let $\sigma\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n)$ be the sum of
$\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(\pi)$ over all overpartitions $\pi$ of $n$. For every positive integer
$n$, $\sigma\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n)$ is odd if $n = j(j+1)/2$ is a triangular number for some
natural number $j$, and even otherwise.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Density of overpartition r-mex sums divisible by powers of two
articles.statement:
Let $m$, $e$ and $k$ be
natural numbers with $k \ge 1$, let $r = 2^m 3^e$, and let
$\sigma_r\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n)$ be the sum over all overpartitions $\pi$ of $n$ of
$\overline{\mathrm{mex}}_r(\pi)$, the least positive integer occurring fewer than $r$ times among
the non-overlined parts of $\pi$. Then the natural numbers $n$ with
$2^k \mid \sigma_r\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n)$ have natural density $1$: the number of such $n$
with $n \le X$, divided by $X$, tends to $1$ as $X \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Theorem 8.

articles.title: Asymptotic formula for the overpartition r-mex sums
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a positive integer and let
$\sigma_r\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n)$ be the sum over all overpartitions $\pi$ of $n$ of
$\overline{\mathrm{mex}}_r(\pi)$, the least positive integer occurring fewer than $r$ times among
the non-overlined parts of $\pi$. Then
$\sigma_r\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n) \sim e^{\pi\sqrt{n}} / (8 \sqrt{r}\, n^{3/4})$ as
$n \to \infty$, that is, the ratio of the two sides tends to $1$.

The denominator $8\sqrt{r}$ follows the published version of the paper; arXiv v1 prints $8r$.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Sums of minimal excludants over overpartitions
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $r$ and $n$,
$\sigma_r\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n)$ is the sum, over all overpartitions $\pi$ of $n$, of
$\overline{\mathrm{mex}}_r(\pi)$, the least positive integer occurring fewer than $r$ times
among the non-overlined parts of $\pi$; for $r = 0$ the value $\overline{\mathrm{mex}}_0(\pi)$
is $0$ by convention, so $\sigma_0\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n) = 0$. We write
$\sigma\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n) = \sigma_1\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n)$.

By direct enumeration, $\sigma\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(n) = 1, 3, 6, 13, 24$ for $n = 0, \dots, 4$,
and $\sigma_2\overline{\mathrm{mex}}(2) = 5$.

## Sources

- Victor Manuel R. Aricheta, Judy Ann L. Donato, *A Minimal Excludant over Overpartitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.1, Definitions of `σmex̄` and `σ_r mex̄`.

articles.title: Permutations of $S_3$ with descent set $\{1\}$
articles.statement:
Exactly two permutations $\tau \in S_3$
have exactly one descent and major index $1$, that is, $\operatorname{des}(\tau) = 1$ and
$\operatorname{maj}(\tau) = 1$; equivalently, their descent set is $\{1\}$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Section 1.

articles.title: Position of the $k$th link of a multifold partition diamond
articles.statement:
For natural numbers
$d_1, \dots, d_M$ (the numbers of folds of the $M$ diamonds) and a natural number $k$, the
position of the $k$th link, counting positions from $0$, is
$L_k = \sum_{m=1}^{\min(k, M)} (d_m + 1)$. In particular $L_0 = 0$, and
$L_k = d_1 + \dots + d_M + M$ for every $k \ge M$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Figure 3 and Section 3.

articles.title: The set of link positions of a multifold partition diamond
articles.statement:
For natural numbers
$d_1, \dots, d_M$, the set of link positions is $\{L_0, L_1, \dots, L_M\}$, where
$L_k = \sum_{m=1}^{k} (d_m + 1)$ is the position of the $k$th link. These positions satisfy
$0 = L_0 < L_1 < \dots < L_M = c - 1$, where $c = d_1 + \dots + d_M + M + 1$ is the number of
parts.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Figure 3.

articles.title: Extending a part vector by zero
articles.statement:
Let $c = d_1 + \dots + d_M + M + 1$ be the number of
parts of the multifold partition diamond whose diamonds have $d_1, \dots, d_M$ folds, and let
$n$ be a natural number. A vector $(a_0, \dots, a_{c-1})$ with entries in $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$
is read as the function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that sends $p$ to $a_p$ for $p < c$ and to
$0$ for $p \ge c$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Section 2.

articles.title: Number of parts of a multifold partition diamond
articles.statement:
The multifold partition diamond whose
$M$ diamonds have $d_1, \dots, d_M$ folds has $c = d_1 + \dots + d_M + M + 1$ parts.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Figure 3 (`c = M(d + 1) + 1`).

articles.title: The first Euler–Mahonian polynomial is $1$
articles.statement:
For every commutative ring $R$ and all
$x, y \in R$, the Euler–Mahonian polynomial $E_1$ satisfies $E_1(x, y) = 1$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Section 1 (`F_1 = 1` in recursion (1)).

articles.title: Recursion for the Euler–Mahonian polynomials
articles.statement:
For every commutative ring $R$, every
natural number $d \ge 1$ and all $x, y \in R$, the Euler–Mahonian polynomials $E_d$ and
$E_{d+1}$ satisfy

$$(1 - y) E_{d+1}(x, y) = (1 - x y^{d+1}) E_d(x, y) - y (1 - x) E_d(xy, y).$$

Together with $E_1 = 1$, this says that the Euler–Mahonian polynomials are the
Dockery–Jameson–Sellers–Wilson polynomials $F_d$, defined by $F_1 = 1$ and
$F_d(q_0, w) = \bigl((1 - q_0 w^d) F_{d-1}(q_0, w) - w (1 - q_0) F_{d-1}(q_0 w, w)\bigr)/(1 - w)$
for $d \ge 2$: since $1 - w$ is a nonzerodivisor in $\mathbb{Z}[q_0, w]$, the recursion is
stated multiplied by $1 - w$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Theorem 1 with recursion (1).

articles.title: Euler–Mahonian polynomial $E_3$ at $(2, 3)$
articles.statement:
Over the integers, the Euler–Mahonian
polynomial $E_3$ takes the value $E_3(2, 3) = 157$.

This agrees with $E_3(x, y) = 1 + 2xy + 2xy^2 + x^2y^3$: the six permutations of $S_3$ have
$(\operatorname{des}, \operatorname{maj})$ equal to $(0, 0)$, $(1, 1)$, $(1, 1)$, $(1, 2)$,
$(1, 2)$ and $(2, 3)$. Only the value at $x = 2$, $y = 3$ is checked, not the polynomial
identity.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Section 1.

articles.title: Euler–Mahonian polynomial
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$ and elements $x, y$ of a commutative
ring, the Euler–Mahonian polynomial evaluated at $(x, y)$ is
$E_d(x, y) = \sum_{\tau \in S_d} x^{\operatorname{des}(\tau)} y^{\operatorname{maj}(\tau)}$,
where $\operatorname{des}(\tau)$ is the number of descents and $\operatorname{maj}(\tau)$ the
major index of the permutation $\tau$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Section 1.

articles.title: Multifold partition diamonds with given fold and link sums
articles.statement:
Let $d_1, \dots, d_M$ be
natural numbers, let $L_k = \sum_{m=1}^{k} (d_m + 1)$ for $0 \le k \le M$ be the link
positions, let $c = L_M + 1$, and let $i$ and $j$ be natural numbers. A function
$b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is a multifold partition diamond with fold sum $i$ and link sum
$j$ when the following hold: for every $k$ with $0 \le k < M$ and every $f$ with
$1 \le f \le d_{k+1}$, we have $b(L_k) \le b(L_k + f) \le b(L_{k+1})$; the sum of $b(p)$ over
the positions $p < c$ different from $L_0, \dots, L_M$ is $i$; and
$b(L_0) + \dots + b(L_M) = j$.

This models the paper's $P$-partitions (order-preserving maps to $\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$) of the
poset in which, for each $k < M$, the folds at positions $L_k + 1, \dots, L_k + d_{k+1}$ lie
above the link at $L_k$ and below the link at $L_{k+1}$. In particular, when every
$d_k \ge 1$, $b(0)$ is the smallest of $b(0), \dots, b(c - 1)$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Sections 2-3.

articles.title: Single-fold diamonds with fold sum 1 and link sum 1
articles.statement:
There is exactly one multifold
partition diamond of shape $(1)$ with fold sum $1$ and link sum $1$. Equivalently, there is exactly
one triple of nonnegative integers $b_0 \le b_1 \le b_2$ with $b_1 = 1$ and $b_0 + b_2 = 1$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, equation (2).

articles.title: Two-fold diamonds with fold sum 1 and link sum 2
articles.statement:
There are exactly two multifold
partition diamonds of shape $(2)$ with fold sum $1$ and link sum $2$. Equivalently, there are
exactly two quadruples $(b_0, b_1, b_2, b_3)$ of nonnegative integers with $b_0 \le b_f \le b_3$
for $f = 1, 2$, $b_1 + b_2 = 1$ and $b_0 + b_3 = 2$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, equation (2).

articles.title: Number of multifold partition diamonds
articles.statement:
Let $d_1, \dots, d_M$ be natural numbers. Put
$L_k = \sum_{m=1}^{k} (d_m + 1)$ for $0 \le k \le M$ and $c = L_M + 1$. A multifold partition
diamond of shape $(d_1, \dots, d_M)$ is a sequence $(b_0, \dots, b_{c-1})$ of nonnegative integers
such that $b_{L_{k-1}} \le b_{L_{k-1} + f} \le b_{L_k}$ for all $1 \le k \le M$ and
$1 \le f \le d_k$. The parts $b_{L_0}, \dots, b_{L_M}$ are its links and the other parts are its
folds; its link sum is $\sum_{k=0}^{M} b_{L_k}$ and its fold sum is the sum of its folds. This is
the number of multifold partition diamonds of shape $(d_1, \dots, d_M)$ with fold sum $i$ and
link sum $j$.

Every part of such a diamond is at most $i + j$, so this number is finite.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, equation (2) and Section 3.

articles.title: The bivariate series of multifold partition diamonds
articles.statement:
For natural numbers
$d_1, \dots, d_M$, $\sigma_{d_1, \dots, d_M}(a, b)$ is the formal power series in
$\mathbb{Z}[[a, b]]$ whose coefficient of $a^i b^j$ is the number of multifold partition diamonds
of shape $(d_1, \dots, d_M)$ with fold sum $i$ and link sum $j$. That is,
$\sigma_{d_1, \dots, d_M}(a, b) = \sum a^{\text{fold sum}} b^{\text{link sum}}$, summed over all
such diamonds. We write $\sigma_{d,M}$ for the case $d_1 = \dots = d_M = d$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, equation (2) and Section 3.

articles.title: Product formula for multifold partition diamonds
articles.statement:
Let $d_1, \dots, d_M$ be positive
integers with $M \ge 1$, and let $\omega_k = \sum_{m=k+1}^{M} d_m$ for $0 \le k \le M$. Let
$\sigma_{d_1, \dots, d_M}(a, b)$ be the generating function of multifold partition diamonds of
shape $(d_1, \dots, d_M)$, where $a$ marks the fold sum and $b$ marks the link sum, and let
$E_d(x, y) = \sum_{\tau} x^{\mathrm{des}(\tau)} y^{\mathrm{maj}(\tau)}$ be the Euler–Mahonian
polynomial, summed over the permutations $\tau$ of $\{1, \dots, d\}$. Then the following
identity holds in $\mathbb{Z}[[a, b]]$:

$$\left(1 - a^{\omega_0} b^{M+1}\right) \prod_{k=1}^{M} \prod_{j=0}^{d_k}
\left(1 - a^{\omega_k + d_k - j} b^{M-k+1}\right) \cdot \sigma_{d_1, \dots, d_M}(a, b) =
\prod_{k=1}^{M} E_{d_k}\left(a^{\omega_k} b^{M-k+1}, a\right).$$

The $k$th diamond (with $d_k$ folds) is the $k$th from the smallest part, as in the paper's poset
$\{1\} \oplus Q_{d_1} \oplus \dots \oplus Q_{d_M}$. If the parts are read in the opposite order,
the formula holds only for the reversed sequence: for $(d_1, d_2) = (1, 2)$ the coefficient of
$ab$ would be $1$, not $2$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Product formula for equal-fold partition diamonds
articles.statement:
Let $d$ and $M$ be positive integers.
Let $\sigma_{d,M}(a, b)$ be the generating function of multifold partition diamonds of shape
$(d, \dots, d)$ ($M$ copies), where $a$ marks the fold sum and $b$ marks the link sum, and let
$E_d(x, y) = \sum_{\tau} x^{\mathrm{des}(\tau)} y^{\mathrm{maj}(\tau)}$ be the Euler–Mahonian
polynomial, summed over the permutations $\tau$ of $\{1, \dots, d\}$. Then the following
identity holds in $\mathbb{Z}[[a, b]]$:

$$\left(1 - a^{Md} b^{M+1}\right) \prod_{n=1}^{M} \prod_{j=0}^{d} \left(1 - a^{nd-j} b^{n}\right)
\cdot \sigma_{d,M}(a, b) = \prod_{n=1}^{M} E_d\left(a^{(n-1)d} b^{n}, a\right).$$

Equivalently, $\sigma_{d,M}(a, b)$ is the product of the $E_d(a^{(n-1)d} b^n, a)$ divided by
$(1 - a^{Md} b^{M+1}) \prod_{n=1}^{M} \prod_{j=0}^{d} (1 - a^{nd-j} b^n)$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Number of descents from the descent set
articles.statement:
For a permutation $\tau$ of
$\{0, 1, \dots, d - 1\}$, the number of descents $\mathrm{des}(\tau) = |\mathrm{Des}(\tau)|$ is the
number of elements of the descent set $\mathrm{Des}(\tau)$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Section 1.

articles.title: Descent set of a permutation
articles.statement:
For a permutation $\tau$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, d - 1\}$, the
descent set is $\mathrm{Des}(\tau) = \{p \in \{1, \dots, d - 1\} : \tau(p - 1) > \tau(p)\}$. If
$\tau$ is read as the permutation $p \mapsto \tau(p - 1) + 1$ of $\{1, \dots, d\}$, this is the
usual descent set: the positions $p$, numbered from $1$, where the value at $p$ exceeds the
value at $p + 1$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Section 1.

articles.title: Major index of a permutation
articles.statement:
For a permutation $\tau$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, d - 1\}$, the
major index is $\mathrm{maj}(\tau) = \sum_{p \in \mathrm{Des}(\tau)} p$, the sum of the
positions, numbered from $1$, in the descent set $\mathrm{Des}(\tau)$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Section 1.

articles.title: Value of a permutation at a natural position
articles.statement:
For a permutation $\tau$ of
$\{0, 1, \dots, d - 1\}$ and a natural number $j$, this is the natural number $\tau(j)$ when
$j < d$, and $0$ when $j \ge d$. It is used to read off descents.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Section 1 (descent statistics).

articles.title: Generating function of Schmidt type $d$-fold partition diamonds
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 1$. A Schmidt
type $d$-fold partition diamond is a finitely supported sequence $(a_p)_{p \ge 0}$ of natural
numbers such that $a_{k(d+1)} \ge a_{k(d+1)+f} \ge a_{(k+1)(d+1)}$ for all $k \ge 0$ and all
$f$ with $1 \le f \le d$; its weight is the sum of its links $a_{k(d+1)}$, $k \ge 0$. Let
$s_d(w)$ be the number of such diamonds of weight $w$, and let
$S_d(q) = \sum_{w \ge 0} s_d(w) q^w \in \mathbb{Z}[[q]]$. Then for all natural numbers $n \le N$,
the coefficient of $q^n$ in $S_d(q) \prod_{m=1}^{N} (1 - q^m)^{d+1}$ equals the coefficient of
$q^n$ in $\prod_{m=1}^{N} E_d(q^m, 1)$, where $E_d$ is the Euler–Mahonian polynomial.

Since every factor $E_d(q^m, 1)/(1 - q^m)^{d+1}$ with $m > N$ is $1$ modulo $q^{N+1}$, the
statement for all $N$ is equivalent to $S_d(q) = \prod_{m \ge 1} E_d(q^m, 1)/(1 - q^m)^{d+1}$.

## Sources

- Matthias Beck and Kobe Wijesekera, *MacMahon's Double Vision: Partition Diamonds Revisited*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A13, Corollary 1, quoting Dockery-Jameson-Sellers-Wilson.

articles.title: Partitions whose even parts are distinct
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $\mathrm{ped}(n)$ is
the number of partitions of $n$ in which every even part occurs exactly once; the odd parts are
unrestricted.

Its generating function is $\sum_{n \ge 0} \mathrm{ped}(n) q^n = (q^4; q^4)_\infty / (q; q)_\infty$.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Section 1 (definition of `ped(n)` before Theorem 1).

articles.title: Values at zero of the restricted partition counts
articles.statement:
The number $\operatorname{ped}(0)$ of
partitions of $0$ in which no even part is repeated, the number $\operatorname{pod}(0)$ of
partitions of $0$ in which no odd part is repeated, the number $P_2(0)$ of partitions of $0$ with
no part congruent to $2$ modulo $4$, and the number $q(0)$ of ordered pairs of partitions into
distinct parts with sizes adding up to $0$ are all equal to $1$, as only the empty partition (or
the pair of empty partitions) is counted.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Sections 1 and 3 (definitions of `ped`, `pod`, `P_2`, `q`).

articles.title: Merca's square recurrence for partitions with distinct even parts
articles.statement:
Let
$\operatorname{ped}(m)$ be the number of partitions of $m$ in which no even part is repeated. For
every $n \ge 0$, the sum $\sum_j (-1)^j \operatorname{ped}(n - 2j^2)$ over the integers $j$ with
$2j^2 \le n$ equals $1$ if $n = k(k+1)/2$ for some integer $k \ge 0$, and $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Theorem 2, quoting M. Merca (via da Silva and Sakai).

articles.title: Merca's triangular recurrence for partitions with distinct even parts
articles.statement:
Let
$\operatorname{ped}(m)$ be the number of partitions of $m$ in which no even part is repeated. For
every $n \ge 0$, the sum $\sum_{j \ge 0} (-1)^{\lceil j/2 \rceil} \operatorname{ped}(n - j(j+1)/2)$
over the $j$ with $j(j+1)/2 \le n$ equals $1$ if $n = k(k+1)$ for some integer $k \ge 0$, and $0$
otherwise.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Theorem 1, quoting M. Merca (via da Silva and Sakai).

articles.title: Partitions whose odd parts are distinct
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $\mathrm{pod}(n)$ is
the number of partitions of $n$ in which every odd part occurs exactly once; the even parts are
unrestricted.

Its generating function is
$\sum_{n \ge 0} \mathrm{pod}(n) q^n = (-q; q^2)_\infty / (q^2; q^2)_\infty$.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Section 3 (definition of `pod(n)` before Theorem 6).

articles.title: Evenness of a triangular sum of partition counts with distinct odd parts
articles.statement:
Let
$\operatorname{pod}(m)$ be the number of partitions of $m$ in which no odd part is repeated. For
every $n > 0$, the sum $\sum_{k \ge 0} \operatorname{pod}(n - k(k+1)/2)$ over the $k$ with
$k(k+1)/2 \le n$ is even.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Bipartitions into distinct parts
articles.statement:
Let $\operatorname{pd}(m)$ be the number of partitions
of $m$ into distinct parts. For a natural number $n$, $q(n)$ is the number of ordered pairs of
partitions into distinct parts whose sizes add up to $n$, that is,
$q(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \operatorname{pd}(k) \operatorname{pd}(n-k)$.

Its generating function is $\sum_{n \ge 0} q(n) x^n = (-x; x)_\infty^2$, where
$(a; x)_\infty = \prod_{i \ge 0} (1 - a x^i)$.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Section 3 (definition of `q(n)` before Theorem 12).

articles.title: Bipartitions into distinct parts from the partition function
articles.statement:
Let $q(n)$ be the number of
ordered pairs of partitions into distinct parts whose sizes add up to $n$, and let $p(m)$ be the
number of partitions of $m$. For every $n \ge 0$, $q(n) = \sum_{k \ge 0} p(n - k(k+1)/2)$, where
the sum runs over the $k$ with $k(k+1)/2 \le n$.

The source states this for $n > 0$; it also holds at $n = 0$, where both sides equal $1$.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Theorem 12.

articles.title: Pentagonal recurrence for partitions into distinct parts
articles.statement:
Let $\operatorname{pd}(m)$ be the
number of partitions of $m$ into distinct parts. For every $n \ge 0$, the sum
$\sum_k (-1)^k \operatorname{pd}(n - k(3k+1))$ over the integers $k$ with $k(3k+1) \le n$ equals
$1$ if $n = m(m+1)/2$ for some integer $m \ge 0$, and $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Corollary 5.

articles.title: Pentagonal recurrence for partitions into distinct odd parts
articles.statement:
Let $\operatorname{pdo}(m)$
be the number of partitions of $m$ into distinct odd parts. For every $n \ge 0$, the sum
$\sum_k (-1)^k \operatorname{pdo}(n - k(3k+1))$ over the integers $k$ with $k(3k+1) \le n$
equals $(-1)^{\lceil m/2 \rceil}$ if $n = m(3m+1)/2$ for some integer $m$, and $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Corollary 4.

articles.title: Overpartitions into odd parts from partitions with distinct odd parts
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathrm{po}(m)$ be the number of overpartitions of $m$ into odd parts and $\mathrm{pod}(m)$
the number of partitions of $m$ whose odd parts are distinct. For every natural number $n$,
$\mathrm{po}(n) = \sum_k \mathrm{pod}(n - k(k+1)/2)$, the sum running over the natural
numbers $k$ with $k(k+1)/2 \le n$.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Overpartitions into odd parts from overpartitions and squares
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{po}(m)$
be the number of overpartitions of $m$ into odd parts and $\overline{p}(m)$ the number of
overpartitions of $m$. For every natural number $n$,
$\mathrm{po}(n) = \sum_k (-1)^k \, \overline{p}(n - 2k^2)$, the sum running over the
integers $k$ with $2k^2 \le n$.

With the partition function $p$ in place of $\overline{p}$ the identity fails at $n = 1$:
$\mathrm{po}(1) = 2$ but $p(1) = 1$.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Theorem 8.

articles.title: Overpartitions into odd parts from partitions and pentagonal numbers
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathrm{po}(m)$ be the number of overpartitions of $m$ into odd parts and $p(m)$ the number
of partitions of $m$. For every natural number $n$,
$\mathrm{po}(n) = \sum_k (-1)^{\lceil k/2 \rceil} p(n - k(3k+1)/2)$, the sum running over
the integers $k$ with $k(3k+1)/2 \le n$.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Overpartitions into odd parts from partitions with no part congruent to 2 modulo 4
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{po}(m)$ be the number of overpartitions of $m$ into odd parts and $P_2(m)$ the
number of partitions of $m$ with no part congruent to $2$ modulo $4$. For every natural
number $n$, $\mathrm{po}(n) = \sum_k P_2(n - k(k+1)/2)$, the sum running over the natural
numbers $k$ with $k(k+1)/2 \le n$.

The case $n = 0$ is included: there both sides equal $1$.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Theorem 11.

articles.title: Overpartitions of even numbers into odd parts
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{po}(m)$ be the number of
overpartitions of $m$ into odd parts and $\overline{p}(m)$ the number of overpartitions of $m$.
For every natural number $n$,
$\mathrm{po}(2n) = \overline{p}(n) + 2 \sum_k \overline{p}(n - 2k^2)$, the sum running over
the integers $k \ge 1$ with $2k^2 \le n$.

The sum cannot start at $k = 0$: at $n = 0$ that would give
$\overline{p}(0) + 2 \, \overline{p}(0) = 3$, whereas $\mathrm{po}(0) = 1$.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Theorem 10.

articles.title: Overpartitions of odd numbers into odd parts
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{po}(m)$ be the number of
overpartitions of $m$ into odd parts and $\overline{p}(m)$ the number of overpartitions of $m$.
For every natural number $n$,
$\mathrm{po}(2n+1) = 2 \sum_k \overline{p}(n - 2k(k+1))$, the sum running over the natural
numbers $k$ with $2k(k+1) \le n$.

With the partition function $p$ in place of $\overline{p}$ the identity fails at $n = 1$.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Theorem 9.

articles.title: Overpartitions of zero into odd parts
articles.statement:
The number $\mathrm{po}(0)$ of overpartitions
of $0$ into odd parts equals $1$: the empty overpartition is the only one.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, value `po(0) = 1` listed after Theorem 5.

articles.title: Overpartitions into odd parts
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $\mathrm{po}(n)$ is the
number of overpartitions of $n$ all of whose parts are odd.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, title and Section 1 (values `po(0), …, po(10)` listed after Theorem 5).

articles.title: Pentagonal recurrence for overpartitions into odd parts
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{po}(j)$ be the
number of overpartitions of $j$ into odd parts. For every natural number $n$, the sum
$\sum_k (-1)^k \, \mathrm{po}(n - k(3k+1)/2)$ over the integers $k$ with $k(3k+1)/2 \le n$
equals $(-1)^{\lceil m/2 \rceil}$ if $n = m(3m+1)/2$ for some integer $m$, and $0$ otherwise.

Such an $m$ is unique, since the numbers $m(3m+1)/2$ with $m$ an integer are distinct.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Overpartitions into odd parts and partitions into distinct odd parts
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathrm{po}(m)$ be the number of overpartitions of $m$ into odd parts and $\mathrm{pdo}(m)$
the number of partitions of $m$ into distinct odd parts. For every natural number $n$, the
sum $\sum_k (-1)^k \, \mathrm{po}(n - k(3k+1)/2)$ over the integers $k$ with
$k(3k+1)/2 \le n$ equals the sum $\sum_k (-1)^k \, \mathrm{pdo}(n - k(3k+1))$ over the
integers $k$ with $k(3k+1) \le n$.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Theorem 13.

articles.title: Square recurrence for overpartitions into odd parts
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{po}(m)$ for the
number of overpartitions of $m$ into odd parts. For every natural number $n$, the sum
$\mathrm{po}(n) + 2 \sum_{k \ge 1,\ 2k^2 \le n} (-1)^k \, \mathrm{po}(n - 2k^2)$ equals $1$ if
$n = 0$, equals $2$ if $n = m^2$ for some integer $m \ge 1$, and equals $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Triangular recurrence for overpartitions into odd parts
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{po}(m)$ for the
number of overpartitions of $m$ into odd parts. For every natural number $n$, the sum
$\sum_{k \ge 0,\ k(k+1)/2 \le n} (-1)^{\lceil k/2 \rceil} \, \mathrm{po}(n - k(k+1)/2)$ equals
$1$ if $n = m(m+1)/2$ for some natural number $m$, and equals $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Overpartitions into odd parts and partitions into distinct parts
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{po}(m)$
for the number of overpartitions of $m$ into odd parts and $\mathrm{pd}(m)$ for the number of
partitions of $m$ into distinct parts. For every natural number $n$,
$\sum_{k \ge 0,\ k(k+1)/2 \le n} (-1)^{\lceil k/2 \rceil} \, \mathrm{po}(n - k(k+1)/2) =
\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z},\ k(3k+1) \le n} (-1)^k \, \mathrm{pd}(n - k(3k+1))$.

The sum on the left runs over $k \ge 0$ only. Taken over all integers $k$ it would double, since
$k$ and $-1 - k$ give the same term, and the identity would fail at $n = 0$.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Theorem 14.

articles.title: Parity form of Euler's pentagonal recurrence
articles.statement:
Write $p(m)$ for the number of partitions
of $m$. For every positive integer $n$, the sum
$\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z},\ k(3k+1)/2 \le n} p(n - k(3k+1)/2)$ is even.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Partitions with no part congruent to 2 modulo 4
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $P_2(n)$ is
the number of partitions of $n$ none of whose parts is congruent to $2$ modulo $4$.

Its generating function is $\sum_{n \ge 0} P_2(n) q^n = (q^2; q^4)_\infty / (q; q)_\infty$.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Section 3 (definition of `P_2(n)` before Theorem 11).

articles.title: Parity of a triangular sum of partitions with no part congruent to 2 modulo 4
articles.statement:
Write
$P_2(m)$ for the number of partitions of $m$ with no part congruent to $2$ modulo $4$. For every
positive integer $n$, the sum $\sum_{k \ge 0,\ k(k+1)/2 \le n} P_2(n - k(k+1)/2)$ is even.

## Sources

- Deepthi G. and S. Chandankumar, *Linear Relations for Overpartitions into Odd Parts*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A60, Corollary 3.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the overpartition of zero
articles.statement: Any two overpartitions of $0$ are equal.

articles.title: Overlined sizes of the fully overlined overpartition
articles.statement:
For every partition $p$ of $n$,
the set of overlined part sizes of the fully overlined overpartition of $p$ is the set of
distinct parts of $p$.

articles.title: Underlying partition of the fully overlined overpartition
articles.statement:
For every partition $p$ of
$n$, the underlying partition of the fully overlined overpartition of $p$ is $p$.

articles.title: Fully overlined overpartition
articles.statement:
For a partition $p$ of $n$, the fully overlined
overpartition of $p$ is the overpartition of $n$ whose underlying partition is $p$ and whose
set of overlined part sizes is the set of all distinct parts of $p$.

articles.title: Overlined sizes in the fully overlined overpartition
articles.statement:
For every partition $p$ of $n$ and
every natural number $a$, $a$ is overlined in the fully overlined overpartition of $p$ if and
only if $a$ is a part of $p$.

articles.title: Characterization of overlined sizes
articles.statement:
For an overpartition $O$ of $n$ and a natural
number $a$, $a$ is overlined in $O$ if and only if $a$ belongs to the set of overlined part
sizes of $O$.

articles.title: Overlined sizes are parts
articles.statement:
If $a$ is overlined in an overpartition $O$ of $n$, then $a$
is a part of the underlying partition of $O$.

articles.title: Overlined sizes are positive
articles.statement:
If $a$ is overlined in an overpartition $O$ of $n$, then
$a > 0$.

articles.title: Overlined part size
articles.statement:
A natural number $a$ is overlined in an overpartition $O$ of $n$
when $a$ belongs to the set of overlined part sizes of $O$.

articles.title: No overlines in a plain partition
articles.statement:
For every partition $p$ of $n$ and every natural
number $a$, $a$ is not overlined in the overpartition whose underlying partition is $p$ and
whose set of overlined part sizes is empty.

articles.title: The overpartition attached to a partition has no overlined sizes
articles.statement:
For every partition
$p$ of a natural number $n$, the overpartition of $n$ attached to $p$ (underlying partition $p$,
no part size overlined) has an empty set of overlined part sizes.

articles.title: The underlying partition of the overpartition attached to a partition
articles.statement:
For every partition
$p$ of a natural number $n$, the underlying partition of the overpartition of $n$ attached to $p$
(underlying partition $p$, no part size overlined) is $p$.

articles.title: The overpartition attached to a partition
articles.statement:
For a partition $p$ of a natural number $n$, the
overpartition of $n$ attached to $p$ has underlying partition $p$ and no overlined part sizes.

articles.title: Overpartitions of zero have no overlined sizes
articles.statement:
Every overpartition of $0$ has no
overlined part sizes.

articles.title: Overpartition
articles.statement:
An overpartition of a natural number $n$ consists of a partition $p$ of $n$
together with a finite set of overlined part sizes, each of which occurs as a part of $p$.

articles.title: Partition generating function with unit weights
articles.statement:
Let $p(n)$ be the number of partitions
of $n$. Over the integers, $\sum_{n \ge 0} p(n)\, x^n$ equals the weighted partition generating
function $\sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{\lambda} \prod_{i} f(i, c_i(\lambda))\, x^n$ with all weights
$f(i, c) = 1$, where $\lambda$ runs over the partitions of $n$, $i$ over the distinct parts of
$\lambda$, and $c_i(\lambda)$ is the number of times $i$ occurs in $\lambda$.

articles.title: Euler's identity for the partition generating function
articles.statement:
Let $p(n)$ be the number of
partitions of $n$. Over the integers,
$\left(\sum_{n \ge 0} p(n)\, x^n\right) \cdot \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^k x^{k(3k-1)/2} = 1$.
By the pentagonal number theorem the second factor equals $\prod_{i \ge 1} (1 - x^i)$.

articles.title: The partition number of one
articles.statement:
Let $p(n)$ be the number of partitions of $n$. Then
$p(1) = 1$: the only partition of $1$ is $1$ itself.

articles.title: The partition number of zero
articles.statement:
Let $p(n)$ be the number of partitions of $n$. Then
$p(0) = 1$: the only partition of $0$ is the empty one.

articles.title: The partition function
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $p(n)$ is the number of partitions of
$n$, that is, of ways of writing $n$ as a sum of positive integers, disregarding order.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagonal_number_theorem ("Pentagonal number theorem").

articles.title: Euler's pentagonal recurrence for the partition function
articles.statement:
Let $p(n)$ be the number of
partitions of $n$, and for an integer $k$ let $g(k) = k(3k - 1)/2$ be the generalized pentagonal
number of $k$. For every natural number $n \ge 1$,
$p(n) = \sum_{k} (-1)^{k+1}\, p(n - g(k))$, where the sum runs over the nonzero integers $k$
with $g(k) \le n$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagonal_number_theorem ("Pentagonal number theorem").

articles.title: Coefficients of the partition polynomial
articles.statement:
For every partition $\lambda$ of a natural
number $n$ and every $j \in \mathbb{N}$, the coefficient of $x^j$ in the partition polynomial
$f_\lambda$ equals the number of parts of $\lambda$ equal to $j$.

articles.title: The partition polynomial at one
articles.statement:
For every partition $\lambda$ of a natural number $n$,
the value $f_\lambda(1)$ of the partition polynomial $f_\lambda$ at $1$ equals the number of
parts of $\lambda$, counted with multiplicity.

articles.title: Derivatives of the partition polynomial via Stirling numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$, let
$m \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, and write $m_i = m(i)$. Assume $m_k \ne 0$ and $m_i = 0$
for every $i$ outside $\{1, \dots, k\}$, so that $m$ lists the part multiplicities of a
partition $\lambda = \langle 1^{m_1}, \dots, k^{m_k} \rangle$ with largest part $k$. Let
$f(y) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} m_i y^i$ for real $y$. Then for every natural number $d \le k$ and every
real $x \ne 0$,

$$f^{(d)}(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} i^d m_i x^{i-d} -
\sum_{j=0}^{d-1} S(d, j)\, x^{j-d} f^{(j)}(x),$$

where $S(d, j)$ are the Stirling numbers of the second kind and $f^{(j)}$ is the $j$th
derivative of $f$; for $d = 0$ the second sum is empty.

## Sources

- Madeline Locus Dawsey, Tyler Russell, and Dannie Urban, "Derivatives and Integrals of Polynomials Associated with Integer Partitions," Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), Article 22.5.1, Theorem 1, lines 108–114, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Dawsey/dawsey3.tex>.

articles.title: Stirling recursion for derivatives, for arbitrary multiplicities
articles.statement:
Let $k$ and $d$ be
natural numbers, let $m \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, write $m_i = m(i)$, and let
$f(y) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} m_i y^i$ for real $y$. Then for every real $x \ne 0$,

$$f^{(d)}(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} i^d m_i x^{i-d} -
\sum_{j=0}^{d-1} S(d, j)\, x^{j-d} f^{(j)}(x),$$

where $S(d, j)$ are the Stirling numbers of the second kind and $f^{(j)}$ is the $j$th
derivative of $f$. No relation between $d$ and $k$ is assumed.

articles.title: Partition polynomial
articles.statement:
For a partition $\lambda$ of a natural number $n$ with parts
$\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_\ell$, listed with multiplicity, the (unnormalized) partition
polynomial of $\lambda$ is $f_\lambda(x) = x^{\lambda_1} + \dots + x^{\lambda_\ell}$, a polynomial
with natural number coefficients.

articles.title: Split replacement in a dimension list
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $q, a, b, c$ and a list $l$ of
natural numbers, the split replacement is defined exactly when $l$ has at least $c$ entries equal
to $a + b$. It removes the last $c$ entries of $l$ equal to $a + b$ and, at the position of the
first of these removed entries, inserts $c$ copies of $a$ followed by $c q^a$ copies of $b$; the
entries of $l$ before that position stay in front, and the entries after it that were not removed
follow in their original order. For $c = 0$ the list is unchanged.

No sorting is performed.

articles.title: Basic ancestors are restricted
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be a prime power and $n > 0$. Let
$(d_0, m_0), \dots, (d_{k-1}, m_{k-1})$ be blocks with $d_i \ge 1$ and $m_i \ge 1$ for all $i$,
$d_0 > d_1 > \dots > d_{k-1}$ and $m_0 d_0 + \dots + m_{k-1} d_{k-1} = n$. Put
$p_i = \sum_{j < i} m_j d_j$, and let the basic dimension list be the concatenation, for
$i = 0, \dots, k - 1$ in order, of $\sum_{j=0}^{m_i - 1} q^{p_i + j d_i}$ copies of $d_i$. If this
list is nonincreasing, then every Gaussian partition whose dimension list equals it is a
restricted Gaussian partition for $q$ and $n$.

The witness realizes every block with an empty branch.

articles.title: Basic block multiplicity
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be a natural number and
$(d_0, m_0), \dots, (d_{k-1}, m_{k-1})$ a list of blocks, and put $p_i = \sum_{j < i} m_j d_j$.
The basic multiplicity of block $i$ is $N_i = \sum_{j=0}^{m_i - 1} q^{p_i + j d_i}$ when $i < k$,
and $N_i = 0$ when $i \ge k$.

articles.title: Final dimensions of a block
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be a natural number,
$(d_0, m_0), \dots, (d_{k-1}, m_{k-1})$ a list of blocks and $C$ a list of chains of branch steps.
The final dimension list of block $i$ is defined when $C$ has an entry $s_1, \dots, s_r$ at index
$i$: start from $N_i$ copies of $d_i$, where $N_i$ is the basic multiplicity of block $i$ (the
empty list when $i \ge k$), and for $t = 1, \dots, r$ in order apply the split replacement of step
$s_t = (a_t, b_t, c_t)$, which replaces $c_t$ copies of $a_t + b_t$ by $c_t$ copies of $a_t$ and
$c_t q^{a_t}$ copies of $b_t$. It is undefined when $C$ has no entry at index $i$ or when one of
these split replacements is undefined.

articles.title: Block
articles.statement:
A block is a pair $(d, m)$ of natural numbers, read as a part size $d$ of an integer
partition together with its multiplicity $m$. No condition is imposed on a single block.

articles.title: First-split exponent
articles.statement:
Let $(d_0, m_0), \dots, (d_{k-1}, m_{k-1})$ be a list of blocks and
put $p_i = \sum_{j < i} m_j d_j$. The first-split exponent of block $i$ is
$u_i = p_i + (m_i - 1) d_i$ when $i < k$, where $m_i - 1$ is taken to be $0$ if $m_i = 0$, and
$u_i = 0$ when $i \ge k$.

articles.title: Branch step
articles.statement:
A branch step is a triple $(a, b, c)$ of natural numbers. It describes one
simultaneous split level: for the ambient parameter $q$, $c$ copies of the parent dimension
$a + b$ become $c$ copies of $a$ and $c q^a$ copies of $b$.

articles.title: Valid branch
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be a natural number, $(d_0, m_0), \dots, (d_{k-1}, m_{k-1})$ a list
of blocks and $i$ an index, and let $u_i$ and $N_i$ be the first-split exponent and the basic
multiplicity of block $i$, with $d_i$ read as $0$ when $i \ge k$. A chain of branch steps
$(a_1, b_1, c_1), \dots, (a_r, b_r, c_r)$ is a valid branch for block $i$ when either $r = 0$, or
$r \ge 1$, the first step satisfies $1 \le b_1 \le a_1$, $a_1 + b_1 = d_i$ and
$1 \le c_1 \le q^{u_i} - 1$ (subtraction truncated at $0$), $N_i \ne 1$, and the chain is
adjacently valid.

articles.title: Adjacently valid chain
articles.statement:
A chain of branch steps
$(a_1, b_1, c_1), \dots, (a_r, b_r, c_r)$ is adjacently valid when for every $j$ with
$1 \le j < r$ we have $a_{j+1} + b_{j+1} = a_j$, $1 \le b_{j+1} \le a_{j+1}$ and
