for every $j \le i$ with $j \ne l$. If exactly the spots $d_1, \dots, d_i$, with $d_l$ replaced
by $q$, are occupied, then the remaining cars $a_{i+1}, \dots, a_n$, arriving in order, all park
under the $k$-Naples rule.

## Sources

- J. P. Carvalho, P. E. Harris, G. Rojas Kirby, N. Tripeny and A. R. Vindas Meléndez, *Enumerating k-Naples Parking Functions through Catalan Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A44, Lemma 2.3.

articles.title: A $2$-Naples parking example
articles.statement:
Under the $2$-Naples rule on the spots $1, \dots, 7$, the
cars with preferences $(6, 6, 6, 5, 5, 2, 1)$, arriving in order into an empty lot, all park, in
the spots $6, 5, 4, 3, 7, 2, 1$ respectively.

## Sources

- J. P. Carvalho, P. E. Harris, G. Rojas Kirby, N. Tripeny and A. R. Vindas Meléndez, *Enumerating k-Naples Parking Functions through Catalan Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A44, Section 1.

articles.title: A $3$-Naples parking example on $\mathbb{Z}$
articles.statement:
Under the $3$-Naples rule on $\mathbb{Z}$,
the cars with preferences $(1, 2, 2, 5, 7, 7, 7, 3)$, arriving in order with no spot occupied,
park in the spots $1, 2, 0, 5, 7, 6, 4, 3$ respectively.

## Sources

- J. P. Carvalho, P. E. Harris, G. Rojas Kirby, N. Tripeny and A. R. Vindas Meléndez, *Enumerating k-Naples Parking Functions through Catalan Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A44, Section 2, Remark 2.

articles.title: A $2$-Naples parking example on $\mathbb{Z}$
articles.statement:
Under the $2$-Naples rule on $\mathbb{Z}$,
the cars with preferences $(4, 2, 2, 2)$, arriving in order with no spot occupied, park in the
spots $4, 2, 1, 0$ respectively.

## Sources

- J. P. Carvalho, P. E. Harris, G. Rojas Kirby, N. Tripeny and A. R. Vindas Meléndez, *Enumerating k-Naples Parking Functions through Catalan Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A44, Section 2, Figure 1.

articles.title: One more backward step keeps the cars in $\{0, \dots, n\}$
articles.statement:
Let $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$ be
integers with $1 \le a_j \le n$ for every $j$. If, under the $k$-Naples rule on $\mathbb{Z}$, the
cars with these preferences, arriving in order with no spot occupied, occupy exactly the spots
$1, \dots, n$, then under the $(k + 1)$-Naples rule on $\mathbb{Z}$ every car parks in a spot $s$
with $0 \le s \le n$.

Every $k \ge 0$ is admitted (the source's proof treats any $k \ge 0$).

## Sources

- J. P. Carvalho, P. E. Harris, G. Rojas Kirby, N. Tripeny and A. R. Vindas Meléndez, *Enumerating k-Naples Parking Functions through Catalan Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A44, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Naples parking on $\mathbb{Z}$
articles.statement:
Starting from a list of occupied spots in $\mathbb{Z}$,
cars with integer preferences $a_1, \dots, a_m$ arrive in order, and each takes the spot given by
the $k$-Naples rule on $\mathbb{Z}$ for the spots occupied when it arrives. The result is the
final list of occupied spots: the spots of the cars, most recent first, followed by the initially
occupied spots.

## Sources

- J. P. Carvalho, P. E. Harris, G. Rojas Kirby, N. Tripeny and A. R. Vindas Meléndez, *Enumerating k-Naples Parking Functions through Catalan Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A44, Section 2 (parking on `ℤ`).

articles.title: Naples parking
articles.statement:
Starting from a list of occupied spots, cars with preferences
$a_1, \dots, a_m \in \mathbb{N}$ arrive in order, and each takes the spot given by the $k$-Naples
rule on the spots $1, \dots, n$ for the spots occupied when it arrives. If every car parks, the
result is the final list of occupied spots: the spots of the cars, most recent first, followed by
the initially occupied spots. If some car cannot park, there is no result.

## Sources

- J. P. Carvalho, P. E. Harris, G. Rojas Kirby, N. Tripeny and A. R. Vindas Meléndez, *Enumerating k-Naples Parking Functions through Catalan Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A44, Section 1.

articles.title: The $k$-Naples rule on $\mathbb{Z}$
articles.statement:
When the spots in a finite list $O$ of integers are
occupied, a car preferring $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ parks in $a$ if $a$ is free; otherwise in the first
free spot among $a - 1, \dots, a - k$, checked in decreasing order with no lower bound; otherwise
in the first free spot among $a + 1, \dots, a + |O| + 1$, checked in increasing order (one of
them is free, so this is the first free spot after $a$).

## Sources

- J. P. Carvalho, P. E. Harris, G. Rojas Kirby, N. Tripeny and A. R. Vindas Meléndez, *Enumerating k-Naples Parking Functions through Catalan Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A44, Section 2 (parking on `ℤ`).

articles.title: The $k$-Naples rule
articles.statement:
On the spots $1, \dots, n$, when the spots in a list $O$ of natural
numbers are occupied, a car preferring $a$ parks in $a$ if $a$ is free; otherwise in the first
free spot among those of $a - 1, \dots, a - k$ that are at least $1$, checked in decreasing
order; otherwise in the first free spot among $a + 1, \dots, n$, checked in increasing order.
The car cannot park if none of these is free, or if $a$ is not one of the spots $1, \dots, n$.

## Sources

- J. P. Carvalho, P. E. Harris, G. Rojas Kirby, N. Tripeny and A. R. Vindas Meléndez, *Enumerating k-Naples Parking Functions through Catalan Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A44, Section 1.

articles.title: The lattice path of $(1, 3, 3, 5, 6, 6)$
articles.statement:
The lattice path of the parking preference
$(1, 3, 3, 5, 6, 6)$ is $\mathrm{UDDUUDDUDUUD}$, where $\mathrm{U}$ is an Up step and
$\mathrm{D}$ a Down step.

## Sources

- J. P. Carvalho, P. E. Harris, G. Rojas Kirby, N. Tripeny and A. R. Vindas Meléndez, *Enumerating k-Naples Parking Functions through Catalan Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A44, Section 3 (Figure 3).

articles.title: Lattice path of a parking preference
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ be a sequence of
natural numbers. Its lattice path is the sequence of $2n$ steps, each an Up step $(1, 1)$ or a
Down step $(1, -1)$, obtained by taking, for each spot $s = 1, \dots, n$ in turn, one Up step
for every index $i$ with $a_i = s$ followed by one Down step, and then appending Down steps
until there are $2n$ steps. When every $a_i$ lies in $\{1, \dots, n\}$ this gives exactly $2n$
steps and nothing is appended; if moreover $\alpha$ is weakly increasing, the $i$-th Up step is
preceded by exactly $a_i - 1$ Down steps.

## Sources

- J. P. Carvalho, P. E. Harris, G. Rojas Kirby, N. Tripeny and A. R. Vindas Meléndez, *Enumerating k-Naples Parking Functions through Catalan Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A44, Section 3 (Remark 3.3).

articles.title: Every $k$-Naples parking function is $(k + 1)$-Naples
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$
and $n$, every $k$-Naples parking function $\alpha$ of length $n$ is also a $(k + 1)$-Naples
parking function.

## Sources

- J. P. Carvalho, P. E. Harris, G. Rojas Kirby, N. Tripeny and A. R. Vindas Meléndez, *Enumerating k-Naples Parking Functions through Catalan Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A44, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Extremely lucky Stirling permutations are counted by the Catalan numbers
articles.statement:
For every
positive integer $n$, the number of Stirling permutations $w$ of order $n$ that are extremely
lucky, that is, whose set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$ of lucky cars has exactly $n$ elements, is the
Catalan number $C_n$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Corollary 2.14 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-cor-20`).

articles.title: Counting extremely unlucky Stirling permutations
articles.statement:
For every integer $n \ge 1$, the number
of Stirling permutations $w$ of order $n$ that are extremely unlucky, that is, whose only lucky
car is car $1$ ($\mathrm{Lucky}(w) = \{1\}$), is $(n - 1)!$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Theorem 2.7 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-thm-13`).

articles.title: Stirling permutations with $n$ nonzero displacements
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the
number of Stirling permutations $w$ of order $n$ in which exactly $n$ cars have nonzero
displacement (equivalently, whose displacement composition $\mathrm{dis}(w)$ has exactly $n$
nonzero parts) is the Catalan number $C_n$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Corollary 5.9 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-cor-45`).

articles.title: Extremely lucky Stirling permutations are determined by their displacements
articles.statement:
Let $w$ and
$w'$ be Stirling permutations of order $n$, and suppose that $w$ is extremely lucky, that is, its
set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$ of lucky cars has exactly $n$ elements. If every car has the same
displacement in $w'$ as in $w$ (that is, $\mathrm{dis}(w') = \mathrm{dis}(w)$), then $w' = w$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Theorem 5.8 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-thm-43`).

articles.title: Extremely lucky Stirling permutations and Dyck words
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, there
is a bijection between the Stirling permutations $w$ of order $n$ that are extremely lucky, that
is, whose set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$ of lucky cars has exactly $n$ elements, and the Dyck words of
semilength $n$ (valid parenthesizations of $n$ pairs of parentheses).

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Theorem 2.12 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-thm-18`).

articles.title: Unlucky cars of an extremely lucky Stirling permutation
articles.statement:
Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a
Stirling permutation of order $n$ that is extremely lucky, that is, its set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$
of lucky cars has exactly $n$ elements, and let $1 \le i \le n$. If car $j$ is unlucky and
exactly $i - 1$ of the cars $1, \dots, j - 1$ are unlucky, then car $j$ prefers spot
$w_j = n - i + 1$ and has displacement $d(j) = 2i - 1$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Lemma 5.7 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-lem-42`).

articles.title: When $\{1, n - 1, 2n - 2\}$ is an admissible lucky set
articles.statement:
For every integer $n \ge 4$, the
set $\{1, n - 1, 2n - 2\}$ is an $n$-admissible lucky set if and only if $n$ is even.

As printed the claim covers all $n$, but it fails at $n = 3$: $w = 133221$ is a Stirling
permutation of order $3$ with $\mathrm{Lucky}(w) = \{1, 2, 4\} = \{1, n - 1, 2n - 2\}$ (its cars
park in spots $1, 3, 4, 2, 5, 6$). The paper's proof assumes $n > 3$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Proposition 4.4 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-prop-35`).

articles.title: Admissible lucky sets with two elements
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $h$ and $i$ be natural numbers with
$h < i \le 2n$. The set $\{h, i\}$ is an $n$-admissible lucky set if and only if $h = 1$ and
either $i > n$ and $i$ is odd, or $i \le n$.

The bound $i \le 2n$ is the paper's standing assumption that lucky sets lie in
$\{1, \dots, 2n\}$; without it $\{1, 2n + 1\}$ would satisfy the right-hand side.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Theorem 4.1 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-thm-32`).

articles.title: Admissible lucky sets
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number. A finite set $S$ of natural numbers
is an $n$-admissible lucky set if $S = \mathrm{Lucky}(w)$ for some Stirling permutation $w$ of
order $n$, where $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$ is the set of lucky cars of $w$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Definition 3.1.

articles.title: Counting admissible lucky sets with two elements
articles.statement:
For every integer $n \ge 1$, the number
of $n$-admissible lucky sets with exactly two elements is $n - 1 + \lceil (n - 1)/2 \rceil$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Corollary 4.2 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-cor-33`).

articles.title: Necessary conditions for admissible lucky sets
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$. If $S$ is an
$n$-admissible lucky set, then $1 \in S$ and $2n \notin S$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Corollary 3.4 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-cor-24`).

articles.title: Number of cars with zero displacement
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $w$ be a Stirling
permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$. The number of cars
$i \in \{1, \dots, 2n\}$ with displacement $d(i) = 0$ is at least $1$ and at most $n$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Corollary 5.6 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-cor-41`).

articles.title: Displacement compositions of 1122 and 11244233
articles.statement:
The displacement composition of a word
$w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ is $\mathrm{dis}(w) = (d(1), \dots, d(2n))$, where $d(i)$ is the
displacement of car $i$. For the Stirling permutations $1122$ of order $2$ and $11244233$ of
order $4$, $\mathrm{dis}(1122) = (0, 1, 1, 2)$ and
$\mathrm{dis}(11244233) = (0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 4, 4, 5)$ (the paper's Example 5.5).

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Definition 5.4 and Example 5.5.

articles.title: Displacement of a car
articles.statement:
Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a word of natural numbers. Car
$i$ prefers spot $q_i = ((w_i - 1) \bmod 2n) + 1$, where $w_i - 1$ is truncated at $0$; when
every $w_i$ lies in $\{1, \dots, 2n\}$, this is $q_i = w_i$. Cars $1, \dots, 2n$ arrive in
order, and car $i$ parks in the least spot $p(i) \in \{q_i, \dots, 2n\}$ not taken by an
earlier car, or in $p(i) = q_i$ if there is no such spot. The displacement of car $i$ is
$d(i) = p(i) - w_i$, where the subtraction is truncated at $0$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Definition 5.1; the tuple `i ↦ d(i + 1)` is the displacement composition `dis(w)` (Definition 5.4).

articles.title: The first preference bounds the lucky cars
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be a Stirling permutation of
order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$, with at least $3$ lucky cars, and let $x$
be the second-smallest lucky car of $w$. If $x \ge n$, then the number of lucky cars of $w$ is
at most $w_1$, and every lucky car parks in one of the spots $1, \dots, w_1$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Lemma 3.10 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-lem-30`).

articles.title: Basic properties of lucky cars
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $w$ be a Stirling permutation of
order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$. Then (a) car $1$ is lucky; (b) the first
car $i$ with $w_i = 1$ is lucky; (c) the number of lucky cars of $w$ is at least $1$ and at
most $n$.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is added: the only Stirling permutation of order $0$ is the empty
word, which has no cars.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Lemma 2.1 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-lem-5`).

articles.title: Characterization of extremely lucky Stirling permutations
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be a Stirling
permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$. Then $w$ has exactly $n$
lucky cars if and only if the second occurrences of the letters of $w$ appear in decreasing
order: for all positions $a < b$ such that $w_a$ also occurs before position $a$ and $w_b$ also
occurs before position $b$, we have $w_b < w_a$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Proposition 2.11 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-prop-17`).

articles.title: Characterization of extremely unlucky Stirling permutations
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $w$
be a Stirling permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$. Then car $1$
is the only lucky car of $w$ if and only if for every $x \in \{2, \dots, n\}$ and every
position $i \le x$, we have $w_i < x$.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is added: the empty word, the only Stirling permutation of order $0$,
has no lucky cars, while the right-hand side holds vacuously.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Corollary 2.5 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-cor-11`).

articles.title: Lucky sets of 1122 and 1221
articles.statement:
Read as parking functions of length $4$, the Stirling
permutation $1122$ has car $1$ as its only lucky car, and $1221$ has exactly cars $1$ and $2$
lucky: $\mathrm{Lucky}(1122) = \{1\}$ and $\mathrm{Lucky}(1221) = \{1, 2\}$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Definitions 1.2 and 3.1.

articles.title: The lucky set of a word
articles.statement:
Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a word of natural numbers. Car
$i$ prefers spot $q_i = ((w_i - 1) \bmod 2n) + 1$, where $w_i - 1$ is truncated at $0$; when
every $w_i$ lies in $\{1, \dots, 2n\}$, this is $q_i = w_i$. Cars $1, \dots, 2n$ arrive in
order, and car $i$ parks in the least spot $p(i) \in \{q_i, \dots, 2n\}$ not taken by an
earlier car, or in $p(i) = q_i$ if there is no such spot. The lucky set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$
is the set of cars $i \in \{1, \dots, 2n\}$ with $p(i) = w_i$; when every $w_i$ lies in
$\{1, \dots, 2n\}$, these are the cars that park in their preferred spot.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Definition 1.2.

articles.title: Left-to-right minima of a Stirling permutation sit at odd positions
articles.statement:
Let
$w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$ and let $j \in \{1, \dots, 2n\}$.
If $w_j < w_i$ for every $i < j$, then $j$ is odd.

In the paper, $j$ is the first car preferring spot $w_j$; the hypothesis $w_j < w_i$ for all
$i < j$ already implies this, and $w_j \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ holds for every Stirling permutation.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Lemma 3.7 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-lem-27`).

articles.title: Parking before the second lucky car
articles.statement:
Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a Stirling permutation
of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$, and let $x$ be a lucky car of $w$ such
that exactly one lucky car of $w$ is smaller than $x$, so that $x$ is the second-smallest element
of the lucky set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$. Then every car $c$ with $2 \le c \le x - 1$ parks in spot
$w_1 + c - 1$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Lemma 3.5 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-lem-25`).

articles.title: Parking spot of a car
articles.statement:
Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a word of natural numbers. Car $i$
prefers spot $q_i = ((w_i - 1) \bmod 2n) + 1$, where $w_i - 1$ is truncated at $0$; when every
$w_i$ lies in $\{1, \dots, 2n\}$, this is $q_i = w_i$. Cars $1, \dots, 2n$ arrive in order, and
car $i$ parks in the least spot $p(i) \in \{q_i, \dots, 2n\}$ not taken by an earlier car, or in
$p(i) = q_i$ if there is no such spot. The parking spot of car $i \in \{1, \dots, 2n\}$ is $p(i)$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Definition 5.1.

articles.title: When the penultimate car is lucky
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a
Stirling permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$. Then car $2n - 1$
is lucky, that is, belongs to the lucky set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$, if and only if $w_{2n-1} = 1$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Theorem 3.11 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-thm-31`).

articles.title: Zero-based preferences of a word
articles.statement:
Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a word of natural
numbers, read as the preferences of $2n$ cars for spots numbered $0, \dots, 2n - 1$. Car
$i \in \{1, \dots, 2n\}$ prefers the spot $(w_i - 1) \bmod 2n$, where $w_i - 1$ is truncated at
$0$. When every $w_i$ lies in $\{1, \dots, 2n\}$, for example when $w$ is a Stirling permutation
of order $n$, this is the spot $w_i - 1$, which is spot $w_i$ in the one-based numbering.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Section 1 (Stirling permutations read as parking functions of length `2n`).

articles.title: Stirling permutations whose second lucky car is $n$
articles.statement:
Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a
Stirling permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$, such that car $n$
is lucky and exactly one lucky car of $w$ is smaller than $n$, so that $n$ is the second-smallest
element of the lucky set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$. (a) If $n$ is even, then $w_1 = 1$, $w_n = n$ and
$\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$ has exactly $2$ elements. (b) If $n$ is odd and $w_1 = 1$, then $w_n = n$ and
$\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$ has exactly $2$ elements.

The paper states this for an admissible lucky set $S$ and a Stirling permutation $w$ with
$\mathrm{Lucky}(w) = S$; here it holds for every such $w$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Lemma 4.3 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-lem-34`).

articles.title: A second lucky car beyond $n$ is odd
articles.statement:
Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a Stirling
permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$, and let $x$ be a lucky car
of $w$ such that exactly one lucky car of $w$ is smaller than $x$, so that $x$ is the
second-smallest element of the lucky set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$. If $x > n$, then $x$ is odd.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Proposition 3.8 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-prop-28`).

articles.title: Preference of the second lucky car
articles.statement:
Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a Stirling permutation
of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$, and let $x$ be a lucky car of $w$ such
that exactly one lucky car of $w$ is smaller than $x$, so that $x$ is the second-smallest element
of the lucky set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$. If $w_1 = 1$, then $x \le w_x \le n$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Lemma 3.9 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-lem-29`).

articles.title: Total displacement of a Stirling permutation is invariant under rearrangement
articles.statement:
Let
$w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$ and let $\sigma$ be a permutation
of $\{1, \dots, 2n\}$. Read words of length $2n$ as parking functions, and let $d(v)$ denote the
total displacement of a word $v$, the sum of the displacements of its cars. Then the rearranged
word $w \circ \sigma = w_{\sigma(1)} \cdots w_{\sigma(2n)}$ satisfies $d(w \circ \sigma) = d(w)$.

The rearranged word $w \circ \sigma$ need not be a Stirling permutation.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Lemma 5.2 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-lem-37`), quoting Elder, Harris, Kretschmann, and Martínez Mori, Lemma 3.1.

articles.title: Total displacement of a Stirling permutation
articles.statement:
Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a Stirling
permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$. Then the total displacement
of $w$, the sum $d(1) + \dots + d(2n)$ of the displacements of its cars, is $n^2$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Corollary 5.3 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-cor-38`).

articles.title: Total displacement of a word
articles.statement:
Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a word of natural numbers,
and for $i \in \{1, \dots, 2n\}$ let $d(i)$ be the displacement of car $i$ in $w$. The total
displacement of $w$ is $d(w) = \sum_{i=1}^{2n} d(i)$.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Definition 5.1.

articles.title: Extending admissible lucky sets
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$. If $S$ is an $n$-admissible lucky set,
then both $S$ and $S \cup \{2n + 1\}$ are $(n + 1)$-admissible lucky sets.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is added: the empty set is $0$-admissible but not $1$-admissible.

## Sources

- L. Colmenarejo et al., *On the Lucky and Displacement Statistics of Stirling Permutations*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.7, Theorem 3.3 (`jis-2024-24.6.7-thm-23`).

articles.title: Ballot paths
articles.statement:
For $k, \ell \in \mathbb{N}$, a ballot path to $(k, \ell)$ is a word of length
$k + \ell$ in up steps and right steps with exactly $\ell$ up steps such that every prefix has at
least as many up steps as right steps; equivalently, a lattice path from $(0,0)$ to $(k, \ell)$
with unit up and right steps that stays on or above the line $y = x$.

articles.title: Number of ballot paths
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k \le \ell$, the number of lattice paths
from $(0,0)$ to $(k, \ell)$ with unit up and right steps that stay on or above the line $y = x$
is $\frac{\ell - k + 1}{\ell + 1} \binom{k + \ell}{k}$.

## Sources

- Steve Butler et al., "Lucky Cars and Lucky Spots in Parking Functions", Lemma 21.

articles.title: Lucky spots of weakly decreasing parking functions as a Catalan convolution
articles.statement:
Number the
cars and spots $0, \dots, n-1$. For cars $i$ and spots $j$, let $q^d_n(i, j)$ be the number of
weakly decreasing parking functions $f$ of length $n$ (that is, $f(0) \ge f(1) \ge \dots \ge
f(n-1)$) with $f(i) = j$ in which car $i$ is lucky. Then for every spot $j$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} q^d_n(i, j) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-j-1} C_{n-1-k} \, C_k,$$

where $C_m$ is the $m$-th Catalan number.

The left side counts the weakly decreasing parking functions in which spot $j$ is lucky, that
is, taken by a car that prefers it.

## Sources

- Steve Butler et al., "Lucky Cars and Lucky Spots in Parking Functions", Theorem 24.

articles.title: Lucky spots of weakly decreasing parking functions as a sum
articles.statement:
Number the cars and spots
$0, \dots, n-1$. For cars $i$ and spots $j$, let $q^d_n(i, j)$ be the number of weakly decreasing
parking functions $f$ of length $n$ (that is, $f(0) \ge f(1) \ge \dots \ge f(n-1)$) with
$f(i) = j$ in which car $i$ is lucky. Then for every spot $j$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} q^d_n(i, j) = \sum_{i=1}^{n-j} \frac{(n-i-j+1)^2}{(n+1-i)(n-j)}
\binom{n-i+j}{j} \binom{n-j+i-2}{i-1}.$$

The left side counts the weakly decreasing parking functions in which spot $j$ is lucky, that
is, taken by a car that prefers it.

## Sources

- Steve Butler et al., "Lucky Cars and Lucky Spots in Parking Functions", Corollary 23.

articles.title: Parking functions with prescribed lucky and unlucky cars
articles.statement:
Number the cars and spots
$0, \dots, n-1$, and let $L$ and $U$ be disjoint sets of cars. The number of parking functions
of length $n$ in which every car in $L$ is lucky and no car in $U$ is lucky equals

$$\prod_{i \in L} (n + 1 - i) \cdot \prod_{i \in U} i \cdot (n + 1)^{n - |L| - |U| - 1},$$

where the power is taken in $\mathbb{Q}$, so the exponent may be negative.

In the paper's numbering of cars from $1$, the factors are $n + 2 - i$ and $i - 1$.

## Sources

- Steve Butler et al., "Lucky Cars and Lucky Spots in Parking Functions", Theorem 4.

articles.title: Factorial moments of the number of lucky cars
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$X(f)$ be the number of lucky cars of a parking function $f$ of length $n$, and let
$P_n(x) = \frac{1}{n+1} \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \bigl((n+1-i)x + i\bigr) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$. Then

$$\frac{1}{(n+1)^{n-1}} \sum_f X(f)\bigl(X(f)-1\bigr)\cdots\bigl(X(f)-\ell+1\bigr) =
\frac{P_n^{(\ell)}(1)}{(n+1)^{n-1}},$$

where $f$ runs over the parking functions of length $n$ and $P_n^{(\ell)}$ is the $\ell$-th
derivative of $P_n$. Since there are $(n+1)^{n-1}$ parking functions of length $n$, the left side
is the $\ell$-th falling-factorial moment of $X$ for a uniformly random parking function.

## Sources

- Steve Butler et al., "Lucky Cars and Lucky Spots in Parking Functions", Proposition 6.

articles.title: Expected number of lucky cars in weakly decreasing parking functions
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 1$, the
sum of the numbers of lucky cars over all weakly decreasing parking functions $f$ of length $n$
(those with $f(0) \ge f(1) \ge \dots \ge f(n-1)$), divided by the Catalan number $C_n$, equals
$\frac{n+1}{2}$.

There are $C_n$ weakly decreasing parking functions of length $n$, so this is the expected number
of lucky cars, which equals the expected number of lucky spots.

## Sources

- Steve Butler et al., "Lucky Cars and Lucky Spots in Parking Functions", Theorem 25.

articles.title: Expected number of lucky cars in weakly increasing parking functions
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$. Number
cars and spots from $0$, and encode a weakly increasing parking function of length $n$ as a
nondecreasing map $a : \{0, \dots, n-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with $a(i) \le i$ for every $i$.
The average, over all such maps $a$, of the number of indices $i$ with $a(i) = i$ equals
$\frac{3n}{n+2}$. Here car $i$ parks in spot $i$ and is lucky exactly when $a(i) = i$, so this
number counts both the lucky cars and the lucky spots.

## Sources

- Steve Butler, Kimberly Hadaway, Victoria Lenius, Preston Martens, and Marshall Moats, "Lucky Cars and Lucky Spots in Parking Functions," Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.1, Corollary, lines 631–633 (supporting lemma lines 619–629), https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL29/Hadaway/had3.tex The corollary attributes the Dyck-path expectation value to Deutsch.

articles.title: Lucky car under greedy parking
articles.statement:
Let $f : \{0, \dots, n-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ give the
preferred spot of each of $n$ cars. Cars $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ arrive in order, and each takes the
least spot at or after its preference not taken by an earlier car, or its preferred spot itself
when there is no such spot. Car $i$ is lucky if the spot it takes is its preferred spot $f(i)$.

For a parking function a free spot always exists.

articles.title: Number of lucky cars
articles.statement:
Let $f : \{0, \dots, n-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ give the preferred
spot of each of $n$ cars, and let cars $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ arrive in order, each taking the least
spot at or after its preference not taken by an earlier car, or its preferred spot itself when
there is no such spot. The number of lucky cars of $f$ is the number of cars $i$ whose spot is
$f(i)$.

articles.title: Generating polynomial of lucky cars
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $0 \le k \le n$, let $c_k$
be the number of parking functions of length $n$ with exactly $k$ lucky cars. Then in
$\mathbb{Q}[x]$,

$$\frac{1}{n+1} \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \bigl((n+1-i)x + i\bigr) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} c_k x^k.$$

## Sources

- Steve Butler et al., "Lucky Cars and Lucky Spots in Parking Functions", Corollary 5.

articles.title: Lucky-car polynomial
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $f_n \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ is the polynomial

$$f_n(x) = \frac{1}{n+1} \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \bigl((n+1-i)\,x + i\bigr).$$

Equivalently, $f_n(x) = \frac{1}{n+1} \prod_{i=1}^{n} \bigl((n+2-i)\,x + (i-1)\bigr)$.

articles.title: Next free spot
articles.statement:
Number the $n$ spots $0, \dots, n-1$. Given a set $S$ of occupied
spots and a spot $a$, the next free spot is the least spot $s \ge a$ with $s \notin S$; when
every spot $s \ge a$ is occupied, it is $a$ itself.

articles.title: Greedy parking from an occupied set
articles.statement:
Number the $n$ spots $0, \dots, n-1$. Given a list
$a_1, \dots, a_m$ of preferred spots and a set $S$ of occupied spots, cars $1, \dots, m$ arrive in
order and car $k$ takes the least spot at or after $a_k$ that is neither in $S$ nor taken by cars
$1, \dots, k-1$ (or $a_k$ itself if there is none). The result is the list of spots taken, in
arrival order.

articles.title: Greedy parking outcome
articles.statement:
Let $f : \{0, \dots, n-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ give the
preferred spot of each of $n$ cars. Starting from an empty lot with spots $0, \dots, n-1$, cars
$0, 1, \dots, n-1$ arrive in order, and each takes the least free spot at or after its preference
(or its preference itself if there is none). The outcome sends each car $i$ to the spot it takes.

articles.title: Boundary values of lucky-car counts (Lemma 9)
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$, number the cars and spots
$0, \dots, n-1$, and let $q_n(i, j)$ be the number of parking functions of length $n$ in which
car $i$ prefers spot $j$ and is lucky. Then for all $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, with powers
taken in $\mathbb{Q}$ (the integer exponents may be negative),

$$q_n(n-1, j) = \binom{n-1}{j} (j+1)^{j-1} (n-j)^{n-j-2},$$



$$q_n(0, j) = \sum_{k=j+1}^{n} \binom{n-1}{k-1} k^{k-2} (n-k+1)^{n-k-1},$$



$$q_n(i, n-1) = n^{n-2},$$



$$q_n(i, 0) = (n+1)^{n-i-2}\, n^{i-1}\, (2n-i).$$

In the one-based indexing of the source, car $i$ and spot $j$ here are car $i+1$ and spot $j+1$.

## Sources

- Steve Butler et al., "Lucky Cars and Lucky Spots in Parking Functions", Lemma 9.

articles.title: Decreasing lucky-car counts (Lemma 22)
articles.statement:
Number the cars and spots $0, \dots, n-1$, and let
$q^{\mathrm{dec}}_n(i, j)$ be the number of weakly decreasing parking functions of length $n$ in
which car $i$ prefers spot $j$ and is lucky. For all $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, if $i + j < n$
then

$$q^{\mathrm{dec}}_n(i, j) = \frac{(n-i-j)^2}{(n-i)(n-j)} \binom{n-i+j-1}{j} \binom{n-j+i-1}{i},$$

and $q^{\mathrm{dec}}_n(i, j) = 0$ otherwise.

In the one-based indexing of the source the condition reads $i + j \le n + 1$.

## Sources

- Steve Butler et al., "Lucky Cars and Lucky Spots in Parking Functions", Lemma 22.

articles.title: Decreasing lucky-car counts
articles.statement:
Number the cars and spots $0, \dots, n-1$. For
$i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, $q^{\mathrm{dec}}_n(i, j)$ is the number of weakly decreasing parking
functions $f : \{0, \dots, n-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with $f(i) = j$ in which car $i$ is lucky,
that is, parks in spot $f(i)$.

In the one-based indexing of Butler et al. this is $q^d_n(i+1, j+1)$.

articles.title: Increasing lucky-car counts (Lemma 18)
articles.statement:
Number the cars and spots $0, \dots, n-1$, let
$q^{\mathrm{inc}}_n(i, j)$ be the number of weakly increasing parking functions of length $n$ in
which car $i$ prefers spot $j$ and is lucky, and let $C_m$ be the $m$-th Catalan number. For all
$i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, $q^{\mathrm{inc}}_n(i, j) = C_i \, C_{n-i}$ if $i = j$, and
$q^{\mathrm{inc}}_n(i, j) = 0$ otherwise.

In the one-based indexing of the source the diagonal value reads $C_{i-1} C_{n-i+1}$.

## Sources

- Steve Butler et al., "Lucky Cars and Lucky Spots in Parking Functions", Lemma 18.

articles.title: Increasing lucky-car counts
articles.statement:
Number the cars and spots $0, \dots, n-1$. For
$i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, $q^{\mathrm{inc}}_n(i, j)$ is the number of weakly increasing parking
functions $f : \{0, \dots, n-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with $f(i) = j$ in which car $i$ is lucky,
that is, parks in spot $f(i)$.

In the one-based indexing of Butler et al. this is $q^i_n(i+1, j+1)$.

articles.title: Lucky-car counts
articles.statement:
Number the cars and spots $0, \dots, n-1$. For
$i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, $q_n(i, j)$ is the number of parking functions
$f : \{0, \dots, n-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with $f(i) = j$ in which car $i$ is lucky, that is,
parks in spot $f(i)$.

In the one-based indexing of Butler et al. this is $q_n(i+1, j+1)$.

articles.title: Number of parking functions in which a given car is lucky
articles.statement:
Number cars and spots
$0, \dots, n-1$, and let $q_n(i, j)$ be the number of parking functions of length $n$ in which
car $i$ prefers spot $j$ and parks there. Then for every $n$ and every car $i < n$,

$$\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} q_n(i, j) = (n + 1 - i)(n + 1)^{n-2},$$

an identity in $\mathbb{Q}$ (for $n = 1$ the exponent is $-1$). The left side is the number of
parking functions of length $n$ in which car $i$ is lucky; in the paper's one-based numbering
the count for the $i$-th car is $(n + 2 - i)(n + 1)^{n-2}$.

## Sources

- Steve Butler et al., "Lucky Cars and Lucky Spots in Parking Functions", Corollary 10.

articles.title: Number of parking functions in which the second spot is lucky
articles.statement:
Number cars and spots
$0, \dots, n-1$, and let $q_n(i, j)$ be the number of parking functions of length $n$ in which
car $i$ prefers spot $j$ and parks there. Then for every $n \ge 2$, in $\mathbb{Q}$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} q_n(i, 1) = \frac{3}{4}(n + 1)^{n-1} - \frac{1}{4}(n - 1)^{n-1}.$$

Since at most one car parks in spot $1$, the left side is the number of parking functions of
length $n$ in which the second spot is lucky, that is, the car parking there preferred it.

## Sources

- Steve Butler et al., "Lucky Cars and Lucky Spots in Parking Functions", Theorem 12.

articles.title: Parking-function shuffles and the first entry
articles.statement:
Let $1 \le m \le n$ and $1 \le k \le n$,
and let $w = (w_1, \dots, w_{m-1})$ be a word with entries in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Then the set
of spots $j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ for which $(j, w_1, \dots, w_{m-1})$ is a partial parking
function with $m$ cars and $n$ spots equals $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$ if and only if $w$ lies in the
set $\mathrm{Sh}_m(k - 1, n - k)$ of $(m, n)$-parking-function shuffles with parameter $k$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Theorem 3, with Definition 6 (the sets `A^n`).

articles.title: Classical parking functions are metered parking functions
articles.statement:
Let $m \le n$. Every partial
parking function $f$ with $m$ cars and $n$ spots is a $t$-metered parking function for every
$t \in \mathbb{N}$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Proposition 4.

articles.title: Metered parking functions with a long meter are classical
articles.statement:
Let $m \le n$ and
$t \ge m - 1$. A map $f : \{0, \dots, m-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is a $t$-metered parking
function if and only if it is a partial parking function with $m$ cars and $n$ spots.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Proposition 3.

articles.title: One-metered parking functions and laces
articles.statement:
Let $0 < m \le n$ and
$f : \{0, \dots, m-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Then $f$ is a $1$-metered parking function if and
only if, in the lace decomposition of $(f(0), \dots, f(m-1))$, the last spot $n - 1$ occurs in
no lace other than as its first entry.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Theorem 1.

articles.title: One-metered parking functions with two spots
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and
$f : \{0, \dots, m-1\} \to \{0, 1\}$. Then $f$ is a $1$-metered parking function with $m$ cars and
$2$ spots if and only if every lace of the lace decomposition of $(f(0), \dots, f(m-1))$ that
contains the value $1$ has length $1$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Corollary 3.

articles.title: Metered parking functions with meter $n - 1$ and more cars than spots
articles.statement:
Let $k > 0$ and
$f : \{0, \dots, n+k-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and let $\pi_0, \dots, \pi_{n-1}$ be the
$(n-1)$-metered outcome of the first $n$ preferences $(f(0), \dots, f(n-1))$ on $n$ spots, where
$\pi_c$ is the spot in which car $c$ parks, if it parks. Then $f$ is an $(n-1)$-metered parking
function if and only if $(f(0), \dots, f(n-1))$ is a parking function and, for every
$i \in \{0, \dots, k-1\}$, car $i \bmod n$ parks in this outcome and $f(n + i) \le \pi_{i \bmod n}$.

The outcome is read periodically: the later preferences $f(n), f(n+1), \dots$ are compared with
$\pi_0, \dots, \pi_{n-1}, \pi_0, \dots$ in turn.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Characterization of $(m-2)$-metered parking functions
articles.statement:
Let $2 < m \le n + 1$,
$f : \{0, \dots, m-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $j \in \mathbb{N}$. Write
$\mathrm{Sh}_p(q - 1, N - q)$ for the set of $(p, N)$-parking-function shuffles with parameter
$q$, words of length $p - 1$ with entries in $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$. Suppose that the middle word
$w = (f(1), \dots, f(m-2))$ lies in $\mathrm{Sh}_{m-1}(k - 1, n - k)$, and that either
$m = n + 1$ and $j = 0$, or $m \le n$, $1 \le j \le k - 1$ and the subsequence $\sigma$ of the
entries of $w$ that are less than $k - 1$, a word of length $m + k - n - 2$ with entries in
$\{0, \dots, k-2\}$, lies in $\mathrm{Sh}_{m+k-n-1}(j - 1, k - 1 - j)$. Then $f$ is an
$(m-2)$-metered parking function if and only if either $f(0) < j$ and $f(m-1) < k$, or
$j \le f(0) < k$ and $f(m-1) \le f(0)$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Metered parking function
articles.statement:
Let $m, n, t \in \mathbb{N}$, number the $n$ spots
$0, \dots, n-1$, and let $f : \{0, \dots, m-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ give the preferred spot of
each of $m$ cars. In the $t$-metered scheme the cars arrive in the order $0, 1, \dots, m-1$, and
car $i$ parks in the least spot $s$ with $f(i) \le s \le n - 1$ that is not occupied by any of the
(at most $t$) cars that arrived just before car $i$; it fails to park if there is no such spot.
Then $f$ is a $t$-metered parking function if every car parks.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Section 1 (definition of `t`-metered parking functions).

articles.title: Number of parking-function shuffles
articles.statement:
Let $1 \le m \le n$ and $1 \le k \le n$, and write
$\mathrm{Sh}_m(k - 1, n - k)$ for the set of $(m, n)$-parking-function shuffles with parameter
$k$, words of length $m - 1$ with entries in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Then
$|\mathrm{Sh}_m(k - 1, n - k)|$ equals $\binom{m-1}{n-k}(n-m+1)\,k^{m-n+k-2}(n-k+1)^{n-k-1}$
if $k > n - m + 1$, equals $m^{m-2}$ if $k = n - m + 1$, and equals $0$ if $k < n - m + 1$.
The exponent $-1$ occurs only on the base $1$ (at $k = n$, and at $m = 1$), and $1^{-1} = 1$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Lemma 4.

articles.title: An example of a parking-function shuffle
articles.statement:
The word $(2, 6, 1, 0, 6, 1)$ with entries
in $\{0, \dots, 7\}$, which is $(3, 7, 2, 1, 7, 2)$ in one-based values, is a
$(7, 8)$-parking-function shuffle with parameter $k = 6$, that is, it lies in
$\mathrm{Sh}_7(5, 2)$. In one-based values it is a shuffle of the parking function
$(3, 2, 1, 2)$ with $4$ cars and $5$ spots and of $(7, 7) = (1, 1) + (6, 6)$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Section 4, Example 5.

articles.title: Parking-function shuffles
articles.statement:
Let $m'$, $n$, $k$ be natural numbers and let
$\pi : \{0, \dots, m' - 1\} \to \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, with one-based letters $w_i = \pi(i) + 1$.
Then $\pi$ is a parking-function shuffle with parameters $(m', n, k)$ when all of the following
hold: no letter $w_i$ equals $k$; exactly $\max(m' + k - n, 0)$ letters satisfy $w_i < k$;
exactly $\max(n - k, 0)$ letters satisfy $w_i > k$; for every $s$ with $1 \le s \le k - 1$, at
most $k - s$ letters satisfy $s \le w_i \le k - 1$; and for every $s$ with $k + 1 \le s \le n$, at
most $n + 1 - s$ letters satisfy $w_i \ge s$.

With $m = m' + 1$, the word $(w_0, \dots, w_{m'-1})$ plays the role of the source's
$(\pi_2, \dots, \pi_m)$, and the conditions express membership in the source's set
$\mathrm{Sh}_m(k - 1, n - k)$ of shuffles of a parking function of $m - n + k - 1$ cars on
$k - 1$ spots (the letters below $k$) with a parking function of length $n - k$ shifted up by
$k$ (the letters above $k$): parking-function membership does not depend on the order of the
letters, and the last two conditions are the usual counting criterion for every car to park.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Section 4, Definition of `(m, n)`-parking function shuffles (`Sh_m(k - 1, n - k)`).

articles.title: Examples of lace decompositions
articles.statement:
The lace decomposition of $(3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 6)$ is
$((3, 3), (3, 3, 4), (6))$, and the lace decomposition of $(4, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 1, 2)$ is
$((4), (1), (2, 2, 3, 4, 5), (5), (1), (2))$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Section 3, example after the definition of the lace decomposition.

articles.title: Lace decomposition
articles.statement:
A lace is a sequence of natural numbers of the form $(p)$ or
$(p, p, p+1, \dots, p+\ell-2)$ for some natural number $p$ and some length $\ell \ge 2$. The lace
decomposition of a finite sequence $(a_1, \dots, a_k)$ of natural numbers is its partition into
blocks of consecutive entries built greedily from left to right: starting with no blocks, each
entry $a_i$ in turn is appended to the last block if the result is again a lace, and otherwise
starts a new block $(a_i)$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Section 3 (definitions of a lace and of the lace decomposition).

articles.title: One step of the lace decomposition
articles.statement:
Given a list of blocks (each a list of natural
numbers) and a natural number $a$: if the last block is $(p)$ with $a = p$, or the last block has
at least two entries and ends with $e$ where $a = e + 1$, then $a$ is appended to the last block;
otherwise, including when there is no block, a new block $(a)$ is added at the end.

Applied to a list of laces, where a lace is $(p)$ or $(p, p, p+1, \dots, p+\ell-2)$ for some
natural number $p$ and some length $\ell \ge 2$, this extends the last lace exactly when the
result is again a lace.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Section 3 (definitions of a lace and of the lace decomposition).

articles.title: Metered parking functions in which every car is lucky
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 2$, $n \ge 2$ and
$t \le m - 1$. The number of $t$-metered $(m, n)$-parking functions in which every car parks in
its preferred spot is $n(n-1)\cdots(n-t+1) \cdot (n-t)^{m-t}$, where the falling factorial
$n(n-1)\cdots(n-t+1)$ has $t$ factors (it equals $1$ for $t = 0$ and $0$ for $t > n$).

The source's companion formula (12) for exactly one lucky car is not stated: it is false as
printed when $m > n + 1$ (for $n = 2$, $m = 4$, $t = 1$ the count is $0$, while the formula
$(t-1)!\,(n-m+1)\,t^{m-t}$ gives $-1$).

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Proposition 8, Equation (13).

articles.title: Lucky cars in the metered scheme
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $t$, $m$, $n$ and a preference
function $f : \{0, \dots, m - 1\} \to \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ (car $i$ prefers spot $f(i)$), the
lucky count of $f$ under the $t$-metered parking scheme on $n$ spots is the number of cars $i$
that park in their preferred spot $f(i)$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Section 2 (`lucky(α)`).

articles.title: Displacement bound in the metered scheme
articles.statement:
Let $t$, $m$, $n$ be natural numbers, let
$f : \{0, \dots, m - 1\} \to \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ be a preference function and let $i < m$ be a
car. Under the $t$-metered parking scheme on $n$ spots, if car $i$ parks in spot $s$ then
$s \le f(i) + t$, that is, its displacement is at most $t$; and if car $i$ fails to park then
$f(i) + t \ge n$.

In the source's one-based numbering, with preference $a_i = f(i) + 1$, a car that fails to park
has $a_i \ge n - t + 1$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Proposition 5.

articles.title: Metered outcomes of a seven-car example on six spots
articles.statement:
On the six spots
$\{0, \dots, 5\}$, for seven cars with preferences $(2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5)$, the $2$-metered
parking scheme parks the cars in spots $(2, 3, 4, 2, 3, 4, 5)$, while in the $1$-metered scheme
the first six cars park in spots $(2, 3, 2, 3, 4, 5)$ and the seventh car fails to park.

In the source's one-based notation, where $O^t_n$ is the outcome of the $t$-metered scheme on
$n$ spots and $X$ marks a car that fails to park, $O^2_6(3,3,3,3,4,5,6) = (3,4,5,3,4,5,6)$ and
$O^1_6(3,3,3,3,4,5,6) = (3,4,3,4,5,6,X)$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, example after the definition of the outcome (Section 2).

articles.title: A 1-metered example in which the third car fails
articles.statement:
In the $1$-metered parking scheme on
two spots $\{0, 1\}$, if three cars arrive with preferences $0$, $0$, $1$, then the first two
cars park in spots $0$ and $1$ and the third car fails to park.

In the source's one-based numbering: with preferences $(1, 1, 2)$, car $3$ fails.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, example after the definition of `t`-metered parking functions (Section 1).

articles.title: A 1-metered example in which every car parks
articles.statement:
In the $1$-metered parking scheme on two
spots $\{0, 1\}$, if three cars arrive all preferring spot $0$, then they park in spots $0$, $1$
and $0$, in that order.

In the source's one-based numbering: preferences $(1, 1, 1)$ give spots $1, 2, 1$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, example after the definition of `t`-metered parking functions (Section 1).

articles.title: Outcome of the metered parking scheme
articles.statement:
Let $t, n \in \mathbb{N}$, number the $n$ spots
$0, \dots, n-1$, and let $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{m-1}$ be a list of preferences in $\mathbb{N}$.
Cars arrive in order, and car $i$ parks in the least spot $s$ with $a_i \le s < n$ that is not
taken by one of the previous $t$ cars (cars $\max(0, i - t), \dots, i - 1$) that parked; if
there is no such spot, car $i$ fails. The outcome is the list whose $i$-th entry is the spot of
car $i$, or a failure marker if car $i$ fails. Thus after car $j$ arrives, car $j - t$ leaves,
and only the cars among the last $t$ entries of the outcome so far occupy spots.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Section 1 (definition of the `t`-metered scheme) and Section 2 (definition of the outcome).

articles.title: Vanishing of metered parking counts
articles.statement:
Let $m, n, t$ be natural numbers with $m > n$ and
$t \ge n$. Then there are no $t$-metered $(m, n)$-parking functions, that is,
$\mathrm{mpf}_{m,n}(t) = 0$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Proposition 2.

articles.title: Binet formula for 1-metered parking functions
articles.statement:
Let $m, n$ be natural numbers with
$m \le n + 1$ and $n > 2$. Then the number $\mathrm{mpf}_{m,n}(1)$ of $1$-metered
$(m, n)$-parking functions satisfies, as real numbers,

$$\mathrm{mpf}_{m,n}(1) = \frac{n(n + \sqrt{n^2-4}) - 2}{n(n + \sqrt{n^2-4}) - 4}
\left(\frac{n + \sqrt{n^2-4}}{2}\right)^m +
\frac{n(n - \sqrt{n^2-4}) - 2}{n(n - \sqrt{n^2-4}) - 4}
\left(\frac{n - \sqrt{n^2-4}}{2}\right)^m.$$

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Corollary 5.

articles.title: 1-metered parking functions with as many cars as spots
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n > 2$, the number of $1$-metered $(n, n)$-parking functions is

$$\mathrm{mpf}_{n,n}(1) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (n-2)^{n-k} \binom{2n+1-k}{k}.$$

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Corollary 4.

articles.title: Lucas-type recursion for 1-metered parking functions
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{mpf}_{m,n}(1)$ for
the number of $1$-metered $(m, n)$-parking functions. For every natural number $n$,
$\mathrm{mpf}_{1,n}(1) = n$ and $\mathrm{mpf}_{0,n}(1) = 1$, and for every natural number $m$
with $1 \le m \le n$,

$$\mathrm{mpf}_{m+1,n}(1) = n \cdot \mathrm{mpf}_{m,n}(1) - \mathrm{mpf}_{m-1,n}(1),$$

where the subtraction is taken in the integers.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Theorem 2.

articles.title: 1-metered parking functions with three cars
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 2$, the
number of $1$-metered $(3, n)$-parking functions is $\mathrm{mpf}_{3,n}(1) = n^3 - 2n$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Proposition 7.

articles.title: 1-metered parking functions with two cars and two spots
articles.statement:
The number of $1$-metered
$(2, 2)$-parking functions is $\mathrm{mpf}_{2,2}(1) = 3$.

This is an entry of the source's Table 1.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Table 1.

articles.title: Metered parking functions with one spot fewer than cars
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 2$ be a natural
number. The number $\mathrm{mpf}_{m,m-1}(m-2)$ of $(m-2)$-metered $(m, m-1)$-parking functions
equals the sum, over all parking functions $f$ of length $m - 1$, of $f(0) + 1$ (the preferred
spot of the first car, with spots numbered from $1$), and it also equals

$$\sum_{i=1}^{m-1} \sum_{s=0}^{m-1-i} \binom{m-2}{s}\, i\, (s+1)^{s-1} (m-s-1)^{m-s-3}.$$

The only negative exponents occur at $s = 0$ and $s = m - 2$, where the base is $1$, so the
formula is the same with exponents truncated at $0$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Corollary 7.

articles.title: Closed form for (m-2)-metered parking functions
articles.statement:
Let $m, n$ be natural numbers with
$2 < m \le n + 1$. Then the number $\mathrm{mpf}_{m,n}(m-2)$ of $(m-2)$-metered
$(m, n)$-parking functions is

$$(n-m+2)^2 (m-1)^{m-3} + \sum_{k=n-m+3}^{n} \binom{m-2}{n-k} (n-k+1)^{n-k-1} S_k,$$

where

$$S_k = \binom{k+1}{2}(n-m+2)\, k^{m-n+k-3} +
\left(k(n-m+1) - \binom{n-m+2}{2}\right)(k-n+m-1)^{k-n+m-3} +
\sum_{j=n-m+2}^{k-1} \left(jk - \binom{j+1}{2}\right) \binom{m-2-n+k}{k-1-j} (n-m+1)\,
j^{j+m-2-n} (k-j)^{k-j-2}.$$

Every subtraction is nonnegative on the summation ranges except in the exponents of the bases
$n - k + 1$ (at $k = n$) and $k - j$ (at $j = k - 1$), which equal $1$ there, so the formula is
the same with exponents truncated at $0$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Metered parking functions with two cars
articles.statement:
For every natural number $t \ge 1$ and every
natural number $n$, the number of $t$-metered $(2, n)$-parking functions is
$\mathrm{mpf}_{2,n}(t) = \max(n^2 - 1, 0)$, that is, $n^2 - 1$ for $n \ge 1$ and $0$ for $n = 0$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Number of metered parking functions
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $t$, $m$ and $n$,
$\mathrm{mpf}_{m,n}(t)$ is the number of $t$-metered $(m, n)$-parking functions, that is, of maps
$f$ from the $m$ cars $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ to the $n$ spots $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ under which every
car parks in the $t$-metered parking scheme.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Section 1 (definition and the notation `mpf_{m,n}(t)`).

articles.title: Window condition for metered parking functions
articles.statement:
Number the cars $1, \dots, m$ and the
spots $1, \dots, n$, and let $a_k$ be the preferred spot of car $k$. If $(a_1, \dots, a_m)$ is a
$t$-metered $(m, n)$-parking function, then for every $i$ with $1 \le i \le n$ and every $j$ with
$1 \le j \le m - t$ (truncated subtraction, so there is no such $j$ when $m \le t$),

$$t + 1 + i \le \#\{k : j \le k \le j + t,\ a_k \le i\} + n,$$

that is, at least $t + 1 - n + i$ of the cars $j, \dots, j + t$ prefer one of the spots
$1, \dots, i$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Equal last-spot counts for 1-metered parking functions
articles.statement:
Let $1 \le m \le j < k \le n$
and number the spots $1, \dots, n$. The number of $1$-metered $(m, n)$-parking functions whose
last car parks in spot $j$ equals the number of those whose last car parks in spot $k$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Lemma 2.

articles.title: 1-metered parking functions whose last car parks in the last spot
articles.statement:
Let $1 \le m \le n$
and number the spots $1, \dots, n$. The number of $1$-metered $(m, n)$-parking functions whose
last car parks in spot $n$ equals $\mathrm{mpf}_{m-1,n}(1)$, the number of $1$-metered
$(m - 1, n)$-parking functions.

The source leaves $1 \le m$ implicit (there is a last car).

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Lucky cars of 1-metered parking are the lace starts
articles.statement:
Let $0 < m \le n$ and let
$\alpha = (a_1, \dots, a_m)$, with each $a_i \in \{1, \dots, n\}$, be any sequence of preferred
spots of $m$ cars on $n$ spots. Under the $1$-metered parking scheme, car $i$ is lucky (it parks
in its preferred spot $a_i$) if and only if position $i$ is the first position of one of the
laces of the lace decomposition $\mathrm{lace}(\alpha)$.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Parking functions with a given first entry
articles.statement:
Let $1 \le m \le n$ and $1 \le j \le n$, and
number the spots $1, \dots, n$. Write

$$S(i) = \binom{m-1}{n-i} (n-m+1)\, i^{i+m-n-2} (n-i+1)^{n-i-1}.$$

If $j > n - m + 1$, the number of partial parking functions with $m$ cars and $n$ spots
(classical $(m, n)$-parking functions) whose first entry is $a_1 = j$ is $\sum_{i=j}^{n} S(i)$;
if $j \le n - m + 1$, it is $m^{m-2} + \sum_{i=n-m+2}^{n} S(i)$. Exponents are natural numbers
with truncated subtraction; the only affected powers are $1^{-1}$, at $i = n$ and at $m = 1$,
which equal the truncated $1^0$.

The text prints the factor $n - m + 1$ as $n - m - 1$, which is false ($m = n = 2$, $j = 1$: two
parking functions, formula $0$); the factor $n - m + 1$ is the one in the source's Lemma 4
($|\mathrm{Sh}_m(k-1, n-k)|$), from which the source derives this corollary, and it matches
exact counts.

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Corollary 6.

articles.title: Lower bound for the number of metered parking functions
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $t$,
$m$ and $n$, $\mathrm{mpf}_{m,n}(t) \ge (n - t)^m$, where $n - t$ is truncated subtraction
(equal to $0$ when $t \ge n$).

## Sources

- Spencer Daugherty, Pamela E. Harris, Ian Klein, and Matt McClinton, *Metered Parking Functions*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A73, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Number of partial parking functions
articles.statement:
Let $s$ and $t$ be natural numbers with
$0 < s \le t$. A partial parking function with $s$ cars and $t$ spots is a map
$f : \{0, \dots, s - 1\} \to \{0, \dots, t - 1\}$ such that for every spot
$k \in \{0, \dots, t - 1\}$ at most $t - k$ cars $i$ have $f(i) \ge k$. The number of partial
parking functions with $s$ cars and $t$ spots is $(t + 1 - s)(t + 1)^{s - 1}$.

The proof is Pollak's circle argument.

## Sources

- Steve Butler, Kimberly Hadaway, Victoria Lenius, Preston Martens, and Marshall Moats, “Lucky Cars and Lucky Spots in Parking Functions”, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.1, proposition at lines 330–332 of https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL29/Hadaway/had3.tex.

articles.title: Chain polynomial
articles.statement:
For a finite partially ordered set $P$ and each natural number $k$, let
$c_k(P)$ be the number of $k$-element chains of $P$, that is, of $k$-element subsets of $P$ any two
of whose elements are comparable; in particular $c_0(P) = 1$, counting the empty chain. The chain
polynomial of $P$ is the polynomial $C(P, t) = \sum_{k \ge 0} c_k(P)\, t^k$ with integer
coefficients.

articles.title: Stanley's Problem 20' has a negative answer
articles.statement:
It is not true that for every finite
distributive lattice $L$ every complex root of the chain polynomial $C(L, t)$ is real, where
$C(L, t) = \sum_{k \ge 0} c_k(L)\, t^k$ and $c_k(L)$ is the number of $k$-element chains of $L$.

For a finite poset $P$ let $J(P)$ be the distributive lattice of its order ideals, and for a
naturally labeled $P$ let $W(P, x) = \sum_{\sigma} x^{\operatorname{des}(\sigma)}$, the sum over
the linear extensions $\sigma$ of $P$, where $\operatorname{des}(\sigma)$ is the number of descents
of $\sigma$. For naturally labeled $P$, real-rootedness of $C(J(P), t)$ is equivalent to that of
$W(P, x)$ (Stanley's text before Problem 20', after Brenti), and Stembridge's naturally labeled
$17$-element posets $P$ have polynomials $W(P, x)$ with non-real zeros, so their lattices $J(P)$
have chain polynomials with non-real zeros.

## Sources

- R. P. Stanley, Positivity Problems and Conjectures in Algebraic Combinatorics (1999), Problem 20' (chain polynomial of a finite distributive lattice); resolution: Stanley, Positivity Problems (1999), text before Problem 20', citing F. Brenti, Mem. Amer. Math. Soc. 413 (1989), Conj. 3; J. R. Stembridge, Counterexamples to the poset conjectures of Neggers, Stanley, and Stembridge, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 359 (2007), 1115-1128; restated in C. A. Athanasiadis and K. Kalampogia-Evangelinou, Chain enumeration, partition lattices and polynomials with only real roots, arXiv:2205.03796, Introduction, Stanley: "When P is natural it can be shown [19, Conj. 3] that Problem 20 is equivalent to the following" (Problem 20', with L = J(P)); Stembridge, Introduction: naturally labeled posets on 17 vertices with non-real W-zeros; Athanasiadis–Kalampogia-Evangelinou: for finite distributive lattices the question is equivalent to the naturally labeled poset conjecture of Neggers, "finally disproved by Stembridge", https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.03796.

articles.title: Stanley's Problem 20' on chain polynomials of distributive lattices
articles.statement:
The proposition that
for every finite distributive lattice $L$, every complex root of the chain polynomial $C(L, t)$ is
real, where $C(L, t) = \sum_{k \ge 0} c_k(L)\, t^k$ and $c_k(L)$ is the number of $k$-element
chains of $L$.

articles.title: Antichains are no larger than the maximum antichain size
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite
partially ordered set. Every antichain $A$ in $\alpha$ has at most as many elements as the
maximum antichain size of $\alpha$.

articles.title: Dilworth's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite partially ordered set. The maximum antichain
size of $\alpha$ equals its minimum chain cover size: the largest number of elements of an
antichain in $\alpha$ equals the smallest number of chains whose union is $\alpha$.

## Sources

- R. P. Dilworth, A decomposition theorem for partially ordered sets, Annals of Mathematics 51 (1950), 161-166, DOI 10.2307/1969503.

articles.title: The maximum antichain size is attained
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite partially ordered set.
Some antichain in $\alpha$ has exactly as many elements as the maximum antichain size of
$\alpha$.

articles.title: The minimum chain cover size is attained
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite partially ordered set.
Some chain cover $C$ of $\alpha$, a finite set of chains of $\alpha$ whose union is $\alpha$,
consists of exactly as many chains as the minimum chain cover size of $\alpha$.

articles.title: Chain cover
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a partially ordered set. A finite set $C$ of finite subsets of
$\alpha$ is a chain cover of $\alpha$ when every member of $C$ is a chain and every element of
$\alpha$ lies in some member of $C$.

articles.title: Maximum antichain size
articles.statement:
For a finite partially ordered set $\alpha$, the maximum antichain
size of $\alpha$ (its width) is the largest number of elements of an antichain in $\alpha$.

articles.title: Chain covers bound the minimum chain cover size
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite partially
ordered set. If $C$ is a chain cover of $\alpha$, that is, a finite set of chains of $\alpha$ whose
union is $\alpha$, then the minimum chain cover size of $\alpha$ is at most the number of chains
in $C$.

articles.title: Minimum chain cover size
articles.statement:
For a finite partially ordered set $\alpha$, the minimum chain
cover size of $\alpha$ is the smallest number of chains in a chain cover of $\alpha$, that is, in
a finite set of chains of $\alpha$ whose union is $\alpha$.

articles.title: Extending a decreasing subsequence
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a real sequence indexed by
$\{0, \dots, N-1\}$, let $k \ge 1$, and let $\varphi$ be a decreasing subsequence of $f$ of length
$k$, that is, indices $\varphi(0) < \dots < \varphi(k-1)$ with
$f(\varphi(0)) > \dots > f(\varphi(k-1))$, whose last index is $\varphi(k-1) = q$. If $p$ is an
index with $q < p$ and $f(p) < f(q)$, then $f$ has a decreasing subsequence of length $k + 1$ that
ends at $p$.

articles.title: The longest decreasing subsequence ending at a point has length at least one
articles.statement:
For every
real sequence $f$ indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and every index $p$, the length of the longest
strictly decreasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $p$ is at least $1$.

articles.title: The longest decreasing subsequence ending at a point is attained
articles.statement:
For every real sequence
$f$ indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and every index $p$, $f$ has a strictly decreasing subsequence
ending at $p$ whose length equals the length of the longest strictly decreasing subsequence of $f$
ending at $p$.

articles.title: Length of the longest decreasing subsequence ending at a point
articles.statement:
For a real sequence $f$
indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and an index $p$, this is the largest $k$ such that $f$ has a
strictly decreasing subsequence of length $k$ ending at $p$, that is, indices
$i_1 < \dots < i_k = p$ with $f(i_1) > \dots > f(i_k)$. The maximum exists: $k = 1$ qualifies, and
every such $k$ is at most $N$.

articles.title: Longest decreasing subsequence lengths grow along a descent
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a real sequence
indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$, and let $q < p$ be indices with $f(p) < f(q)$. Then the length of
the longest strictly decreasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $q$ is strictly less than the length
of the longest strictly decreasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $p$.

articles.title: Erdős–Szekeres theorem
articles.statement:
Let $r, s \ge 1$ be natural numbers, let $N = (r - 1)(s - 1) + 1$,
and let $f$ be an injective real sequence indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$. Then $f$ has a strictly
increasing subsequence of length $r$, that is, indices $i_1 < \dots < i_r$ with
$f(i_1) < \dots < f(i_r)$, or a strictly decreasing subsequence of length $s$, that is, indices
$j_1 < \dots < j_s$ with $f(j_1) > \dots > f(j_s)$.

articles.title: Appending a later index keeps indices increasing
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and let
$\varphi : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ be strictly increasing with last value
$\varphi(k-1) = q$. If $p$ is an index with $q < p$, then the map on $\{0, \dots, k\}$ obtained by
appending $p$ to $\varphi$, which sends each $i < k$ to $\varphi(i)$ and sends $k$ to $p$, is
strictly increasing.

articles.title: The last entry of an appended map
articles.statement:
For every map
$\varphi : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and every $p \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}$, the map
obtained by appending $p$ to $\varphi$ takes the value $p$ at its last index $k$.

articles.title: Appending an entry to a map of indices
articles.statement:
Given
$\varphi : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and $p \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}$, the appended map
on $\{0, \dots, k\}$ sends each $i < k$ to $\varphi(i)$ and sends $k$ to $p$.

articles.title: No strict pair in a one-element set
articles.statement: There are no $i, j \in \{0\}$ with $i < j$.

articles.title: Entries of a strictly increasing index map lie at or below its last entry
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$
and let $\varphi : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ be strictly increasing with
$\varphi(k-1) = q$. Then $\varphi(i) \le q$ for every $i < k$.

articles.title: Extending an increasing subsequence
articles.statement:
Let $f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$k \ge 1$, and let $\varphi$ be an increasing subsequence of $f$ of length $k$ (indices and values
strictly increasing) with last index $\varphi(k-1) = q$. If $p \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ satisfies
$q < p$ and $f(q) < f(p)$, then $f$ has an increasing subsequence of length $k + 1$ ending at
$p$.

articles.title: Longest increasing subsequences ending at a position have length at least one
articles.statement:
For every
$f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$ and every position $p$, the length of the longest
increasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $p$ is at least $1$.

articles.title: The longest increasing subsequence ending at a position is attained
articles.statement:
For every
$f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$ and every position $p$, $f$ has an increasing subsequence
ending at $p$ whose length equals the length of the longest increasing subsequence of $f$ ending
at $p$.

articles.title: Length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at a position
articles.statement:
For
$f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$ and a position $p$, this is the largest $k \le N$ such that
$f$ has an increasing subsequence of length $k$ ending at $p$, where indices and values both
increase strictly.

articles.title: Longest increasing subsequence lengths increase strictly along increasing pairs
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $q < p$ be positions with $f(q) < f(p)$. Then the
length of the longest increasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $q$ is strictly less than the
length of the longest increasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $p$.

articles.title: Decreasing subsequence ending at a position
articles.statement:
For $f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$,
a position $p$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the statement that $k \ge 1$ and $f$ has a
decreasing subsequence $\varphi$ of length $k$ (indices strictly increasing and values strictly
decreasing) ending at $p$, that is, with $\varphi(k-1) = p$.

articles.title: Decreasing subsequence
articles.statement:
For $f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
a map $\varphi : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ is a decreasing subsequence of $f$ of
length $k$ when $\varphi(i) < \varphi(j)$ and $f(\varphi(j)) < f(\varphi(i))$ for all $i < j$.

articles.title: Increasing subsequence ending at a position
articles.statement:
For $f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$,
a position $p$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the statement that $k \ge 1$ and $f$ has an
increasing subsequence $\varphi$ of length $k$ (indices and values strictly increasing) ending at
$p$, that is, with $\varphi(k-1) = p$.

articles.title: Increasing subsequence
articles.statement:
For $f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
a map $\varphi : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ is an increasing subsequence of $f$ of
length $k$ when $\varphi(i) < \varphi(j)$ and $f(\varphi(i)) < f(\varphi(j))$ for all $i < j$.

articles.title: The last value is the smallest along a strictly decreasing selection
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a real
sequence indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$, let $k \ge 1$, and let $\varphi$ map
$\{0, \dots, k-1\}$ to $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ so that $f(\varphi(j)) < f(\varphi(i))$ whenever
$i < j < k$. If $\varphi(k-1) = q$, then $f(q) \le f(\varphi(i))$ for every $i < k$.

articles.title: Bound by the longest decreasing subsequence ending at a position
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a real
sequence indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and let $p$ be a position. If $f$ has a strictly
decreasing subsequence of length $k$ ending exactly at $p$, then $k$ is at most the length of the
longest strictly decreasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $p$.

articles.title: Bound by the longest increasing subsequence ending at a position
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a real
sequence indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and let $p$ be a position. If $f$ has a strictly
increasing subsequence of length $k$ ending exactly at $p$, then $k$ is at most the length of the
longest strictly increasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $p$.

articles.title: One-term subsequences are decreasing
articles.statement:
For every real sequence $f$ indexed by
$\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and every position $p$, the subsequence of length $1$ consisting of the term
at position $p$ is a strictly decreasing subsequence of $f$.

articles.title: One-term subsequences are increasing
articles.statement:
For every real sequence $f$ indexed by
$\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and every position $p$, the subsequence of length $1$ consisting of the term
at position $p$ is a strictly increasing subsequence of $f$.

articles.title: A positive natural number exceeds its predecessor
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k > 0$,
$k - 1 < k$.

articles.title: Subsequences are no longer than the sequence
articles.statement:
If
$\varphi \colon \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ is strictly increasing, that is
$\varphi(i) < \varphi(j)$ whenever $i < j$, then $k \le N$.

articles.title: Decreasing subsequences of every smaller length
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a real sequence indexed by
$\{0, \dots, N-1\}$. If $f$ has a strictly decreasing subsequence of length $k$, then for every
$s \le k$ it has a strictly decreasing subsequence of length $s$.

articles.title: Increasing subsequences of every smaller length
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a real sequence indexed by
$\{0, \dots, N-1\}$. If $f$ has a strictly increasing subsequence of length $k$, then for every
$r \le k$ it has a strictly increasing subsequence of length $r$.

articles.title: The last value is the largest along a strictly increasing selection
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a real
sequence indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$, let $k \ge 1$, and let $\varphi$ map
$\{0, \dots, k-1\}$ to $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ so that $f(\varphi(i)) < f(\varphi(j))$ whenever
$i < j < k$. If $\varphi(k-1) = q$, then $f(\varphi(i)) \le f(q)$ for every $i < k$.

articles.title: The chosen linear extension is bijective
articles.statement:
For every finite poset $\alpha$ with
$n$ elements, the chosen linear extension of $\alpha$, viewed as a rank function
$\alpha \to \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, is a bijection.

articles.title: The number of linear extensions is positive
articles.statement:
For every finite poset $\alpha$,
the number of linear extensions of $\alpha$ is positive.

So this count is a valid denominator for probabilities over linear extensions.

articles.title: Ranking a Szpilrajn linear extension
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite poset with $n$
elements, and fix a linear order on $\alpha$ extending its partial order (one exists by
Szpilrajn's extension theorem; it is chosen once and for all). This is the order
isomorphism from $\alpha$ with that linear order onto $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ with its usual
order.

articles.title: Linear extensions of a finite poset
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite poset with $n$
