For a natural number $n$, a set partition $P$ of the integer
interval $[-n, n] = \{-n, \dots, n\}$ is of type $B$ if for every block $\beta$ of $P$ the set
$-\beta = \{-x : x \in \beta\}$ is again a block of $P$, and exactly one block $\beta$ of $P$
satisfies $-\beta = \beta$.

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Definition 1.

articles.title: Length of the doubled word
articles.statement:
For every finite set $S$ of natural numbers with elements
$s_1 < \dots < s_k$, the doubled word $f(S) = s_1 s_1 s_2 s_2 \cdots s_k s_k$ has length $2|S|$.

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Lemma 3 (the map `f`).

articles.title: Length of the wrapped word
articles.statement:
For every finite set $S$ of natural numbers with elements
$s_1 < \dots < s_k$, the wrapped word $g(S) = s_1 s_2 s_2 \cdots s_k s_k s_1$ (the empty word when
$S = \emptyset$) has length $2|S|$.

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Lemma 3 (the map `g`).

articles.title: Flattened Stirling permutations and type $B$ set partitions
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n \ge 1$, the set of flattened Stirling permutations of order $n + 1$ is in bijection with the
set of type $B$ set partitions of $[-n, n] = \{-n, \dots, n\}$.

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Theorem 2.

articles.title: A word that is not flattened
articles.statement:
The word $123321445566778899$ is not flattened.

This word is a Stirling permutation of order $9$; its runs $1233$, $2$, $1445566778899$ have
leading letters $1, 2, 1$, which do not weakly increase.

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Section 1 (example).

articles.title: The word of a set partition of $(-n, n)$, as a list
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let
$P$ be a set partition of $[-n, n] = \{-n, \dots, n\}$. For a finite set $S$ of integers let
$h(S) = \{|i| + 1 : i \in S\}$, and for a finite set $T$ of natural numbers with elements
$t_1 < \dots < t_k$ let $f(T) = t_1 t_1 t_2 t_2 \cdots t_k t_k$ and
$g(T) = t_1 t_2 t_2 \cdots t_k t_k t_1$ (both empty when $T = \emptyset$). Let $P_0$ be the set of
nonnegative elements of the block of $P$ containing $0$. Let $p_1 < \dots < p_m$ be the integers $p$
with $1 \le p \le n$ such that every positive element of the block of $P$ containing $p$ is at
least $p$ and every negative element $q$ of that block satisfies $p < -q$, and let $N_i$ and $P_i$
be the sets of negative and of positive elements of the block containing $p_i$. The list of $P$ is
the list of natural numbers

$$g(h(P_0))\, f(h(N_1))\, g(h(P_1)) \cdots f(h(N_m))\, g(h(P_m)).$$

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Proposition 1 (map `φ`), with Definition 2.

articles.title: The word of a type $B$ set partition is a flattened Stirling permutation
articles.statement:
For every
natural number $n$ and every type $B$ set partition $P$ of $[-n, n] = \{-n, \dots, n\}$, the word
$\varphi(P) = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_{2(n+1)}$ of $P$ is a Stirling permutation of order $n + 1$ and is
flattened.

## Sources

- arXiv:2306.13034, Proposition 3.6; the INTEGERS record is truncated after "let `π_i = N_i P_i` be as in", and the statement is completed from the arXiv text.
- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Proposition 1.

articles.title: The word of a set partition of $(-n, n)$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a set partition
$P$ of $[-n, n] = \{-n, \dots, n\}$, let $L(P)$ be the list of $P$: the list of natural numbers
built from the blocks of $P$ (via the shift map and the doubled and wrapped words). The word
$\varphi(P) = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_{2(n+1)}$ has $w_i$ equal to the $i$-th entry of $L(P)$ when $L(P)$
has at least $i$ entries, and $w_i = 0$ otherwise.

Restricted to type $B$ set partitions, this is the map $\varphi$ of Proposition 1.

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Proposition 1 (map `φ`).

articles.title: An example of the shift map
articles.statement:
For the map $h(S) = \{|i| + 1 : i \in S\}$ on finite sets
of integers, $h(\{-2, 0, 1\}) = \{1, 2, 3\}$.

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Lemma 2 (the map `h`).

articles.title: The shift map
articles.statement:
For a finite set $S$ of integers, $h(S) = \{|i| + 1 : i \in S\}$, a
finite set of natural numbers.

In particular, for every natural number $n$, $h$ sends subsets of $[-n, n]$ to subsets of
$\{1, \dots, n + 1\}$.

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Lemma 2 (the map `h`).

articles.title: Number of runs of the word of a type $B$ set partition
articles.statement:
Let $\pi$ be a type $B$ set
partition of $[-n, n]$ and let $\varphi(\pi)$ be the word of length $2(n + 1)$ that the map
$\varphi$ of Proposition 1 assigns to it. Write $P_0$ for the set of nonnegative elements of the
block of $\pi$ containing $0$. Let $\beta_1, \dots, \beta_m$ be the blocks kept by Adler's
labelling, exactly one from each pair $\{\beta, -\beta\}$ of distinct blocks, namely the block
containing the smallest magnitude of the pair as a positive element; write $N_i$ and $P_i$ for
the sets of negative and positive elements of $\beta_i$. Then the number of runs of
$\varphi(\pi)$ is

$$1 + |\{i \ge 1 : |N_i| \ge 1\}| + |\{i \ge 0 : |P_i| \ge 2\}|.$$

The paper states this for a flattened Stirling permutation $w$ of order $n + 1$ and the
partition $\varphi^{-1}(w)$; since $\varphi$ is a bijection from the type $B$ set partitions of
$[-n, n]$ onto these permutations (Theorem 3), this is the same as the statement for
$w = \varphi(\pi)$ over all $\pi$.

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Number of runs of a word
articles.statement:
A run of a word $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{m-1}$ of natural numbers is
a maximal contiguous weakly increasing subword. The number of runs of $w$ is the number of
positions $i < m$ that start a run, that is, with $i = 0$ or $w_{i-1} > w_i$; the empty word has
no runs.

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Section 1 (runs).

articles.title: Start of a run
articles.statement:
Position $i$ of a word $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{m-1}$ of natural numbers
starts a run when $i = 0$ or the letter before it is larger, that is, $w_{i-1} > w_i$. Runs are
the maximal contiguous weakly increasing subwords, so these are exactly the positions where a run
begins.

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Section 1 (runs).

articles.title: Wrapped word of the empty set
articles.statement:
The wrapped word $g(\emptyset)$ of the empty set is the
empty word.

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Lemma 3 (the map `g`).

articles.title: Wrapped word of a singleton
articles.statement:
For every natural number $s$, the wrapped word of the
singleton $\{s\}$ is $g(\{s\}) = s\,s$, the word of length two both of whose letters are $s$.

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Lemma 3 (the map `g`).

articles.title: Wrapped word of a finite set
articles.statement:
For a finite set $S = \{s_1 < s_2 < \dots < s_k\}$ of natural
numbers, the wrapped word $g(S)$ is $s_1 s_2 s_2 \cdots s_k s_k s_1$: the smallest element, then
each larger element written twice in increasing order, then the smallest element again. For
$S = \emptyset$, $g(S)$ is the empty word.

## Sources

- Buck, Elder, Figueroa, Harris, Harry, Simpson, *Flattened Stirling Permutations*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A104, Lemma 3 (the map `g`).

articles.title: Characterization of minimal permutations with a given number of descents
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a
permutation of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ and let $d$ be a natural number. A descent of a permutation
$\tau$ of $\{1, \dots, k\}$ is an index $1 \le i \le k - 1$ with $\tau(i+1) < \tau(i)$, and $\tau$
occurs in $\sigma$ if there are positions $\varphi(1) < \dots < \varphi(k)$ in $\{1, \dots, n\}$
with $\tau(a) < \tau(b)$ exactly when $\sigma(\varphi(a)) < \sigma(\varphi(b))$. Then $\sigma$ has
exactly $d$ descents and no permutation $\tau$ of $\{1, \dots, k\}$ with $0 < k < n$ occurring in
$\sigma$ has exactly $d$ descents if and only if $\sigma$ has exactly $d$ descents and every
ascent $i$ of $\sigma$ (an index $1 \le i \le n - 1$ with $\sigma(i) < \sigma(i+1)$) satisfies
$2 \le i \le n - 2$ and either $\sigma(i) < \sigma(i-1) < \sigma(i+2) < \sigma(i+1)$ or
$\sigma(i) < \sigma(i+2) < \sigma(i-1) < \sigma(i+1)$; that is, the entries at positions
$i-1, i, i+1, i+2$ form the pattern $2143$ or $3142$.

## Sources

- Stefano Bilotta, Elisabetta Grazzini, and Elisa Pergola, "Enumeration of Two Particular Sets of Minimal Permutations", Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.10.2, Theorem `thm:characterization`, lines 230-237, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Grazzini/graz3.tex>.

articles.title: Minimal permutations of length two more than their number of descents
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $d$, the number of permutations $\sigma$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, d + 1\}$ such that $\sigma$ has
exactly $d$ descents (positions $0 \le i \le d$ with $\sigma(i) > \sigma(i + 1)$) and, for every
position $j$, deleting the entry at position $j$ leaves a sequence of $d + 1$ entries with fewer
than $d$ descents, equals $2^{d+2} - (d + 1)(d + 2) - 2$.

## Sources

- Stefano Bilotta, Elisabetta Grazzini, and Elisa Pergola, "Enumeration of Two Particular Sets of Minimal Permutations", Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.10.2, Theorem `thm:enum`, lines 324-326, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Grazzini/graz3.tex>.

articles.title: Average number of correct positions in the second guess
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 2$ and let $S$ be a
permutation Wordle strategy (a permutation $S[m]$ of $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ for each $m$) whose
component $S[n]$ has no fixed point. For a secret permutation $\pi$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ let
$\gamma_2$ be the second guess of $S$. The sum, over all derangements $\pi$ of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, of the number of positions $i$ with $\gamma_2(i) = \pi(i)$, divided by the
number of derangements of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, equals $n/(n-1)$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Proposition 4 (`jis-2026-26.1.7-prop-4`).

articles.title: Derangements solved in three guesses by cyclic shift
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 3$, exactly
$2^n - (2n + 1)$ derangements $\pi$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ are guessed by the cyclic shift
strategy in exactly three guesses.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Lemma 9 (`jis-2026-26.1.7-lem-9`).

articles.title: Among inductive strategies, cyclic shift left minimizes three-guess solves first correct at guess two
articles.statement:
**Among inductive strategies, cyclic shift left minimizes three-guess solves first correct at
guess two.** Let $n \ge 4$ and let $S$ be an inductive strategy of length $n$ whose component
$S[n]$ is not the left cyclic shift $i \mapsto i - 1 \pmod n$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Let
$\mathrm{CSL}_n$ be the cyclic shift left strategy, whose component on $n$ positions is the left
cyclic shift and whose component on $m \ne n$ positions is the rotation $i \mapsto i + 1 \pmod m$.
Then the number of permutations $\pi$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that $\mathrm{CSL}_n$ guesses in
exactly three guesses, with the second guess being the first guess that has a correct position,
is strictly smaller than the number of permutations $\pi$ that $S$ guesses in exactly three
guesses with the second guess being the first guess that has a correct position.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Theorem 16 (`jis-2026-26.1.7-thm-16`).

articles.title: Three-guess solves of permutations with a fixed point
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 4$ and let $S$ be a
permutation Wordle strategy (a permutation $S[m]$ of $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ for each $m$) with
$S[m]$ equal to the cyclic shift $j \mapsto j + 1 \bmod m$ for every $m < n$. The number of
permutations $\pi$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that $S$ guesses in exactly three guesses and whose
first guess (the identity) has a correct position, that is, $\pi$ has a fixed point, is
$1 - 2^{n+1} + 3^n + n^2/2 + 5n/2 - n \cdot 2^n$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Theorem 10 (`jis-2026-26.1.7-thm-10`).

articles.title: A unique three-guess solve with no early correct position
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 4$ and let $S$ be
a permutation Wordle strategy (a permutation $S[m]$ of $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ for each $m$) whose
component $S[n]$ is an $n$-cycle. Exactly one permutation $\pi$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is
guessed by $S$ in exactly three guesses with the third guess being the first guess that has a
correct position.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Theorem 11 (`jis-2026-26.1.7-thm-11`).

articles.title: Upper bound on three-guess solves first correct at guess two
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 4$ and let $S$
be an inductive strategy of length $n$ whose component $S[n]$ is not the cyclic shift
$j \mapsto j + 1 \bmod n$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Then fewer than $2^n - 2n - 2$ permutations
$\pi$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ are guessed by $S$ in exactly three guesses with the second guess
being the first guess that has a correct position.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Theorem 13 (`jis-2026-26.1.7-thm-13`).

articles.title: Lucas-number count for the left-shift strategy
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 4$ and let $\mathrm{CSL}_n$
be the strategy whose component on $n$ positions is the left cyclic shift
$j \mapsto j - 1 \bmod n$ and whose component on $m \ne n$ positions is the cyclic shift
$j \mapsto j + 1 \bmod m$. The number of permutations $\pi$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that
$\mathrm{CSL}_n$ guesses in exactly three guesses, with the second guess being the first guess
that has a correct position, is $L_n - n - 1$, where $L_n$ is the $n$-th Lucas number
($L_0 = 2$, $L_1 = 1$, $L_{k+2} = L_{k+1} + L_k$).

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Theorem 15 (`jis-2026-26.1.7-thm-15`).

articles.title: Three-guess solves of cyclic shift first correct at guess two
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 4$, the number
of permutations $\pi$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that the cyclic shift strategy guesses in exactly
three guesses, with the second guess being the first guess that has a correct position, is
$2^n - 2n - 2$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Theorem 12 (`jis-2026-26.1.7-thm-12`).

articles.title: Non-top components of the left-shift strategy
articles.statement:
For all $n$ and $m$ with $m \ne n$, the
component on $m$ positions of the left-shift strategy $\mathrm{CSL}_n$ is the cyclic shift
$j \mapsto j + 1 \bmod m$ of $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 4.3.

articles.title: Top component of the left-shift strategy
articles.statement:
For every $n$, the component on $n$ positions
of the left-shift strategy $\mathrm{CSL}_n$ is the left cyclic shift $j \mapsto j - 1 \bmod n$
of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the inverse of the cyclic shift $j \mapsto j + 1 \bmod n$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 4.3.

articles.title: Cyclic shift left strategy
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the strategy $\mathrm{CSL}_n$ assigns
to each $m$ a permutation of $m$ positions: for $m = n$ the left cyclic shift
$[m, 1, 2, \dots, m-1]$ in one-line notation, that is, $i \mapsto i - 1 \pmod m$, and for every
$m \ne n$ the right cyclic shift $[2, 3, \dots, m, 1]$, that is, $i \mapsto i + 1 \pmod m$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 4.3.

articles.title: Components of the cyclic shift strategy
articles.statement:
For every $m$, the component of the cyclic shift
strategy on $m$ positions is the rotation $i \mapsto i + 1 \pmod m$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 2.

articles.title: Cyclic shift strategy
articles.statement:
A strategy assigns to each $m$ a permutation of $m$ positions, used
to rearrange the entries on the $m$ incorrect positions of a guess. The cyclic shift strategy
$\mathrm{CS}$ has component $\mathrm{CS}[m] = [2, 3, \dots, m, 1]$ in one-line notation, that is,
the rotation $i \mapsto i + 1 \pmod m$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 2.

articles.title: Inductive strategy
articles.statement:
A strategy $S$ (a permutation $S[m]$ of $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ for each
$m$) is inductive of length $n$ when $S[m]$ is the rotation $i \mapsto i + 1 \pmod m$ for every
$m < n$, and $S[n]$ is an $n$-cycle, that is, a single cycle moving every element of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 3.1.

articles.title: One- and two-guess counts for deranged strategies
articles.statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $S$ be
a strategy whose component $S[m]$ has no fixed point for every $2 \le m \le n$, and write
$[x^r] f_S$ for the number of permutations of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that $S$ guesses in exactly $r$
guesses. Then $[x^1] f_S = 1$ and $[x^2] f_S = 2^n - n - 1$, the Eulerian number $A(n, 1)$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Theorem 5 (`jis-2026-26.1.7-thm-5`).

articles.title: Cyclic shift left minimizes three-guess solves among inductive strategies
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 4$
and let $S$ be an inductive strategy of length $n$ whose component $S[n]$ is not the left cyclic
shift $i \mapsto i - 1 \pmod n$. Then strictly fewer permutations of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ are
guessed in exactly three guesses with the cyclic shift left strategy $\mathrm{CSL}_n$ than with
$S$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Theorem 14 (`jis-2026-26.1.7-thm-14`).

articles.title: Cyclic shift maximizes three-guess solves among inductive strategies
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 4$ and let
$S$ be an inductive strategy of length $n$ whose component $S[n]$ is not the rotation
$i \mapsto i + 1 \pmod n$. Then strictly fewer permutations of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ are guessed in
exactly three guesses with $S$ than with the cyclic shift strategy.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Theorem 7 (`jis-2026-26.1.7-thm-7`).

articles.title: No permutation is guessed in zero guesses
articles.statement:
For every strategy $S$ and every $n$, write
$f_S$ for the generating function whose coefficient $[x^r] f_S$ is the number of permutations of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that $S$ guesses in exactly $r$ guesses. Then the constant coefficient
$[x^0] f_S$ vanishes.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 4.

articles.title: Coefficients of the guess-count generating function
articles.statement:
For a strategy $S$ and natural
numbers $n$ and $r$, the coefficient $[x^r] f_S(x)$ of the generating function of $S$ at length
$n$ is the number of secret permutations of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that $S$ guesses in exactly $r$
guesses.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 4.

articles.title: Permutations with a correct entry in the first guess
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, a strategy
$S$ and a permutation $\pi$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, write $\rho_S(\pi) = r$ when the $r$-th guess
is the first guess with a correct position for the secret $\pi$. Then $\rho_S(\pi) = 1$, that is,
the first guess (the identity) already has a correct position, exactly when $\pi$ has a fixed
point.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, proof of Theorem 10.

articles.title: First guess with a correct position in permutation Wordle
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a strategy, that
is, a permutation $S_m$ of $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ for every $m$, let $\pi$ be a permutation of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and let $\gamma_1, \gamma_2, \dots$ be the guesses of permutation Wordle with
strategy $S$ and secret $\pi$. For a natural number $r$, $\rho_S(\pi) = r$ means that $r \ge 1$,
that $\gamma_r(k) = \pi(k)$ for some position $k$, and that for every $j$ with $1 \le j < r$ there
is no position $k$ with $\gamma_j(k) = \pi(k)$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 4.2.

articles.title: The second guess against a derangement
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a strategy for permutation Wordle,
that is, a permutation $S_m$ of $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ for every $m$, and let $\pi$ be a permutation
of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with no fixed point. Then the second guess $\gamma_2$ of permutation Wordle
with strategy $S$ and secret $\pi$ is the inverse permutation $S_n^{-1}$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, proof of Proposition 4.

articles.title: Recurrence for the guesses of permutation Wordle
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a strategy, that is, a
permutation $S_m$ of $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ for every $m$, let $\pi$ be a permutation of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and let $\gamma_1, \gamma_2, \dots$ be the guesses of permutation Wordle with
strategy $S$ and secret $\pi$. For every $r \ge 1$, the guess $\gamma_{r+1}$ is the guess that one
round of the game with strategy $S$ and secret $\pi$ produces from $\gamma_r$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 2.

articles.title: Guesses of permutation Wordle
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a strategy, that is, a permutation $S_m$ of
$\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ for every $m$, and let $\pi$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. The
guesses $\gamma_1, \gamma_2, \dots$ of permutation Wordle with strategy $S$ and secret $\pi$ are
the maps from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to itself defined recursively: $\gamma_1$ is the identity, and
$\gamma_{r+1}$ is the guess that one round of the game with strategy $S$ and secret $\pi$
produces from $\gamma_r$. The sequence is indexed from $0$: its term at index $r$ is
$\gamma_{r+1}$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 2.

articles.title: Correct positions stay locked
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a strategy, that is, a permutation $S_m$ of
$\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ for every $m$, let $\pi$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and let
$g$ be a map from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to itself. If $g(i) = \pi(i)$ at a position $i$, then the
guess that one round of permutation Wordle with strategy $S$ and secret $\pi$ produces from $g$
also takes the value $g(i)$ at $i$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 2.

articles.title: One round of permutation Wordle
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a strategy, that is, a permutation $S_m$ of
$\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ for every $m$, let $\pi$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ (the
secret), and let $g$ be a map from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to itself (the current guess). Let $I$ be
the set of incorrect positions, the $k$ with $g(k) \ne \pi(k)$, and let $m$ be the number of
elements of $I$. The next guess agrees with $g$ at every position outside $I$ and permutes the
entries of $g$ on $I$ by $S_m$: writing $I = \{i_0 < i_1 < \dots < i_{m-1}\}$, it takes the value
$g(i_j)$ at $i_{S_m(j)}$ for every $j < m$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 2.

articles.title: Games won with the first guess
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a strategy, that is, a permutation $S_m$ of
$\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ for every $m$, and let $\pi$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Then
permutation Wordle with strategy $S$ and secret $\pi$ ends after exactly one guess if and only if
$\pi$ is the identity.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, proof of Theorem 5.

articles.title: Permutation Wordle games solved in a given number of guesses
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a strategy, that
is, a permutation $S_m$ of $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ for every $m$, let $\pi$ be a permutation of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and let $\gamma_1, \gamma_2, \dots$ be the guesses of permutation Wordle with
strategy $S$ and secret $\pi$. For a natural number $r$, the game ends after exactly $r$ guesses
when $r \ge 1$, $\gamma_r = \pi$, and $\gamma_j \ne \pi$ for every $j$ with $1 \le j < r$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 4.

articles.title: Permuting along all positions
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and
let $g$ be a map from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to itself. Applying $\sigma$ to the entries of $g$
along the set of all positions $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, listed in increasing order, gives the map
$g \circ \sigma^{-1}$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, proof of Proposition 4 (`γ₂ = S[n]⁻¹`).

articles.title: Permuting the entries of a map along a set of positions
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be a subset of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with $k$ elements, listed in increasing order as
$i_0 < i_1 < \dots < i_{k-1}$, let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, and let $g$
be a map from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to itself. Applying $\sigma$ to $g$ along $I$ gives the map that
takes the value $g(i_j)$ at $i_{\sigma(j)}$ for every $j < k$ and agrees with $g$ outside $I$.

## Sources

- Aurora Hiveley, *Experimenting with Permutation Wordle*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.7, Section 2 (the action of a strategy component on `𝓘_r`).

articles.title: Recursion for the Taylor coefficients of the Buchstab function
articles.statement:
Let $\omega$ be a real
function with $\omega(x) = 1/x$ for $1 \le x \le 2$ and
$x\,\omega(x) = 1 + \int_1^{x-1} \omega(t)\,dt$ for $x \ge 2$, and let $c_{n,i}$ ($n, i \ge 0$)
be real numbers such that for every integer $n \ge 1$ and every real $z$ with $-1 \le z < 1$ the
series $\sum_{i \ge 0} c_{n,i} z^i$ converges absolutely to $\omega(n + (1+z)/2)$. Then
$c_{1,i} = \frac{2}{3} \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^i$ for every $i \ge 0$, and for every $n \ge 1$

$$c_{n+1,0} = \frac{1}{2n+3} \sum_{i \ge 0} c_{n,i} \left(2(n+1) + \frac{(-1)^i}{i+1}\right)$$

and, for every $i \ge 1$,

$$c_{n+1,i} = \frac{1}{2n+3} \left(\frac{c_{n,i-1}}{i} - c_{n+1,i-1}\right).$$

The printed statement of Theorem 3 has $c_{n,i}/n$ in place of $c_{n,i-1}/i$; the recursion above
is the identity $(2n+3) c_{n+1,i} + c_{n+1,i-1} = c_{n,i-1}/i$ derived in the paper's proof.

## Sources

- Claude Gravel and Daniel Panario, *Evaluating the Generalized Buchstab Function and Revisiting the Variance of the Distribution of the Smallest Components of Combinatorial Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A7, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Recursion for the Taylor coefficients of the generalized Buchstab function
articles.statement:
Let $K > 0$,
let $\Omega$ be a real function with $\Omega(x) = 1$ for $1 \le x < 2$ and
$\Omega(x) = 1 + K \int_2^x \frac{\Omega(u-1)}{u-1}\,du$ for $x \ge 2$, and let $c_{n,i}$
($n, i \ge 0$) be real numbers such that for every integer $n \ge 1$ and every real $z$ with
$-1 \le z < 1$ the series $\sum_{i \ge 0} c_{n,i} z^i$ converges absolutely to
$\Omega(n + (1+z)/2)$. Then $c_{1,0} = 1$, $c_{1,i} = 0$ for every $i \ge 1$,

$$c_{2,0} = 1 + K \sum_{i \ge 0} \frac{(-1)^i}{(i+1)\,2^{i+1}},$$



$$c_{2,i} = K \sum_{j \ge 0} \frac{(-1)^{j+i-1} \binom{j+i}{i}}{(j+i)\,2^{j+i}} \quad (i \ge 1),$$

and for every $n \ge 3$, writing
$\alpha_{n,m} = \sum_{j=0}^{m} \frac{(-1)^{m-j}}{(2n-1)^{m-j}}\, c_{n-1,j}$ for $m \ge 0$,

$$c_{n,0} = \sum_{i \ge 0} c_{n-1,i} -
\frac{K}{2n-1} \sum_{i \ge 0} \frac{(-1)^{i+1} \alpha_{n,i}}{i+1}$$

and $c_{n,i} = \dfrac{K\, \alpha_{n,i-1}}{(2n-1)\, i}$ for every $i \ge 1$.

Here $c_{2,0} = 1 + K \log(3/2)$. The printed statement of Theorem 4 has
$c_{2,0} = 1 + K \sum_{i \ge 1} 1/(i\, 2^i)$, which omits the sign $(-1)^{i-1}$.

## Sources

- Claude Gravel and Daniel Panario, *Evaluating the Generalized Buchstab Function and Revisiting the Variance of the Distribution of the Smallest Components of Combinatorial Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A7, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Mean length of the smallest cycle of a random permutation
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 1$ let $X_n$ be the
length of the smallest cycle of a uniformly random permutation of $\{1, \dots, n\}$. Then
$\mathbb{E}(X_n) / (e^{-\gamma} \log n) \to 1$ as $n \to \infty$, where $\gamma$ is the
Euler–Mascheroni constant.

The paper states this as $\mathbb{E}(X_n) = e^{-\gamma} \log n \, (1 + O(h(n)/\log n))$ for some
$h(n) = o(\log n)$, which is equivalent.

## Sources

- Claude Gravel and Daniel Panario, *Evaluating the Generalized Buchstab Function and Revisiting the Variance of the Distribution of the Smallest Components of Combinatorial Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A7, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Higher moments of the smallest cycle length
articles.statement:
Let $\omega$ be a real function with
$\omega(x) = 1/x$ for $1 \le x \le 2$ and $x\,\omega(x) = 1 + \int_1^{x-1} \omega(t)\,dt$ for
$x \ge 2$, and for $n \ge 1$ let $X_n$ be the length of the smallest cycle of a uniformly random
permutation of $\{1, \dots, n\}$. For every integer $\ell \ge 2$ there are real constants
$\varepsilon > 0$ and $C$ such that for every $n \ge 1$

$$\left| \mathbb{E}(X_n^\ell) - \ell\, n^{\ell-1} \int_1^\infty \frac{\omega(x)}{x^\ell}\,dx \right|
\le C\, n^{\ell-1} n^{-\varepsilon}.$$

## Sources

- Claude Gravel and Daniel Panario, *Evaluating the Generalized Buchstab Function and Revisiting the Variance of the Distribution of the Smallest Components of Combinatorial Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A7, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Variance of the smallest cycle length
articles.statement:
Let $\omega$ be a real function with
$\omega(x) = 1/x$ for $1 \le x \le 2$ and $x\,\omega(x) = 1 + \int_1^{x-1} \omega(t)\,dt$ for
$x \ge 2$, and for $n \ge 1$ let $X_n$ be the length of the smallest cycle of a uniformly random
permutation of $\{1, \dots, n\}$. There are real constants $\varepsilon > 0$ and $C$ such that for
every $n \ge 1$

$$\left| \operatorname{Var}(X_n) - 2n \int_1^\infty \frac{\omega(x)}{x^2}\,dx \right|
\le C\, n \cdot n^{-\varepsilon}.$$

## Sources

- Claude Gravel and Daniel Panario, *Evaluating the Generalized Buchstab Function and Revisiting the Variance of the Distribution of the Smallest Components of Combinatorial Objects*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A7, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Stirling permutations
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number. A word $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_{2n}$ of
natural numbers is a Stirling permutation of order $n$ if every letter lies in $\{1, \dots, n\}$,
each $i \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ occurs exactly twice, and every letter strictly between the two
occurrences of $i$ is greater than $i$.

articles.title: The set of Stirling permutations
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $Q_n$ is the set of all
Stirling permutations of order $n$, viewed as words $w_1 w_2 \cdots w_{2n}$ of natural numbers.

articles.title: A sum rule for derangements
articles.statement:
For every natural number $p$,
$\sum_{n=0}^{p} n\, D(n) = \lfloor (p + 1)!/e \rfloor$, where $D(n)$ is the number of
derangements of $n$ objects.

## Sources

- Jean-Christophe Pain, *A Sum Rule for Derangements*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A84, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Zagier's formula for products of two cyclic permutations
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $k$ be integers
with $n \ge 1$ and $1 \le k \le n$. Call a permutation of an $n$-element set cyclic when it has
exactly one cycle, fixed points counted as cycles. Write $c(n+1, k)$ for the unsigned Stirling
number of the first kind, the number of permutations of $n + 1$ elements with exactly $k$
cycles. If $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are chosen independently and uniformly among the cyclic
permutations of an $n$-element set, then the probability that $\sigma\tau$ has exactly $k$
cycles, fixed points included, is

$$\frac{1 + (-1)^{n-k}}{(n+1)!} \, c(n+1, k).$$

Proof: We formalize the plane-permutation transposition and reflection bijections of
Chen and Reidys, arXiv:1502.07674, lines 786-1074, and their specialization to Zagier's
recurrence, lines 1167-1370. A generating-polynomial coefficient identity supplies the
matching Stirling recurrence; descending induction on the cycle count finishes.

## Sources

- R. Cori and G. Hetyei, *On Reduced Unicellular Hypermonopoles*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.3, Theorem [Zagier], lines 351-359, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL28/Hetyei/hetyei2.tex>, quoting D. Zagier.

articles.title: Point reflection between the two triangles of a parallelogram
articles.statement:
Let $u$ and $v$ be
linearly independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and let $P$ be the parallelogram they span. The map
$p \mapsto u + v - p$ is a bijection from the set of points of the triangle
$\operatorname{conv}\{0, u, v\}$ that lie in the interior of $P$ onto the set of points of the
triangle $\operatorname{conv}\{u, v, u + v\}$ that lie in the interior of $P$.

The map sends $s u + t v$ to $(1 - s) u + (1 - t) v$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Clean parallelograms are unimodularly equivalent to standard ones
articles.statement:
Let $u$ and $v$ be
lattice points spanning a clean lattice parallelogram $P$ whose area is an integer $n \ge 2$. Then
there is an integer $a$ with $1 \le a < n$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$ such that $P$ is unimodularly
equivalent to the standard clean parallelogram $P_{a,n}$.

For area $1$ (the unit square) there is no such $a$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Theorem 3.

articles.title: A determinant of three convergent vectors
articles.statement:
Let $1 \le a < n$ be integers, let
$n / a = [q_0; q_1, \dots, q_m]$ be the regular continued fraction of $n / a$, where $m$ is the
least index at which it terminates, and let $v_j = (B_j, A_j)$ be its convergent vectors. Then
for every natural number $i$ with $i + 2 \le m$, the determinant of the $3 \times 3$ matrix with
rows $(1, B_{i-2}, A_{i-2})$, $(1, B_i, A_i)$ and $(1, B_{i+2}, A_{i+2})$ equals
$(-1)^{i+1} q_i q_{i+1} q_{i+2}$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Lemma 10.

articles.title: Distances of the convergent vectors to the line $y = (n / a) x$
articles.statement:
Let $1 \le a < n$ be
coprime integers, let $n / a = [q_0; q_1, \dots, q_m]$ be the regular continued fraction of
$n / a$, where $m$ is the least index at which it terminates, and let $v_j = (B_j, A_j)$ be its
convergent vectors. For $p = (x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ let $d(p) = |n x - a y| / \sqrt{n^2 + a^2}$
be the distance from $p$ to the line $y = (n / a) x$. Then: if $m \ge 1$, then
$d(v_0) < n / (2 \sqrt{n^2 + a^2})$ and $d(v_{m-1}) > 0$; for every natural number $i$ with
$i + 1 < m$ we have $d(v_{i+1}) < d(v_i)$, so the distances strictly decrease along
$v_0, v_1, \dots, v_{m-1}$; and for every $i$ with $1 \le i \le m - 1$, every lattice point
$(\beta, \alpha)$ with $0 < \beta < a$, $0 < \alpha < n$, $\beta \le B_i$ and
$(\beta, \alpha) \ne v_{i-1}, v_i$ satisfies $d(\beta, \alpha) > d(v_{i-1})$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Initial convergent vectors
articles.statement:
For every rational number $x$, the convergent vectors of the
regular continued fraction of $x$ begin with $v_{-2} = (1, 0)$, $v_{-1} = (0, 1)$ and
$v_0 = (1, \lfloor x \rfloor)$, and its zeroth partial quotient is $q_0 = \lfloor x \rfloor$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Section 3 (CF algorithm, Step 1 and Step 2).

articles.title: Convergent vectors in the quarters of $P_{a,n}$
articles.statement:
Let $1 \le a < n$ be coprime integers,
let $n / a = [q_0; q_1, \dots, q_m]$ be the regular continued fraction of $n / a$, where $m$ is
the least index at which it terminates, and let $v_i$ be its convergent vectors. The lines
$y = (n / a)(x - 1/2)$ and $y = n / 2$ cut the parallelogram $P_{a,n}$ with vertices $(0, 0)$,
$(1, 0)$, $(a, n)$, $(a + 1, n)$ into four closed parallelograms: $P_1$ (lower left), spanned by
$(1/2, 0)$ and $(a/2, n/2)$, and its translates $P_2 = P_1 + (1/2, 0)$ (lower right),
$P_3 = P_1 + ((a + 1)/2, n/2)$ (upper right) and $P_4 = P_1 + (a/2, n/2)$ (upper left). Let
$S(p) = (a + 1, n) - p$. Then for every $i$ with $0 \le i < m$: if $i$ is even, then
$v_i \in P_1$ and $S(v_i) \in P_3$; if $i$ is odd, then $v_i + (1, 0) \in P_2$ and
$S(v_i + (1, 0)) \in P_4$.

These points form the sets $V_1$ and $V_2$ of the paper.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Lemma 8.

articles.title: Lattice points of the parallelogram of two consecutive convergent vectors
articles.statement:
Let
$1 \le a < n$ be integers, let $n / a = [q_0; q_1, \dots, q_m]$ be the regular continued fraction
of $n / a$, where $m$ is the least index at which it terminates, and let $v_i$ be its convergent
vectors. For every integer $i$ with $-2 \le i < m$, the lattice points of the parallelogram
spanned by $v_i$ and $v_{i+1}$ are exactly $0$, $v_i$, $v_{i+1}$ and $v_i + v_{i+1}$, and every
point of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ equals $s v_i + t v_{i+1}$ for some integers $s$ and $t$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Recurrence for convergent vectors
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a rational number with regular continued
fraction $[q_0; q_1, q_2, \dots]$ and convergent vectors $v_{-2}, v_{-1}, v_0, \dots$, and let
$i \ge 0$. If the expansion of $x$ has a term $b$ in position $i + 2$ (it does not terminate
before $q_{i+2}$), then $q_{i+2} = b$ and $v_{i+2} = v_i + b \, v_{i+1}$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Section 3 (CF algorithm, Step 3).

articles.title: Lattice points of the triangle with vertices $0$, $v_{i-2}$, $v_i$
articles.statement:
Let $1 \le a < n$ be
integers, let $n / a = [q_0; q_1, \dots, q_m]$ be the regular continued fraction of $n / a$, where
$m$ is the least index at which it terminates, and let $v_j$ be its convergent vectors. For every
integer $i$ with $0 \le i \le m$, let $T_i$ be the closed triangle with vertices $0$, $v_{i-2}$
and $v_i$. Then the segment $[v_{i-2}, v_i]$ contains exactly $q_i + 1$ lattice points, the
interior of $T_i$ contains no lattice point, and every lattice point of $T_i$ other than its
vertices lies on the segment $[v_{i-2}, v_i]$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Lemma 9.

articles.title: Convergent vectors of a continued fraction
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a rational number with regular
continued fraction $[q_0; q_1, q_2, \dots]$, and let $A_j$ and $B_j$ be the numerators and
denominators of its convergents, given by $A_{-2} = 0$, $A_{-1} = 1$, $B_{-2} = 1$, $B_{-1} = 0$
and $A_j = q_j A_{j-1} + A_{j-2}$, $B_j = q_j B_{j-1} + B_{j-2}$ for $j \ge 0$. Stark's
convergent vectors of $x$ are $v_j = (B_j, A_j)$ for $j \ge -2$, so $v_{-2} = (1, 0)$,
$v_{-1} = (0, 1)$ and $v_j = v_{j-2} + q_j v_{j-1}$ for every $j \ge 0$ for which $q_j$ exists.

If the expansion terminates with $q_m$, then $v_j = v_m$ for all $j > m$; for $j < -2$ the
value is set to $v_0$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Section 3 (CF algorithm).

articles.title: Euclid's algorithm on small inputs
articles.statement:
Euclid's algorithm takes exactly one division step
on $(2, 1)$, two division steps on $(3, 2)$ and five division steps on $(13, 8)$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Section 5.3.

articles.title: Number of steps of Euclid's algorithm
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $u$ and $v$, the number of
division steps of Euclid's algorithm on $(u, v)$ is $0$ if $v = 0$, and otherwise one more than
the number of division steps on $(v, u \bmod v)$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Section 5.3 (division steps of the Euclidean algorithm).

articles.title: Vertices of the interior hull of a standard clean parallelogram
articles.statement:
Let $1 \le a < n$ with
$\gcd(a, n) = 1$, let $P_{a,n} = \{s (1, 0) + t (a, n) : 0 \le s \le 1,\ 0 \le t \le 1\}$, and let
$n / a = [q_0; q_1, \dots, q_m]$ be the regular continued fraction of $n / a$, with $m \ge 2$.
Write $A_i / B_i$ for its $i$-th convergent, and put $v_{-1} = (0, 1)$, $v_i = (B_i, A_i)$ for
$i \ge 0$, $u_i = v_i + (1, 0)$ (so $u_{-1} = (1, 1)$) and $w = (a + 1, n)$. Then the vertices of
the convex hull of the lattice points in the interior of $P_{a,n}$ are exactly $u_{-1}$ and
$w - u_{-1}$, the points $u_i$ and $w - u_i$ for odd $i$ with $0 \le i < m$, and the points $v_i$
and $w - v_i$ for even $i$ with $0 \le i < m$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Clean interior hulls and Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$,
$F_{k+2} = F_{k+1} + F_k$ be the Fibonacci numbers. Let $1 \le a < n$ with $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, let
$P_{a,n} = \{s (1, 0) + t (a, n) : 0 \le s \le 1,\ 0 \le t \le 1\}$, and let $H$ be the convex
hull of the lattice points in the interior of $P_{a,n}$. Then the lattice points on the boundary of
$H$ are exactly the vertices of $H$ if and only if there is a natural number $k$ with $n = F_k$
and either $a = F_{k-1}$ or $a = F_{k-2}$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Vertices and area of the interior hull of a standard clean parallelogram
articles.statement:
Let
$1 \le a < n$ with $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, let
$P_{a,n} = \{s (1, 0) + t (a, n) : 0 \le s \le 1,\ 0 \le t \le 1\}$, let
$n / a = [q_0; q_1, \dots, q_m]$ be the regular continued fraction of $n / a$, and let $H$ be the
convex hull of the lattice points in the interior of $P_{a,n}$. If $H$ has positive area, then
$H$ has $2(m + 1)$ vertices when $q_0 > 1$ and $2m$ vertices otherwise (that is, when $q_0 = 1$),
and $q_0 + q_1 + \dots + q_m = \mathrm{area}(P_{a,n}) - \mathrm{area}(H)$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Lemma 11.

articles.title: Interior lattice points of a standard clean parallelogram
articles.statement:
Let $1 \le a < n$ with
$\gcd(a, n) = 1$, let $P_{a,n} = \{s (1, 0) + t (a, n) : 0 \le s \le 1,\ 0 \le t \le 1\}$, and
write $\langle x \rangle = x - \lfloor x \rfloor$ for the fractional part of a real number $x$.
The lattice points in the interior of $P_{a,n}$ are exactly the points
$\langle k(n - a)/n \rangle \, (1, 0) + (k/n) \, (a, n)$ for $k = 1, \dots, n - 1$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Clean lattice parallelogram
articles.statement:
For points $u, v \in \mathbb{R}^2$, the parallelogram
spanned by $u$ and $v$ is clean when $u$ and $v$ are lattice points and the lattice points on the
boundary of the parallelogram are exactly $0$, $u$, $v$ and $u + v$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Section 2 (definition after Reznick).

articles.title: Lamé's theorem (1844)
articles.statement:
Let $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$, $F_{k+2} = F_{k+1} + F_k$ be the
Fibonacci numbers, and let $N \ge 1$. Let $u > v > 0$ be natural numbers on which Euclid's
algorithm takes exactly $N$ division steps, and suppose that $u \le u'$ whenever $u' > v' > 0$
are natural numbers on which it takes exactly $N$ division steps. Then $u = F_{N+2}$ and
$v = F_{N+1}$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Parallelogram spanned by two vectors
articles.statement:
For $u, v \in \mathbb{R}^2$, the parallelogram
spanned by $u$ and $v$ is the set $\{s u + t v : 0 \le s \le 1,\ 0 \le t \le 1\}$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Section 1.1.

articles.title: The integer lattice in the plane
articles.statement:
The lattice points of $\mathbb{R}^2$ are the points
$(a, b)$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$; they form the image of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Section 1.

articles.title: The last partial quotient of $n/a$ is at least $2$
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $n$ be natural numbers
with $1 \le a < n$, and let $n/a = [q_0; q_1, \dots, q_m]$ be the regular continued fraction of
$n/a$, where $q_0 = \lfloor n/a \rfloor$ and $m$ is the number of partial quotients after $q_0$
produced by the continued fraction algorithm (so $m = 0$ exactly when $a$ divides $n$). Then
$q_m \ge 2$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Lemma 7.

articles.title: Partial quotients of a rational number
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a rational number. The continued
fraction algorithm sets $x_0 = x$ and $q_0 = \lfloor x_0 \rfloor$ and, as long as $x_j$ is not an
integer, $x_{j+1} = 1/(x_j - q_j)$ and $q_{j+1} = \lfloor x_{j+1} \rfloor$; it stops at the first
index $m$ for which $x_m$ is an integer, so that $x = [q_0; q_1, \dots, q_m]$. For a natural
number $i$, the $i$-th partial quotient of $x$ is $q_i$ when $i \le m$ and $0$ when $i > m$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Section 3.

articles.title: The point reflection symmetry of $P_{a,n}$
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $n$ be natural numbers with
$1 \le a < n$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, let $P_{a,n} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be the parallelogram
with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, $(a, n)$, $(a + 1, n)$, and let
$S : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be $S(x, y) = (a + 1 - x, n - y)$. Then $S(P_{a,n}) = P_{a,n}$,
and $S$ is an isometry of $\mathbb{R}^2$ for the maximum distance
$d((x, y), (x', y')) = \max(|x - x'|, |y - y'|)$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Unimodular equivalences between the parallelograms $P_{b,n}$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$
and $n$ let $P_{b,n}$ be the parallelogram spanned by $(1, 0)$ and $(b, n)$, with vertices
$(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, $(b, n)$, $(b + 1, n)$. Let $n$, $a$ and $a'$ be natural numbers with $n > 1$,
$1 \le a < n$, $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, $1 \le a' < n$ and $a a' \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$. Then $P_{a,n}$ is
unimodularly equivalent to each of $P_{n-a,n}$, $P_{a',n}$ and $P_{n-a',n}$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Lemma 2.

articles.title: The parallelogram $P_{a,n}$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$ and $n$, the set
$P_{a,n} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ is the closed parallelogram spanned by $(1, 0)$ and $(a, n)$,
that is, the set of points $s (1, 0) + t (a, n)$ with $0 \le s \le 1$ and $0 \le t \le 1$. For
$n \ge 1$ it is the parallelogram with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, $(a, n)$ and $(a + 1, n)$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Section 2.

articles.title: Lowest and highest interior lattice points of $P_{a,n}$ on each vertical line
articles.statement:
Let $a$
and $n$ be natural numbers with $1 \le a < n$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, let $P_{a,n}$ be the
parallelogram with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, $(a, n)$, $(a + 1, n)$, and for an integer $k$
let $S_k$ be the set of integers $y$ such that $(k, y)$ lies in the interior of $P_{a,n}$. If
$a = 1$, the least element of $S_1$ is $1$ and the greatest is $n - 1$. If $a > 1$, then: for
every integer $k$ with $2 \le k \le a - 1$, the least element of $S_k$ is
$\lceil (k - 1) n / a \rceil$ and the greatest is $\lfloor k n / a \rfloor$; the least element of
$S_1$ is $1$ and the greatest is $\lfloor n / a \rfloor$; and the least element of $S_a$ is
$\lceil (a - 1) n / a \rceil$ and the greatest is $n - 1$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Lowest and highest interior lattice points of $P_{a,n}$ on paired vertical lines
articles.statement:
Let $a$
and $n$ be natural numbers with $1 \le a < n$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, let $P_{a,n}$ be the
parallelogram with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, $(a, n)$, $(a + 1, n)$, and for an integer $k$
let $S_k$ be the set of integers $y$ such that $(k, y)$ lies in the interior of $P_{a,n}$. Let
$k, l \ge 1$ be natural numbers with $k + l = a + 1$, and suppose that $y_L$ is the least element
of $S_k$ and $y_H$ is the greatest element of $S_l$. Then $y_L + y_H = n$, and $(l, y_H)$ lies on
the boundary of the convex hull of the points of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ in the interior of $P_{a,n}$ if
and only if $(k, y_L)$ does.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Lemma 6.

articles.title: Interior lattice points of $P_{a,n}$ on a vertical line
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$ and $n$,
let $P_{a,n}$ be the parallelogram spanned by $(1, 0)$ and $(a, n)$, with vertices $(0, 0)$,
$(1, 0)$, $(a, n)$, $(a + 1, n)$. For an integer $k$, the set $S_k$ is the set of integers $y$
such that $(k, y)$ lies in the interior of $P_{a,n}$, that is, the $y$-coordinates of the lattice
points in the interior of $P_{a,n}$ on the line $x = k$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Section 2.

articles.title: Integer affine maps of the plane
articles.statement:
For a $2 \times 2$ integer matrix $M$ with entries
$m_{ij}$ and an integer vector $u = (u_1, u_2) \in \mathbb{Z}^2$, the map
$T_{M,u} : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is
$T_{M,u}(x, y) = (m_{11} x + m_{12} y + u_1, m_{21} x + m_{22} y + u_2)$, that is,
$p \mapsto M p + u$. It is an affine unimodular map when $\det M = \pm 1$; the definition itself
puts no condition on $\det M$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Section 1.1.

articles.title: Unimodular equivalence is reflexive
articles.statement:
Every subset $P$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is unimodularly
equivalent to itself (take the identity matrix and the zero translation).

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Section 1.1.

articles.title: Unimodularly equivalent sets
articles.statement:
Two sets $P, Q \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ are unimodularly
equivalent when some affine unimodular map sends $P$ onto $Q$: there are a $2 \times 2$ integer
matrix $M$ with $\det M = 1$ or $\det M = -1$ and an integer vector $u \in \mathbb{Z}^2$ such that
$\{M x + u : x \in P\} = Q$.

In the paper's notation, where $T$ is the map and $P_1$ and $P_2$ are the two sets, the displayed
condition $T(P_1) = T(P_2)$ is a typo for $T(P_1) = P_2$.

## Sources

- Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan, Riaz R. Khan, and Peng Zhao, *A Geometric Relationship between Continued Fractions and Clean Lattice Parallelograms*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A10, Section 1.1.

articles.title: Colour group of a 2-coloured sphere triangulation
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a finite simplicial
2-sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$, let a colouring assign white or black to every finite set of points of
$\mathbb{R}^3$, and let $c$ be one of the two colours. The colour group of $X$ for $c$ is the
abelian group generated by the vertices of $X$ with the relations $u + v + w = 0$ for each
triangle $\{u, v, w\}$ of $X$ (a face with exactly three vertices) of colour $c$; that is, the
free abelian group $\mathbb{Z}^{(V)}$ on the vertex set $V$ of $X$ modulo the subgroup generated by
the indicator functions of the triangles of $X$ of colour $c$.

articles.title: Proper colourings of the triangles of a sphere triangulation
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a finite
simplicial 2-sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$, and let a colouring assign white or black to every finite
set of points of $\mathbb{R}^3$. The colouring is proper on $X$ if any two distinct triangles of
$X$ (faces with exactly three vertices) that have exactly two vertices in common receive different
colours.

articles.title: Blackburn–McCourt theorem (Kourovka Problem 17.35)
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a finite simplicial 2-sphere in
$\mathbb{R}^3$, and let a colouring assign white or black to every finite set of points of
$\mathbb{R}^3$ so that any two distinct triangles of $X$ (faces with exactly three vertices) with
exactly two vertices in common receive different colours. Let $G_W$ be the abelian group generated
by the vertices of $X$ with the relations $u + v + w = 0$ for each white triangle $\{u, v, w\}$ of
$X$, and let $G_B$ be defined in the same way from the black triangles. Then $G_W$ and $G_B$ are
isomorphic.

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 17.35 (I. M. Wanless, N. J. Cavenagh); resolution: S. R. Blackburn and T. A. McCourt, Triangulations of the sphere, bitrades and abelian groups, Combinatorica 34 (2014), 527-546, Theorem 1 (for any finite triangulation of the sphere with properly black-white coloured faces, A_W ≅ A_B); Kourovka Archive, Problem 17.35 (Conjecture is proved), https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.5423.

articles.title: Kourovka Problem 17.35 (statement)
articles.statement:
The statement that for every finite simplicial
2-sphere $X$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and every colouring of the finite sets of points of $\mathbb{R}^3$
white or black such that any two distinct triangles of $X$ (faces with exactly three vertices)
with exactly two vertices in common receive different colours, the groups $G_W$ and $G_B$ are
isomorphic. Here $G_W$ is the abelian group generated by the vertices of $X$ with the relations
$u + v + w = 0$ for each white triangle $\{u, v, w\}$ of $X$, and $G_B$ is defined in the same way
from the black triangles.

articles.title: Triangles of a sphere triangulation
articles.statement:
For a finite simplicial 2-sphere $X$ in
$\mathbb{R}^3$, the triangles of $X$ are its faces with exactly three vertices, that is, its
2-dimensional faces.

articles.title: The basis polynomials $b^d_j$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $d$ and $j$, $b^d_j$ is the complex
polynomial $b^d_j = \prod_{i=0}^{d-1} (X + d - j - i)$.

Integer constants are used before mapping to $\mathbb{C}$, avoiding any convention about rising
versus falling Pochhammer symbols.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, definition of `bᵈⱼ`.

articles.title: Binomial polynomial
articles.statement:
For an integer $n$ and a natural number $d$, the binomial polynomial
$\binom{X+n}{d}$ is the real polynomial $\frac{1}{d!} \prod_{i=0}^{d-1} (X + n - i)$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Lemma 7.

articles.title: The set of attainable canonical-line roots is connected
articles.statement:
For every positive integer $d$,
the set $\Omega_d$ of canonical-line roots of degree-$d$ CL-polynomials satisfying
$(\diamondsuit)$ is a nonempty connected subset of $\mathbb{C}$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Theorem 6.

articles.title: The set $\Omega_d$ of attainable canonical-line roots
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$,
$\Omega_d$ is the set of complex numbers $z$ on the canonical line such that $z$ is a root of
some CL-polynomial of degree $d$ satisfying $(\diamondsuit)$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, definition of `Ω_d`.

articles.title: Canonical line
articles.statement:
The canonical line $\mathrm{CL}$ is the vertical line of complex numbers
with real part $-1/2$, that is, $\mathrm{CL} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Re} z = -1/2\}$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Definition of `CL`.

articles.title: Parameter bound for SNN CL-polynomials
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a complex polynomial of degree $d$
that is a CL-polynomial with real scale $a$ and list of real parameters $c_1, \dots, c_m$, and
suppose that $f$ is SNN. Then for each parameter $c_k$ there is a real number $\beta$ such that
$-\tfrac12 + \beta i$ is a root of the symmetric basis polynomial $p^d_0$ and
$c_k \le \tfrac14 + \beta^2$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Theorem 7 (restatement of Theorem 4).

articles.title: Product of quadratic canonical-line factors
articles.statement:
For a finite list $c_1, \dots, c_m$ of real
numbers, this is the monic complex polynomial $\prod_{k=1}^{m} (X^2 + X + c_k)$; the empty list
gives the constant polynomial $1$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, factored definition of CL-polynomials.

articles.title: Values of CL-polynomials on the canonical line
articles.statement:
If $f$ is a CL-polynomial of degree $d$,
then for every $z$ on the canonical line there is a real number $r$ with $f(z) = r\, i^d$; that
is, $f$ maps the canonical line into $\mathbb{R}\, i^d$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Interlacing on the canonical line
articles.statement:
A complex polynomial $f$ CL-interlaces a complex
polynomial $g$ when $f$ and $g$ are nonzero, $\deg g = \deg f + 1$, all roots of $f$ and of $g$
lie on the canonical line, and, writing $d = \deg f$ and listing the roots with multiplicity as
$a_1, \dots, a_d$ for $f$ and $b_1, \dots, b_{d+1}$ for $g$, each list sorted by increasing
imaginary part, they alternate:
$\operatorname{Im} b_1 \le \operatorname{Im} a_1 \le \operatorname{Im} b_2 \le \cdots \le
\operatorname{Im} a_d \le \operatorname{Im} b_{d+1}$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, definition of CL-interlacing.

articles.title: Ehrhart CL-spans of reflexive polytopes in dimension at most 9
articles.statement:
Let $d \le 9$, let
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be the convex hull of a finite set of integer points, and suppose
that $P$ is reflexive. Let $\Delta^d_{sr}$ be the standard reflexive simplex, with vertices
$e_1, \dots, e_d$ and $-(e_1 + \cdots + e_d)$. Let $E$ and $E'$ be complex polynomials such
that, for every natural number $k$, $E(k)$ is the number of integer points of $kP$ and $E'(k)$
is the number of integer points of $k\Delta^d_{sr}$. Then
$\operatorname{clspan} E \subseteq \operatorname{clspan} E'$.

Reflexivity is Hibi's interior-point characterization, up to a lattice translation, which does
not change the Ehrhart polynomial.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Proposition 4.

articles.title: CL-span bound for SNN CL-polynomials
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a complex polynomial of degree $d$ that
is both a CL-polynomial and an SNN polynomial. Then the CL-span of $f$ is contained in the
CL-span of the symmetric basis polynomial $p^d_0$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Theorem 4.

articles.title: CL-span of the zero polynomial
articles.statement:
The zero polynomial has empty CL-span (its root multiset
is empty).

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Section 2 (definition of `clspan`).

articles.title: CL-span
articles.statement:
The CL-span of a complex polynomial $f$ is the convex hull, in $\mathbb{C}$
viewed as a real vector space, of the set of roots of $f$ lying on the canonical line, the line
of complex numbers with real part $-1/2$. Here the zero polynomial is regarded as having no
roots, so its CL-span is empty.

When nonempty, the CL-span is an interval of the canonical line.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Section 2 (definition of `clspan`).

articles.title: Coefficientwise limits preserve real interlacing
articles.statement:
Let $(f_n)$ and $(g_n)$ be sequences
of real polynomials with only real roots, and let $f$ and $g$ be nonzero real polynomials such
that, for every $k$, the coefficient of $X^k$ in $f_n$ tends to that in $f$ and the coefficient
of $X^k$ in $g_n$ tends to that in $g$ as $n \to \infty$. Suppose that for all sufficiently
large $n$ the degree of $f_n$ equals the degree of $f$ and the degree of $g_n$ equals the degree
of $g$, and that $f_n$ interlaces $g_n$ for every $n$, in the sense of real interlacing. Then $f$
interlaces $g$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Proposition 3 (quoting Fisk, Corollary 1.41).

articles.title: Complex binomial polynomial
articles.statement:
For an integer $n$ and a natural number $d$, the complex
binomial polynomial $\binom{X+n}{d} \in \mathbb{C}[X]$ is

$$\binom{X+n}{d} = \frac{1}{d!} \prod_{i=0}^{d-1} (X + n - i).$$

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Theorem 3 (quoting Braun and Develin, Theorem 2.3).

articles.title: Polynomial counting the lattice points of dilates
articles.statement:
Let $V \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^d$ be a
finite set and let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be the lattice polytope spanned by $V$, its convex
hull. A complex polynomial $E$ counts the lattice points of $P$ when, for every natural number
$k$, $E(k)$ equals the ordinary Ehrhart count $|kP \cap \mathbb{Z}^d|$, the number of points of
$\mathbb{Z}^d$ of the form $kx$ with $x$ a rational point of $P$.

By Ehrhart's theorem such a polynomial exists, and it is unique.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, definition of the Ehrhart polynomial.

articles.title: Classical bounds on Ehrhart roots
articles.statement:
Let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a full-dimensional
lattice polytope, the convex hull of a finite set of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, and let $E$ be a
complex polynomial with $E(k) = |kP \cap \mathbb{Z}^d|$ for every natural number $k$. Then every
complex root $\alpha$ of $E$ satisfies $|\alpha| \le 1 + (d+1)!$, and every real root $\alpha$
of $E$ satisfies $-d \le \alpha < \lfloor d/2 \rfloor$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Theorem 1 (quoting Beck, De Loera, Develin, Pfeifle, and Stanley, Theorem 1.2).

articles.title: Braun's disc for Ehrhart roots
articles.statement:
Let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a full-dimensional
lattice polytope, the convex hull of a finite set of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, and let $E$ be a
complex polynomial with $E(k) = |kP \cap \mathbb{Z}^d|$ for every natural number $k$. Then every
root $\alpha$ of $E$ lies in the closed disc centered at $-1/2$ with radius $d(d - 1/2)$, that
is, $|\alpha + 1/2| \le d(d - 1/2)$.

By Ehrhart's theorem, $E$ has degree $d$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Theorem 2 (quoting Braun, Theorem 1).

articles.title: Functional equation versus palindromic h-star coefficients
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a nonzero complex
polynomial of degree $d$ with $h^*$-coefficients $h^*_0(f), \dots, h^*_d(f)$. Then
$f(X-1) = (-1)^d f(-X)$ as polynomials if and only if $h^*_i(f) = h^*_{d-i}(f)$ for every
$i \le d$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Lemma 1 (quoting Corollary 2.2 in Kölbl's [11]).

articles.title: The h-star coefficients of a polynomial
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a complex polynomial of degree $d$,
with $d = 0$ for the zero polynomial. For a natural number $i$, the $i$-th $h^*$-coefficient of
$f$ is

$$h^*_i(f) = \sum_{j=0}^{i} (-1)^j \binom{d+1}{j} f(i-j),$$

the coefficient of $t^i$ in the power series $(1-t)^{d+1} \sum_{k \ge 0} f(k)\, t^k$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, definition of the `h*`-polynomial.

articles.title: Property (♢)
articles.statement:
For a complex polynomial $f$ of degree $d$ and a natural number $i$, let
$h^*_i(f)$ be the coefficient of $t^i$ in $(1 - t)^{d+1} \sum_{k \ge 0} f(k)\, t^k$. Then $f$ has
property (♢) when $f \ne 0$ and its $h^*$-coefficients $h^*_0(f), \dots, h^*_d(f)$ are real,
nonnegative and palindromic, that is, $h^*_i(f) = h^*_{d-i}(f)$ for $0 \le i \le d$.

For CL-polynomials the paper notes that palindromicity is automatic; it is kept here as part of
the property.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, definition of `(♢)`.

articles.title: Real-rooted polynomials
articles.statement:
A real polynomial $f$ has only real roots when $f \ne 0$ and the
number of real roots of $f$, counted with multiplicity, equals the degree of $f$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Proposition 2 (quoting Fisk, Lemma 1.26).

articles.title: Hibi's lower bound
articles.statement:
Let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be the lattice polytope spanned by a
finite set of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, and suppose that $P$ is full-dimensional. Let $E$ be a
complex polynomial with $E(k) = |kP \cap \mathbb{Z}^d|$ for every natural number $k$, and write
$h^*_i$ for the $h^*$-coefficients of $E$. If $h^*_d \ne 0$, then
$\operatorname{Re} h^*_1 \le \operatorname{Re} h^*_k$ for every $k$ with $1 \le k < d$.

The $h^*$-coefficients are defined as complex numbers, so the inequality compares real parts.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Theorem 5 (quoting Hibi's lower bound theorem).

articles.title: CL-polynomials
articles.statement:
A complex polynomial $f$ of degree $d$ is a CL-polynomial when there are
a real number $a \ne 0$ and real numbers $c_1, \dots, c_m \ge 1/4$ with $m = \lfloor d/2 \rfloor$
such that $f = a \prod_{i=1}^{m} (X^2 + X + c_i)$ if $d$ is even and
$f = a (2X + 1) \prod_{i=1}^{m} (X^2 + X + c_i)$ if $d$ is odd.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, definition of CL-polynomial.

articles.title: CL-polynomials with given parameters
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a complex polynomial of degree $d$, let
$a$ be a real number, and let $c_1, \dots, c_m$ be a list of real numbers. Then $f$ is a
CL-polynomial with scale $a$ and parameters $c_1, \dots, c_m$ when $a \ne 0$, every $c_i \ge 1/4$,
$m = \lfloor d/2 \rfloor$, and $f = a \prod_{i=1}^{m} (X^2 + X + c_i)$ if $d$ is even and
$f = a (2X + 1) \prod_{i=1}^{m} (X^2 + X + c_i)$ if $d$ is odd.

The parameters form a list so that later statements can refer to individual parameters.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, definition of CL-polynomial.

articles.title: Full-dimensional sets
articles.statement:
A subset $P$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ is full-dimensional when it is
nonempty and the direction of its affine span is all of $\mathbb{R}^d$ (equivalently, the affine
span of $P$ is $\mathbb{R}^d$).

Nonemptiness matters only for $d = 0$: the empty subset of $\mathbb{R}^0$ has an affine span
whose direction $\{0\}$ is all of $\mathbb{R}^0$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, full-dimensional lattice-polytope convention.

articles.title: SNN polynomials
articles.statement:
For a complex polynomial $f$ of degree $d$ and a natural number $i$, let
$h^*_i(f)$ be the coefficient of $t^i$ in $(1 - t)^{d+1} \sum_{k \ge 0} f(k)\, t^k$. Then $f$ is
SNN when $f \ne 0$ and its $h^*$-coefficients $h^*_0(f), \dots, h^*_d(f)$ are real and
nonnegative.

Coefficients beyond the degree, which vanish by the generating-series identity, are not part of
the condition.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, definition of SNN-polynomial.

articles.title: Lattice points as real points
articles.statement:
A lattice point $x = (x_1, \dots, x_d) \in \mathbb{Z}^d$
is regarded as the point of $\mathbb{R}^d$ with the same coordinates $x_1, \dots, x_d$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, definition of a lattice polytope.

articles.title: Lattice polytopes
articles.statement:
The lattice polytope spanned by a finite set $V \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^d$
is the convex hull in $\mathbb{R}^d$ of the points of $V$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, definition of a lattice polytope.

articles.title: Fisk's Leibniz rule for interlacing
articles.statement:
Let $f, f_1, g, g_1$ be real polynomials with
positive leading coefficients, each having only real roots, such that $f$ and $g$ have no common
real root, $f_1$ interlaces $f$, and $g_1$ interlaces $g$. Then $f_1 g_1$ interlaces
$f g_1 + f_1 g$, the polynomial $f g_1 + f_1 g$ interlaces $f g$, the roots of $f g_1 + f_1 g$
alternate with those of $f g_1$ and with those of $f_1 g$, and $f g_1 + f_1 g$ has only real
roots.

Here $p$ interlaces $q$ when $p$ and $q$ are nonzero, $\deg q = \deg p + 1$, and both have only
real roots, whose sorted lists $a_1 \le \dots \le a_n$ and $b_1 \le \dots \le b_{n+1}$ (with
multiplicity) satisfy $b_1 \le a_1 \le b_2 \le \dots \le a_n \le b_{n+1}$. The roots of $p$ and
$q$ alternate when $p$ and $q$ are nonzero of the same degree $n$ and have only real roots, whose
sorted lists satisfy $a_1 \le b_1 \le \dots \le a_n \le b_n$ or
$b_1 \le a_1 \le \dots \le b_n \le a_n$.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Proposition 2 (quoting Fisk, Lemma 1.26, “Leibnitz rule”).

articles.title: Alternating lists of equal length
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a binary relation on a type $\alpha$ and
let $n \ge 0$. A list $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$ alternates with a list $(b_1, \dots, b_n)$ with
respect to $r$ when
$a_1 \mathrel{r} b_1 \mathrel{r} a_2 \mathrel{r} \cdots \mathrel{r} a_n \mathrel{r} b_n$,
that is, $a_k \mathrel{r} b_k$ for $1 \le k \le n$ and $b_k \mathrel{r} a_{k+1}$ for
$1 \le k < n$. Two empty lists alternate, and lists of different lengths never alternate.

This equal-length companion of interlacing is used only for the same-degree clauses in Fisk's
Leibniz rule.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Proposition 2 (quoting Fisk, Lemma 1.26).

articles.title: Interlacing lists
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a binary relation on a type $\alpha$ and let $d \ge 0$.
A list $(a_1, \dots, a_d)$ interlaces a list $(b_1, \dots, b_{d+1})$ with respect to $r$ when
$b_1 \mathrel{r} a_1 \mathrel{r} b_2 \mathrel{r} \cdots \mathrel{r} a_d \mathrel{r} b_{d+1}$,
that is, $b_k \mathrel{r} a_k$ and $a_k \mathrel{r} b_{k+1}$ for $1 \le k \le d$. Two lists
interlace only when the second has exactly one more entry than the first; in particular the
empty list interlaces every one-element list.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, definition of interlacing.

articles.title: Asymptotics of the largest root of the model polynomial
articles.statement:
For $d \ge 0$ let
$M_d = \binom{X+d}{d} + \binom{X}{d}$ be the model polynomial. Let $(\beta_d)_{d \ge 0}$ be a
sequence of complex numbers such that for every $d \ge 1$, $\beta_d$ is a root of $M_d$ and
$|\gamma| \le |\beta_d|$ for every root $\gamma$ of $M_d$. Then
$|\beta_d + \tfrac12| - d^2/\pi = O(1)$ as $d \to \infty$.

No condition is placed on $\beta_0$ because $M_0$ is constant; this does not affect the
asymptotic statement.

## Sources

- Max Kölbl, *Properties of Ehrhart Polynomials Whose Roots Lie on the Canonical Line*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A68, Theorem 3 (quoting Braun and Develin, Theorem 2.3).

articles.title: Model polynomial
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, the model polynomial is the complex
polynomial $M_d = \binom{X+d}{d} + \binom{X}{d}$, where for an integer $n$ the binomial
polynomial $\binom{X+n}{d}$ is $\frac{1}{d!}\prod_{i=0}^{d-1} (X + n - i)$.

For $d \ge 1$, $d!\,M_d$ is the symmetric basis polynomial $p^d_0$; the paper emphasizes that
$M_d$ need not be an Ehrhart polynomial.

## Sources
