numbers, let $D$ be a set of positive integers, and write $D + c = \{d + c : d \in D\}$. Suppose
that for every coloring of $D$ with $r - 1$ colors and every $k \ge 1$ there are
$x_0, \dots, x_{k-1} \in D$, all of the same color, that form a $(D + c)$-diffsequence, that is,
$x_{i+1} - x_i \in D + c$ for every $i < k - 1$. Then $D + c$ is $r$-accessible.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Theorem 10.

articles.title: One part of an accessible union is accessible
articles.statement:
Let $D$, $D_1$ and $D_2$ be sets of
natural numbers with $D = D_1 \cup D_2$. If $D$ is accessible, then $D_1$ is accessible or $D_2$
is accessible.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Corollary 3.

articles.title: Colorings avoiding long diffsequences under fractional-part bounds
articles.statement:
Let $r \ge 1$, let
$d_0 < d_1 < \cdots$ be a strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers with $d_0 > 0$, and let
$D = \{d_n : n \ge 0\}$. Suppose there are real numbers $\alpha$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ such that
for every $n$ the fractional part of $\alpha d_n$ lies in the closed interval
$[\varepsilon, (r-1)/r]$. Then there is a coloring of the positive integers with $r$ colors that
has no monochromatic $D$-diffsequence of positive integers of length
$\lceil 1/(r\varepsilon) \rceil + 1$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Theorem 12.

articles.title: The primes are 2-accessible
articles.statement:
The set of prime numbers is $2$-accessible: for every colouring
$c : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, 1\}$ of the natural numbers with two colours and every length $k \ne 1$
there is a sequence $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of natural numbers, all of the same colour, such that
each difference $x_{i+1} - x_i$ is a prime number.

Quester proves this as a special case of Theorem 1 of the paper, using the
Frantzikinakis–Host–Kra recurrence theorem along shifted primes.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, The Primes are 2-Accessible, arXiv preprint (2026), arXiv:2606.00410, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00410; Nikos Frantzikinakis, Bernard Host, Bryna Kra, The polynomial multidimensional Szemeredi theorem along shifted primes, Israel J. Math. 194 (2013), 331-348, arXiv:1009.1484, https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.1484.

articles.title: 2-accessibility of the primes
articles.statement:
The statement that the set of prime numbers is
$2$-accessible: for every colouring $c : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, 1\}$ of the natural numbers with two
colours and every length $k \ne 1$ there is a sequence $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of natural numbers,
all of the same colour, such that each difference $x_{i+1} - x_i$ is a prime number. Open Problem
Garden question OPG-1797 asks whether this holds.

## Sources

- `OPG-1797` (Open Problem Garden, node 1797, http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/2_accessibility_of_primes): "Is the set of prime numbers 2-accessible?"

articles.title: The even Fibonacci set is not 2-accessible
articles.statement:
Let $F_m$ denote the $m$-th Fibonacci number,
with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$. The even Fibonacci set
$\{F_{3n+3} : n \ge 0\} = \{2, 8, 34, \dots\}$ is not $2$-accessible.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Proposition 2 (consequence).

articles.title: The even Fibonacci numbers have degree of accessibility $1$
articles.statement:
The even Fibonacci set
$\{2, 8, 34, \dots\}$ is $1$-accessible, and it is not $r$-accessible for any natural number
$r \ge 2$.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Even Fibonacci set
articles.statement:
Let $F_m$ denote the $m$-th Fibonacci number, with $F_0 = 0$ and
$F_1 = 1$. The even Fibonacci set is $\{F_{3n+3} : n \ge 0\}$; its first terms are
$2, 8, 34, \dots$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Proposition 2.

articles.title: A 2-coloring with no monochromatic 4-term even-Fibonacci diffsequence
articles.statement:
Let $F_m$ denote
the $m$-th Fibonacci number, with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$, and let
$E = \{F_{3n+3} : n \ge 0\} = \{2, 8, 34, \dots\}$ be the even Fibonacci set. There is a coloring
of the positive integers with $2$ colors under which no four positive integers
$x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3$ of the same color satisfy $x_{i+1} - x_i \in E$ for $i = 0, 1, 2$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Proposition 2 (coloring claim).

articles.title: Fibonacci numbers divided by the golden ratio
articles.statement:
Let $F_n$ be the $n$-th Fibonacci number,
with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$, and let $\varphi = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2$ be the golden ratio. For every
natural number $n \ge 2$,

$$\frac{F_n}{\varphi} - F_{n-1} = (-1)^{n+1} \varphi^{-n}.$$

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Arithmetic progressions with Fibonacci gaps are not $2$-regular
articles.statement:
There is a coloring of the
positive integers with two colors that admits no monochromatic $5$-term arithmetic progression
with gap in the positive Fibonacci set $\{1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \dots\}$, that is, no positive integers
$x_0, \dots, x_4$ of one color with $x_i = a + i d$ for all $i < 5$, for a positive integer $a$ and
a positive Fibonacci number $d$. Moreover, the positive Fibonacci set is $1$-large, and it is not
$r$-large for any natural number $r \ge 2$.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Theorem 2.

articles.title: The positive Fibonacci set is not 2-large
articles.statement:
Let $F_n$ denote the $n$-th Fibonacci number,
with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$. The positive Fibonacci set
$\{F_n : n \ge 2\} = \{1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \dots\}$ is not $2$-large.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Proposition 1 (consequence).

articles.title: The morphism $\nu$
articles.statement:
The morphism $\nu$ is given on the letters $0$ and $1$ by
$\nu(0) = 1$ and $\nu(1) = 00$.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Definition 1.

articles.title: The Fibonacci numbers have degree of accessibility at most $3$
articles.statement:
The positive Fibonacci set
$\{1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \dots\}$ is not $r$-accessible for any natural number $r \ge 4$. Moreover, some
coloring of the positive integers with four colors admits no monochromatic $4$-term
diffsequence with differences in the positive Fibonacci set: there are no positive integers
$x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3$ of one color such that $x_{i+1} - x_i$ is a positive Fibonacci number for
$i = 0, 1, 2$.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Theorem 1.

articles.title: A 2-coloring with no monochromatic 6-term progression with positive Fibonacci gap
articles.statement:
There
is a coloring of the positive integers with two colors such that no 6-term arithmetic progression
$a, a + d, \dots, a + 5d$ of positive integers whose gap $d$ is a positive Fibonacci number is
monochromatic.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Proposition 1 (coloring claim).

articles.title: Beatty-sequence descriptions of the words $F_\infty$, $S$ and $T$
articles.statement:
Let
$\varphi = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2$ be the golden ratio and $F_\infty = 010010100\cdots$ the infinite
Fibonacci word. Let $S = \mu(F_\infty)$ be its image under the morphism $\mu$ with $\mu(0) = 10$
and $\mu(1) = 01$, and $T = \nu(F_\infty)$ its image under the morphism $\nu$ with $\nu(0) = 1$
and $\nu(1) = 00$. For a word $W$ and an integer $n \ge 1$, write $W(n)$ for the $n$-th letter of
$W$, counting from $1$. Then:
(i) for every integer $n \ge 1$, $F_\infty(n) = 0$ if and only if $n = \lfloor m\varphi \rfloor$
for some integer $m$;
(ii) for every integer $n$, positive or not, if $n \ne \lfloor m\varphi \rfloor$ for every
integer $m$, then $n + 1 = \lfloor m'\varphi \rfloor$ and $n - 1 = \lfloor m''\varphi \rfloor$ for
some integers $m'$ and $m''$;
(iii) for every integer $n \ge 1$, $S(n) = 0$ if and only if either $n$ is even and
$n/2 = \lfloor m\varphi \rfloor$ for some integer $m$, or $n$ is odd and
$(n+1)/2 \ne \lfloor m\varphi \rfloor$ for every integer $m$;
(iv) for every integer $n \ge 1$, $T(n) = 1$ if and only if $n = 2\lfloor m\varphi \rfloor - m$
for some integer $m$.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Finite unions of lacunary sets are not 2-large
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$ and all lacunary sets
$D_1, \dots, D_n$, the union $D_1 \cup \dots \cup D_n$ is not 2-large.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Theorem 8.

articles.title: $4$ is half of an even Fibonacci number
articles.statement:
Let $F_m$ be the $m$-th Fibonacci number, with
$F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$. The number $4$ belongs to the set
$G = \{F_{3n}/2 : n \ge 1\} = \{1, 4, 17, 72, \dots\}$ of halves of the positive even Fibonacci
numbers; indeed $4 = F_6/2$.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Section 2 (notation `G`, `g_n`).

articles.title: Fractional parts of shifted Fibonacci numbers divided by $\sqrt{5}$
articles.statement:
Let $F_n$ be the
$n$-th Fibonacci number, with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$, let $\varphi = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2$ be the
golden ratio, so that $2\varphi - 1 = \sqrt{5}$, and write $\{y\} = y - \lfloor y \rfloor$ for the
fractional part. Let $n \ge 13$ be a natural number and $\varepsilon \in \{-4, 0, 4\}$, let
$c_{n,\varepsilon}$ be Wesley's constant, which depends on $n \bmod 4$ and $\varepsilon$, and put
$y = (F_n + \varepsilon)/(2\varphi - 1)$. Then
(i) $\{y\} = -2(-\varphi)^{-n}/5 + c_{n,\varepsilon}$, and
(ii) $\lfloor y \rfloor$ is even if and only if $\varepsilon = 0$ and
$n \equiv 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 \pmod{12}$, or $\varepsilon = 4$ and
$n \equiv 0, 2, 3, 9, 10 \pmod{12}$, or $\varepsilon = -4$ and
$n \equiv 0, 1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 11 \pmod{12}$.

The paper prints $+2(-\varphi)^{-n}/5$ in (i). The sign $-$ is the one its proof derives
(Equation (1)); the printed sign fails for every $n \ge 13$, since this term is nonzero.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Differences of fractional parts of multiples of the golden ratio
articles.statement:
Let $F_m$ be the $m$-th
Fibonacci number, with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$, let $\varphi = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2$ be the golden
ratio, and write $\{y\} = y - \lfloor y \rfloor$ for the fractional part. Let $i \ge 1$ be a
natural number, put $g_i = F_{3i}/2$ (an integer, since $F_{3i}$ is even), and let
$x_1, x_2, m_1, m_2$ be integers. Then:
(i) if $g_i$ is even, $2(x_2 - x_1) = g_i$, $x_1 = \lfloor m_1\varphi \rfloor$ and
$x_2 = \lfloor m_2\varphi \rfloor$, then
$\{m_2\varphi\} - \{m_1\varphi\} \le (\varphi^{-3i+1} - \varphi)/4 < -0.38$;
(ii) if $g_i$ is odd, $2(x_2 - x_1) = g_i + 1$, $x_1 = \lfloor m_1\varphi \rfloor$ and
$x_2 + 1 = \lfloor m_2\varphi \rfloor$, then
$\{m_2\varphi\} - \{m_1\varphi\} < (3\varphi - 6)/4 < -0.28$;
(iii) if $g_i$ is odd, $i > 1$, $2(x_2 - x_1) = g_i - 1$, $x_1 + 1 = \lfloor m_1\varphi \rfloor$
and $x_2 = \lfloor m_2\varphi \rfloor$, then
$\{m_2\varphi\} - \{m_1\varphi\} < (-5\varphi + 6)/4 < -0.52$.

The paper states (i) with a strict inequality, but equality occurs: $i = 2$, $m_1 = 1$, $m_2 = 2$,
$x_1 = 1$, $x_2 = 3$ give $\{2\varphi\} - \{\varphi\} = (\varphi^{-5} - \varphi)/4$.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Furstenberg–Weiss correspondence for translation-invariant families
articles.statement:
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be
a collection of finite sets of integers that is closed under translation, that is,
$A + t \in \mathcal{A}$ for all $A \in \mathcal{A}$ and $t \in \mathbb{Z}$, and let $r \ge 1$.
For a homeomorphism $T$ and an integer $a$, write $T^{-a}(U)$ for the preimage of $U$ under the
$a$-th power of $T$. Then the following three conditions are equivalent: (a) for every coloring
of $\mathbb{Z}$ with $r$ colors there are a color $i$ and a set $A \in \mathcal{A}$ all of whose
elements have color $i$; (b) for every nonempty compact metric space $X$, every homeomorphism
$T$ of $X$ and every cover of $X$ by $r$ open sets $U_1, \dots, U_r$, there are $i$ and
$A \in \mathcal{A}$ such that $\bigcap_{a \in A} T^{-a}(U_i)$ is nonempty; (c) the same holds
for every nonempty compact metric space $X$, every minimal homeomorphism $T$ of $X$ and every
cover of $X$ by $r$ clopen sets $U_1, \dots, U_r$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Halves of even Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let $F_m$ be the $m$-th Fibonacci number, with $F_0 = 0$
and $F_1 = 1$. The set of halves of the positive even Fibonacci numbers is
$G = \{F_{3n}/2 : n \ge 1\} = \{1, 4, 17, 72, \dots\}$; its elements are written
$g_n = F_{3n}/2$ for $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Section 2 (notation `G`, `g_n`).

articles.title: Accessibility means $r$-accessibility for every $r \ge 1$
articles.statement:
A set $D$ of natural numbers
is accessible if and only if it is $r$-accessible for every natural number $r \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (r-accessible).

articles.title: Accessible sets
articles.statement:
A set $D$ of natural numbers is accessible if it is $r$-accessible for
every natural number $r \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (r-accessible).

articles.title: Characterization of chromatically intersective sets
articles.statement:
A set $D$ of natural numbers is
chromatically intersective if and only if every element of $D$ is positive and, for every
natural number $r \ge 1$ and every coloring of the positive integers with $r$ colors, there are
positive integers $a$ and $b$ of the same color whose difference $a - b$, computed in the
integers, lies in $D$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Theorem 13(iv).

articles.title: Chromatically intersective sets
articles.statement:
A set $D$ of natural numbers is chromatically
intersective if every element of $D$ is positive and, for every natural number $r \ge 1$ and
every coloring of the positive integers with $r$ colors, there are positive integers $a$ and $b$
of the same color whose difference $a - b$, computed in the integers, lies in $D$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Theorem 13(iv).

articles.title: Characterization of arithmetic progressions with gap in $D$
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a set of natural
numbers, $k$ a natural number and $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ positive integers. Then
$x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ is a $k$-term arithmetic progression with gap in $D$ if and only if there
are a positive integer $a$ and an element $d \in D$ such that $x_i = a + i d$ for every $i < k$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (r-large).

articles.title: Arithmetic progressions with gap in $D$
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a set of natural numbers and $k$ a
natural number. A sequence $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of positive integers is a $k$-term arithmetic
progression with gap in $D$ if there are a positive integer $a$ and an element $d \in D$ such
that $x_i = a + i d$ for every $i < k$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (r-large).

articles.title: Characterization of $D$-diffsequences
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a set of natural numbers and
$x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ integers. Then $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ is a $D$-diffsequence if and only if
for every $i$ with $i + 1 < k$ there is $d \in D$ such that $x_{i+1} - x_i = d$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (D-diffsequence).

articles.title: $D$-diffsequences
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a set of natural numbers and $k$ a natural number. A
finite sequence $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of integers is a $D$-diffsequence when for every $i$ with
$i + 1 < k$ there is $d \in D$ with $x_{i+1} - x_i = d$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (D-diffsequence).

articles.title: Characterization of lacunary sequences
articles.statement:
A sequence $(m_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of natural numbers
is lacunary if and only if $m_n > 0$ for every $n$ and there is a real number $q > 1$ such that
$m_{n+1} \ge q \, m_n$ for every $n \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Context (lacunary sequence).

articles.title: Characterization of lacunary sets
articles.statement:
A set $D$ of natural numbers is lacunary if and only
if there is a lacunary sequence $(m_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of natural numbers with
$D = \{m_n : n \ge 0\}$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Context (lacunary set).

articles.title: Lacunary set
articles.statement:
A set $D$ of natural numbers is lacunary when $D = \{m_n : n \ge 0\}$ for
some lacunary sequence $(m_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of natural numbers.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Context (lacunary set).

articles.title: Lacunary sequence
articles.statement:
A sequence $(m_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of natural numbers is lacunary when
$m_n > 0$ for every $n$ and there is a real number $\lambda > 1$ such that
$m_{n+1} \ge \lambda m_n$ for every $n \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Context (lacunary sequence).

articles.title: Characterization of large sets
articles.statement:
A set $D$ of natural numbers is large if and only if it
is $r$-large for every natural number $r \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (r-large).

articles.title: Large set
articles.statement:
A set $D$ of natural numbers is large when it is $r$-large for every natural
number $r \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (r-large).

articles.title: Characterization of $\ell$-topological recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $\ell$ be a natural number and $D$
a set of natural numbers. Then $D$ is a set of $\ell$-topological recurrence if and only if every
element of $D$ is positive and, for every compact metric space $X$, every minimal homeomorphism
$T \colon X \to X$ and every nonempty open set $U \subseteq X$, there is $d \in D$ such that
$\bigcap_{j=0}^{\ell} T^{-jd}(U)$ is nonempty, where $T^{-jd}(U)$ is the preimage of $U$ under
the $jd$-th iterate of $T$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (ℓ-topological recurrence).

articles.title: Sets of $\ell$-topological recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $\ell$ be a natural number. A set $D$ of
natural numbers is a set of $\ell$-topological recurrence when every element of $D$ is positive
and, for every compact metric space $X$, every minimal homeomorphism $T \colon X \to X$ and
every nonempty open set $U \subseteq X$, there is $d \in D$ such that
$\bigcap_{j=0}^{\ell} T^{-jd}(U)$ is nonempty, where $T^{-jd}(U)$ is the preimage of $U$ under
the $jd$-th iterate of $T$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (ℓ-topological recurrence).

articles.title: Characterization of minimal systems
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a compact metric space and
$T \colon X \to X$ a homeomorphism. Then $T$ is minimal if and only if there is no closed set
$K \subseteq X$ with $K \ne \emptyset$, $K \ne X$ and $T(K) = K$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (topological dynamical system, minimal).

articles.title: Minimal system
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a compact metric space and $T$ a homeomorphism of $X$. The
system $(X, T)$ is minimal when there is no closed set $K \subseteq X$ that is nonempty, different
from $X$ and invariant, meaning $T(K) = K$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (topological dynamical system, minimal).

articles.title: Monochromatic finite sequences
articles.statement:
Given a colouring $c : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, \dots, r - 1\}$
of the natural numbers with $r$ colours, a finite sequence $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of natural
numbers is monochromatic when all its terms have the same colour: $c(x_i) = c(x_j)$ for all
$i, j < k$.

## Sources

- `OPG-1797` (Open Problem Garden, node 1797, http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/2_accessibility_of_primes): formalizes "monochromatic sequence" from the definition of `r`-accessible.

articles.title: Monochromatic sequences of positive integers
articles.statement:
Let $r$ and $k$ be natural numbers and let
$c$ color the positive integers with the colors $0, 1, \dots, r - 1$. A sequence
$x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of positive integers is monochromatic for $c$ when $c(x_i) = c(x_j)$ for
all $i, j < k$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (r-large).

articles.title: Characterization of multiple topological recurrence
articles.statement:
A set $D$ of natural numbers is a set
of multiple topological recurrence if and only if $D$ is a set of $\ell$-topological recurrence for
every natural number $\ell \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (ℓ-topological recurrence).

articles.title: Sets of multiple topological recurrence
articles.statement:
A set $D$ of natural numbers is a set of multiple
topological recurrence when it is a set of $\ell$-topological recurrence for every natural number
$\ell \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (ℓ-topological recurrence).

articles.title: $r$-accessible sets of natural numbers
articles.statement:
A set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is $r$-accessible
when for every colouring $c : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, \dots, r - 1\}$ with $r$ colours and every
length $k \ne 1$ there is a sequence $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of natural numbers that is
monochromatic for $c$ and is an $S$-diffsequence: for each $i$ with $i + 1 < k$ there is
$d \in S$ with $x_{i+1} = x_i + d$.

## Sources

- `OPG-1797` (Open Problem Garden, node 1797, http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/2_accessibility_of_primes): `S` is `r`-accessible if for every `r`-coloring of `ℕ` and every `k ∈ ℕ \ {1}` there is a monochromatic `S`-diffsequence of length `k`.

articles.title: Characterization of $r$-accessible sets
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a natural number and $D$ a set of
natural numbers. Then $D$ is $r$-accessible if and only if every element of $D$ is positive,
$r \ge 1$, and for every coloring $c$ of the positive integers with the colors $0, 1, \dots, r - 1$
and every natural number $k \ge 1$ there are positive integers $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ that are
monochromatic for $c$ and form a $D$-diffsequence: $x_{i+1} - x_i \in D$, the difference taken in
the integers, for every $i$ with $i + 1 < k$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (r-accessible).

articles.title: $r$-accessibility for colorings of the positive integers
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a natural number. A set
$D$ of natural numbers is $r$-accessible when every element of $D$ is positive, $r \ge 1$, and for
every coloring $c$ of the positive integers with the colors $0, 1, \dots, r - 1$ and every natural
number $k \ge 1$ there are positive integers $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ that are monochromatic for $c$
and form a $D$-diffsequence: $x_{i+1} - x_i \in D$, the difference taken in the integers, for every
$i$ with $i + 1 < k$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (r-accessible).

articles.title: Characterization of $r$-large sets
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a natural number and $D$ a set of natural
numbers. Then $D$ is $r$-large if and only if every element of $D$ is positive, $r \ge 1$, and for
every coloring $c$ of the positive integers with the colors $0, 1, \dots, r - 1$ and every natural
number $k \ge 1$ there are positive integers $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ that are monochromatic for $c$
and form a $D$-AP: there are a positive integer $a$ and some $d \in D$ with $x_i = a + i d$ for
all $i < k$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (r-large).

articles.title: $r$-large sets
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a natural number. A set $D$ of natural numbers is $r$-large when
every element of $D$ is positive, $r \ge 1$, and for every coloring $c$ of the positive integers
with the colors $0, 1, \dots, r - 1$ and every natural number $k \ge 1$ there are positive integers
$x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ that are monochromatic for $c$ and form a $D$-AP: there are a positive
integer $a$ and some $d \in D$ with $x_i = a + i d$ for all $i < k$.

Quantifying over every length $k \ge 1$ formalizes "arbitrarily long" monochromatic $D$-APs.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (r-large).

articles.title: Finite $S$-diffsequences
articles.statement:
For a set $S$ of natural numbers, a finite sequence
$x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of natural numbers is an $S$-diffsequence when each term is the previous
one plus an element of $S$: for every $i$ with $i + 1 < k$ there is $d \in S$ with
$x_{i+1} = x_i + d$.

## Sources

- `OPG-1797` (Open Problem Garden, node 1797, http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/2_accessibility_of_primes): formalizes "`S`-diffsequence", i.e. `x_{i+1} - x_i ∈ S`, stated additively as `x (i+1) = x i + d` with `d ∈ S`.

articles.title: Topological recurrence is $1$-topological recurrence
articles.statement:
A set $D$ of natural numbers is a
set of topological recurrence if and only if it is a set of $\ell$-topological recurrence for
$\ell = 1$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (ℓ-topological recurrence).

articles.title: Sets of topological recurrence
articles.statement:
A set $D$ of natural numbers is a set of topological
recurrence when it is a set of $\ell$-topological recurrence for $\ell = 1$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (ℓ-topological recurrence).

articles.title: Iterated preimage as a preimage under a power
articles.statement:
For a homeomorphism $T$ of a topological
space $X$, an integer $s$ and a subset $U \subseteq X$, the iterated preimage $T^{-s} U$ is the
preimage $(T^s)^{-1}(U)$ of $U$ under the $s$-th power $T^s$ of $T$ in the group of
homeomorphisms of $X$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (ℓ-topological recurrence).

articles.title: Iterated preimage
articles.statement:
For a homeomorphism $T$ of a topological space $X$, an integer $s$ and
a subset $U \subseteq X$, the iterated preimage $T^{-s} U$ is defined as the preimage
$(T^s)^{-1}(U)$ of $U$ under the $s$-th power $T^s$ of $T$ in the group of homeomorphisms of $X$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (ℓ-topological recurrence).

articles.title: Dilates of a finite union of lacunary sets stay away from the integers
articles.statement:
Let $\ell \ge 1$
and let $S_0, \dots, S_{\ell-1} \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be lacunary sets with union
$S = \bigcup_i S_i$. Then there are real numbers $\alpha$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ such that the
infimum over $s \in S$ of the distance $|\alpha s - \operatorname{round}(\alpha s)|$ from
$\alpha s$ to its nearest integer $\operatorname{round}(\alpha s)$ equals $\varepsilon$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Largeness is partition regular
articles.statement:
If $D_1, D_2 \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and their union
$D = D_1 \cup D_2$ is large, then $D_1$ is large or $D_2$ is large.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Theorem 4.

articles.title: The Lucas numbers are not $4$-accessible
articles.statement:
Let $L = \{2, 1, 3, 4, 7, \dots\}$ be the set of
Lucas numbers $L_0 = 2$, $L_1 = 1$, $L_{n+2} = L_{n+1} + L_n$. There is a coloring of the positive
integers with the colors $0, 1, 2, 3$ for which no sequence $x_0, x_1, x_2$ of positive integers is
both monochromatic and an $L$-diffsequence; and $L$ is not $r$-accessible for any $r \ge 4$.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Lemma 6.

articles.title: Membership in the even Fibonacci set
articles.statement:
Write $F_m$ for the $m$-th Fibonacci number, with
$F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$. A natural number $d$ belongs to the even Fibonacci set if and only if
$d = F_{3n+3}$ for some natural number $n$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Proposition 2.

articles.title: Membership in the positive Fibonacci set
articles.statement:
Write $F_n$ for the $n$-th Fibonacci number,
with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$. A natural number $d$ belongs to the positive Fibonacci set if and
only if $d = F_n$ for some natural number $n \ge 2$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Accessibility with more colors implies accessibility with fewer
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a set of
natural numbers and let $r, s$ be natural numbers with $1 \le r \le s$. If $D$ is
$s$-accessible, then $D$ is $r$-accessible.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Definition (r-accessible).

articles.title: Halved even Fibonacci numbers and $4$-accessibility of the Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Write $f_n$
for the $n$-th Fibonacci number ($f_0 = 0$, $f_1 = 1$). Let $F = \{1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \dots\}$ be the
set of positive Fibonacci numbers and $G = \{f_{3n}/2 : n \ge 1\} = \{1, 4, 17, 72, \dots\}$ the set
of halves of the even Fibonacci numbers. If $G$ is not $2$-accessible, then $F$ is not
$4$-accessible.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Fast eventual growth rules out 2-accessibility
articles.statement:
Let $d_0 < d_1 < d_2 < \cdots$ be a
strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers with $d_0 > 0$, and let
$D = \{d_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$. Suppose there are a real number $\delta > 0$ and a natural
number $N \ge 1$ such that $d_{n+1} \ge (3 + \delta) d_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n + 1 \ge N$. Then $D$ is not $2$-accessible.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Sets growing by a factor of three are not 2-large
articles.statement:
Let $d_0 < d_1 < d_2 < \cdots$ be a
strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers with $d_0 > 0$ and $d_{n+1} \ge 3 d_n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $D = \{d_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$. Then $D$ is not $2$-large.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Positive values of a polynomial vanishing at zero form a large set
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a
polynomial with integer coefficients, positive leading coefficient and $p(0) = 0$. Then the set
of positive integers $d$ such that $p(n) = d$ for some positive integer $n$ is large.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Theorem 9.

articles.title: Positive Fibonacci set
articles.statement:
The positive Fibonacci set is $\{F_n : n \ge 2\}$, where the
Fibonacci numbers are $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$ and $F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n$. Equivalently, it is the
set $\{1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \dots\}$ of positive Fibonacci numbers, each counted once.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Finite removal preserves $r$-largeness
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a natural number. If a set
$D \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is $r$-large and $F \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is finite, then $D \setminus F$
is $r$-large.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Topological recurrence, accessibility and chromatic intersectivity
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a set
of positive integers. Say that $D$ has *diffsequence recurrence* if for every compact metric
space $X$, every minimal homeomorphism $T$ of $X$, every nonempty open set $U \subseteq X$ and
every $k \ge 1$ there are integers $s_1, \dots, s_k$ forming a $D$-diffsequence such that
$U \cap T^{-s_1}U \cap \dots \cap T^{-s_k}U$ is nonempty, where $T^{-s}U$ is the preimage of $U$
under the integer power $T^s$. Then the following are equivalent: $D$ is a set of topological
recurrence; $D$ has diffsequence recurrence; $D$ is accessible; $D$ is chromatically
intersective.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Theorem 13.

articles.title: The Thue–Morse morphism $\mu$
articles.statement:
The morphism $\mu$ on binary words sends the letter $0$ to
the word $10$ and the letter $1$ to the word $01$.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Definition 1.

articles.title: One part of a union inherits $k$-topological recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number
and let $D_1, D_2 \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $D_1 \cup D_2$ is a set of $k$-topological recurrence,
then $D_1$ or $D_2$ is a set of $k$-topological recurrence.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Theorem 14.

articles.title: Sets containing their own long diffsequences are 2-accessible
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a set of
positive integers. If for every $k \ge 1$ there are positive integers $x_1, \dots, x_k$, all in
$D$, that form a $D$-diffsequence, then $D$ is $2$-accessible.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Two-colorings avoiding long $D$-progressions
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a set of positive integers,
let $\alpha$ be a real number and let $\varepsilon > 0$ be such that
$\lVert \alpha d \rVert \ge \varepsilon$ for every $d \in D$, where $\lVert t \rVert$ denotes the
distance from $t$ to the nearest integer. Then there is a $2$-coloring of the positive integers
with no monochromatic $D$-arithmetic progression of length $\lceil 1/(2\varepsilon) \rceil + 1$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Theorem 7.

articles.title: 2-large sets contain multiples of every positive integer
articles.statement:
Every $2$-large set $D$ of
positive integers contains a multiple of each positive integer $m$.

## Sources

- Oscar Quester, *On Some Properties of Accessible Sets*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A64, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Wesley's constant $c_{n,0}$ for $n \equiv 0 \pmod 4$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ with
$n \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, Wesley's constant satisfies $c_{n,0} = 2/5$.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Lemma 5 (definition of `c_{n,ε}`).

articles.title: Wesley's constants $c_{n,\varepsilon}$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and an integer
$\varepsilon$, the real number $c_{n,\varepsilon}$ is defined by the residue of $n$ modulo $4$:
if $n \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, then $c_{n,\varepsilon} = (4 + (2\sqrt5 - 5)\varepsilon)/10$;
if $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, then $c_{n,\varepsilon} = (11 - 4\sqrt5)/5$ when $\varepsilon = -4$ and
$c_{n,\varepsilon} = (4 + (4\sqrt5 - 5)\varepsilon)/20$ otherwise;
if $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, then $c_{n,\varepsilon} = (6 + (2\sqrt5 - 5)\varepsilon)/10$;
if $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, then $c_{n,\varepsilon} = (9 - 4\sqrt5)/5$ when $\varepsilon = -4$ and
$c_{n,\varepsilon} = (8 + (2\sqrt5 - 5)\varepsilon)/10$ otherwise.

Lemma 5 uses these constants only for $\varepsilon \in \{-4, 0, 4\}$.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Lemma 5 (definition of `c_{n,ε}`).

articles.title: Wesley's word $S$
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be the morphism of binary words with $0 \mapsto 10$ and
$1 \mapsto 01$, and let $f_0 = 0$, $f_1 = 01$, $f_2 = 010$, $\dots$ be the finite Fibonacci words.
The word $S$ is the infinite binary word, indexed from $0$, whose letter at index $n$ is the
letter at index $n$ of $\mu(f_{n+2})$.

Since each $f_k$ is a prefix of $f_{k+1}$, $S = \mu(F_\infty) = 1001101001\dots$, where
$F_\infty = 010010100\dots$ is the infinite Fibonacci word.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Definition 1.

articles.title: Wesley's word $T$
articles.statement:
Let $\nu$ be the morphism of binary words with $0 \mapsto 1$ and
$1 \mapsto 00$, and let $f_0 = 0$, $f_1 = 01$, $f_2 = 010$, $\dots$ be the finite Fibonacci words.
The word $T$ is the infinite binary word, indexed from $0$, whose letter at index $n$ is the
letter at index $n$ of $\nu(f_{n+2})$.

Since each $f_k$ is a prefix of $f_{k+1}$, $T = \nu(F_\infty) = 1001100100\dots$, where
$F_\infty = 010010100\dots$ is the infinite Fibonacci word.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Definition 1.

articles.title: The first ten letters of Wesley's words $S$ and $T$
articles.statement:
Indexing letters from $0$, the
letters of $S$ at indices $0, 1, \dots, 9$ are $1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1$ and the letters of
$T$ at indices $0, 1, \dots, 9$ are $1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0$; that is, $S$ begins with
$1001101001$ and $T$ begins with $1001100100$.

## Sources

- William J. Wesley, *Improved Ramsey-Type Theorems for Fibonacci Numbers and Other Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A29, Definition 1.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 984: a two-colouring with short monochromatic progressions exists
articles.statement:
There is a
colouring of the positive integers with two colours such that for every real $\varepsilon > 0$
there is a real constant $C_\varepsilon$ with the following property: whenever $a \ge 1$,
$d \ge 1$ and $k \ge 0$ are integers and $a, a + d, \dots, a + (k - 1)d$ all have the same
colour, $k \le C_\varepsilon a^\varepsilon$.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #984, https://www.erdosproblems.com/984 (status PROVED); resolution: Z. Hunter, proof in the erdosproblems.com/984 comments, using Green's red-blue colourings for off-diagonal van der Waerden numbers, erdosproblems.com/984: 'Zach Hunter has proved the answer is yes (see the comments)'; the comment colours each block I_t = [100^t, 100^{t+1}) with no red 3-term progression and no blue progression of length k_t = |I_t|^{o(1)} for odd t (colours swapped for even t), https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/984.

articles.title: Statement of Erdős Problem 984 on short monochromatic progressions
articles.statement:
The proposition that
there is a colouring of the positive integers with two colours such that for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real constant $C_\varepsilon$ with the following property: whenever
$a \ge 1$, $d \ge 1$ and $k \ge 0$ are integers and $a, a + d, \dots, a + (k - 1)d$ all have the
same colour, $k \le C_\varepsilon a^\varepsilon$.

articles.title: Forcing a monochromatic descending wave
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, the statement
that for every colouring of the natural numbers with two colours there is a monochromatic $k$-term
descending wave all of whose terms lie in $\{1, \dots, n\}$. Equivalently, every colouring of
$\{1, \dots, n\}$ with two colours has a monochromatic $k$-term descending wave, so the statement
says $f(k) \le n$, where $f(k)$ is the least $n$ with this property.

articles.title: Descending wave
articles.statement:
A $k$-term descending wave is a sequence $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of
natural numbers with $x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_{k-1}$ and $x_{j-1} + x_{j+1} \le 2 x_j$ for every
$j$ with $0 < j < k - 1$.

articles.title: Alon–Spencer: the descending-wave number has cubic order
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, say
that $n$ forces a $k$-term wave if every colouring of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ with two colours has a
monochromatic $k$-term descending wave. There are real numbers $c > 0$ and $C$ such that for all
sufficiently large $k$, every natural number $n$ that forces a $k$-term wave satisfies
$n \ge c k^3$, and the natural number $\lfloor \max(C k^3, 0) \rfloor$ forces a $k$-term wave.
Writing $f(k)$ for the least $n$ that forces a $k$-term wave, this says $f(k) \asymp k^3$.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #781, https://www.erdosproblems.com/781 (status DISPROVED); resolution: N. Alon and J. Spencer, Ascending waves, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 52 (1989), 275-287; T. C. Brown, P. Erdős and A. R. Freedman, Quasi-progressions and descending waves, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 53 (1990), 81-95, Alon-Spencer Theorem 1.1: c_1 k³ ≤ f(k) ≤ c_2 k³ for all k ≥ 1, the upper bound being Brown, Erdős and Freedman's f(k) ≤ k³/3 - 4k/3 + 3; Brown, Erdős and Freedman also proved k² - k + 1 ≤ f(k) and asked whether it is the exact value, and Alon and Spencer: 'Here we show that this is false', https://web.math.princeton.edu/~nalon/PDFS/Publications1/Ascending%20waves.pdf.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 781, cubic order of the wave number
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, say
that $n$ forces a $k$-term wave if every colouring of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ with two colours has a
monochromatic $k$-term descending wave. The statement that there are real numbers $c > 0$ and $C$
such that for all sufficiently large $k$, every natural number $n$ that forces a $k$-term wave
satisfies $n \ge c k^3$, and the natural number $\lfloor \max(C k^3, 0) \rfloor$ forces a $k$-term
wave. Writing $f(k)$ for the least $n$ that forces a $k$-term wave, this says $f(k) \asymp k^3$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 781 is false
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, say that $n$ forces a $k$-term
wave if every colouring of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ with two colours has a monochromatic $k$-term
descending wave. It is not the case that for every natural number $k \ge 1$ the number
$k^2 - k + 1$ forces a $k$-term wave and the number $k^2 - k$ does not. Writing $f(k)$ for the
least $n$ that forces a $k$-term wave, this says that $f(k) \ne k^2 - k + 1$ for some $k \ge 1$.

Alon and Spencer proved $f(k) \ge c k^3$ for some $c > 0$, so $f(k) > k^2 - k + 1$ for all large
$k$.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #781, https://www.erdosproblems.com/781 (status DISPROVED); resolution: N. Alon and J. Spencer, Ascending waves, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 52 (1989), 275-287; T. C. Brown, P. Erdős and A. R. Freedman, Quasi-progressions and descending waves, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 53 (1990), 81-95, Alon-Spencer Theorem 1.1: c_1 k³ ≤ f(k) ≤ c_2 k³ for all k ≥ 1, the upper bound being Brown, Erdős and Freedman's f(k) ≤ k³/3 - 4k/3 + 3; Brown, Erdős and Freedman also proved k² - k + 1 ≤ f(k) and asked whether it is the exact value, and Alon and Spencer: 'Here we show that this is false', https://web.math.princeton.edu/~nalon/PDFS/Publications1/Ascending%20waves.pdf.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 781, the exact-value question
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, say that $n$
forces a $k$-term wave if every colouring of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ with two colours has a monochromatic
$k$-term descending wave. The statement that for every natural number $k \ge 1$ the number
$k^2 - k + 1$ forces a $k$-term wave and the number $k^2 - k$ does not; that is,
$f(k) = k^2 - k + 1$ for every $k \ge 1$, where $f(k)$ is the least $n$ that forces a $k$-term
wave.

articles.title: Solution of Erdős Problem 190 on monochromatic or rainbow progressions
articles.statement:
For a natural number
$k$, let $H(k)$ be the least natural number $N$ such that every colouring
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ has a good $k$-term arithmetic progression below $N$, that is,
there are natural numbers $a$ and $d > 0$ with $a + d(k - 1) < N$, where $k - 1$ is natural-number
subtraction, such that the colours $f(a + di)$ for $i < k$ are all equal or pairwise distinct;
let $H(k) = 0$ if no such $N$ exists. Then $H(k)^{1/k}/k \to \infty$ as $k \to \infty$.

This answers Erdős Problem 190 affirmatively; it was proved by Bae and, independently, by Fox and
Hunter.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problem #190, erdosproblems.com (live page, LaTeX source and forum threads read 2026-10-22), https://www.erdosproblems.com/190; J. H. Bae, A resolution of Erdős Problem #190 via Erdős-Lovász, BCT, and Baker-Harman-Pintz, arXiv:2604.20588 (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.20588; J. Fox and Z. Hunter, Three-color van der Waerden numbers grow super-exponentially, arXiv:2606.02541 (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.02541.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 190 on monochromatic or rainbow progressions
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, let
$H(k)$ be the least natural number $N$ such that every colouring $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
has a good $k$-term arithmetic progression below $N$, that is, there are natural numbers $a$ and
$d > 0$ with $a + d(k - 1) < N$, where $k - 1$ is natural-number subtraction, such that the colours
$f(a + di)$ for $i < k$ are all equal or pairwise distinct; let $H(k) = 0$ if no such $N$ exists.
The proposition asserts that $H(k)^{1/k}/k \to \infty$ as $k \to \infty$.

articles.title: Monochromatic-or-rainbow progression number
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, $H(k)$ is the least
natural number $N$ such that every colouring $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ has a good $k$-term
arithmetic progression below $N$, that is, there are natural numbers $a$ and $d > 0$ with
$a + d(k - 1) < N$, where $k - 1$ is natural-number subtraction, such that the colours $f(a + di)$
for $i < k$ are all equal or pairwise distinct. If no such $N$ exists, then $H(k) = 0$.

articles.title: Good arithmetic progressions
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a colouring and let
$N$ and $k$ be natural numbers. The colouring $f$ has a good $k$-term arithmetic progression below
$N$ if there are natural numbers $a$ and $d > 0$ with $a + d(k - 1) < N$, where $k - 1$ is
natural-number subtraction (so it is $0$ when $k = 0$), such that the colours $f(a + di)$ for
$i < k$ are either all equal (the progression is monochromatic) or pairwise distinct (it is
rainbow). For $k \ge 1$ the condition $a + d(k - 1) < N$ says that every term $a + di$ with
$i < k$ lies in $\{0, \dots, N - 1\}$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 645 is true
articles.statement:
For every colouring of the positive integers with two colours
there are positive integers $x$ and $d$ with $d > x$ such that $x$, $x + d$ and $x + 2d$ all
have the same colour.

Brown and Landman proved more: for every increasing function $f$ there is such a monochromatic
progression with $d > f(x)$. Erdős Problems also records a short argument of Alweiss.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #645, https://www.erdosproblems.com/645 (status PROVED (LEAN)); resolution: T. C. Brown and B. M. Landman, Monochromatic arithmetic progressions with large differences, Bull. Austral. Math. Soc. (1999), 21-35, erdosproblems.com/645: first proved by Brown and Landman, with d > f(x) for any increasing f; the page records a short argument of Alweiss, https://www.erdosproblems.com/645.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 645
articles.statement:
The statement that for every colouring of the positive integers with
two colours there are positive integers $x$ and $d$ with $d > x$ such that $x$, $x + d$ and
$x + 2d$ all have the same colour.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 966 holds
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k \ge 2$ and $r \ge 2$ there is a set $A$
of natural numbers that contains no arithmetic progression of $k + 1$ distinct terms and such
that for every colouring $c$ of the natural numbers with $r$ colours there are a subset
$t \subseteq A$ that is an arithmetic progression of $k$ distinct terms and a colour $i$ with
$c(x) = i$ for every $x \in t$.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #966, https://www.erdosproblems.com/966 (status PROVED (LEAN)); resolution: formal proof linked from erdosproblems.com/966 (found with Aristotle, posted in the comment thread); P. Erdős, Problems and results in combinatorial number theory (1975), 295-310, reports that Spencer had shown that such a sequence exists, erdosproblems.com/966 status 'proved (Lean)'; formal proof cited by formal-conjectures, https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos966.lean.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 966: progression-free sets that are Ramsey for shorter progressions
articles.statement:
This
is the statement that for all natural numbers $k \ge 2$ and $r \ge 2$ there is a set $A$ of
natural numbers that contains no arithmetic progression of $k + 1$ distinct terms and such that
for every colouring $c$ of the natural numbers with $r$ colours there are a subset
$t \subseteq A$ that is an arithmetic progression of $k$ distinct terms and a colour $i$ with
$c(x) = i$ for every $x \in t$.

Only the colours of elements of $A$ matter, so the colouring condition says that every
colouring of $A$ with $r$ colours has a monochromatic progression of $k$ distinct terms.

articles.title: Intervals forcing the van der Waerden number $W(3, k)$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $N$ and $k$,
the interval $\{1, \dots, N\}$ forces $W(3, k)$ if every red/blue colouring of the natural numbers
has, inside $\{1, \dots, N\}$, a red $3$-term arithmetic progression or a blue $k$-term arithmetic
progression (progressions have common difference $d > 0$). Equivalently $W(3, k) \le N$, where the
van der Waerden number $W(3, k)$ is the least $n$ such that every red/blue colouring of
$\{1, \dots, n\}$ has a red $3$-term or a blue $k$-term arithmetic progression.

articles.title: Monochromatic arithmetic progressions in an initial interval
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a red/blue
colouring of the natural numbers, given as a map to the Booleans ($\mathrm{true}$ is red,
$\mathrm{false}$ is blue), let $b$ be a colour and let $\ell$ and $N$ be natural numbers. Then $c$
has an $\ell$-term arithmetic progression of colour $b$ inside $\{1, \dots, N\}$ if there are
natural numbers $a$ and $d > 0$ such that for every $i < \ell$ we have $1 \le a + id \le N$ and
$c(a + id) = b$.

articles.title: Monochromatic arithmetic progression
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a colouring of the natural numbers with
the two colours true and false, let $b$ be a colour and let $l, N$ be natural numbers. Then $c$
has a monochromatic progression of colour $b$ and length $l$ in $\{1, \dots, N\}$ when there are
natural numbers $a \ge 1$ and $d \ge 1$ with $a + (l - 1) d \le N$, where $l - 1$ is read as $0$
when $l = 0$, such that $c(a + j d) = b$ for every $j < l$.

articles.title: The off-diagonal van der Waerden numbers are not polynomially bounded
articles.statement:
There are no
natural numbers $C$ and $A$ such that for every $k \ge 1$, every colouring of the natural numbers
in red and blue has a red $3$-term or a blue $k$-term arithmetic progression $a, a + d, \dots$
with $a \ge 1$, $d \ge 1$ and all terms in $\{1, \dots, C k^A\}$.

Equivalently, the van der Waerden number $W(3, k)$, the least $n$ such that every red/blue
colouring of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ has a red $3$-term or a blue $k$-term arithmetic progression, is
not bounded by $C k^A$ for any constants $C$ and $A$. Green proved that for some constant $c > 0$
and all sufficiently large $k$, $W(3, k) \ge k^{b(k)}$ with
$b(k) = c (\log k / \log \log k)^{1/3}$, which tends to infinity (the colours of his colouring are
swapped relative to this statement, which is symmetric).

## Sources

- AIM workshop Graph Ramsey theory, problem list, https://www.overleaf.com/read/mnvcscjjysvg, Problem 43 (same text: AimPL, Graph Ramsey Theory, section 25, http://aimpl.org/graphramsey/1/); resolution: B. Green, New lower bounds for van der Waerden numbers, Forum Math. Pi 10 (2022), e18, arXiv:2102.01543, abstract and main theorem: there is a red-blue colouring of [N] with no blue 3-term progression and no red progression of length e^{C (log N)^{3/4} (log log N)^{1/4}}, so w(3, k) ≥ k^{b(k)} with b(k) = c (log k / log log k)^{1/3} → ∞; Z. Hunter (arXiv:2111.01099) improved this to w(3, k) ≥ k^{c log k / log log k}, https://doi.org/10.1017/fmp.2022.12.

articles.title: Polynomial growth of the off-diagonal van der Waerden numbers (claim)
articles.statement:
There are natural
numbers $C$ and $A$ such that for every $k \ge 1$, every colouring of the natural numbers in red
and blue has a red $3$-term or a blue $k$-term arithmetic progression $a, a + d, \dots$ with
$a \ge 1$, $d \ge 1$ and all terms in $\{1, \dots, C k^A\}$. Equivalently, the van der Waerden
number $W(3, k)$, the least $n$ such that every red/blue colouring of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ has a red
$3$-term or a blue $k$-term arithmetic progression, satisfies $W(3, k) \le C k^A$ for every
$k \ge 1$.

This is the AIM question (Graph Ramsey theory, Problem 43) stated as a claim.

articles.title: Schoen's subexponential upper bound for $W(3, k)$
articles.statement:
Write $W(3, k)$ for the van der Waerden
number: the least $n$ such that every red/blue colouring of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ has a red $3$-term
or a blue $k$-term arithmetic progression (progressions have common difference $d > 0$). Say that
$N$ forces $W(3, k)$ if every red/blue colouring of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ has a red $3$-term or a
blue $k$-term arithmetic progression. There is a real constant $c < 1$ such that for all
sufficiently large natural numbers $k$ some natural number $N < \exp(k^c)$ forces $W(3, k)$.
Equivalently, $W(3, k) < \exp(k^c)$ for all large $k$.

Schoen proved $W(3, k) \le \exp(O(k^{1-\delta}))$ for an absolute constant $\delta > 0$, which gives
this statement; erdosproblems.com/721 records Schoen as the first to show it. The best known bound
is now $\exp(O((\log k)^9))$, via Bloom and Sisask.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #721, https://www.erdosproblems.com/721 (status SOLVED); resolution: T. Schoen, A subexponential upper bound for van der Waerden numbers W(3, k), Electron. J. Combin. 28 (2021), Paper 2.34; B. Green, New lower bounds for van der Waerden numbers, Forum Math. Pi 10 (2022), e18, Schoen's abstract: N ≤ exp(O(k^{1-c})) for an absolute c > 0 whenever {1, …, N} splits into a 3-AP-free part and a k-AP-free part; abstract of arXiv:2102.01543 (Green): w(3, k) ≥ k^{b(k)} with b(k) = c (log k / log log k)^{1/3}; erdosproblems.com/721: both specific challenges of Erdős have been met, https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/v28i2p34.

Waerden number: the least $n$ such that every red/blue colouring of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ has a red
$3$-term or a blue $k$-term arithmetic progression (progressions have common difference
$d > 0$). Say that $N$ forces $W(3, k)$ if every red/blue colouring of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ has a red
$3$-term or a blue $k$-term arithmetic progression. This is the proposition that there is a real

articles.title: Green's superpolynomial lower bound for $W(3, k)$
articles.statement:
Write $W(3, k)$ for the van der Waerden
number: the least $n$ such that every red/blue colouring of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ has a red $3$-term
or a blue $k$-term arithmetic progression (progressions have common difference $d > 0$). Say that
$N$ forces $W(3, k)$ if every red/blue colouring of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ has a red $3$-term or a
blue $k$-term arithmetic progression. There is a real constant $c > 0$ such that for all
sufficiently large natural numbers $k$, no natural number
$N < \exp\bigl(c (\log k)^{4/3} / (\log \log k)^{1/3}\bigr)$ forces $W(3, k)$. Equivalently,
$W(3, k) \ge \exp\bigl(c (\log k)^{4/3} / (\log \log k)^{1/3}\bigr)$ for all large $k$.

Green's colouring has no $3$-term progression in one colour and no long progression in the other;
it disproves Graham's guess $W(3, k) \ll k^2$. Hunter improved the bound to
$\exp(c (\log k)^2 / \log \log k)$ (erdosproblems.com/721).

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #721, https://www.erdosproblems.com/721 (status SOLVED); resolution: T. Schoen, A subexponential upper bound for van der Waerden numbers W(3, k), Electron. J. Combin. 28 (2021), Paper 2.34; B. Green, New lower bounds for van der Waerden numbers, Forum Math. articles.title: Van der Waerden's theorem
articles.statement:
For all positive integers $r$ and $k$ there is a natural
number $N$ such that for every coloring of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ with $r$ colors there are natural
numbers $a \ge 1$ and $d \ge 1$ with $a + (k - 1)d \le N$ such that each of the $k$ terms
$a, a + d, \dots, a + (k - 1)d$ has the same color as $a$.

Proof: apply the Hales–Jewett theorem to the digit-sum encoding $x \mapsto 1 + \sum_i x_i$
of words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, k - 1\}$, so that a combinatorial line becomes an
arithmetic progression. This follows the standard derivation in Graham, Rothschild, and
Spencer, *Ramsey Theory*, Section 2.3, from van der Waerden (1927).

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Waerden%27s_theorem

articles.title: Nonzero solutions of a two-equation system modulo primes greater than 3 congruent to 3 mod 4
articles.statement:
**Nonzero solutions of a two-equation system modulo primes greater than 3 congruent to 3
mod 4.** Let $n > 3$ be a prime with $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. Then there are nonzero
$x, y \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ and an integer $r \in \{2, 3\}$ such that $x + ry = 0$ and
$xy^r = 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.

The source prints the second equation as $xy r = 1$; it is read as $xy^r = 1$, as in the proof,
whose first case computes $xy^2 = x^3/4 = 1$.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Lemma 6.

articles.title: The sum-plus-product family is $1$-vanishing over $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$
articles.statement:
Let $F_1$ be
the family over $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ sending a block $(b_1, \dots, b_l)$ to
$\sum_i b_i + \prod_i b_i$. Then $F_1$ is $1$-vanishing: every sequence over
$\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ contains a block of consecutive terms, of some length $l > 1$, on which
$F_1$ vanishes.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Every family is $0$-vanishing
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and every family $F$ of
functions $f^{(l)} : (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^l \to M$, $l \ge 0$, into a type $M$ with a zero
element, $F$ is $0$-vanishing.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Section 2 (definition of `m`-vanishing).

articles.title: $m$-vanishing family
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $F = (f^{(l)})_{l \ge 0}$ be a
family of functions $f^{(l)} : (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^l \to M$ into a type $M$ with a zero
element. For a natural number $m$, $F$ is $m$-vanishing if for every sequence
$a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ of elements of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ there are a length $l > 1$ and a
start $s \ge 0$ such that $f^{(l)}(a_{s+jl}, a_{s+jl+1}, \dots, a_{s+jl+l-1}) = 0$ for every
$j < m$; that is, the sequence contains $m$ consecutive blocks of a common length $l > 1$ on each
of which $f^{(l)}$ vanishes.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Section 2 (definition of `m`-vanishing).

articles.title: The sum-minus-product family is vanishing modulo prime powers
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime,
$k > 0$ and $n = p^k$, and let $F_{-1}$ be the family over $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ sending a
block $(b_1, \dots, b_l)$ to $\sum_i b_i - \prod_i b_i$. Then $F_{-1}$ is vanishing.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Theorem 4.

articles.title: The sum-plus-product family is vanishing over $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}$
articles.statement:
**The sum-plus-product family is vanishing over $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ and
$\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}$.** Let $n \in \{4, 8\}$ and let $F_1$ be the family over
$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ sending a block $(b_1, \dots, b_l)$ to $\sum_i b_i + \prod_i b_i$. Then
$F_1$ is vanishing.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Lemma 2.

articles.title: The sum-plus-product family is vanishing over $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$
articles.statement:
Let $F_1$ be the
family over $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ sending a block $(b_1, \dots, b_l)$ to
$\sum_i b_i + \prod_i b_i$. Then $F_1$ is vanishing.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Zero-sum van der Waerden theorem
articles.statement:
For every positive integer $n$, the family over
$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ sending a block $(b_1, \dots, b_l)$ to $\sum_i b_i$ is vanishing: for
every $m > 0$, every sequence over $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ contains $m$ consecutive blocks of a
common length $l > 1$, each with sum zero.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Vanishing of families of sums of transformed entries
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a positive integer, $d$ a
natural number and $g_1, \dots, g_d : \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ maps.
Then the family over $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ sending a block $(b_1, \dots, b_l)$ to the vector
$\left(\sum_i g_1(b_i), \dots, \sum_i g_d(b_i)\right) \in (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^d$ is
vanishing, where a block counts as vanishing when all $d$ coordinates of this vector are zero.

The source assumes $d > 0$; for $d = 0$ the statement is trivial.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Vanishing family
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number. A family $F$ of functions on blocks over
$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ with values in a type with a zero is vanishing if it is $m$-vanishing for
every positive integer $m$.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Section 2 (definition of vanishing).

articles.title: Monotonicity of $m$-vanishing
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a family of functions on blocks over
$\mathbb{Z}/n$ with values in a type $M$ with a zero. If $F$ is $m$-vanishing and $m' \le m$,
then $F$ is $m'$-vanishing.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Section 2 (definition of `m`-vanishing).

articles.title: $F_{\pm 1}$ over $\mathbb{Z}/6$ is not $m$-vanishing for $m > 1$
articles.statement:
For every $m > 1$,
neither of the sum-plus-product families $F_{-1}$ and $F_1$ over $\mathbb{Z}/6$, where
$F_c(b_1, \dots, b_l) = b_1 + \dots + b_l + c\, b_1 \cdots b_l$, is $m$-vanishing.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Lemma 4.

articles.title: $F_1$ modulo a prime $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ is not $m$-vanishing for $m > 0$
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be
a prime with $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. Then for every $m > 0$ the sum-plus-product family $F_1$
over $\mathbb{Z}/n$, $F_1(b_1, \dots, b_l) = b_1 + \dots + b_l + b_1 \cdots b_l$, is not
$m$-vanishing.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Lemma 5, quoting Theorem 3.6 of Bialostocki and Dierker.

articles.title: $F_1$ modulo a prime $n > 3$ with $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ is not $m$-vanishing for $m > 0$
articles.statement:
Let $n > 3$ be a prime with $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. Then for every $m > 0$ the sum-plus-product
family $F_1$ over $\mathbb{Z}/n$, $F_1(b_1, \dots, b_l) = b_1 + \dots + b_l + b_1 \cdots b_l$, is
not $m$-vanishing.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Lemma 7.

articles.title: $F_1$ modulo $8u$ with $u > 1$ is not $m$-vanishing for $m > 0$
articles.statement:
Let $u > 1$ be a natural
number and $n = 8u$. Then for every $m > 0$ the sum-plus-product family $F_1$ over $\mathbb{Z}/n$,
$F_1(b_1, \dots, b_l) = b_1 + \dots + b_l + b_1 \cdots b_l$, is not $m$-vanishing.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Lemma 8.

articles.title: $F_1$ modulo $9u$ with $u > 0$ is not $m$-vanishing for $m > 0$
articles.statement:
Let $u > 0$ be a natural
number and $n = 9u$. Then for every $m > 0$ the sum-plus-product family $F_1$ over $\mathbb{Z}/n$,
$F_1(b_1, \dots, b_l) = b_1 + \dots + b_l + b_1 \cdots b_l$, is not $m$-vanishing.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Lemma 9.

articles.title: $F_c$ with $c \notin \{0, \pm 1\}$ is not $m$-vanishing for $m > 0$
articles.statement:
Let $n > 1$ and let
$c \in \mathbb{Z}/n$ with $c \ne 0$, $c \ne 1$ and $c \ne -1$. Then for every $m > 0$ the
sum-plus-product family $F_c$ over $\mathbb{Z}/n$,
$F_c(b_1, \dots, b_l) = b_1 + \dots + b_l + c\, b_1 \cdots b_l$, is not $m$-vanishing.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Theorem 2.

articles.title: The sum-plus-product family on blocks of length two
articles.statement:
For $c \in \mathbb{Z}/n$ and
$b_0, b_1 \in \mathbb{Z}/n$, the sum-plus-product family $F_c$ over $\mathbb{Z}/n$ satisfies
$F_c(b_0, b_1) = b_0 + b_1 + c\, b_0 b_1$.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Section 2 (the family `F_c`).

articles.title: The sum-plus-product family $F_c$
articles.statement:
For $c \in \mathbb{Z}/n$, the family $F_c$ over
$\mathbb{Z}/n$ sends a block $(b_1, \dots, b_l)$ of elements of $\mathbb{Z}/n$, of any length
$l \ge 0$, to $b_1 + \dots + b_l + c\, b_1 b_2 \cdots b_l$, where an empty sum is $0$ and an
empty product is $1$.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Section 2 (the family `F_c`).

articles.title: Classification of vanishing for the sum-plus-product family $F_1$
articles.statement:
Let $n > 1$ and let
$F_1$ be the family over $\mathbb{Z}/n$ given by
$F_1(b_1, \dots, b_l) = b_1 + \dots + b_l + b_1 \cdots b_l$. If $n \notin \{2, 3, 4, 6, 8\}$,
then $F_1$ is not $m$-vanishing for any $m > 0$. If $n \in \{2, 3, 4, 8\}$, then $F_1$ is
vanishing. If $n = 6$, then $F_1$ is $1$-vanishing but not $m$-vanishing for any $m > 1$.

## Sources

- Arie Bialostocki and Vladyslav Oles, *On Generalizing the Van Der Waerden Theorem to Some Symmetric Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A25, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Layman's Catalan-sum Hankel determinant, including the empty matrix
articles.statement:
Let $C_m$ denote the
$m$-th Catalan number and $F_m$ the $m$-th Fibonacci number, with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$. For
every natural number $n$, the determinant of the $n \times n$ integer matrix whose $(i, j)$ entry
is $C_{i+j+1} + C_{i+j+2}$ for $0 \le i, j \le n-1$ equals $F_{2n+2}$. For $n = 0$ the matrix is
empty and both sides equal $1$.

articles.title: Layman's Catalan-sum Hankel determinant
articles.statement:
Let $C_m$ denote the $m$-th Catalan number and
$F_m$ the $m$-th Fibonacci number, with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$. For every integer $n \ge 1$, the
determinant of the $n \times n$ integer matrix whose $(i, j)$ entry is $C_{i+j+1} + C_{i+j+2}$ for
$0 \le i, j \le n-1$ equals $F_{2n+2}$.

## Sources

- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL16/Bouras/bouras4.tex>, lines 109–117.

articles.title: Hankel transform
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $(a_k)_{k \ge 0}$ be a sequence
in $R$. The Hankel transform of $a$ is the sequence $(h_n)_{n \ge 0}$ in $R$ whose term $h_n$ is
the determinant of the $(n + 1) \times (n + 1)$ Hankel matrix $(a_{i+j})_{0 \le i, j \le n}$.

articles.title: Jacobi continued fraction expansion
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a ring, not necessarily commutative, let
$(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$, $(\alpha_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and $(\beta_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be sequences in $K$, let
$\mu_0 \in K$, and let $(F_i)_{i \ge 0}$ be a sequence of formal power series over $K$ in the
variable $x$. These data form a Jacobi continued fraction expansion of $a$ when
$\sum_{n \ge 0} a_n x^n = \mu_0 F_0$ and, for every $i \ge 0$,
$(1 - \alpha_i x - \beta_{i+1} x^2 F_{i+1}) F_i = 1$. Informally, the power series $F_i$ are the
tails of the continued fraction

$$
\sum_{n} a_n x^n = \cfrac{\mu_0}{1 - \alpha_0 x - \cfrac{\beta_1 x^2}{1 - \alpha_1 x - \cdots}}.
$$

This records only the continued fraction identities, not Heilermann's formula for the Hankel
determinants of $a$.

## Sources

- Paul Barry, "From Fibonacci to Robbins: Series Reversion and Hankel Transforms," JIS 24 (2021), Article 21.10.2, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL24/Barry2/barry461.tex>, lines 110-117.

articles.title: Weighted Motzkin recurrence for the coefficients of a Jacobi fraction
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a ring,
let $a$, $\alpha$, $\beta$ be sequences in $K$ and let $\mu_0 \in K$. Suppose that $a$ has Jacobi
fraction data $(\alpha, \beta, \mu_0)$: there are power series $F_0, F_1, \dots$ over $K$ with
$\sum_{n \ge 0} a_n x^n = \mu_0 F_0$ and $(1 - \alpha_i x - \beta_{i+1} x^2 F_{i+1}) F_i = 1$ for
every $i \ge 0$. Then there is an array $(M_{n,j})_{n, j \ge 0}$ in $K$ with $M_{0,0} = 1$ and,
for all $n, j \ge 0$, $M_{0,j+1} = 0$, $M_{n+1,0} = \alpha_0 M_{n,0} + \beta_1 M_{n,1}$ and
$M_{n+1,j+1} = M_{n,j} + \alpha_{j+1} M_{n,j+1} + \beta_{j+2} M_{n,j+2}$, such that
$a_n = \mu_0 M_{n,0}$ for every $n \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Paul Barry, *From Fibonacci to Robbins: Series Reversion and Hankel Transforms*, Journal of Integer Sequences 24 (2021), Article 21.10.2, lines 110–117, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL24/Barry2/barry461.tex. Barry does not explicitly state this auxiliary tableau lemma; it is a coefficientwise bridge for the displayed fraction.

articles.title: Hankel transforms of Jacobi fractions do not depend on the linear coefficients
articles.statement:
Let $K$
be a commutative ring. Say that a sequence $a$ in $K$ has Jacobi fraction data
$(\alpha, \beta, \mu_0)$, where $\alpha$, $\beta$ are sequences in $K$ and $\mu_0 \in K$, when there
are power series $F_0, F_1, \dots$ over $K$ with $\sum_{n \ge 0} a_n x^n = \mu_0 F_0$ and
$(1 - \alpha_i x - \beta_{i+1} x^2 F_{i+1}) F_i = 1$ for every $i \ge 0$. If $a$ has Jacobi fraction
data $(\alpha, \beta, \mu_0)$ and $a'$ has Jacobi fraction data $(\alpha', \beta, \mu_0)$, with the
same $\beta$ and $\mu_0$ but arbitrary $\alpha$ and $\alpha'$, then $a$ and $a'$ have the same
Hankel transform: for every $n \ge 0$ the determinants of the $(n+1) \times (n+1)$ matrices
$(a_{i+j})_{0 \le i, j \le n}$ and $(a'_{i+j})_{0 \le i, j \le n}$ are equal.

## Sources

- Paul Barry, "From Fibonacci to Robbins: Series Reversion and Hankel Transforms," Journal of Integer Sequences 24 (2021), Article 21.10.2, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL24/Barry2/barry461.tex>, lines 110-117. Stated over a commutative ring.

articles.title: Heilermann's formula
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a commutative ring, let $a$, $\alpha$, $\beta$ be
sequences in $K$ and let $\mu_0 \in K$. Suppose that $a$ has Jacobi fraction data
$(\alpha, \beta, \mu_0)$: there are power series $F_0, F_1, \dots$ over $K$ with
$\sum_{n \ge 0} a_n x^n = \mu_0 F_0$ and $(1 - \alpha_i x - \beta_{i+1} x^2 F_{i+1}) F_i = 1$ for
every $i \ge 0$. Then for every $n \ge 0$ the Hankel transform of $a$ at $n$, the determinant of
the $(n+1) \times (n+1)$ matrix $(a_{i+j})_{0 \le i, j \le n}$, equals

$$\mu_0^{n+1} \prod_{j=0}^{n-1} \beta_{j+1}^{\,n-j},$$

that is, $\mu_0^{n+1} \beta_1^n \beta_2^{n-1} \cdots \beta_n$, which is $\mu_0$ for $n = 0$.

## Sources

- Paul Barry, "From Fibonacci to Robbins: Series Reversion and Hankel Transforms," Journal of Integer Sequences 24 (2021), Article 21.10.2, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL24/Barry2/barry461.tex>, lines 110-117. Zero-indexed: `hankelTransform a n` is the determinant of the `(n + 1) x (n + 1)` Hankel matrix, and the product over `Finset.range n` with shift `beta (j + 1)` and exponent `n - j` gives `beta_1 ^ n, ..., beta_n ^ 1`; for `n = 0` the empty product yields `mu0`. Scope: only the determinant identity is stated; the Jacobi continued fraction data itself is carried by `HasJacobiFraction`.

articles.title: Heilermann's formula for weighted Motzkin arrays
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a commutative ring, let
$\alpha$, $\beta$ be sequences in $K$, let $\mu_0 \in K$, and let $(M_{n,j})_{n, j \ge 0}$ be an
array in $K$ with $M_{0,0} = \mu_0$ and, for all $n, j \ge 0$, $M_{0,j+1} = 0$,
$M_{n+1,0} = \alpha_0 M_{n,0} + \beta_1 M_{n,1}$ and
$M_{n+1,j+1} = M_{n,j} + \alpha_{j+1} M_{n,j+1} + \beta_{j+2} M_{n,j+2}$. Then for every
$n \ge 0$ the Hankel transform of the column $(M_{m,0})_{m \ge 0}$ at $n$, the determinant of the
$(n+1) \times (n+1)$ matrix $(M_{i+j,0})_{0 \le i, j \le n}$, equals

$$\mu_0^{n+1} \prod_{j=0}^{n-1} \beta_{j+1}^{\,n-j},$$

that is, $\mu_0^{n+1} \beta_1^n \beta_2^{n-1} \cdots \beta_n$, which is $\mu_0$ for $n = 0$.

No hypothesis that the $\beta_i$ are nonzero is needed.

## Sources

- Paul Barry, *From Fibonacci to Robbins: Series Reversion and Hankel Transforms*, Journal of Integer Sequences 24 (2021), Article 21.10.2, lines 110–117, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL24/Barry2/barry461.tex.

articles.title: Layman's theorem: the binomial transform preserves the Hankel transform
articles.statement:
For every
sequence of integers $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$, the Hankel transform of the binomial transform of $a$
equals the Hankel transform of $a$. Here the binomial transform of $a$ is the sequence
$b_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} a_i$, and the Hankel transform of a sequence $c$ is the
sequence whose $n$-th term, for $n \ge 0$, is the determinant of the $(n+1) \times (n+1)$
matrix $(c_{i+j})_{0 \le i, j \le n}$.

## Sources

- John W. Layman, *The Hankel Transform and Some of its Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 4 (2001), Theorem 1, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL4/LAYMAN/hankel.pdf>. Campaign source passage: Mahid M. Mangontarum, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL20/Mangontarum/mango4.tex>, lines 535-557.

articles.title: Specialized Stieltjes matrix
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be an additive monoid with one and let
$a, b, \lambda, \mu \in R$. The specialized Stieltjes matrix is the tridiagonal Stieltjes
production matrix with $a_1 = a + \lambda$, $b_1 = b + \mu$ and the same $a$ and $b$: the infinite
matrix $S$ with rows and columns indexed by $\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ whose entries are
$S_{i, i+1} = 1$ for every $i$, $S_{0,0} = a + \lambda$, $S_{1,0} = b + \mu$, $S_{i,i} = a$ and
$S_{i+1,i} = b$ for every $i \ge 1$, and $S_{i,j} = 0$ for all other $i, j$.

This specialization corresponds to the inverse Riordan pair with numerator
$1 - \lambda x - \mu x^2$ over $1 + a x + b x^2$.

articles.title: Tridiagonal Stieltjes production matrix
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be an additive monoid with one and let
$a_1, b_1, a, b \in R$. The Stieltjes matrix $S$ is the infinite matrix with rows and columns
indexed by $\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ whose entries are $S_{i, i+1} = 1$ for every $i$,
$S_{0,0} = a_1$, $S_{1,0} = b_1$, $S_{i,i} = a$ and $S_{i+1,i} = b$ for every $i \ge 1$, and
$S_{i,j} = 0$ for all other $i, j$. So row $0$ is $a_1, 1, 0, \dots$, row $1$ is
$b_1, a, 1, 0, \dots$, and each row $i \ge 2$ has $b$ below the diagonal, $a$ on the diagonal, $1$
above the diagonal and $0$ elsewhere.

articles.title: Even noncrossing partitions and Dyck paths with even descents
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n$, there is a bijection between the noncrossing partitions of $\{0, \dots, 2n - 1\}$ all of
whose blocks have even size and the Dyck paths of semilength $2n$ all of whose descents have even
length. Here the descents of a Dyck path are the lengths of its maximal runs of down steps, one
