for each peak $UD$: the run of down steps starting at the $D$ of that peak.

## Sources

- Taras Goy and Mark Shattuck, *Determinants of Toeplitz-Hessenberg Matrices with Fuss-Catalan Entries*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.2, Lemma 10 (`jis-2026-26.1.2-lem-10`).

articles.title: Toeplitz–Hessenberg determinants with Catalan entries
articles.statement:
Write $\det(a_0; a_1, \dots, a_n)$
for the determinant of the $n \times n$ Toeplitz–Hessenberg matrix whose entry in row $i$ and
column $j$ is $a_{i+1-j}$ for $j \le i + 1$ and $0$ above the superdiagonal (so $a_0$ fills the
superdiagonal and $a_1, \dots, a_n$ the first column); for $n = 0$ it is $1$. Let $C_n$ be the
$n$-th Catalan number, $C(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} C_n x^n \in \mathbb{Q}[[x]]$, and
$K_m = C_{m+2} - C_{m+1}$ for $m \ge -1$, so that $K_{-1} = 0$. Then the following hold.
(1) $\sum_{n \ge 1} \det(-1; C_1, C_3, \dots, C_{2n-1})\, x^{2n} = x^2 C(x)^2 C(-x)^2$.
(2) $\bigl(\sum_{n \ge 0} \det(-1; C_2, \dots, C_{n+1})\, x^n\bigr) \bigl(2 - C(x)^2\bigr) = 1$.
(3) For every $n \ge 1$,
$\det(1; K_{-1}, K_0, \dots, K_{n-2}) = (-1)^{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} C_i$.
(4) For every $n \ge 1$, $\det(1; K_0, K_1, \dots, K_{n-1}) = (-1)^{n-1} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} C_i$.
(5) $\bigl(\sum_{n \ge 1} \det(-1; K_0, K_1, \dots, K_{n-1})\, x^n\bigr) \bigl(1 - x C(x)^3\bigr) =
x C(x)^3$.

Thus the determinants in (2) have generating function $1/(2 - C(x)^2)$ and those in (5) have
generating function $x C(x)^3/(1 - x C(x)^3)$, the generating function of OEIS A026674; the
determinants in (1) form OEIS A066357.

## Sources

- Taras Goy and Mark Shattuck, *Determinants of Toeplitz-Hessenberg Matrices with Fuss-Catalan Entries*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.2, Theorem 6 (`jis-2026-26.1.2-thm-6`).

articles.title: Special Toeplitz–Hessenberg determinants of Fuss–Catalan numbers
articles.statement:
Write
$\det(a_0; a_1, \dots, a_n)$ for the determinant of the $n \times n$ Toeplitz–Hessenberg matrix
whose entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is $a_{i+1-j}$ for $j \le i + 1$ and $0$ above the
superdiagonal. For natural numbers $p, r \ge 1$ let $A_n(p, r) = \frac{r}{pn + r} \binom{pn + r}{n}$
be the generalized Fuss–Catalan number, put
$D_n(p, r) = (-1)^{n-1} \det(1; A_1(p, r), \dots, A_n(p, r))$, and let $C_n$ be the $n$-th
Catalan number. Then, in $\mathbb{Q}$: $D_n(2, 3) = C_{n-1} - C_{n-2}$ for every $n \ge 2$;
$D_n(2, 4) = C_{n-1} - 2 C_{n-2}$ for every $n \ge 3$;
$D_n(3, 1) = \frac{1}{n} \binom{3n - 2}{n - 1}$ for every $n \ge 1$; and
$D_n(3, 2) = \frac{2}{n} \binom{3n - 3}{n - 1}$ for every $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Taras Goy and Mark Shattuck, *Determinants of Toeplitz-Hessenberg Matrices with Fuss-Catalan Entries*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.2, Corollary 4 (`jis-2026-26.1.2-cor-4`).

articles.title: Toeplitz–Hessenberg determinants of Fuss–Catalan numbers
articles.statement:
Write
$\det(a_0; a_1, \dots, a_n)$ for the determinant of the $n \times n$ Toeplitz–Hessenberg matrix
whose entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is $a_{i+1-j}$ for $j \le i + 1$ and $0$ above the
superdiagonal. For natural numbers $p, r, n$ let $A_n(p, r) = \frac{r}{pn + r} \binom{pn + r}{n}$
be the generalized Fuss–Catalan number, taken to be $0$ when $pn + r = 0$. Then for all natural
numbers $p, r$ and every $n \ge 1$,

$$\det(1; A_1(p, r), \dots, A_n(p, r)) = (-1)^{n-1} \frac{r}{n} \binom{pn - r - 1}{n - 1}$$

in $\mathbb{Q}$, where the binomial coefficient has an integer, possibly negative, upper index:
$\binom{x}{k} = x (x - 1) \cdots (x - k + 1)/k!$.

This includes $p = r = 0$, which the paper's standing assumption excludes; there every entry
$A_i(0, 0)$ is $0$ and both sides vanish.

## Sources

- Taras Goy and Mark Shattuck, *Determinants of Toeplitz-Hessenberg Matrices with Fuss-Catalan Entries*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.2, Theorem 3 (`jis-2026-26.1.2-thm-3`).

articles.title: Generating function of Toeplitz–Hessenberg determinants
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and
$a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ a sequence in $R$. Write $\det(a_0; a_1, \dots, a_n)$ for the determinant
of the $n \times n$ Toeplitz–Hessenberg matrix whose entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is
$a_{i+1-j}$ for $j \le i + 1$ and $0$ above the superdiagonal. In the ring of formal power series
over $R$ let $f(x) = \sum_{n \ge 1} \det(a_0; a_1, \dots, a_n)\, x^n$ and
$H(x) = \sum_{i \ge 1} a_i (-a_0)^{i-1} x^i$. Then $f = H + H f$.

When $a_0$ is invertible, $H(x) = -g(-a_0 x)/a_0$ with $g(x) = \sum_{i \ge 1} a_i x^i$, and the
identity is the paper's $f(x) = (-g(-a_0 x)/a_0)/(1 + g(-a_0 x)/a_0)$. The form $f = H + H f$
needs no hypothesis on $a_0$; for $a_0 = 0$ it gives $\det(0; a_1, \dots, a_n) = a_1^n$.

## Sources

- Taras Goy and Mark Shattuck, *Determinants of Toeplitz-Hessenberg Matrices with Fuss-Catalan Entries*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.2, Lemma 2 (`jis-2026-26.1.2-lem-2`).

articles.title: Toeplitz–Hessenberg determinants of ternary Fuss–Catalan numbers
articles.statement:
Write
$\det(a_0; a_1, \dots, a_n)$ for the determinant of the $n \times n$ Toeplitz–Hessenberg matrix
whose entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is $a_{i+1-j}$ for $j \le i + 1$ and $0$ above the
superdiagonal, and let $H_n = \frac{1}{3n + 1} \binom{3n + 1}{n}$ and
$J_n = \frac{2}{3n + 2} \binom{3n + 2}{n}$. Then, in $\mathbb{Q}$,
$\det(1; H_2, H_3, \dots, H_{n+1}) = \frac{2 (-1)^{n-1}}{n} \binom{3n - 3}{n - 1}$ for every
$n \ge 2$, and $\det(-1; J_0, J_1, \dots, J_{n-1}) = H_n$ for every $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Taras Goy and Mark Shattuck, *Determinants of Toeplitz-Hessenberg Matrices with Fuss-Catalan Entries*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.2, Theorem 8, formulas (4) and (6) (`jis-2026-26.1.2-thm-8`).

articles.title: Small generalized Fuss–Catalan numbers
articles.statement:
For the generalized Fuss–Catalan numbers
$A_n(p, r) = \frac{r}{pn + r} \binom{pn + r}{n}$, one has $A_3(2, 1) = 5$, $A_2(2, 3) = 9$,
$A_3(3, 1) = 12$ and $A_2(3, 2) = 7$.

With $C_n$ the $n$-th Catalan number, $A_3(2, 1) = C_3$ and $A_2(2, 3) = C_4 - C_3$.

## Sources

- Taras Goy and Mark Shattuck, *Determinants of Toeplitz-Hessenberg Matrices with Fuss-Catalan Entries*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.2, Sections 1-2 (`C_n = A_n(2, 1)`, `K_n = A_n(2, 3)`, `H_n = A_n(3, 1)`, `J_n = A_n(3, 2)`).

articles.title: Trudi multi-sums of Fuss–Catalan numbers
articles.statement:
For $s \in \mathbb{Q}$ and rational numbers
$a_1, \dots, a_n$ let $T_s(a_1, \dots, a_n)$ be the sum of
$s^{|\alpha|} \binom{|\alpha|}{\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n} a_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots a_n^{\alpha_n}$
over all $(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n) \in \mathbb{N}^n$ with
$\alpha_1 + 2 \alpha_2 + \dots + n \alpha_n = n$, where $|\alpha| = \alpha_1 + \dots + \alpha_n$.
Let $A_n(p, r) = \frac{r}{pn + r} \binom{pn + r}{n}$ be the generalized Fuss–Catalan number,
taken to be $0$ when $pn + r = 0$; let $C_n$ be the $n$-th Catalan number,
$K_m = C_{m+2} - C_{m+1}$ for $m \ge -1$ (so $K_{-1} = 0$), $H_n = A_n(3, 1)$ and
$J_n = A_n(3, 2)$. Then the following hold.
(1) For all natural numbers $p, r$ and every $n \ge 1$,
$-T_{-1}(A_1(p, r), \dots, A_n(p, r)) = \frac{r}{n} \binom{pn - r - 1}{n - 1}$, where the
binomial coefficient has an integer, possibly negative, upper index:
$\binom{x}{k} = x (x - 1) \cdots (x - k + 1)/k!$.
(2) For every $n \ge 1$, $-T_{-1}(K_{-1}, K_0, \dots, K_{n-2}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} C_i$.
(3) For every $n \ge 1$, $-T_{-1}(K_0, K_1, \dots, K_{n-1}) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} C_i$.
(4) For every $n \ge 2$, $-T_{-1}(H_2, H_3, \dots, H_{n+1}) = \frac{2}{n} \binom{3n - 3}{n - 1}$.
(5) For every $n \ge 1$, $T_1(J_0, J_1, \dots, J_{n-1}) = H_n$.

Identity (1) includes $p = r = 0$, which the paper's standing assumption excludes; there both
sides are $0$.

## Sources

- Taras Goy and Mark Shattuck, *Determinants of Toeplitz-Hessenberg Matrices with Fuss-Catalan Entries*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.2, Corollary 9 (`jis-2026-26.1.2-cor-9`).

articles.title: Inverse of a Riordan array from its A- and Z-sequences
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, let
$g, f, A, Z, \bar f$ be formal power series over $K$, and let $d_{00} \in K$ with $d_{00} \ne 0$.
Suppose that $g(0) = d_{00}$, $f(0) = 0$, $A(0) \ne 0$ and $\bar f(0) = 0$; that
$f(\bar f(x)) = x$ and $\bar f(f(x)) = x$, so that $\bar f$ is the compositional inverse of $f$;
that $f(x) = x\, A(f(x))$, so that $A$ is the generating function of the A-sequence; and that
$g(x) = d_{00} \bigl(1 - x\, Z(f(x))\bigr)^{-1}$, so that $Z$ is the generating function of the
Z-sequence. Then

$$\left(\frac{1}{g(\bar f(x))},\ \bar f(x)\right) =
\left(\frac{A(x) - x\, Z(x)}{d_{00}\, A(x)},\ \frac{x}{A(x)}\right).$$

The pair on the left is the inverse of the Riordan array $(g, f)$. The hypothesis
$\bar f(f(x)) = x$ is not needed for the conclusion; it is kept to match the source.

## Sources

- Paul Barry and Aoife Hennessy, "Meixner-Type Results for Riordan Arrays and Associated Integer Sequences," Journal of Integer Sequences 13 (2010), Article 10.9.4, Lemma, lines 280-283, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL13/Barry5/barry96s.tex>. The paper attributes this formula to Luzon.

articles.title: Inverse of a Riordan array from its A- and Z-sequences (one-sided form)
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a
field, let $g, f, A, Z, \bar f$ be formal power series over $K$, and let $d_{00} \in K$ with
$d_{00} \ne 0$. Suppose that $g(0) = d_{00}$, $f(0) = 0$, $A(0) \ne 0$, $\bar f(0) = 0$,
$f(\bar f(x)) = x$, $f(x) = x\, A(f(x))$ and $g(x) = d_{00} \bigl(1 - x\, Z(f(x))\bigr)^{-1}$.
Then

$$\left(\frac{1}{g(\bar f(x))},\ \bar f(x)\right) =
\left(\frac{A(x) - x\, Z(x)}{d_{00}\, A(x)},\ \frac{x}{A(x)}\right).$$

Here $A$ and $Z$ are the generating functions of the A- and Z-sequences of the Riordan array
$(g, f)$, and the pair on the left is its inverse. Only $f(\bar f(x)) = x$ is assumed, not also
$\bar f(f(x)) = x$.

articles.title: A- and Z-sequence characterization of integer Riordan arrays
articles.statement:
Let $(d_{n,k})_{n,k \ge 0}$ be
an integer matrix that is lower triangular, that is, $d_{n,k} = 0$ whenever $n < k$. Then the
following are equivalent: (i) there are power series $g, f \in \mathbb{Z}[[x]]$ with $g(0) = 1$,
$f(0) = 0$ and $[x^1]\, f \ne 0$ such that $d_{n,k} = [x^n]\, g f^k$ for all $n, k \ge 0$;
(ii) $d_{0,0} = 1$ and there are rational sequences $(A_j)_{j \ge 0}$ and $(Z_j)_{j \ge 0}$ with
$A_0 \ne 0$ such that, for all $n, k \ge 0$,

$$d_{n+1,k+1} = \sum_{j=0}^{n} A_j\, d_{n,k+j} \quad\text{and}\quad
d_{n+1,0} = \sum_{j=0}^{n} Z_j\, d_{n,j}.$$

The sequences are rational because $A_0 = [x^1]\, f$ need not be a unit in $\mathbb{Z}$.

Correction to the cited source: Barry's Proposition displays the hypothesis $Z_0 \ne 0$, but the
identity Riordan array has $Z_0 = 0$, so that condition cannot hold in general. This statement
therefore drops $Z_0 \ne 0$ — a deliberate correction to the source, not just a normalization —
and instead imposes the Riordan normalization $d_{0,0} = 1$.

Proof: The forward implication uses coefficientwise triangular expansions in powers of $f$; the
converse reconstructs $g$ and $f$ from columns zero and one and proves rowwise uniqueness. This is
the route of Barry's Proposition Char following He and Sprugnoli's Theorems 2.1 and 2.2.

## Sources

- P. Barry, *A Note on a Family of Generalized Pascal Matrices Defined by Riordan Arrays*, Journal of Integer Sequences 16 (2013), Article 13.5.4, Proposition Char, lines 173-180, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL16/Barry2/barry231.tex>, after Theorems 2.1 and 2.2 of He.

articles.title: Matrix power formula for Barry's triangle
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be Barry's triangle recurrence and let
$2 \le a \le n$. Let $M$ be the $(a - 1) \times (a - 1)$ lower bidiagonal matrix of natural
numbers with diagonal entries $M_{i,i} = i(a - i)$ for $i = 1, \dots, a - 1$, entries
$M_{i+1,i} = 1$ just below the diagonal, and all other entries $0$. Then $s(0, n, a)$ is the
bottom-left entry $(M^{n-2})_{a-1,1}$ of the power $M^{n-2}$.

## Sources

- Khaidarov, *Enumeration of Certain k-Block Partitions of Barry*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.2.8, main result announced in the abstract, equation (7) (`jis-2026-26.2.8-abstract-main`).

articles.title: Matrix-free formula for Barry's triangle
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be Barry's triangle recurrence and let
$2 \le a \le n$. Then

$$s(0, n, a) = \sum_{p_1 + \dots + p_{a-1} = n - a} \prod_{i=1}^{a-1} \bigl(i(a - i)\bigr)^{p_i},$$

where the sum runs over all tuples $(p_1, \dots, p_{a-1})$ of natural numbers with sum $n - a$.

## Sources

- Khaidarov, *Enumeration of Certain k-Block Partitions of Barry*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.2.8, main result announced in the abstract, equation (11) (`jis-2026-26.2.8-abstract-main`).

articles.title: Small values of Barry's triangle
articles.statement:
Barry's triangle recurrence $s$ takes the values
$s(0, 2, 2) = 1$, $s(0, 4, 3) = 4$ and $s(0, 6, 4) = 67$.

## Sources

- Khaidarov, *Enumeration of Certain k-Block Partitions of Barry*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.2.8, Table 1.

articles.title: Defining recurrence of Barry's triangle
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $\beta, n, k$, Barry's
triangle recurrence $s$ satisfies
$s(\beta, n + 1, k + 1) = s(\beta + 1, n, k) + \beta (k + 1)\, s(\beta, n, k + 1)$.

## Sources

- Khaidarov, *Enumeration of Certain k-Block Partitions of Barry*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.2.8, equation (1).

articles.title: Barry's triangle recurrence
articles.statement:
The function $s(\beta, n, k)$ of natural numbers
$\beta, n, k$, with natural-number values, is defined by $s(\beta, 0, 0) = 1$, by
$s(\beta, n, k) = 0$ if exactly one of $n, k$ is $0$, and by

$$s(\beta, n, k) = s(\beta + 1, n - 1, k - 1) + \beta k\, s(\beta, n - 1, k)$$

if $n, k \ge 1$.

The triangle OEIS A080416 is $s(0, n, k)$ for $2 \le k \le n$.

## Sources

- Bulat Khaidarov, *Enumeration of Certain k-Block Partitions of Barry*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.2.8, equation (1).

articles.title: Bell matrix
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A Bell matrix over $R$ is given by a formal
power series $g \in R[[X]]$ whose constant coefficient is a unit of $R$. The corresponding
Riordan-array pair is $(g, Xg)$.

articles.title: Central coefficients of Bell matrices
articles.statement:
Let $g \in \mathbb{Z}[[X]]$ be the power series of a
Bell matrix over $\mathbb{Z}$, with constant coefficient $g(0) = 1$, and let
$u \in \mathbb{Z}[[X]]$ be a power series with constant coefficient $0$ such that substituting
$u$ for $X$ in $X \, g(X)^{-1}$ gives $X$. Then for every natural number $n$, the entry of the
Bell matrix in row $2n$ and column $n$ equals $(n+1)$ times the coefficient of $X^{n+1}$ in $u$.

The source writes the right-hand side as $(n+1)\,[x^n]\,\tfrac{1}{x} u(x)$.

## Sources

- Paul Barry, "On the Central Coefficients of Bell Matrices," Journal of Integer Sequences 14 (2011), Article 11.4.3, Theorem `laterthm`, lines 167-169, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL14/Barry3/barry132.tex>.

articles.title: Entries of a Bell matrix
articles.statement:
For a Bell matrix over a commutative ring $R$ given by the
power series $g$, and natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the entry in row $n$ and column $k$ is the
coefficient of $X^n$ in $g \cdot (Xg)^k$.

articles.title: Second component of a Bell matrix
articles.statement:
For a Bell matrix over a commutative ring $R$ given by
the power series $g$, the second component of its Riordan-array pair is the power series
$h = Xg \in R[[X]]$.

articles.title: Binary binomial interpolated triangle
articles.statement:
For real numbers $a_0, a_1, \alpha, \beta$, a real
array $(a_{n,k})_{n,k \ge 0}$ is the binary binomial interpolated triangle
$BT(a_0, a_1, \alpha, \beta; \alpha, \beta)$ when $\alpha\beta \ne 0$, $|a_0| + |a_1| \ne 0$,
$a_{0,0} = a_0$, $a_{1,0} = a_1$, $a_{n,0} = \alpha\, a_{n-1,0} + \beta\, a_{n-2,0}$ for every
$n \ge 2$, and $a_{n,k} = \alpha\, a_{n,k-1} + \beta\, a_{n-1,k-1}$ for all $1 \le k \le n$.
Entries $a_{n,k}$ with $k > n$ are not constrained.

articles.title: Rising diagonals of a binary binomial interpolated triangle are constant
articles.statement:
Let
$a_0, a_1, \alpha, \beta$ be real numbers and let $a = (a_{n,k})_{n,k \ge 0}$ be a real array that
is the binary binomial interpolated triangle $BT(a_0, a_1, \alpha, \beta; \alpha, \beta)$. Then
for every $n \ge 0$ the rising diagonal of $a$ at level $n$ is constant: $a_{n-i,i} = a_{n-j,j}$
for all $0 \le i, j \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$.

articles.title: Rising diagonal
articles.statement:
For a real array $a = (a_{n,k})_{n,k \ge 0}$ and $n \ge 0$, the rising
diagonal of $a$ at level $n$ is the finite sequence $k \mapsto a_{n-k,k}$ indexed by
$0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$.

articles.title: Constant term of the degenerate exponential series
articles.statement:
For every real number $\lambda$, the
constant term of the degenerate exponential series $e_\lambda(t)$ is $1$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Equation (1).

articles.title: The zeroth degenerate Bernoulli number
articles.statement:
For every real number $\lambda$, the degenerate
Bernoulli number $\beta_{0,\lambda}$ equals $1$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Equation (6).

articles.title: Degenerate Bernoulli numbers
articles.statement:
For a real number $\lambda$, let $(1)_{0,\lambda} = 1$ and
$(1)_{m,\lambda} = 1 \cdot (1 - \lambda) \cdots (1 - (m - 1)\lambda)$ for $m \ge 1$ (the
generalized falling factorial of $1$ with increment $\lambda$). For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the
degenerate Bernoulli number $\beta_{n,\lambda}$ is $n!$ times the coefficient of $t^n$ in the
inverse of the formal power series $\sum_{m \ge 0} (1)_{m+1,\lambda} \, t^m / (m + 1)!$ over
$\mathbb{R}$, whose constant term is $1$.

Since this power series is $(e_\lambda(t) - 1) / t$ for the degenerate exponential series
$e_\lambda(t)$, the numbers $\beta_{n,\lambda}$ satisfy
$t / (e_\lambda(t) - 1) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \beta_{n,\lambda} \, t^n / n!$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Equation (6).

articles.title: The zeroth degenerate Daehee number
articles.statement:
For every real number $\lambda \ne 0$, the degenerate
Daehee number $D_{0,\lambda}$ equals $1$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Equation (9).

articles.title: Degenerate Daehee numbers
articles.statement:
For a real number $\lambda$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the
degenerate Daehee number is $D_{n,\lambda} = n! \binom{\lambda}{n+1} / \lambda$, where
$\binom{\lambda}{k} = \lambda (\lambda - 1) \cdots (\lambda - k + 1) / k!$ is the generalized
binomial coefficient (for $\lambda = 0$ the value is $0$, by the convention $x / 0 = 0$).

For $\lambda \ne 0$ the degenerate logarithm $\log_\lambda(1 + t) = ((1 + t)^\lambda - 1) / \lambda$
satisfies $\log_\lambda(1 + t) / t = \sum_{n \ge 0} \binom{\lambda}{n+1} t^n / \lambda$, so the
numbers $D_{n,\lambda}$ are given by
$\log_\lambda(1 + t) / t = \sum_{n \ge 0} D_{n,\lambda} \, t^n / n!$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Equations (2) and (9).

articles.title: The zeroth degenerate Euler number
articles.statement:
For every real number $\lambda$, the degenerate Euler
number $\varepsilon_{0,\lambda}$ equals $1$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Equation (7).

articles.title: Degenerate Euler numbers
articles.statement:
For a real number $\lambda$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the
degenerate Euler number $\varepsilon_{n,\lambda}$ is $n!$ times the coefficient of $t^n$ in the
formal power series $2 / (e_\lambda(t) + 1)$ over $\mathbb{R}$, where $e_\lambda(t)$ is the
degenerate exponential series; that is,
$2 / (e_\lambda(t) + 1) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \varepsilon_{n,\lambda} \, t^n / n!$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Equation (7).

articles.title: Degenerate exponential series
articles.statement:
For a real number $\lambda$, the degenerate exponential
series is the formal power series $e_\lambda(t) = \sum_{n \ge 0} (1)_{n,\lambda} \, t^n / n!$
over $\mathbb{R}$, where $(1)_{0,\lambda} = 1$ and, for $n \ge 1$,
$(1)_{n,\lambda} = 1 \cdot (1 - \lambda) \cdots (1 - (n - 1)\lambda)$ is the generalized falling
factorial of $1$ with increment $\lambda$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Equation (1) at `x = 1`.

articles.title: Alternating binomial sum of degenerate harmonic numbers
articles.statement:
Let $\lambda > 0$ be real and let
$H_{k,\lambda} = H_{k,\lambda}(1)$ be the degenerate harmonic numbers, that is, the generalized
degenerate harmonic numbers at $\alpha = 1$. Then for every integer $n \ge 1$,
$\sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{k+1} \binom{n}{k} H_{k,\lambda} = \binom{n + \lambda - 1}{n} / \lambda$,
where $\binom{n + \lambda - 1}{n}$ is the generalized binomial coefficient.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Degenerate Bernoulli and Euler sums of higher-rank degenerate harmonic numbers
articles.statement:
Let
$\lambda > 0$ and $\alpha > 0$ be real and let $n \ge 1$ be an integer. Write $\beta_{k,\lambda}$
and $\varepsilon_{k,\lambda}$ for the degenerate Bernoulli and Euler numbers,
$H_{m,\lambda}(\alpha)$ for the generalized degenerate harmonic numbers, and
$H_\lambda(m, r, \alpha)$ for the generalized degenerate harmonic numbers of rank $r$. Then
$\sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^k \beta_{k,\lambda} H_\lambda(n, k - 1, \alpha) / k! =
\alpha H_{n+1,\lambda}(\alpha) - 1$, and if moreover $\alpha \ne 1/2$, then
$\sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k+1} \varepsilon_{k,\lambda} H_\lambda(n, k - 1, \alpha) / k! =
((2\alpha)^{-n} - 1) / (2\alpha - 1)$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Theorem 8.

articles.title: Degenerate harmonic numbers of rank and degenerate Stirling numbers of the first kind
articles.statement:
Let
$\lambda > 0$ and $\alpha > 0$ be real and let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Write
$(1)_{k,\lambda} = 1 \cdot (1 - \lambda) \cdots (1 - (k-1)\lambda)$ for the generalized falling
factorial, $H_\lambda(m, r, \alpha)$ for the generalized degenerate harmonic numbers of rank $r$,
and $S_{1,\lambda}(k, i)$ for the degenerate Stirling numbers of the first kind. Then

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{(1)_{k,\lambda}}{k!} H_\lambda(n, k-1, \alpha) =
\sum_{k=1}^{n} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{(-1)^{k+i} (1)_{i,\lambda} S_{1,\lambda}(k, i)}{\alpha^k k!}.$$

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Alternating degenerate exponential sum of degenerate harmonic numbers of rank
articles.statement:
Let
$\lambda > 0$ and $\alpha > 0$ be real and let $n$ be a natural number. Write
$(1)_{k,\lambda} = 1 \cdot (1 - \lambda) \cdots (1 - (k-1)\lambda)$ for the generalized falling
factorial (so $(1)_{0,\lambda} = 1$), $H_\lambda(m, r, \alpha)$ for the generalized degenerate
harmonic numbers of rank $r$, and $H_{m,\lambda}(\alpha)$ for the generalized degenerate harmonic
numbers. Then

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k \frac{(1)_{k,\lambda}}{k!} H_\lambda(n+1, k, \alpha) =
H_{n+1,\lambda}(\alpha) - \frac{H_{n,\lambda}(\alpha)}{\alpha}.$$

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Shifted alternating degenerate exponential sum of degenerate harmonic numbers of rank
articles.statement:
Let $\lambda > 0$ and $\alpha > 0$ be real and let $n$ be a natural number. Write
$(1)_{k,\lambda} = 1 \cdot (1 - \lambda) \cdots (1 - (k-1)\lambda)$ for the generalized falling
factorial and $H_\lambda(m, r, \alpha)$ for the generalized degenerate harmonic numbers of rank $r$.
Then

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k \frac{(1)_{k+1,\lambda}}{(k+1)!} H_\lambda(n+1, k, \alpha) =
\frac{1}{\alpha}.$$

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Degenerate harmonic numbers of rank and degenerate Stirling numbers of the second kind
articles.statement:
Let $\lambda > 0$ and $\alpha > 0$ be real and let $m$ and $n$ be natural numbers with
$1 \le m \le n$. Write $S_{2,\lambda}(k, m)$ for the degenerate Stirling numbers of the second kind
and $H_\lambda(n, r, \alpha)$ for the generalized degenerate harmonic numbers of rank $r$. Then

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} \frac{(-1)^k S_{2,\lambda}(k, m) H_\lambda(n, k-1, \alpha)}{k!} =
\frac{(-1)^m}{m! \, \alpha^m}.$$

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Theorem 9.

articles.title: Partial sums of degenerate harmonic numbers of rank as a convolution
articles.statement:
Let $\lambda > 0$
and $\alpha > 0$ be real and let $n$ and $r$ be natural numbers. Write $H_\lambda(k, r, \alpha)$
for the generalized degenerate harmonic numbers of rank $r$ and $H_{m,\lambda}(\alpha)$ for the
generalized degenerate harmonic numbers. Then

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} H_\lambda(k, r+1, \alpha) =
\sum_{k=0}^{n} H_{n-k,\lambda}(\alpha) \, H_\lambda(k, r, \alpha).$$

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Degenerate harmonic numbers of rank vanish at index zero
articles.statement:
For all real $\lambda$ and
$\alpha$ and every natural number $r$, the generalized degenerate harmonic number of rank $r$
satisfies $H_\lambda(0, r, \alpha) = 0$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Section 1.

articles.title: Degenerate harmonic numbers of rank zero
articles.statement:
For all real $\lambda$ and $\alpha$ and every
natural number $n$, the generalized degenerate harmonic number of rank $0$ equals the generalized
degenerate harmonic number: $H_\lambda(n, 0, \alpha) = H_{n,\lambda}(\alpha)$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Section 1.

articles.title: Generalized degenerate harmonic numbers of a given rank
articles.statement:
For real $\lambda$ and $\alpha$,
let $\ell_0 = 0$ and $\ell_m = (-1)^{m-1} \binom{\lambda}{m} / (\lambda \alpha^m)$ for $m \ge 1$,
where $\binom{\lambda}{m}$ is the generalized binomial coefficient and a quotient by $0$ is read
as $0$, and let $L(t) = \sum_{m \ge 0} \ell_m t^m$ as a formal power series. For
$\lambda, \alpha > 0$ this is the expansion of $-\log_\lambda(1 - t/\alpha)$, where
$\log_\lambda(1 + t) = ((1 + t)^\lambda - 1)/\lambda$ is the degenerate logarithm. For natural
numbers $n$ and $r$, the generalized degenerate harmonic number of rank $r$, written
$H_\lambda(n, r, \alpha)$, is the sum of the coefficients of $t^0, t^1, \dots, t^n$ in
$L(t)^{r+1}$. Equivalently, $\sum_{n \ge 0} H_\lambda(n, r, \alpha) t^n = L(t)^{r+1} / (1 - t)$.

Expanding the power, $H_\lambda(n, r, \alpha)$ is the sum of $\ell_{k_0} \cdots \ell_{k_r}$ over
all $k_0, \dots, k_r \ge 1$ with $k_0 + \cdots + k_r \le n$, which is the explicit definition in
the source.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Section 1, Equation (5).

articles.title: Degenerate harmonic term of index one
articles.statement:
For every real $\lambda \ne 0$ and every real
$\alpha$, the degenerate harmonic term of index $1$,
$H^0_{1,\lambda}(\alpha) = \binom{\lambda}{1} / (\lambda \alpha)$, equals $1/\alpha$.

At $\alpha = 0$ both sides are $0$, under the convention that a quotient by $0$ is $0$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Section 1.

articles.title: Degenerate harmonic term of index zero
articles.statement:
For all real $\lambda$ and $\alpha$, the
degenerate harmonic term of index $0$, $H^0_{0,\lambda}(\alpha)$, is $0$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Section 1.

articles.title: Degenerate harmonic terms
articles.statement:
For real numbers $\lambda$ and $\alpha$ and a natural number
$n$, the degenerate harmonic term is $0$ when $n = 0$ and
$(-1)^{n-1} \binom{\lambda}{n} / (\lambda \alpha^n)$ when $n \ge 1$, where
$\binom{\lambda}{n} = \lambda(\lambda - 1)\cdots(\lambda - n + 1)/n!$.

These are the coefficients of $t^n$ in $-\log_\lambda(1 - t/\alpha)$, where
$\log_\lambda(1 + t) = \sum_{n \ge 1} \binom{\lambda}{n} t^n / \lambda$; the series has no constant
term. For $n \ge 1$ the term is the paper's $H^0_{n,\lambda}(\alpha)$; at $n = 0$ the value $0$
follows the paper's convention $H^r_{0,\lambda}(\alpha) = 0$ and the generating function.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Section 1 (`H⁰_{n,λ}(α)` and Equation (2)).

articles.title: Alternating and binomial sums of degenerate hyperharmonic numbers
articles.statement:
Let $\lambda > 0$ and
$\alpha > 0$ be real numbers and let $n$ be a natural number. Write $H_{m,\lambda}(\alpha)$ for the
generalized degenerate harmonic numbers, $H^s_{m,\lambda}(\alpha)$ for the generalized degenerate
hyperharmonic numbers of order $s$, and $D_{n,\lambda}$ for the degenerate Daehee numbers. Then

$$
\sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k H^{k+1}_{n-k+1,\lambda}(\alpha) =
\frac{(-1)^n D_{n,\lambda}}{\alpha^{n+1}\, n!},
$$

and for every natural number $r$,

$$
\sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{k+r}{r} H_{n-k+1,\lambda}(\alpha) = H^{r+2}_{n+1,\lambda}(\alpha).
$$

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Theorem 1.

articles.title: A binomial sum equal to a degenerate hyperharmonic number
articles.statement:
Let $\lambda > 0$ and
$\alpha > 0$ be real numbers and let $r \le n$ be natural numbers. Write
$\binom{\lambda}{j} = \lambda(\lambda - 1)\cdots(\lambda - j + 1)/j!$ and $H^s_{m,\lambda}(\alpha)$
for the generalized degenerate hyperharmonic numbers of order $s$. Then

$$
\sum_{k=r}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} \frac{\binom{\lambda}{n-k+1}}{\lambda\, \alpha^{n-k+1}} \binom{k}{r} =
H^{r+1}_{n-r+1,\lambda}(\alpha).
$$

The hypothesis $r \le n$ makes the summation range $r \le k \le n$ nonempty, as in the paper.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Degenerate Stirling numbers of the first kind in column zero
articles.statement:
For every real number
$\lambda$ and every natural number $n$, the degenerate Stirling number of the first kind
$S_{1,\lambda}(n, 0)$ equals $1$ if $n = 0$ and $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Equation (8).

articles.title: Degenerate Stirling numbers of the first kind
articles.statement:
For a real number $\lambda$, let
$\log_\lambda(1 + t)$ be the formal power series $\sum_{m \ge 1} \binom{\lambda}{m} t^m / \lambda$,
where $\binom{\lambda}{m} = \lambda(\lambda - 1)\cdots(\lambda - m + 1)/m!$. For natural numbers
$n$ and $k$, the degenerate Stirling number of the first kind $S_{1,\lambda}(n, k)$ is $n!/k!$
times the coefficient of $t^n$ in $(\log_\lambda(1 + t))^k$. Equivalently,
$(\log_\lambda(1 + t))^k / k! = \sum_{n \ge k} S_{1,\lambda}(n, k) t^n / n!$, and
$S_{1,\lambda}(n, k) = 0$ for $n < k$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Equations (2) and (8).

articles.title: Degenerate Stirling numbers of the second kind in column zero
articles.statement:
For every real number
$\lambda$ and every natural number $n$, the degenerate Stirling number of the second kind
$S_{2,\lambda}(n, 0)$ equals $1$ if $n = 0$ and $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Equation (8).

articles.title: Degenerate Stirling numbers of the second kind
articles.statement:
For a real number $\lambda$, let
$e_\lambda(t) = \sum_{n \ge 0} (1)_{n,\lambda} t^n / n!$ be the degenerate exponential series,
where $(1)_{0,\lambda} = 1$ and $(1)_{n,\lambda} = 1 (1 - \lambda) \cdots (1 - (n - 1)\lambda)$.
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the degenerate Stirling number of the second kind
$S_{2,\lambda}(n, k)$ is $n!/k!$ times the coefficient of $t^n$ in $(e_\lambda(t) - 1)^k$.
Equivalently, $(e_\lambda(t) - 1)^k / k! = \sum_{n \ge k} S_{2,\lambda}(n, k) t^n / n!$, and
$S_{2,\lambda}(n, k) = 0$ for $n < k$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Equation (8).

articles.title: Recurrence for generalized degenerate harmonic numbers
articles.statement:
For all real numbers $\lambda$ and
$\alpha$ and every natural number $n$, the generalized degenerate harmonic numbers satisfy

$$
H_{n+1,\lambda}(\alpha) = H_{n,\lambda}(\alpha) +
\frac{(-1)^n \binom{\lambda}{n+1}}{\lambda\, \alpha^{n+1}},
$$

where $\binom{\lambda}{n+1} = \lambda(\lambda - 1)\cdots(\lambda - n)/(n+1)!$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Section 1.

articles.title: The zeroth generalized degenerate harmonic number
articles.statement:
For all real numbers $\lambda$ and
$\alpha$, the generalized degenerate harmonic number $H_{0,\lambda}(\alpha)$ is $0$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Section 1.

articles.title: Generalized degenerate harmonic numbers
articles.statement:
For real numbers $\lambda$ and $\alpha$ and a
natural number $n$, Dağlı's generalized degenerate harmonic number is

$$
H_{n,\lambda}(\alpha) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{(-1)^{k-1} \binom{\lambda}{k}}{\lambda\, \alpha^k},
$$

where $\binom{\lambda}{k} = \lambda(\lambda - 1)\cdots(\lambda - k + 1)/k!$; in particular
$H_{0,\lambda}(\alpha) = 0$. At $\alpha = 1$ these are the degenerate harmonic numbers
$H_{n,\lambda}$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Section 1.

articles.title: Generalized degenerate hyperharmonic numbers of order one
articles.statement:
For all real numbers
$\lambda$ and $\alpha$ and every natural number $n$, the generalized degenerate hyperharmonic
number of order $1$ equals the generalized degenerate harmonic number:
$H^1_{n,\lambda}(\alpha) = H_{n,\lambda}(\alpha)$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Section 1.

articles.title: Generalized degenerate hyperharmonic numbers of positive order vanish at zero
articles.statement:
For all
real numbers $\lambda$ and $\alpha$ and every natural number $r$, the generalized degenerate
hyperharmonic number of order $r + 1$ at index $0$ is zero: $H^{r+1}_{0,\lambda}(\alpha) = 0$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Section 1.

articles.title: Generalized degenerate hyperharmonic numbers
articles.statement:
For real numbers $\lambda$ and $\alpha$,
the generalized degenerate hyperharmonic numbers $H^r_{n,\lambda}(\alpha)$, indexed by natural
numbers $r$ (the order) and $n$, are defined by recursion on $r$. At order $0$ they are the
degenerate harmonic terms: $H^0_{0,\lambda}(\alpha) = 0$ and
$H^0_{n,\lambda}(\alpha) = (-1)^{n-1} \binom{\lambda}{n} / (\lambda \alpha^n)$ for $n \ge 1$,
where $\binom{\lambda}{n}$ is the generalized binomial coefficient. For every order $r$,
$H^{r+1}_{n,\lambda}(\alpha) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} H^r_{k,\lambda}(\alpha)$.

In particular $H^r_{0,\lambda}(\alpha) = 0$ for $r \ge 1$, and $H^1_{n,\lambda}(\alpha)$ is the
generalized degenerate harmonic number
$H_{n,\lambda}(\alpha) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k-1} \binom{\lambda}{k} / (\lambda \alpha^k)$.

## Sources

- Ömer Duran, Neşe Ömür and Sibel Koparal, *Generalized Degenerate Harmonic Numbers and Their Applications with Riordan Arrays*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A41, Section 1.

articles.title: Right-down diagonal families of order $k$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, a family
$(A_j)_{0 \le j \le k+1}$ of integer sequences $A_j : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ is a family of
right-down diagonal sequences of order $k$ when $k \ge 1$ and, for every $j$ and every natural
number $n \ge \lfloor k/2 \rfloor + 1$,

$$A_j(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} c_k(i)\, A_j(n-1-i),$$

where $c_k(i) = (-1)^i \binom{k+1-i}{i+1}$ is the right-down diagonal coefficient.

## Sources

- László Németh and László Szalay, *Sequences Involving Square Zig-Zag Shapes*, Journal of Integer Sequences 24 (2021), Article 21.5.2.

articles.title: Right-down diagonal coefficient
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $i$, the coefficient
$c_k(i)$ of the right-down diagonal recurrence is the integer $(-1)^i \binom{k+1-i}{i+1}$ when
$i \le k+1$, and $0$ when $i > k+1$.

articles.title: Diagonal sums of an array
articles.statement:
For a doubly indexed array $(a_{i,j})_{i, j \ge 0}$ with entries
in an additive commutative monoid $M$, the $n$-th diagonal sum is
$d_n = \sum_{i + j = n} a_{i,j} = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_{k,n-k}$.

If $a$ is a lower-triangular array with $a_{i,j}$ in row $i$ and column $j$, these are its sums
along rising diagonals. For a Riordan array $(g, f)$, whose column $j$ has generating function
$g(x) f(x)^j$, the sequence $(d_n)$ has generating function $g(x) / (1 - x f(x))$.

articles.title: Exponential Pascal-type matrix
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring that is a
$\mathbb{Q}$-algebra and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$. The exponential Pascal-type matrix with
parameter $r$ is the exponential Riordan array $[e^t, t + r t^2/2]$ over $R$: the matrix with
rows and columns indexed by the natural numbers whose $(n, k)$ entry is

$$\frac{n!}{k!} \, [t^n] \, e^t \left(t + \frac{r}{2} t^2\right)^k,$$

where $[t^n]$ takes the coefficient of $t^n$ in a formal power series over $R$ and the
rational number $n!/k!$ acts on $R$ through its $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra structure.

articles.title: Generating pair of the exponential Pascal-type matrix
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring
that is a $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$. This is the pair of formal power
series $\left(e^t, t + \frac{r}{2} t^2\right)$ over $R$, written $[e^t, t + r t^2/2]$ in
exponential Riordan array notation.

articles.title: Second series of the exponential Pascal-type pair
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring
that is a $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$. This is the formal power series
$t + \frac{r}{2} t^2$ over $R$, the second component of the generating pair
$[e^t, t + r t^2/2]$ of the exponential Pascal-type matrix.

articles.title: Morgan–Voyce coefficients
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the Morgan–Voyce coefficient
$d(n, k)$ is the binomial coefficient $\binom{n + k}{n - k}$ if $k \le n$, and $0$ if $k > n$.

These numbers form the lower-triangular Riordan array
$\left(\frac{1}{1 - x}, \frac{x}{(1 - x)^2}\right)$, OEIS A085478.

articles.title: Morgan–Voyce polynomials
articles.statement:
For a semiring $R$ and a natural number $n$, the Morgan–Voyce
polynomial of index $n$ over $R$ is

$$b_n(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} d(n, k)\, x^k \in R[x],$$

where $d(n, k) = \binom{n + k}{n - k}$ is the Morgan–Voyce coefficient, read in $R$ through the
map from the natural numbers.

The coefficients of $b_n$ form row $n$ of the Riordan array
$\left(\frac{1}{1 - x}, \frac{x}{(1 - x)^2}\right)$, OEIS A085478.

## Sources

- OEIS A085478.

articles.title: Entry formula for the ordinary Riordan Pascal-like triangle
articles.statement:
For natural numbers
$n, k$ and an integer $r$, the ordinary Riordan Pascal-like matrix entry $T(n, k; r)$ equals
$\sum_{j=0}^{k} \binom{k}{j} \binom{\max(n - j, 0)}{k} r^j$; this holds by definition.

articles.title: Ordinary Riordan Pascal-like triangle
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n, k$ and an integer $r$,
the entry $T(n, k; r)$ is the integer

$$T(n, k; r) = \sum_{j=0}^{k} \binom{k}{j} \binom{\max(n - j, 0)}{k} r^j.$$

This is the entry formula of the ordinary Riordan array
$\bigl(1/(1 - x),\ x(1 + rx)/(1 - x)\bigr)$, denoted $T(r)$. Terms with $j > n - k$ vanish,
because then $\max(n - j, 0) < k$. For $r = 0$ this is Pascal's triangle and for $r = 1$ the
Delannoy triangle.

articles.title: Closed form of the Pascal column generating functions
articles.statement:
For every natural number $j$ and
every real number $x$ with $|x| < 1$, the column generating function $\alpha_j$ of the infinite
Pascal matrix satisfies $\alpha_j(x) = x^j / (1 - x)^{j+1}$.

articles.title: Column generating functions of the Pascal matrix
articles.statement:
For a natural number $j$ and a real
number $x$, the column generating function of the infinite Pascal matrix is
$\alpha_j(x) = \sum_{i \ge 0} \binom{i}{j} x^i$, where $\binom{i}{j}$ is the entry in row $i$ and
column $j$; the sum is taken to be $0$ when the series is not summable.

articles.title: Entries of the infinite Pascal matrix
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $i$ and $j$, the entry of the
infinite Pascal matrix in row $i$ and column $j$ is the binomial coefficient $\binom{i}{j}$.

articles.title: Total generating function of the Pascal matrix
articles.statement:
For every real number $x$ with
$|x| < 1/2$, the sum $\sum_{j \ge 0} \alpha_j(x)$ of the column generating functions of the
infinite Pascal matrix equals $\sum_{i \ge 0} (2x)^i$, and
$\sum_{i \ge 0} (2x)^i = \frac{1}{1 - 2x}$.

articles.title: Summing the Pascal column generating functions
articles.statement:
For every real number $x$ with
$|x| < 1/2$, the sum $\sum_{j \ge 0} \alpha_j(x)$ of the column generating functions of the
infinite Pascal matrix equals $\sum_{j \ge 0} \sum_{i \ge 0} \binom{i}{j} x^i$, where
$\binom{i}{j}$ is the entry in row $i$ and column $j$, and it also equals
$\sum_{j \ge 0} x^j / (1 - x)^{j+1}$.

articles.title: Reversing the order of summation in the Pascal matrix
articles.statement:
For every real number $x$ with
$|x| < 1/2$, writing $\binom{i}{j}$ for the entry of the infinite Pascal matrix in row $i$ and
column $j$, we have
$\sum_{j \ge 0} \sum_{i \ge 0} \binom{i}{j} x^i = \sum_{i \ge 0} \sum_{j \ge 0} \binom{i}{j} x^i$,
and this sum equals $\frac{1}{1 - x} \sum_{j \ge 0} \left(\frac{x}{1 - x}\right)^j$.

articles.title: Summing the Pascal matrix row by row
articles.statement:
For every real number $x$ with $|x| < 1/2$,
writing $\binom{i}{j}$ for the entry of the infinite Pascal matrix in row $i$ and column $j$, we
have $\sum_{i \ge 0} x^i \sum_{j=0}^{i} \binom{i}{j} = \frac{1}{1 - 2x}$.

articles.title: Generalized Pell matrix as a Riordan array, for every k
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number
and let $p(n, m)$, for natural numbers $n$ and $m$, be natural numbers such that for every $n$
the power series $\sum_{m \ge 0} p(n, m)\, x^m$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ satisfies
$\left(\sum_{m \ge 0} p(n, m)\, x^m\right)(1 - x)^{n+1} = (1 + x + \dots + x^k)^n$. Then for all
natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the coefficient of $x^n$ in
$\frac{1}{1-x} \left(\frac{x(1 + x + \dots + x^k)}{1-x}\right)^m$ is $p(m, n - m)$ if $m \le n$
and $0$ otherwise. That is, the lower-triangular matrix whose entry in row $n$ and column $m$
is $p(m, n - m)$ is the Riordan array
$\left(\frac{1}{1-x}, \frac{x(1 + x + \dots + x^k)}{1-x}\right)$.

articles.title: Generalized Pell matrix as a Riordan array
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ be a natural number and let
$p(n, m)$, for natural numbers $n$ and $m$, be natural numbers such that for every $n$ the power
series $\sum_{m \ge 0} p(n, m)\, x^m$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ satisfies
$\left(\sum_{m \ge 0} p(n, m)\, x^m\right)(1 - x)^{n+1} = (1 + x + \dots + x^k)^n$. Then for all
natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the coefficient of $x^n$ in
$\frac{1}{1-x} \left(\frac{x(1 + x + \dots + x^k)}{1-x}\right)^m$ is $p(m, n - m)$ if $m \le n$
and $0$ otherwise. That is, the lower-triangular matrix whose entry in row $n$ and column $m$
is $p(m, n - m)$ is the Riordan array
$\left(\frac{1}{1-x}, \frac{x(1 + x + \dots + x^k)}{1-x}\right)$.

## Sources

- Jhon J. Bravo, Jose L. Herrera, and José L. Ramírez, "Combinatorial Interpretation of Generalized Pell Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 23 (2020), Article 20.2.1, Theorem, lines 269–272, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL23/Bravo/bravo4.tex It follows from `pell_riordan_general`; the hypothesis `hk` is unused and keeps the source's shape.

articles.title: Barry–Hennessy generalized Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
For a real number $r$ and a natural number
$n$, the $r$-parameter generalized Fibonacci number is the real number

$$F_r(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} \binom{n-k}{k} r^k.$$

## Sources

- Paul Barry and Aoife Hennessy, *Notes on a Family of Riordan Arrays and Associated Integer Hankel Transforms*, Journal of Integer Sequences 12 (2009), Article 09.5.3.

articles.title: Constant term and row sum of a shifted array
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, let
$(A_{i,k})_{i,k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be an array with entries in $R$, and let $r \in R$ and
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. For $s \in R$ let $A^{(s)}$ be the $s$-shifted array with entries
$A^{(s)}_{i,j} = \sum_{k=j}^{i} \binom{k}{j} A_{i,k} s^{k-j}$ (an empty sum when $j > i$), and let
$p(X) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} A^{(r)}_{n,k} X^k \in R[X]$ be the $n$-th row polynomial of $A^{(r)}$.
Then $p(0) = A^{(r)}_{n,0} = \sum_{k=0}^{n} A_{n,k} r^k$ and
$p(1) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} A^{(r)}_{n,k} = A^{(r+1)}_{n,0}$.

## Sources

- José Agapito, Ângela Mestre, Maria M. Torres, and Pasquale Petrullo, "On One-Parameter Catalan Arrays," Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.5.1, Corollary (equations eqColumn0Rr and eqRowsumsRr), lines 240–245, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Agapito/agapito2.tex

articles.title: Total positivity of Bell-type Riordan arrays from a Pólya frequency series
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and
$A$ be formal power series over $\mathbb{R}$ with $P(0) \ne 0$, write $[x^n]F$ for the
coefficient of $x^n$ in a power series $F$, and let $r, s, t \ge 0$ be real numbers with
$s^2 \ge 4t$. Suppose that $P$ is a Pólya frequency series, that is, every minor of the lower
Toeplitz matrix of its coefficients (whose entry in row $n$ and column $k$ is $[x^{n-k}]P$ for
$k \le n$ and $0$ otherwise) is nonnegative, and that

$$A(x)\,(P(x) - rx) = P(x)^2 + sxP(x) + tx^2.$$

Let $R$ be the Riordan array with $A$-sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and $Z$-sequence
$(z_n)_{n \ge 0}$, where $a_n = [x^n]A$ and $z_n = a_{n+1}$ (a Bell-type Riordan array). Then
$R$ is totally positive: every minor of $R$ is nonnegative.

Since $P(0) \ne 0$, the series $P(x) - rx$ is invertible, so the hypothesis on $A$ says
$A = (P^2 + sxP + tx^2)/(P - rx)$.

## Sources

- Lili Mu, Yuanyuan Xing and Sai-Nan Zheng, *A New Criterion for the Total Positivity of Riordan Arrays*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.5, Corollary 6 (`jis-2025-25.7.5-cor-6`).

articles.title: Bell-type Riordan arrays with a Pólya frequency A-sequence are totally positive
articles.statement:
Let $g$
be a formal power series over $\mathbb{R}$ with $g(0) \neq 0$, write $[x^n]F$ for the coefficient
of $x^n$ in a power series $F$, and let $D = (d_{n,k})_{n,k \ge 0}$ be the Bell-type Riordan array
$(g(x), x g(x))$, with entries $d_{n,k} = [x^n]\, g(x) (x g(x))^k$. Let $(a_j)_{j \ge 0}$ be a
real sequence, the $A$-sequence of $D$, such that for all $n, k \ge 0$

$$d_{n+1,k+1} = \sum_{j=0}^{n} a_j\, d_{n,k+j}.$$

If $(a_j)$ is a Pólya frequency sequence, that is, every minor of its lower Toeplitz matrix
(whose entry in row $n$ and column $k$ is $a_{n-k}$ for $k \le n$ and $0$ otherwise) is
nonnegative, then $D$ is totally positive: every minor of $D$ is nonnegative.

The sum stops at $j = n$ because $d_{n,m} = 0$ for $m > n$.

## Sources

- Lili Mu, Yuanyuan Xing and Sai-Nan Zheng, *A New Criterion for the Total Positivity of Riordan Arrays*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.5, Proposition 5.

articles.title: Riordan array with given A- and Z-sequences
articles.statement:
For real sequences $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and
$(z_n)_{n \ge 0}$, an infinite real matrix $R = (r_{n,k})_{n,k \ge 0}$ is the Riordan array with
$A$-sequence $(a_n)$ and $Z$-sequence $(z_n)$ when $r_{0,0} = 1$, $r_{0,k} = 0$ for $k \ge 1$, and
for all $n, k \ge 0$

$$r_{n+1,0} = \sum_{j=0}^{n} z_j\, r_{n,j}, \qquad r_{n+1,k+1} = \sum_{j=0}^{n} a_j\, r_{n,k+j}.$$

The sums stop at $j = n$ because the recurrence forces $r_{n,m} = 0$ for $m > n$.

## Sources

- Lili Mu, Yuanyuan Xing and Sai-Nan Zheng, *A New Criterion for the Total Positivity of Riordan Arrays*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.5, Section 1, equation (1).

articles.title: Entries in row 1 of a Riordan array
articles.statement:
If $R = (r_{n,k})_{n,k \ge 0}$ is the Riordan array
with $A$-sequence $(a_n)$ and $Z$-sequence $(z_n)$, for real sequences $(a_n)$ and $(z_n)$, then
$r_{1,0} = z_0$ and $r_{1,1} = a_0$.

## Sources

- Lili Mu, Yuanyuan Xing and Sai-Nan Zheng, *A New Criterion for the Total Positivity of Riordan Arrays*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.5, Section 1, equation (1).

articles.title: A total positivity criterion for Riordan arrays
articles.statement:
Let $P, Q, A, Z$ be formal power series
over $\mathbb{R}$ with $P(0) \ne 0$, write $[x^n]F$ for the coefficient of $x^n$ in a power
series $F$, and let $a, b, r, s, t \ge 0$ be real numbers. Suppose that

$$A(x)\,(P(x) - rx) = P(x)^2 + sxP(x) + tx^2$$

and

$$Z(x)\,(P(x)^2 - rxP(x)) =
(P(x)^2 + sxP(x) + tx^2)\,Q(x) + (aP(x) + bx)(P(x) - xQ(x)),$$

and let $R$ be the Riordan array whose $A$-sequence is $([x^n]A)_{n \ge 0}$ and whose
$Z$-sequence is $([x^n]Z)_{n \ge 0}$. Let $J(Q(x), P(x))$ be the coefficient matrix whose row
$n \ge 0$ reads $[x^n]Q, [x^n]P, [x^{n-1}]P, \dots, [x^0]P, 0, 0, \dots$. Call a matrix totally
positive when every minor of it is nonnegative. If $J(Q(x), P(x))$ is totally positive,
$s^2 \ge 4t$ and $as + a\sqrt{s^2 - 4t} \ge 2b$, then $R$ is totally positive.

Since $P(0) \ne 0$, the series $P(x) - rx$ and $P(x)^2 - rxP(x)$ are invertible, so the two
hypotheses say $A = (P^2 + sxP + tx^2)/(P - rx)$ and
$Z = ((P^2 + sxP + tx^2)Q + (aP + bx)(P - xQ))/(P^2 - rxP)$.

## Sources

- Lili Mu, Yuanyuan Xing and Sai-Nan Zheng, *A New Criterion for the Total Positivity of Riordan Arrays*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.5, Theorem 2 (`jis-2025-25.7.5-thm-2`).

articles.title: Total positivity of a Riordan array from its coefficient matrix
articles.statement:
Let $(a_n)$ and $(z_n)$
be real sequences with generating functions $A(x)$ and $Z(x)$, and let $R$ be the Riordan array
with $A$-sequence $(a_n)$ and $Z$-sequence $(z_n)$. If the coefficient matrix $J(Z(x), A(x))$ is
totally positive, that is, every minor of it is nonnegative, then every minor of $R$ is
nonnegative.

## Sources

- Lili Mu, Yuanyuan Xing and Sai-Nan Zheng, *A New Criterion for the Total Positivity of Riordan Arrays*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.5, Proposition 1 (`jis-2025-25.7.5-prop-1`).

articles.title: First two columns of the coefficient matrix of a Riordan array
articles.statement:
For real sequences
$(z_n)$ and $(a_n)$ with generating functions $Z(x)$ and $A(x)$, and for every $n \ge 0$, the
coefficient matrix $J(Z(x), A(x))$ has entry $z_n$ in row $n$, column $0$, and entry $a_n$ in
row $n$, column $1$.

## Sources

- Lili Mu, Yuanyuan Xing and Sai-Nan Zheng, *A New Criterion for the Total Positivity of Riordan Arrays*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.5, Section 1.

articles.title: Coefficient matrix of a Riordan array
articles.statement:
For real sequences $(z_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and
$(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ with generating functions $Z(x)$ and $A(x)$, the coefficient matrix
$J(Z(x), A(x))$ is the infinite real matrix, with rows and columns indexed by $n, k \ge 0$, whose
entry in row $n$ and column $k$ is $z_n$ if $k = 0$, is $a_{n+1-k}$ if $1 \le k \le n + 1$, and is
$0$ if $k > n + 1$. Thus row $n$ reads $z_n, a_n, a_{n-1}, \ldots, a_0, 0, 0, \ldots$

## Sources

- Lili Mu, Yuanyuan Xing and Sai-Nan Zheng, *A New Criterion for the Total Positivity of Riordan Arrays*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.5, Section 1.

articles.title: The binomial array at $(4, 2)$
articles.statement:
For the parameters
$(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma') = (0, 0, 1; 0, 0, 1)$ of the binomial
coefficients (Table 1), the triangular array $a$ satisfies $a_{4,2} = 6$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Table 1.

articles.title: Triangular array of a linear recurrence
articles.statement:
Given integer parameters
$(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$, the array $a_{n,k} \in \mathbb{Q}$,
$n, k \ge 0$, is defined by $a_{0,k} = \delta_{k,0}$ and, for $n \ge 1$, by the recurrence (1)
$a_{n,k} = (\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma)\, a_{n-1,k} +
(\alpha' n + \beta' k + \gamma')\, a_{n-1,k-1}$, where $a_{n-1,-1} = 0$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Equation (1).

articles.title: Linear Diophantine equations
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, c, u, v \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $a \ne 0$ or
$b \ne 0$, let $d = \gcd(a, b)$, and suppose $a u + b v = d$ (Bézout). If $d \mid c$, then the
integers $x, y$ with $a x + b y + c = 0$ are exactly those of the form
$x = -(c/d) u + m (b/d)$, $y = -(c/d) v - m (a/d)$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$. If $d \nmid c$, then
$a x + b y + c = 0$ has no solution in integers $x, y$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Negative-negative numbers on and below the diagonal (auxiliary)
articles.statement:
For integer parameters
$(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$ and $p, q \ge 0$, put $n = -(p + 1)$ and
$k = n - q$. The rational numbers $b_{p,q}$ are defined by recursion on $p$ and then on $q$ through
$b_{p,q} = (c - (\alpha(n+1) + \beta(k+1) + \gamma)\, e) / (\alpha'(n+1) + \beta'(k+1) + \gamma')$,
where $c = b_{p-1,q}$ if $p \ge 1$, $c = 1$ if $p = q = 0$, and $c = 0$ if $p = 0 < q$; and
$e = b_{p,q-1}$ if $q \ge 1$, $e = 0$ if $q = 0$. Division by $0$ gives $0$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Definition 2.

articles.title: Knuth-type duality
articles.statement:
For integers $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$, let $a$ and $b$ be the arrays with
parameters $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; 0, 0, 1)$ and $(\beta, \alpha, -\gamma; 0, 0, 1)$. Then their
negative-negative numbers satisfy $a^{NN}_{-n,-k} = b^{NN}_{k-1,n-1}$ for all $n, k \in \mathbb{Z}$.

This generalizes the identity $[-n, -k] = \{k, n\}$ between the Stirling numbers $[n, k]$ of the
first kind and $\{n, k\}$ of the second kind.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Proposition 2.

articles.title: Negative-negative numbers at $(-1, -1)$ and $(-1, 0)$
articles.statement:
For all parameters
$(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$, the negative-negative numbers $a^{NN}$ satisfy
$a^{NN}_{-1,-1} = 1/\gamma'$ (read as $0$ when $\gamma' = 0$) and $a^{NN}_{-1,0} = 0$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Definition 2.

articles.title: Recurrence for the negative-negative numbers
articles.statement:
For all parameters
$(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$ and all integers $k < n \le -2$, the
negative-negative numbers $a^{NN}$ satisfy
$a^{NN}_{n,k} = (a^{NN}_{n+1,k+1} - (\alpha(n+1) + \beta(k+1) + \gamma)\, a^{NN}_{n,k+1}) /
(\alpha'(n+1) + \beta'(k+1) + \gamma')$, where division by $0$ gives $0$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Definition 2.

articles.title: Negative-negative numbers
articles.statement:
For parameters
$(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$ with triangular array $a_{n,k}$ ($n, k \ge 0$),
the negative-negative numbers $a^{NN}_{n,k} \in \mathbb{Q}$, $n, k \in \mathbb{Z}$, are defined
as follows (Definition 2): $a^{NN}_{0,k} = \delta_{k,0}$ for all $k$; $a^{NN}_{n,k} = a_{n,k}$ for
$n > 0$ and $k \ge 0$; $a^{NN}_{n,k} = 0$ for $n > 0 > k$ and for $n < 0$, $k > n$; and, for
$k \le n < 0$,
$a^{NN}_{n,k} = (a^{NN}_{n+1,k+1} - (\alpha(n+1) + \beta(k+1) + \gamma)\, a^{NN}_{n,k+1}) /
(\alpha'(n+1) + \beta'(k+1) + \gamma')$, where division by $0$ gives $0$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Definition 2.

articles.title: Negative-positive numbers at negative rows (auxiliary)
articles.statement:
For integer parameters
$(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$ and $p, k \ge 0$, put $n = -(p + 1)$. The
rational numbers $c_{p,k}$ are defined by recursion on $p$ and then on $k$ through
$c_{p,k} = (r - (\alpha'(n+1) + \beta' k + \gamma')\, s) / (\alpha(n+1) + \beta k + \gamma)$,
where $r = c_{p-1,k}$ if $p \ge 1$, $r = 1$ if $p = k = 0$, and $r = 0$ if $p = 0 < k$; and
$s = c_{p,k-1}$ if $k \ge 1$, $s = 0$ if $k = 0$. Division by $0$ gives $0$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Definition 1.

articles.title: Generating function of the negative-positive numbers for $\beta = \beta' = 0$
articles.statement:
Let
$\alpha, \gamma, \alpha', \gamma'$ be integers and let $a^{NP}$ be the negative-positive numbers
for the parameters $(\alpha, 0, \gamma; \alpha', 0, \gamma')$. For every $n \ge 0$, in the ring
$\mathbb{Q}[[u]]$ of formal power series,

$$
\sum_{k \ge 0} a^{NP}_{-n,k} u^k =
\Bigl(\prod_{j=0}^{n-1} \bigl((\gamma - j\alpha) + (\gamma' - j\alpha') u\bigr)\Bigr)^{-1},
$$

where the inverse of a power series with constant term $0$ is taken to be $0$.

Coefficientwise in $x^n/n!$ this is Theorem 1, which says that the exponential generating
function $\bar F(u, x) = \sum_{n,k \ge 0} a^{NP}_{-n,k} u^k x^n/n!$ equals the hypergeometric
series ${}_0F_1(-; b; -x/(\alpha + \alpha' u))$
with $b = -(\gamma + \gamma' u)/(\alpha + \alpha' u)$, and $e^{x/(\gamma + \gamma' u)}$ when
$\alpha = \alpha' = 0$: the rising factorial $b^{\overline{n}} = b(b+1)\cdots(b+n-1)$ satisfies
$b^{\overline{n}} (-(\alpha + \alpha' u))^n =
\prod_{j\lt n} (\gamma + \gamma' u - j(\alpha + \alpha' u))$. The paper's existence hypothesis
($\gamma - j\alpha \ne 0$ for all $j$) is not needed: a zero divisor makes both sides $0$ from
that row on.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Theorem 1.

articles.title: The negative-positive number at $(-1, 0)$
articles.statement:
For every triangular recurrence with
parameters $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$, its negative-positive number at
row $-1$ and column $0$ is $a^{NP}_{-1,0} = 1/\gamma$, computed in $\mathbb{Q}$ with $1/0 = 0$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Definition 1.

articles.title: Recurrence for the negative-positive numbers
articles.statement:
For every triangular recurrence with
parameters $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$ and all integers $n \le -2$ and
$k \ge 1$, the negative-positive numbers satisfy

$$
a^{NP}_{n,k} = \frac{a^{NP}_{n+1,k} - (\alpha'(n+1) + \beta' k + \gamma')\, a^{NP}_{n,k-1}}
  {\alpha(n+1) + \beta k + \gamma},
$$

where the division is in $\mathbb{Q}$ and division by $0$ gives $0$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Definition 1.

articles.title: Negative-positive numbers
articles.statement:
Let $a_{n,k}$ ($n, k \ge 0$) be the triangular array of a
triangular recurrence with parameters $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$. Its
negative-positive numbers $a^{NP}_{n,k} \in \mathbb{Q}$, for $n, k \in \mathbb{Z}$, are defined by
$a^{NP}_{n,k} = a_{n,k}$ for $n, k \ge 0$, $a^{NP}_{n,k} = 0$ for $k < 0$, and, for $n < 0 \le k$,
recursively by

$$
a^{NP}_{n,k} = \frac{a^{NP}_{n+1,k} - (\alpha'(n+1) + \beta' k + \gamma')\, a^{NP}_{n,k-1}}
  {\alpha(n+1) + \beta k + \gamma},
$$

where division by $0$ gives $0$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Definition 1.

articles.title: NP/NN duality
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be the array of a triangular recurrence with parameters
$(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$, with weights
$w(n, k) = \alpha(n + 1) + \beta k + \gamma$ and $w'(n, k) = \alpha'(n + 1) + \beta' k + \gamma'$,
and let $\tilde a$ be the array of the reflected recurrence, with parameters
$(\alpha' + \beta', -\beta', \gamma'; \alpha + \beta, -\beta, \gamma)$ and weights $\tilde w$,
$\tilde w'$. Then for all integers $n, k$ the negative-positive and negative-negative numbers
satisfy $\tilde a^{NP}_{n,k} = a^{NN}_{n,n-k}$ and $\tilde a^{NN}_{n,n-k} = a^{NP}_{n,k}$.
Moreover, $\tilde w(n, k) \ne 0$ for all integers $n < 0 \le k$ if and only if
$w'(n, k + 1) \ne 0$ for all integers $k \le n < 0$; and $\tilde w'(n, k + 1) \ne 0$ for all
integers $k \le n < 0$ if and only if $w(n, k) \ne 0$ for all integers $n < 0 \le k$.

Thus the divisor condition of Definition 1 for $\tilde a$ is equivalent to that of Definition 2
for $a$, and conversely, so the left-hand sides exist exactly when the right-hand sides do.
With junk value $0$ for a zero divisor, the two identities need no existence hypothesis.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Proposition 3.

articles.title: Reflection of triangular recurrences is an involution
articles.statement:
Reflecting a triangular
recurrence with parameters $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$ twice gives back the
recurrence with parameters $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, proof of Proposition 3.

articles.title: Reflected triangular recurrence
articles.statement:
The reflection of a triangular recurrence with
parameters $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$ is the triangular recurrence with
parameters $(\alpha' + \beta', -\beta', \gamma'; \alpha + \beta, -\beta, \gamma)$.

If $a_{n,k}$ is the triangular array of the original recurrence, these are the parameters of the
reflected array $\tilde a_{n,k} = a_{n,n-k}$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Proposition 3.

articles.title: Triangular recurrence
articles.statement:
A triangular recurrence is a tuple
$(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$ of six integers, the parameters of the linear
recurrence

$$
a_{n,k} = (\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma)\, a_{n-1,k} +
  (\alpha' n + \beta' k + \gamma')\, a_{n-1,k-1}.
$$

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Equation (1).

articles.title: Second weight of a triangular recurrence
articles.statement:
For a triangular recurrence with parameters
$(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$ and integers $n, k$, the second weight is the
rational number $\alpha'(n + 1) + \beta' k + \gamma'$.

It is the divisor in the recurrence defining the negative-negative number $a^{NN}_{n,k-1}$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Definition 2.

articles.title: First weight of a triangular recurrence
articles.statement:
For a triangular recurrence with parameters
$(\alpha, \beta, \gamma; \alpha', \beta', \gamma')$ and integers $n, k$, the first weight is the
rational number $\alpha(n + 1) + \beta k + \gamma$.

It is the divisor in the recurrence defining the negative-positive number $a^{NP}_{n,k}$.

## Sources

- Lars Palapies, *On Extensions of Triangular Arrays to Negative Row Indices and Their Generating Functions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A83, Definition 1.

articles.title: Peart–Woodson triple factorization of Riordan arrays
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be an integer, let
$\varepsilon$, $\delta$ and $\lambda$ be real numbers, and let $g$ and $f$ be formal power series
over $\mathbb{R}$ with $g(0) = 1$ and $f(0) = 0$. Write $r_{n,k}$ for the coefficient of $x^n$
in $g f^k$, and suppose that for all natural numbers $n$ and $k$

$$r_{n+1,0} = (b + \varepsilon)\, r_{n,0} + (\lambda + \delta)\, r_{n,1},$$



$$r_{n+1,k+1} = r_{n,k} + b\, r_{n,k+1} + \lambda\, r_{n,k+2},$$

that is, the Riordan array $(g, f)$ has dot diagram
$[b + \varepsilon, \lambda + \delta; 1, b, \lambda]$. With the Riordan product
$(p_1, p_2) \ast (q_1, q_2) = (p_1 \cdot q_1(p_2),\, q_2(p_2))$, let
$P_b = \bigl(1/(1 - bx),\, x/(1 - bx)\bigr)$ and
$C_\lambda = \bigl(c(\lambda x^2),\, x\, c(\lambda x^2)\bigr)$, where
$c(x) = \sum_{m \ge 0} C_m x^m$ is the generating function of the Catalan numbers $C_m$, and let
$F_{\varepsilon,\delta} = \bigl(1/(1 - \varepsilon x - \delta x^2),\, x\bigr)$. Then
$(g, f) = (P_b \ast C_\lambda) \ast F_{\varepsilon,\delta}$.

## Sources

- Cameron and Nkwanta, Riordan multiplication at lines 113–117 and the dot-diagram recursions at lines 124–138.
- Naiomi T. Cameron and Asamoah Nkwanta, *On Some (Pseudo) Involutions in the Riordan Group*, Journal of Integer Sequences 8 (2005), Article 05.3.7, Triple Factorization theorem due to Peart and Woodson, line 339, reused in the proof at line 373, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL8/Cameron/cameron46.tex>.

articles.title: Twin Powers Theorem for pseudo-involutions
articles.statement:
Let $l$ be a natural number, let
$n = 2l + 1$, and let $g$ be a formal power series over $\mathbb{R}$ with $g(0) \ne 0$. Put
$f(x) = x\, g(x^n)$ and $h(x) = x\, g(x)^n$. Call a power series $p$ pseudo-involutory if
$p(0) = 0$, the coefficient of $x$ in $p$ is nonzero, and the compositional inverse $\bar p$ of
$p$ satisfies $\bar p(x) = -p(-x)$; call $B$ a B-function of $p$ if
$p(x) - x = x\, p(x)\, B(x\, p(x))$. Let

$$P(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{l} \frac{2l+1}{2j+1} \binom{l+j}{2j} x^j.$$

Suppose that $B_f$ is a B-function of $f$, that $B_h$ is a B-function of $h$, and that $f$ or $h$
is pseudo-involutory. Then $f$ and $h$ are both pseudo-involutory, and

$$x^n B_h(x^n)^2 = x B_f(x)^2 \, P\bigl(x B_f(x)^2\bigr)^2.$$

## Sources

- Alexander Burstein and Louis W. Shapiro, "Pseudo-Involutions in the Riordan Group," Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), Article 22.3.6, The Twin Powers Theorem, lines 1129–1146, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Burstein/burstein14.tex

articles.title: Binomial transform as a binomial sum
articles.statement:
For every integer sequence $(a_i)_{i \ge 0}$ and
every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the $n$-th term of the binomial transform of $a$ equals
$\sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} a_i$.

articles.title: Binomial transform
articles.statement:
The binomial transform of an integer sequence $(a_i)_{i \ge 0}$ is the
falling k-binomial transform of $a$ with $k = 1$, the sequence whose $n$-th term is
$\sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} 1^{n-i} a_i$.

articles.title: Exponential generating function of the binomial transform
articles.statement:
Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and
$(b_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be real sequences with $b_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} a_k$ for every $n$,
and let $A : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be any function. For every real number $t$, if the series
$\sum_{n \ge 0} a_n t^n / n!$ converges absolutely with sum $A(t)$, then the series
$\sum_{n \ge 0} b_n t^n / n!$ converges absolutely with sum $e^t A(t)$.

The formulation is pointwise: convergence of the exponential generating function of $a$ is
assumed only at the point $t$ under consideration.

## Sources

- Ayhan Dil, Veli Kurt, and Mehmet Cenkci, *Algorithms for Bernoulli and Related Polynomials*, Journal of Integer Sequences 10 (2007), Article 07.5.4, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL10/Dil/dil11.tex>, Proposition `prop2` (proof attributed to Seidel), lines 221-233; the binomial-transform relation `a_0^n = Σᵢ C(n,i) a_i^0` is equation (8)/(9), lines 188-199.

articles.title: The k-fold binomial transform is the falling k-binomial transform
articles.statement:
For every integer
sequence $a$ and every integer $k$: if $k \ge 0$, applying the binomial transform $k$ times to
$a$ gives the falling $k$-binomial transform of $a$; if $k < 0$, applying the inverse binomial
transform (the falling $(-1)$-binomial transform) $-k$ times to $a$ gives the falling
$k$-binomial transform of $a$. In both cases the equality is one of integer sequences.

## Sources

- Michael Z. Spivey and Laura L. Steil, "The k-Binomial Transforms and the Hankel Transform", Journal of Integer Sequences 9 (2006), Article 06.1.1, Theorem `falling_equiv`, lines 636-640, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL9/Spivey/spivey7.tex>.

articles.title: Falling k-binomial transform
articles.statement:
For an integer $k$ and an integer sequence $(a_i)_{i \ge 0}$,
the falling $k$-binomial transform of $a$ is the integer sequence $(b_n)_{n \ge 0}$ given by

$$b_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} k^{n-i} a_i.$$

articles.title: Generating function of the binomial transform over a field
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and let
$a : \mathbb{N} \to K$ be a sequence with ordinary generating function
$A(X) = \sum_n a_n X^n \in K[[X]]$. Then the ordinary generating function of the binomial
transform $n \mapsto \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} a_k$ of $a$ equals
$(1 - X)^{-1} \cdot A\big(X (1 - X)^{-1}\big)$ in $K[[X]]$, where $A\big(X (1 - X)^{-1}\big)$ is
the power series obtained by substituting $X (1 - X)^{-1}$ for $X$ in $A$.

articles.title: Multiple binomial transform
articles.statement:
The binomial transform sends an integer sequence
$(a_i)_{i \ge 0}$ to the sequence $(b_n)_{n \ge 0}$ given by
$b_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} a_i$. For a natural number $r$, the $r$-fold binomial
transform of $a$ is obtained by applying the binomial transform $r$ times in succession; the
$0$-fold transform of $a$ is $a$ itself.

* Jiaqiang Pan, *Multiple Binomial Transforms and Families of Integer Sequences*,
  Journal of Integer Sequences 13 (2010), lines 128–150:
  <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL13/Pan/pan8.tex>.
* Jiaqiang Pan, *Some Properties of the Multiple Binomial Transform and the Hankel Transform of
  Shifted Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 14 (2011), lines 104–118:
  <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL14/Pan/pan12.tex>.

Concept `jis_term_c157679dc9eb88c4ba264101`; source statements
`jis_565fc7c3315ad99b5942cc67` and `jis_a569298bba80b28850af1658`.

## Sources

-

articles.title: Ordinary generating function of the binomial transform
articles.statement:
Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$
be a real sequence with ordinary generating function $A(X) = \sum_n a_n X^n \in \mathbb{R}[[X]]$.
Then the ordinary generating function of the binomial transform
$n \mapsto \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} a_k$ of $a$ equals
$(1 - X)^{-1} \cdot A\big(X (1 - X)^{-1}\big)$ in $\mathbb{R}[[X]]$, where
$A\big(X (1 - X)^{-1}\big)$ is the power series obtained by substituting $X (1 - X)^{-1}$ for $X$
in $A$.

## Sources

- Ayhan Dil, Veli Kurt, and Mehmet Cenkci, "Algorithms for Bernoulli and Related Polynomials," Journal of Integer Sequences 10 (2007), Article 07.5.4, Proposition, lines 205–218 (proof attributed to Euler there). <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL10/Dil/dil11.tex> It is the case `K = ℝ` of `mk_sum_choose_mul_eq_inv_one_sub_mul_subst`.

articles.title: Barry's Catalan transform and its inverse
articles.statement:
Let $a, b \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Q}$ be
sequences such that, for every $n \ge 0$,

$$b_n = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{2k+1}{n+k+1} (-1)^{k-j}
\binom{2n}{n-k} \binom{k}{j} a_j.$$

Then for every $n \ge 1$ both

$$b_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{k}{2n-k} \binom{2n-k}{n-k} a_k$$

and

$$b_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{k}{n} \binom{2n-k-1}{n-k} a_k$$

hold, and for every $n \ge 0$ both

$$a_n = \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} (-1)^k \binom{n-k}{k} b_{n-k}$$

and

$$a_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} \binom{k}{n-k} b_k$$

hold.

In the hypothesis, the terms with $j > k$ vanish because $\binom{k}{j} = 0$ there.

## Sources

- Paul Barry, "A Catalan Transform and Related Transformations on Integer Sequences", Journal of Integer Sequences 8 (2005), Article 05.4.5, proposition lines 302--311, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL8/Barry/barry84.tex>.

articles.title: Recovering a sequence term from its generating function
articles.statement:
Let $t_0, t_1, t_2, \dots$ be
natural numbers and let $c$, $m$, $N$ be natural numbers with $c \ge 2$ and $2 \le m \le N$.
Suppose that the real series $\sum_{k \ge 0} t_k \, (c^{-N})^k$ is summable and that
$t_j < c^{j-2}$ for every $j \ge m$. Then

$$t_N = \Bigl\lfloor c^{N^2} \sum_{k \ge 0} t_k \, (c^{-N})^k \Bigr\rfloor \bmod c^N.$$

## Sources

- M. Prunescu and J. M. Shunia, "On Modular Representations of C-Recursive Integer Sequences", Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.5.3, Theorem `ThmExtraction1`, source lines 169–173, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL28/Prunescu/prunescu3.tex>. The paper attributes the result to Prunescu and Sauras-Altuzarra. Only the first representation (for `N ≥ m ≥ 2` with `t j < c ^ (j - 2)`) is recorded, not the `c ≥ 8` variant for all `n ≥ 1`.

articles.title: Hadamard product of two Fibonacci-type series
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let
$a, b \in R$, and let $n \ge 2$ be a natural number. For each $k$, let $f_k$ be the coefficient of
$x^k$ in $1/(1 - ax - x^2)$ and $g_k$ the coefficient of $x^k$ in $1/(1 - bx - x^n)$, the
inverses taken in $R[[x]]$. Then the Hadamard product $\sum_{k \ge 0} f_k g_k x^k$ equals

$$
\frac{1 - f_{n-2}\, x^n}{1 - ab\, x - b^2 x^2 - (f_n + f_{n-2})\, x^n -
(2b f_{n-1} - ab f_{n-2})\, x^{n+1} + (-1)^n x^{2n}}
$$

in $R[[x]]$, where the denominator has constant coefficient $1$ and so is invertible.

## Sources

- Jong Hyun Kim, "Hadamard Products and Tilings", Journal of Integer Sequences 12 (2009), Article 09.7.4, Theorem `eq:61`, lines 430-437, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL12/Kim/kim18.tex>.

articles.title: Boyadzhiev's and Katsuura's formulas for alternating binomial power sums
articles.statement:
Let
$p_{\ell,m}(x, y) = \sum_{k=0}^{m} (-1)^k \binom{m}{k} (kx + y)^\ell$ and let $S(j, m)$ denote the
Stirling numbers of the second kind. For all complex numbers $x, y$ and natural numbers
$\ell, m$:
(i) (Boyadzhiev) $p_{\ell,m}(x, y) = \sum_{j=m}^{\ell} \binom{\ell}{j} (-1)^m m!\, S(j, m)\,
x^j y^{\ell-j}$, where the sum is empty (hence $0$) when $\ell < m$;
(ii) (Katsuura) if $\ell < m$ then $p_{\ell,m}(x, y) = 0$, and $p_{m,m}(x, y) = (-1)^m x^m m!$.

## Sources

- Daniele Parisse, *On Hypersequences of an Arbitrary Sequence and Their Weighted Sums*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A70, Proposition 1.

articles.title: A value of the alternating binomial power sum
articles.statement:
The alternating binomial power sum
$p_{\ell,m}(x, y) = \sum_{k=0}^{m} (-1)^k \binom{m}{k} (kx + y)^\ell$ satisfies
$p_{1,1}(1, 1) = 1 - 2 = -1$.

## Sources

- Daniele Parisse, *On Hypersequences of an Arbitrary Sequence and Their Weighted Sums*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A70, Section 3, Equation (3.9).

articles.title: Recurrences for alternating binomial power sums
Small cases of alternating binomial power sums
Special values of alternating binomial power sums
articles.statement:
Let
$p_{\ell,m}(x, y) = \sum_{k=0}^{m} (-1)^k \binom{m}{k} (kx + y)^\ell$, with $0^0 = 1$, and let
$S(j, m)$ denote the Stirling numbers of the second kind. For all complex numbers $x, y$ and
natural numbers $\ell, m$:
(i) $p_{\ell,m}(x, x) = (-1)^m m!\, S(\ell + 1, m + 1)\, x^\ell$, and in particular
$p_{\ell,m}(1, 1) = (-1)^m m!\, S(\ell + 1, m + 1)$;
(ii) $p_{\ell,m}(0, y) = 0^m y^\ell$;
(iii) $p_{\ell,m}(x, 0) = (-1)^m m!\, S(\ell, m)\, x^\ell$, and in particular
$p_{m+1,m}(1, 0) = (-1)^m m! \binom{m+1}{2}$;
(iv) $p_{\ell,m}(-1, m) = m!\, S(\ell, m)$.
