$g \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, this is the natural number
$\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} g(i)!\,\bigl((i+1)!\bigr)^{g(i)}$.

articles.title: Extension of a vector by zero
articles.statement:
A vector $(a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ of natural numbers
extends to the sequence $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that sends $j$ to $a_j$ for $j < n$ and to $0$
for $j \ge n$.

articles.title: Generalized Stirling numbers of the second kind with parameter k
articles.statement:
For a positive
integer $k$, the numbers $S_2(k; n, m)$, for natural numbers $n$ and $m$, are defined by
$S_2(k; 0, 0) = 1$, by $S_2(k; 0, m) = 0$ and $S_2(k; m, 0) = 0$ for $m \ge 1$, and by

$$S_2(k; n + 1, m + 1) = ((k - 1)n + m + 1)\, S_2(k; n, m + 1) + S_2(k; n, m).$$

articles.title: The hat M32 partition number array
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a positive integer and let $p$ be a
partition of $n$ with multiplicity vector $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$, so that exactly $a_j$ parts of $p$
equal $j$ and $\sum_j j a_j = n$. Write $S_2(k; j, 1)$ for the generalized Stirling numbers of
the second kind with parameter $k$. The entry $\widehat{M}_{32}(k; p)$ is the natural number
$\prod_{j=1}^{n} S_2(k; j, 1)^{a_j}$.

articles.title: Denominator of the M3 partition number
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a partition of $n$ with multiplicity
vector $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$, so that exactly $a_j$ parts of $p$ equal $j$ and $\sum_j j a_j = n$.
The $M_3$ denominator of $p$ is the natural number $\prod_{j=1}^{n} a_j!\,(j!)^{a_j}$.

articles.title: The M3 partition number
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a partition of $n$ with multiplicity vector
$(a_1, \dots, a_n)$, so that exactly $a_j$ parts of $p$ equal $j$ and $\sum_j j a_j = n$. The
number $M_3(p)$ is the quotient of $n!$ by $\prod_{j=1}^{n} a_j!\,(j!)^{a_j}$ in natural-number
division.

This division is exact, so $M_3(p) = n! / \prod_{j=1}^{n} a_j!\,(j!)^{a_j}$.

articles.title: The M31 partition number array
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a positive integer and let $p$ be a
partition of $n$ with multiplicity vector $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$, so that exactly $a_j$ parts of $p$
equal $j$ and $\sum_j j a_j = n$. Write $M_3(p)$ for the M3 partition number of $p$, and for
$j \ge 1$ write $c_j = (j + k - 2)!/(k - 1)!$, the absolute value of the generalized Stirling
number of the first kind $S_1(k; j, 1)$. The entry $M_{31}(k; p)$ is the natural number
$M_3(p) \prod_{j=1}^{n} c_j^{a_j}$.

articles.title: The partition number array $M_{32}(k)$
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a positive integer and let
$a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ be a partition multiplicity vector of $n$, that is, nonnegative integers
with $\sum_{j=1}^{n} j\,a_j = n$, where $a_j$ counts the parts equal to $j$. Then
$M_{32}(k; a) = M_3(a) \prod_{j=1}^{n} S_2(k; j, 1)^{a_j}$, where $M_3(a)$ is $n!$ divided by
$\prod_{j=1}^{n} a_j!\,(j!)^{a_j}$ (the division is exact), and
$S_2(k; j, 1) = \prod_{i=1}^{j-1} ((k - 1)i + 1)$ is the first column of the generalized
Stirling numbers of the second kind.

articles.title: Weighted size of a multiplicity vector
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and nonnegative integers
$a_1, \dots, a_n$, the weighted size is $\sum_{j=1}^{n} j\,a_j$, the sum of the parts of the
partition with $a_j$ parts equal to $j$.

articles.title: Number of parts of a partition
articles.statement:
Let $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$ be a partition multiplicity
vector of $n$, that is, nonnegative integers with $\sum_{j=1}^{n} j\,a_j = n$, where $a_j$
counts the parts equal to $j$. Its part count is $\sum_{j=1}^{n} a_j$.

articles.title: Partition multiplicity vectors
articles.statement:
A partition multiplicity vector of $n \in \mathbb{N}$
is a tuple $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$ of nonnegative integers with $\sum_{j=1}^{n} j\,a_j = n$. It
encodes the partition of $n$ that has $a_j$ parts equal to $j$.

articles.title: Finite power product
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and functions
$g, f \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, this is the product $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} f(i)^{g(i)}$,
with the convention $0^0 = 1$.

articles.title: Absolute first column of the generalized Stirling numbers of the first kind
articles.statement:
For
positive integers $k$ and $j$, the absolute value $|S_1(k; j, 1)|$ is defined as the quotient
$(j + k - 2)!/(k - 1)!$.

articles.title: Index-weighted partial sum
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a function
$f \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, this is the sum $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (i + 1)\,f(i)$.

articles.title: Surjective restricted-growth strings
articles.statement:
A word $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{n-1}$ of length $n$
with letters in $\{0, 1, \dots, k-1\}$ is a surjective restricted-growth string if every letter
$0, \dots, k-1$ occurs in $w$ and, for every position $i$ and every letter $m < w_i$, some
position $j < i$ has $w_j = m$.

articles.title: Non-symmetric peaks of a word
articles.statement:
For a word $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_\ell$ of natural numbers,
a non-symmetric peak is a position $i$ with $1 < i < \ell$ such that $w_{i-1} < w_i$,
$w_{i+1} < w_i$ and $w_{i-1} \ne w_{i+1}$. The non-symmetric peak count of $w$ is the number of
such positions; in particular it is $0$ when $\ell < 3$.

A peak with $w_{i-1} = w_{i+1}$ is a symmetric peak instead.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *Counting Symmetric and Non-Symmetric Peaks in a Set Partition*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A8, Section 1.

articles.title: Generating function for the total number of non-symmetric peaks in set partitions
articles.statement:
Fix
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ and, for each $n$, let $P_{n,k}$ be the set of surjective restricted-growth
strings of length $n$ with letters in $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$; these encode the partitions of
$\{1, \dots, n\}$ into exactly $k$ blocks. For $w \in P_{n,k}$ let $\operatorname{nsp}(w)$ be the
number of non-symmetric peaks of $w$. In the ring $\mathbb{Z}[[x]]$ of formal power series let
$F_k(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} |P_{n,k}| x^n$. Then

$$
\sum_{n \ge 0} \Big(\sum_{w \in P_{n,k}} \operatorname{nsp}(w)\Big) x^n =
\binom{k - 1}{2} x F_k(x) + F_k(x) \sum_{m=3}^{k} 2 \binom{m}{3} \frac{x^3}{1 - m x},
$$

where $k - 1$ is read as $0$ when $k = 0$ and $1/(1 - m x)$ is the inverse of $1 - m x$ in
$\mathbb{Z}[[x]]$.

If $NSP_k(x, q) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{w \in P_{n,k}} q^{\operatorname{nsp}(w)} x^n$, then
$F_k(x) = NSP_k(x, 1)$ and the left side is the derivative of $NSP_k(x, q)$ in $q$ at $q = 1$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *Counting Symmetric and Non-Symmetric Peaks in a Set Partition*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A8, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Peak generating function for set partitions
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$. Work in the fraction field of
the ring $\mathbb{Z}[q][[x]]$ of power series in $x$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$. For
a word $w = w_0 \cdots w_{n-1}$, let $\mathrm{pk}(w)$ be the number of positions $a$ with
$a + 2 < n$ and $w_a < w_{a+1} > w_{a+2}$, and let $W_{n,k}$ be the set of surjective
restricted-growth strings of length $n$ with letters in $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$. Let
$t = 1 + x^2 (1-q)/2$, let $U_m = U_m(t)$ for $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, where $U_m$ is the Chebyshev
polynomial of the second kind extended to negative indices by its recurrence (so $U_{-1} = 0$
and $U_{-2} = -1$), and let $R_j = (U_j - U_{j-1})/(U_{j-1} - U_{j-2})$. Then

$$\sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{w \in W_{n,k}} q^{\mathrm{pk}(w)} x^n = x^k (1-q)^k \prod_{j=1}^{k}
\frac{1 + x + x^2 (1-q) - R_j}{1 + x (1-q) - R_j}.$$

Set partitions of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ with $k$ blocks are encoded by the strings in $W_{n,k}$, and
$\mathrm{pk}(w)$ counts the peaks of the encoded partition. Division is total in the fraction
field, so the statement carries no nonvanishing hypotheses.

Proof: Following Mansour and Shattuck, Lemmas 2.1, 2.2, and 2.6 and Theorem 2.7,
the proof combines first-occurrence decompositions with the Chebyshev recurrence.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, "Counting Peaks and Valleys in a Partition of a Set," Journal of Integer Sequences 13 (2010), Article 10.6.8, Theorem, lines 313–317, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL13/Shattuck/shattuck3.tex>.

articles.title: Total number of non-symmetric peaks over set partitions with $k$ blocks
articles.statement:
For natural
numbers $n$ and $k$, let $P_{n,k}$ be the set of surjective restricted-growth strings of length $n$
with letters in $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$ (these encode the partitions of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ into exactly
$k$ blocks). For $w \in P_{n,k}$ let $\operatorname{nsp}(w)$ be the number of non-symmetric peaks
of $w$, and denote by $S(a, b)$ the Stirling numbers of the second kind. Then

$$
\sum_{w \in P_{n,k}} \operatorname{nsp}(w) = \binom{k - 1}{2} S(n - 1, k) +
2 \sum_{j=3}^{k} \binom{j}{3} \sum_{i=3}^{n-k} j^{i-3}\, S(n - i, k),
$$

where the differences $k - 1$, $n - 1$ and $n - k$ of natural numbers are truncated at $0$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *Counting Symmetric and Non-Symmetric Peaks in a Set Partition*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A8, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Total number of symmetric peaks over set partitions with $k$ blocks
articles.statement:
For natural numbers
$n$ and $k$, let $P_{n,k}$ be the set of surjective restricted-growth strings of length $n$ with
letters in $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$ (these encode the partitions of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ into exactly $k$
blocks). For $w \in P_{n,k}$ let $\operatorname{sp}(w)$ be the number of symmetric peaks of $w$,
and denote by $S(a, b)$ the Stirling numbers of the second kind. Then

$$
\sum_{w \in P_{n,k}} \operatorname{sp}(w) = (k - 1)\, S(n - 1, k) +
\sum_{j=2}^{k} \binom{j}{2} \sum_{i=3}^{n-k} j^{i-3}\, S(n - i, k),
$$

where the differences $k - 1$, $n - 1$ and $n - k$ of natural numbers are truncated at $0$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *Counting Symmetric and Non-Symmetric Peaks in a Set Partition*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A8, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Peaks of the word $1322141251$
articles.statement:
The word $1322141251$ (the list
$1, 3, 2, 2, 1, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1$) has exactly one symmetric peak, the factor $141$, and exactly two
non-symmetric peaks, the factors $132$ and $251$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *Counting Symmetric and Non-Symmetric Peaks in a Set Partition*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A8, Section 1.

articles.title: Generating function for the total number of symmetric peaks in set partitions
articles.statement:
Fix
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ and, for each $n$, let $P_{n,k}$ be the set of surjective restricted-growth
strings of length $n$ with letters in $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$; these encode the partitions of
$\{1, \dots, n\}$ into exactly $k$ blocks. For $w \in P_{n,k}$ let $\operatorname{sp}(w)$ be the
number of symmetric peaks of $w$. In the ring $\mathbb{Z}[[x]]$ of formal power series let
$F_k(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} |P_{n,k}| x^n$. Then

$$
\sum_{n \ge 0} \Big(\sum_{w \in P_{n,k}} \operatorname{sp}(w)\Big) x^n =
\max(k - 1, 0)\, x F_k(x) + F_k(x) \sum_{m=1}^{k} \binom{m}{2} \frac{x^3}{1 - m x},
$$

where $1/(1 - m x)$ is the inverse of $1 - m x$ in $\mathbb{Z}[[x]]$.

If $SP_k(x, q) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{w \in P_{n,k}} q^{\operatorname{sp}(w)} x^n$, then
$F_k(x) = SP_k(x, 1)$ and the left side is the derivative of $SP_k(x, q)$ in $q$ at $q = 1$.

## Sources

- Walaa Asakly and Noor Kezil, *Counting Symmetric and Non-Symmetric Peaks in a Set Partition*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A8, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Total number of peaks over set partitions
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, call a word
$\pi = \pi_1 \cdots \pi_n$ on the alphabet $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$ a restricted growth word if it uses
every letter and, for every position $i$, every letter smaller than $\pi_i$ occurs among
$\pi_1, \dots, \pi_{i-1}$; these words encode the partitions of $[n]$ into $k$ blocks. A peak of
$\pi$ is a position $i$ with $1 < i < n$ and $\pi_{i-1} < \pi_i > \pi_{i+1}$. Then the total
number of peaks, summed over all restricted growth words of length $n$ on $k$ letters, equals

$$\binom{k}{2} S(n-1, k) + \sum_{j=2}^{k} \left(j \binom{j}{2} - \binom{j+1}{3}\right)
\sum_{i=3}^{n-k} j^{i-3}\, S(n-i, k),$$

where $S(m, k)$ is the Stirling number of the second kind, $n - 1$ is read as $0$ when $n = 0$,
and the inner sum is empty when $n - k < 3$.

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Mark Shattuck, "Counting Peaks and Valleys in a Partition of a Set", Journal of Integer Sequences 13 (2010), Article 10.6.8, Corollary 2, lines 388-394, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL13/Shattuck/shattuck3.tex>.

articles.title: Counting reduced unicellular hypermonopoles with a cyclic vertex permutation
articles.statement:
Let
$n \ge 2$ and $k \ge 1$ be natural numbers with $2k \le n$, let $\sigma$ be the cyclic
permutation $i \mapsto i + 1$ (modulo $n$) of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$, and write $z(\pi)$ for
the number of cycles of a permutation $\pi$, fixed points included. Let $r(n, k)$ be the number
of permutations $\alpha$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ with no fixed point such that
$z(\alpha^{-1} \circ \sigma) = 1$ and $z(\alpha) = k$. Then, in terms of the cyclic product
numbers $H$,

$$r(n, k) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} (-1)^i \binom{n}{i} H(n - i, k - i).$$

In the terms of the source, $r(n, k)$ counts the reduced unicellular hypermonopoles
$(\sigma, \alpha)$ with $\sigma = (1, \dots, n)$ and $z(\alpha) = k$.

## Sources

- Robert Cori and Gábor Hetyei, *On Reduced Unicellular Hypermonopoles*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.3, Proposition 12 (`jis-2025-25.3.3-prop-12`).

articles.title: Unicellular hypermonopoles with a cyclic vertex permutation
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural
numbers, let $\sigma$ be the cyclic permutation $i \mapsto i + 1$ (modulo $n$) of
$\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$, and write $z(\pi)$ for the number of cycles of a permutation $\pi$,
fixed points included. Then the number of permutations $\alpha$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ with
$z(\alpha^{-1} \circ \sigma) = 1$ and $z(\alpha) = k$ is the cyclic product number $H(n, k)$.

In the terms of the source, these $\alpha$ are the unicellular hypermonopoles $(\sigma, \alpha)$
with $\sigma = (1, \dots, n)$ and $z(\alpha) = k$.

## Sources

- Robert Cori and Gábor Hetyei, *On Reduced Unicellular Hypermonopoles*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.3, Corollary 8 (`jis-2025-25.3.3-cor-8`).

articles.title: Cycle count of a fixed-point-free permutation
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\alpha$ be a
permutation of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ with no fixed point. Then the number $z(\alpha)$ of
cycles of $\alpha$ satisfies $1 \le z(\alpha)$ and $2 z(\alpha) \le n$.

This is the source's bound $1 \le z(\alpha) \le n / 2$ for a reduced unicellular
hypermonopole $(\sigma, \alpha)$ on $n$ points: only $n \ge 1$ (forced by $z(\sigma) = 1$) and
the absence of buds (fixed points of $\alpha$) are used.

## Sources

- Robert Cori and Gábor Hetyei, *On Reduced Unicellular Hypermonopoles*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.3, Corollary 11 (`jis-2025-25.3.3-cor-11`).

articles.title: Vanishing of the cyclic product numbers for odd $n - k$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$
such that $n + k$ is odd (equivalently, $n - k$ is odd), the cyclic product number $H(n, k)$ is
$0$.

## Sources

- Robert Cori and Gábor Hetyei, *On Reduced Unicellular Hypermonopoles*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.3, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Small cyclic product numbers
articles.statement:
The cyclic product numbers satisfy $H(3, 1) = 1$,
$H(4, 2) = 5$, $H(5, 1) = 8$ and $H(7, 1) = 180$.

## Sources

- Robert Cori and Gábor Hetyei, *On Reduced Unicellular Hypermonopoles*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.3, Table 1 (values of `H(n, k)`).

articles.title: Cyclic product numbers with second argument zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the
cyclic product number $H(n, 0)$ is $0$, since the unsigned Stirling number of the first kind
$c(n + 1, 0)$ is $0$.

## Sources

- Robert Cori and Gábor Hetyei, *On Reduced Unicellular Hypermonopoles*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.3, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Cyclic product numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, write $c(m, j)$ for the unsigned
Stirling numbers of the first kind. The cyclic product number $H(n, k)$ is the quotient
$c(n + 1, k) / \binom{n + 1}{2}$, rounded down to a natural number, when $n + k$ is even
(equivalently, $n - k$ is even), and $0$ when $n + k$ is odd. Division by zero gives $0$, so
$H(0, k) = 0$ for every $k$.

These are the numbers displayed in Theorem 5 of the source. The numbers $H(n + 1, k)$ are the
Hultman numbers (OEIS A164652).

## Sources

- Robert Cori and Gábor Hetyei, *On Reduced Unicellular Hypermonopoles*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.3, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Genus bounds for reduced unicellular hypermonopoles
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ and $\alpha$ be
permutations of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$, and write $z(\pi)$ for the number of cycles of a
permutation $\pi$, fixed points included. Suppose that $z(\sigma) = 1$, that
$z(\alpha^{-1} \circ \sigma) = 1$, that $\alpha$ has no fixed point, and that the natural
number $g$ satisfies $n + 2 = z(\sigma) + z(\alpha) + z(\alpha^{-1} \circ \sigma) + 2g$. Then
$2g + 1 \le n \le 4g$.

In the terms of the source, $(\sigma, \alpha)$ is a reduced unicellular hypermonopole on $n$
points and $g$ is its genus, given by Jacques' formula.

## Sources

- Robert Cori and Gábor Hetyei, *On Reduced Unicellular Hypermonopoles*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.3, Lemma 2 (`jis-2025-25.3.3-lem-2`).

articles.title: Criterion for a hypermap with a cyclic vertex permutation to have no bud
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be
the cyclic permutation $i \mapsto i + 1$ (modulo $n$) of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$. A permutation
$\alpha$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ has no fixed point if and only if
$\pi = \alpha^{-1} \circ \sigma$ satisfies $\pi(i) \ne i + 1$ (modulo $n$) for every $i$.

In the terms of the source, a bud of the hypermap $(\sigma, \alpha)$ is a fixed point of $\alpha$.
The source assumes the hypermap is a unicellular hypermonopole; the equivalence does not use that
assumption, so it is stated for every $\alpha$.

## Sources

- Robert Cori and Gábor Hetyei, *On Reduced Unicellular Hypermonopoles*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.3, Lemma 10 (`jis-2025-25.3.3-lem-10`).

articles.title: Vanishing of the reduced unicellular hypermonopole counts
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma_n$ be the cyclic
permutation $i \mapsto i + 1$ (modulo $n$) of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$, write $z(\pi)$ for the
number of cycles of a permutation $\pi$, fixed points included, and let $r(n, k)$ be the number
of permutations $\alpha$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ with no fixed point such that
$z(\alpha^{-1} \circ \sigma_n) = 1$ and $z(\alpha) = k$. Then $r(n, k) = 0$ for all natural
numbers $n$ and $k$ with $n - k$ odd; $r(3, k) > 0$ for some natural number $k$ with $2k \le 3$;
and $r(n, k) = 0$ whenever $n < 3$ and $2k \le n$.

So the least $n$ with $r(n, k) > 0$ for some $k \le n / 2$ is $n = 3$. In the terms of the
source, $r(n, k)$ counts the reduced unicellular hypermonopoles $(\sigma_n, \alpha)$ with
$\sigma_n = (1, \dots, n)$ and $z(\alpha) = k$.

## Sources

- Robert Cori and Gábor Hetyei, *On Reduced Unicellular Hypermonopoles*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.3, Corollary 13 (`jis-2025-25.3.3-cor-13`).

articles.title: Counting reduced unicellular hypermonopoles by genus
articles.statement:
Fix $g \in \mathbb{N}$. For
each $n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $\zeta_n$ be the cyclic permutation of $\{0, \ldots, n - 1\}$
sending $i$ to $i + 1$ modulo $n$, and let $z(\pi)$ be the number of cycles of a permutation
$\pi$, fixed points included. Let $U_g$ be the set of pairs $(n, \alpha)$, with
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\alpha$ a permutation of $\{0, \ldots, n - 1\}$, such that
$z(\zeta_n) = 1$, $z(\alpha^{-1} \zeta_n) = 1$ (the product applies $\zeta_n$ first), $\alpha$
has no fixed point, and $n + 2 = z(\zeta_n) + z(\alpha) + z(\alpha^{-1} \zeta_n) + 2g$. Then
$U_g$ is finite and its number of elements is $\sum_{n = 2g + 1}^{4g} r(n, n - 2g)$, where
$r(n, k)$ is the number of permutations $\alpha$ of $\{0, \ldots, n - 1\}$ without fixed
points such that $z(\alpha^{-1} \zeta_n) = 1$ and $z(\alpha) = k$.

The pairs in $U_g$ are the reduced unicellular hypermonopoles $(\zeta_n, \alpha)$ of genus
$g$, with the genus given by Jacques' formula and the vertex permutation normalized to
$\zeta_n$. The paper writes $u(g)$ for the number of elements of $U_g$; its first value is
$u(1) = 2$.

## Sources

- Robert Cori and Gábor Hetyei, *On Reduced Unicellular Hypermonopoles*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.3, Proposition 15 (`jis-2025-25.3.3-prop-15`).

articles.title: Generating polynomial of the cyclic product numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, let
$H(n, k)$ be the cyclic product numbers, viewed as rational numbers. Then in the polynomial
ring $\mathbb{Q}[x]$

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} H(n, k) x^k = c_n (x (x + 1) \cdots (x + n) - x (x - 1) \cdots (x - n)),$$

where $c_n = \frac{1}{(n + 1) n}$ for $n \ge 1$ and $c_0 = 0$; for $n = 0$ both sides are $0$.

## Sources

- Robert Cori and Gábor Hetyei, *On Reduced Unicellular Hypermonopoles*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.3, Lemma 6 (`jis-2025-25.3.3-lem-6`), quoting S. Grusea and A. Labarre.

articles.title: Restricted-growth word generating function
articles.statement:
Fix $k \ge 0$. A word $u_1 u_2 \cdots u_n$
in the letters $1, \dots, k$ is a restricted-growth word if for every $i$, either $u_i = 1$ or
$u_i \le u_j + 1$ for some $j < i$ (so a nonempty such word begins with $1$). For
$d = (d_1, \dots, d_k) \in \mathbb{N}^k$, let $r(d)$ be the number of restricted-growth words in
which each letter $a$ occurs exactly $d_a + 1$ times. Then, in the ring of formal power series
in $x_1, \dots, x_k$ over $\mathbb{Q}$,

$$\sum_{d} r(d)\, x_1^{d_1} \cdots x_k^{d_k} = \prod_{j=1}^{k} (1 - x_1 - \cdots - x_j)^{-1}.$$

Proof: Decompose restricted-growth words by their first letter to obtain a coefficient
recurrence, lift it to multivariate power series, and iterate power-series inverse
cancellation. The combinatorial route follows Ehrenborg, Hedmark, and Hettle, Theorem 1.

## Sources

- Richard Ehrenborg, Dustin Hedmark, and Cyrus Hettle, "A Restricted Growth Word Approach to Partitions with Odd/Even Size Blocks," Journal of Integer Sequences 20 (2017), Article 17.5.5, Theorem 1, lines 190-200, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL20/Ehrenborg/ehren4.tex>.

articles.title: Generating function for set partitions by rises
articles.statement:
Fix $k \ge 1$. For $n, r \ge 0$ let
$a_{n,r}$ be the number of words $\pi = \pi_1 \cdots \pi_n$ on the alphabet $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$
that use every letter, satisfy the restricted growth condition that each $\pi_i$ is at most the
number of distinct letters among $\pi_1, \dots, \pi_{i-1}$, and have exactly $r$ rises (the
source's $2$-rises), that is, positions $i < n$ with $\pi_i < \pi_{i+1}$. These words encode the
partitions of $[n]$ into $k$ blocks. Then, in the ring $\mathbb{Q}[[x, y]]$ of formal power
series,

$$\sum_{n, r \ge 0} a_{n,r}\, x^n y^r =
\frac{x^k y^{k-1} (1-y)^k}{\prod_{j=1}^{k} \bigl((1 - x + xy)^j - y\bigr)}.$$

## Sources

- Toufik Mansour and Augustine O. Munagi, “Enumeration of Partitions by Long Rises, Levels, and Descents”, Journal of Integer Sequences 12 (2009), Article 09.1.8, Theorem `thrise2`, lines 505-510, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL12/Munagi/munagi15.tex>.

articles.title: Gould–Quaintance double-sum formula for Bell numbers
articles.statement:
Write $B_n$ for the $n$-th Bell
number and $s(p, m) = (-1)^{p-m} {p \brack m}$ for the signed Stirling number of the first kind,
where ${p \brack m}$ is the number of permutations of $p$ elements with exactly $m$ cycles. For all
natural numbers $n$ and $p$, with the convention $0^0 = 1$,

$$B_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-p)^{n-k} \binom{n}{k} \sum_{m=0}^{p} B_{k+m}\, s(p, m).$$

The source states the formula for $p \ge 1$; with $0^0 = 1$ it also holds for $p = 0$.

## Sources

- H. W. Gould and Jocelyn Quaintance, "Implications of Spivey's Bell Number Formula," Journal of Integer Sequences 11 (2008), Article 08.3.7, Theorem, equation (E:4), lines 177–182, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL11/Gould/gould35.tex

articles.title: Bell numbers are row sums of Stirling numbers of the second kind
articles.statement:
For every
natural number $n$, the Bell number $B_n$ equals $\sum_{k=0}^{n} S(n, k)$, where $S(n, k)$ is the
Stirling number of the second kind.

## Sources

- Michael Z. Spivey, *A Generalized Recurrence for Bell Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 11 (2008), Article 08.2.5, equation `Stir`, lines 107–108 (quoting the classical formula), <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL11/Spivey/spivey25.tex>.

articles.title: Dobinski's formula
articles.statement:
Let $B_n$ denote the $n$-th Bell number, the number of partitions of
an $n$-element set. For every natural number $n$, the real series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k^n / k!$
is summable with sum $e \cdot B_n$, so $B_n = \frac{1}{e} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{k^n}{k!}$.
At $n = 0$ the term $k = 0$ is $0^0 / 0! = 1$, matching the exponential series.

## Sources

- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL14/Mezo/mezo9.tex>, lines 283-293. Only the classical Bell-number identity is stated here; the r-Bell generalizations are excluded.

articles.title: Falling factorial in terms of signed Stirling numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the
identity of polynomials with integer coefficients

$$x (x - 1) \cdots (x - n + 1) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} s(n, k)\, x^k$$

holds, where $s(n, k)$ is the signed Stirling number of the first kind.

## Sources

- Benjamin Schreyer, *Rigged Horse Numbers and their Modular Periodicity*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.1, Proposition 2 (`jis-2025-25.4.1-prop-2`).

articles.title: Eventual periodicity of the Fubini numbers modulo $K$
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a natural number, let
$\lambda(K)$ be the value of the Carmichael function at $K$, and let $R$ be the largest exponent
in the prime factorization of $K$ ($R = 0$ for $K \le 1$). Then the Fubini numbers $F(n)$
satisfy $F(n + \lambda(K)) \equiv F(n) \pmod K$ for every natural number $n \ge R$.

## Sources

- Benjamin Schreyer, *Rigged Horse Numbers and their Modular Periodicity*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.1, Corollary 10 (`jis-2025-25.4.1-cor-10`).

articles.title: Eventual periods of the Fubini numbers modulo an odd number
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be an odd natural
number and let $\lambda(K)$ be the value of the Carmichael function at $K$. Then a natural number
$p$ is divisible by $\lambda(K)$ if and only if there is a natural number $N$ such that the Fubini
numbers $F(n)$ satisfy $F(n + p) \equiv F(n) \pmod K$ for all $n \ge N$. In particular, the
eventual period of the Fubini numbers modulo $K$ is exactly $\lambda(K)$.

## Sources

- Benjamin Schreyer, *Rigged Horse Numbers and their Modular Periodicity*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.1, Corollary 11 (`jis-2025-25.4.1-cor-11`).

articles.title: A Carmichael congruence for all residues modulo $K$
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a natural number, let
$\lambda(K)$ be the value of the Carmichael function at $K$, and let $R$ be the largest exponent
in the prime factorization of $K$ ($R = 0$ for $K \le 1$). Then
$a^R \equiv a^{\lambda(K) + R} \pmod K$ for every natural number $a < K$.

## Sources

- Benjamin Schreyer, *Rigged Horse Numbers and their Modular Periodicity*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.1, Proposition 4 (`jis-2025-25.4.1-prop-4`).

articles.title: Eventual periodicity of the $r$-Fubini numbers modulo $K$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $r \ge 1$
and a natural number $m$, let $F_r(m)$ be the number of pairs $(k, f)$ of a natural number
$k \le m$ and a surjection $f : \{0, \dots, m - 1\} \to \{0, \dots, k - 1\}$ that is injective on
the elements less than $r$; equivalently, $F_r(m)$ counts the weak orderings of $m$ elements in
which the elements less than $r$ are pairwise untied. Let $K$ be a natural number, let
$\lambda(K)$ be the value of the Carmichael function at $K$, and let $R$ be the largest exponent
in the prime factorization of $K$ ($R = 0$ for $K \le 1$). Then
$F_r(n + \lambda(K)) \equiv F_r(n) \pmod K$ for every natural number $n \ge r - 1 + R$.

## Sources

- Benjamin Schreyer, *Rigged Horse Numbers and their Modular Periodicity*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.1, Corollary 12 (`jis-2025-25.4.1-cor-12`).

articles.title: Alternating recurrence for the Fubini numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the Fubini
number $F(n)$ satisfies

$$F(n) = n! - \sum_{j=1}^{n} s(n, n-j)\, F(n-j),$$

where $s(n, k)$ is the signed Stirling number of the first kind.

## Sources

- Benjamin Schreyer, "Rigged Horse Numbers and their Modular Periodicity," Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.1, Corollary, lines 253–257, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL28/Schreyer/schreyer7.tex

articles.title: Fubini numbers as sums of Stirling numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the Fubini
number $F(n)$ equals $\sum_{k=0}^{n} S(n,k)\, k!$, where $S(n,k)$ is the Stirling number of the
second kind.

articles.title: Fubini number of one
articles.statement: The Fubini number $F(1)$ equals $1$.

articles.title: Fubini number of three
articles.statement: The Fubini number $F(3)$ equals $13$.

articles.title: Fubini number of two
articles.statement: The Fubini number $F(2)$ equals $3$.

articles.title: Fubini number of zero
articles.statement:
The Fubini number $F(0)$ equals $1$: the empty set has exactly
one weak ordering.

articles.title: Fubini numbers
articles.statement:
The Fubini number (ordered Bell number) of a natural number $n$ is
$F(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} S(n,k)\, k!$, where $S(n,k)$ is the Stirling number of the second kind.

$F(n)$ counts the weak orderings, equivalently the ordered set partitions, of an $n$-element set.

articles.title: Generalized Bell numbers
articles.statement:
For a commutative ring $R$, elements $s, h \in R$ and a natural
number $n$, the generalized Bell number is

$$\mathfrak{B}_{s;h}(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(n, k),$$

where the generalized Stirling numbers $\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(a, j) \in R$ are defined for all
natural numbers $a$ and $j$ by $\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(0, 0) = 1$,
$\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(0, j + 1) = \mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(a + 1, 0) = 0$ and
$\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(a + 1, j + 1) = \mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(a, j) +
h\,(j + 1 + s \max(a - j - 1, 0))\,\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(a, j + 1)$; here the natural number
$\max(a - j - 1, 0)$ is viewed as an element of $R$.

articles.title: Generalized Bell polynomials at one
articles.statement:
For a commutative ring $R$, elements $s, h \in R$ and
a natural number $n$, the generalized Bell polynomial $\mathfrak{B}_{s;h|n}$ evaluated at $x = 1$
equals the generalized Bell number $\mathfrak{B}_{s;h}(n)$.

articles.title: Generalized Bell polynomials
articles.statement:
For a commutative ring $R$, elements $s, h \in R$, a natural
number $n$ and $x \in R$, the generalized Bell polynomial evaluated at $x$ is

$$\mathfrak{B}_{s;h|n}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(n, k)\, x^k,$$

where the generalized Stirling numbers $\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(a, j) \in R$ are defined for all
natural numbers $a$ and $j$ by $\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(0, 0) = 1$,
$\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(0, j + 1) = \mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(a + 1, 0) = 0$ and
$\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(a + 1, j + 1) = \mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(a, j) +
h\,(j + 1 + s \max(a - j - 1, 0))\,\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(a, j + 1)$; here the natural number
$\max(a - j - 1, 0)$ is viewed as an element of $R$.

articles.title: Recurrence for generalized Stirling numbers
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and
$s, h \in R$. The generalized Stirling numbers $\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(n, k) \in R$ are defined by
$\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(0, 0) = 1$, $\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(0, k + 1) = \mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(n + 1, 0) = 0$
and the recurrence below. For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$,

$$\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(n + 1, k + 1) = \mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(n, k) +
h\,(k + 1 + s \max(n - k - 1, 0))\,\mathfrak{S}_{s;h}(n, k + 1).$$

Here $\max(n - k - 1, 0)$ is a natural number viewed as an element of $R$.

articles.title: Turán-type identity for the Bell numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 2$, the Bell
numbers $B_m$ satisfy

$$B_{n-1} B_{n+1} - B_n^2 = \frac{1}{2e^2} \sum_{k=2}^{\infty} \sum_{j=1}^{k-1}
\frac{j^{n-1} (k-j)^{n-1}}{j! \, (k-j)!} \, (k-2j)^2,$$

where $e = \exp(1)$.

Every summand is nonnegative and the summand with $k = 3$, $j = 1$ is positive, so the identity
refines Engel's inequality $B_n^2 \le B_{n-1} B_{n+1}$ to a strict inequality.

## Sources

- Horst Alzer, "On Engel's Inequality for Bell Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 22 (2019), Article 19.7.1, Theorem with Equation (E3), lines 114–120, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL22/Alzer/alzer6.tex>.

articles.title: Engel's inequality for Bell numbers
articles.statement:
For every integer $n \ge 1$, the Bell numbers
satisfy $B_n^2 \le B_{n-1} B_{n+1}$, where $B_n$ is the number of partitions of an $n$-element
set.

This non-strict inequality is Eq. (E2) of Horst Alzer, "On Engel's Inequality for Bell
Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 22 (2019); Alzer's strict refinement is a different
result.

## Sources

- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL22/Alzer/alzer6.tex>, lines 79--104, where `B_n` is defined as the Bell number and Eq. (E2) states `B_n^2 ≤ B_{n-1} B_{n+1}` for every integer `n ≥ 1`. The source attributes this inequality to K. Engel, "On the average rank of an element in a filter of the partition lattice," J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 65 (1994), 67--78.

articles.title: Partial Bell polynomial
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, let $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$
and let $x_1, x_2, \dots$ be a sequence in $R$. The partial Bell polynomial $B_{n,k}(x)$ is
the sum, over all tuples $(m_1, \dots, m_{n+1})$ of natural numbers with
$\sum_j j\, m_j = n$ and $\sum_j m_j = k$, of

$$\frac{n!}{\prod_j m_j!\,(j!)^{m_j}} \prod_j x_j^{m_j},$$

where the quotient is a natural number, mapped into $R$.

## Sources

- Mihoubi, *Some Congruences for the Partial Bell Polynomials*, J. Integer Seq. 12 (2009), Article 09.4.1.

articles.title: Howard's formula for potential polynomials
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero,
let $r \ge 1$ and $n$ be natural numbers, and let $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ be a sequence in $K$
with $a_r \ne 0$. Let $g$ be the formal power series

$$g(x) = \sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{r!\, a_{r+k}}{a_r\, (r+k)!}\, x^k,$$

let $g^{-1}$ be its inverse in $K[[x]]$, and write $[x^n]\, f$ for the coefficient of $x^n$ in a
power series $f$. Let $P \in K[X]$ be a polynomial of degree at most $n$ such that
$P(m) = n!\, [x^n]\, (g^{-1})^m$ for every natural number $m \le n$. Then

$$P(X) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i \left(\frac{r!}{a_r}\right)^i \frac{n!\, i!}{(n+ri)!} \cdot
\frac{X(X+1)\cdots(X+i-1)}{i!} \cdot \frac{(X+n)(X+n-1)\cdots(X+i+1)}{(n-i)!} \cdot
B_{n+ri,\,i}(\tilde a),$$

where empty products equal $1$, $B_{n+ri,\,i}$ is the partial Bell polynomial, and $\tilde a$
is the sequence with $\tilde a_j = a_j$ for $j \ge r$ and $\tilde a_j = 0$ for $j < r$.

## Sources

- G. Nemes, Journal of Integer Sequences 13 (2010), https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL13/Nemes/nemes2.tex, lines 120-133 (generic) and 166-173 (specialization).

articles.title: Howard's formula for the series $\sum_{k \ge 0} 2x^k/(k+2)!$
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural
number, let

$$h(x) = \sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{2}{(k+2)!}\, x^k \in \mathbb{Q}[[x]],$$

let $h^{-1}$ be its inverse in $\mathbb{Q}[[x]]$, and write $[x^n]\, f$ for the coefficient of
$x^n$ in a power series $f$. Let $G_n \in \mathbb{Q}[X]$ be a polynomial of degree at most $n$
such that $G_n(m) = n!\, [x^n]\, (h^{-1})^m$ for every natural number $m \le n$. Then

$$G_n(X) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i\, 2^i\, \frac{n!\, i!}{(n+2i)!} \cdot
\frac{X(X+1)\cdots(X+i-1)}{i!} \cdot \frac{(X+n)(X+n-1)\cdots(X+i+1)}{(n-i)!} \cdot
B_{n+2i,\,i}(0, 1, 1, \dots),$$

where empty products equal $1$ and $B_{n+2i,\,i}(0, 1, 1, \dots)$ is the partial Bell
polynomial evaluated at the sequence whose first term is $0$ and whose other terms are all $1$.

## Sources

- G. Nemes, Journal of Integer Sequences 13 (2010), https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL13/Nemes/nemes2.tex, lines 120-133 (generic) and 166-173 (specialization).

articles.title: Schreyer's Fubini formula for r-horse numbers
articles.statement:
Let $r \le n$ be natural numbers. For each
$k$, count the surjections $f : \{0, \dots, n - 1\} \to \{0, \dots, k - 1\}$ whose values on the
first $r$ points are strictly increasing, $f(0) < f(1) < \dots < f(r - 1)$, and let $H$ (the
$r$-horse number) be the sum of these counts over $0 \le k \le n$. Then, as rational numbers,

$$
H = \frac{1}{r!} \sum_{j=0}^{r} (-1)^j \, c(r, r - j) \, F_{n-j},
$$

where $c(r, i)$ is the unsigned Stirling number of the first kind (the number of permutations of
$r$ elements with exactly $i$ cycles) and $F_m$ is the $m$-th Fubini number.

The proof follows Schreyer's: the signed falling-factorial expansion is evaluated at integers and
transported to surjection counts by image decomposition and binomial inversion, rather than by
shift operators.

## Sources

- Benjamin Schreyer, "Rigged Horse Numbers and their Modular Periodicity," Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.1, Theorem, lines 211–215, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL28/Schreyer/schreyer7.tex

articles.title: Spivey's Bell number formula
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $m$ and $n$,

$$B_{n+m} = \sum_{j=0}^{m} \sum_{k=0}^{n} j^{n-k} \, S(m, j) \binom{n}{k} B_k,$$

where $B_k$ is the $k$-th Bell number, $S(m, j)$ is the Stirling number of the second kind, and
$0^0 = 1$.

## Sources

- Michael Z. Spivey, *A Generalized Recurrence for Bell Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 11 (2008), Article 08.2.5, equation `Bell_Gen`, lines 113–117, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL11/Spivey/spivey25.tex>.

articles.title: Spivey's recurrence for Bell numbers
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n$ and $m$,

$$B_{n+m} = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \sum_{j=0}^{m} j^{n-k} \, S(m, j) \binom{n}{k} B_k,$$

where $B_k$ is the $k$-th Bell number, $S(m, j)$ is the Stirling number of the second kind, and
$0^0 = 1$. This is Spivey's Bell number formula with the two finite sums interchanged.

## Sources

- Jacob Katriel, "On a Generalized Recurrence for Bell Numbers", Journal of Integer Sequences 11 (2008), Article 08.3.8, equation (Spivey), lines 77–81, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL11/Katriel/katriel6.tex (quoting Michael Z. Spivey, "A generalized recurrence for Bell numbers", Journal of Integer Sequences 11 (2008), Article 08.2.5).

articles.title: The (p, q)-deformed Spivey formula
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $q$ be real numbers with
$0 < q < p \le 1$, and for $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put $[k] = (p^k - q^k)/(p - q)$. Define real numbers
$S(n, k)$ for $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ by $S(0, 0) = 1$, $S(0, k) = 0$ for $k \ge 1$,
$S(n + 1, 0) = 0$, and, for $k \ge 1$,
$S(n + 1, k) = p^{n + 1 - k} q^{k - 1} S(n, k - 1) + [k] \, S(n, k)$, where the exponent
$n + 1 - k$ is read as $0$ when $k > n + 1$. Put $\tilde S(n, k) = p^{\binom{k}{2}} S(n, k)$ and
$\tilde B_n(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \tilde S(n, k) \, x^k$ for real $x$. Then for all
$m, n \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$\tilde B_{n+m}(1) = \sum_{k=0}^{m} \sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{n}{j} \tilde S(m, k) \, [k]^{n-j} \,
q^{jk} \, \tilde B_j\bigl(p^{n+m-j}\bigr),$$

with $0^0 = 1$.

Proof: We formalize the operator proof around equations `eq1`, `eq2'`, `eq4`, `meq`,
`pqexpn`, and `lasteq` in Oussi's paper, using formal power series in place of convergent series.

## Sources

- L. Oussi, *A (p,q)-Deformed Recurrence for the Bell Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 23 (2020), Article 20.5.2, main theorem equation `lasteq`, lines 214-220, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL23/Oussi/oussi5.tex>.

articles.title: The zeroth term of a Carlitz-type sequence
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be a real number. If $(T_n)$ is a
Carlitz-type $q$-polynomial sequence with associated real sequence $(a_k)$, then $T_0(x) = a_0$
for every real $x$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Definition in Section 2.1.

articles.title: Sum of consecutive Bernoulli numbers via Stirling numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$,
$B_n + B_{n+1} = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k \frac{k!}{k+2} S(n,k)$, where $B_n$ are the Bernoulli numbers
with $B_1 = -1/2$ (generating function $t/(e^t - 1)$, the paper's convention) and $S(n,k)$ are the
Stirling numbers of the second kind.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Corollary 2.19.

articles.title: Binomial inversion
articles.statement:
For real sequences $(u_n)$ and $(v_n)$, the identities
$u_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} v_k$ hold for all natural numbers $n$ if and only if the
identities $v_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} \binom{n}{k} u_k$ hold for all natural numbers $n$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Lemma 2.2.

articles.title: Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli numbers via $q$-Stirling numbers
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$ with $q \ne 1$, write
$[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$, $[x]_k = [x][x - 1] \cdots [x - k + 1]$ and $[k]! = [1][2] \cdots [k]$
(empty products are $1$), and let $\beta_n = \beta_n(0)$ be Carlitz's $q$-Bernoulli numbers. If
real numbers $S_q(m,k)$ satisfy $[x]^m = \sum_{k=0}^{m} q^{k(k-1)/2} S_q(m,k) [x]_k$ for every
natural number $m$ and every real $x$ (this is the defining identity of Carlitz's $q$-Stirling
numbers of the second kind), then for every natural number $n$,
$\beta_n + q \beta_{n+1} = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k \frac{[k]!}{[k+2]} S_q(n,k)$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Corollary 2.18.

articles.title: The zeroth Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli polynomial
articles.statement:
For real $q \ne 1$ and every real $x$, the
Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli polynomial $\beta_0(x)$ equals $1$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Section 2.1.

articles.title: Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli polynomials
articles.statement:
For real $q$, write $[y] = (q^y - 1)/(q - 1)$. For
natural $n$ and real $x$, Carlitz's $q$-Bernoulli polynomial is
$\beta_n(x) = (q - 1)^{-n} \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} \binom{n}{k} \frac{k + 1}{[k + 1]} q^{kx}$;
that is, $(\beta_n)$ is the Carlitz-type sequence with associated sequence
$a_k = (k + 1)/[k + 1]$. The Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli numbers are $\beta_n = \beta_n(0)$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Section 2.1 (examples after Theorem 2.1); after L. Carlitz (1948).

articles.title: Carlitz's initial value $\eta_1 = 0$
articles.statement:
For real $q \ne 1$, the value $\eta_1 = \eta_1(0)$ of
Carlitz's $q$-polynomial $\eta_1$ at $0$ equals $0$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Sections 1 and 2.1.

articles.title: The zeroth Carlitz $q$-polynomial
articles.statement:
For all real $q$ and $x$, Carlitz's $q$-polynomial
$\eta_0(x)$ equals $1$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Section 2.1.

articles.title: Carlitz $q$-polynomials $\eta_n$
articles.statement:
For real $q$, write $[y] = (q^y - 1)/(q - 1)$ and let
$a_0 = 1$ and $a_k = k/[k]$ for $k \ge 1$. For natural $n$ and real $x$, Carlitz's $q$-polynomial
is $\eta_n(x) = (q - 1)^{-n} \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} \binom{n}{k} a_k q^{kx}$; that is,
$(\eta_n)$ is the Carlitz-type sequence with associated sequence $(a_k)$. Its values at $0$ are
written $\eta_n = \eta_n(0)$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Section 2.1 (examples after Theorem 2.1); after L. Carlitz (1948).

articles.title: Symbolic recurrence for Carlitz-type sequences
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$ with $q \ne 1$, write
$[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$, let $r$ be a natural number, let $P$ be a real polynomial and let
$(a_k)$ be a real sequence with $[k + r]\, a_k = P(k)$ for every natural number $k$. If $(T_n)$ is
a Carlitz-type sequence with associated sequence $(a_k)$ and $t_n = T_n(0)$, then for every natural
number $n$ greater than the degree of $P$ (taken to be $0$ when $P = 0$),
$q^r \sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{n}{j} q^j t_j = t_n$, which in umbral notation reads
$q^r (q t + 1)^n = t^n$.

The hypothesis $[k + r]\, a_k = P(k)$ encodes $a_k = P(k)/[k + r]$; for $r = 0$ it forces
$P(0) = 0$ and leaves $a_0$ free.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Theorem 2.5.

articles.title: Extended Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli numbers via $q$-Stirling numbers
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$ with
$q \ne 1$ be real, write $[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$ for real $x$, $[x]_m = [x][x-1] \cdots [x-m+1]$
(with $[x]_0 = 1$) and $[m]! = [1][2] \cdots [m]$ (with $[0]! = 1$), and let $\beta_n^{(r)}(x)$
be the extended Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli polynomials, with numbers $\beta_n^{(r)} = \beta_n^{(r)}(0)$.
Let $r \ge 1$ and $n$ be natural numbers, and let $S(m, k)$ be real numbers such that
$[x]^m = \sum_{k=0}^{m} q^{k(k-1)/2} S(m, k) [x]_k$ for every natural number $m$ and every real
$x$ (the defining identity of Carlitz's $q$-Stirling numbers of the second kind). For natural $k$
put $\varphi_r(q, k) = (-1)^k [k]! \sum_{i=0}^{r-1} q^{ik} [r-1]_i / [k+r]_{i+1}$. Then

$$\beta_n^{(r)} = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \varphi_r(q, k) S(n, k),$$

and for every natural number $k$,

$$
\varphi_r(q, k) = (-1)^k [k]! \, [r-1]! \, q^{1-r} \sum_{i=0}^{r-1}
\frac{(q-1)^i q^{i(i+1)/2 - i(r-1)}}{[r-1-i]! \, [k+i+1]}.
$$

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Theorem 2.13.

articles.title: Series for the extended Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli numbers
articles.statement:
Let $0 < q < 1$, write
$[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$, and let $\beta_n^{(r)} = \beta_n^{(r)}(0)$ be the extended Carlitz
$q$-Bernoulli numbers. For every natural number $n \ge 1$,
$\beta_n^{(0)} = -n \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} q^k [k]^{n-1} + (1 - q)^{-n}$, and for every natural number
$r \ge 1$,

$$
\beta_n^{(r)} = -n \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} q^{(r+1)k} [k]^{n-1} +
r (1 - q) \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} q^{rk} [k]^n.
$$

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Theorem 2.11.

articles.title: Closed forms for the extended Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli polynomials
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$ with
$q \ne 1$ be real, write $[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$, let $r$ be a natural number, and let
$\beta_n^{(r)}(x)$ be the extended Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli polynomials. Put $a_k = (k + r)/[k + r]$
for natural $k$ with $k + r \ne 0$, and $a_0 = 1$ if $r = 0$. Then:
(i) for every natural $n$ and real $x$,
$\beta_n^{(r)}(x) = (q - 1)^{-n} \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} \binom{n}{k} a_k q^{kx}$;
(ii) for every natural $n$ and real $x$,
$\beta_n^{(r)}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} \beta_k^{(r)}(0) q^{kx} [x]^{n-k}$;
(iii) for every natural $n \ge 2$,
$q^r \sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{n}{j} q^j \beta_j^{(r)}(0) = \beta_n^{(r)}(0)$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Proposition 2.9.

articles.title: Recurrence for the extended Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli polynomials
articles.statement:
For every real $q$, natural
numbers $r$ and $n$, and real $x$, the extended Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli polynomials satisfy
$\beta_n^{(r+1)}(x) = q^{-x} \bigl(\beta_n^{(r)}(x) + (q - 1) \beta_{n+1}^{(r)}(x)\bigr)$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Section 2.2.

articles.title: Extended Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli polynomials of order zero
articles.statement:
For every real $q$, natural number
$n$ and real $x$, the extended Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli polynomial $\beta_n^{(0)}(x)$ equals Carlitz's
$q$-polynomial $\eta_n(x)$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Section 2.2.

articles.title: Extended Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli polynomials
articles.statement:
For real $q$, the extended Carlitz
$q$-Bernoulli polynomials $\beta_n^{(r)}(x)$, indexed by natural numbers $r$ and $n$ and evaluated
at real $x$, are defined by recursion on $r$: $\beta_n^{(0)}(x) = \eta_n(x)$ is Carlitz's
$q$-polynomial, and
$\beta_n^{(r+1)}(x) = q^{-x} \bigl(\beta_n^{(r)}(x) + (q - 1) \beta_{n+1}^{(r)}(x)\bigr)$.
The extended Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli numbers are $\beta_n^{(r)} = \beta_n^{(r)}(0)$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Section 2.2 (definition of the extended family).

articles.title: Characterization of Carlitz-type sequences
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$ with $q \ne 1$ be real and write
$[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$. A sequence of functions $T_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is
Carlitz-type with some associated real sequence $(a_k)$ if and only if for every natural $n$ and
every real $x$, $T_n(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} T_k(0) q^{kx} [x]^{n-k}$.

This is a $q$-analogue of the characterization of Appell sequences.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Theorem 2.1.

articles.title: Closure properties of Carlitz-type sequences
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$ with $q \ne 1$ be real, and let
$(T_n)$ be a Carlitz-type sequence of functions $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with associated real
sequence $(a_k)$. Then:
(i) $n q^x T_{n-1}(x)$ is Carlitz-type with associated sequence $(q - 1) k a_{k-1}$;
(ii) if $a_0 = 0$, then $q^{-x} T_{n+1}(x)/(n + 1)$ is Carlitz-type with associated sequence
$a_{k+1}/((q - 1)(k + 1))$;
(iii) $q^{-x} (T_n(x) + (q - 1) T_{n+1}(x))$ is Carlitz-type with associated sequence $a_{k+1}$;
(iv) $n (T_{n-1}(x) + (q - 1) T_n(x))$ is Carlitz-type with associated sequence $(q - 1) k a_k$.
At $n = 0$ the functions in (i) and (iv) are $0$, and at $k = 0$ the associated sequence in (i)
is $0$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Proposition 2.6.

articles.title: Carlitz-type sequences
articles.statement:
For real $q$, a sequence of functions
$T_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $n \ge 0$, is Carlitz-type with associated real sequence
$(a_k)_{k \ge 0}$ if for every natural number $n$ and every real $x$,
$T_n(x) = (q - 1)^{-n} \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} \binom{n}{k} a_k q^{kx}$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Definition in Section 2.1.

articles.title: The $q$-number of $1$
articles.statement:
For real $q \ne 1$, the $q$-analogue $[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$
satisfies $[1] = 1$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Section 1.

articles.title: The $q$-analogue of $0$ is $0$
articles.statement:
For every real number $q$, $[0]_q = 0$, where
$[x]_q = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$ is the $q$-analogue of a real number $x$, taken to be $0$ when
$q = 1$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Section 1.

articles.title: The $q$-analogue of a real number
articles.statement:
For real numbers $q$ and $x$, the $q$-analogue of $x$
is

$$[x]_q = \frac{q^x - 1}{q - 1},$$

where $q^x$ is the real power; we write $[x]$ when $q$ is fixed. When $q = 1$ the denominator is
$0$ and the quotient is taken to be $0$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Section 1.

articles.title: Partial fraction decomposition of $q^{kx}$ over a $q$-falling factorial
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$ with
$q \ne 1$, let $[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$, write $[m]! = [1][2]\cdots[m]$ (with $[0]! = 1$) and
$\binom{k}{i}_q = [k]!/([i]!\,[k-i]!)$. Then for every natural number $k$ and every real number
$x \notin \{0, 1, \dots, k\}$,

$$\frac{q^{kx}}{[x][x-1]\cdots[x-k]} = \frac{1}{[k]!} \sum_{i=0}^{k} (-1)^{k-i} \binom{k}{i}_q
\frac{q^{(k^2+k)/2 + (i^2-i)/2}}{[x-i]}.$$

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Proposition 2.16.

articles.title: Weighted $q$-power sums via Carlitz's $q$-Bernoulli polynomials
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$ with
$q \ne 1$, let $[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$, and let $\beta_n(x)$ be Carlitz's $q$-Bernoulli
polynomials, with $\beta_n = \beta_n(0)$. Then for all natural numbers $n$ and $N$,

$$n \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} q^{2k} [k]^{n-1} + (q - 1) \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} q^k [k]^n =
q^N \beta_n(N) - \beta_n,$$

where $0^0 = 1$, and the first term is $0$ when $n = 0$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Corollary 2.8.

articles.title: Sums of $q^k (k)^{n-1}$ via Carlitz's $q$-polynomials $\eta_n$
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$ with $q \ne 1$,
let $[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$, and let $\eta_n(x)$ be Carlitz's $q$-polynomials, with
$\eta_n = \eta_n(0)$. Then for every natural number $n \ge 1$ and every natural number $N$,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} q^k [k]^{n-1} = \frac{\eta_n(N) - \eta_n}{n},$$

where $0^0 = 1$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Corollary 2.7.

articles.title: Weighted $q$-power sums via the extended Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli polynomials
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$
with $q \ne 1$, let $[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$, and let $\beta_n^{(r)}(x)$ be the extended Carlitz
$q$-Bernoulli polynomials, with $\beta_n^{(r)} = \beta_n^{(r)}(0)$. Then for all natural numbers
$r$, $n$ and $N$,

$$n \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} q^{(r+1)k} [k]^{n-1} + (q - 1) r \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} q^{rk} [k]^n =
q^{rN} \beta_n^{(r)}(N) - \beta_n^{(r)},$$

where $0^0 = 1$, and the first term is $0$ when $n = 0$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Theorem 2.10.

articles.title: Sums of $q^{rk} (k)^{n-d}$ via Carlitz-type sequences
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$ with $q \ne 1$, let
$[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$, and let $r$, $d$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $r \ge 1$, $d \le r$
and $d \le n$. Write $(k)_d = k(k-1)\cdots(k-d+1)$ for the falling factorial (with $(k)_0 = 1$).
Let $T_m(x)$ ($m \in \mathbb{N}$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$) be the Carlitz-type sequence with associated
sequence $a_k = (q - 1)^{d-1} (k)_d / [k + r - d]$, that is,

$$T_m(x) = (q - 1)^{-m} \sum_{k=0}^{m} (-1)^{m-k} \binom{m}{k} a_k q^{kx}$$

for all $m$ and all real $x$. Then for every natural number $N$,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} q^{rk} [k]^{n-d} = \frac{q^{(r-d)N} T_n(N) - T_n(0)}{(n)_d},$$

where $0^0 = 1$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Theorem 2.4.

articles.title: Sums of $q^{rk} (k)^n$ via Carlitz-type sequences
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$ with $q \ne 1$, let
$[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$, and let $r \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $S_m(x)$
($m \in \mathbb{N}$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$) be the Carlitz-type sequence with associated sequence
$a_k = 1/((q - 1)[k + r])$, that is,

$$S_m(x) = (q - 1)^{-m} \sum_{k=0}^{m} (-1)^{m-k} \binom{m}{k} a_k q^{kx}$$

for all $m$ and all real $x$. Then for all natural numbers $n$ and $N$,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} q^{rk} [k]^n = q^{rN} S_n(N) - S_n(0),$$

where $0^0 = 1$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Theorem 2.3.

articles.title: Sums of $q^{ir}$ times $q$-falling factorials
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$ with $q \ne 1$, let
$[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$, and write $[x]_m = [x][x-1]\cdots[x-m+1]$ for the $q$-falling factorial
(with $[x]_0 = 1$). Then for all natural numbers $r \ge 1$, $k$ and $N$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} q^{ir} [i]_k = \left(\sum_{\ell=0}^{r-1}
\frac{q^{(r-\ell-1)N + (\ell+1)k} \, [r-1]_\ell}{[k+r]_{\ell+1}}\right) [N]_{k+1}.$$

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Proposition 2.14.

articles.title: Second closed form of a limit of $q$-interpolated falling-factorial sums
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$
with $q \ne 1$, let $[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$, write $[x]_m = [x][x-1]\cdots[x-m+1]$ and
$[m]! = [1][2]\cdots[m]$ (both equal to $1$ when $m = 0$), and let $r \ge 1$ and $k$ be natural
numbers. Let $P$ be a real polynomial such that

$$P(q^N) = q^{k(k-1)/2} \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} q^{ir} [i]_k$$

for every integer $N \ge 1$. Then, as $x \to 0$ through real numbers $x \ne 0$, $P(q^x)/[x]$
tends to

$$g_r(q, k) = (-1)^k [k]! \, [r-1]! \, q^{1-r} \sum_{i=0}^{r-1}
\frac{(q-1)^i \, q^{i(i+1)/2 - i(r-1)}}{[r-1-i]! \, [k+i+1]}.$$

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Proposition 2.17.

articles.title: Limit of the $q$-power-sum interpolant at $0$: first closed form
articles.statement:
Let $q > 0$ with
$q \ne 1$, let $r \ge 1$ and $k \ge 0$ be integers, and for real $x$ write
$[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$, $[x]_m = [x][x-1]\cdots[x-m+1]$ (with $[x]_0 = 1$) and
$[k]! = [1][2]\cdots[k]$. Let $P$ be a real polynomial such that
$P(q^N) = q^{k(k-1)/2} \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} q^{ir} [i]_k$ for every positive integer $N$. Then
$P(q^x)/[x]$ tends, as $x \to 0$ with $x \ne 0$, to

$$(-1)^k [k]! \sum_{i=0}^{r-1} \frac{q^{ik} [r-1]_i}{[k+r]_{i+1}}.$$

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Corollary 2.15.

articles.title: Bernoulli numbers as a limit as $q \to 1^-$
articles.statement:
Let $r \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$ be integers and,
for real $q$ and $x$, write $[x] = (q^x - 1)/(q - 1)$. Then, as $q$ tends to $1$ from below,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(r q^{rk} - (n + r) q^{(r+1)k}\right) [k]^{n-1} \to B_n,$$

where $B_n$ is the $n$-th Bernoulli number, with the convention $B_1 = -1/2$.

## Sources

- Bakir Farhi, *q-Analogues of Sums of Consecutive Powers of Natural Numbers and Extended Carlitz q-Bernoulli Numbers and Polynomials*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A85, Corollary 2.12.

articles.title: Closed form of the Euler–Seidel matrix
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid and let
$(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence in $M$. For all $n, k \ge 0$, the entry $a_n^k$ of the
Euler–Seidel matrix of $a$ equals $\sum_{i=0}^{k} \binom{k}{i} a_{n+i}$.

articles.title: Euler–Seidel matrix
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a type with an addition and let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a
sequence in $M$. The Euler–Seidel matrix of $a$ is the array $(a_n^k)_{n, k \ge 0}$, with entry
$a_n^k$ in position $(n, k)$, defined by $a_n^0 = a_n$ and
$a_n^k = a_n^{k-1} + a_{n+1}^{k-1}$ for $k \ge 1$.

articles.title: Closed form for the array $R(k, m)$
articles.statement:
Let $k$ and $m$ be natural numbers with
$1 \le m \le k$, and let $R(k, m) = \sum_{j=0}^{m} (-1)^j \binom{2m}{j} (m - j)^{2k}$. Then

$$R(k, m) = 2^{2k+m-1}\, m! \sum_{b} \frac{(2k)!}{b_1! \cdots b_k!}
\prod_{r=1}^{k} \left(\frac{1}{4^r (2r)!}\right)^{b_r},$$

where the sum runs over all $k$-tuples $b = (b_1, \dots, b_k)$ of natural numbers with
$b_1 + 2 b_2 + \dots + k b_k = k$ and $b_1 + \dots + b_k = m$ (each such $b_r$ is at most $k$).

## Sources

- José L. Cereceda, "Sums of Powers of Integers and the Sequence A304330", Corollary 6.

articles.title: The array $R(k, m)$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $m$, $R(k, m)$ is the integer
$\sum_{j=0}^{m} (-1)^j \binom{2m}{j} (m - j)^{2k}$.

articles.title: The array $U(k, m)$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $m$, $U(k, m)$ is the rational number
$\frac{2}{(2m)!} \sum_{j=0}^{m} (-1)^j \binom{2m}{j} (m - j)^{2k}$.

articles.title: The Faulhaber coefficients $b_{k,r}$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $p$ and $q$, let
$R(p, q) = \sum_{j=0}^{q} (-1)^j \binom{2q}{j} (q - j)^{2p}$, and for natural numbers $q$
and $s$ let $\mathrm{Ps}_q^{(s)}$ be the Legendre–Stirling number of the first kind, the
coefficient of $x^s$ in $\prod_{i=0}^{q-1} (x - i(i+1))$. For natural numbers $k$ and $r$,
$b_{k,r}$ is the rational number
$\sum_{m=r}^{k} \frac{3 \cdot 2^r}{(2m+1)!}\, R(k, m)\, \mathrm{Ps}_m^{(r)}$.

articles.title: The Faulhaber coefficients $c_{k,r}$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $p$ and $q$, let
$R(p, q) = \sum_{j=0}^{q} (-1)^j \binom{2q}{j} (q - j)^{2p}$, and for natural numbers $q$
and $s$ let $\mathrm{Ps}_q^{(s)}$ be the Legendre–Stirling number of the first kind, the
coefficient of $x^s$ in $\prod_{i=0}^{q-1} (x - i(i+1))$. For natural numbers $k$ and $r$,
$c_{k,r}$ is the rational number
$\sum_{m=r}^{k} \frac{2^{r+1}}{(2m+2)!\,(m+1)}\, R(k+1, m+1)\, \mathrm{Ps}_{m+1}^{(r+1)}$.

articles.title: Inversion formula for the arrays $u(k, m)$ and $U(k, m)$ (Butzer et al.)
articles.statement:
For natural
numbers $k$ and $m$, let $u(k, m)$ be the first-kind Jacobi–Stirling number $J(k, m; 0)$, the
coefficient of $x^m$ in $\prod_{i=0}^{k-1} (x - i^2)$, and let
$U(k, m) = \frac{2}{(2m)!} \sum_{j=0}^{m} (-1)^j \binom{2m}{j} (m - j)^{2k}$. For all sequences
$(a_k)_{k \ge 0}$ and $(b_k)_{k \ge 0}$ of real numbers, $a_k = \sum_{m=1}^{k} u(k, m)\, b_m$
holds for every $k \ge 1$ if and only if $b_k = \sum_{m=1}^{k} U(k, m)\, a_m$ holds for every
$k \ge 1$.

## Sources

- José L. Cereceda, "Sums of Powers of Integers and the Sequence A304330", Lemma 5.

articles.title: Even power sums in terms of $\binom{2n+m+1}{2m+1}$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k \ge 1$ and
$n$, write $S_{2k}(n) = 1^{2k} + 2^{2k} + \dots + n^{2k}$ and
$R(k, m) = \sum_{j=0}^{m} (-1)^j \binom{2m}{j} (m - j)^{2k}$. Then
$2^{2k} S_{2k}(n) = \sum_{m=1}^{k} R(k, m) \binom{2n+m+1}{2m+1}$.

## Sources

- José L. Cereceda, "Sums of Powers of Integers and the Sequence A304330", Theorem 1.

articles.title: Odd power sums in terms of $\binom{n+m}{2m-1}$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k \ge 1$ and $n$,
write $S_{2k-1}(n) = 1^{2k-1} + 2^{2k-1} + \dots + n^{2k-1}$, let
$R(p, q) = \sum_{j=0}^{q} (-1)^j \binom{2q}{j} (q - j)^{2p}$, and let $Q_{k,1}(n) = n^{2k-1}$ and
$Q_{k,m}(n) = 2 \sum_{j=m}^{k} \binom{2k-1}{2j-2} R(j-1, m-1)\, n^{2k-2j+1}$ for $m \ge 2$. Then
$2^{2k-1} S_{2k-1}(n) = \sum_{m=1}^{k} Q_{k,m}(n) \binom{n+m}{2m-1}$.

## Sources

- José L. Cereceda, "Sums of Powers of Integers and the Sequence A304330", Theorem 10.

articles.title: Knuth's correspondence between even and odd power sums
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ be a natural
number, let $(a_m)_{m \ge 0}$ be a sequence of real numbers, and write
$S_j(n) = 1^j + 2^j + \dots + n^j$. Then
$\frac{S_{2k}(n)}{2n+1} = \sum_{m=1}^{k} a_m \binom{n+m}{2m}$ for every natural number $n$
if and only if $S_{2k-1}(n) = \sum_{m=1}^{k} \frac{2m+1}{m}\, a_m \binom{n+m}{2m}$ for every
natural number $n$.

## Sources

- José L. Cereceda, "Sums of Powers of Integers and the Sequence A304330", Proposition 2.

articles.title: Knuth's formula for even power sums
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k \ge 1$ and $n$, write
$S_{2k}(n) = 1^{2k} + 2^{2k} + \dots + n^{2k}$ and
$R(k, m) = \sum_{j=0}^{m} (-1)^j \binom{2m}{j} (m - j)^{2k}$. Then
$S_{2k}(n) = \sum_{m=1}^{k} R(k, m)\, \frac{2n+1}{2m+1} \binom{n+m}{2m}$.

## Sources

- José L. Cereceda, "Sums of Powers of Integers and the Sequence A304330", Proposition 3.

articles.title: Faulhaber form of the even power sums
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k \ge 1$ and $n$,
writing $S_j(n) = 1^j + 2^j + \cdots + n^j$ for the power sums and $b_{k,r}$ for the Faulhaber
coefficients of Proposition 12, the rational numbers satisfy
$S_{2k}(n) = S_2(n) \sum_{r=1}^{k} b_{k,r} \, S_1(n)^{r-1}$.

## Sources

- José L. Cereceda, "Sums of Powers of Integers and the Sequence A304330", Proposition 12.

articles.title: Knuth's binomial formula for the odd power sums
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k \ge 1$ and
$n$, the power sum $S_{2k-1}(n) = 1^{2k-1} + 2^{2k-1} + \cdots + n^{2k-1}$ satisfies

$$S_{2k-1}(n) = \sum_{m=1}^{k} R(k, m) \cdot \frac{1}{m} \binom{n + m}{2m},$$

where $R(k, m) = \sum_{j=0}^{m} (-1)^j \binom{2m}{j} (m - j)^{2k}$ is the array of OEIS A304330.

## Sources

- José L. Cereceda, "Sums of Powers of Integers and the Sequence A304330", Proposition 3.

articles.title: Faulhaber form of the odd power sums
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k \ge 1$ and $n$,
writing $S_j(n) = 1^j + 2^j + \cdots + n^j$ for the power sums and $c_{k,r}$ for the Faulhaber
coefficients of Proposition 12, the rational numbers satisfy
$S_{2k+1}(n) = S_1(n)^2 \sum_{r=1}^{k} c_{k,r} \, S_1(n)^{r-1}$.

## Sources

- José L. Cereceda, "Sums of Powers of Integers and the Sequence A304330", Proposition 12.

articles.title: Power sums
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, the power sum $S_k(n)$ is the rational
number $\sum_{i=1}^{n} i^k = 1^k + 2^k + \cdots + n^k$, which is $0$ when $n = 0$.

articles.title: Sum of $i \binom{i+k-1}{2k-1}$
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$,

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} i \binom{i + k - 1}{2k - 1} = \frac{k(2n + 1)}{2k + 1} \binom{n + k}{2k}.$$

## Sources

- José L. Cereceda, "Sums of Powers of Integers and the Sequence A304330", Lemma 7.

articles.title: Vanishing alternating sum of the A304330 array
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k \ge 2$,

$$\sum_{m=1}^{k} (-1)^m \frac{((m-1)!)^2}{(2m)!} R(k, m) = 0,$$

where $R(k, m) = \sum_{j=0}^{m} (-1)^j \binom{2m}{j} (m - j)^{2k}$ is the array of OEIS A304330.

## Sources

- José L. Cereceda, "Sums of Powers of Integers and the Sequence A304330", Proposition 15.

articles.title: Sum of $2i \binom{2i+k-1}{2k-1}$
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$,

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} 2i \binom{2i + k - 1}{2k - 1} = k \binom{2n + k + 1}{2k + 1}.$$

## Sources

- José L. Cereceda, "Sums of Powers of Integers and the Sequence A304330", Lemma 4.

articles.title: The polynomials $Q_{k,m}$ of Theorem 10
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$, write
$R(a, b) = \sum_{i=0}^{b} (-1)^i \binom{2b}{i} (b - i)^{2a}$ for the array of OEIS A304330.
The rational number $Q_{k,m}(n)$ is $n^{2k-1}$ if $m = 1$, and otherwise

$$Q_{k,m}(n) = 2 \sum_{j=m}^{k} \binom{2k-1}{2j-2} R(j-1, m-1) \, n^{2k-2j+1}.$$

Differences of natural numbers such as $2k - 1$ and $m - 1$ are truncated at $0$.

articles.title: Garabedian's formula for the Bernoulli numbers, including $n = 0$
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $n$,

$$2(1 - 2^n) B_n = n \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{(-1)^{n-k} (k-1)!\, S(n, k)}{2^{k-1}},$$

where $B_n$ is the $n$-th Bernoulli number, with $B_1 = -\frac{1}{2}$, and $S(n, k)$ is the
Stirling number of the second kind. At $n = 0$ both sides are $0$.

articles.title: Garabedian's formula for the Bernoulli numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 1$,

$$2(1 - 2^n) B_n = n \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{(-1)^{n-k} (k-1)!\, S(n, k)}{2^{k-1}},$$

where $B_n$ is the $n$-th Bernoulli number, with $B_1 = -\frac{1}{2}$, and $S(n, k)$ is the
Stirling number of the second kind.

The identity also holds for $n = 0$, where both sides are $0$.

## Sources

- Schehrazade Zerroukhat and Laala Khaldi, "A Note on Explicit Formulas for Bernoulli and Genocchi Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.7, equation (g19), lines 188–191 of the official TeX, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL28/Zerroukhat/zerrou3.tex>, which displays `2(1-2^n)B_n = G_n = n ∑ ...` and notes Garabedian's formula is equivalent to it; this article states the outer (Bernoulli-to-sum) equality. Original: H. L. Garabedian, "A new formula for the Bernoulli numbers," Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 46 (1940), 531–533.

articles.title: Garabedian's formula for the Genocchi numbers, including $n = 0$
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $n$, the Genocchi number $G_n$, defined by $\sum_{m \ge 0} G_m x^m / m! = 2x/(e^x + 1)$,
satisfies

$$G_n = n \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{(-1)^{n-k} (k-1)!\, S(n, k)}{2^{k-1}},$$

where $S(n, k)$ is the Stirling number of the second kind. At $n = 0$ both sides are $0$.

articles.title: Garabedian's formula for the Genocchi numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 1$, the
Genocchi number $G_n$, defined by $\sum_{m \ge 0} G_m x^m / m! = 2x/(e^x + 1)$, satisfies

$$G_n = n \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{(-1)^{n-k} (k-1)!\, S(n, k)}{2^{k-1}},$$

where $S(n, k)$ is the Stirling number of the second kind.

The identity also holds for $n = 0$, where both sides are $0$.

The formula is due to H. L. Garabedian, "A new formula for the Bernoulli numbers," Bulletin of
the American Mathematical Society 46 (1940), 531–533, DOI 10.1090/S0002-9904-1940-07255-6.

## Sources

- Schehrazade Zerroukhat and Laala Khaldi, "A Note on Explicit Formulas for Bernoulli and Genocchi Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.7, lines 184–194 of the official TeX: <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL28/Zerroukhat/zerrou3.tex>.

articles.title: Exponential generating function of the Euler coefficients
articles.statement:
Let $E_n$ denote the Euler
coefficients, let $e^x$ be the exponential series, and let $e^{-x}$ be the series obtained from
it by replacing $x$ with $-x$. In the ring $\mathbb{Q}[[x]]$ of formal power series with rational
coefficients, $(e^x + e^{-x}) \sum_{n \ge 0} E_n x^n / n! = 2 + e^x - e^{-x}$.

Since $e^x + e^{-x} = 2 \cosh x$ and $2 + e^x - e^{-x} = 2 (1 + \sinh x)$, and $\cosh x$ is
invertible, this says that the exponential generating function of the $E_n$ is
$\operatorname{sech} x + \tanh x$.

articles.title: Recurrence for the Euler coefficients
articles.statement:
Let $E_m$ denote the Euler coefficients, and let
$\varepsilon_m$ be $1$ if $m$ is odd and $0$ if $m$ is even. For every natural number $n$,
$E_{n+1} = \varepsilon_{n+1} - \sum_j \binom{n+1}{j} E_{n+1-j}$, where the sum runs over the even
$j$ with $2 \le j \le n+1$.

It comes from comparing coefficients in
$\cosh x \cdot (\operatorname{sech} x + \tanh x) = 1 + \sinh x$.

articles.title: The zeroth Euler coefficient
articles.statement: The Euler coefficient $E_0$ equals $1$.

articles.title: Euler coefficients
articles.statement:
Let $\varepsilon_n$ be $1$ if $n$ is odd and $0$ if $n$ is even. The
Euler coefficients $E_n$ are the integers defined by $E_0 = 1$ and, for $n \ge 1$,
$E_n = \varepsilon_n - \sum_j \binom{n}{j} E_{n-j}$, where the sum runs over the even $j$ with
$2 \le j \le n$.

They are the coefficients in $\operatorname{sech} x + \tanh x = \sum_{n \ge 0} E_n x^n / n!$: the
recurrence compares coefficients in $\cosh x \cdot (\operatorname{sech} x + \tanh x) = 1 + \sinh x$.
The first values are $1, 1, -1, -2, 5, 16, -61$.

articles.title: The list of the first Euler coefficients
articles.statement:
Let $\varepsilon_N$ be $1$ if $N$ is odd and $0$
if $N$ is even. For each natural number $n$, this is the list $[c_0, c_1, \dots, c_n]$ of integers
with $c_0 = 1$ and, for $1 \le N \le n$, $c_N = \varepsilon_N - \sum_j \binom{N}{j} c_{N-j}$, where
the sum runs over the even $j$ with $2 \le j \le N$. The Euler coefficient $E_n$ is its last entry
$c_n$. The list is built one entry at a time, so each step reuses the earlier values.

The recurrence comes from $\cosh x \cdot (\operatorname{sech} x + \tanh x) = 1 + \sinh x$.

articles.title: Initial row for the median Euler numbers
articles.statement:
Let $E_m$ denote the Euler coefficients. This is
the integer sequence $(a_m)_{m \ge 0}$ with $a_0 = 0$ and $a_m = E_m$ for $m \ge 1$. It is the
initial row of the Euler–Seidel matrix from which the median Euler numbers are read off.

articles.title: Median Euler numbers modulo three and five
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 1$, the median
Euler number $R_n$ is divisible by $3$, and $R_n / 3 \equiv 3^{n-1} \pmod 5$.

articles.title: Median Euler numbers
articles.statement:
Let $E_m$ denote the Euler coefficients, and let $(a_n^k)$ be the
Euler–Seidel matrix of the initial row $a_0 = 0$, $a_m = E_m$ for $m \ge 1$, so that $a_n^0 = a_n$
and $a_n^{k+1} = a_n^k + a_{n+1}^k$. The median Euler number $R_n$ is the natural number
$|a_{n+1}^n|$. Equivalently, $R_n = \left|\sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} E_{n+1+i}\right|$.

The first values are $R_0 = 1$, $R_1 = 3$, $R_2 = 24$ and $R_3 = 402$.

articles.title: Genocchi numbers via Bernoulli numbers
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the Genocchi number $G_n$
is the rational number $G_n = 2(1 - 2^n) B_n$, where $B_n$ is the $n$-th Bernoulli number with the
convention $B_1 = -\tfrac{1}{2}$.

articles.title: Divisibility of the median Genocchi numbers
articles.statement:
Let $H_{2m+1}$ denote the odd-indexed median
Genocchi values, with the signs given by their defining sum, so that $H_5 = 2$, $H_7 = -8$ and
$H_9 = 56$. For every natural number $n \ge 1$ there is an integer $z$ with $H_{2n+3} = 2^n z$,
and $z \equiv 1 \pmod 6$ if $n$ is odd, while $z \equiv 4 \pmod 6$ if $n$ is even.

Proof: The antisymmetry of the Euler–Seidel matrix of the Genocchi numbers writes $H_{2n+3}$ as
an alternating sum of Legendre–Stirling numbers times $k!\,(k+1)!$. Pulling a power of two out of
each term gives the factor $2^n$; in the remaining sum every term from the fourth on is divisible
by $6$, which gives the residue. The divisibility and residue arguments are Chen's, applied to
this finite sum instead of his continued fraction.

## Sources

- Kwang-Wu Chen, *An Interesting Lemma for Regular C-fractions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 6 (2003), Article 03.4.8: <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL6/Chen/chen50.tex>.

articles.title: Odd-indexed median Genocchi numbers
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, let $B_m$ be the $m$-th
Bernoulli number and $G_m = 2(1 - 2^m) B_m$ the $m$-th Genocchi number. For a natural number $n$,
the median Genocchi number $H_{2n+1}$ is the rational number defined by $H_1 = 1$ and, for
$n \ge 1$,

$$H_{2n+1} = \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor} \binom{n}{2k+1} G_{2n-2k}.$$

These values carry signs: $H_3 = -1$ and $H_5 = 2$.

articles.title: Tangent numbers: 2-adic divisibility and a congruence mod 6
articles.statement:
Let $T \colon \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{Z}$ satisfy $T(0) = 0$ and, for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$T(m+1) = [m = 0] - \sum_{k=0}^{m} \binom{m}{k} T(k)\, T(m-k),$$

where $[m = 0]$ is $1$ if $m = 0$ and $0$ otherwise. Then for every $n \ge 1$, $2^n$ divides
$T(2n+1)$ and $T(2n+1)/2^n \equiv (-1)^n 4^{n-1} \pmod 6$.

These conditions determine $T$: its values are the coefficients of the exponential generating
function of $\tanh x$, the signed tangent numbers (unsigned, OEIS A009006). The source defines
the tangent numbers through $1 + \tanh x$, which agrees with this recurrence at odd indices.

## Sources

- Kwang-Wu Chen, "An Interesting Lemma for Regular C-fractions," Journal of Integer Sequences 6 (2003), Article 03.4.8, Theorem, equation, lines 362–369 (tangent numbers defined at lines 351–360), https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL6/Chen/chen53.tex

articles.title: Weighted affine power sum
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a ring, $a, b$ integers, $u \in R$ and $n, p$
natural numbers. The weighted affine power sum is

$$S_p(a, b; u, n + 1) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} u^k (ak + b)^p,$$

computed in $R$ with $a$, $b$ and $k$ mapped into $R$.

Unlike later generating-function identities in the source, this finite definition does not
require $u$ to be nonzero.

articles.title: Number of permutations with all cycles of length $r$
articles.statement:
Let $r \ge 2$ and $n \ge 0$. The
number of permutations of $n$ objects all of whose cycles, fixed points counted as cycles of
length one, have length exactly $r$ equals $n!/(r^{n/r}\,(n/r)!)$ if $r$ divides $n$, and $0$
otherwise.

When $r$ divides $n$ the quotient is an integer, so the natural-number division is exact.

## Sources

- Imboa-Navalona Manjaka Rakotoson and Fanja Rakotondrajao, *Associated Stirling Eulerian Numbers and Their q-Analogues*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.5.7, Corollary 25 (`jis-2025-25.5.7-cor-25`).

articles.title: Circular Eulerian numbers are shifted Eulerian numbers
articles.statement:
An excedance of a permutation
$\sigma$ of $n$ objects $1, \dots, n$ is an index $i$ with $\sigma(i) > i$. Let $C_{n,m}$ be the
number of circular permutations of $n$ objects (permutations with a single cycle through all
$n \ge 1$ points) with exactly $m$ excedances, and let $A_{n,m}$ be the number of permutations of
$n$ objects with exactly $m$ excedances (the $0$-associated Stirling Eulerian number, which
counts the permutations all of whose cycle lengths exceed $0$, that is, all permutations). Then
$C_{1,0} = 1$; for all $n \ge 2$ and $1 \le m \le n$ we have $C_{n,m} = A_{n-1,m-1}$; and for
every $n \ge 2$ the polynomial identity $C_n(x) = x\,A_{n-1}(x)$ holds in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$, where
$C_n(x) = \sum_{m=0}^{n} C_{n,m} x^m$ and $A_{n-1}(x) = \sum_{m=0}^{n-1} A_{n-1,m} x^m$.

## Sources
